0.title: Romans
0.overview:
Martin Luther called the letter to the Romans "the chief part of the New Testament and the very purest gospel." John Calvin wrote that "when anyone understands this Epistle, he has a passage opened to him to the understanding of the whole Scripture." Martyn Lloyd-Jones preached 366 sermons on it over some thirteen years and still felt he had not exhausted it. Romans is not one letter among many; it is the theological heart of the New Testament, the fullest and most systematic exposition of the gospel that God ever moved a human pen to write.

Paul wrote to a church he had never visited, in the capital of the empire, at the height of his apostolic ministry — probably from Corinth around AD 57. His purpose was not merely to introduce himself before a planned visit to Spain. It was to set before these believers, Jew and Gentile alike, the full panorama of the gospel: the universal guilt of humanity, the righteousness of God revealed in Christ, justification by faith alone, the transforming work of the Spirit, the sovereign purposes of God in election and in the mystery of Israel, and the shape of the redeemed life in the world. No letter covers more ground. No letter has changed more lives.

The structure follows the gospel's own logic. Chapters 1–3 establish the diagnosis: all humanity — pagan, moralist, and Jew — stands guilty before the righteous God, with no resources of its own to secure acquittal. Chapters 3–5 announce the remedy: the righteousness of God given freely through faith in Jesus Christ, who bore the wrath we deserved. Chapters 6–8 trace the fruit: union with Christ, death to sin, life in the Spirit, adoption as children, and the unshakeable security of those whom God has called. Chapters 9–11 address the mystery: if Israel is the covenant people, why has Israel largely rejected its Messiah? And chapters 12–16 show what the gospel-transformed life looks like in home, church, city, and empire.

Who were the Christians in Rome? No apostle founded the church. Luke lists visitors from Rome in the Pentecost crowd (Acts 2:10), and the gospel probably reached the capital through Jewish believers like them. Some years before this letter Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2), and for a time the congregations were largely Gentile. When Jewish believers returned after his death, they came back to churches whose leaders and habits had changed. That tension between Jewish and Gentile Christians lies behind much of the letter, especially chapters 9–11 and 14–15 (cf. 1:7).

And what of the New Perspective on Paul? Since the 1970s scholars such as E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright have argued that first-century Judaism was not a religion of earning salvation; that works of the law means chiefly the marks that set Jews apart, such as circumcision, the food laws and the Sabbath; and that justification is mainly about who belongs to God’s people. They are right that the unity of Jew and Gentile is a real concern of Romans (3:29–30; 15:7), and that Judaism has sometimes been described unfairly. But the more likely reading is the Reformation one. Paul’s charge in 1:18–3:20 is not that Jews kept Gentiles out but that all have broken God’s law and stand guilty before him, so that every mouth may be stopped (3:19). Justification answers that guilt. It is God’s verdict of acquittal, given freely to the ungodly (4:5) on the ground of Christ’s blood (5:9). Belonging to God’s people follows from that verdict; it is not what the verdict means.

We will draw on the great Reformed interpreters of this letter: Calvin's magisterial commentary, Luther whose reading of 1:17 unlocked the Reformation, Lloyd-Jones whose fourteen volumes remain the richest English-language treatment, John Stott whose Message of Romans is a model of accessible depth, Timothy Keller's Romans for You, and scholars Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner. Come expecting to be undone and remade. Romans has that effect on everyone who takes it seriously.

1.title: The Gospel and the Wrath of God
1.overview:
Romans 1 opens with one of the most carefully crafted sentences in ancient literature — a single Greek sentence spanning seven verses, in which Paul introduces himself, his gospel, and his Lord with the precision of a theologian and the ardour of a man in love with what he believes. By the time the chapter ends, the same pen that wrote of the gospel as "the power of God for salvation" has traced the terrifying arc of divine wrath against human idolatry. These two things belong together: the good news is only truly good when the bad news is truly bad.

The movement of the chapter is deliberate. Paul establishes the gospel (vv. 1–17), then demonstrates the need for it (vv. 18–32). The power of God for salvation is proportionate to the depth of human lostness — and that depth, as Paul will show, is vertiginous. The world Paul describes in vv. 18–32 is not ancient history; it is every human culture that has suppressed the knowledge of the God it cannot stop knowing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Paul, the Gospel, and the Grace of Apostleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's opening sentence is a controlled explosion of theology. In seven verses he identifies himself as a slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God — a gospel promised in the Old Testament Scriptures, concerning God's Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and declared to be the Son of God in power by the resurrection from the dead. Every phrase is a chapter of theology waiting to be unfolded. This is not a man warming up; this is a man who knows exactly what he believes and why it matters.

The word that unlocks everything is euangelion — gospel. It meant, in the first-century Roman world, the proclamation of good news, typically the accession of a new emperor or a great military victory. Paul seizes the word and repurposes it entirely. The great news is not that Caesar has triumphed; it is that Jesus Christ, Son of God, Lord, has been raised from the dead and now reigns over all things. This is a message with empire-shaking implications — which is precisely why Paul is eager to preach it in Rome itself.

The address of grace and peace — "to all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints" — is not a formality. It is a theological declaration. These people, in the capital of pagan power, are loved by God. They are called. They are saints — not by virtue of their moral achievement but by virtue of their union with Jesus Christ who is holy, and who has made them holy in him. Before Paul preaches a word of gospel to them, he speaks a word of gospel over them. This is the Pauline method: ground identity before applying imperatives.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pre-Pauline Gospel

One of the most important features of Romans 1:1–4 is Paul's insistence that the gospel he preaches was "promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures." The gospel is not a Pauline invention or a Gentile innovation — it is the fulfilment of Israel's own scriptures. Jesus is the descendant of David (2 Samuel 7), declared Son of God by resurrection (Psalm 2). Calvin saw in this the unity of the two testaments: the Old Testament is the gospel in promise; the New Testament is the gospel in fulfilment. Any reading of the Old Testament that does not find Christ there has missed its point.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's designation of himself as a doulos — slave — of Christ Jesus was shocking in a world where slavery was degradation. He inverts the social order: the highest dignity available to a human being is not freedom but bondage to Jesus Christ. Now: In an age that prizes autonomy above all things, the Christian claim that the best possible life is one of radical submission to Christ still provokes the same offence — and still offers the same liberation to those who discover that the lordship of Christ is the only yoke that is easy and the only burden that is light.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God,

Meaning first. Romans is Paul’s fullest explanation of the gospel. Written from Corinth around AD 57 to a church he had never visited, it lays out the whole plan of salvation: all are sinners under God’s wrath (1:18–3:20); God justifies the ungodly by faith in Christ alone (3:21–5:21); the justified are set free from sin’s power and given the Spirit (6–8); God’s purpose for Israel is not frustrated (9–11); and the gospel shapes a whole new way of life (12–16). Luther called it the clearest gospel of all, and Augustine, Luther, Wesley and countless others were converted through it. Chapter 1 opens with Paul’s greeting and theme, and then begins the long argument: the wrath of God against a humanity that knew God and turned from him.

Three names in one breath. Paul introduces himself three ways before his name is fully out of his mouth: a slave (doulos), called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel. The first is ownership: Paul belongs entirely to Christ. The second is commission: he did not volunteer; he was apprehended on the Damascus road. The third is a single purpose: as Jeremiah was set apart from the womb, Paul has been reserved for one thing, the gospel of God. Everything else in his life is subordinate to it.

A servant of Christ Jesus. Take the first word slowly, because we have domesticated it. Most English Bibles render doulos as “servant”, and a servant is a man with a job. That is not what the word meant. A slave in the Roman world was not an employee but a possession, in law a thing and not a person. He owned nothing, because anything that came into his hands belonged to his master. He had no right to his own time, his own body or his own plans. He could not refuse. He was often given his name by the man who bought him.

The word read aloud in Rome. Remember where this letter is going. In Rome something like a third of the population was enslaved, and the church met in houses. When this letter was read aloud, there were slaves in the room, and almost certainly people who owned slaves. Into that room the greatest missionary in Christian history introduces himself by the legal status of the lowest people present. He is not reaching for a humble-sounding word. He is reaching for the one word in the Roman vocabulary that meant a man belongs entirely to somebody else, and wearing it as a title.

The highest title in Israel. Yet a Jewish reader would have heard something else in the same instant, and Paul intends both. Servant of the LORD is one of the great titles of the Old Testament. It belongs to Moses, to Joshua, to David, to the prophets, and supremely to the Servant of Isaiah on whom everything turns. So in one word Paul takes the lowest rung on the Roman ladder and the highest title in Israel’s Scriptures and says they are the same rung. That is not a rhetorical trick. It is the shape of the whole gospel he is about to spend sixteen chapters explaining.

Called to be an apostle. Not self-appointed (Galatians 1:1). An apostle is one sent with authority, an eyewitness of the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 9:1). And watch the word, because it does something you may not expect. The Greek adjective, klētos, called, turns up twice more before the sentence is over. You also are called to belong to Jesus Christ (v. 6). You are called to be saints (v. 7). Three times in seven verses, the same word each time. Paul has no special vocabulary for his own vocation and an ordinary one for everybody else’s. Whatever happened to him on the Damascus road and whatever happened to you are named with the same word: neither of you volunteered, and neither of you was consulted.

Set apart for the gospel of God. There is a quiet irony here that Paul, of all men, could not have missed. “Set apart” (aphōrismenos) shares its root with the likely meaning of the name Pharisee: the separated ones, a movement whose entire discipline was separation from everything and everyone that might defile. Paul had been an expert in it. And God takes the separated man, keeps the verb, and reverses the preposition. He is no longer set apart from people; he is set apart for a message, and the message sends him straight to the Gentiles he had spent decades avoiding. It is the same word God used of him before he was born (Galatians 1:15) and the same word the Spirit used when the church at Antioch was told to release him (Acts 13:2). Nothing about him was wasted. It was requisitioned. And “the gospel of God” means it comes from God: it is his good news before it is anyone’s message.

The title his Lord wore first. When Paul wants to describe what the Son of God did in coming to us, he reaches for this same word: Christ “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), the form of a doulos. So Paul is not claiming a humility that Jesus did not stoop to. He is the slave of the one who became a slave. The title is not beneath him, because it was not beneath his Lord. The Son who owned everything took the form of the one who owns nothing, so that people who belonged to sin could come to belong to him.

What it does not mean. Paul is describing ownership, not exhaustion. The Master in question is the one who ordered a sabbath, who told his workers to come away and rest a while (Mark 6:31), and who slept through a storm. A church that quotes this verse at a tired person to extract more work from them has understood neither the slave nor the Master. Nor does it mean that every Christian has, or should manufacture, a dramatic calling like Paul’s. His assignment is not yours. But if you belong to Christ you were called, in exactly the sense he was.

Are there apostles today? Not in Paul’s sense. An apostle of Christ had to have seen the risen Lord and been sent by him personally (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8), and Paul calls himself the last to see him. The apostles laid the foundation of the church once for all (Ephesians 2:20), and their teaching is now in the New Testament. Missionaries and church planters are sent ones in a general sense, but no one today carries an apostle’s authority. So when we want to hear an apostle, we open this letter.

In a sentence. Paul introduces himself as a slave of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God.

On a Tuesday. A slave’s defining condition is that he does not own his own time, and the quickest way to find out what you believe about ownership is to listen to yourself when a day is interrupted. Notice the word that arrives: my morning, my weekend, my evening, and the quality of the resentment when someone spends it for you. That reaction is not a small sin to be scolded over; it is information about who you think holds the deed. And if you have ever suspected that you are not the kind of person God calls, that other people have callings and you have a routine, notice that the letter opens by putting the apostle and the reader under the same word. The parts of your history you consider unusable are the parts God is most practised at requisitioning.

For worship. Behold the Master whom Paul serves. Christ Jesus is Lord of all, and yet he knelt to wash his disciples’ feet (John 13:5) and was valued at the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32; Matthew 26:15). He asks nothing of Paul that he did not first give himself. And he claims his people not with a whip but with a price paid in his own blood (1 Corinthians 6:20), so that to belong to him is the only true freedom. Praise the God whose gospel this is, who set apart a Pharisee for the Gentiles, and whose Son is the Servant who reigns.
verseByVerse.note: “Servant” translates the ordinary word for a slave, one wholly owned by his master. Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, probably around AD 57, before taking the collection to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh
verseByVerse.commentary:
which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh

The oldest thing in the world. The gospel Paul preaches is not a novelty. It is the fulfilment of God’s long-standing promise, written in the Scriptures of Israel (Genesis 3:15; 12:3; Isaiah 53). Calvin saw in this the unity of the two testaments: the Old Testament is the gospel in promise; the New Testament is the gospel in arrival. And “promised beforehand” answers an objection the Roman church was certainly hearing. Rome respected age and distrusted new religions as superstition, so the charge was easy to make: this is a sect barely twenty-five years old, gathered round an executed provincial. Paul’s reply is that it is nothing of the kind. The gospel is older than the Scriptures that promised it, and what happened outside Jerusalem was not the start of something but the keeping of something. “Holy Scriptures” is the first use of the phrase in the New Testament.

Promised. A promise is only as good as the one who makes it, and the interval is the test. God said he would crush the serpent’s head in a garden, and then let millennia pass. He swore to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed in his offspring, and then the family went down to Egypt and was enslaved for four centuries. He told David that a son of his would have a throne for ever, and then the dynasty collapsed, the city burned, and the line dwindled to a carpenter in a village nobody respected. At every point it would have been reasonable to conclude that the promise had lapsed. And then it did not. The word settles the character of God before a single doctrine is argued: he is the God who keeps his word across centuries.

Through his prophets in the holy Scriptures. When Paul preached the gospel he preached it out of a book his hearers already owned. He had no New Testament. Every sermon in Acts is an exposition of the Old. So any reading of the Old Testament that does not find Christ there has missed its point, and the two-thirds of your Bible you find hardest is not the run-up to the gospel. It is the gospel in promise. Jesus said as much on the road to Emmaus, when beginning with Moses and all the Prophets he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27).

How do I find Christ in the Old Testament without forcing it? Read each passage for its plain meaning first, in its own setting. Then ask where it is heading: which promise it carries forward (a seed, a king, a new covenant), which pattern it sets up that Christ fulfils (the Passover lamb, the priest, the temple), and which longing it leaves open that only he answers. The New Testament shows the way, because Jesus and the apostles read the Old Testament like this. You are not hunting for hidden codes. You are following a road to where it arrives.

Concerning his Son. The gospel is about a person. Not first a system, a method or a moral code, but God’s Son. Everything Paul will argue for fifteen chapters is the unfolding of this one phrase.

Descended from David according to the flesh. His human nature: a true man, born of David’s line, fulfilling the promise of an eternal son of David (2 Samuel 7:12–16). “According to the flesh” means according to his human descent. And Paul is not being decorative. God’s Son entered a genealogy. He had an ancestry that could be traced, a family with a documented history, and if you have read that family’s history you know what is in it. David, who arranged a man’s death to conceal an adultery. Solomon, who ended in idolatry. Manasseh, who filled Jerusalem with innocent blood. The line runs through a foreign widow, a prostitute in Jericho, and a succession of kings the Bible itself calls evil. That is the family the Son of God consented to join, and he did not join it at a safe distance. He took their flesh.

A report, not a principle. The promise required a real descendant: an actual body, in an actual bloodline, in an actual town, at a datable moment. Christianity is not a set of timeless spiritual principles that a thoughtful person could have discovered in any century. It is a report about something that happened, to a particular man, in a family whose paperwork survives. Which is why it could be false, and why, if it is true, it is not merely inspiring but binding.

In a sentence. God promised this gospel long ago through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, and it concerns his Son, who as a man was a descendant of David.

On a Tuesday. If you are waiting on God for something he has said, and it has been a long time, a prayer for a child who has walked away, a marriage you cannot see mending, a wrong you have watched go unaddressed for years, the argument of this verse is not that your wait will be short. It is that God’s delays run to centuries and he has never yet failed to arrive. The promises of Genesis were kept in Bethlehem, and many who had been waiting died waiting. That is not a soothing thought. It is a solid one: the interval proves nothing except that we are not the ones who set the timetable.

For worship. So the Son of God has a great-grandfather. The promise God made in a garden, renewed to a wandering herdsman and sworn to a shepherd king, came to rest at last not in a programme but in a person with an address. The long silence between the promise and the keeping of it was never God losing interest. It was God taking the time to become one of us.

parallels.desc: the promised son of David

verseByVerse.quote: and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,
verseByVerse.commentary:
and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,

Declared, not made. The resurrection is the divine verdict on Jesus: he who was Son of God in weakness and humiliation has been publicly declared Son of God in power by his rising. “Declared” (horisthentos) means appointed, marked out, installed in the open. It does not mean made. This verse has been used for a long time to argue that Jesus became the Son of God at some point, a man whom God promoted and adopted at the resurrection. The answer is in the sentence itself. One verse earlier the gospel is “concerning his Son, who was descended from David”: the Son is the one who did the descending. He was already the Son before there was a genealogy to enter. A man cannot be promoted into a position he occupied before he arrived.

In power. What changed at the resurrection was not the Son but the public record. He moved from weakness to power, from humiliation to exaltation (Philippians 2:6–11). Two stages: descended from David in weakness, declared Son in power. A verdict does not create the fact it announces. A man wrongly convicted and later exonerated is not made innocent by the second trial; he was innocent throughout, and the court has finally said so. That is the resurrection. The world had reached its verdict on Jesus and published it in three languages over his head, and the grave was the establishment’s last word on the matter. Then God overturned it, and the overturning was not private. Peter puts it as a straight contradiction: God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified (Acts 2:36).

According to the Spirit of holiness. Paul has just said “according to the flesh”, and now he balances it. Two spheres are in view: the realm of ordinary human descent, in which Jesus is David’s descendant, and the realm of the Spirit, in which he is declared God’s Son in power. Both are true of the same person at once. The Spirit of holiness is most probably the Holy Spirit, by whose power he was raised. And the Spirit is not incidental: the same Spirit who raised him is the one Paul says lives in you, so that he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you (8:11). The power that opened that tomb has a residential address.

By his resurrection from the dead. The proof (Acts 13:33; 17:31). And the reason it matters for the whole letter is that Paul will say the same thing about believers: Christ was raised for our justification (4:25). If the Father’s verdict on the Son was reversed in public, then the verdict on everyone joined to him has been reversed with it. The empty tomb is God’s receipt. The debt was accepted as paid, and he said so by opening the grave.

Jesus Christ our Lord. Paul has spent four verses on titles of enormous altitude, Son of God, descendant of David, declared in power, Spirit of holiness, and he lands on a possessive pronoun. Not the Lord: our Lord. Kyrios was what the Greek Old Testament used to render the divine name, and it was also what the empire required people to say of Caesar; Paul is claiming both fields at once. But he does not leave it at altitude. The one who holds the name above every name is spoken of, by a slave writing to a house church in the capital, as though he belongs to them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus became the Son of God at the resurrection, as adoptionists taught. He is the eternal Son, who took flesh and was exalted.

In a sentence. By his resurrection from the dead, he was declared with power to be the Son of God by the Spirit of holiness: Jesus Christ our Lord.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you would say if someone told you tomorrow that they had found the body. Not whether you could refute it, but whether it would matter. If your faith is mainly a set of values, a way of being decent and hopeful, the news would be sad but survivable. Paul’s faith would not survive it for an hour, and he says so plainly: if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:14–19). He staked everything on an event that could in principle be disproved by a corpse. The risen Jesus reigns in power; serve him as your Lord.

For worship. The resurrection is not the happy ending appended to the story of a good man. It is the Father standing up in the courtroom of the world, after the sentence has been carried out and the body sealed in rock, and announcing that the accused was his Son the whole time. The Son who was never not the Son, who had the Father’s glory before there was a world to be glorious in, consented to be reduced to a corpse in a borrowed grave, so that the announcement could be made from the one place where no one could argue with it. Death had him for a weekend. It has never recovered from the loan.

parallels.desc: you are my Son

verseByVerse.quote: ...through whom we have received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations, including you who are called to belong to Jesus Christ... — Romans 1:5-6
verseByVerse.commentary:
through whom we have received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations, including you who are called to belong to Jesus Christ,

Through whom we have received grace and apostleship. Paul is almost certainly not listing two separate gifts. He means the grace that consisted in being made an apostle, and to feel why, remember who is writing. The man given the commission to preach had been arresting preachers. He held the coats at a stoning. He went to Damascus with letters to drag Christians back in chains and was intercepted on the road doing exactly that. He never got over it: I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God; but by the grace of God I am what I am (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). So the commission was not a reward that followed the pardon. The commission was the pardon. God did not merely forgive the persecutor; he handed him the message and sent him to the people he had been hunting.

To bring about the obedience of faith. A phrase that brackets the entire letter: it appears again at the very end (16:26). The grammar allows more than one reading. It may be the obedience that consists in faith, so that believing the gospel is itself the first act of obedience to God; or the obedience that springs from faith, the life that follows believing; or obedience to “the faith”, the body of Christian teaching. Paul would probably have been puzzled by our need to choose, and the decisive evidence is where he puts the phrase: as a pair of bookends, with everything between them as the explanation. Verdict: faith is the first thing God commands, and the root from which every other obedience grows: not faith versus obedience, but faith working through love (Galatians 5:6).

Faith is not passive. This is the letter above all others which insists that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law, that the wages of work are debt and not grace, that Abraham was counted righteous while he was still uncircumcised. And it opens and closes by calling for obedience. Paul saw no tension, and neither should you. Faith is not obedience’s substitute, and obedience is not faith’s wage. It is easy to admire Jesus, and it costs nothing to agree that the gospel is probably true. What this phrase asks is that you stop underwriting your own life, and that is not a mild request. It is why the New Testament can speak of unbelief as disobedience without changing the subject.

So am I saved by obeying? No. Paul will spend chapters 3 and 4 proving that no one is declared right with God by works (3:20, 28). Obedience is never the ground of our acceptance; Christ’s obedience is (5:19). But real faith never stays alone. The faith that rests on Christ is the same faith that begins to follow him, and the obedience that grows from it is the fruit of being accepted, not the price of it.

For the sake of his name. Not for the sake of the nations, though he loves them, nor for the sake of the church growing, though he wants it: for the sake of the name. The goal of all mission is Christ’s glory among every people.

Among all the nations. This is not a general enthusiasm for scale. It is a quotation waiting to be recognised. God told Abraham that in his offspring all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 22:18), the promise this passage has just said was made beforehand in the holy Scriptures (v. 2). So Paul’s travel plans are not an apostolic hobby. They are the means by which a promise sworn to a childless herdsman two thousand years earlier is being kept, in real time, on actual roads, by a man with a tentmaker’s hands.

Including you who are called to belong to Jesus Christ. It lands with a quiet thud that is easy to miss. Paul has been describing something enormous and far away: a mission to all the nations, for the sake of the name, in fulfilment of an ancient oath. Then: including you. The Christians in Rome are not the audience of this mission, watching it happen elsewhere. They are the thing itself, what “all the nations” looks like when the sentence stops being a plan and becomes a room with people in it. “Called” means effectually called, summoned by God (8:28–30), the second of the three callings in this opening. And note what they are called to: not to achieve, or to understand, or to be useful. Called to belong. It is the word of ownership again, the word Paul used of himself before he used it of them.

In a sentence. Through Christ Paul received grace and apostleship to bring people from all nations to the obedience that comes from faith, for his name’s sake, including the Roman believers called to belong to Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone you long to see come to Christ, and ask honestly why. Most of our reasons are decent and partial: so that they would be happier, so that they would stop making choices that frighten us, so that the family would be at peace. Now run the harder version. If that person came to faith and never thanked you, never joined your church, never became easy to be with, and their life stayed every bit as hard, would you still count it everything you had prayed for? If yes, you are praying for the sake of his name. If something hesitates, that is not a reason for shame. It is simply the place where Paul’s motive and ours are not yet the same, and it will bear praying about.

For worship. The greatest missionary who ever lived introduces his life’s work, names the ends of the earth as his parish, roots it in a promise older than the nation of Israel, and then turns to a few dozen believers meeting in borrowed rooms in a hostile city and tells them that they are not the spectators of that story. They are the evidence that it is true. You are called to belong to Jesus Christ, and the name for whose sake the whole world is being reached has been written over you.

parallels.desc: the obedience of faith

verseByVerse.quote: To all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. — Romans 1:7
verseByVerse.commentary:
To all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Who was in that room. This greeting is warmer than the situation was. Some years before, the emperor Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome; Luke mentions it in passing, which is how Priscilla and Aquila came to be in Corinth (Acts 18:2). The Jewish believers, including many of the founders, were gone, and for several years the Roman congregations were Gentile congregations. Then Claudius died, the edict lapsed, and the exiles came home to churches that had learned to function without them, with other leaders and other customs. Hold that in mind and much of this letter stops being abstract: the argument that Jew and Gentile are equally guilty and equally justified, the ache of chapters 9 to 11 over Israel, the warning to Gentiles not to be arrogant toward the broken branches, the whole of chapter 14 on the strong and the weak. Paul is writing into a congregation with a seam running through it. And the first thing he does is address them all with one description: loved by God, called, saints. One greeting over one church.

To all those in Rome who are loved by God. Before they are anything else, they are loved. And the phrase is passive: these people did not love their way into God’s favour; they were loved before they did anything. Do not let the grammar pass as a technicality, because it decides how the whole letter will be read. They were loved before they did anything, they will be loved after they have failed at a good deal, and the letter will eventually say it plainly: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (5:8). The love was at full strength at the worst possible moment. It has nowhere to grow to.

And called to be saints. Not aspiring to be saints, but already saints by the call of God that placed them in Christ. Centuries of church usage have made the word mean the opposite of what Paul intends: a category of exceptional Christians, mostly dead, with stained glass. In the Old Testament the root belongs first to things: the holy place, the holy garments, the holy vessels, and what made them holy was not their quality but their designation. A bowl in the tabernacle was not a better bowl. It was a bowl set aside for God, no longer available for anything else. So when Paul calls a mixed room of tradesmen, slaves and immigrants the holy ones, he is not describing their record. He is describing what has happened to them. Saints are all believers, not a special class (Acts 9:13): made holy by God’s call, not by their own achievement.

Be what you are. If holiness began as your achievement you would have to keep proving it, and every failure would put your status back in question. If holiness is a designation, then failure is a contradiction of what you are, not a disproof of it. That is exactly how Paul writes to the most disorderly church he knew, opening a letter about lawsuits, drunkenness at the Lord’s table and a man sleeping with his stepmother by calling them saints (1 Corinthians 1:2). He does not withdraw the word in order to rebuke them. He rebukes them on the strength of it.

How do I know I am called? Paul’s word means God’s effective summons, the call that actually brings a person to Christ (8:30). You do not need to remember a dramatic moment. If you trust Christ, rest your hope on him and want to follow him, that faith is the evidence that God called you, because no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44).

Grace to you and peace. Paul’s greeting joins the Greek and the Hebrew. Grace (charis) is a play on the standard Greek hello, chairein, and peace is the Jewish shalom, spoken across the Mediterranean every day; and Paul, writing to a church with Greeks and Jews eyeing each other across a room, opens with both. Even his hello is integrated. Grace is God’s undeserved favour; peace is what that favour produces once the war between humanity and God has been ended by the blood of the cross: reconciliation with God and wholeness of life. The order never reverses in Scripture. Nobody has ever found peace and then gone looking for grace. And Paul pronounces both before he has written a sentence of argument: the gospel is gift before it is demand.

From God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Jesus is set alongside the Father as the single source of grace and peace. Only God gives grace, so this is a quiet but clear statement of Christ’s deity. And notice the first time this letter says “God our Father”. It will not be the last: by chapter 8 Paul will have a room full of former slaves and shopkeepers crying Abba, and will make their adoption the ground of their security. But he says it here, at the door, before the argument begins.

In a sentence. Paul writes to all in Rome loved by God and called to be saints: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. There is a way of being a Christian in which you are, in effect, auditioning: you believe God loves you, and you also believe the love is roughly proportional to how the week went. Here is a test, and it takes ten seconds. Ask: does God love me more today than he did this time last year? If the honest answer is yes, and the reason is that you have been doing better, then the love has quietly become a wage. Paul’s passive rules it out. Begin each day where he begins: loved by God, called to be holy.

For worship. That is the shape of the gospel in a single greeting. The God who is about to spend a chapter and a half describing his own wrath is introduced to these people, by name, as their Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ stands beside him as the giver of the same grace and the same peace.
verseByVerse.note: “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people — all believers. The church at Rome was not founded by Paul; he had never been there.

parallels.desc: visitors from Rome at Pentecost

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Paul's Longing and His Debt to All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having established his gospel and his greeting, Paul opens his heart. He has prayed for the Roman Christians unceasingly. He has longed to visit them. He has been prevented — more than once. This passage is often passed over quickly on the way to the theological fireworks of vv. 16–17, but it deserves careful attention: it shows us what a gospel-shaped pastor looks like. Paul's longing is not merely strategic (Rome as a missionary base) but personal. He wants to see them, to be mutually encouraged, to share with them some spiritual gift.

The phrase "I am under obligation" (v. 14) — literally "I am a debtor" — is startling. Paul does not feel that preaching the gospel to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish, is above and beyond the call of duty. He feels indebted to them. They have a claim on him. The grace that was lavished on him on the Damascus road was not for his private enrichment; it was for their benefit. He owes them what he received for free. This is the logic of all gospel ministry: grace received creates obligation discharged.

"I am not ashamed of the gospel" (v. 16) — the understatement implies the opposite: he is eagerly proud of it, itching to proclaim it in Rome's very centre. Rome was the most intimidating platform imaginable: the seat of empire, the crossroads of civilization, the city that had crucified the Lord of the gospel. And Paul cannot wait to get there.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pastoral and Missionary Logic of Paul

Romans 1:8–15 reveals that Paul's missionary strategy is inseparable from his pastoral affection. He does not view the Roman church as an audience for his theology or a resource for his mission; he views them as beloved brothers and sisters in whom he longs to rejoice. Reformed missiology has always insisted that mission and church are inseparable — the mission proceeds from the church, through the church, and for the establishment of the church. Paul's eagerness to visit Rome exemplifies this: he is not a lone-ranger evangelist but an apostle embedded in the body of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's sense of debt to all people — Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish — erased every cultural and social hierarchy. The gospel belonged to no class or culture. Now: The contemporary church is perpetually tempted to preach a gospel shaped for those who are already culturally similar to us. Paul's "debtor" language is a rebuke: the gospel is owed to every person in our reach, regardless of whether they seem like likely converts or comfortable neighbours.

verseByVerse.quote: First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed in all the world. For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I mention you
verseByVerse.commentary:
First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed in all the world. For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I mention you

First, I thank my God. This is Paul’s settled habit, the way he opens letter after letter, including letters to churches about to be told very hard things. The Corinthians were tearing themselves apart over leaders, tolerating incest and getting drunk at the Lord’s table, and he still opens by thanking God for them. Which makes the one exception worth noticing: Galatians has no thanksgiving at all. He goes straight from the greeting to “I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you.” When Paul omits the thanksgiving, something is seriously wrong. Here it is present, warm and first. And “my God” is personal.

Through Jesus Christ. Easy to read as a formula, and it is not one. Paul cannot even say thank you to God on his own account. Gratitude goes up through the Mediator, because the problem the whole letter is about to describe is not merely that we sin but that we have no standing, and a man with no standing cannot simply address the throne. So the smallest prayer in the Christian life travels the same road as the greatest. Every thank you before a meal is carried by the same blood that carried the thief into paradise.

For all of you, because your faith is proclaimed in all the world. Notice what he thanks God for. Not their numbers, their generosity, their organisation or their strategic position in the capital. Their faith, and faith is itself God’s gift, so the Giver receives the thanks. Rome was the hub of the empire; every road led there and out again, and travellers, traders, soldiers and slaves carried news along them constantly. Something about these believers had got into the traffic. What travelled out of Rome was that these people believed God.

For God is my witness. Why would a man need to swear to something as unremarkable as praying for people? Because they had no way of checking, and reason to wonder. Paul had never been to Rome. He is writing to a church he did not found, in a city he hopes to use as a base for a mission further west (15:24). It would have been easy for someone in that room to conclude that the famous apostle’s sudden interest was strategic, that they were a stopping point on somebody else’s route. So he calls God to witness what nobody else can verify: that for years, unseen, they have been on his list. He had been ministering to Rome on his knees for years before he set foot there.

Whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son. The word for serve, latreuō, is temple language, the word for priestly service: the sacrifices, the incense, the work done in the holy place by men in linen. Paul takes the vocabulary of the most sacred building in the world and applies it to talking about Jesus, mostly to small groups of unimportant people in rented rooms, workshops and prisons up and down the roads of the empire (15:16). He is not saying his work is like worship. He is saying it is the real thing, and that the smoke of the altar has moved outdoors. His prayer life and his preaching were not two compartments; they were one act of worship.

That without ceasing I mention you. Before this phrase flattens you, be clear about what it does not mean. Paul was not praying every waking second; he made tents, argued in synagogues, sailed, wrote, ate and slept. The phrase was ordinary Greek for something regular and unremitting. It means these people never dropped off his list. He did not forget them for six months and then feel guilty. A reader who takes it as a demand for continuous spoken prayer will conclude within a week that he cannot pray at all, which is exactly the result the verse was not written to produce.

How do I pray for people like this? Make it small enough to keep. Write down the names God has put on your heart, and pray for a few each day, so that every name comes round each week. Pray Paul’s own prayers for them (Ephesians 1:17–19; Philippians 1:9–11; Colossians 1:9–12), so that you are asking for what matters most, not only for problems to go away. And when you remember someone during the day, turn the thought into a sentence to God on the spot.

In a sentence. First Paul thanks his God through Jesus Christ for them all, because their faith is being reported throughout the world; and God, whom he serves wholeheartedly in the gospel of his Son, knows that he remembers them constantly.

On a Tuesday. If people two countries away were talking about your congregation, what would they have heard? That it is large, or well run, or has good music, or holds the right line on a contested question? All of that can be true of a church whose faith is not the thing being reported. And look at what fills your praying. For most of us it is situations: the diagnosis, the interview, the money, the decision; when the situation resolves, the subject disappears. Paul’s prayer life was populated by people, most of them absent, some not yet met. In the last chapter of this letter he greets about two dozen of them by name in a city he had never visited. He had been holding them up one at a time.

For worship. The Christians in Rome had no idea any of this was happening. They had never seen his face, and they would only find out when this letter was read aloud. That is almost certainly true of you as well: somewhere there is an old woman, or a friend from a church you left, or a parent, who mentions your name to God with a regularity you know nothing about. And above every one of them is the Son himself, who always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and has never once let your name drop off his list.

verseByVerse.quote: always in my prayers, asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
always in my prayers, asking that somehow by God’s will I may now at last succeed in coming to you.

Always in my prayers. Constant intercession, for a church he had never seen.

Now at last. The sound of a man who has been waiting a long time. He says a few verses later that he has often intended to come and been prevented (v. 13), and in chapter 15 he puts a number on it: I have longed for many years to come to you (15:23). This is not a fortnight’s postponement. A plan he believed was right, formed for the best reasons, had been blocked repeatedly over years, and he was still asking.

Somehow by God’s will. “Somehow”: Paul did not know how. “By God’s will”: submitted. This is not pious filler, nor the verbal tic that “if it be your will” often becomes, a disclaimer attached in advance so that nothing has really been asked and nothing can be seen to fail. Paul asks for the specific thing, plainly and repeatedly, and then submits the outcome. James says the same to men making business plans: you ought to say, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (James 4:15). The point is not that we should stop planning. It is that we are creatures who do not know whether we will be alive on Thursday.

Desire held within God’s sovereignty. Notice what he does not do with the delay. He does not decide the door is shut for good and stop asking. He does not conclude that the desire itself was wrong, that wanting Rome was ambition dressed up as mission. Nor does he force it, treating the obstacles as opposition to be overridden by determination. He keeps wanting it, keeps asking, and leaves the timing where it belongs. Most of us can manage desire without submission, which is impatience, or submission without desire, which is resignation wearing a pious face. Burning desire held within the bounds of God’s sovereignty is the mark of genuine gospel ministry.

The delays are not neglect. Most delays do not feel like providence at the time. They feel like a door closing for no reason: the job that went to somebody else, the treatment that did not work, the years of waiting for a child, the ministry you were sure God had given you that quietly failed. Paul did not always know what the prevention was for. When the Spirit blocked him from Bithynia (Acts 16:7) he was given no explanation; only later did a man from Macedonia appear in a dream. So the honest form of this doctrine is not that every delay has a visible reason you will eventually be shown. It is that the delays are not random and are not neglect. And the proof in this case is in your hands. If Paul had reached Rome when he first wanted to, we would almost certainly not have this letter. The greatest exposition of the gospel ever written exists because a man could not get to the city he wanted to visit and had to write instead.

How do I know whether a closed door is God’s no, or something to push through? Do not try to read God’s will from circumstances alone; doors can close for many reasons. Ask first what Scripture says: God’s commands settle what is right, and no open door can make a wrong thing right. Within what is right, use wisdom, take counsel from mature believers, keep praying, and keep trying where it is wise to try, as Paul did for years. Then accept the outcome God gives. Providence is understood looking back, not used as a signal looking forward. Paul did not know why Bithynia was closed until Macedonia opened.

Answered in his way. When the prayer was finally answered, it was answered in a form he had not asked for. He reached Rome as a prisoner, after arrest, two years in custody at Caesarea and a shipwreck, at the empire’s expense, chained to a soldier (Acts 27–28). He got the city. He did not get the itinerary. And the last verse of Acts leaves him there, welcoming all who came to him and proclaiming the kingdom of God with all boldness and without hindrance, which is a remarkable thing for Luke to say about a man under guard, and exactly what this prayer had asked for.

In a sentence. In his prayers he always asks that now at last, by God’s will, he might succeed in coming to them.

On a Tuesday. You may be asking, as Paul was, for something good, for the right reasons, and getting nothing but closed doors. Keep asking for the specific thing, and keep leaving the timing with God. This verse does not promise that the door will open on your terms. It promises that the one who is not opening it has not stopped listening.

For worship. The God who blocked the road to Rome was writing Romans. He is never idle when he says not yet, and the thing he does instead may be the thing people are still reading two thousand years later.

verseByVerse.quote: For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you — that is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith, both yours and mine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you — that is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith, both yours and mine.

For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you. Paul begins confidently, and the three phrases all travel one way, from the apostle to the church. The phrase “spiritual gift” (charisma pneumatikon) does not describe a technique for handing over one of the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12 like a parcel. Paul is deliberately vague: some gift, because he does not yet know what these particular people will need when he arrives, and he trusts the Giver to supply it then. He means a spiritual blessing that comes through his ministry among them: teaching, encouragement and the strengthening of their faith. “To strengthen” (stērichthēnai) is to make firm, as a building is made stable.

That is. Then he hears himself, and the self-correction is visible in the grammar. “That is” is the sound of a man stopping mid-flow and reaching for a better sentence: that we may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith, both yours and mine. He does not delete the first version; he lets us watch him revise it. The greatest theologian in the church’s history heard a note of condescension in his own draft and corrected it before he reached the full stop. Even the apostle expected to receive from those to whom he ministered (Acts 28:15).

What the correction cost. Paul had every credential a man could have. He had seen the risen Christ. He had been caught up to the third heaven. He wrote Scripture. The believers in Rome were tradesmen, slaves and immigrants, some only a year or two old in the faith, and there was nothing they could teach him about justification. But that is not what he says he needs from them. He expects to be encouraged by their faith, and faith is not expertise. A frightened woman still trusting God after a bad year has something the most learned man in the room cannot generate for himself by knowing more. He can only watch it and be strengthened.

The body has no passengers. This quietly demolishes the way most of us picture Christian growth, in both directions. If you are the one who normally teaches, leads, hosts or fixes, notice what Paul thinks a strong Christian is: not a man with no needs, but a man who knows he has them and says so to people less impressive than himself. And if you are newer, quieter, convinced you are in the room only to receive, the apostle to the Gentiles was looking forward to being helped by people exactly like you. The body of Christ has no passengers. And the currency of Christian encouragement is not cheerfulness or advice or competence. It is somebody in front of you still trusting God. That is why sitting with a believer who is suffering well can leave you steadier than a conference will.

In a sentence. Paul longs to see them to share some spiritual gift to strengthen them, or rather that they might encourage each other by their shared faith.

On a Tuesday. When did you last tell another Christian, in plain words, that you needed their help: not a general “please pray for me”, but the actual thing? If you cannot remember, you are living in a posture Paul refused to adopt, probably at a cost you have stopped noticing: the loneliness of the person everyone assumes is fine. Usually it is not humility. Usually it is that being the one who needs help means giving up being the one who is depended upon.

For worship. The apostle books his visit to the capital of the world, and the reason he gives is not that Rome needs him. It is that he needs Rome. Christ has so made his body that its greatest member cannot do without its least, and the faith he gives to the weakest believer is a gift to the strongest.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented), in order that I may reap some harvest among you as well as among the rest of the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented), in order that I may reap some harvest among you as well as among the rest of the Gentiles.

I do not want you to be unaware, brothers. A signal Paul uses deliberately, when he is about to tell his readers something they do not know and might otherwise get wrong (he uses it of the hardening of Israel in 11:25 and of those who have died in 1 Thessalonians 4:13). Someone in Rome had almost certainly noticed the obvious: the apostle to the Gentiles has been working the Mediterranean for twenty years and has never once come to the largest Gentile city on earth. The natural conclusion was unflattering: he does not think we matter, or he is avoiding a church he did not found. Paul corrects it. The ESV notes that “brothers” includes sisters in the church: brothers and sisters in God’s family.

But thus far have been prevented. He does not say he was too busy, which would have been true. He says he was prevented, and the word puts an agent behind the obstacle. Part of the hindrance was the work elsewhere (15:22); and the same Spirit who forbade him Bithynia (Acts 16:6–7) had other work for him first. Paul will not describe his own life in terms of scheduling. The two accounts of an identical year are entirely different to live inside. “I never got round to it” leaves you the manager of a life that is not going well. “I was prevented” leaves you a servant whose Master has other arrangements.

In order that I may reap some harvest among you. Not to teach them or hold meetings: harvest (karpos, fruit), conversions and growth. Harvest carries three things a lecture does not. It is slow: nobody harvests in the week he sows. It is not manufactured: a farmer can plough, sow and water, and cannot make a single seed germinate; I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). And it is seasonal, which is why he can be prevented for years without the work being lost. A field left unvisited is not a field abandoned. It is a field not yet ripe.

As well as among the rest of the Gentiles. And notice what he assumes about the Roman church. Their faith is talked about all over the empire (v. 8). By any measure they are a success, and Paul still expects a harvest among them. He does not think of a healthy church as a finished one. A building is completed and then maintained; a field is never finished, and is either being worked or going back to weeds.

In a sentence. Paul wants them to know that he had often planned to come but had been prevented until now, so that he might have a harvest among them as among other Gentiles.

On a Tuesday. Think of the situation you have privately written off: the relative who will never believe, the colleague who is too far gone, the part of your own character you have decided is simply how you are. Ask when you stopped expecting anything there. Not when you stopped trying; when you stopped expecting. And if you are the one doing the sowing and have seen nothing, the parent who has prayed for a son for eleven years, the teacher of teenagers who seem to absorb nothing, the Christian at work who has been kind and honest for a decade and never once been asked why: often one sows and another reaps (John 4:37–38). The growing is not your department, and the absence of fruit in June says nothing about what is happening underground.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest is the one who gives the growth. He prevents and he permits, he holds back a field for years and ripens it in a season, and no seed sown in his name has ever been lost in the ground.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “brothers” can include sisters in the church.

verseByVerse.quote: I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome. — Romans 1:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome.

I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians. Paul does not say he is willing to preach to them, or burdened for them, or available. He says he is a debtor (opheiletēs). That is the language of the ledger: a man who owes something and has not yet paid it. And it raises an obvious question, because Paul had never met these people, borrowed nothing from them and done them no wrong. How do you come to be in debt to strangers? There are two ways to owe a man money. You can borrow from him, and Paul had not. Or somebody can hand you a sum with instructions to deliver it to him, and then you are in debt to a person you have never met, for money that was never yours, until he has it in his hand. That is Paul’s position. On the Damascus road he was given something that was not for him: a message with a name on it, addressed to the nations. To withhold it would be theft.

Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish. The first-century way of saying everyone. Greeks were the cultured, literate world; barbarians were everyone else, whose languages sounded to Greek ears like “bar-bar”. Two pairs, each covering the whole field from opposite ends: the cultured and the crude, the clever and the slow. Paul is naming the two groups a preacher instinctively avoids for opposite reasons. The sophisticated frighten us, because they can argue and we suspect we would lose. The unsophisticated bore us, or seem unpromising. Paul says he is in debt to both. The church does not get to choose its creditors. His gospel has no cultural prerequisites: the Athenian philosopher and the rough Scythian stand equally in need of the same grace and are equally able to receive it.

So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome. Even to believers: Christians need the gospel preached to them too. And note what Paul feels: not guilt but eagerness. He is not dragging himself towards Rome under the lash of an unpayable bill; he can hardly wait to get there. The debt has become a desire.

What it does not mean. A debt can be preached in a way that crushes. If you owe everybody, and the payment is their eternal life, then every conversation you did not have becomes a debt in arrears, and a sensitive Christian can be flattened by that arithmetic. But Paul is one man with one life who cannot reach Spain and Rome in the same year, and does not pretend otherwise. Your debt is to the people God has actually put in your reach: the ones whose names you know, whose kitchens you sit in, who work at the next desk. Not to the world. He never asked you to be the apostle to the Gentiles; that post is filled.

How do I pay the debt without being pushy? Begin with the people you already know, and with honesty about yourself. Live in a way that raises questions, and answer them gently and respectfully when they come (1 Peter 3:15). Pray for opportunities and notice them: a friend’s grief, a question about why you go to church, a conversation about what makes life worth living. Say what Christ has done in plain words, and leave the result to God. You are responsible to deliver the message, not to produce the response.

In a sentence. Paul is under obligation to Greeks and non-Greeks, wise and foolish, so he is eager to preach the gospel to those in Rome too.

On a Tuesday. If the gospel is my possession, telling someone about it is generosity, and generosity is optional and can wait until I feel equipped. If the gospel is a delivery, none of that applies. A courier does not congratulate himself for handing over a parcel, and he does not decide the recipient looks unlikely to appreciate it. So name the last five people you have spoken to about Christ, or would consider speaking to. How many are recognisably a version of you? If the list is uniform, the problem may not be courage. You may have unconsciously decided who the message is for, and Paul’s pairs exist to stop that decision being made.

For worship. Grace received creates a debt of love. The one who owes nothing to anyone came and paid what we owed, and every person you meet is someone he has addressed a message to. Paul does not describe the people of the world as his audience or his mission field. He describes them as his creditors, because Christ had made him rich with something that belonged to them.
verseByVerse.note: Greeks thought of all non-Greek speakers as “barbarians.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–17 — The Theme: The Righteousness of God by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two verses. The entire letter in miniature. Everything Paul will argue across sixteen chapters is compressed here with the density of a diamond. "I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written: 'The righteous shall live by faith.'" This is the thesis statement of Romans, and it is the sentence that changed the world.

Martin Luther, tormented by the phrase "the righteousness of God" — understanding it as the terrifying standard by which God condemns sinners — wrestled with it until the light broke. "At last," he wrote, "meditating day and night...I began to understand that the righteousness of God is that by which the righteous lives by a gift of God, namely by faith. And this is the meaning: the righteousness of God is revealed by the gospel, namely, the passive righteousness with which the merciful God justifies us by faith. Here I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates." The Reformation began in these two verses.

The gospel is power — not advice, not inspiration, not a moral framework, but the very power of God actively at work to save. It is power for salvation — not merely forgiveness of past sins, but the complete rescue of a human being from the dominion of sin and death and the wrath of God, and the restoration of that person to the full flourishing of life in God. And it is for everyone who believes — the one condition, the one instrument, the one hand that receives what God freely gives: faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Righteousness of God: Attribute or Gift?

Reformed exegesis has understood "the righteousness of God" in Romans 1:17 as a righteousness that originates with God and is given by God to the believing sinner — what the Reformers called iustitia aliena, an alien righteousness, a righteousness that is not our own. Luther's breakthrough was recognising that this righteousness is not the demanding standard that condemns but the gracious gift that saves. This is the doctrine of imputation: Christ's perfect righteousness is credited to the account of the believing sinner, so that God can be simultaneously just (the sin has been punished in Christ) and the justifier (the sinner is declared righteous). Calvin called this the "wonderful exchange" — Christ takes our sin; we receive his righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Luther's discovery of Romans 1:17 broke the back of a system of salvation by merit and religious performance that had enslaved Western Christendom for centuries. The Reformation was, at its heart, a rediscovery of these two verses. Now: Every generation re-erects the system of merit that the gospel demolishes. Every human heart, left to itself, believes it must earn its standing with God. Romans 1:16–17 is the permanent, repeatable antidote: the gospel is not something you do; it is something done for you, received by faith, given by the merciful God who justifies the ungodly.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. — Romans 1:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.

For I am not ashamed of the gospel. The negative tells you the pull was real. It is worth being concrete about what there was to be ashamed of, because we have had two thousand years to get used to the cross and Paul’s readers had not. Crucifixion was not merely a cruel execution; it was a deliberately degrading one, reserved in practice for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals, and Roman citizens were normally exempt from it by law. Cicero, arguing a case a century earlier, said the very word ought to be kept away not only from the body of a Roman citizen but from his thoughts, his eyes and his ears. And the message Paul is carrying into the capital has at its centre a Jewish provincial who was put to death that way: foolishness to Greeks and a stumbling block to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Alexamenos worships his god. We even have a picture of how it looked from outside. Scratched into plaster on the Palatine in Rome, a century or two after this letter arrived, someone drew a cartoon: a figure on a cross with the head of a donkey, and a man beside it with his hand raised in worship. Underneath, in scrawled Greek: Alexamenos worships his god. It is a schoolboy’s joke, and it is exactly the social reality Paul is writing into. To confess this gospel in Rome was to be the person everyone else found faintly ridiculous.

A man who had felt the pull. Paul had private reasons for the sentence too. The years just behind this letter are not a record of triumph: run out of Philippi after a beating, hurried out of Thessalonica by night, moved on from Berea, politely dismissed by the philosophers in Athens, and then Corinth, where he arrived by his own admission in weakness and in fear and much trembling (1 Corinthians 2:3). This is not a man who has never felt the pull. It is a man who has felt it repeatedly and decided where he stands.

For it is the power of God for salvation. The theme of the whole letter, and not the reason we would give. He does not say the gospel is true, though it is, or reasonable, though he will argue it for eleven chapters, or beautiful, though it is. He says it is power, and the grammar matters: not that the gospel has power or brings power, but that it is the power of God. The message is not a description of something powerful happening elsewhere; it is the instrument God uses to do the thing. That is why ordinary preaching, and ordinary Christians saying ordinary sentences about Christ, keep producing results out of all proportion to the people involved. The Rome of the Caesars thought it knew what power was; the gospel is greater. One small correction: preachers sometimes say this word (dynamis) gives us “dynamite”, but the arrow points the other way. Nobel named his explosive after the Greek word, and a detonation is not Paul’s picture. His word means effective might, the capacity to accomplish. “Salvation” is rescue from sin, wrath and death into eternal life.

To everyone who believes. The condition, and the only one. No other qualification is offered anywhere in the sentence: not to everyone who obeys the law, but to everyone who believes. It is open to all.

Then why doesn’t everyone believe when it is preached? The same message that saves some is folly to others (1 Corinthians 1:18). The gospel is God’s power, but it is the power of a living God who works through it as he wills; the Spirit must open blind eyes (2 Corinthians 4:4–6; Acts 16:14). That is why we preach and pray together. We are never the power. We carry it, and ask God to use it.

To the Jew first and also to the Greek. What does “first” (prōton) mean? Not that Jews are saved more easily or more fully, or by a different way: Paul will insist that there is no distinction, for all have sinned and all are justified the same way, by faith (3:22–23; 10:12). First means first in time and in the privilege of history. God made his promises to Israel; the Messiah came from Israel as Israel’s king; the gospel was preached first in Jerusalem, and in every city Paul went first to the synagogue (Acts 13:46; 17:1–2). The gospel is the fulfilment of Israel’s own story, and it belongs to them first. “Greek” means everyone who is not a Jew, the whole Gentile world. And for a congregation with a seam running through it (see on 1:7), Paul has already settled the thing that mattered most in that room: one power, one condition, two peoples, and the same door.

Does it set a priority in mission today? Some Christians read “to the Jew first” as a standing rule that the church must take the gospel to Jewish people before others. The more likely reading is that it describes the order of salvation history, which Paul’s own practice followed. It does not put one people ahead of another in the queue. But it does forbid the opposite error. Paul’s heart’s desire and prayer to God for Israel is that they may be saved (10:1), and a church that left Jewish people out of its witness would have forgotten whose promises it is preaching.

In a sentence. Paul is not ashamed of the gospel, because it is God’s power to save everyone who believes, first the Jew and then the Greek.

On a Tuesday. Almost nobody reading this will be asked to deny Christ under interrogation. Shame is quieter than that. It is the sentence you began and did not finish. It is the small disclaimer, “I’m not really religious, but”, attached in advance so that nobody misfiles you. It is how you describe your Sunday to a colleague on Monday: vague, edited so that it will not require a follow-up question. Watch for the edit this week. Not the denial; the edit. And when you find it, the answer is not to work up more nerve, because the verse does not end with a demand for courage. It ends with an argument: I am not ashamed, for it is the power of God. Confidence in this message grows in the person who has watched it work, who has seen someone he had written off become a Christian, or watched it hold a friend together through something that should have destroyed him.

For worship. The cross was shameful, and the world was right about what it looked like. But Jesus endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God (Hebrews 12:2). He took the humiliation and did not think it too high a price. So Paul is not being brave about an embarrassing story; he is refusing to be ashamed of something his Lord was willing to be shamed by, and no servant may be more fastidious than his Master. No army carried this message. No philosophy underwrote it. It travelled the trade roads in the mouths of slaves and weavers and dockhands, and within three centuries it had emptied the temples of the empire that crucified its subject. It is still running. Nothing else from that century is.

verseByVerse.quote: For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, 'The righteous shall live by faith.' — Romans 1:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, “The righteous shall live by faith.”

For in it the righteousness of God is revealed. Everything turns on what “the righteousness of God” means, and it can be read three ways. It might mean an attribute: God’s own perfect rightness, the standard he is and measures by. It might mean an activity: God acting to put things right. Or it might mean a gift: a righteous status God gives to people who have none of their own. Notice what happens to a guilty man under each reading. If the gospel reveals God’s standard, that is not good news; it is the problem restated more clearly. And this is where the verse becomes a biography.

The monk and the open gates. Martin Luther was a monk who took sin seriously enough to be destroyed by it. He fasted, kept vigils, confessed for hours at a stretch until his confessor lost patience, and found no peace, because he knew the standard and he knew himself. When he came to this verse it was the worst sentence in the Bible: the one thing a man in his condition could not survive was more of God’s righteousness. He later wrote that he had hated the phrase, and the God he thought stood behind it. Then the meaning broke open. He saw that the righteousness revealed in the gospel is not the standard God demands but the standing God gives; not the righteousness by which he condemns, but the righteousness with which he clothes (3:21–22; Philippians 3:9). Meditating day and night, he wrote, he understood that this is the righteousness with which the merciful God justifies us by faith, and he felt that he was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates. The Reformation came out of that sentence.

An alien righteousness. The Reformers had a name for what Luther saw: iustitia aliena, an alien righteousness, alien not as strange but as belonging to someone else. It is not produced in you; it is credited to you, the way a sum can be entered into an account that did not earn it. Christ’s obedience is reckoned as yours; your sin was reckoned as his and dealt with at the cross. Luther called it the joyful exchange. And it is the only arrangement that lets God be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (3:26): the debt paid, not waived, and the guilty acquitted, not excused. So God’s righteousness revealed in the gospel is both his own righteous character, shown in saving justly through the cross (3:25–26), and the righteous status he gives to all who believe.

If my righteousness is credited, does it matter how I live? Paul saw the question coming and gives chapter 6 to it: shall we go on sinning that grace may abound? By no means (6:1–2). The faith that receives Christ’s righteousness unites us to Christ himself, and no one can be joined to Christ and stay as he was. Holiness is not the payment for acceptance; it is the life of someone who has been accepted. You are not made right with God by how you live, but you will not stay comfortable living as if you were not.

Is revealed. Present tense, continuous, still happening. Paul does not say it was revealed once in Palestine and is now a matter of record. Every time this gospel is preached the curtain goes back again, and what Luther saw is shown to somebody else.

From faith for faith. The phrase (ek pisteōs eis pistin) has been read several ways: (1) from God’s faithfulness to our faith; (2) from the faith of the preacher to the faith of the hearer; (3) from Old Testament faith to New Testament faith; (4) faith growing from one degree to another; (5) faith from first to last.
