Everything presently disputed or hidden is on a schedule to be uncovered. Nothing is being lost; it is being kept.

He will render to each one according to his works. Paul is quoting his Bible (Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12), and the psalm puts it in the same breath as something else: to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love, for you will render to a man according to his work. Steadfast love and exact recompense, addressed to the same God. And “each one”: not nations or generations, each. No one will be graded on a curve against the people around him or lost in a crowd, which is unnerving and is also the only arrangement that could be just (Matthew 16:27; Revelation 20:12).

Does judgment by works contradict justification by faith? No; they answer different questions. Works are what is produced in court as evidence, not what is paid at the counter. Nobody is saved by evidence, and there will be evidence. The tree is not made alive by its fruit, but at harvest the inspection is of fruit. See the notes on vv. 7–8 and 13.

Will Christians be judged too? Yes, but not to decide whether we belong to God. That was settled at the cross: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (8:1). Believers will stand before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), where their lives are opened and what was done for him is acknowledged and rewarded, and some work that was worthless is lost, though the believer himself is saved (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). It is a Father’s assessment of his children, not a court deciding their fate. That should make us serious and not afraid.

In a sentence. Because of your stubborn, unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself for the day of wrath, when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed and he will repay each person according to what they have done.

On a Tuesday. Take something you know is wrong in your life and ask what has actually happened about it in the last six months. Has anything changed, not perfectly, but in some direction you could point to? Or has there only been a cycle of failure, discomfort, and a private promise to do better that nobody, including you, expected to be kept? A heart that repents moves. A heart that merely regrets goes in circles, and mistakes the circling for movement because it comes with so much feeling. Every day without repentance adds to the store. Repent today, and the account is cleared in Christ.

For worship. The one thing this letter insists on is that the balance can be changed: not by a man improving his deposits, which is the only remedy he can think of and the one thing that cannot work, but by being credited with an account that was never his (see on 1:17). The treasury of wrath he had been filling was emptied at the cross, onto the Son. The treasury he receives, he did not fill.

parallels.desc: you will render to a man according to his work

verseByVerse.quote: to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life; but for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury.
verseByVerse.commentary:
to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life; but for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury.

To those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life. This is the verse in Romans that most often stops a careful reader, and the difficulty should be stated rather than stepped around. Paul has said the gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes (1:16), and will say that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law (3:28). Here he says God will give eternal life to those who persist in doing good. Taken alone, that sounds like salvation by works. “Patience” (hypomonē) is steady endurance under weight; “well-doing” is good work; “seek” means their lives are aimed at God’s glory and the immortality only he can give.

Where Christians differ: who receives eternal life in vv. 7, 10 and 13? There are two main readings among those who hold firmly to justification by faith alone. The first (taken, for example, by Douglas Moo) sees these verses as stating God’s standard in principle: if anyone did persist in doing good, they would receive eternal life; but Paul will show in 3:9–20 that no one does, so the verses shut every mouth and drive us to Christ. The terms are honest, like a scholarship advertised for candidates with a flawless record: the money is real, and the reason nobody collects is not that the committee is dishonest. The second (taken, for example, by C. E. B. Cranfield and Thomas Schreiner) sees them as describing real people: believers, whose lives, changed by the Spirit, show persevering good works, and whom God will vindicate on the last day. Support for this comes later in the same chapter, where the Gentile who keeps the law is one whose heart is circumcised by the Spirit (vv. 26–29), and from Paul’s teaching that those who sow to the Spirit will reap eternal life (Galatians 6:8). Verdict: the second reading is most likely, and the first contains an important truth. God’s judgment will follow the evidence of a person’s life (v. 6). The only people who will be found persevering in good are those whom God has justified freely by faith and renewed by his Spirit (Ephesians 2:8–10; Philippians 1:6). Their good works are not the ground of their acceptance, which is Christ’s righteousness alone (3:21–26), but the fruit and evidence of it. And no one can reach this standard by the law in his own strength, which is exactly what Paul goes on to prove.

The direction of a life. Look at the words Paul chose. Not achievement but patience, staying at something under weight; and seeking, not possessing or having arrived but oriented, still after it. He is not describing a man who has produced a spotless record. He is describing the direction a life faces over time. And he does not contrast the successful with the failing; he contrasts those who seek glory, honour and immortality with those who are self-seeking. Both are seeking. The last day asks not how much was accomplished but what the life was after. And wanting glory, honour and immortality is not condemned as ambition. It is the right ambition. Our desires are not too strong but too weak: the second group wanted it for themselves, and settled for it far too cheaply.

But for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury. “Self-seeking” (eritheia) is selfish ambition, the spirit of faction and self-promotion. And the language of obeying unrighteousness is striking: sin is presented not as weakness but as allegiance, a rival lordship willingly served. Their deeds show their hearts.

I keep falling into the same sin. Does that mean I am not persevering in well-doing? No. Perseverance is not sinlessness; Paul assumes interruption, which is why his word is patience. The question is the direction of travel and what you do when you fall. A believer falls and gets up again, hates the sin, confesses it, and fights it, sometimes for years (7:15–25; 1 John 1:8–9). What Scripture warns against is the settled life that has made peace with sin and stopped fighting. If you are grieved by your sin and still running to Christ with it, that grief and that running are themselves the Spirit’s work in you.

In a sentence. To those who persist in doing good, seeking glory, honour and immortality, God will give eternal life, but for the self-seeking who reject the truth and follow evil, there will be wrath and anger.

On a Tuesday. Draw a line through the last five years and ask which way it points. Not whether this month was good; not whether you fell last week. Over five years, is there anything you now hate that you used to excuse? Anything you now do that once seemed impossible? Is God more to you than he was, or less? A car that stalls repeatedly is still going somewhere; a car that is stationary and revving is not, however loud it is.

For worship. If you have read this verse and concluded that you fall short of patient continuance in well-doing, you have read it correctly; the man who thinks he qualifies has misread it. And the letter goes on to tell you who kept these terms. Christ endured with patience, did good without a break, sought his Father’s glory and not his own, and never once obeyed unrighteousness. He met verse 7 in full, and what he earned by it is given to people who plainly did not. Eternal life is what Christ merited by a life exactly like the one described here. Your patient well-doing is not the payment for it. It is the evidence that it has already been given to you.

verseByVerse.quote: There will be tribulation and distress for every human being who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek, but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There will be tribulation and distress for every human being who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek, but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek.

There will be tribulation and distress for every human being who does evil. Paul has just said this and now says it backwards: verses 7 and 8 ran good then evil; 9 and 10 run evil then good, so the two destinies sit at the centre of a mirror. It is the construction of a man who does not want to be misheard. And the words are concrete. Tribulation is pressure, the crushing of something under weight. Distress is literally narrow space: being hemmed in, with no room to turn. Paul pictures the outcome of a life apart from God not as a distant fire but as a closing in. “Every human being”: no exceptions.

The shape of sin. Anybody can verify this in ordinary life. Every temptation presents itself as an enlargement: more freedom, more experience, and the people who declined were narrow and missed out. Then watch what it delivers over twenty years. The man who drinks ends with a world the size of one room. The bitter woman ends with a life organised around a single grievance she can no longer put down. The pornography habit that promised variety produces a man who cannot look at his own wife properly. Whatever is finally meant by tribulation and distress, it is this, continued, with the restraints gone.

But glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good. Verse 7 promised immortality; here the third word is peace, shalom, not merely the absence of conflict but everything in its proper place, working. And glory in Hebrew is weight, substance. So the contrast is not pleasure against pain. It is expansion against contraction: a life given room to become what it was made for, or a life closing in until nothing is left but the thing it chose.

The Jew first and also the Greek. The same phrase as 1:16, now cutting the other way. Every Jewish believer knew what first meant: first to be called, to receive the promises, to be given the law. Paul uses the identical word about the dock. First in privilege, first in responsibility. Amos put it more bluntly: you only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities (Amos 3:2). Election is the ground of the severer reckoning, not an exemption from it. To whom much was given, of him much will be required (Luke 12:48).

Who is first today? The person raised in a Christian home who cannot remember not knowing the gospel. The one who has sat under good preaching for thirty years, owns four Bibles, could answer any doctrinal question, and has friends who pray for him by name. Every one of those is a mercy, and this verse quietly turns each into an entry on an account. The most dangerous seat in any church is not the back row. It is the one occupied by somebody who has heard everything and been changed by very little.

In a sentence. There will be trouble and distress for everyone who does evil, Jew first and then Greek, but glory, honour and peace for everyone who does good, Jew first and then Greek.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last time a sermon, a passage or a conversation genuinely landed on you, the moment you thought, that is about me, and it is true. Ask what happened in the seven days afterwards. Not what you felt; what changed by the following Sunday. Do that with the last three occasions you can remember, and you will have a fair measure of what your light is doing in you. The more you know of God, the more you are responsible for. Live up to your light, and ask him to make it grow.

For worship. If this frightens you, two things. The same “first” that meant first in accountability meant first in the offer: the gospel came to them first, and it has come to you, which is the very mercy now unsettling you. And the weight of the greater light was carried in the end by the only man who ever had all of it and wasted none. He was crushed so that the narrowing could stop, and what he opens, at the far end of this letter, is room.

verseByVerse.quote: For God shows no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God shows no partiality.

For God shows no partiality. The principle behind it all (Deuteronomy 10:17; Acts 10:34). The word is a picture from the Old Testament courtroom: literally face-receiving, the judge who lifts the face of the man before him because he was somebody. Israel’s law forbade it: you shall not be partial in judgment, you shall not defer to the great (Leviticus 19:15), for the LORD your God is not partial and takes no bribe. Paul is applying the oldest principle in Israel’s law to Israel.

Both directions. We usually hear only one. Nothing you bring can raise your chin: not your family, not having been in church since you were four, not your giving, competence or reputation. But run it the other way, because this is the half that goes unpreached. If no advantage lifts a face, no disadvantage lowers one. God is not more ready to hear the articulate, the theologically trained, the emotionally stable, or those whose lives look tidy. The woman who cannot pray aloud, the man who came to Christ at sixty with a wrecked history, the believer with a criminal record: none of them is further down the list, because there is no list. Impartiality is terrifying to anyone trading on advantage, and the best news in the world to anyone who has none.

Peter learned it the hard way. It took a vision and a two-day journey. Standing in a Gentile’s house, having spent his life certain such a house would defile him, his first words were: truly I understand that God shows no partiality (Acts 10:34). He was not conceding a point in a debate. He was watching a wall come down that he had believed held up the roof.

Does impartiality mean God loves everyone the same? It means no status can move his judgment, and his love cannot be bought. It does not mean he has no particular love for particular people; chapter 8 insists on the opposite in the warmest words in Greek. God plays no favourites, and he has, extravagantly, beloved.

In a sentence. For God does not show favouritism.

On a Tuesday. James makes it a rule about Sunday morning: if a man in fine clothes is given the good seat and the poor man told to stand, have you not become judges with evil thoughts (James 2:1–4)? The modern version rarely involves seating. It is who gets followed up after missing three weeks, whose name is remembered, which visitor is introduced to someone and which gets a handshake at the door. Think of the last two conversations you had at church and ask what those people could do for you. Then ask when you last sought out the person who can do nothing for you at all, and whose company is slightly hard work. God shows no favouritism. Neither should you.

For worship. God will not lift your face because of anything you bring to court. But he will lift it. You, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head (Psalm 3:3). By the end of this letter it is clear how a guilty man has his head lifted in that courtroom: not because the Judge was impressed by him, but because the Judge’s own Son stood in his place, and there was nothing left on the charge sheet to keep his eyes on the floor.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified. — Romans 2:12–13
verseByVerse.commentary:
For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified.

For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law. Hear the symmetry Paul builds: sinned without the law, perish without the law; sinned under the law, judged by the law. Each person is measured by the light he was actually given, and there is real mercy in that. Nobody will be arraigned for a revelation that never reached him; the tribesman who never heard of Sinai will not be tried by Sinai (see on 1:19–20). But the mercy does not end where we would like. He is judged by less, and he still perishes, for sins against what he knew (1:20; 2:15). Fewer rules did not mean he kept them.

And all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. Jews will be judged by the law they had.

For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God. “Hearers” (akroatai) would have gone straight through a Jewish reader. Israel’s central confession begins Hear, O Israel, and every Sabbath in every synagogue in Rome the law was read aloud to people who had come specifically to hear it. Many assumed that possessing it put them right with God. And Paul says that the thing you do faithfully every Sabbath, for your whole life, will not make one person righteous. The modern equivalent needs no translation. No generation has had such easy access to preaching, and the danger is exact, because hearing feels like doing. Something genuinely happens when a passage lands: recognition, warmth, resolve. It is possible to have that every week for thirty years and be unaltered, which is why James says the hearer who does not do is deceiving himself (James 1:22). The deception is that agreement feels like obedience.

But the doers of the law who will be justified. “Will be justified” (dikaiōthēsontai): future, at the final judgment. This is the first appearance in the letter of the verb to justify, the word on which Romans turns and over which the Reformation was fought, and Paul introduces it in the very form that seems to contradict everything he will build with it. He wants the standard understood at full strength before he says who has met it. In principle a perfect law-keeper would be justified; but no one keeps it perfectly (3:10, 20, 23), so this shuts the mouth of anyone relying on having the law. Yet the verse also points forward: those justified by faith in Christ and given the Spirit begin truly to do what the law requires (8:4), and on the last day God will acknowledge them as righteous. See the note on vv. 7–8.

Where Christians differ: does Paul teach salvation by works here? Roman Catholic teaching, and some recent scholars, read vv. 6–13 as teaching that final justification depends in part on the good works a person does with God’s help. Verdict: no. Paul establishes that God judges according to deeds, and that hearing or possessing the law saves no one. He then shows that no one meets the law’s standard (3:9–20), so justification must be by faith apart from works (3:21–28; 4:4–5). The good works of believers are the evidence of a true and living faith, not its ground. We are justified by faith alone, and judged according to works that show whether that faith was real (James 2:14–26). There is no contradiction between Romans 2 and Romans 3: the first shows the standard and the evidence; the second shows the only ground of acceptance.

Two kinds of hearing. Paul says here that hearers are not justified; eight chapters later he says faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (10:17). Both are true, because there are two kinds of hearing. There is the hearing that receives information and files it, which changes nothing and can go on for a lifetime. And there is the hearing a drowning man does when someone on the bank tells him where the rope is. That second kind is not the opposite of doing. It is the first thing a man does, and it is the only kind that has ever justified anybody.

In a sentence. Everyone who sins without the law will perish without the law, and everyone who sins under the law will be judged by the law, for it is not those who hear the law who are righteous before God, but those who obey it who will be declared righteous.

On a Tuesday. Listen for the sentence “yes, that is a good point” in your own mouth this week, after a sermon, a book, or a friend who told you the truth about yourself. Notice what it does. It sounds like agreement, and it works as a full stop. A person who intends to act does not usually say “good point”; he says “what do I do about that?” So after the next sermon, before you leave the building, decide one specific thing you will do differently this week, and tell someone.

For worship. No one has kept the law perfectly except Christ. He heard the Father’s word and did it, every day, in every detail, so that he could say: I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29). He is the one doer of the law, and he kept it for those who could not.

verseByVerse.quote: For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them

For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires. Pagans who do not have Moses’ law still often do what it requires: honour parents, refuse murder, keep promises. This is common grace. Paul is not teaching that Gentiles can be saved by following their conscience; he is establishing that people without the written law still have a moral framework that makes them accountable.

They are a law to themselves. Not that they make up their own rules, but that their own nature carries God’s law within. The moral law is built into human nature as part of the image of God. Every culture knows that some things are wrong.

While their conscience also bears witness. The word (syneidēsis) is built from two pieces meaning to know with: co-knowing. It names the strange fact that a human being can stand at a slight distance from himself and pass judgment on what he finds. You are the only creature that can be ashamed of itself. A dog can fear consequences; it cannot lie awake at four in the morning because of what it said to somebody in 1998. And Paul describes it as a courtroom: a witness bearing testimony, thoughts that come forward to accuse and thoughts that come forward to excuse. A full proceeding, going on inside people who have never read a page of the Bible. And even the excusing is revealing: nobody mounts a defence in a court he does not believe exists. Mostly, though, it accuses.

Where Christians differ: who are these Gentiles? Some, from Augustine to Cranfield, take them to be Gentile Christians, in whom the new covenant writes the law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). Others say Paul means unbelieving Gentiles who show moral awareness. Verdict: the context points to unbelieving Gentiles. Paul is still proving that everyone is accountable (1:18–3:20); he speaks of what Gentiles do “by nature” and of a conscience that accuses (v. 15), and of people who “perish without the law” (v. 12). Jeremiah promised the law itself written on the heart; Paul speaks here of the work of the law, its demands. This is not saving obedience, but evidence of accountability.

Conscience is a witness, not the judge. Paul is careful: it bears witness at a trial conducted by somebody else. A witness can be mistaken: it can testify from a distorted upbringing, a frightening father, or a church that taught a rule God never made. Conscience is real, God-given, and not infallible, and confusing those last two facts has damaged many Christians. There are two opposite failures. One is the conscience that will not stop accusing: believers who confess the same forgiven sin nightly for years and cannot receive assurance. To them Scripture says: whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything (1 John 3:20). He knows more than your accusing heart, including what his Son has done. The other is the conscience seared like scar tissue (1 Timothy 4:2), which is quiet, and whose quietness is its danger.

Should I always follow my conscience? Never act against it, but always be willing to have it corrected. To do what you believe is wrong is sin, even if the thing itself is allowed, because it is done without faith (14:23). But a conscience can be too strict or too loose, so it must be trained by Scripture. When your conscience troubles you about something God’s word does not forbid, do not simply override it: study what Scripture says, ask mature believers, and let the truth reshape it over time. When it is silent about something God’s word condemns, believe the word over the silence.

In a sentence. When Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do what it requires, they show that its requirements are written on their hearts, as their consciences also testify, with their thoughts sometimes accusing them and sometimes defending them.

On a Tuesday. Do not ask whether you feel guilty; that measures the volume, not the accuracy. Take the last thing your conscience convicted you about and ask two questions. Can I name the command of God this broke? If so, that is real conviction, and the answer is repentance, not reassurance. If there is nothing behind it but a vague feeling of not being good enough, it may be a witness giving evidence it does not have. And does this drive me toward God or away from him? The Spirit’s conviction is specific and takes you to the cross. The accuser is vague, and always advises you to keep your distance for a while.

For worship. If the law is written on the heart, it was there before you were converted, in every year you were running. That is why a memory from twenty years ago can still make you wince: that faculty was doing its work all along, and it was one of the means God used to bring you home. It accused you accurately, and then it was answered: not by your improvement, and not by its own eventual silence, but by a verdict handed down from a higher bench, where the blood of Christ purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14).
verseByVerse.note: Conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong that God has given to every person.

parallels.desc: I will write it on their hearts

verseByVerse.quote: on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus.

On that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men. God judges the secrets: not only what we do in public, but hidden thoughts and motives (1 Corinthians 4:5; Hebrews 4:13). Nothing escapes.

According to my gospel. The strangest phrase in the verse. Judgment is not the awkward small print at the end of the good news; Paul files it under the good news. The good news is not that there is no judgment, but that there is a way to be safe in it, and that the universe is just. Ask who the doctrine is good news for. Ask the woman whose abuser was never charged and kept his job and his pew. Ask the man whose career was destroyed by a lie he could never disprove. Ask a family whose village was burned by men who were promoted afterwards. The world has told every one of them that the file is closed. This verse says the file is open, the evidence is kept, and a date has been set. A universe with no judgment is not gentler. It is one in which the powerful got away with it permanently.

The hidden good. There is a side of “the secrets” that is rarely preached. Jesus said: give in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you (Matthew 6:4). If that day uncovers what was hidden, it does not uncover only hidden wrong. The eleven years of caring for a parent with dementia that nobody watched. The money given quietly by a man everyone thought was tight-fisted. The prayers said at night for someone who never knew. None of it was recorded by anyone else, and none of it was lost. For a great many obscure people, that day will be the first time anyone has seen what they actually did with their lives.

By Christ Jesus. Jesus is the judge (Acts 17:31; John 5:22). The Father has given him authority to execute judgment because he is the Son of Man (John 5:27): because he is human. He was poor, exhausted, misrepresented, betrayed by a friend, and tried in a rigged court himself. Nobody will be able to say the Judge did not understand the circumstances. The one who died for sinners will judge them, and for those in him, the Judge is their Saviour.

Should I be afraid of that day as a Christian? Not afraid of condemnation, because your standing was settled at another bar: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (8:1). What is assessed for a believer is his work, not his welcome, and Scripture is honest that some work will not survive the fire, while he himself will be saved (1 Corinthians 3:15). Loss is possible; losing Christ is not. So the right response is not dread but honesty now: bring your secrets into the light with God, confess them, and where it is right, to a trusted believer (James 5:16). What is confessed now is covered.

In a sentence. This will happen on the day when God judges people’s secrets through Christ Jesus, as Paul’s gospel declares.

On a Tuesday. Think of one thing that would genuinely surprise the people who think well of you. Not to tell anyone; just notice that you did not have to search for it. It arrived immediately, because you have known about it all along. That gap between the you that is known and the you that is real is exactly the material of this verse, and every one of us maintains it. Bring it to Christ today.

For worship. The Judge before whom the secrets will be opened is not going to learn anything. He has known every one of them from the beginning, in full, without your explanations attached, and he went to the cross already holding the complete file. No evidence produced on that day will change his mind about you, because none of it will be new to him. You are not going to be found out. You were found out long ago, and he came anyway.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–29 — The Failure of Israel: Circumcision of the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now addresses the Jewish interlocutor directly, and the charge he levels is devastating. The Jew who possesses the Torah, who teaches it to others, who relies on it for his identity — does he keep it himself? "You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?" The indictment is not that the Torah is worthless but that it cannot save those who merely possess and teach it without obeying it from the heart.

The climax of the argument comes in the citation from Isaiah and Ezekiel: "The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you." This is the ultimate indictment. Israel, entrusted with the oracles of God, called to be a light to the nations, had become in its hypocrisy a reason for the nations to despise the God of Israel. The covenant privilege had become a covenant disgrace. Nothing has changed in principle: every generation of the church must face the same charge — does our life commend the God we profess?

The solution Paul gestures toward is one of the most important concepts in the entire letter: "circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter" (v. 29). This is the Old Testament's own vision — Deuteronomy 10:16, Deuteronomy 30:6, Jeremiah 31:33, Ezekiel 36:26 — now being fulfilled in the new covenant. The mark of true belonging to God is not an outward physical sign but the inward transformation of the heart by the Spirit. This will be Paul's great theme in chapters 6–8.

One move in the middle of the section should not be passed over, because it is the sharpest thing in it. At verse 27 Paul does not merely say that circumcision without obedience is worthless. He says that the physically uncircumcised man who keeps the law will judge the man who has the letter, the circumcision, and a record of breaking it. The outsider is called as the prosecution witness. It is the same reversal our Lord made when he said of a Roman soldier that he had not found such faith in all Israel (Matthew 8:10), and it is designed to be intolerable to anyone whose security rests in the marking rather than in the obedience the marking was given to signify.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Purpose and Limits of the Law

Romans 2:17–29 is the first extended treatment of the law's purpose and limits in the letter. Calvin identified three uses of the law: to reveal sin, to restrain wickedness in society, and to guide the redeemed life. Paul is here invoking the first use: the law reveals sin. The Jew who possesses the Torah has a clearer mirror than the Gentile — and therefore a clearer sight of his own failure to meet its demands. The law cannot save; it can only expose the need for a Saviour. This is precisely why chapters 3–4 follow: the righteousness the law demands but cannot provide is given freely in the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish confidence in circumcision as the defining covenant mark was absolute in Paul's day. To question its saving significance was to question the entire structure of Second Temple Jewish identity. Paul does not question circumcision's historical significance; he relativises it entirely: the physical sign points to a spiritual reality, and when the sign is present without the reality, it is worse than useless. Now: The equivalent is any Christian community that trusts in the outward marks of religion — baptism, church attendance, doctrinal orthodoxy, moral reputation — as substitutes for the inward transformation of the heart by the Spirit. Paul's word stands: God looks at the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God and know his will and approve what is excellent, because you are instructed from the law;
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God and know his will and approve what is excellent, because you are instructed from the law;

But if you call yourself a Jew. Now Paul names his hearer directly: the Jew who has every privilege. And notice the shape. Verses 17 to 20 are one long suspended sentence, if you call yourself a Jew, and rely, and boast, and know, and approve, and are sure you are a guide, a light, an instructor, a teacher: nine clauses of mounting credentials with no main verb. Paul lets a man talk himself up for four verses without interruption, and the sentence has no floor under it until verse 21 brings it down. A boast is most effectively answered by being allowed to finish. And the name carries a pun Paul will spring at the end of the chapter: Jew comes from Judah, named by his mother with the words this time I will praise the LORD (Genesis 29:35). Judah means praise. Hold that until verse 29.

And rely on the law. “Rely” (epanapauē) means to rest on, to lean back, to settle one’s weight. Trusting in having the law, rather than in God. The law was given as a path to walk, and he has made furniture of it. A path only helps while you are moving along it; a chair helps most when you have stopped.

And boast in God. Boasting in God can be good: let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31), and we boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ (5:11). The fault is not that this man is proud of God, but that he is proud of having God. From inside they are hard to tell apart; from outside the difference is plain. Boasting in God makes a person smaller and warmer. Boasting in having God makes him larger and colder.

And know his will and approve what is excellent, because you are instructed from the law. “Approve what is excellent” is literally to test and distinguish the things that differ: the same verb as the mind that refused to test God (1:28) and the renewed mind that discerns his will (12:2). Paul credits this man with something real: a trained moral palate. These are real privileges (9:4–5). The problem is not the privileges, but trusting in them. And it removes his last excuse, because his problem is provably not that he cannot see.

In a sentence. If you call yourself a Jew, relying on the law and boasting in God, knowing his will and approving what is best because you are taught by the law...

On a Tuesday. When someone asks what you believe, listen to what comes out. Do you describe a position: what you hold, what your church teaches, where you stand relative to people who have it wrong? Or do you describe a Person? Both may be orthodox. Only one sounds like someone who has met him. And does knowing God make you feel nearer to people who do not know him, or further from them? Church membership, a Christian upbringing and Bible knowledge are gifts. They cannot save you. Trust Christ, not your privileges.

For worship. The modern list is easy to write: raised in it, taught well, doctrinally sound, able to spot an error at forty paces. Every line is a gift, and not one line of it is a pulse. Life is not in the possession of truth but in the Person the truth is about: this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3).

verseByVerse.quote: and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—
verseByVerse.commentary:
and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—

And if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness. Israel had been called to be a light to the nations (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6). A real calling: the self-description is not invented arrogance but a genuine vocation recited by a man who has stopped noticing that a vocation makes demands. And every one of the four titles is a teaching role. He does not describe himself as a worshipper, a servant or a forgiven sinner. He defines himself by his position relative to people who know less. Jesus called the Pharisees blind guides (Matthew 15:14; 23:16).

An instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children. Teachers of Gentile converts. And here is the occupational hazard of every teacher: parents, preachers, elders, Sunday school teachers, the person in the small group who always knows the answer. The danger is not error. It is that his relationship to the truth becomes professional. He reads a passage and his first thought is that it would preach; he hears a sermon and assesses it. None of this is dishonest, and all of it quietly puts him beside the word rather than under it. The Bible stops being a word addressed to him and becomes material.

Having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth. The law really did embody truth. The word (morphōsis) is the outline, the formed representation, and here it is positive: the law is the outline of what God is like. But Paul uses the same word of people in the last days having the appearance of godliness but denying its power (2 Timothy 3:5). The word is neutral. Everything depends on whether there is anything inside the shape. Having it is not obeying it.

Should I stop teaching if I fall short of what I teach? No. Paul does not tell this man to put the law down. He asks him a question: do you not teach yourself? The remedy for standing beside the word is not silence but getting back underneath it. Keep teaching, and let every passage you prepare speak to you first. Be honest with those you teach that you need it too; a teacher who admits his own struggle teaches grace better than one who seems to have none. If there is a sin you are living in, deal with it before God, and if it is serious, step back while it is put right. But the answer to hypocrisy is repentance, not resignation.

In a sentence. ...and if you are convinced that you are a guide for the blind, a light for those in darkness, an instructor of the foolish and a teacher of little children, because you have in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth...

On a Tuesday. Take the last passage of Scripture you studied properly and ask what it said to you: not to your class, your children, or the person you have been worrying about. If the answer takes searching while the application to others came instantly, you have found the condition Paul describes. And remember that the people you teach are not chiefly formed by your instruction. Children raised in Christian homes rarely abandon the faith because the doctrine was wrong; more often they watched a version of it up close for eighteen years and concluded it did not do anything. You are always teaching two lessons, and only one is prepared.

For worship. There is one Teacher who never stood beside the word, because he is the Word. He taught with authority and lived every syllable, and he calls himself gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). If you teach others, be taught by him first. Humility is the teacher’s first lesson, and he is the one who gives it.
verseByVerse.note: Israel had been called to be a light to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? While you preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?
verseByVerse.commentary:
you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? While you preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?

You then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? The question that brings the long boast of vv. 17–20 down. Every teacher, preacher and parent must ask it. And notice the form: Paul does not say you steal; he asks. An accusation can be argued with: tell a man what he is and he starts building a case. A question leaves him alone in the room with the answer. It is the method God used on the first man who hid from him, who was not handed a list of charges but asked, where are you? (Genesis 3:9). God knew the answer. The question was so that the man would have to say it himself.

While you preach against stealing, do you steal? While you say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? Paul is not asserting that Jewish people were characteristically thieves and adulterers; he argues in the manner of the lecture hall, putting to an imagined objector the standard charges any moralist would recognise. He is a Jew himself, and seven chapters on he will say he could wish himself cut off from Christ for their sake. The point is that the law you teach condemns you too. And Jesus showed that the law reaches the heart: lust is adultery and hatred is murder (Matthew 5:21–28).

You who abhor idols, do you rob temples? The most searching of the three. Israel was forbidden not only to worship idols but to profit from them: you shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them or take it for yourselves (Deuteronomy 7:25). Pagan temples were full of precious metal, and there was money for anyone prepared to melt it down and ask no questions. The charge was live: the town clerk of Ephesus defends Paul’s companions as neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess (Acts 19:37), using the word for temple-robbers. So the accusation is exact: you denounce idolatry at the front and take the silver off it at the back. It may also point to robbing God himself (Malachi 3:8), as the Pharisees condemned idols while loving money (Luke 16:14).

The shape of our inconsistency. That third question is the most modern of the three, because it is the shape most of our hypocrisy takes. We rarely do the thing we condemn. We benefit from it. You do not spread the gossip; you listen to all of it. You disapprove of how a colleague got the result, and you were glad of the result. You have views about where money comes from, and there are questions about your own you have decided not to ask. None of this feels like hypocrisy, because you genuinely do abhor the idol. You simply also take the gold.

The law as a mirror. The Reformers spoke of three uses of the law: it restrains wickedness in society, it guides the redeemed life, and first of all it shows a person what he really is. That first use is at work here. The law is a mirror: superbly designed to show you the dirt on your face, and it has never once removed any of it, and nobody blames a mirror for that. The error of the man in these verses is not that he owns a mirror. It is that he has framed it, hung it on the wall, and started showing it to visitors as evidence of how he looks. The mirror is meant to send us to the only place we can be washed.

In a sentence. You who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say not to commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who hate idols, do you rob temples?

On a Tuesday. Name one thing you criticise in public and profit from in private: not something you do, but something you are content to benefit from while keeping your hands apparently clean. Most of us can find one inside a minute, and the finding is the point. Then do one concrete thing about it this week: stop listening, give something back, ask the question you have avoided. Preach to yourself before you preach to others.

For worship. Only one teacher could ask these questions of everyone and answer them all about himself. Which of you convicts me of sin? (John 8:46). And he did not stand in judgment over the hypocrites from a distance. He took their place, so that the mirror which could only show our dirt is followed by the fountain that washes it: the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7).

verseByVerse.quote: You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law.

You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law. The sentence closes a circle. The section opened with a man who boasts in God (v. 17) and ends with a man who boasts in the law: the same verb, six verses apart. The problem was never that he valued the law too highly. He valued it as a possession rather than a demand, and a possession is something you display. And the verdict is one weighted word: he dishonours God. Chapter 1 said humanity refused to honour God and was given up to the dishonouring of their bodies (1:21, 24); the same idea returns with the religious man in the frame. The pagan dishonours God by worshipping something else. The religious man dishonours him by claiming him loudly and living as though he were not there.

Why it is worse. A man who makes no profession and does wrong has damaged himself. A man who has told everyone he belongs to God, and does the same wrong, has attached God’s name to it. Without intending anything of the kind, he has made a statement about what God is like, and other people will believe it, because a life is more persuasive than a doctrine. This is the logic of the third commandment. Taking the Lord’s name in vain is not chiefly about swearing. It is carrying his name and treating it as though it weighed nothing. And it needs no scandal. It is the Christian known at work for being sharp about money; the father whose family go quiet when he comes in; the believer whose neighbours have concluded, without discussing theology, that whatever he has does not seem to make him kinder.

Does my failure really damage God’s honour? Not God himself: he is not diminished by being misrepresented, any more than the sun is dimmed by a bad photograph of it. What is at stake is what the people around you are being shown. So the answer to failure is not to hide it, which adds a lie to the sin, but to own it. When you have dishonoured Christ in front of others, say so plainly to them, apologise without excuses, and put right what you can. Nothing honours God in front of unbelievers more than a Christian who admits he was wrong and shows where he goes for forgiveness.

In a sentence. You who boast in the law dishonour God by breaking it.

On a Tuesday. Think of three people who know both that you are a Christian and what you are actually like: a colleague, a neighbour, an adult child. Ask what conclusion about God a reasonable person would draw from your life if yours were the only evidence. Not what you would want them to conclude; what the evidence supports. Then ask God to make your life honour him there, and start with the one relationship where it is hardest.

For worship. The honour God was owed and did not receive from us has been paid in full by somebody. One life on this earth made no false statement about the Father at any point: I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). This letter exists to say that his record is put to the account of people whose own record reads like verse 23.

verseByVerse.quote: For, as it is written, "The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For, as it is written, “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”

For, as it is written, “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.” From Isaiah 52:5 and Ezekiel 36:20. In the prophets the setting is exile. The nations mocked God’s name not because Israel behaved badly but because Israel had been defeated: Ezekiel quotes the taunt, these are the people of the LORD, and yet they had to go out of his land. So much for their God. Paul applies the sentence to a different mechanism. In the prophets the name suffered because of what happened to God’s people; here because of what is done by them. Both are the same thing: the world forms its opinion of God from the people who carry his name. You are evidence either way. Christians who live badly cause the name of Christ to be blasphemed (1 Timothy 6:1; Titus 2:5).

Hypocrisy is not persecution. Say the modern form plainly. When a church covers up the abuse of children to protect its reputation, when a ministry’s finances turn out to be a private fortune, when a celebrated preacher was a different man off the platform, the contempt that follows is not persecution. It is an accurate response to the evidence, and Christians should be the last to confuse the two. Peter draws the line: if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer (1 Peter 4:15–16). Being despised for the cross is an honour. Being despised for hypocrisy is a bill. And when such things are exposed, the right response is truth, justice for the wronged and repentance, never protecting the institution.

Because of you. But do not let the headlines carry this verse. Paul writes because of you, the same singular man he has been questioning. Most people do not form their view of Christianity from scandals. Nobody in your street has met a famous pastor. They have met you. Their working theory of what God does to a person is assembled from two or three Christians they happen to know, in unguarded moments, and that sample includes you.

Ezekiel’s answer. Paul has chosen his ground with care. Ezekiel 36 does not stop at verse 20. Having stated the problem, God announces the remedy in the same chapter: I will sprinkle clean water on you; I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you; I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes (Ezekiel 36:25–27). That is exactly where Paul is going in five verses: a circumcision of the heart, by the Spirit (v. 29). And between the problem and the remedy stands God’s motive: it is not for your sake that I am about to act, but for the sake of my holy name (36:22).

In a sentence. As Scripture says, God’s name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last time your Christianity was visible to someone who does not share it: a disagreement at work, a contested conversation, a moment when you were tired and provoked. What came across? Not what you said; what came across. Was it Christ, or your certainty, your irritation, your need to be seen to be right? Most of us have never blasphemed God’s name. Rather more of us have made it look uninteresting, brittle or unkind, which does more damage, because nobody argues with a thing he has simply stopped finding attractive. People judge Christ by Christians. Ask him to make you a fair exhibit.

For worship. His people had dragged his reputation through the nations, and God did not respond by demanding that they repair it. He undertook to repair it himself, and the way he chose was to change them from the inside. The name that was blasphemed because of us will finally be honoured because of what he does in us.

parallels.desc: my name is continually despised

verseByVerse.quote: For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?

For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law. Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham (Genesis 17), the sign of belonging to God’s people. And it is hard for us to feel the force of this sentence. Circumcision was not a ceremony someone had attended; it was a permanent mark on the body, made on the eighth day of life, carried to the grave. It was the one credential a Jewish man could not lose or be argued out of, and many believed it guaranteed a place in the age to come. Paul begins by granting it: it is of value, genuinely. God gave it, and it meant something. What he denies is that it works on its own, regardless of the life attached to it.

But if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. The sign without the reality is worthless. A circumcised law-breaker is no better than a pagan. To the man Paul addresses, that is close to saying the covenant can be voided by conduct, and it is meant to take the floor out from under him. But Paul is quoting Moses, not spiritualising him away. The command to circumcise the heart is in the law itself (Deuteronomy 10:16), and Jeremiah said it six hundred years earlier: the days are coming when God will punish all who are circumcised merely in the flesh, for all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart (Jeremiah 9:25–26). A sign is not a machine. A wedding ring is a real thing given for real reasons, and it has never kept anyone faithful; on the hand of a man conducting an affair it does not become neutral. It becomes a lie in metal.

So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision? Who is this man? Some take him as hypothetical, like the doers of the law in v. 13. Others take him as a real person, a Gentile believer whose heart the Spirit has changed, so that the law’s requirement is beginning to be fulfilled in him (8:4). The second is more likely here, because Paul is moving toward the true circumcision of v. 29, which is by the Spirit. Such a man’s obedience is not perfect and is not the ground of his acceptance; it is the evidence of a heart God has circumcised. And notice the verb, “regarded”: an accountant’s word, to credit to an account. It will dominate chapter 4, where Abraham believes God and it is counted to him as righteousness. Here, on its first outing as a word of crediting, God is counting an outsider in.

A lesson for baptism and the Lord’s Supper. The same applies to the signs Christ has given his church. They are valuable and commanded, but they do not save without faith. A baptised unbeliever is no better off than an unbaptised one; and for this app, which holds believer’s baptism, baptism is meant to follow and declare faith, not replace it. Very few people today trust in circumcision. Many trust in an event: a decision at fourteen at a summer camp, a card signed, a baptism, a week when everything seemed clear. The event may have been entirely genuine. Paul’s question is whether the thing it signified is present now.

What it does not mean. This is not an argument that the signs God has given are unimportant, and nobody should conclude their baptism was a formality; Paul says the opposite in his first words. The error is the sign detached from what it points to. And some readers will now be examining a conversion they can barely remember and concluding that no vivid moment means no real faith. It does not. Assurance was never meant to rest on the quality of your memory of the beginning. Nobody proves he is alive by producing a birth certificate; he proves it by breathing, now. A person who cannot date his conversion and loves Christ today is in an incomparably better position than one with a certificate and no pulse.

How can I know my faith is real? Look for present evidence, not only a past event. Do you trust Christ alone for forgiveness, not your record? Do you hate your sin and fight it, even when you lose? Do you love other believers and want to be with them (1 John 3:14)? Do you want to obey God, and grieve when you do not? Is Christ precious to you? None of these needs to be strong; each only needs to be real. And the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (8:16). If you find these marks, however weak, take comfort. If you find none, do not despair: go to Christ now, because he receives everyone who comes.

In a sentence. Circumcision has value if you keep the law, but if you break it, you are as if uncircumcised, and if an uncircumcised person keeps the law’s requirements, will he not be regarded as circumcised?

On a Tuesday. Answer one honest question: what is the evidence for your Christianity that is dated later than your conversion? Not the story of how it began; the evidence from this year. A sin you have fought. A prayer you actually pray. A love for someone you have no natural reason to love. A grief over your own hardness. None needs to be impressive; it only needs to be current.

For worship. Every outward sign points beyond itself to Christ: circumcision to the cutting away he would accomplish, baptism to the death and resurrection he went through, the Supper to his body given and blood shed. Do not trust the signs. Trust the one they point to, and let them do what they were given for, which is to send you to him.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you who have the written code and circumcision but break the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you who have the written code and circumcision but break the law.

Then he who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you. Feel the courtroom Paul has been building since verse 1. The man in the dock has spent the chapter as a judge: passing verdicts on the pagans of chapter 1, teaching the blind, instructing the foolish. Now someone else is brought in, and it is the last person he expected: the uncircumcised man, the outsider he had been instructing. He does not merely turn out to be acceptable; he condemns. And not by argument. His existence is the verdict. Jesus used the same device: the men of Nineveh and the queen of the South will rise up at the judgment and condemn this generation, because they responded to less, and something greater is here (Matthew 12:41–42). They make no speech. They just stand there, having done with a candle what others would not do with the sun.

You who have the written code and circumcision but break the law. “Written code” (gramma) is the letter: the outward, written law, without the Spirit. Literally, you who through letter and circumcision break the law. The possessions are implicated: the code and the mark had become the very things that made the breaking possible, because they gave him a reason not to look. A man with no credentials at least knows he has nothing to plead. Give him a credential and you have handed him somewhere to hide.

The convert who shames us. The same figure walks around every congregation. Somewhere near you is a believer who came to Christ four years ago with no advantages at all: no Christian family, no grounding in the faith, a history that would make yours look sheltered. He mangles the theological terms and cannot find the minor prophets. And he prays as though God were in the room, forgives people who have truly wronged him, gives more than he can afford, and talks about Jesus to his neighbours without finding it difficult. He is not trying to rebuke anyone. He is a rebuke.

What it does not mean. This verse does not say ignorance is safer than knowledge, and it must not become an argument for keeping people uninstructed. The Gentile is commended for keeping the law, not for lacking it, and the whole chapter insists that light is a mercy. The problem was never that this man had too much; it is that he had a great deal and it stayed on the outside of him.

In a sentence. The one who is not physically circumcised but obeys the law will condemn you who, though you have the written code and circumcision, break the law.

On a Tuesday. Think of a believer you find slightly irritating: the enthusiastic one, the recent convert whose zeal seems naive, the person whose theology is thin and whose obedience is not. Ask what the irritation is made of. Sometimes it is real discernment. Very often it is the discomfort of watching someone do easily what you have stopped doing, and the quickest way to manage that feeling is to find something in him to correct. Instead, thank God for him, and ask him what has been helping him.

For worship. Turn the reversal round and there is something tender in it. If the insider’s credentials cannot save him, the outsider’s lack of them cannot damn him. Everyone who has come late, from the wrong background, with the wrong history and no religious furniture, stands where the man in verse 27 stands, and in this chapter that is the better place to stand. Christ came for the outsiders, and made them his own.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter. His praise is not from man but from God. — Romans 2:28–29
verseByVerse.commentary:
For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter. His praise is not from man but from God.

For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. Being a true member of God’s people is not a matter of race or ritual. Paul defines Jewish identity from the inside out, and he is not inventing a new category; he is completing the logic of the Old Testament itself.

But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart. The Old Testament already said it: circumcise your hearts (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 4:4). And Moses says it twice with the same image: first as a command, circumcise the foreskin of your heart (Deuteronomy 10:16), and later, when it was plain no one had, as a promise: the LORD your God will circumcise your heart (Deuteronomy 30:6). Between the command and the promise stands the whole history of Israel, and the reason the promise was necessary. The prophets never promised that Israel would try harder. They promised that God would operate. And circumcision was the one act of covenant obedience a man could not perform on himself; someone else held the knife. Nobody has ever circumcised his own heart. It is an operation performed on you, which is exactly why it produces no boast.

By the Spirit, not by the letter. The Spirit does what the written law cannot: he changes the heart (2 Corinthians 3:6; Ezekiel 36:26–27). This is the new covenant, fully unveiled in chapter 8. The contrast is not between spirit and law as such; Paul is not against the law. It is between the outward written requirement and the inward power of the Spirit, who creates the obedience the law commands but cannot produce. And it is Ezekiel 36 argued out: the diagnosis quoted at v. 24, the cure given here, heart and Spirit, in the prophet’s own order.

Where Christians differ: has the church replaced Israel? Some read this verse as saying that Gentile believers are now the true Jews, linking it with Philippians 3:3, we are the circumcision. Verdict: that is not quite what this verse says. Paul is still speaking to the Jew of v. 17, and he is saying who is a Jew in the full sense: not everyone with the outward mark, but the one whose heart God has changed, as Moses and the prophets had said all along (compare 9:6). He does not erase Israel. In the next breath he asks what advantage the Jew has and answers, much in every way (3:1–2), and chapters 9–11 still speak of Israel as a people with a future in God’s purposes. Gentile believers belong to Abraham’s family by faith (4:11–12; Galatians 3:29), but this verse makes a narrower point: within Israel the outward mark never made anyone God’s.

Then do Jewish people today need Christ to be saved? Yes, and Paul says so with tears. The same heart-circumcision Moses promised comes only through the Spirit whom Christ gives, and there is no other name by which anyone is saved (Acts 4:12). That is why Paul’s heart’s desire and prayer for Israel was that they might be saved (10:1), and why he went to the synagogue first in every city. Love for Jewish people, and gratitude for the Messiah who came from them, mean sharing him with them, humbly and gladly, never with contempt.

His praise is not from man but from God. The sentence Paul has been walking toward since verse 17. Remember what Jew means: Judah, named with the words this time I will praise the LORD. The name means praise. So the closing line is a definition delivered as a pun: the true Praise is the one whose praise comes from God. He began by addressing a man who calls himself a Jew, and ends by telling him what the name he has carried all his life actually means, and that it is not awarded by the people who can see you. And the contrast is not between external and sincere; a merely private religion is no better than a merely public one, and chapters 12–16 will demand very visible obedience. The contrast is between what people can see and award, and what God sees and awards. The circumcision Paul describes has only one competent witness.

In a sentence. A person is not a Jew who is one only outwardly, nor is circumcision merely outward and physical, but a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code; such a person’s praise comes from God, not from people.

On a Tuesday. How much of your Christian life would survive if nobody ever found out about it? Take away the congregation, the reputation, the people who think well of you for it, and ask what would still be there on a wet Tuesday with nobody watching. Whatever is left when the audience is removed is the part that is from God. Ask the Spirit to circumcise your heart, to cut away what you cannot cut away yourself, and seek his praise, not people’s.

For worship. There is great relief here for the Christian nobody notices. You will not be asked at the end to produce the visible things: the platform, the record, the esteem of the sound. Paul has spent a whole chapter taking away every commendation human beings can give, in order to hand you one they cannot give and therefore cannot take back. One day God will speak it aloud, about people nobody thought worth mentioning. It will come from the one who saw all of it, including what was done badly and what was done at cost and never noticed by a living soul, and it will be spoken because of his Son: well done, good and faithful servant (Matthew 25:21). Nothing in it will be exaggerated, because he has no need to flatter, and nothing will be left out. It will be the first entirely accurate sentence ever spoken about a human life.

parallels.desc: the LORD will circumcise your heart

Jesus.<sup>17</sup>But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God<sup>18</sup>and know his will and approve what is excellent, because you are instructed from the law;<sup>19</sup>and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness,<sup>20</sup>an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—<sup>21</sup>you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? While you preach against stealing, do you steal?<sup>22</sup>You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?<sup>23</sup>You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law.<sup>24</sup>For, as it is written, “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”<sup>25</sup>For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision.<sup>26</sup>So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?<sup>27</sup>Then he who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you who have the written code and circumcision but break the law.<sup>28</sup>For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical.<sup>29</sup>But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter. His praise is not from man but from God.

3.title: No One Righteous — But Now, Righteousness
3.overview:
Romans 3 is one of the most concentrated pieces of theological argument in the entire Bible. It moves through three distinct but connected moments: the faithfulness of God despite human faithlessness (vv. 1–8), the universal verdict of guilt on the entire human race from the Old Testament's own testimony (vv. 9–20), and then — with the two most beautiful words in the letter — "But now" (v. 21): the announcement of a righteousness from God that is apart from the law, given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe.

The emotional architecture of the chapter is deliberate. Paul has spent two chapters building the case for universal human guilt — the Gentile guilty through creation and conscience, the Jew guilty despite law and covenant. Now he delivers the verdict that springs from the evidence: no one righteous, not even one. And then, from within the deepest valley of human hopelessness, he sounds the trumpet of the gospel: the righteousness of God has been manifested. The darkness is real. The light is realer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — God's Faithfulness and Human Faithlessness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If Jewish identity and covenant privilege provide no buffer against divine judgment (chapter 2), an obvious question arises: what advantage has the Jew? Was the entire covenant history of Israel pointless? Paul will not allow this conclusion. The advantage is real and great: "they were entrusted with the oracles of God." The Torah, the prophets, the promises — these are not nothing. They are the priceless repository of God's self-revelation and covenant purposes. The problem is not the oracles; the problem is the people who received them.

But what about God's faithfulness? If Israel has been faithless to the covenant, does that mean God's covenant promises have failed? Never, Paul declares — and the energy of his negation (mē genoito — "by no means!", "God forbid!", the strongest possible denial in Greek) is palpable. God's faithfulness is not contingent on human faithfulness. He remains true even when every human being is a liar. The covenant will not fail because the Covenant God cannot fail.

This brief passage anticipates the great argument of chapters 9–11: the apparent failure of Israel to embrace her Messiah does not represent a failure of God's word. His purposes stand. His faithfulness endures. The mystery of Israel's unbelief is not the defeat of God's plan but a part of it — and Paul will unfold that mystery with breathtaking scope later in the letter.

The second half of the section (vv. 5–8) turns to a pair of objections that Paul was evidently hearing in real life, and both are attempts to turn grace into a licence. If our unrighteousness only serves to display God’s righteousness more brightly, is God not unjust to punish it? And if my lie makes his truth more evident, why am I still condemned — why not simply “do evil that good may come”? Paul reports that last slander as something people were actually saying he taught, which tells us how radical his gospel of free grace sounded to its first hearers; no one ever accused the Pharisees of encouraging sin. He does not argue the point here — he refuses it, notes that God could judge nothing at all if the objection held, and reserves the full answer for chapter 6. But the objection itself is a compliment in disguise. A gospel that cannot be misheard as permission is probably not the gospel Paul preached.
verseByVerse.theology:
Divine Faithfulness and Human Failure

The question of whether human sin can thwart God's covenant purposes is one of the deepest in all theology. Romans 3:3–4 gives the Reformed answer: it cannot. God's faithfulness is not a function of human response; it is grounded in his own immutable character. Calvin wrote that God's truth stands firm even against the unfaithfulness of the whole world. This has practical implications for Christian assurance: our standing in the covenant does not rest on our faithfulness but on God's. He who called us is faithful; he will do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish readers would have been relieved by Paul's affirmation of Israel's covenant privileges, but troubled by his insistence that these privileges provide no exemption from judgment. The tension — covenant advantage, yet equal accountability — was genuinely new, though rooted in the Old Testament prophets. Now: Christians face the same tension. The advantages of covenant community — Scripture, sacrament, preaching, prayer — are real and great. They are also not saving substitutes for personal faith and repentance. Privilege and accountability always travel together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision? Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision? Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.

Meaning first. Romans 3 is the hinge of the letter. First Paul answers objections: if Jews are no better off, what was the point of being God’s people? (vv. 1–8). Then he closes the case: all, Jews and Gentiles, are under sin; no one is righteous; every mouth is stopped (vv. 9–20). Then come the greatest verses in the Bible on how God saves. But now the righteousness of God has been revealed apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe. All have sinned; all who believe are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption in Christ, whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, so that God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (vv. 21–26). Boasting is excluded; we are justified by faith apart from works (vv. 27–31). The chapter that brings the whole human race into the dock ends with the Judge himself providing the righteousness the prisoners could never bring.

Then what advantage has the Jew? Paul has just argued that circumcision without obedience is worthless, and he knows exactly what the man in front of him is now thinking: then none of it meant anything, and two thousand years of covenant history were a waste of everyone’s time. Notice that Paul asks the question at all, and that he asks it against himself. A lesser writer would have let the misunderstanding stand rather than complicate a good argument. Paul stops the flow of his own case to answer it, which tells you something about the difference between winning a debate and telling the truth.

Much in every way. The answer is not a grudging concession. Paul does not retreat an inch from chapter 2, and he does not allow the privileges to be belittled; in chapter 9 he will list them with an ache in his voice: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, the Christ (9:4–5). Both things are true at once, and holding them together is the whole art of this passage: a gift can be genuinely magnificent and genuinely insufficient to save the man holding it.

They were entrusted. The word Paul chooses is not the language of a possession but of a deposit: something handed to you which belongs to somebody else and about which you will be asked. A trustee does not own the fund. He administers it, and he is accountable for what happens to it. That quietly answers the question the whole passage raises. The advantage is real precisely because it is a trust, and a trust is the one kind of advantage that increases your liability rather than reducing it.

The oracles of God. The utterances, the things God actually said: the Scriptures, God’s very words, entrusted to Israel to keep and to pass on.
