It is worth pausing on how strange this is as an answer. Paul could have named the temple, the land or the throne. He names one thing, and it is that God had spoken and that they had it in writing. Through them, the whole world received the Bible. Every Gentile believer who has ever opened the Psalms is in debt to the scribes of Israel who copied them, letter by letter, for a thousand years.

A people with sentences. Consider what that meant in the ancient world, because familiarity has flattened it for us. Every nation had gods, and every nation had priests who could tell you what the gods were thought to want: read from entrails, from stars, from the flight of birds, from the ambiguous mutterings of a woman at Delphi, and always open to interpretation and revision. Israel alone had sentences. Not impressions of the divine will but actual words, in a known language, that could be copied, memorised, checked, argued about, and read aloud to a child. In a world of religious guesswork, one people had a text, because the living God had chosen to speak.

The advantage we hold. This is exactly the advantage a Christian holds today, and we hold it more fully than they did. You own, in a language you can read, more of God’s speech than Isaiah ever saw, and most of us keep several copies. The whole thrust of chapter 2 falls on this point: the deposit does not benefit a man who never opens it. There is no category in Scripture called owning the word of God. There is only hearing it and doing it, or hearing it and not.

The problem was never the gift. This is the sentence that should govern how you read the rest of the chapter. Everything Paul is about to say about human ruin is said by a man who has just insisted, in the strongest terms available to him, that what God gave was magnificent. The indictment of chapters 1 to 3 is not the story of a deficient revelation. It is the story of what happened to a priceless deposit in the hands of people exactly like us.

Do Jewish people still have an advantage today? Paul’s answer to that belongs to chapters 9 to 11, and Christians who love those chapters read the details differently. But this much he says plainly: the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (11:29), the privileges of 9:4–5 were never a mistake, and God has not rejected his people (11:1). What no privilege can do is justify. A Jewish heritage of Scripture, like a Christian upbringing, is a great mercy and a heavy responsibility, and it saves no one apart from faith in Christ. The proper response of a Gentile believer is gratitude, not arrogance (11:18), and a longing that the people who gave us the Bible should receive its Messiah.

Is the Old Testament still God’s word for me? Yes, every page of it. Paul calls it the oracles of God, the words God himself spoke, and he never treats them as out of date. Jesus said the Scriptures bear witness about him (John 5:39), and Paul says that whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope (15:4). Not every command applies to you in the same way: the sacrifices are fulfilled in Christ, and Israel’s civil laws governed a nation. But all of it is God speaking, all of it points to his Son, and all of it is for you.

In a sentence. What advantage is there in being a Jew, or in circumcision? A great deal, above all that the Jews were entrusted with the very words of God.

On a Tuesday. You have been entrusted with God’s word too, and here is a small test, factual rather than introspective. Over the past month, how many hours did you spend with the oracles of God, reading, hearing and thinking about them, compared with the hours you spent on what you would call recreation? Do not moralise the answer; just get the number. It is the truest available measure of what you actually believe you have been entrusted with, and it is probably not the number you would have guessed. Then do the simplest possible thing about it: open the Book today, before the screen.

For worship. The God of Israel did not leave the world to guess at him. He spoke, he put his words in writing, he guarded them through exile, conquest and the slow centuries of copying, and then he sent the Word himself, made flesh, of whom every one of those sentences had been speaking. The God who could have remained silent chose to be the God who talks to his creatures, and the book on your table is the evidence that he has never stopped.
verseByVerse.note: “The oracles of God” are the Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar, as it is written, "That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar, as it is written, “That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged.”

What if some were unfaithful? If Israel failed, does God fail? Has he broken his promises? The sentence turns on a play that English cannot keep. Their faithlessness (apistia) and God’s faithfulness (pistis) are the same root in Greek, negated on one side, as if to say: does their un-faith un-faith the faith of God? Paul sets the two words against each other so that the answer is visible before it is argued. One is a quality of God, and the other is merely its absence in somebody else. An absence cannot cancel a substance. The dark in a room has never once put out a lamp.

By no means! Mē genoito: the strongest negative Paul has, a phrase he uses ten times in this letter, always when a conclusion is not merely wrong but intolerable. The older translations reached for God forbid, which is not a literal rendering and catches the tone exactly. This is not the language of a man weighing a proposition. It is the language of a man recoiling from one.

Let God be true though every one were a liar. One of the great rules of the Christian mind. God’s faithfulness does not depend on ours (2 Timothy 2:13): even if every human being failed, God would remain true. And it is worth turning that into the working principle it is, because every believer meets the situation it was built for. Sooner or later what God has said and what you can see will fail to agree. He says he works all things for good, and you are standing in a hospital corridor. He says he is near to the brokenhearted, and you have felt nothing for eight months. He says his discipline is love, and it does not feel like love. In that moment one of two things has to give, and Paul tells you which: God is true. The consensus of the human race, your own eyes, and your own heart at four in the morning are all admitted as evidence, and they lose. Not because your experience is unreal, but because a witness who has been wrong before is not permitted to overrule one who never has.

What it does not mean. It is not a call to pretend. Paul does not say let God be true and every man be silent. The Bible is full of people telling God exactly what they see, at length and without editing; half the Psalter does little else. You are allowed to say that it looks as though he has forgotten you. What you are not allowed to do is conclude it. Say the whole of what you see; then let his word have the last sentence rather than the first.

That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged. Go and look at the psalm Paul quotes, because a citation left unopened is a claim left unproved, and this one is startling. The words come from Psalm 51:4, and Psalm 51 is David after Bathsheba: after the adultery, after the pregnancy, after arranging for a loyal soldier to be abandoned in the front line so that the husband would not come home. That is the man saying, against you, you only, have I sinned, so that you may be justified in your words and blameless in your judgment. He is not defending himself. He is agreeing with the verdict in advance, without conditions, declaring that when God judges him, God will be in the right.

Displayed, not damaged. That is exactly why Paul reaches for it here. He needs to show that God’s truthfulness is not damaged by human failure but displayed by it, and the proof is a man at the bottom of his own life saying so. The worst thing David ever did did not make God’s word less reliable. It demonstrated it: God had said what such a man is, and such a man turned out to be exactly that. Human sin shows God’s righteousness in judging it.

Did God’s faithfulness mean every Israelite was saved anyway? No. God’s faithfulness is faithfulness to what he promised, and he never promised to save people who refused him. Paul answers this directly later: not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel (9:6). God kept his word by preserving a believing remnant, chosen by grace (11:5), and by sending the Messiah through Israel exactly as he had said. He also kept his word when he judged unbelief, because his covenant always carried warnings as well as promises. His faithfulness is not a guarantee that no one will be lost. It is a guarantee that nothing he has said will fail.

If I am faithless, will God still keep me? If you belong to Christ, yes. He remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself (2 Timothy 2:13). But read the line before it too: if we deny him, he also will deny us (2 Timothy 2:12). Paul is distinguishing the believer who wavers, doubts and fails, as Peter did on the night of the trial, from the person who finally and deliberately turns his back on Christ for good. The first is held, because what holds him is God’s faithfulness and not his own grip. The second shows he never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). If you are worried about your faithlessness and still turning to Christ, that worry is a sign of life, not of abandonment.

In a sentence. If some were unfaithful, does their unfaithfulness cancel God’s faithfulness? Not at all! Let God be true and every human a liar, as Scripture says: so that you may be proved right in your words and win when you are judged.

On a Tuesday. Take the last time you were rebuked, by Scripture, by a sermon, or by a person who loved you enough to say it. Did you come out of it agreeing with God, or explaining yourself? Almost all of us explain. We supply the context, the provocation, the tiredness, the other party’s share, and every syllable of explanation is a small attempt to keep the verdict from being wholly just. David does something that costs a great deal more and pays a great deal better: he stops arguing and lets God be right about him. Try it once this week, with one specific thing, in one plain sentence to God, with no clause beginning with but.

For worship. If God’s faithfulness rose and fell with ours, the assurance of every Christian would track the quality of his last fortnight. It does not. The fixed point of your life is not your grip on him; it is his character, which was never in your keeping and therefore was never at risk. Kings have broken treaties, nations have broken covenants, friends have broken promises, and you have broken more vows to God than you can count. He has never broken one. In a universe of human unreliability, he is true, and he will be true when every liar has fallen silent.

parallels.desc: so that you may be justified in your words
all mankind are liars

verseByVerse.quote: But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.) By no means! For then how could God judge the world?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.) By no means! For then how could God judge the world?

But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? A twisted objection: if my sin makes God look good, why does he punish me? It is worth stating it in modern dress, because in Paul’s terms it can sound like an academic curiosity, and it is nothing of the kind. God gets glory from forgiving sinners. No sinners, no forgiveness; no forgiveness, no glory. Therefore my sin is, in a roundabout way, a service, and it is a bit hard for God to be furious about the raw material of his own reputation. Nobody says this out loud. A great many people run some version of it quietly, and it is the oldest trick in the human repertoire: to find a way in which the thing you were going to do anyway turns out to be useful.

I speak in a human way. Watch what Paul does with it, because his method is as instructive as his answer. First he flags his own sentence. He has just voiced an argument he considers close to blasphemy, and he does not want it left in the air with his name attached; he is almost embarrassed to have said it. Then he refuses it with the same explosive negative as two verses earlier. And then he does not construct a philosophical rebuttal. He asks a question.

By no means! For then how could God judge the world? That is not evasion; it is the argument. Every party to this conversation, Jew or Greek, agreed on one thing: God will judge the world. Abraham had said it long ago: shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Genesis 18:25). It is the fixed point. And the objection, followed to its end, abolishes it, because if evil that serves God’s glory cannot be punished, and all evil somehow serves God’s glory, then nothing whatever can be punished, and there is no judgment of anything by anybody. The objector has not found a loophole. He has sawn off the branch he is sitting on, and Paul simply points at the saw.

Good out of evil. The flaw underneath recurs in a hundred forms, so name it. God can and does bring good out of evil; he is not thereby implicated in the evil, and the evil is not thereby made good. Joseph told his brothers exactly this and softened neither half: as for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). Both clauses stand. The brothers’ intention was wicked and God’s was good, and the fact that the second used the first does not convert it into the second. The supreme instance is the cross, where the worst act in human history accomplished the salvation of the world, and Peter, preaching it, puts both truths in one sentence: delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed him (Acts 2:23). Nobody at Pentecost heard that as an acquittal.

Does God cause sin, then, if he uses it? No. Scripture holds two truths together without apology: God rules over all things, including the evil acts of men, and God is never the author of sin, and the men who do it are fully responsible (Westminster 3.1; 5.4). Joseph’s brothers chose freely and wickedly; God overruled their choice for good. We cannot fully explain how both are true, any more than we can explain how a Person can be both God and man, but we can see both in the same story and refuse to give up either. The practical point is simple: God’s sovereignty is a comfort when you are sinned against, and never an excuse when you are the one sinning.

The permission slip. This is not really a debating point. It is a mechanism people use, and the modern versions are easy to recognise once named. God can bring good out of this. He knows my heart. I will be more help to people afterwards for having been through it. My testimony will be all the more powerful. Every one of those sentences is true in its place, and every one can be deployed in advance, as a permission slip, which is the precise moment it stops being theology and becomes a lie.

In a sentence. If our unrighteousness highlights God’s righteousness, is God unjust to punish us? Paul speaks in human terms. Certainly not! Otherwise how could God judge the world?

On a Tuesday. The test turns on tense rather than content. Notice when you reach for the sovereignty of God. Afterwards, looking back on something you regret, saying that God has been better to you than you deserved and has brought something out of the wreckage: that is faith, and it is what Genesis 50:20 is for. Beforehand, while a decision is still open, saying that God can work anything out: that is not faith. It is the objection of verse 5, in your own voice, doing exactly the work Paul says it does. The same sentence is worship in the past tense and self-permission in the future one. Never excuse your sin by thinking God can use it. He will, but you are still responsible.

For worship. Paul does not defend God’s justice by explaining it. He assumes that a God who did not punish evil would be a worse God, not a kinder one, and that a Judge who could be argued out of a verdict by a clever man would be no protection to anybody. The Judge of all the earth will do right. He cannot be talked round when the argument is in your favour, and so he cannot be talked round when it is not; the widow, the orphan and the murdered have their hope in exactly that. And this same unbending Judge is the one who, in a few verses, will provide the propitiation himself. His justice is not the obstacle to the gospel. It is the gospel’s foundation.

parallels.desc: shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?

verseByVerse.quote: But if through my lie God's truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner? And why not do evil that good may come? — as some people slanderously charge us with saying. Their condemnation is just.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if through my lie God’s truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner? And why not do evil that good may come? — as some people slanderously charge us with saying. Their condemnation is just.

But if through my lie God’s truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner? The same objection, stated personally, and then pushed to its logical extreme.

And why not do evil that good may come? If God’s glory is served by human sin, why not maximise the glory by maximising the sin? This is where every attempt to conscript God’s purposes into an excuse for sin ends, if it is followed honestly. Paul will not pause to refute it at length here, and the reason is worth seeing below.

As some people slanderously charge us with saying. Do not hurry past the most remarkable detail in these two verses, which is not the objection but the aside. People were going round claiming that this was Paul’s actual teaching. He had preached free grace so unreservedly, righteousness apart from works, God justifying the ungodly, nothing to bring and nothing to pay, that respectable religious people concluded he must be telling converts that sin no longer mattered (see 6:1). His gospel was so radical that people thought it encouraged sin.

A test of preaching. That charge works as a test of preaching that has never failed. Nobody ever accused the Pharisees of encouraging immorality. Nobody has ever misheard a sermon about trying harder as permission to sin. The charge of licence is only ever levelled at a message of grace so free that it sounds dangerous. If your gospel has never once been misunderstood in this direction, it is worth asking whether you have actually preached the thing Paul was preaching. A gospel nobody could possibly abuse is usually a gospel with a condition quietly attached.

How Paul handles a slander. Notice how he treats a false accusation about his own ministry, because it is not what we would do. He gives it one clause. He does not devote a paragraph to clearing his name, does not list the ways he has been misrepresented, and does not appeal for fairness. He corrects the record in a few words and moves on to the argument, which was always more important than his reputation. Anyone who has ever been misquoted knows how much restraint that takes.

Their condemnation is just. The sentence stops the reader with its brevity. Paul has been asked a question and answers with a verdict rather than an argument, and some readers find that unsatisfying. But it is deliberate, and it is right. Some propositions are not to be debated but refused, because to argue them on their merits is already to concede that they might have some. A man who asks whether it might be good to do evil has not made an intellectual error you can correct with information. He has revealed what he wants, and dressed it in a syllogism.

Why the full answer waits. Paul will come back to this exact question in chapter 6, are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?, and the answer there is not a rule but a fact: you died to sin, so how can you still live in it? He defers it because the full answer needs a doctrine he has not yet laid out, namely union with Christ. He cannot explain why a Christian will not want to sin more until he has explained what a Christian is. So here he simply blocks the road, and three chapters later he shows you the country on the other side of it.

This is forgivable. The everyday form is not the bald proposition but something subtler. Almost nobody thinks, I shall sin in order that grace may abound. What people think, at eleven at night, is: this is forgivable. And it is. That is the whole trouble. The doctrine is being used, in the moment before the act, to reduce the cost of it. That is not the abuse of a bad doctrine but the abuse of the best one there is, and it is only possible because grace really is that free.

I have used grace as an excuse before. Is there hope for me? Yes, and the very fact that it troubles you is part of the hope. The men of verse 8 were not troubled; they had turned grace into an argument. If you see that you have treated forgiveness as a discount and you are grieved by it, then grace is doing exactly what it does: it trains us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12). Bring that very sin to Christ, the sin of presuming on him, and he will forgive it as freely as any other (1 John 1:9). Then let the cost of the forgiveness, not the fear of losing it, make the next temptation heavier. What Scripture warns against is not a Christian who has fallen this way, but a settled life that has made peace with it.

In a sentence. If my lie makes God’s truth shine more brightly for his glory, why am I still condemned as a sinner? Why not do evil that good may result, as some slanderously claim we say? Their condemnation is deserved.

On a Tuesday. When you consider doing something you know is wrong, does the thought of God’s forgiveness make it easier or harder? For a man who has understood the gospel the answer moves in a direction that surprises him: knowing what the forgiveness cost makes the sin more expensive, not less. He is not restrained by fear of punishment, because that was settled. He is restrained by something considerably stronger: the difficulty of casually doing the thing that killed his friend. If forgiveness is working in you as a discount, then whatever you are believing at that moment, it is not this gospel.

For worship. Grace was never a permission. It is a power, and the difference shows in what it produces. The grace of God that brings salvation does not merely pardon; it takes a man by the hand and teaches him to walk (Titus 2:11–12). The men of verse 8 had heard of the pardon and never met the Teacher, which is why Paul does not argue with them; you cannot reason someone into a household he has not entered. But the Saviour who was slandered as the friend of sinners has a household full of former sinners who no longer want what they once wanted, and he did that not by making grace smaller but by making it so free, and so costly, that it changed them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — No One Is Righteous: The Verdict of Scripture
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul has argued the guilt of the Gentile from creation and conscience. He has argued the guilt of the moralist and the Jew from their own failure to live by the law they possess. Now he seals the case with the testimony of Israel's own scriptures. The catena of Old Testament citations in vv. 10–18 — drawn from Psalms 14, 5, 140, 10, 36, and Isaiah 59 — forms a comprehensive indictment: no one is righteous, no one understands, no one seeks God; their throats are open graves, their mouths full of cursing and bitterness, their feet swift to shed blood, and there is no fear of God before their eyes.

The theological move is masterful. Paul is not importing foreign charges against Israel; he is using Israel's own sacred texts to establish Israel's own guilt. The Torah was given to the Jew; and the Torah says that no one is righteous. Therefore the Jew who trusts in the Torah as a source of righteousness has not read the Torah carefully enough. The law's purpose is not to provide righteousness but to reveal the absence of it: "through the law comes knowledge of sin" (v. 20).

"No one" — the universality is relentless. Not most people. Not unreformed people. Not people without religion. No one. The scope of the verdict prepares for the scope of the remedy: the gospel is for everyone because everyone needs it equally. There are no moral high achievers who need it slightly less. There are no spiritual derelicts for whom it is too late. The ground is completely level: all have sinned, all fall short (v. 23), all are justified freely by grace (v. 24).

And the section closes with a courtroom image worth naming, because it is the most vivid thing in it. The purpose of the whole indictment, Paul says, is “so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God” (v. 19). A stopped mouth is what happens at the end of a trial that has gone badly: the defendant who arrived with explanations has run out of them, and the silence in the dock is the verdict arriving before the judge speaks it. That silence is not the aim of the passage but its precondition — because a man still talking is a man still defending himself, and nobody has ever been justified by grace while he was still presenting a case.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity

Romans 3:9–20 is the locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of total depravity. The doctrine does not mean that every human being is as bad as possible, but that sin has corrupted every dimension of human nature — the mind ("no one understands"), the will ("no one seeks for God"), the affections, the speech, the conduct, the very orientation of the soul. No part of the human person is untouched by the fall. This means that the human contribution to salvation is precisely zero: we do not contribute our goodwill, our moral achievement, our religious sensitivity. Salvation is entirely of God from beginning to end. This is why Paul can say in v. 24 that justification is "freely" given — there is nothing in us to which it could be a response.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The catena of psalms and prophets Paul deploys was drawn from Israel's own worship book. These were texts sung in the temple, prayed in the synagogue, memorised by devout Jews. Their application to Israel's own guilt was deeply confrontational — like a church being indicted by its own hymns. Now: The contemporary church sometimes prefers a more optimistic anthropology — emphasising human potential and the image of God while minimising the ravages of the fall. Romans 3:9–20 is the permanent corrective. The doctrine of human depravity is not pessimism; it is realism. And realism about the disease is the precondition for gratitude for the cure.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin, as it is written: "None is righteous, no, not one;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin, as it is written: “None is righteous, no, not one;

Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. Privileges, yes; a better verdict, no. Does this contradict verse 2, which answered much in every way? No. The advantage was real: Israel had been entrusted with the oracles of God. But privilege is not a better standing before the Judge. In the courtroom, having the law only means being judged by it, and so Jew and Gentile stand together under sin.

For we have already charged. Notice the legal vocabulary, because Paul has been building a case and this is the moment he sums up. The word belongs to a prosecutor bringing a formal accusation. Chapters 1 and 2 were not a survey of human behaviour; they were the presentation of evidence, and the reader has been in a courtroom since 1:18 without necessarily realising it.

That all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin. The charge, when it comes, is not the one we expect. Paul does not say that all have committed sins. He says that all are under sin: under its power and its guilt, the same construction you would use for a soldier under orders or a slave under a master (7:14; Galatians 3:22). The plural sins are the symptom; the singular Sin is the disease. And these are two different diagnoses of the human condition. If the problem is sins, then the problem is a record, and what a man needs is a pardon. If the problem is Sin, then the problem is a power he is under, and he needs to be rescued. This letter will say that God did both, and it will spend chapter 3 on the first and chapters 6 to 8 on the second.

But I know decent people. Someone always says it. Of course. Paul is not saying that everyone is a criminal or that no unbeliever is kind; he has just conceded that Gentiles sometimes do by nature what the law requires (2:14). He is saying something less visible and more serious. A man may be honest, generous, faithful to his wife, admired by everyone who knows him, and still be living his entire life without reference to the God who made him, and that is what being under sin looks like in a respectable neighbourhood. The chains are not always the kind that chafe.

As it is written. Paul strings together quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah to prove it from Scripture (Psalm 14:1–3; 53:1–3; 5:9; 140:3; 10:7; Isaiah 59:7–8; Psalm 36:1), a chain of texts in the way the rabbis argued. And notice how he uses the first. Psalm 14 opens with the fool who says in his heart there is no God, and the original singers knew exactly who that was about: the nations, the enemies of Israel, the people outside. It was a comfortable psalm if you were inside. Paul turns it round on the very people who sang it, like a congregation being indicted by its own hymnbook: the words are familiar, everyone knows the tune, and this morning they are about you.

None is righteous, no, not one. Paul is not content with the general statement. He adds the clause that closes the last exit, because the human mind, presented with a universal negative, immediately begins hunting for the exception, and it always has a candidate in view, usually itself. Not one is there to prevent the search. Not one person is righteous before God.

What about babies, who have done nothing? Scripture teaches that we are sinners from birth, not only from our first wrong act: in sin did my mother conceive me (Psalm 51:5), and in Adam all were made sinners (5:12, 19). So no one, not even an infant, stands before God on the ground of innocence. That is exactly why the hope for little ones who die is grace, not their goodness. The app’s view, with the Reformed confessions, is that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (Westminster 10.3), and grieving parents may rest their child in the hands of the God who is rich in mercy and took little children in his arms (Mark 10:16).

In a sentence. Are we Jews any better? Not at all, for Paul has already charged that Jews and Gentiles alike are all under the power of sin, as Scripture says: no one is righteous, not even one.

On a Tuesday. As you read the chain that follows, throats, tongues, feet, eyes, watch what your mind does with it. Most of us begin quietly assigning the verses: this one fits my brother-in-law, that one describes the state of the country, and here is a good description of somebody at work. That reflex is the very thing chapter 2 exposed, and it is remarkably persistent. Read the next eight verses with one discipline: every time you find yourself thinking of another person, stop and ask where the sentence touches you. It takes about four minutes and it is one of the more uncomfortable things you can do with a Bible. Not one is righteous, including you. That is the bad news that makes the gospel good.

For worship. Christianity does not think poorly of people. The physician who tells you the growth is malignant is not a pessimist about your body; he is the only person in the room who is going to be any use to you. Paul is levelling the ground, and he is levelling it because he is about to build something on it that will not fit on an uneven site. Fourteen verses from now the same word comes back: all have sinned, and all who believe are justified freely by his grace. The verdict is total because the remedy is. There is one Righteous One, and he came for the unrighteous, so that not one of the not-one need be lost.
verseByVerse.note: Paul strings together quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah to show that all are under sin.

parallels.desc: not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins

verseByVerse.quote: no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one."
verseByVerse.commentary:
no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one.”

No one understands. Three negations follow, no understanding, no seeking, no good, and they are universal. Begin with the mind, because Paul does. This is not a comment on intelligence. It is the claim that something is wrong with the faculty itself where God is concerned, which is why the most brilliant people alive can examine the evidence and come away unmoved while a person of no education grasps the gospel and is transformed by it. Paul says elsewhere that the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them (1 Corinthians 2:14). Not unwilling merely. Not able.

No one seeks for God. Every generation objects: the world is full of seekers. There are pilgrimages, retreats, bookshops with whole walls of spirituality, people who describe themselves as on a journey. How can Paul say nobody is looking? Because of what is actually being sought. Human beings look tirelessly for what God gives: meaning, peace, forgiveness, a sense that their life amounts to something, the assurance that they are loved. Nobody has to be persuaded to want any of that. What nobody seeks, left to himself, is God on his own terms: a God with authority over him, who has the right to name his sin, who will not be edited, and whose company he cannot leave when it becomes inconvenient. We look for the benefits. We do not look for the Person, and religion is very often the most sophisticated method available for having the first without the second.

Behind a tree. That is exactly what happened the first time. In the garden, after the fall, God comes walking in the cool of the day, and the man is not looking for him; he is hiding among the trees (Genesis 3:8). The whole Bible follows that pattern. It is not the record of humanity’s search for God but of God’s search for humanity. He calls to Adam, he comes down to Moses, he pursues Jonah across a sea, he sends prophet after prophet to a people who kill them. And in the end our Lord defines his own mission in the same terms: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). If nobody is searching, then somebody has to come.

All have turned aside. Turned off the road. It is the shepherd’s picture Isaiah chose for the same condition: all we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned, every one, to his own way (Isaiah 53:6). Note the last phrase, because it saves the doctrine from a caricature. Nobody has to be taught to sin, and nobody follows a common script; each turns to his own way. Depravity does not produce uniformity. It produces a world of highly individual people going, with great originality, in the same general direction.

Together they have become worthless. The word (ēchreiōthēsan) means useless, gone sour, like milk that has turned. It was used in the Greek Old Testament for things spoiled beyond use. The creature made to bear God’s image and fill the earth with his glory has become, in the matter for which he was made, good for nothing.

No one does good, not even one. Not that no one does anything kind, but that no one does what is truly good before God: from a heart that loves him, in obedience to his word, for his glory.

Where Christians differ: how bad is human nature? Some believe people are basically good, or that fallen humans keep the ability to seek God on their own. Verdict: Scripture teaches total depravity: not that people are as bad as they could be, but that every part of human nature, mind, will and affections, is affected by sin, and no one can, by his own power, seek God or do spiritual good (8:7–8; Ephesians 2:1–3). This is why salvation must be entirely by grace.

Then are the good deeds of unbelievers worthless? Not in every sense. When an unbeliever nurses the sick, tells the truth or gives to the poor, the deed itself may be right and is a real blessing to others, and God, in his common kindness, restrains sin and preserves a great deal of good in the world. What such deeds cannot do is please God as acceptable worship or earn his favour, because they do not come from a heart made right with him by faith, nor aim at his glory (Hebrews 11:6; Westminster 16.7). So we can honestly admire a good neighbour and still say he needs Christ. Admiration and evangelism are not in tension.

Is there any point in an unbeliever reading the Bible or coming to church? Every point. That no one seeks God by nature does not mean God does not use means to seek them. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (10:17). The Spirit works through the word read, preached and explained, and many have begun to read out of curiosity, or come to church to please a friend, and found that God was the one doing the seeking. The invitation of the gospel is sincere and goes to everyone. Keep inviting, keep praying, and keep the Bible open in front of the people you love.

In a sentence. No one understands, no one seeks God; all have turned away and become worthless together; no one does good, not even one.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test that settles the question in your own case, and it is uncomfortably simple. Think of what you most want God to do for you at the moment. Now suppose he offered you that thing on condition that you would have nothing further to do with him: the healing, the restored relationship, the job, the peace of mind, delivered in full, and God himself off the table. Would you take it? Everyone knows his own answer within about two seconds. This is the difference between seeking God’s hand and seeking his face, and Psalm 73 has been the test case for three thousand years: whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you (Psalm 73:25).

For worship. If you are reading this and find that you do want God, that his existence is a comfort rather than a threat, that you would not take the gift without the Giver, then you have just produced evidence that something has happened to you which this verse says does not happen naturally. You did not seek him first. The wanting is itself the sign of a work already done, which is why our Lord could say that no one can come to him unless the Father who sent him draws him (John 6:44). The seeking you are conscious of is the far end of a search that began in eternity, in the heart of a God who came walking into the garden calling, and who came at last in his Son to find you behind your tree.

verseByVerse.quote: "Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive." "The venom of asps is under their lips." "Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive.” “The venom of asps is under their lips.” “Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness.”

Their throat is an open grave. Before the images, notice the proportions, because they are startling once you count. Paul is walking down a body: throat, tongue, lips, mouth, then feet (v. 15), then eyes (v. 18). Six items, and four of the six are the organs of speech. Out of the whole of human wickedness, with murder and violence available to him and duly mentioned, he gives more than half his anatomy to the mouth. Sin shows itself first in words.

Out of the abundance of the heart. That is not an accident of the texts he strung together; it is a judgment about where the trouble surfaces. Our Lord said the same and gave the reason: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matthew 12:34). Speech is where the inside becomes audible. You can conceal your character in almost every other department for years, because nobody sees your thoughts and conduct can be managed, but you cannot talk for long without giving yourself away. Which is why he added, in the same breath, that on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word (Matthew 12:36). Not the considered ones. The careless ones, because those are the ones that were not edited.

An open grave. The first image, from Psalm 5:9, is worse than it sounds in English. For a Jewish reader the phrase carried two things at once. There is the obvious one: a tomb standing open gives off the smell of what is inside, and the throat is simply the passage from a man’s interior to the outside world, so if what comes up out of him smells of death, the report is about what is down there. But there is also a ritual weight we miss entirely. Under the law, a man who so much as touched a grave was unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16). An open grave did not merely offend; it contaminated, and it contaminated people who had done nothing but come near. That is Paul’s claim about human speech. It does not stay with the speaker.

They use their tongues to deceive. The four organs are not four ways of saying one thing; they are a sequence. The throat is the source, what comes up from inside. The tongue is the method: they keep on deceiving, and the tense is habitual rather than occasional.

The venom of asps is under their lips. From Psalm 140:3, and the sharpest of the four. The venom of a snake is not on the fangs where you could see it but under them, and by the time you know it is there, it is in you. Stay with the image, because it names something we have no other word for: speech that is lethal precisely because it is smooth. Not the shouted insult, which at least announces itself and can be answered. The compliment with a hook in it. The concerned question that plants a doubt about somebody and leaves no fingerprints. The sentence beginning, I only say this because I care about you, which is very occasionally true. The observation made in front of others that is perfectly accurate and perfectly timed to humiliate. None of it would stand out on a recording. All of it is under the lip.

Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness. From Psalm 10:7, and the overflow: the point at which a man stops bothering to hide it. James wrote a whole paragraph on the subject and reached for the same pictures: the tongue is a fire, a restless evil, full of deadly poison, and no human being can tame it (James 3:6–8). He also makes the observation that puts this verse in a church rather than a gutter: with the same mouth we bless our Lord and Father and curse people who are made in the likeness of God (James 3:9). The mouth that has been singing in the service is the mouth that dismantles somebody in the car afterwards, and it does not even change gear.

The open grave with a distribution network. Our generation has industrialised this in a way Paul could not have imagined. Most people in history spoke to a few dozen others, and their words died in the air. We now speak constantly, in writing, to strangers, at speed, with no tone of voice to soften anything, and the words do not decay. A sentence composed in ninety seconds of irritation can reach thousands of people and still be sitting there in five years.

How do I actually change the way I speak? Start where Jesus starts, with the heart, because the mouth only reports what is there. Ask God to deal with the bitterness or contempt underneath, and pray David’s prayer before the day begins: set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips (Psalm 141:3). Then build small habits. Be quick to hear, slow to speak (James 1:19). Before you speak or post about someone, ask whether it is true, whether it is needed, and whether it builds them up (Ephesians 4:29). When you have wounded someone, go back and name it plainly rather than waiting for it to fade. And fill the mouth with better things: thanks, Scripture, encouragement, prayer.

In a sentence. Their throats are open graves, their tongues practise deceit, the poison of vipers is on their lips, and their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness.

On a Tuesday. Make the test precise to the image rather than general. Do not ask whether you swear. Think of one sentence you said this week that was entirely polite, that nobody in the room would have called unkind, and that you knew, as you were forming it, would land somewhere tender. Perhaps you told yourself it was honesty. That sentence is not on your lips. It is under them, and it is the one this verse is about. Watch your words today. They show what is in your heart.

For worship. Scripture gives the way out in a man who made exactly this diagnosis about himself. Isaiah, shown the throne, does not only cry that the nation has unclean lips. He says, I am a man of unclean lips, and a burning coal is taken from the altar and touched to his mouth, and his guilt is taken away (Isaiah 6:5–7). The fire came not from his effort at better speech but from an altar where something had died. And that mouth was then sent to speak. This is the reversal the letter is heading for: the organ that chapter 3 calls an open grave is, in chapter 10, the mouth that confesses Jesus as Lord and is saved (10:9–10). The Word made flesh, in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Peter 2:22), went down into a real open grave, so that graves like ours might be made into mouths of praise.

parallels.desc: their throat is an open grave
the venom of asps
his mouth is filled with cursing

verseByVerse.quote: "Their feet are swift to shed blood;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Their feet are swift to shed blood;

Their feet are swift to shed blood. From Isaiah 59:7, and from words to deeds. Two words carry the line, and the second is the disturbing one. Not that their feet shed blood: that would be an indictment of what people do. Swift. It is an indictment of how quickly they get there, and speed is a measure of desire. Nobody hurries toward something he is reluctant about. The verse is not describing a journey that occasionally ends in violence; it describes an eagerness, and it is the eagerness rather than the violence that tells you what is in the runner. Human history is a story of bloodshed, from Cain onwards.

Belonging. The same words echo Proverbs, and the proverb describes not a mob but a recruitment. It is the father in Proverbs 1 warning his son about the men who will invite him along: come with us, let us lie in wait for blood, we shall find all precious goods, throw in your lot among us. Then comes the father’s comment: their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed blood (Proverbs 1:11–16). The point of the passage is that the invitation is attractive. It offers company, adventure and a share of the proceeds. Evil rarely presents itself as evil; it presents itself as belonging.

Feet are how intention becomes history. Feel the change of gear in the chain. Everything up to here has been the inside of a man and the noise he makes. Now the body is in motion, and something has crossed a line that cannot be uncrossed. Thought is private, speech can sometimes be recovered, but a man who has gone somewhere and done something has produced a fact in the world.

The sixth commandment at its root. A modern reader will want to file this verse under people unlike himself, and Paul’s whole argument forbids it. Our Lord traced the sixth commandment back to its root: everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment, and whoever says you fool will be liable to the hell of fire (Matthew 5:21–22). John said it flatly: everyone who hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15). This is not a claim that a harsh word equals a killing in its consequences. It is a claim about the substance being measured: the desire to see someone diminished, silenced, humiliated, ended. That desire is available to respectable people at their own kitchen tables. Most of us never reach the deed because we lack the opportunity, the nerve or the anonymity, which is a mercy but is not innocence.

Clean bloodshed. Bloodshed has always had its tidy forms, in which nobody’s feet appear to move at all. David never touched Uriah; he sent a letter and let the Ammonites do it. Ahab did not stone Naboth; a court was convened and witnesses were found. Pilate washed his hands in public and gave the order anyway. The distance between the decision and the death is the oldest device in the world for keeping one’s feet unmarked, and it works on the conscience without deceiving the Judge for a moment.

Is all anger sinful, then? No. Scripture says be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26), and Jesus himself was angry at hardness of heart (Mark 3:5). Righteous anger is aimed at what is genuinely evil, is grieved on God’s behalf rather than merely offended on mine, and wants the wrong put right and the wrongdoer restored. The anger Jesus calls murder in seed form is different: it is about me, it nurses itself, and it wants the other person to be smaller. The test is what it wants. If your anger is pushing you to pray, to protect the vulnerable or to speak the truth in love, it may be right. If it is pushing you to rehearse speeches and enjoy imagining someone’s downfall, it has already crossed the line.

In a sentence. Their feet are quick to shed blood.

On a Tuesday. Make the test about speed rather than deeds. Notice what you move toward quickly. When somebody you resent is in difficulty, how fast does the news reach you, and how fast do you pass it on? When there is an argument at church, how quickly are you across the room and in it? When a story arrives that confirms what you already thought about someone, how long does it take you to believe it? Nobody has to be dragged toward those things. Our feet are perfectly capable of hurrying, and what they hurry toward is evidence in this trial. Pray for peace in a violent world, and be quick to forgive, not to harm.

For worship. Scripture uses the identical image in the opposite direction. Isaiah watched a runner come over the mountains and wrote that his feet were beautiful, because of what he was carrying: good news, peace, salvation; and Paul quotes it later in this letter of the people who bring the gospel (Isaiah 52:7; Romans 10:15). The same organ, the same haste. Feet that ran to shed blood are not, in the end, cut off. They are sent somewhere else, in a hurry, carrying something worth the speed. And it was made possible because the only feet that never ran to evil were nailed to a tree, and the only blood shed for the life of the world was his own.

parallels.desc: their feet run to evil

verseByVerse.quote: "in their paths are ruin and misery, and the way of peace they have not known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
in their paths are ruin and misery, and the way of peace they have not known.”

In their paths are ruin and misery. From Isaiah 59:7–8. Notice where the ruin is. It is not in front of them as a destination; it is in their paths: behind them, along the route, in the places they have already been. This is the only line in the chain that looks at the damage from the outside, and it changes the camera angle entirely. Every other verse examines the sinner, his throat, his tongue, his feet, his eyes. This one steps back and photographs the road he has walked down. Sin leaves destruction behind.

The wreckage we cannot see. That is the part of sin we are least equipped to see, because we experience our own lives from the inside, as a sequence of understandable decisions, each with its reasons. The wreckage is not in our field of vision. It is in other people: the child who grew up learning to read a father’s mood before coming into a room; the friend who stopped calling and was never asked why; the colleague made to look foolish in a meeting eleven years ago who still thinks about it; the marriage that did not end but went quiet. None of that appears on the sinner’s own account of his life. All of it is in the path.

Ruin and misery. The two words are worth separating. Ruin is breakage: something that was whole is now not. Misery is what the breakage costs the people living in it. So the verse gives both the fact and the feeling, a thing destroyed and somebody carrying it. Sin is never only an offence against God registered in heaven; it always has a second address, and there is usually a person at it.

And the way of peace they have not known. Peace here is not the absence of trouble but shalom: everything in its proper place, working, whole. Fallen humanity cannot find it, with God, with others, or within. And the wording is exact: not that they refuse the way of peace, but that they have not known it. There is real pathos in that. The whole human race is trying to arrive somewhere it cannot find, which is why every generation produces its own confident method, better education, better systems, better technology, better politics, and why each produces a fresh crop of ruin along the way. Isaiah, from whom this comes, watched his own nation do it and said they groped for the wall like the blind and stumbled at noon as in the twilight (Isaiah 59:10).

But many unbelievers seem to live peaceful lives? Many do, in the ordinary sense, and we should be thankful: God in his kindness restrains evil and gives order, friendship and quiet to people who do not know him. But the peace in view here is deeper. It is peace with God, which no one has apart from Christ (5:1), and the wholeness that flows from it. A life can be calm on the surface and still be at war with its Maker, and at death the surface calm comes to an end. Equally, a believer may live through great turmoil and still have the peace of God guarding his heart (Philippians 4:7). The question is not how quiet your life is but whether you have been reconciled.

Do I need to go back and put things right with people? Where you can, yes. Repentance in Scripture often involves other people and not only God. Zacchaeus did not merely confess; he worked out fourfold and started paying (Luke 19:8). Our Lord told a man to leave his gift at the altar and go and be reconciled to his brother first (Matthew 5:23–24), interrupting an act of worship for the sake of a repair. But not every path can be walked back down. Some people are dead, some are unreachable, and some would be harmed by your return; there the road back is closed, and God’s forgiveness is not thereby withheld. Where it is open, walk it, humbly and without demanding a particular response. It is usually the last thing we want to do, and often the most freeing.

In a sentence. Ruin and misery mark their ways, and they do not know the way of peace.

On a Tuesday. This test is harder than the usual sort because you cannot run it alone. Pick the three people closest to you and ask, honestly, what it costs to be in a relationship with you. Not what you provide; what it costs. Where do they walk carefully? What subject do they avoid? What have they stopped expecting? Most of us can answer for other people immediately and go blank about ourselves, which is the point. The braver version is to ask one of them. The answer will not be a catalogue of atrocities. It will be small, specific and about ten years old, and it will be in your path.

For worship. The way of peace was not known, so somebody had to come and be it. He himself is our peace, Paul writes to another church, of the one who made peace by the blood of his cross and came and preached peace to those who were far off and to those who were near (Ephesians 2:14–17). The road nobody could find turned out not to be a road at all. It is a Person, the Prince of Peace, and he came looking for the people leaving ruin in their paths, and this letter will shortly say that he died for them while they were still doing it (5:8). He walked the whole way of peace without a single step of ruin, and then walked into the ruin of the cross, so that people like us could walk out of ours.

parallels.desc: the way of peace they do not know

verseByVerse.quote: "There is no fear of God before their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“There is no fear of God before their eyes.”

There is no fear of God before their eyes. From Psalm 36:1, and the root of it all. Notice that the body is now complete: throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet, and finally eyes. Paul has built the chain backwards. He begins with what a man says, moves to where he goes, and arrives last at what he is looking at. Five charges of symptom, and then the cause. Everything above this line is a consequence of this line. Sin is, at bottom, a failure of worship before it is a failure of morality.

What the fear of God is. The phrase has been damaged by association. It does not mean terror, or a nervous religion of cringing before a temperamental deity. We use the idea ourselves in exactly the right sense and never notice. That boy has no fear of his father, we say, and nobody hearing it thinks we mean the father ought to be frightening. We mean that the father’s reality does not weigh with the boy. He is not restrained by it, does not consult it, and behaves in his father’s presence exactly as he would in his absence. That is the charge here. Not that these people are insufficiently scared, but that God’s existence makes no practical difference to them at all: no reverence, no sense of accountability to him.

Before their eyes. The phrase is precise: it describes what a man keeps in view while he is deciding. Everyone knows a speed limit exists, yet the appearance of a patrol car in the mirror alters behaviour instantly. Nothing about the belief has changed; only what is in the frame. That is how it works with God, which is why almost nobody sins while consciously aware of him. The Christian’s problem is rarely that he stops believing. It is that at the moment of choosing, God is simply not in the picture, and the picture is what governs conduct.

The beginning of wisdom. This verse belongs at the end of the list rather than anywhere else. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (Proverbs 1:7), and the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10); its absence is the beginning of folly and sin. So it explains the first charge in the chain as well as the last. Verse 11 said no one understands; verse 18 says why. It is not that these people are unintelligent, but that they have removed from view the one fact that makes sense of every other, and a man reasoning about his life with God left out of the frame will reason with great sophistication to conclusions that are reliably wrong.

Is a Christian supposed to fear God? Yes, though not with the fear of punishment. John says that perfect love casts out fear, and he is careful about which fear, adding that fear has to do with punishment (1 John 4:18). The dread of being condemned is gone, and this letter will say so in the plainest words at 8:1. What is not gone, and grows, is the other thing. A child of a good father is not afraid of him and would not dream of being flippant about him; the boy is entirely at ease on his knee and would go white if he heard someone speak of his father with contempt. Both at once, and neither weakening the other. That is the fear this verse says is missing, and it is a covenant gift: I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me (Jeremiah 32:40). The fear is given as the thing that keeps a man. It is not the opposite of assurance; it is part of the means by which God holds on to his people.

How do I grow in the fear of God? Not by working yourself into a state of reverence, which does not last past Tuesday. Look at God as he has shown himself. Read the passages where his holiness is on display, Isaiah 6, Exodus 19 and 20, Revelation 4 and 5, and let them be large. Above all, look at the cross, because Scripture says something surprising: with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared (Psalm 130:4). Nothing makes God weightier to a forgiven sinner than knowing what his forgiveness cost. Then practise remembering him in the ordinary hours: a sentence of prayer before a hard conversation, a pause before you open something you should not. And ask him for it; he has promised to give it.

In a sentence. There is no fear of God before their eyes.

On a Tuesday. The test is exact to the phrase. Ask what you would do differently in the next hour if Christ were standing in the room, visible. Not next year, and not a heroic change: the next hour. What would you not open, not say, not watch, not put off? Whatever appears on that list measures how much of your day is lived with God out of the frame, and the gap is not a matter of belief, because you already believe he is there. It is a matter of sight. Ask God to put his fear before your eyes. It is the start of wisdom.

For worship. Paul’s last quotation carries its own cure, if you follow it home. This line comes from Psalm 36, which opens with the wicked man who has no fear of God before his eyes, and then turns, a few verses later, to say: your steadfast love, O LORD, extends to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds; for with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light (Psalm 36:5, 9). The psalm that diagnoses the eye is the psalm that supplies the light. The chain ends in darkness, and Paul knew perfectly well where the rest of it goes: to the God whose glory shines in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), the one sight that, once seen, puts the fear of God before the eyes for ever.

parallels.desc: there is no fear of God before his eyes

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be held accountable to God. For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin. — Romans 3:19-20
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be held accountable to God. For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin.

Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law. Take the first clause on its own, because it closes the last door and most readers walk straight past it. Paul has just quoted a chain of passages, and every one comes from Israel’s own Scriptures. That invites an obvious escape. A Jewish reader could grant every word and conclude that the psalmist was describing the nations, the wicked, the enemies of God: bad people, elsewhere. Paul blocks it with a single procedural observation. Those texts were addressed to the people who possess them. Scripture speaks first to the congregation that owns it. You do not get to receive the Bible as a description of somebody else.

Hearing a sermon on behalf of others. The instinct is identical in a church. We are all competent at hearing a sermon for other people: this would help my son, my wife should be here for this, I do hope he is listening. The rule of verse 19 is that the word lands first on the people in the room, and there is no arrangement whereby you may pass it along without receiving it yourself.

So that every mouth may be stopped. The picture is a courtroom where the defendant, having heard the indictment, has nothing to say: no excuses, no protests, no plea of mitigating circumstances, no claim of comparative righteousness. Before God, no one can say but I was better than most, or consider what I did achieve. And notice the order Paul builds: the law speaks, mouths are stopped, and only then is the world held accountable. A man does not become guilty when he stops arguing; he was guilty already. What the silence does is end the defence, and until the defence ends, nothing can be given. A man who is still presenting his case is asking for a verdict on his record, and grace has nothing to say to a man who still believes he might win.

And the whole world may be held accountable to God. The whole world, Jew and Gentile, religious and irreligious, guilty before God’s court. Chapter 1 caught the pagan, chapter 2 the moralist and the man with the law; here the doors are shut and the room is full.

For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight. This is the sentence the letter has been walking toward since chapter 2, the conclusion of 1:18–3:20, echoing Psalm 143:2: enter not into judgment with your servant, for no one living is righteous before you. Read it as the answer to a question already asked. At 2:7 Paul stated the standard: patience in well-doing, and God will give eternal life. At 2:13 he stated the rule: not the hearers of the law but the doers will be justified. Both left one question open: who has done it? Here is the answer, delivered as a verdict: no one is declared righteous before God by keeping the law. Not one. The standard was real. The finding is that nobody meets it. Chapter 2 was the statute; chapter 3 is the judgment.

The road is impassable. Note the exact wording, because it does not say what people often hear. It does not say the law is bad, or that obedience does not matter, or that God has lowered the standard. It says that by this road no one arrives. The road is not condemned; it is reported to be impassable, and the report is made by the surveyor who laid it out.

Where Christians differ: what are works of the law? The New Perspective on Paul argues that works of the law means mainly the Jewish identity markers, circumcision, the food laws and the Sabbath, so that Paul is opposing ethnic pride rather than any attempt to earn salvation. Verdict: the identity markers are included, and in vv. 29–30 the question of Jew and Gentile comes to the surface. But Paul’s argument here is wider. The verse ends, through the law comes knowledge of sin, and the whole case since 1:18 has been about guilt for wrongdoing, not badges of belonging; no one keeps the law (vv. 10–18; 2:21–23). Works of the law are any obedience to God’s commands offered as a basis for acceptance, and Paul’s point is that no human obedience can justify, because all have sinned (v. 23; 4:4–5).

Since through the law comes knowledge of sin. The law’s purpose is not to save but to show sin (7:7). It is a mirror, not a washbasin; a mirror, not a ladder. The word is the stronger one, full recognition rather than vague awareness. Everyone knows in some general way that he is not what he should be. The law converts that fog into an itemised statement. This is what the Reformers called a use of the law: to show us our sin and drive us to Christ (see on v. 31). That is why an honest reading of the Ten Commandments is more use to an unconverted man than any amount of encouragement: you cannot want a Saviour while your problem remains a mood.

What about those who have never heard of Christ? This verse says the whole world is accountable, and Paul has already explained on what basis: those without the written law are judged by the light they had, creation and conscience, and they have not lived up to it (1:20; 2:12–15). No one will be condemned for failing to believe a gospel he never heard; he will be judged for real sin against real light. But no one is saved apart from Christ, and Paul is plain that people cannot call on one of whom they have never heard (10:14). The answer of this letter is not speculation but mission: the reason Paul was going to Spain. The question should send us to our knees and to our neighbours.

In a sentence. We know that what the law says applies to those under it, so that every mouth is silenced and the whole world is accountable to God, for no one will be declared righteous in his sight by works of the law; rather, through the law we become conscious of sin.

On a Tuesday. The test here is not another examination of conscience but a question about what you do with the results. When Scripture shows you something true about yourself, where do you go next? Some go to despair, which is the law doing half its work and stopping. Some go to resolve, which is the law doing none of it: the man has heard that he cannot climb and responds by training harder. The law has done its full work only when a man stops climbing and starts looking for a rescue. Stop defending yourself before God. Let your mouth be stopped, and then open it to call on Christ.

For worship. This is the darkest sentence in the letter, and it is not the end of the paragraph. Every mouth stopped, the whole world accountable, no human being justified, and the next words Paul writes are: but now. He has spent two and a half chapters demolishing every refuge, not because he enjoys demolition, but because what he is about to offer will only be received by people who have nowhere else to stand. The silence in that courtroom is not the end of the trial. It is the hush before the Judge rises and announces that he has provided a righteousness of his own.

parallels.desc: no one living is righteous before you

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — But Now: The Righteousness of God Through Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"But now" — nuni de. Two words in Greek that change everything. After three chapters of unrelenting diagnosis — the Gentile without excuse, the moralist self-condemned, the Jew convicted by his own scriptures, the entire world accountable to God — these two words open a door out of a sealed room. The righteousness of God has been manifested. Apart from the law. Through faith in Jesus Christ. For all who believe. Freely. By grace. Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

This is the centre of Romans. This is the centre of Paul's gospel. This is the theological core of the Reformation. Every word of vv. 21–26 has been weighed and debated and celebrated for two millennia — and still it burns with the same fire. God put Christ forward as a propitiation — a mercy seat, a place of atonement — by his blood, to be received by faith. In this act, God demonstrated his own righteousness: He passed over former sins (under the patient forbearance of the old covenant) and he condemned the sin that deserved condemnation — in his own Son, at Calvary. The God who justifies the ungodly (4:5) is not a God who winks at sin. He is a God who bore its full weight in the person of his Son.

Boasting is excluded (v. 27). The person who is justified by faith through Christ has nothing to boast of but Christ. The Jew cannot boast in the Torah; the Greek cannot boast in philosophy; the moralist cannot boast in her record; the religious cannot boast in his devotion. The ground is level. There is one God, and he justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. The gospel is the great leveller — and the great glorifier, because it redirects all glory from the creature to the Creator.

Two things at the edges of the section should not be lost. The first is the sentence on which the whole offer rests, and it is the shortest in the passage: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (v. 23). It is not an insult dropped into a paragraph about grace; it is the reason there is a paragraph about grace, and everything from 1:18 onward has been written to make that sentence land as a plain description rather than an accusation. The second is the question Paul asks last, which is the one his critics had been asking loudly: do we then overthrow the law by this faith (v. 31)? He has just said righteousness comes apart from the law, and the obvious inference is that the law has been discarded — the very charge of 3:8. His answer is the strongest denial in his vocabulary, and then four words that will take him the whole of chapter 4 to prove: we uphold the law. Justification by faith does not abolish the Old Testament. It is what the Old Testament was about.
verseByVerse.theology:
Propitiation: The Heart of the Atonement

Romans 3:25 introduces one of the most important words in the New Testament: hilastērion — propitiation. This word carries the specific meaning of an offering that averts divine wrath by satisfying it. Leon Morris demonstrated exhaustively that this is the correct reading against C.H. Dodd's attempted substitution of "expiation" (which only removes sin, without reference to wrath). Christ's death on the cross was not merely a moral demonstration or a removal of guilt; it was the bearing of the holy wrath of God against sin, so that God could be both just (the sin was punished) and the justifier (the sinner is acquitted). The Reformed tradition has always insisted on this: without propitiation, justification has no foundation. If the wrath was not truly satisfied, the forgiveness is not truly free.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The language of vv. 24–25 deliberately echoes the Day of Atonement ritual of Leviticus 16: the mercy seat (hilastērion) where blood was sprinkled to cover the sins of the people. Paul is saying: what the Day of Atonement pointed to, Christ has accomplished — once for all, for all who believe. The entire sacrificial system of the old covenant found its fulfilment and its terminus in the cross. Now: Every human religion has some mechanism for dealing with the problem of guilt — sacrifice, ritual, moral achievement, reincarnation, denial. Romans 3:21–31 announces that the only mechanism that actually works is the one God provided: the substitutionary death of his own Son, received by faith. There is no other name, no other blood, no other righteousness that avails.

verseByVerse.quote: But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it—the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction:
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it — the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction:

But now. Two of the greatest words in the Bible. Stand still at the hinge, because the whole letter turns on it. Everything from 1:18 has been a closing down. Creation leaves nobody an excuse; conscience convicts the man without the law; the law convicts the man who has it; the moralist is condemned by the standard he applies to others; the Scriptures themselves supply the verdict, until every mouth is stopped and there is nothing left to say. It is the most sustained demolition in the Bible. And into that silence: but now. God has acted (Ephesians 2:13).

Not therefore. Paul does not say therefore. There is nothing in chapters 1 to 3 from which grace follows. He does not present the gospel as the conclusion of an argument but as an interruption of one: an announcement from outside the courtroom, which is what gospel always meant, news, not advice.

The righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law. Not constructed or invented, but revealed, brought into the open, and the tense is a completed act with standing results. It is not on offer pending conditions. It has happened, in public, at a datable moment, and the announcement is catching up with it. This is the righteous standing that God gives (1:17), revealed in Christ, apart from law-keeping.

His character, or his gift? Paul holds both together. It is a righteousness that comes through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe, and so a status God gives: his verdict that a sinner is in the right with him (compare Philippians 3:9, the righteousness from God that depends on faith). Yet in vv. 25–26 the same cross shows God’s own righteousness, so that he is just and the justifier. Luther found the gospel when he saw that God’s righteousness in this letter is not only the standard that condemns us but the gift that clothes us.

Although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it. Apart from the law, and yet witnessed by it: those look like opposite claims and are not. The law is not the source of this righteousness; it never produced any, as the last verse established. But it has been pointing at it from the beginning (Genesis 15:6; Habakkuk 2:4), and chapter 4 will prove it. Every sacrifice, every high priest going in on the Day of Atonement, every prophet who spoke of a servant wounded for our transgressions, was a signpost. A signpost is apart from the destination in that you cannot live in it, and utterly connected to it in that it exists for nothing else. Paul is not founding a new religion; he is announcing that the old one has arrived at what it was for. The God of the gospel and the God of Israel are not two Gods with two schemes.

Through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. Received through faith in Christ: not earned, but received. And then the phrase that decides who this is for: for all who believe. Not for all who believe and. There is no second clause anywhere in the sentence: no period of probation, no minimum standard of improvement, no requirement that you first become the sort of person to whom such an offer could decently be made. Paul has spent three chapters establishing that no such person exists, precisely so that the offer could be phrased this way. Open to all, with one condition, faith, and faith is not a condition you meet but the empty hand that receives.

Where Christians differ: faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ? The Greek (pisteōs Iēsou Christou) can mean faith in Jesus Christ or the faithfulness of Jesus Christ, and some scholars prefer the second, emphasising Christ’s obedience unto death. Verdict: Christ’s faithful obedience is indeed the ground of our justification (5:19), but here the phrase most naturally means faith in Christ, since Paul immediately adds for all who believe. We are justified by faith in Christ, whose faithful obedience is credited to us. Both truths stand, and nobody who holds both has lost anything.

For there is no distinction. Jew and Gentile alike, the moralist and the pagan, the man with four Bibles and the man who has never opened one. The ground was levelled in vv. 9–20 so that one door could serve everyone.
