Justification. To be justified is to be declared righteous by God as judge: a legal verdict, not a process of being made righteous. God, the judge, declares the believing sinner righteous on the basis of Christ’s work. The word belongs to the courtroom: its opposite is to condemn (8:33–34), and no one thinks that to condemn a man means to make him wicked. Being made holy, which Scripture calls sanctification, really does begin at the same moment and always follows, but it is a different gift, and justification never rests on it.

Is that not a legal fiction, calling me righteous when I am not? No, because the verdict rests on something real. God does not pretend you have kept the law. He declares you righteous because you are joined to Christ by faith, and Christ really has kept it, and really has borne the penalty for your breaking it. His obedience is reckoned to your account as truly as your sin was reckoned to his (2 Corinthians 5:21). A fiction would be God saying the debt never existed. The gospel is God saying it has been paid, by the one who had the right to pay it. And the person God justifies he also begins to change, so the verdict is never left alone.

What exactly is faith? More than believing facts, though it includes them. Faith knows who Christ is and what he has done; it agrees that this is true and that it is true for me; and it trusts him, leaning the whole weight of your hope on him. The Westminster Confession calls it accepting, receiving and resting upon Christ alone for justification (Westminster 14.2). Think of a chair: knowing it is there, agreeing it would hold you, and then sitting down. Faith is the sitting down. It is not a feeling, and it is not the strength of your confidence; it is where you are resting.

In a sentence. But now God’s righteousness has been revealed apart from the law, as the Law and the Prophets testify: a righteousness from God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe, without distinction.

On a Tuesday. The test is not an examination of your life but of what you are resting on, and it is best run where it is hardest. Think of your worst week this year, the one with the failure in it that you have told nobody about. Now ask what changed about your standing with God during that week. If the honest answer is that it dropped and has since partly recovered, then you are still living under chapter 2, whatever you believe about chapter 3. A righteousness manifested apart from the law is not affected by your performance under the law, because it never rested on it at any point. But now: whatever your past, these words mean God has acted for you. Believe.

For worship. Two words stand at the hinge of this letter and of history. Everything before them is a courtroom filling up and every mouth in it closing. And then: but now. Not a mitigation. Not a discount, or a reduced charge, or a quiet decision to overlook the file. A righteousness from God, apart from law, held out to the very people the law had that moment finished condemning, and priced at the life of the only innocent man who ever lived. The verdict did not soften. It fell somewhere else. Blessed be the God who did not wait for us to climb up to him, but came down, in his Son, with a righteousness already finished in his hands.
verseByVerse.note: To be “justified” is to be declared righteous by God as judge.

verseByVerse.quote: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,

For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. Notice first that these are not two sentences but one. We are used to hearing verse 23 on its own; it is the verse people memorise, and it gets quoted as a standalone verdict on the human race. In Paul it has no full stop. All have sinned, and are justified by his grace as a gift. The diagnosis and the remedy arrive in a single breath. It may be the most important comma in the Bible.

All. The word is doing something the English can miss. Paul has spent three chapters building a list long enough to catch everybody, the idolater, the moralist, the gossip, the man with four Bibles, precisely so that when this sentence arrives it lands as a description rather than an insult. Nobody in the room gets to feel singled out, because nobody has been. This is the universal problem.

Fall short of the glory of God. It is not a moral score. The glory of God is what we were made to reflect, his image (Genesis 1:27), and what we were meant to share. Human beings were made to be the one creature in the world that shows what he is like, and the charge is that we do not. We miss the mark, like an archer whose arrow drops short of the target. That explains the peculiar ache that comes with being human: the sense, available to everyone, of falling short of yourself. You know you were meant for more than you are. Not more successful; more real. That intuition is not vanity and it is not neurosis. It is accurate reporting, and this verse is its explanation.

Have sinned, and fall short. Note the tenses, because Paul does not leave it in the past. Have sinned is a completed fact, a matter of record. Fall short is present and continuous: we keep falling short. The second verb is not describing the day you were converted. It is describing this morning. That is worth saying to any Christian who assumes this half of the sentence has stopped applying to him: you are still falling short as you read, and the next clause is written in the same present tense.

And are justified by his grace as a gift. The universal remedy. Justified: declared righteous. By his grace: undeserved favour. As a gift (dōrean): freely, for nothing, gratis, at no cost to the one who receives it. The same word turns up in a sentence our Lord applied to himself: they hated me without a cause (John 15:25). It is used for hatred that had no reason in its object and for grace that has no reason in its object. There was nothing in him to justify the hatred, and there is nothing in you to justify the gift. The verb is present, because this is what is always true of every believer: justified, once for all, and standing in it today as fully as on the first day.

Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. The word that stops the sentence being sentimental. Redemption (apolytrōsis) belongs to the marketplace: the price paid to buy a slave’s freedom or release a prisoner of war. Christ paid the price to free us from sin (Mark 10:45; 1 Peter 1:18–19). That tells you two things at once. It tells you what your position was: not a man with a poor record, but a man owned by somebody else. And it tells you that grace was free to you and to nobody else. A gift that cost the giver nothing is a formality; a gift that cost him everything, given to someone who could not contribute a penny, is what this verse means by grace. Free is not the same as cheap. Grace is free for us, though infinitely costly for God.

To whom was the ransom paid? Some early Christian writers said it was paid to the devil, who held humanity captive. Scripture never says so. The debt was owed to God’s justice, which is why Paul goes straight on to propitiation (v. 25). The ransom picture tells us what our release cost and what it achieved; it is not meant to be pressed further.

Does all have sinned and are justified mean that everyone is saved? No. The all who are justified are the all who believe (v. 22); the sentence runs straight on from for all who believe, for there is no distinction. Every human being has sinned. Every believer, without exception, is justified. The gift is offered to all without distinction of race or record, and received only by faith. Paul will say the same in chapter 5: those who receive the abundance of grace reign in life (5:17). The good news is not that everyone is already forgiven, but that anyone, however far gone, who comes to Christ is.

In a sentence. For all have sinned and fall short of God’s glory, and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Most of us pass this verse too quickly, so say it in the first person and see whether it survives: I have sinned, and I fall short of the glory of God. Most people can affirm the doctrine and flinch at the pronoun. Then try the second half the same way: and I am justified freely by his grace. Notice which of the two is harder to say without qualifying it. For most Christians it is the second, and the reason is instructive: we can accept a diagnosis that puts us with everybody else far more readily than a gift that puts us in debt to somebody. Say both today, and do not add anything to the second.

For worship. The great danger with this verse is that it becomes a slogan. Read alone, it makes Christianity a low view of people. Read as Paul wrote it, in one sentence with what follows, it says something no religion has ever said: the same all that condemns is the all to whom the gift is held out, and the only qualification for receiving it is the one every human being already possesses, need. The Lord of glory, whom we fell short of reflecting, came down to where we had fallen, and bought back his own image out of the slave market with his own blood. All have sinned. All who believe are justified freely. You are both. Rejoice.
verseByVerse.note: “Redemption” was the word for buying a slave’s freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: ...whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. — Romans 3:25-26
verseByVerse.commentary:
whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.

Whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood. Now the sentence the whole letter was built to say. God put Christ forward, and the initiative is entirely divine. It is not a reluctant God being persuaded by a loving Son; it is the loving God providing the means to satisfy his own justice. The love of God and the justice of God meet at the cross, not in opposition but in unity. God shows his love by giving his Son (5:8); God shows his justice by not passing over sin but bearing it in his Son. The cross is at once the greatest act of love and the most rigorous expression of justice in the history of the universe.

Propitiation. A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. The word (hilastērion) is used in the Greek Old Testament for the mercy seat, the lid of the ark of the covenant, where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15; Hebrews 9:5). Christ is the true mercy seat, where God’s wrath against sin is satisfied and his mercy given. This letter has prepared for the word: wrath is real, personal and being revealed (1:18; 2:5), and at the cross it was absorbed rather than deflected.

Carried outside and shown to the crowd. Note where Paul places the mercy seat. In Israel it stood in the innermost room, where once a year, in the dark, blood was sprinkled and God met his people over the covering of a box that held the law they had broken. Only the high priest went in, once, with blood that had to be brought again the following year. Paul says God put Christ forward: set him out in the open, in public, in daylight, on a hill outside a city wall, where anybody could see. The holiest thing in Israel had been hidden behind a curtain for a thousand years. At the cross it was carried outside and shown to the crowd.

Where Christians differ: propitiation or expiation? Some translate hilastērion as expiation, the removing of sin, and deny that God’s wrath needed to be satisfied; others prefer simply mercy seat. The mercy seat picture is real, since the same word is used in Hebrews 9:5. Verdict: the context is God’s wrath (1:18; 2:5) and his justice (vv. 25–26), and in 5:9 Paul says that since we are justified by Christ’s blood, we shall be saved by him from the wrath of God. Christ’s death removes sin, yes, but by bearing the wrath it deserved. This is penal substitution: Christ suffered the penalty of our sins in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13). It is the centre of the gospel.

To be received by faith. The means of receiving it. The atonement, accomplished once at Calvary outside any of us, is received by each of us through faith. Faith is the bridge between what Christ did and what the sinner receives: not a deserving act, but the God-given instrument of receiving. Faith does not earn the righteousness; it lays hold of it. It is the hand that takes the gift, not the labour that earns the wage.

Because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. Why did the cross have to happen at all? Paul’s answer is not, in the first place, that we needed rescuing, true as that is. It is that God had a problem with his own record. For centuries he had been forgiving people. Abraham lied twice about his wife and remained the friend of God. David committed adultery and murder and was told that the LORD had put away his sin (2 Samuel 12:13). The whole sacrificial system ran on the blood of animals, which, as Hebrews says flatly, can never take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). So an accusation was accumulating against heaven itself: on what grounds had all this been let through? The word here is not the ordinary word for forgiveness. It means to let go by, to leave unpunished for the present, and it puts God in the position of a judge who had been suspending sentences for two thousand years without explaining himself. Was God unjust? The cross shows he was not: he punished those sins in Christ.

This was to show God’s righteousness. That is why Paul calls the cross a demonstration: a public exhibit, evidence produced in court. God was not merely saving sinners at Calvary. He was clearing his own name. The saints of the Old Testament were forgiven on credit, and at the cross the account was settled.

So that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. The heart of the gospel, and the summit of the letter. Hold the two halves apart and feel the difficulty, because we have heard it too often to be startled by it. A judge who acquits the guilty is not merciful; he is corrupt, and every legal system on earth knows it. Proverbs says so without qualification: he who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD (Proverbs 17:15). God’s own law forbade the very thing his gospel appears to do. The question of Romans is not how a loving God can forgive. It is how a just God can, and remain just. The answer: he punished sin in his Son. God is just: sin is punished. God is the justifier: the sinner who believes is declared righteous. Nothing was waived. The sentence was carried out in full, on somebody else, by arrangement, with the Judge providing the substitute out of his own household. That is why God can pronounce a guilty man righteous without a fiction: the penalty is not overlooked, it is paid, and the acquittal rests on an execution that has already taken place.

Is it not unjust to punish an innocent person instead of the guilty? It would be, if God took an unwilling third party and punished him for others. That is not what happened. The one who bore the penalty is God himself in the person of the Son, who came willingly: no one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). The Judge did not lay the cost on a stranger; he bore it in himself. And the substitute is not a stranger to us either: he took our nature and stands as the head of his people, so that what he did, he did as us and for us (5:12–19). The Father did not love us less than the Son did, nor the Son love justice less than the Father. Father, Son and Spirit together planned it, accomplished it and apply it.

In a sentence. God presented Christ as a sacrifice of atonement, a propitiation through his blood, received by faith, to demonstrate his righteousness, since in his patience he had left earlier sins unpunished, and to show his justice now, so that he would be both just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus.

On a Tuesday. This test goes to what your assurance is made of. Ask yourself why God accepts you, and listen for whether the answer leans on God’s kindness, his willingness to overlook, his understanding of your circumstances. If it does, your assurance rests on his character as you imagine it, and it will not hold at four in the morning, because a God who overlooks things could presumably also change his mind about overlooking them. The answer this passage gives is harder and infinitely steadier: he accepts you because the debt was paid, and it would be unjust of him to collect it twice. Justice, the thing you feared, has become the ground you stand on. At the cross, God’s justice and mercy kissed. Your sins were punished there, so you will never face that wrath.

For worship. The old preachers loved to say that steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other (Psalm 85:10). At the cross God did not choose between being loving and being just, and he did not balance them in some compromise where each got less than its due. He satisfied both, completely, at his own expense, and the only person in the transaction who lost anything was himself. Every religion ever devised has had to choose between a God who is holy and a God who forgives, and each has quietly given up something to keep the other. At the cross the choice was refused. The cost of refusing it was carried by the one who refused it. God set forth his own Son as the place where the wrath would land, so that he might be at the same moment the Judge who does not bend and the Father who runs to the guilty.
verseByVerse.note: A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. The same word is used in the Greek Old Testament for the “mercy seat,” the lid of the ark where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement.

parallels.desc: blood on the mercy seat

verseByVerse.quote: Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.

Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. Boasting is the assertion of merit before God, and the word Paul uses is stronger than excluded suggests in modern English. It is the word for shutting a door: barred out, locked outside, slammed out the door. Boasting is not discouraged, or moderated, or permitted in small quantities among mature believers. It has been put out of the building and the door has been closed behind it. If salvation is God’s gift, received by faith, no one can boast (Ephesians 2:8–9; 1 Corinthians 1:29–31). The proud Jew of 2:17, boasting in the law, and the proud moralist: all silenced.

By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith. Law here means principle. A system of works would allow boasting; the principle of faith excludes it. Notice what has done the excluding, because it is not what we would expect. Paul does not say boasting is excluded by humility, or by a rule against it, or by a proper sense of proportion. It is excluded by the structure of how salvation works. That matters in practice, because a man told to stop boasting will simply learn to boast more quietly, and self-congratulation driven underground becomes harder to detect and no less pleasant to indulge. What Paul describes is not a prohibition but a demolition: there is nothing left to boast about. You cannot be proud of a gift you did not choose, earn, deserve or contribute to. The impulse is not forbidden. It is unemployed. Faith is empty hands, receiving.

Why has God arranged salvation this way? Why by faith and not by effort, when effort would at least keep people trying? Part of the answer is here. If any element of your standing rested on you, then somewhere in the last analysis you would have grounds for comparison, and comparison is the seedbed of everything Paul has denounced since chapter 2. God has closed off boasting not because he cannot bear rivals, but because boasting is a poison, and the only cure for it is a salvation in which no one has anything to show. And the deepest reason is his glory: he saves in such a way that the whole praise goes to the one who did the saving (1 Corinthians 1:31).

For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law. The sentence that changed the history of the West, and the thesis of the Reformation. Notice the verb: we hold, we reckon, we count it settled. Paul is not floating a proposal. He has been building a case for two and a half chapters and this is the finding, entered into the record. How it sits with judgment according to works has been answered already (see on 2:6–8).

Luther’s word. Luther translated the verse into German as by faith alone (allein), and was attacked for adding a word for the rest of his life. The word is not in the Greek. It is, however, exactly what the sentence means, because apart from works is what alone is for: if works are excluded, faith is the only thing left standing. Luther inserted a word that was already doing its work in the sentence, and every opponent who objected had to explain what else, besides faith, Paul had left in. Faith is not a work that earns; it is the hand that receives Christ.

Where Christians differ: faith alone? The Council of Trent (1547) condemned the teaching that we are justified by faith alone. Verdict: apart from works of the law leaves faith alone as the instrument. Not faith plus baptism, faith plus penance, or faith plus good works. Good works are the necessary fruit of justifying faith (Ephesians 2:10; James 2), but they are not part of its ground. This is sola fide, the article on which the church stands or falls.

But does James not say the opposite? James says that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (James 2:24). The apostles are answering different questions and using justify in different senses. Paul asks how a guilty sinner is put right with God, and answers: by faith, apart from works. James asks what kind of faith is real, and answers that faith without works is dead (James 2:17): a person is shown to be righteous by what he does. Paul opposes works as the ground of acceptance; James opposes a faith that is only words. Paul agrees that true faith works, faith working through love (Galatians 5:6), and James agrees that Abraham was counted righteous when he believed (James 2:23). We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

What about baptism? Is it not needed to be saved? Baptism matters greatly: Christ commanded it, and it is the sign of a believer’s union with him in his death and resurrection (6:3–4). This commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that it is for those who profess faith, and many paedobaptist brothers, with the Westminster Confession, baptise the children of believers too. But both agree on this verse: baptism is not the instrument of justification, and grace and salvation are not so tied to it that no one can be saved without it (Westminster 28.5). The thief on the cross was promised paradise unbaptised. Be baptised because Christ commands it, not in order to be justified.

What it does not mean. This is the point at which people become anxious about their faith instead of their works, which is the same disease at a new address. If you find yourself asking whether your faith is strong enough, sincere enough or free enough of doubt to count, you have begun to treat faith as a work: something you produce, of a certain quality, which God then rewards. It is not. Faith is not the payment; it is the receiving. A weak hand and a strong hand take hold of the same rope, and the rope does the holding. What saves is not the excellence of your grip but the strength of what you are gripping.

In a sentence. Where then is boasting? It is excluded, not by a principle of works but by the principle of faith, for we maintain that a person is justified by faith apart from the works of the law.

On a Tuesday. Notice what you find yourself mentioning when you want somebody to think well of you spiritually: how long you have been a Christian, what you have read, what you gave up, how much you serve, the hardship you have borne well. Nobody is exempt; the currency simply varies with the congregation. In some circles it is zeal, in others doctrinal precision, in others suffering, in others how relaxed one is about the things other Christians worry over. Whatever it is, it is a boast, and this verse says the door it is trying to come in by has been locked. When you catch yourself, turn the sentence round and say something true about Christ instead.

For worship. The locked door turns out to be a kindness rather than a deprivation. A religion of achievement requires you to keep score, and keeping score is exhausting in both directions: it makes you anxious when you are losing and insufferable when you are winning. Paul has removed the scoreboard. There is only one thing left for anybody to say, and he says it in another letter: far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Galatians 6:14). Not nothing to boast about: nothing of ours. You have nothing to boast of before God except Christ, and in him you have everything, so that the mouth stopped in verse 19 is opened at last, not to plead its record, but to praise its Redeemer.

verseByVerse.quote: Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also, since God is one—who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also, since God is one — who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.

Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? If salvation were by the law, only Jews could have it. The question is put as a question rather than an assertion, and that is deliberate. Nobody in the synagogue would have said aloud that God was the God of Jews only; the Scriptures they read every week said the opposite in a hundred places, from the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed to Isaiah’s house of prayer for all peoples (Isaiah 56:7). Paul is not correcting their doctrine. He is showing them that their practice had quietly contradicted a creed they could recite in their sleep, which is a considerably more uncomfortable thing to be shown.

Since God is one. The phrase echoes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one (Deuteronomy 6:4). Feel the audacity of what Paul does with it. Every Jewish household said those words morning and evening; it was the first thing a child learned and the last thing a dying man wanted to hear. And its obvious force, for centuries, had been separation: the nations have many gods, we have the one true God, and that is what makes us different. Paul takes the same words and turns them outward. If there is only one God, then he is not our God as opposed to theirs. He is theirs too, whether they know it or not, and a God who belongs to everybody cannot have arranged a way of salvation that only one group is able to use. If there is one God, he is God of all, and he saves all the same way.

Who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. Same God, same way, for all. And a small detail repays attention: two different prepositions, by faith and through faith. Commentators have debated whether Paul intends any distinction, and the likeliest answer is the most elegant one: he is refusing to let either group have the standard phrasing. Had he written the same words twice, one form might have seemed the normal one and the other the variant, the insiders and the people admitted on the insiders’ terms. By varying it, he gives neither party the definite article. Two doors, the same width, and neither of them is the tradesman’s entrance.

The fight that nearly tore the church apart. This sounds settled to us and was not settled at all. Whether Gentiles had to become Jews first, circumcision, food laws, calendar, before they could be Christians filled a council at Jerusalem (Acts 15), produced the letter to the Galatians, and put Paul in open conflict with Peter at a common table in Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14). Nobody was denying that Gentiles could be saved. The question was on what terms, and Paul saw, with a clarity that cost him dearly, that a gospel with a cultural entrance fee is not the gospel at all.

The modern form. It is rarely doctrinal, which is what makes it hard to see. No congregation holds that outsiders must first become like us. It simply turns out, over time, that the people who thrive there are the ones who already share the accent, the education, the politics, the family shape, the taste in music, the ease with a particular vocabulary. Nobody voted for this. It assembles itself, and the tell is not what a church believes about who may come. It is who is comfortable once they have.

Does one God for all mean every religion leads to him? It means the opposite. Paul’s argument is that because God is one, there is one way to him for everyone, and that way is faith in Jesus Christ (v. 22). There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Jesus said no one comes to the Father except through him (John 14:6), and the apostles said there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12). Other religions are not different roads up the same mountain; they are human attempts, sometimes earnest, to reach a God who has come down to us by one road. That is not narrowness. It is the widest door in the world: open to every nation, every culture and every record, through the one Saviour.

In a sentence. Is God the God of Jews only, and not of Gentiles too? Yes, of Gentiles too, since there is only one God, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through the same faith.

On a Tuesday. This test can be run this Sunday. Look around the room and ask who is missing who lives within two miles. Then ask a harder question: think of the last person who came, stayed a few weeks and did not return, and ask whether anyone found out why. If a church requires no circumcision but does require a hundred smaller things that nobody has ever written down, it has reinvented the problem of Romans 3 without ever disputing the doctrine. There is one God and one way of salvation for every person on earth. Tell them, and make room for them.

For worship. The comfort in the argument is aimed at individuals as much as at groups. If God justified people on any basis a human being can possess, nationality, upbringing, temperament, intelligence, moral aptitude, religious sensitivity, that basis would be unevenly distributed, and some people would be nearer the door than others through no doing of their own. Faith is the one qualification that levels every field, because it is not an achievement; it is looking away from yourself to Christ. So the door Paul describes has no step. God is one, and therefore he has exactly one way in, and it is the same width for everybody who ever lived. One day a multitude no one can number, from every nation, tribe, people and language, will stand before the throne crying that salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb (Revelation 7:9–10), and the Shema will be sung in every tongue.
verseByVerse.note: “God is one” echoes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession.

parallels.desc: the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.

Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? The obvious objection: if salvation is by faith, is the law pointless? This is not a stray thought at the end of a paragraph. It is Paul answering, at last, the slander he reported at 3:8, that he taught people to do evil so that good might come, a charge he there refused even to argue with. Now that the doctrine has been fully stated, he turns and faces it. If righteousness comes apart from the law, has the law been thrown away?

By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law. The same violent negative he used at 3:4 and 3:6, and then he claims the exact opposite. The verb is stronger than uphold suggests: it is a word for making something stand, establishing it, setting it firmly on its feet. So the claim is not that the law survives the gospel, or that a place has been found for it. It is that the law was never standing properly until now.

How the law is lowered. That sounds extravagant until you ask what the alternative does to it. A man trying to be justified by the law must, if he is to have any peace, lower it. He cannot live with a standard that says you shall not covet and means it, so he quietly translates the commandments into things that can be achieved: no adultery becomes no affair, no murder becomes no violence, honour your father becomes a phone call at Christmas. He has kept the law in the sense that he has redefined it down to his own size. That is not upholding it. It is the most thorough disrespect the law ever suffers, and it is always done by its admirers.

How faith establishes it. The gospel does the reverse. It lets every commandment stand at full height: the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good, Paul will say (7:12). Faith takes the law’s verdict seriously: we are guilty, and we need a substitute. Christ fulfilled the law’s demands and bore its penalty (8:3–4). Nothing is discounted. The demand is met in full by somebody, the penalty is paid in full by somebody, and the sinner is justified without a single letter of the standard being adjusted in his favour. And those justified by faith are given the Spirit, who enables them to fulfil the law’s righteous requirement (8:4; 13:8–10). Only the man who has stopped needing the law to be manageable is free to see how magnificent it is.

The law itself testified. There is a second sense in which faith establishes the law, and Paul will spend the next chapter proving it. He has just said something that sounds like a break with the Old Testament, and the obvious objection is that he has invented a new religion. So he does not argue the point abstractly; he goes and gets Abraham. The man the whole nation traced itself to, reckoned righteous by believing God before he was circumcised and centuries before the law was given, is Paul’s proof that justification by faith is not a novelty smuggled in past Moses. It is the oldest thing in the book. Chapter 4 exists to make the four words at the end of chapter 3 stick.

The law in the Christian life. Reformed theology speaks of three uses of the law: to restrain sin in society, to show us our sin and drive us to Christ, and to guide believers in grateful obedience. The law cannot save, but it shows the shape of the love that salvation produces. Paul is not here mainly discussing the law as a rule of life for the believer, though he holds that too and will come to it in chapters 6, 8 and 13. He is answering a charge about the doctrine. But the answer has the same shape everywhere: grace does not lower the standard; it produces people who begin, unevenly and gradually, to love it.

So is a Christian still bound by the Ten Commandments? Yes, as a rule of life, though not as a way of earning life. The Reformed confessions distinguish the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments and in love for God and neighbour, which binds everyone always, from the ceremonial laws, fulfilled in Christ’s sacrifice, and the civil laws of Israel as a nation, which expired with that state (Westminster 19.3–5). Christ does not cancel the moral law for believers; he frees us from its curse and writes it on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). Christians differ, honourably, on how the fourth commandment applies now that Christ has risen on the first day of the week, and this commentary sets out those views where the Sabbath is discussed, taking the view that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (see on 14:5–6). But every Christian agrees that the law shows us how to love.

In a sentence. Do we then nullify the law by this faith? Not at all! Rather, we uphold the law.

On a Tuesday. This is a good test for anybody who has grasped justification by faith and wonders whether he has grasped it too comfortably. Read the Sermon on the Mount slowly this week and watch your own reaction. If your instinct is to soften it, he cannot mean that literally, this is hyperbole, allowances must be made, then something in you is still trying to pass, because only a candidate needs the exam to be easier. If you can let it stand at full height, agree with every word, and find that it does not frighten you, that is what this verse means by upholding the law. The man who is not being examined can afford to admire the standard.

For worship. Paul has spent three chapters showing that the law cannot save anybody, and he ends by insisting he has not said a word against it. Both are true, and they are the same truth. The law was never a ladder that broke under the weight; it was always a mirror, and a mirror is not discredited because it cannot wash a face. It is honoured at last by a man who stops arguing with it and goes to be washed. And it is honoured above all by the Son, who said he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17), who loved his Father with all his heart and his neighbour as himself every hour of his life, and who then bore the law’s curse for people who had kept none of it. The law shows you your need of Christ, and in Christ it shows you how to love him.

For there is no distinction:<sup>23</sup>for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,<sup>24</sup>and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,<sup>25</sup>whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith.
