It is excluded. By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith.<sup>28</sup>For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.<sup>29</sup>Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also,<sup>30</sup>since God is one—who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.<sup>31</sup>Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.

4.title: Abraham: The Father of All Who Believe
4.overview:
If justification is by faith and not by works of the law, Paul faces an immediate objection from Jewish readers: what about Abraham? Abraham is the father of the Jewish nation, the recipient of the covenant, the model of obedience. If he was justified by his works, then surely righteousness is earned, not given. Romans 4 is Paul's extended answer — and it is devastating in its exegetical precision and its theological reach.

The answer is simple and irrefutable: Abraham was justified by faith before he was circumcised (Genesis 15:6 precedes Genesis 17), and before the law was given (by four centuries). The very man whom Judaism claimed as the exemplar of covenant faithfulness is in fact the exemplar of justifying faith — and therefore the father not only of circumcised Jewish believers but of all Gentile believers as well. The gospel does not contradict the covenant with Abraham; it fulfils it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Abraham Justified by Faith, Not Works or Circumcision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's argument from Abraham is both simple and lethal to the works-righteousness position. He goes directly to Genesis 15:6: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." The verb "counted" (Greek: logizomai; Hebrew: chashab) is an accounting term — to reckon to someone's account. God reckoned Abraham righteous — not because Abraham had earned it but because Abraham believed. The righteousness was credited; it was not achieved.

Paul then deploys a second argument from David. Psalm 32:1–2 speaks of the blessedness of the man whose sins are not counted against him. David was not speaking of a man who earned God's favour; he was speaking of a man who received forgiveness he did not deserve. Blessed is the man whose iniquity is forgiven — not whose record is clean. The whole Old Testament agrees: righteousness before God is received, not achieved.

The third and clinching argument concerns the timing of Abraham's circumcision. The justification of Genesis 15:6 precedes the circumcision of Genesis 17 by perhaps fourteen to twenty-four years. Abraham was declared righteous while still uncircumcised — which means circumcision was a sign and seal of a righteousness already received by faith, not the means by which that righteousness was obtained. This means Abraham is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not: his pattern is faith, not ethnicity.

And at the centre of it stands a phrase so shocking that Paul can only have chosen it deliberately: God “justifies the ungodly” (v. 5). Not the sincere, not the searching, not the imperfect but well-intentioned. The ungodly — the very people the God of the Old Testament had sworn he would not acquit, since his own law had called the justifying of the wicked an abomination. Paul is not softening the difficulty; he is naming it in the strongest available terms, because the cross has already answered it (3:25–26). This is the sentence the whole chapter is arranged around, and every reader who has ever wondered whether he is too far gone should notice which category is being justified here.
verseByVerse.theology:
Imputation: The Reckoning of Righteousness

The word logizomai (count, reckon, credit, impute) appears eleven times in Romans 4. This is deliberate. The doctrine of imputation — that God credits Christ's righteousness to the believing sinner's account — is the hinge of the doctrine of justification. Luther's language of the "wonderful exchange" captures it: Christ takes our sin; we receive his righteousness. Not infused into us (as Rome taught), but credited to us — declared righteous in Christ, clothed in a righteousness that is not ours by achievement but ours by gift. Luther called this the "alien righteousness" (iustitia aliena) — foreign to us by nature, ours by grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's appeal to Abraham was the ultimate trump card in Jewish theological discussion. If Abraham himself was justified by faith and not by works, the works-righteousness position has lost its founding father. Paul turns the Jewish trump card against itself. Now: Every form of religious merit-earning — "I'm basically a good person," "I attend church," "I pray every day," "I've never done anything really terrible" — collapses before Romans 4. Abraham, the father of the faithful, stood before God with nothing but faith in the promise. So must we.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.

Meaning first. Romans 4 proves from the Old Testament that justification has always been by faith. Paul takes the greatest example in Jewish history, Abraham, and shows that he was counted righteous because he believed God, not because he worked, and before he was circumcised. So Abraham is the father of all who believe, Jew and Gentile. His faith trusted the God who gives life to the dead, and ours does the same: we believe in the God who raised Jesus, who was handed over for our sins and raised for our justification. The chapter is the Old Testament foundation of by faith alone, and it ends where the whole Bible ends, at an empty tomb.

Why the whole chapter exists. This is not a devotional excursion into the life of a patriarch. Paul has just made an enormous claim, that justification by faith upholds the law rather than abolishing it (3:31), and a claim like that has to be proved from the Scriptures or it is worthless. So he goes and gets the one witness no opponent could dismiss. Not a prophet, not a psalm, but the man the entire nation traced its existence to. If Abraham was justified by faith, the argument is over, because there is nobody further back to appeal to.

What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? This was a bolder move than it looks, because Abraham was not a neutral exhibit. Jewish teachers held him up as the great example of a righteous man, who kept the law before it was given and was tested and found faithful. If anyone was justified by works, surely Abraham was. One well-known book of the period, 1 Maccabees, quotes the very verse Paul is about to use and attaches it to the binding of Isaac: Abraham was found faithful when tested, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (1 Maccabees 2:52). On that reading, Genesis 15:6 is a verdict on Abraham’s proven obedience, which is very nearly the opposite of Paul’s point. He is not merely quoting a text. He is taking it back from an established interpretation, and his instrument will be the calendar: what Genesis 15 says, and when Genesis 15 happened.

For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about. Feel the force of the concession before Paul takes it away. He does not say Abraham had nothing to show. At the human level the man had an extraordinary record. He left a settled city, a family and an inheritance on the strength of a word from a God he had not previously known. He turned down the spoils of a war he had won so that no king could say he had made Abraham rich. He pleaded with God for a wicked city and would not stop at fifty, or forty, or ten. He welcomed strangers who turned out to be more than strangers. And at the end he was willing to give up the one thing he had waited a lifetime for. Any tribunal on earth would have decorated him. He is the only man in Scripture called the friend of God (James 2:23).

But not before God. Paul grants the whole of it and then adds four words that empty it. They are the hinge of the verse and easy to read as a throwaway. The record is real, and it belongs to a different courtroom. Before other men Abraham towers. Before God he is a man counted righteous on the basis of having believed a promise, which is exactly the position of everybody else who has ever been counted righteous. No one can boast before God (3:27). It is not that boasting has been forbidden by a rule; the ground of it has been removed, and here Paul shows it was never there even in the strongest case anybody could produce.

Does God then not care about my good works? He cares very much, and delights in them. Scripture says he is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love you have shown for his name (Hebrews 6:10), and that labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). He even promises to reward it. But he receives your works as a Father receives the gifts of his children, not as an employer pays a wage. They are the fruit of your acceptance, made possible by his grace, never the price of it. That is why you can offer them gladly and without anxiety: they are not being weighed to decide whether you belong.

In a sentence. What did Abraham, the forefather of the Jewish people, discover? If he was justified by works, he had something to boast about, but not before God.

On a Tuesday. Write down the three things you would most want said about you at your funeral: the real ones, the achievements or qualities you quietly hope will be mentioned. Then read them again and ask what weight any of them would carry in a courtroom where the charge is that you have not loved God with all your heart and your neighbour as yourself. The point is not to make the list look shabby. Most people’s lists are genuinely creditable. The point is that everything on it is testimony in a different case. Even the greatest believers had nothing to boast of before God. Neither do you, and that is freedom.

For worship. Notice what Paul does not do with Abraham. He does not diminish him to make room for grace, does not hunt through Genesis for his failures, and does not suggest that his obedience was less than it appears. He leaves the man exactly as tall as he is, and then observes, quietly, that height was never the measurement being taken. Before the Holy One, the friend of God stands where the thief on the cross stands: with empty hands and a promise. And the God who will not share his glory with the greatest of men has never once refused his mercy to the least of them.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish teachers held up Abraham as the great example of a righteous man.

verseByVerse.quote: For what does the Scripture say? "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.” Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.

For what does the Scripture say? Paul settles it by Scripture, not by tradition or argument. The question is not what the teachers have said about Abraham but what God has said.

Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. From Genesis 15:6, the key verse of the chapter, quoted also in Galatians 3:6 and James 2:23. Counted (logizomai) is a bookkeeping word: credited to his account. Paul leans on it eleven times in these twenty-five verses. That is not a stylistic habit; he is hammering one nail. The whole argument turns on a single question, how does righteousness get onto a person’s account?, and the answer is that it is put there. Righteousness was entered on Abraham’s account, though he did not earn it.

An old man under the stars. Go back to Genesis and see what the verse describes, because it is not a man in a devotional frame of mind. Abraham is old and childless, and God has just taken him outside at night and told him to number the stars if he can, and said: so shall your offspring be (Genesis 15:5). There is no child. There is no evidence. There is an old man standing in the dark, looking up, with nothing in his hands and nothing in his future but a sentence somebody said to him. And the next line is: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness. Faith in the Bible is not a mood or a temperament. It is taking God at his word when the word is the only thing you have.

Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due. A simple illustration, and exact. A ledger can be altered in only two ways. Either a sum is earned, in which case entering it is not generosity but bookkeeping: the employer who pays on Friday is not being kind, he is settling a debt, and a man thanked for his wages is being insulted. Or a sum is credited from outside, in which case the recipient contributed nothing but an account number. Wages are earned; a gift is free. You cannot have it both ways. If righteousness were earned, it would be wages. It is credited as a gift. And if you ever find yourself feeling that God owes you something, after a hard season of faithfulness or a sacrifice nobody noticed, you have quietly moved yourself into the first column, and the first column has no grace in it anywhere.

What was not counted. Not Abraham’s obedience, which was considerable. Not his character, which was better than most. What was counted was that he believed God, which is why faith can never be reclassified as a small work that earns the rest. There is nothing meritorious in accepting a gift; the hand that takes a parcel has not contributed to its contents. Faith justifies not because it is a fine quality but because of what it lays hold of.

Credited, not infused. Two things are being credited in this chapter, and they are easy to blur. God does not merely decline to count Abraham’s sins; that comes in vv. 6–8, and it is only half the transaction. Something positive is put on the account: righteousness, a standing the man did not have. This is what the Reformers meant by imputation, and the distinction matters. The righteousness is not infused into you like a medicine that gradually improves your condition; it is credited to you like a sum entered in a book. If it were infused, your standing would rise and fall with your progress, and you would never know where you stood on any given evening. Because it is credited, it is complete on the day it is entered. A Christian ten minutes old and a Christian of fifty years stand in exactly the same righteousness, and neither has more of it than the other.

But does James not say the opposite? James 2:21–24 says that Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac, and that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. Readers rightly ask how Paul and James fit together. Three things resolve it. First, they are speaking of different moments in Abraham’s life: Paul quotes Genesis 15, when Abraham first believed and was counted righteous; James points to Genesis 22, perhaps thirty years later, when Abraham’s faith was tested and proved real. Second, they are answering different errors: Paul opposes those who think they can earn acceptance with God by works; James opposes those who think a faith that produces no works can save. Third, they use justified in different senses: Paul means declared righteous before God; James means shown to be righteous, vindicated, proved genuine before others (James 2:18, show me your faith). James himself quotes Genesis 15:6 and says Abraham’s works fulfilled it (James 2:23): his obedience showed what his faith had always been. So the two agree. We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone; it always works (Galatians 5:6).

Was Abraham saved by believing in Christ, or only in a promise about children? By believing the promise, and the promise was Christ. God promised offspring, and Paul says the offspring in view was ultimately one person: and to your offspring, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Jesus himself said that Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day (John 8:56). Abraham did not know the name Jesus or the details of the cross, but he trusted the God who promised to bless the world through his seed, and that seed came. Old Testament believers were saved exactly as we are, by grace through faith in God’s promised Redeemer; they looked forward to him, and we look back.

In a sentence. Scripture says Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness, and wages are not credited to a worker as a gift but as what he is owed.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last time you did something genuinely costly for God: the giving that hurt, the forgiveness that was expensive, the years in an unglamorous ministry. Now notice what you expected afterwards. Was there any part of you that looked for a return: that things should go better now, that the prayer should be answered, that God should notice? That expectation is not wickedness, and it is nearly universal. But it is the arithmetic of wages, and it is worth catching, because it is the way grace quietly turns back into religion. Catch it, name it, and thank God instead for what you never earned.

For worship. Abraham had no child, no land he owned, and no evidence, and that night he had a righteousness credited to him that he had done nothing whatever to produce. Most of what he was later famous for came afterwards, and none of it was the ground of his standing. God did not enter the sum because the account looked promising. He entered it because he had decided to, and the account was empty. The same God has written the same entry against the name of every believer, and the righteousness he credits is the spotless righteousness of his own Son. Righteousness is credited to your account by faith. You did not earn it. Blessed be the God who gives.
verseByVerse.note: “Counted” is a bookkeeping word: credited to his account.

parallels.desc: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,

And to the one who does not work. Not that believers do no good works, but that they do not work in order to be justified. They stop trying to earn it. Paul is describing what a man brings to the transaction, and it means, unavoidably, that the qualification for being justified is having nothing to offer. That is why this is the hardest verse in the Bible for respectable people. If you have been decent all your life, attended faithfully, given generously and raised your children well, you must still come to God on precisely the same terms as the man who has wrecked everything he ever touched: as one of the ungodly, working nothing, holding nothing out. Most people would rather be forgiven a great deal than be told their record is not currency.

But believes in him who justifies the ungodly. One of the most astonishing phrases in Scripture, and we have been anaesthetised to it by familiarity. The texts behind it are God’s own instructions to his own judges. He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD (Proverbs 17:15). I will not acquit the wicked (Exodus 23:7). These are not obscure verses; they are the working standard of Israel’s justice. Paul takes the phrase straight out of them and makes it a description of God: he is the one who justifies the ungodly. It is as if a man defined the Almighty by the one thing his own law calls an abomination.

The ungodly. Paul is not being careless, and he does not soften the word. He does not say God justifies the weak, or the struggling, or the sincere but inconsistent. The word (asebēs) is the root of the ungodliness of 1:18, the thing against which the wrath of God is revealed. Paul reaches back to the first charge in the letter, puts the same people in the dock, and says they are the ones being acquitted. Not the good, not the improving, not the religious, but the ungodly. Good news for the worst sinner.

How God can do it. The reason he can say it without contradiction has already been given, and this verse depends on it entirely: God does it justly, because Christ bore their punishment (3:25–26). The guilt was not overlooked; it was transferred and dealt with. Justification is not God deciding that the ungodly are not so bad after all. It is God pronouncing a verdict that has already been paid for. So the gospel is not the announcement that God is lenient. A lenient God would be a corrupt judge, and there would be no comfort in him at all, because a judge who can be talked round can be talked round by your accuser as well. This is what Calvin and the Reformers loved to call the wonderful exchange: Christ takes our ungodliness, and we receive his righteousness.

His faith is counted as righteousness. Faith is not itself the righteousness, as if faith were a good work God accepts instead of obedience. Faith is the hand that receives Christ’s righteousness. It is counted for righteousness because it unites us to Christ, who is our righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30; Philippians 3:9).

Two readers. This verse is written for two opposite readers in the same breath. If you are the one who has been quietly afraid that you are too far gone, that there is a thing in your past which puts you outside the ordinary offer, that God might save people like you in general but not you in particular, read the category again. He justifies the ungodly. Not the improved ungodly, and not those who have sorted themselves out enough to be presentable. If God only justified good people, your fear would be entirely rational. He does not, and the whole verse exists to say so. And if you are the other reader, for whom none of this feels urgent because you have never done anything that would frighten a congregation, the word ungodly is yours too, and the letter spent three chapters establishing it. There is one door, and it is marked with a description you would not have chosen for yourself.

If I still feel ungodly after years as a Christian, was I ever justified? Feeling ungodly is not evidence against your justification; it is the condition God justifies. The verdict was never based on how godly you felt, and it does not move when your feelings do. What you are experiencing is the ongoing war of a justified sinner against remaining sin, which Paul himself describes with anguish (7:15–25). God declares you righteous in an instant, and then spends the rest of your life making you holy, slowly and truly. If you hate your sin and keep running to Christ with it, that is exactly what a justified person looks like from the inside. Keep looking at him, not at the feeling.

In a sentence. To the one who does not work but trusts God who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness.

On a Tuesday. Complete this sentence honestly: God accepts me even though I... Most Christians can finish it easily. Now complete this one: God accepts me even though there is nothing about me that recommends the arrangement. If the second produces a flicker of resistance, a wish to add some small qualification about your sincerity or your effort or your intentions, that flicker is precisely what verse 5 was written to remove, and it will keep coming back for the rest of your life. If you are waiting until you are in a fit state to come, you are waiting to be disqualified. God justifies the ungodly. If you feel ungodly, you qualify. Trust him.

For worship. There is a phrase here that no other faith on earth would dare to print. Not the God who rewards the righteous: every religion in history has managed that one. The God who justifies the ungodly. Set those words side by side and they ought not to be able to stand together: a holy God pronouncing right the people who are demonstrably wrong, and doing it without telling a lie. They stand because a cross is holding them up. The Holy One took the place of the ungodly, so that the ungodly might take the place of the Holy One’s beloved, and he calls it not a compromise but the display of his righteousness.

parallels.desc: I will not acquit the wicked

verseByVerse.quote: just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: "Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;

Just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works. A second witness, from the Psalms, and the shape of the argument is a legal habit: only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established (Deuteronomy 19:15). Paul has produced Abraham, the founder of the nation, from the age before the law. Now he produces David, the greatest of its kings, from the age under the law. Two men, a thousand years apart, on opposite sides of Sinai, and both righteous by reckoning rather than by record. Nobody can answer the case by saying that Abraham was a special case from before the rules were made.

Done nothing, and done something. There is a second reason David is the right witness. Abraham shows you that a man can be counted righteous without having earned it. David shows you that a man can be counted righteous after having forfeited it. Abraham answers the question, can God credit a man who has done nothing? David answers the harder one: can God credit a man who has done something?

Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven. From Psalm 32:1, traditionally read as written after David’s adultery and murder. Every instinct in a religious person says the blessed man is the man with a clean record. David says the blessed man is the one whose lawless deeds are forgiven, which means the blessed man is by definition a man with lawless deeds. His blessing does not lie in some area of his life where he did well. It lies precisely at the point of his worst failure, because that is where the forgiveness is. There is no beatitude in this psalm for anything David got right.

And whose sins are covered. The two verbs answer two different fears. Forgiven is a word for lifting and carrying away: the load taken off a man’s back and removed. Covered means hidden from God’s judgment, under the blood (Psalm 85:2). Think of the mercy seat: the lid over the ark, blood on the covering, the broken law underneath and God meeting his people above it. So one word deals with the weight and the other with the exposure. If your trouble is that you cannot carry it, the first word is for you. If your trouble is that you cannot bear to have it seen, the second is.

What it does not mean. Covered does not mean that God has agreed to look the other way, or that the file has been mislaid, or that enough time has passed. That kind of covering would be a fiction, and every honest person would know it. That is why the psalm begins where it does, and why David spends its opening verses describing what it was like before the covering: while he kept silent his bones wasted away, day and night God’s hand was heavy on him, his strength dried up as by the heat of summer (Psalm 32:3–4). The relief in this psalm is not the relief of a man who has decided to stop thinking about it. It is the relief of a man who said it out loud and discovered it had been dealt with.

Do I have to confess every single sin to be forgiven, even the ones I forget? Your justification does not hang on the completeness of your list. When you came to Christ, all your sins were forgiven and covered, including the ones you have forgotten and the ones you never noticed (Psalm 19:12). Confession is not a fresh payment each time; it is the honesty of a child with his Father, which keeps the relationship open and warm. God promises that if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9). So confess what you know, specifically and without excuses, and ask him to cleanse you from what you do not know. Then rest. The blood covers more than your memory does.

In a sentence. David also speaks of the blessedness of the one to whom God credits righteousness apart from works: blessed are those whose lawless acts are forgiven and whose sins are covered.

On a Tuesday. This test separates two things that look alike from the outside. Take the thing in your life you would least want read aloud, and ask which you actually have: is it unmentioned, or is it covered? Unmentioned means nobody knows and you are managing it, and the arrangement holds as long as nothing surfaces. Covered means it has been brought out, named to God without qualification, and dealt with at the cost of blood, and a covered sin is safe precisely because it has already been fully seen. The difference between the two is the difference between Psalm 32:3–4 and Psalm 32:1–2. If it is only unmentioned, say it to God today.

For worship. David, of all people, is the man Paul wanted. The blessing he pronounces is not the sigh of a man whose life went smoothly. It is the verdict of a man who had wrecked everything that mattered to him and found, on the other side of it, that the God against whom he had done it had covered his sin: not by pretending, but at a price that would not be revealed for another thousand years, when David’s greater Son hung on a cross outside David’s city. Blessed are you if your sins are forgiven. That is the greatest happiness there is, and it was bought for you by the one man who never needed it for himself.

parallels.desc: blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven

verseByVerse.quote: "blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin.”

Blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin. Psalm 32:2, and the other side of imputation. The construction Paul quotes (ou mē logisētai) is stronger than any English version can carry. It is the double negative Greek reserves for absolute denial: not merely will not, but will never, under any circumstances. It is the same emphatic form our Lord used when he said that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37), and that his sheep will never perish (John 10:28). So this is not a statement about God’s present mood, which might soften or harden with time. It is a door welded shut. There is no set of future circumstances in which the Lord reopens the ledger and enters the sin after all.

The great exchange. God credits righteousness to the believer (v. 6) and does not credit his sin to him. Both: the negative and the positive. Sin not counted against us, because it was counted against Christ (2 Corinthians 5:19–21). Righteousness counted to us, because Christ’s righteousness is ours. And the positive half is the one usually missing from how we feel about ourselves. Most Christians are clear that their sins are not counted. Far fewer live as though a positive righteousness has been counted to them. A man whose debts are cancelled has nothing; a man whose debts are cancelled and whose account is then filled from someone else’s fortune is rich. Justification is not being returned to zero. It is being given a standing you did not have even before you sinned.

What about the sins I have not committed yet? It is the question any honest Christian eventually asks, usually at night. A man converted at thirty has fifty years of failure in front of him, and it is natural to assume the past was dealt with at the cross and the future is on some kind of running account. But look at the tense of the promise. It does not say the Lord has not counted his sin. It says he will not count it: the verb faces forward. When Christ died, every sin you would ever commit was still future. The ones you committed last week were no more unknown to him then than the ones you committed as a child.

Then why do I still pray, forgive us our debts? Because you are now a child, not a defendant. Justification settles once for all that you will never be condemned. But a justified believer can still grieve his Father and fall under his fatherly displeasure, and needs to come back humbly, confess and ask for the joy of fellowship to be restored (Westminster 11.5). David prayed restore to me the joy of your salvation (Psalm 51:12), not restore my salvation. So you pray the Lord’s Prayer not to be readmitted to the family, but because you are in it, and children who love their Father do not let wrongs sit unspoken between them.

What it does not mean. Paul will spend the whole of chapter 6 on this, so it is enough to name it. A verdict this absolute is precisely the kind of thing a man can turn into permission: if the Lord will never count my sin, the arithmetic of sinning has changed in my favour. Paul does not answer the objection by weakening the promise. He answers it by pointing to what has happened to the person. A man who has been treated like this and concludes he may now do as he likes has not understood what was done to him. You do not respond to that kind of mercy by testing its limits, any more than a man pardoned at the scaffold spends the afternoon looking for another capital offence.

In a sentence. Blessed is the one whose sin the Lord will never count against him.

On a Tuesday. The test is not whether you believe you are forgiven, since most believers say yes. It is what happens next. When you have failed badly and confessed it, do you then keep your distance for a few days, praying less, reading less, not quite able to sing on Sunday, until you feel you have re-established something? That interval is the tell. It is the behaviour of a man who believes his sins are not counted but suspects his standing must be earned back, and the two halves of this verse are the cure. There is nothing to re-establish. The account was never yours in the first place. God will never count your sin against you, if you are in Christ. Live in that freedom, today, without the waiting period.

For worship. Notice where David is standing when he says it. This is the work of a man who had done two things his own law punished with death, who had been caught, who had been confronted by a prophet in his own throne room and had nothing to say. That man wrote blessed. Not relieved, not tolerated, not permitted to remain in office: blessed, the same word the Psalter uses of the righteous man in Psalm 1. The Lord will never count his sin, and before the psalm is over he is telling other sinners where to come. The sin David could never pay for was counted, in full, to his Son and Lord, and the Lord who counted it there will never count it anywhere else.

parallels.desc: blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity

verseByVerse.quote: Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised.

Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? The key question for Jew and Gentile. Paul has just quoted David’s beatitude, and beatitudes are the sort of thing people quietly assume belong to their own kind. The question is whether the forgiveness of Psalm 32 is house property, available to the insiders, on application, through the proper channels. And the answer is settled not by an appeal to God’s generosity but by a date.

How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? A brilliant argument from the order of events, and the calendar argument promised at the start of the chapter. Notice how quietly devastating it is. Paul does not dispute a single word of the text his opponents value. He does not argue that circumcision was unimportant, or that Genesis has been misread, or that the covenant was provisional. He simply asks when. The whole case turns on the order of two chapters, and once the question is put there is no answer available, because Genesis 15 comes before Genesis 17, and no amount of theology can move it.

It was not after, but before he was circumcised. Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15 and circumcised in Genesis 17, at least fourteen years later. Between them lie the birth of Ishmael and thirteen more years: the boy is thirteen when the command comes (Genesis 16:16; 17:24–25). So for a decade and a half the man the whole nation traced itself to was walking around justified before God and physically indistinguishable from any pagan in Canaan. Had he died in that period he would have died righteous, with nothing to show for it that anyone could inspect. He was justified as an uncircumcised man. So circumcision was not necessary for justification, and Gentiles can be justified without it.

Justified as a Gentile. That does something generous to the argument. Paul is not saying Abraham was a Jew who happened to be justified. He is saying Abraham was justified while he was, in every visible respect, a Gentile: a man from Mesopotamia, from a family that served other gods (Joshua 24:2), with no law, no temple, no priesthood, no sign and no religious community whatever. The founder of the covenant people entered his righteousness from outside the covenant people, because at that moment there was no covenant people to be inside.

The arrangement. All of this has an edge for a reader who has never once thought about circumcision. The instinct Paul is dismantling is not Jewish; it is human, and it survives every change of religion. It is the assumption that the blessing arrives through the arrangement: that the promises of Scripture are addressed, in practice, to people who are properly inside things, baptised, confirmed, on the roll, in the right church, taught by the right people. The assumption is rarely stated, which is why it is rarely examined. It shows up in the quiet confidence of those who have the arrangement, and in the hesitancy of those who do not.

What it does not mean. The sign is not thereby made worthless, and Paul says so in the next verse. God commanded it, Abraham obeyed, and Genesis 17 is not an afterthought. The argument is about sequence, not value. What Paul has established is that the sign could not have produced what its owner already had, and that a man who has the sign and nothing else has the receipt without the purchase.

Does it matter which church I belong to, then? Yes, but not for this. Belonging to a faithful church matters a great deal: for sound teaching, for the Lord’s Supper and baptism rightly given, for care, discipline and love (Hebrews 10:24–25). Christ loves his church and you should too. But no church membership, however orthodox, justifies anyone, and no believer is shut out of God’s promises because he came to faith in an unremarkable congregation, or late, or alone. The church is the family the justified belong to, not the door by which they become justified. That door is Christ, received by faith.

In a sentence. Is this blessing only for the circumcised, or for the uncircumcised too? Faith was credited to Abraham as righteousness, and when? Before he was circumcised, not after.

On a Tuesday. Think of a promise of God you find hard to apply to yourself: that he is near to the brokenhearted, that nothing can separate you from his love, that he will not cast you out. Ask what you think stands between you and it. If the honest answer is anything that could be called a credential, that you came to faith too late, that you were never properly discipled, that your background is wrong, that you are not the sort of person these things are written for, then this passage is about you, and its answer is a date. Abraham had none of it either. He had a promise and he believed it, and the paperwork came fourteen years later.

For worship. God accepted Abraham before any ritual, while he was still in every outward way a stranger to the covenant. He accepts you the same way: by faith. The God of Abraham has never been the God of the insiders only. He went looking for a pagan in Ur, made him his friend under the open sky, and then built a nation around him so that, in the fullness of time, the door of that nation could be thrown open to the whole world through Abraham’s Son.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15 and circumcised in Genesis 17, some years later.

verseByVerse.quote: He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well, and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well, and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.

He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith. A sign points to something; a seal confirms it. Seal is a legal term, not a decorative one. In the ancient world a seal was pressed into wax on a document to certify it. It did not create the agreement; it authenticated one already made, and it identified whose the thing was. Nobody ever became the owner of a field by acquiring a seal; the seal declared publicly what a transaction had already accomplished. That is exactly the relation Paul sets between the sign and the righteousness, and it settles the order for good. Circumcision did not make Abraham righteous; it confirmed the righteousness he already had by faith. A seal on an empty page certifies nothing.

And our sign? Christians do not circumcise, so the obvious question is what our equivalent is, and whether this passage devalues it. It does not. Baptism stands in a similar relation to faith: commanded by God, genuinely meaningful, and never the thing itself. Paul’s argument cuts equally against a man who trusts his circumcision and a man who trusts his baptism, and it guards against the opposite error too. The sign is not nothing; it is a seal, and a seal is issued by an authority. What it cannot do is manufacture what it certifies.

Where Christians differ: circumcision, baptism and infants. Paedobaptists argue that baptism replaces circumcision as the sign and seal of the covenant (Colossians 2:11–12), and since circumcision was given to infants, baptism should be too; they also point to the households baptised in Acts (16:15, 33). Those are serious arguments, held by many godly Christians. Verdict: Paul says circumcision sealed the righteousness Abraham had by faith; it followed faith in Abraham’s case. Circumcision was given to all Abraham’s physical descendants, Ishmael as well as Isaac, believing or not. In the new covenant, all its members know the Lord (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11), and the sign is given to those who believe (Acts 2:41; 8:12), as Colossians itself says: buried with him in baptism, raised with him through faith (Colossians 2:12). Credobaptists hold that baptism belongs to believers, while honouring paedobaptist brothers and sisters as fellow heirs of Abraham.

I was baptised as a baby, so should I be baptised now? If you hold, as this commentary does with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism is for those who profess faith, then being baptised now is not a second baptism but obedience to Christ’s command for the first time as a believer. Many Christians come to that conviction and take the step gladly. Others, persuaded of the paedobaptist view, believe their infant baptism was valid and that what they need is to own it by faith, which they do. Whatever you conclude, do it from Scripture and a clear conscience, after talking with your pastor, and never treat brothers and sisters who differ as anything less than fellow children of Abraham. The faith the sign points to matters more than either view of the sign.

The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised. Abraham is the father of Gentile believers: spiritual descent, by faith, not by blood (Galatians 3:7, 29). Paul has been proving a point about chronology, and now he shows what the chronology was for. Because Abraham was justified before he was circumcised, he is not merely an example Gentiles may study from a distance; he is their father. The relationship is not a comparison. A believing Gentile is not like one of Abraham’s children. He is one.

A lineage. That is a considerable thing to say to people with no ancestral claim on the promises at all. If you came to Christ out of a family with no faith in it, or a hostile one, or simply an indifferent one, if you are the first Christian anybody in your line can remember, this verse hands you a lineage. You are not a recent addition tolerated at the edge of somebody else’s story. Your family history runs back four thousand years to a man standing under the stars in Canaan, and Paul argues it not as sentiment but as fact, from the order of two chapters in Genesis.

And to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith. And of believing Jews: not merely circumcised, but following his faith. The qualifier does real work: possessing the sign does not by itself put a man in the family. And the picture is walking in footsteps, which is what a child does behind his father in a field, placing his feet where the bigger prints already are. Sonship is shown by direction of travel, not by paperwork. Abraham’s true children are those who believe.

My faith feels far too small to walk in his footsteps. Paul is describing a pattern, not a standard of performance. He will shortly admit that Abraham considered his own body as good as dead, and Genesis records his lapses with complete honesty. The footsteps are not evidence of a great faith; they are evidence of a faith pointed at the same object. A child does not have to fill his father’s footprint. He only has to be going the same way.

In a sentence. Abraham received circumcision as a sign, a seal of the righteousness he had by faith while uncircumcised, so that he would be the father of all who believe without being circumcised, and also of the circumcised who walk in the footsteps of his faith before circumcision.

On a Tuesday. Ask which of Abraham’s footprints your own life is placing feet into. He left security on the strength of a promise. He waited twenty-five years for something God had said, without any evidence arriving in the meantime. He believed a thing that was, on the face of it, physically impossible. Take one of those and ask where in your life there is anything like it: any point at which you are actually depending on something God has said, in a way that would look foolish if he turned out not to exist. If nothing comes to mind, that is worth knowing. It is possible to hold every one of Abraham’s doctrines and stand in none of his footprints. Walk in his footsteps of faith. You are his child if you believe.

For worship. So the section ends with one man, two families, and a single door between them. The Gentile who believes and the Jew who believes turn out to be brothers, and what makes them brothers is not the sign that once divided them but the faith that came before it. God promised Abraham a family like the stars, and he has been keeping that promise ever since, one name at a time, in every language under heaven, and yours is among them.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and confirmed that something was genuine.

parallels.desc: the sign of the covenant

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Promise Through Faith: Abraham's Hope Against Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul argues that God’s promise that Abraham and his descendants would inherit the world never depended on keeping the law but on the righteousness that comes by faith. If it rested on law, faith would be pointless and the promise void, since the law exposes transgression and brings wrath. So the promise rests on grace through faith, and it is guaranteed to all Abraham’s offspring, Jews and Gentiles who share his faith, for he is the father of many nations. Abraham trusted the God who gives life to the dead and creates out of nothing. Though he was about a hundred and Sarah was barren, he kept hoping when there was no human ground for hope, grew strong in faith, gave God glory and was fully convinced God would do what he had promised. That is why it was counted to him as righteousness, and Scripture records it for our sake too: righteousness will be counted to us who trust the God who raised Jesus, who was handed over for our sins and raised for our justification.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith and the Resurrection

Romans 4:24–25 ties justification directly to the resurrection of Jesus. Christ was raised "for our justification" — His resurrection is not merely the proof of his deity but the declaration that his atoning work was accepted by the Father. The resurrection is the Father's public vindication of the Son's sacrifice. This means that Christian faith is not merely belief in the ethical teachings of Jesus or even in his death; it is faith in the God who raised him from the dead. Easter is not the happy ending of a sad story; it is the announcement that the story of sin and death and wrath has been definitively answered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The promise to Abraham that he would be "heir of the world" (v. 13) goes beyond what Genesis explicitly states but draws on the expansive reading of the Abrahamic covenant in Jewish tradition. Paul is claiming that the full scope of that promise — a redeemed humanity, a renewed creation — is fulfilled in Christ and received by faith. The Jewish hope for the world is the Christian gospel. Now: Abraham's "hope against hope" (v. 18) is the model for Christian faith in every situation where the circumstances shout impossibility. The God who gave life to Abraham's dead body and Sarah's dead womb is the same God who raises the dead today — physically at the last day, spiritually in every conversion. No situation is beyond him.

verseByVerse.quote: For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void.

For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world. God promised Abraham the land of Canaan (Genesis 12:7; 15:18). Paul sees that the promise was bigger: the whole world. All nations blessed in him (Genesis 12:3), and his offspring, Christ, inheriting the earth (Psalm 2:8; Matthew 5:5). The land was a down payment on the new creation. Be straightforward about the phrase itself, because a careful reader who goes back to Genesis will not find it there. God promised a land, an innumerable offspring, and that in Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed. Paul is compressing, and he does it the way his contemporaries already did, reading the promise in its full scope. The seed of it is in the text: a blessing for all the families of the earth is not a local arrangement, and a promise of that size was never going to be exhausted by a strip of land on the eastern Mediterranean.

Did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. The law came 430 years later (Galatians 3:17). The promise was made, ratified and believed long before Sinai, so it cannot have depended on the law.

For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void. If inheritance depended on law-keeping, no one would inherit, since no one keeps it, and the promise would be empty. Law and promise work on different principles. And the two verbs are stronger than they look. Null means emptied, hollowed out, drained of content; void means made inoperative, put permanently out of use. Paul does not say faith would be reduced or the promise weakened. Both would be cancelled outright. If the estate goes to those who perform, then performance is the mechanism, and trust has nothing left to do. Faith would survive as a feeling that accompanies the transaction without contributing to it, decorative rather than load-bearing. Two mechanisms cannot operate on the same inheritance. One will be doing the work and the other will be sentiment.

A promise, not a contract. That is why the difference is not a nicety. A contract binds two parties, and either can void it; each has obligations, each watches the other, and the whole arrangement is only as secure as the weaker signatory. A promise binds one party and names another as the recipient. The recipient’s conduct is not what keeps it in force, because he never undertook anything in the first place.

The God who walked alone. Abraham had been shown that in the most extraordinary way, in the very chapter Paul keeps quoting. When he asked how he could know he would inherit, God told him to bring animals, cut them in half, and lay the pieces opposite each other (Genesis 15:9–10). That was a covenant ceremony, and its meaning was understood across the ancient world: the parties walked between the severed halves, calling the same fate down on themselves if they broke the agreement (compare Jeremiah 34:18). So Abraham prepared the pieces and waited. Then a deep sleep fell on him, and a dreadful darkness, and when the sun had gone down a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch, the presence of God, passed between the pieces alone (Genesis 15:12, 17). Abraham never walked. He was asleep for the ratification. God swore by himself, took the entire liability, and left the other party lying on the ground.

Heir. The word Paul chooses belongs to the same world. Nobody earns an inheritance; the only thing required of an heir is that he be named. And Scripture does not leave unstated one more feature of an inheritance: it takes effect by a death (Hebrews 9:16–17). The promise made over the divided animals in Genesis 15 was finally executed when the one who had walked between them alone kept its terms in his own body.

Does the land promise still belong to the Jewish people? Christians answer this differently, and the question deserves care. Dispensational Christians hold that it does: God promised Canaan to Abraham’s descendants as an everlasting possession (Genesis 17:8), and a promise of God cannot be cancelled. Many others, including this commentary, read it as not cancelled but enlarged. Paul says Abraham would be heir of the world; Hebrews says he was looking forward to the city that has foundations (Hebrews 11:10); Jesus says the meek shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). On this reading Canaan was the down payment, and the renewed creation is the inheritance, belonging to all who are Christ’s, Jew and Gentile: if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29). What God will yet do for ethnic Israel Paul takes up in chapter 11.

In a sentence. The promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would inherit the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith, for if those who rely on the law are heirs, faith means nothing and the promise is worthless.

On a Tuesday. This test is about the size of your expectations rather than the state of your soul. Try to describe what you are actually going to inherit. Most Christians, pressed, produce something vague and largely elsewhere: a good place, after death, somewhere else. Paul says heir of the world, and he means it: this creation, healed; a body that works; work worth doing; the earth under a good King. If your hope is essentially an evacuation, it is smaller than the promise. The Bible does not end with the saints leaving the world. It ends with the dwelling place of God with man, on a new earth (Revelation 21:1–3). Let that shape how you treat the world now: as an estate you will inherit, not a waiting room you will leave.

For worship. If the inheritance ran on performance, everything would depend on your keeping it up, and you would spend your life auditing your grip. It runs on a promise, and the security is located somewhere other than you: in an oath sworn between the pieces by a God who walked that path alone, while the man who would inherit the world lay asleep in the dark, having contributed nothing to the ceremony but the animals he laid out. In Christ you will inherit the world. The meek shall inherit the earth, because the Lord of the earth was made meek for them, and bore in himself the curse of the broken covenant so that the promise could never fail.

verseByVerse.quote: For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression. That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring — not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression. That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring — not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,

For the law brings wrath. The law is good (7:12), but given to sinners it cannot give life; it exposes and condemns. It turns sin into transgression, and transgression brings God’s judgment (orgē, wrath). That was a devastating thing to say to people whose whole hope rested on possessing it. They had assumed the law was the mechanism of the inheritance. Paul says it is the mechanism of the indictment. Giving the law to sinners is like installing a speed camera on a road everyone was already speeding down. Nothing has been made worse. Everything has been made explicit, and the fines have started arriving.

But where there is no law there is no transgression. Transgression (parabasis) means stepping over a line. This does not mean that people without the law do not sin, or are innocent. Paul will say that sin was in the world before the law was given, and death reigned from Adam to Moses (5:13–14), and that Gentiles without the law still perish for their sin (2:12). Transgression is a particular kind of sin: the deliberate breaking of a known, stated command. You can be lost without a map, but you cannot be a trespasser until somebody has put up a fence. When God gave the law, sin became visible and wilful rebellion against his spoken word, and so more serious (5:20; 7:13). The point for Paul’s argument is that if the promise depended on the law, it would bring wrath, not blessing; so the promise must rest on faith and grace instead.

That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace. Faith and grace go together: faith receives what grace gives. If it depended on us, it would be uncertain. Read the logic backwards, because Paul states the purpose before the mechanism. What God wanted was a promise that was guaranteed. That was the requirement. And so, working back from the outcome, it had to depend on faith and rest on grace, because there is no other way to build a promise that cannot fail. Grace is not simply the kinder option. It is the only one that produces certainty, since any arrangement involving human performance is only as reliable as the human, and we have three chapters of evidence about that.

And be guaranteed to all his offspring. Guaranteed (bebaian): firm, sure. The word belonged to business and law: a title that would hold up, a contract legally secure, a transaction that could not be overturned later, a deed that stands when challenged. So Paul is not offering a warm hope but a valid title, and the difference is the difference between wanting something to be true and being able to produce the paperwork. Because it rests on grace, not on our performance, it is certain. Assurance is possible because salvation is by grace through faith.

The ordinary Christian week. Feel what this does to the week, because it is the pastoral point of the verse. If your standing depended on your performance, it would necessarily move, and you would know where you were by how the last few days had gone. There would be Sundays when you could sing and Sundays when you could not quite. There would be a low audit running at the back of your mind at all times, loudest precisely when you most need to pray. That is not a defect of temperament. It is the inevitable condition of anyone whose inheritance runs on law, and the only cure is to change the instrument.

Who is the father of us all. Jew and Gentile believers alike. These are the quiet triumph of the whole argument. Not the father of one nation with an annexe for outsiders. Paul has been arguing about law and promise and wrath and guarantee, and it lands on a family, which is what a promise, unlike a contract, is finally able to produce.

Can I really be sure I am saved? Yes, and this verse is one of the reasons. Assurance does not come from looking at how well you are doing, but from three things God gives together: his promises, which cannot fail because they rest on grace; the fruit of his grace in you, however small, such as love for Christ and hatred of sin; and the witness of his Spirit with your spirit that you are a child of God (8:16; Westminster 18.2). A true believer may lose the feeling of assurance for a time and have to wait for it, but the title itself does not change. Doubt about your assurance is not the same as the loss of your salvation.

What it does not mean. A guarantee can be misheard as an invitation to relax into nothing at all. Paul is not saying that the heir’s life is irrelevant; he is saying it is not the ground. The promise is guaranteed to all his offspring, and the previous verses described what Abraham’s offspring look like: people who walk in the footsteps of his faith. Security and indifference are not the same thing. A man who has understood that his inheritance cannot be lost does not become careless about the Father who gave it. He becomes free to obey without negotiating.

In a sentence. The law brings wrath, and where there is no law there is no transgression, so the promise depends on faith, so that it may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all Abraham’s offspring, not only to those of the law but to those who share Abraham’s faith, for he is the father of us all.

On a Tuesday. Think about how you feel when you approach God after a week in which you have done well: you prayed, you resisted something, you were generous. Now compare how you feel approaching him after a week in which you did none of it. If those feel very different, notice what has happened: something has been fluctuating, and it is not the promise. This does not make you a hypocrite; almost every believer lives with some version of it. But it locates the work still to be done, and the work is not more effort. It is learning to believe that the title is secure in both weeks. Because your salvation rests on grace, it is guaranteed. You can be sure.

For worship. Every human guarantee is only as good as the one who gives it, and every human guarantor dies. This one was given by the God who cannot lie, ratified in the blood of his Son, sealed by his Spirit, and stands as firm on your worst day as on your best. He did not build salvation on the sand of our performance but on the rock of his own grace, so that every child of Abraham, from the weakest to the strongest, might stand on exactly the same ground and sing the same song: it is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: as it is written, "I have made you the father of many nations" — in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, "So shall your offspring be."
verseByVerse.commentary:
as it is written, “I have made you the father of many nations” — in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, “So shall your offspring be.”

I have made you the father of many nations. From Genesis 17:5, when God renamed Abram, exalted father, as Abraham, father of a multitude. Look at the tense, which is easily read past and is the whole thing. God does not say I will make you the father of many nations. He says I have made you: past tense, spoken to a childless old man with no evidence of any kind. God speaks of the future as done, because for him it is. He does not describe reality; he establishes it. That is why Abraham’s name was changed before anything happened. He was addressed, by everyone he met, as father of a multitude while the promised son had not been born. Every conversation was a small act of faith or a small humiliation, depending on whether the One who named him could be relied on.

In the presence of the God in whom he believed. A phrase in the middle of the sentence decides the whole character of this faith. Abraham is not a man reasoning his way to a conclusion about a distant deity. He is standing before someone. Faith in the Bible is never a calculation about probabilities; it is a posture in front of a Person, which is why it can survive evidence that a calculation could not.

Who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. What kind of God did Abraham trust? The God of resurrection and creation. He had the whole Old Testament to choose from, and he picks these two, because between them they cover the only two situations in which a human being has nothing whatever to contribute: when there is nothing there yet, and when what was there has died. Every other predicament admits of some human input, effort, ingenuity, time. These two do not. A corpse cannot cooperate with its own raising, and nothing cannot assist in its own creation.

Both apply to Abraham literally. The offspring did not yet exist: nothing, waiting to be called. And the bodies through which they would come were finished: Abraham’s and Sarah’s, as good as dead (v. 19), waiting to be quickened. Later God would give life to Isaac on the altar too, in a figure (Hebrews 11:19), and supremely he would give it to Jesus. Abraham was standing in the only two circumstances where God works without a collaborator, and he became the father of many nations from inside both of them. Faith trusts a God who can do the impossible.

In hope he believed against hope. Humanly, there was no hope; he hoped in God. With nothing in the situation to hope for, he hoped. This is not positive thinking, and it is not the refusal to admit facts; the next verse says outright that he faced them. Hope in Scripture is not a mood about the future but a settled expectation resting on something said. So the question is never how much hope you can generate. It is whether the One who spoke can do it.

So shall your offspring be. From Genesis 15:5. As the stars. And Paul is writing to people who will have to believe something at least as unlikely: that a man they never met, executed in a province they have never visited, is alive, and that his death has settled their account with God. Every visible indicator argues against it. So he gives them a father who was in exactly that position, and shows what his faith actually rested on: not a reason to expect a child, but a God who does this sort of thing.

What it does not mean. This verse has been used to promise people outcomes God never promised. Abraham had a specific word from God about a specific thing, and his faith was in that word, not in his own conviction that it ought to happen. Believing hard that a particular result will come is not the faith described here, and when the result does not come, the collapse is severe. Faith fastens on what God has said. Where he has spoken plainly, that he will forgive, that he will keep you, that he will raise the dead, that he works all things for the good of those who love him, you may believe against every appearance and you will not be put to shame. Where he has not spoken about your particular case, ask, leave the answer with him, and keep believing what he has said while you wait.

Will God really raise my believing loved ones who have died? Yes. This is exactly the God described here: the one who gives life to the dead. The Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies (8:11), and since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:14). Their souls are already with the Lord, and their bodies will be raised, recognisable and glorious, when Christ returns. You may grieve, but not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The grave is not a category God finds difficult.

In a sentence. As Scripture says, God made him the father of many nations, in the sight of the God he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into being things that do not exist, and against all hope Abraham believed in hope that he would become the father of many nations, just as he had been told his offspring would be.

On a Tuesday. Take the thing you are praying for and cannot see any way through: the marriage, the son, the diagnosis, the part of your own character that has not moved in twenty years. Ask which of the two descriptions in verse 17 your situation falls under. Is it something that does not exist and would have to be created? Or something that was alive and is now dead? Those are the two categories named in this verse, and they are named as the specialities of the God you are praying to. There is no third category here, no department for cases that are merely difficult, which suggests that difficulty was never the relevant measurement.

For worship. If God were merely very powerful, hopeless cases would still be hopeless, and the question of every prayer would be whether your situation had gone too far. But God is not described here as the God who improves things. He is the God who works with nothing and with the dead, which means that having nothing to work with is not a disadvantage in his hands. It is his usual raw material. He spoke, and a universe stood up out of nothing. He spoke, and a dead womb bore a son. He spoke, and on the third day a dead man walked out of a tomb. Your God gives life to the dead and calls things into being from nothing. Nothing is impossible for him.
