so shall your offspring be

verseByVerse.quote: He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb. No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah’s womb. No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,

He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead. Faith is not ignoring reality. The word for considered is not a glance; it is the verb for taking careful stock, examining a thing closely and reaching a conclusion about it. Abraham faced the facts: he was about a hundred, and Sarah ninety and barren. He did the arithmetic, got the right answer, and believed God anyway. A good deal of Christian teaching implies the opposite, that doubt is what you get for looking too hard at reality and the remedy is to look less. Paul says the reverse. Abraham looked, and named what he saw with brutal accuracy. The word is blunter than piety would like: his body was already dead.

The deadness was the material. Put the two verses side by side. Verse 17 said God gives life to the dead. Verse 19 says Abraham considered his own body as good as dead. He was not applying a general doctrine about God’s power to an unrelated problem. He was standing inside the exact category God had just named. The deadness was not the obstacle to the promise. It was the material the promise was going to work with, and Abraham could see both facts at once.

No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God. A great many Christians have quietly used this sentence against themselves. Read alone it sounds like a man of unbroken confidence, and it produces a familiar despair: my faith wavers weekly, so I am not what Abraham was. But did Abraham not laugh (Genesis 17:17), and take Hagar (Genesis 16)? Yes. Genesis records that in this same period he lied about his wife to save himself, took Hagar because waiting had become unbearable, and when God repeated the promise he fell on his face and laughed, and said in his heart, shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Sarah laughed too, behind the tent door, and was asked about it. His faith was not perfect. But in the end it did not turn from the promise itself.

A man who staggers, not a man who defects. Paul is not rewriting the history; his readers knew Genesis better than we do. He is describing the direction of a life rather than auditing every hour of it. Abraham’s faith had bad days, poor decisions and at least one outright laugh, and it did not turn back. This is God’s summary of a long life, and the striking thing about it is not that God failed to notice the failures. It is that this is how he chooses to remember a believer. God graciously remembers Abraham’s faith, not his failures (Hebrews 11:8–12).

But he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God. Faith grows by looking at God, not at ourselves. It is not strengthened by trying to have more faith, which is like trying to fall asleep by concentrating: the harder you work at it, the more awake you are. Faith is not a substance you can increase by direct effort. It grows by attention to its object. Giving glory to God means saying back to him what he is like: that he keeps his word, that nothing is too hard for him, that he has never failed anyone yet. The man who does that finds, without aiming at it, that believing has become easier. And faith gives glory to God simply by trusting him to keep his word, as unbelief calls him a liar (1 John 5:10).

What should I do with my doubts? Bring them to God rather than hiding them from him. The father in the Gospel cried, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24), and Jesus healed his son. Doubt is not the same as unbelief: unbelief refuses God, while doubt is faith struggling and asking. Talk to a mature Christian; doubts grow in the dark. Go back to the evidence God has given, above all the resurrection of Jesus and the promises of Scripture. And do what Abraham did: turn your attention from the size of your faith to the greatness of God, and praise him for what you know is true. Faith is often strengthened not by solving every question but by looking longer at him.

Does faith mean I should ignore medical facts or refuse help? No. Abraham considered the facts honestly; faith never requires pretending. Trusting God and using the means he provides go together: the same God who heals is the God who gave us doctors, medicine and wisdom (1 Timothy 5:23; Colossians 4:14). Refusing treatment to prove your faith is not faith but presumption, putting the Lord your God to the test (Matthew 4:7). Pray for healing, take the treatment, and leave the outcome with God. Faith says, God is able, and God is good, whatever he decides; it does not say that facts are lies.

In a sentence. Without weakening in faith, he faced the fact that his body was as good as dead, since he was about a hundred, and that Sarah’s womb was also dead, yet he did not waver in unbelief at God’s promise but was strengthened in faith and gave glory to God.

On a Tuesday. This is really a prescription. Next time you catch yourself wavering, notice what you instinctively reach for. Most of us reach inward: we examine our faith, take its temperature, worry about its size, and end up with a smaller faith more closely observed. Abraham did the opposite. Try it deliberately. Take fifteen minutes and do nothing but rehearse what God has actually done, in Scripture and in your own life: name five things, out loud, specifically. It will feel mechanical for the first ten minutes. Then notice what has happened to the size of the thing you were worrying about. Face your impossible situation honestly, then look at God and give him glory by trusting his promise.

For worship. Look at what Abraham’s faith was like from the inside: twenty-five years of nothing happening; a wife long past childbearing; a household that must have wondered; two episodes of frank cowardice; a laugh. And one line in the New Testament that says he did not waver, which tells you what God does with a faith that staggers and keeps facing the same way. Abraham was not given more faith so that he could face his dead body. He looked at his dead body, and then he looked at God, and the second look was the longer one. The God who wrote that line over Abraham’s life has a gentler pen than any of us, because he reads his children through the faithfulness of his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.

Fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised. The definition of faith: full conviction that God can and will do what he says. Faith rests on two things, God’s promise and God’s power; not on our feelings or our ability. Notice how narrow the object of the conviction is, because this is the mercy of the verse. Abraham was not fully convinced that he would enjoy the experience, or that he understood what God was doing, or that the waiting had been reasonable. He was convinced of one thing: that God was able to do what he had promised. That is far smaller and far harder than general spiritual confidence, and it is the whole of what is required.

Able, and willing. Most of our difficulty is not really about God’s ability at all. Ask almost any Christian whether God could heal the illness, restore the marriage, save the son, break the habit, and the answer comes back at once: of course he could. The doubt sits somewhere else and is rarely said out loud: whether he will bother, whether he has particularly noticed, whether in this case he is inclined to. The verse addresses power, and the letter spends chapters addressing the other question, which is why it can afford to be brief here. He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (8:32). A God who did not spare his own Son has already answered any doubt about whether he is disposed toward you.

Fully convinced. The word means to be filled completely, carried to the full, the way a sail is full or a hold is full. It is not a decision made once but a settled state. Which raises an obvious question for a Christian who does not feel full of anything. Is this the standard? Must I attain it before God will count anything to me? No, and the reason is the whole argument of the chapter. Faith does not justify because it reaches a certain intensity; it justifies because of what it is attached to. The chapter has already shown Abraham lying about his wife and laughing at the promise. What Paul describes here is the direction his faith settled into over twenty-five years, the character it had by the end, not its state on the first morning. Full assurance of this kind is the fruit of a long walk with God, not the fee for beginning one.

What he had promised. Then the small phrase almost nobody notices. Faith in Scripture is never free-floating. It always has a word behind it, and it can only go as far as that word goes. Abraham was not exercising a general spiritual attitude; he was holding on to a specific sentence God had spoken to him about a specific thing, and his confidence was exactly as wide as the promise and not one inch wider. That tells you what to do when your faith is thin. Do not try to generate more conviction; you cannot, any more than you can decide to find something funny. Go and find the promise.

How do I know which promises are really mine? Read them in context, and ask to whom they were made. Some promises were given to particular people for particular events: Abraham’s son, Gideon’s victory, Paul’s safe arrival in Rome. Those show you God’s character, but they are not addressed to you. Others are made to all who belong to Christ, and those are yours in full, for all the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). That he will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5), that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6), that nothing can separate you from his love (8:38–39): these are written to you. Learn them by heart, and lean on them by name.

In a sentence. He was fully persuaded that God had power to do what he had promised.

On a Tuesday. Most Christians fail this test the first time. Name the promise you are currently relying on. Not a doctrine, not a general impression that God is good: a sentence from Scripture, which you could say aloud, which speaks to the thing you are actually worried about. If nothing comes, that is not a verdict on your faith. It is a diagnosis of why it feels so hard to exercise: you have been trying to trust without holding anything. Find the sentence today, write it where you will see it, and put your weight on it.

For worship. This verse, which sounds like the most demanding in the chapter, is really the most freeing. It does not ask you to be strong. It asks you to be convinced about somebody else’s strength. The whole of Abraham’s greatness, in the end, was that he thought better of God than his circumstances did, and God has never yet let down anyone who thought well of him. He is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think (Ephesians 3:20), and he has never made a promise he could not keep or would not. Be fully convinced: God is able to do what he has promised you.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: That is why his faith “was counted to him as righteousness.” But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. — Romans 4:22–24a
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is why his faith “was counted to him as righteousness.” But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also.

That is why his faith was counted to him as righteousness. Repeating Genesis 15:6, the sentence the whole chapter has been unfolding. The pattern for Abraham is identical to the pattern for us, because the God is the same and the way he deals with sinners is the same: by faith, through grace, credited and not earned.

But the words it was counted to him were not written for his sake alone. Notice exactly what Paul says was written for us, because it is more precise than a general claim that the Bible is relevant. He does not say Abraham’s life was recorded for us, or that his example is inspiring. He says the words, it was counted to him, were not written for his sake alone. It is the specific phrase that is addressed to us. Moses wrote a sentence about one man, and Paul says that sentence had a second audience in view from the beginning, thousands of years before any of us were born.

But for ours also. Scripture was written for us (15:4; 1 Corinthians 10:11). Abraham’s story is the pattern of every believer’s salvation; what was true for him is true for you. The verse was true of Abraham on the night it happened. He was the one being justified, and nothing about his experience was diminished because others would read about it. But it was also being written down, and the writing was not merely archival. When God did something for a childless man in Canaan, part of what he was doing was making a record that would hold your weight.

How Paul has argued. Stand back from the whole chapter and notice its method. Paul has not asked anyone to accept a new doctrine. He has asked them to read an old text carefully: what it says, what order it comes in, which words it uses. And the doctrine has come out of the reading. That is how he has answered the charge that justification by faith is a novelty. He did not find a clever way round the Old Testament. He found justification by faith in it, in the founding story of the nation whose Scriptures they were, and his opponents had been reading past it.

Not first a gallery of examples. This also settles how to read Old Testament stories, and it is the most useful thing in these verses for ordinary reading. Most of us were taught the narratives as moral examples: be brave like David, be faithful like Daniel, be patient like Job. That reading has two defects. It exhausts you, because you are asked to produce qualities you do not have. And it is not what the stories are first for. Paul does not say be like Abraham. He says the way God dealt with Abraham is the way God deals with you. The point of the story is not the patriarch’s faith but the Lord’s reckoning.

So should I never read Old Testament stories as examples? You should, but second, not first. Paul himself says that these things happened to them as an example, and were written down for our instruction (1 Corinthians 10:11), and Hebrews 11 sets the faith of the saints before us to imitate. The difference is the order. First ask what the story shows of God: his grace, his promises, his judgment, his patience, and how it points to Christ. Then ask what kind of response that God deserves, and you will find the example in its proper place: not a standard to reach in your own strength, but the shape of a life that trusts the same God.

In a sentence. This is why his faith was credited to him as righteousness, and the words it was credited to him were written not for him alone, but also for us.

On a Tuesday. Run this test on your own Bible reading. Take the last Old Testament passage you read and ask what you came away with. If it was a resolution, I should be more like that, I should try harder at this, you read it as a moral example. Now go back and ask a different question: what does this show me about what God is like, and what he does with people who have nothing? That is the question this verse authorises, and it is the reason a chapter about a man dead for four thousand years can settle where you stand tonight. Read the Bible as written for you. It is.

For worship. Paul does not say the words can be applied to us, as though we were borrowing something. He says they were written for us; the intention was there in the writing. You are not reading somebody else’s mail and hoping some of it fits. The letter has your name on it, and it was addressed before you existed, by the God who knew the end from the beginning and had you in mind when he took an old man outside to count the stars.

verseByVerse.quote: It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. — Romans 4:24b–25
verseByVerse.commentary:
It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification.

It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord. Our faith is like Abraham’s: trust in the God who gives life to the dead. Notice how Paul names the God we believe in, because he could have said it a hundred ways and chose this one, and it closes the loop of the chapter. Abraham believed in the God who gives life to the dead (v. 17) and looked at a body that was as good as dead (v. 19). We believe in the God who gave life to the dead and look at a body that was truly dead, in a tomb, for three days. Abraham believed God would bring life from his dead body; we believe God brought life from Jesus’ dead body. It is not an analogy. It is faith in the same God doing the same kind of thing, and the second instance is the one the first was pointing at.

Who was delivered up for our trespasses. Delivered up (paredothē): handed over, the word of Isaiah 53:12 in the Greek Old Testament, and of Judas’s betrayal. By God, for our sins, to pay for them. And the verb has been waiting since chapter 1. It is the same verb that fell three times like a gavel when God gave them up to the desires of their hearts, to dishonourable passions, to a debased mind (1:24, 26, 28). There, God handed sinners over to what they had chosen. Here, God hands his own Son over to what they deserved. The letter’s most terrible verb and its most merciful one are the same word, and one handing over is the answer to the other.

Who handed Jesus over, Judas, the rulers, Pilate or God? All of them, in different ways and with opposite purposes. Judas handed him over for money, the rulers out of envy, Pilate out of cowardice, and each was guilty. Yet Peter says he was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23), and the church prayed that Herod, Pilate and the peoples did whatever God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27–28). Above them all, the Father gave him up for us all (8:32), and the Son gave himself: the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). Men meant it for evil; God meant it for the salvation of the world.

And raised for our justification. Because of our justification, or to secure it. The parallel repays reading slowly. Delivered up because of our trespasses; raised because of our justification. The same small preposition governs both halves, which suggests that our trespasses were the reason he went to the cross, and our justification, accomplished there, was the reason he came out of the grave. He was raised because the work was done. The resurrection proves that the payment was accepted. If Christ had stayed dead, we would not know our sins were paid. His resurrection is God’s receipt, declaring the debt settled, and the living Christ applies his righteousness to us (5:10; 8:34).

The receipt. Imagine the case without the empty tomb. A man dies claiming to bear the sins of the world, and stays dead. There is then no way on earth to know whether the payment was accepted, or whether he simply died as other men die, under the same sentence, one more casualty of the thing he claimed to defeat. Death holding him would have meant the account was unsettled. Death releasing him is the public statement that there was nothing left to hold him for. Most of us locate our assurance at the cross, and rightly; but a payment can always be doubted by a man in a bad mood at three in the morning: was it enough, for this, for me? The resurrection is God’s own signature on the transaction, given publicly, in daylight, before witnesses who were later killed for saying so. The Father does not raise men whose work is unfinished.

Why does the resurrection matter for my justification, and not only the cross? Because the cross is where the debt was paid, and the resurrection is where God declared it paid. Without the resurrection, Paul says, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). The risen Christ is also the one who now lives to apply what he won: he is at the right hand of God, interceding for us (8:34), and it is to a living Saviour, not a dead martyr, that faith is joined. So the gospel is not only Christ died for our sins, but that he was buried and raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Both halves belong in your confidence.

In a sentence. Righteousness will be credited to us who believe in the God who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was handed over to death for our sins and raised to life for our justification.

On a Tuesday. When you have sinned badly and the accusation arrives, you cannot possibly be forgiven for that, notice what you reach for in reply. If it is your repentance, or how sorry you are, or a resolution about the future, the accusation will win, because none of those is strong enough and you know it. The answer this verse puts in your hand is a historical event you had nothing to do with: he was raised. Nothing you have done this week can un-empty that tomb. The verdict was published before you were born and cannot be appealed by anybody, including you. Say it back to the accuser, and to yourself: he was delivered up for my trespasses, and raised for my justification.

For worship. So the chapter that began with an old man in Canaan ends outside a grave in Jerusalem, and the same sentence covers both. It was counted to him. It will be counted to us. Between the two lies the only event in history that makes the accounting honest: a Son handed over by his Father, and handed back. Stand at the two ends of that sentence. At one end, a hill outside a city wall, and a body taken down in a hurry because a feast was coming. At the other, a garden at first light, a stone moved, and grave clothes lying where a body had been. Between them lies the one weekend on which the standing of the whole human race was suspended, and it hung on the Father’s verdict concerning his Son, and on nothing anyone else had done or would ever do. He was handed over for your sins and raised for your justification. Your sins are paid; you are declared righteous. Rejoice.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh?<sup>2</sup>For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.<sup>3</sup>For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”<sup>4</sup>Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.<sup>5</sup>And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,<sup>6</sup>just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works:<sup>7</sup>“Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;<sup>8</sup>blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin.”<sup>9</sup>Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness.<sup>10</sup>How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised.<sup>11</sup>He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well,<sup>12</sup>and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.<sup>13</sup>For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith.<sup>14</sup>For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void.<sup>15</sup>For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression.<sup>16</sup>That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring—not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,<sup>17</sup>as it is written, “I have made you the father of many nations”—in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.<sup>18</sup>In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, “So shall your offspring be.”<sup>19</sup>He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah’s womb.<sup>20</sup>No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,<sup>21</sup>fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.<sup>22</sup>That is why his faith was “counted to him as righteousness.”<sup>23</sup>But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone,<sup>24</sup>but for ours also. It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord,<sup>25</sup>who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification.

5.title: Peace, Joy, and the Two Adams
5.overview:
Romans 5 is the hinge of the letter. Behind us lie three chapters of diagnosis and one chapter of remedy; ahead lie three chapters of Christian experience and life. Chapter 5 stands at the turning point, summarising the achievements of justification (vv. 1–11) before setting those achievements within the grandest possible framework: the story of two men, Adam and Christ, whose actions determined the destiny of all humanity (vv. 12–21).

The opening "therefore" connects everything that follows to everything Paul has argued. Because we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God. We have access to grace. We stand in hope. We can even boast in our sufferings. And the love of God — poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit — is the guarantee that the hope will not put us to shame. The person justified by faith does not merely have a changed legal status; she has entered a new world, a new relationship, a new story whose ending is already written.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Peace, Access, Hope, and the Love of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." This sentence is the great sigh of relief at the centre of the letter. Three chapters of accumulated guilt — the Gentile without excuse, the moralist self-condemned, the universal verdict of Scripture, the silencing of every mouth — and now: peace. Not merely the absence of war, but the shalom of a relationship fully restored. The hostility between the holy God and the sinful creature has been dealt with at the cross, and the one who has received the verdict of justification stands in the peace of a fully settled relationship with God.

Paul adds to peace the gift of access (v. 2) — "through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand." Access was a technical term for the privilege of being brought into the presence of a king. The justified sinner has not merely been acquitted; she has been given permanent, unimpeded access to the throne of God. She does not approach on the basis of her spiritual performance on any given day; she stands in grace — a position of favour that does not fluctuate with her feelings or her faithfulness.

The boasting in sufferings (vv. 3–5) is one of the most counter-intuitive things Paul writes. He does not merely say we can endure suffering; he says we rejoice in it — because suffering produces endurance, endurance produces character, character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame because the love of God has been poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit. The chain is unbreakable. And the certainty of hope rests not on our own resilience but on the Spirit-given experience of being loved by God.

And then Paul does something the rest of the section depends on: he proves that love rather than asserting it. Verses 6 to 8 fix the timing of the cross — Christ died for us while we were still weak, still ungodly, still sinners. Not after we improved, and not in anticipation of our improving. He sets it against the best human parallel he can find and shows that there is none: one might barely die for a good man, but God shows his love in that while we were still sinners Christ died for us (v. 8). From there the argument runs from the harder thing to the easier. If God did that for enemies, the lesser question of whether he will finish the work in friends answers itself — since we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved from wrath through him (vv. 9–10). The section ends where it must: not with the benefits but with the giver. We rejoice, finally, not in peace or access or hope, but in God himself, through whom we have now received reconciliation (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Peace with God and the Assurance of Faith

Romans 5:1 is a foundation stone of the Reformed doctrine of assurance. The believer has peace with God — not the peace she feels on spiritually good days, but the objective peace established by the accomplished work of Christ received by faith. The Reformation recovered this against the Roman Catholic teaching that assurance is presumption: on the contrary, to doubt one's justification when God has spoken the verdict is to call God's word into question. As Calvin taught, faith without assurance is not the faith of the New Testament. The peace of Romans 5:1 is not a feeling; it is a fact grounded in the finished work of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The first-century world had no shortage of philosophical frameworks for enduring suffering — Stoic resignation, Epicurean avoidance, Platonic transcendence. None of them grounded suffering in the love of a personal God or gave it redemptive purpose. Paul's rejoicing in suffering (vv. 3–5) was genuinely new: suffering has a trajectory, and that trajectory ends in hope that is guaranteed by the Spirit. Now: In an age that treats suffering as the enemy of the good life, to be medicated, minimised, or avoided at all costs, Romans 5:3–5 offers a radically different framework. Suffering is not the enemy of Christian hope; it is one of its primary instruments. The Christian who suffers well — who endures, who builds character, who hopes — is not an anomaly but a disciple.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand... — Romans 5:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in hope of the glory of God.

Meaning first. Romans 5 shows what justification brings. First, its fruits: peace with God, access to his grace, hope of glory, joy even in suffering, the love of God poured into our hearts, and certainty of final salvation, since if God loved us when we were enemies, he will surely save us now we are his friends (vv. 1–11). Then the great comparison of Adam and Christ (vv. 12–21): through one man’s sin, condemnation and death came to all in him; through one man’s obedience, righteousness and life come to all in him. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more. The chapter that begins with a man at peace with God ends with grace seated on a throne, and both are the work of one Man.

Therefore. Start with the first word, because it carries four chapters. This is the hinge of the whole letter. Everything from 1:18 has been a court case: the charge, the evidence, the silencing of every mouth, the verdict, and then the astonishing provision by which the guilty are declared righteous. Chapters 1 to 4 establish the verdict. Chapters 5 to 8 describe what it is like to live inside it. Paul is no longer arguing that you can be justified. He is telling you what is now true of you because you are.

Since we have been justified by faith. A completed fact. Not hoping to be, not trying to be, but have been: the verdict has been pronounced and the court has risen. Everything that follows in this chapter rests on this, and none of it rests on anything else.

We have peace with God. Peace with God is not the same as peace about God. It is not subjective tranquillity or the absence of spiritual anxiety; it is the objective end of hostility between the holy God and the sinful creature. The war is over. Christ made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). And it is worth seeing what the hostility actually consisted of, because it ran in both directions and not in the same way. On our side it was real enmity: alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds (Colossians 1:21). On God’s side it was not temper but settled judicial opposition, his wrath, which chapter 1 said is being revealed from heaven. Both had to be dealt with, and only one of them could be dealt with by persuasion. That is why the word is peace and not ceasefire. A ceasefire is an agreement to stop shooting and can be revoked by either party on an afternoon’s notice. A peace treaty settles the terms, and this one was signed in blood by the offended party.

We have, or let us have? A brief word about a footnote you may find in your Bible, since it can be unsettling to discover that the manuscripts differ here. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read let us have peace. The difference is a single letter in Greek, a long o for a short one, and the two were pronounced identically in Paul’s day, so a scribe taking dictation could easily write one for the other. Nearly all translations read we have, and rightly: the context is a list of what we have, and Paul is drawing a conclusion from the argument he has just finished, not issuing an exhortation. And even on the other reading the peace would still be a fact. It would mean let us enjoy the peace we have, never let us try to obtain it.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ. The only way. Peace was not negotiated by us and is not maintained by us. It was made by him, and it stands as long as he stands.

Through him we have also obtained access. The word (prosagōgē) described the office of the official who introduced people at a royal court. Nobody simply walked in to see a king; you were brought in, by someone with the standing to bring you. So the word contains both the privilege and the fact that it is not your own. And notice the tense: we have obtained access, a completed action with permanent effect. The introduction has already been made. You are not applying each morning to see whether today is a day on which you may approach.

Into this grace in which we stand. Grace here is not a mood or a transaction but a place: something you can be standing on, which means it is underneath you and bearing your weight. The verb is again the perfect: we took our stand and we are still standing. And a floor is the sort of thing you stop noticing, which is exactly right. Nobody spends the day generating the floor. The man who has understood this verse does not have to re-establish his position with God every morning, any more than he has to re-lay the floorboards before he can cross the room.

And we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. “Rejoice” (kauchōmetha) is boast, exult: the same word as the boasting that was excluded in 3:27. The boasting of the man who trusted his own record has been shut out, and a right boasting has taken its place, in God’s glory, which we will share (8:18, 30). And this is one of the quiet masterstrokes of the letter. Go back two chapters. The charge sheet against the human race reached its summary in exactly these words: all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (3:23). That was the indictment; this is the hope. Paul has taken the precise phrase in which our ruin was stated and made it the description of our future. The thing we lost is the thing we are promised. Not merely forgiveness for having fallen short of it, but the glory itself, restored to the creature it was made for.

Hope is not wishful thinking. In ordinary speech, hope means I would like it but I am not sure: I hope it does not rain. In the New Testament it means confident expectation of something God has promised and not yet delivered. The uncertainty is only about the date, never about the thing. Christian hope is as sure as the one who made the promise, and it is called hope only because we have not yet seen it.

Peace behind, ground beneath, glory ahead. Notice the escalation, which is deliberate: peace (v. 1), then a standing in grace, then hope of glory (v. 2). Justification does not merely settle the past; it opens the future. The present standing and the future destination are both secured by the same grace received by the same faith. Paul piles up three things in two verses and none of them fluctuates: peace behind you, a place to stand beneath you, and glory ahead of you.

If I have peace with God, why do I still feel anxious or guilty? Because feelings report on many things, and the verdict of God is not one of the things they are good at reporting. Your peace with God is a fact about God’s judgment of you, settled in Christ, and it is not reopened by a bad night. Guilt you still feel may be pointing to something real you need to confess, and then the answer is to confess it and believe 1 John 1:9. Or it may be the leftover echo of sins already forgiven, and then the answer is to argue with it from this verse. Anxiety may be temperament, tiredness or illness, none of which alters your standing. Do not try to feel your way into peace. Look at the verdict, and let the feelings follow when they can.

In a sentence. Since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we now stand, and we rejoice in the hope of God’s glory.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it goes to which half of the letter you are actually living in. Which of these two sentences describes your normal week: I am trying to get right with God, or I am right with God? Both are said by sincere Christians and only one of them is true. If the first is your instinct, if the ordinary background hum of your spiritual life is effortful and slightly anxious, a project not yet completed, then you are living in chapters 1 to 4 with a doctrine from chapter 5, and the word to hear is Paul’s first one: therefore. The case is closed. The verdict is in. Pray today not as a man applying for an audience but as one who has been brought in and is still standing there. What remains is not to secure the peace but to live in it.

For worship. The God who had every right to remain at war with us made the peace himself, paid for it himself, and then took us by the hand and brought us into his presence, and has never once asked us to leave. The war is over, the ground is firm, and the glory we threw away in Eden is held out to us again, not as a reward but as an inheritance. All of it is through our Lord Jesus Christ: the peace was his blood, the access is his hand, and the glory is his own, shared.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “let us have peace.”

verseByVerse.quote: Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope,

Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings. Paul has just spoken of rejoicing in the hope of the glory of God (v. 2); now he speaks of rejoicing in sufferings, and “not only that” suggests the second is as natural to the Christian as the first. Not just in spite of them, but in them. The verb is the same boast, exult. The joy of verse 2 looks at the future; the joy of verse 3 is found in the middle of the present at its worst (James 1:2–4; 1 Peter 1:6–7).

What it does not mean. Two things need saying at once, before the chain, or this passage will do damage. The first is what Paul does not say. He does not say suffering is good, or that it should be sought, or that a Christian ought to feel positively about a diagnosis. Scripture never calls evil good; the Lord himself wept at a grave he was about to empty. And he does not say rejoice because of your sufferings, as though the thing itself were the cause of the joy. The word is in: joy located inside a situation that remains bad, on account of something else that is true about it. The second is that this is not a formula and not a promise about outcomes. Paul is not saying every sufferer automatically becomes stronger. He knows better, and so does anybody who has watched a man come out of a hard decade smaller and harder than he went in. Suffering by itself does not produce endurance. It produces bitterness at least as often, and the difference is not the quantity of the pain but what the sufferer is holding on to while it lasts. That is why the paragraph ends where it does, at the love of God poured into the heart by the Spirit (v. 5).

Knowing that suffering produces endurance. “Suffering” (thlipsis) is pressure, affliction, the crushing of something under weight. “Endurance” (hypomonē) is not passive resignation. It is the compound that means remaining under: staying put beneath a load rather than crawling out from under it. And it can only be produced one way. There is no exercise that develops it in the abstract; nobody has ever become patient in a comfortable year. That is worth knowing about the Christian life generally: several of the qualities we most want are only manufactured in conditions we would never choose.

And endurance produces character. The Greek word (dokimē) is a metallurgist’s: the quality of metal that has been through the assay and come out proved. It shares its root with the failed test at 1:28, where a mind that would not keep God in view was handed over as metal that did not pass. Here the metal passes. And notice what a proving actually is: it does not create the quality, it demonstrates it, and it demonstrates it to the man himself. Most of us do not know what we believe until something has tried to take it away from us. That is why a Christian who has been through something often has a settledness that no amount of reading produces. He is not cleverer than you. He has been tested, and he has the certificate. Faith that has been through trouble is proven real.

And character produces hope. The surprising link. We would have expected the chain to run the other way, with hope enabling endurance. Paul says hope is the output. And the logic is exactly right once you have lived it. The reason a tested believer hopes is that he has evidence: he has been in the place where he was certain he could not go on, and he went on, and looking back he can see that he was carried. Hope is not optimism about the future; it is a conclusion drawn from the past. The man who has been held before has grounds for expecting to be held again. So the chain runs: suffering, endurance, proven character, hope.

If I cannot feel any joy in this. One more guard, for the reader in the middle of it rather than looking back on it. If you are suffering now and can find no joy in it whatever, you have not failed this passage. Paul is describing a trajectory, not a mood available on demand, and he is writing to people at various points along it. Endurance is mostly indistinguishable from simply not leaving. If today you have not walked away from God, if you are still, in some ragged fashion, holding on, then the first link of this chain is being forged in you at this moment, and it will not feel like anything at all while it happens.

Does this include suffering I brought on myself? Yes, though differently. Peter distinguishes suffering for doing good from suffering for doing wrong (1 Peter 2:20), and the second calls first for repentance, not celebration. But God does not waste even the consequences of our own folly. The man reaping what he sowed, the woman living with the results of a bad decision she cannot undo: once the sin has been confessed and forgiven, the pressure that remains is still pressure, and the same God still works endurance, character and hope through it. Paul’s word covers every kind of affliction a believer carries, including the ones with his own fingerprints on them. Grace is not too proud to work with the wreckage.

Does God send suffering, then? Scripture holds two things together without embarrassment. Suffering is an intruder in God’s world, the fruit of the fall that this very chapter goes on to describe, and God takes no pleasure in it for its own sake (Lamentations 3:33). And nothing reaches a believer that has not passed through his hands, and he works all of it for good (8:28). Joseph could say to his brothers that they meant it for evil and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20), in the same sentence, about the same event. You do not have to call the thing good. You may call God good in it.

In a sentence. Not only so, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance, perseverance produces proven character, and character produces hope.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test that costs nothing and does a great deal. Write down, specifically, the three hardest things you have been through since becoming a Christian. Beside each one, write what you were afraid would happen: that you would lose your faith, that you would not cope, that you would never be happy again. Then write what actually happened. Most people find, doing this honestly, that the thing they feared did not occur and that they cannot now reconstruct how they got through. That inability is the point. It was not resilience; you were carried, and you have already forgotten it. That list is the raw material of hope, and this is exactly how Paul says hope gets made. Keep it, and read it at the start of the next hard thing.

For worship. The God who wastes nothing has taken the worst things in a fallen world and set them to work for his children: the pressure that was meant to crush us becomes the furnace that proves us, and the fire that should have destroyed our faith becomes the evidence that it was real. He did not spare his own Son suffering, and the Son, though he was a son, learned obedience through what he suffered (Hebrews 5:8). Every link of this chain he forged first in himself, and he walks the road with us, so that even our affliction becomes a path to glory.

verseByVerse.quote: and hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

And hope does not put us to shame. The phrase is not primarily about embarrassment. In the Old Testament, to be put to shame is what happens to a man whose confidence turns out to have been misplaced: the one who trusted an ally that did not come, or a god that could not answer. It is the shame of having backed the wrong thing in public (Psalm 25:3; Isaiah 28:16). Hope in that sense is a risk: every hope is a bet on something, and most of them eventually expose the person who made them. Paul says this one will not. We will not stand on the last day like someone who trusted a false promise. Not because we hope sincerely, but because of what is holding the other end.

Because God’s love has been poured into our hearts. The reason he gives is not the one we would expect. Having just said that hope is produced by tested character, he might have grounded its reliability in the same place: you have come through before, therefore you will come through again. Instead he goes outside the chain entirely and points to something given. The chain of verses 3 and 4 is real, but it is not what makes hope safe. What makes it safe is that God has already done something inside you.

Whose love? Note the direction of the love, since it can be read either way and the difference is everything. This is not first our love for God, welling up. It is his love for us, poured in: the sense of being loved by God arriving in a human heart as an experienced thing rather than an inferred one. Paul is not describing a doctrine you hold; he is describing something that has happened to you. Not only believed, but known.

Poured. The verb (ekkechytai) is extravagant. It is the word for a downpour, for something emptied out without measuring: the word used of the Spirit being poured out at Pentecost (Acts 2:17), and of the blood poured out at the cross. Not administered in a therapeutic dose. God is not careful with this. And the tense is perfect: it has been poured, an act completed with results that remain, which means the reservoir was filled before today and is not depleted by a bad week.

Through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. Every believer has the Spirit, given at conversion (8:9), and it is the Spirit who assures us of God’s love, so that we cry Abba, Father (8:15–16). He is the firstfruits of the coming glory, God’s own pledge that the hope will be honoured. This internal witness to the love of God is what sustains the rejoicing of verses 3 and 4 through the darkest seasons of suffering.

What if I have never felt anything of the kind? A great many faithful Christians read a verse like this and conclude that whatever Paul is describing has not happened to them. So three things, carefully. First, this is not describing a particular kind of experience: not a moment, not an emotional register, not the sort of thing that could be arranged at a meeting. It shows up in more ways than one. It is in the man who finds, to his surprise, that he wants to pray. It is in the sudden and inexplicable conviction, halfway through an ordinary Tuesday, that you are not facing your life alone. It is in tears at a line of a hymn you have sung a hundred times. It is in the fact that you mind about your sin at all. None of those announces itself as the love of God being poured out, and all of them are.

Temperament and health are real. Second, some people feel everything strongly and some feel very little, and the difference is largely how they were made and how they slept. There are believers who have loved Christ for forty years with the emotional volume permanently low, and others whose capacity for felt experience has been flattened by depression or exhaustion or grief. Scripture never treats intensity of feeling as the measure of anything, and a man whose illness has taken his feelings has not thereby lost the Spirit who was given to him.

The evidence is not only inward. Third, and most usefully: Paul says the love was poured in through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, and the presence of that Spirit is demonstrable in ways that do not depend on your feelings today. Do you call God Father, and mean it? That is the Spirit (8:15). Do you want holiness, even while failing at it? Is Christ precious to you in a way he was not at nineteen? Those are not achievements. They are symptoms.

Does every Christian have the Spirit, or is he a later blessing for some? Every Christian has him. Paul says plainly that anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (8:9), and here he speaks of the Spirit as given to us, all of us, the whole church in Rome. There is no second class of believers who have been given him and a first class who are still waiting. Christians may be filled afresh, strengthened and led more deeply as they grow (Ephesians 5:18), and you should ask for that. But you do not need to seek the Spirit as though you lacked him. You need to believe what he has already been given to do in you.

In a sentence. And hope does not disappoint us, because God has poured out his love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, whom he has given us.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it is better than asking whether you feel loved. Ask when you last noticed something that would be inexplicable if God were not real and did not care for you. Not a miracle: a comfort that arrived from nowhere at the right moment, a peace you could not account for, a word in Scripture that landed as though addressed to you. Most Christians have a small collection of these and have never counted them, because each one on its own seems too slight to mention. Count them tonight, and thank God for each by name. That is the pouring, and it has been going on longer than you thought.

For worship. The chain from suffering to hope would be a cruel arrangement if it ran on human strength, because the people who most need it are precisely those who have least of it. It does not. Underneath the endurance and the testing and the hope is something poured in from outside, by a Spirit who was given and not earned. The Father loved us, the Son died to make the love righteous, and the Spirit carries it into the heart and empties it out without measuring. That is why the man at the bottom of the pit can still be told that his hope will not let him down: the love holding the other end is the love of God himself.

parallels.desc: in you they trusted and were not put to shame

verseByVerse.quote: For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will scarcely die for a righteous person — though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die —
verseByVerse.commentary:
For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will scarcely die for a righteous person — though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die —

For while we were still weak. Notice that Paul is now doing something he has not done before in this letter: he is offering proof of the love he has just asserted. Verse 5 said God’s love has been poured into our hearts, and a sceptic, or a Christian on a bad night, might reasonably answer that this is exactly what one would expect a religion to claim, and that inward feelings are not evidence of anything. So Paul goes outside us altogether. The proof is not a state of mind. It is a death, in public, at a datable moment, and its evidential force lies entirely in when it happened. And “weak” (asthenōn) is worth resisting the urge to soften. It does not mean we were doing our best in difficult circumstances. It means without strength: the word used of the physically helpless, the invalid who cannot get himself to the water. The picture is not a man who needed assistance. It is a man who could not have contributed to his own rescue if he had wanted to.

At the right time Christ died for the ungodly. “At the right time” (kata kairon): the crucifixion was not an accident of history but an event scheduled in the eternal purpose of God, when the fullness of time had come (Galatians 4:4), falling at the precise moment of human helplessness. And “for the ungodly” means in their place, on their behalf: not for those who had earned divine favour, but for those in active opposition to God. It is the same word as 4:5, where God justifies the ungodly. The timing is repeated with insistence across three verses: while we were still weak, for the ungodly, while we were still sinners. Every one of them is a state we were in at the time. If Christ had died for the repentant, the cross would prove that God responds well to repentance. If he had died for the promising, it would prove God has an eye for potential. He died for people who were at that moment incapable, opposed and guilty, which proves something about God and nothing whatever about us.

For one will scarcely die for a righteous person. Then Paul does something unexpected, and readers often skim it as rhetorical padding. It is not. He is conducting a search: going out into human experience to find the highest instance of love he can, so that he can measure God’s against it. And watch him qualify himself twice as he goes. For a righteous man, the upright, correct, admirable sort, one will scarcely die.

Though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die. Then he corrects himself: perhaps for a good man, the warm and generous kind, a benefactor you would actually be fond of, someone might dare it. Even that is hedged with perhaps and dare. This is the best the human race can offer, and Paul cannot state it without qualification. And his estimate is right. People do die for others: a mother for her child, a soldier for the man beside him, occasionally a stranger in a river. But notice the invariable condition: there is always something in the object that draws it out. Love, in us, is a response to worth or to belonging. Nobody has ever laid down his life for a man he found contemptible, who had wronged him, and who would not be grateful. That is not cynicism about human beings; it is a fair description of where our ceiling is. Christ died for neither the righteous nor the good. He died for the ungodly.

A different kind of love. This means these verses are doing more than praising God warmly. They establish that divine love is a different kind of thing, not a larger quantity of the same thing. Ours is drawn out; his originates. Ours responds to something; his creates the something it will later delight in. And that is why the question what does God see in me? has no answer: not because the answer is disappointing, but because the question assumes the wrong mechanism. He was not looking for something to see.

Does this mean Christ died for me in particular? Paul writes we and us: he is speaking to believers about what Christ did for them. But look at the description: weak, ungodly. Those are not the names of a select class you might fail to qualify for. They are the names of everyone, and the gospel is offered freely to every one of them. No one who comes to Christ will discover that he was not included. If you are trusting him, you may say with Paul that he loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20), and if you are not yet, the only qualification for coming is the one you already have: being ungodly.

In a sentence. When we were still powerless, at just the right time Christ died for the ungodly, and very rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person someone might possibly dare to die.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it is not about your feelings toward God but about what you think you are bringing. When you try to believe that God loves you, notice what you instinctively reach for as the reason. Most of us produce something, even if we would never say it out loud: that we have been trying, that we mean well, that we are not as bad as we might be, that at least we care about this. Now take whatever you produced and set it against verse 6. Christ died for the weak and the ungodly: categories that contain not a single reason. Whatever you were holding was not what secured this and cannot be what maintains it. Put it down.

For worship. If God’s love were like ours, it would have been drawn out by something in us, and it could therefore be exhausted by something in us. A love with a reason can lose its reason. But the love demonstrated at a specific hour, for people who were at that hour helpless and hostile, has nothing in us to lose. The Son of God did not wait for us to become good enough to die for. He came down to the ungodly, at the time his Father had appointed, and laid down his life for people who could not lift a finger to help him, and that is the love that holds us still.
