If you have stopped, start today: the door out is still open.

In a sentence. Should we go on sinning so that grace may increase? Certainly not! How can we who died to sin keep living in it?

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it follows the verb rather than the general subject. Do not ask whether you sinned this week; you did. Ask instead whether there is anything in your life you have stopped fighting: not lost to repeatedly, but quietly stopped contesting. Something you have arranged your week around, made room for, and no longer bring to God because you have privately settled that this is simply how things are. That is not a lapse. That is an address. And Paul’s question is not how could you have done that? (he knows perfectly well how) but how can you still be living there? Name it to God today, and move out. You have died to sin. Do not live as if you were still its slave.

For worship. The man who hears about free grace and concludes that he may now sin as he likes has revealed that he still regards sin as the good thing he is being asked to give up, and grace as the permission slip. He has the transaction backwards. Grace did not let us off a punishment and leave us in the same house. Christ came into the house, took its whole debt on himself, died there, and carried us out with him when he rose. He did not merely forgive us for living under sin’s roof. He ended the tenancy.
verseByVerse.note: Paul answers a charge his teaching of grace invited.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.

Do you not know? Notice how Paul opens. He is not teaching them something new. He is reminding them of something they were told at the beginning and have evidently not been using, which is the commonest condition in the Christian life. Most of us are not short of information. We are short of the habit of standing on what we already have.

All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. “Baptised into Christ” means united with him. Baptism is the sign of union with Christ, and especially with his death: when he died, we died with him. And the little word that does the heaviest lifting appears twice: baptised into Christ Jesus, baptised into his death. Not baptised because of his death, or in memory of it. Into. Paul is not describing a benefit transferred to you at a distance, like a payment made into your account by a stranger. He is describing your being placed inside an event. What happened to Christ is reckoned to have happened to you, because you are in him, which is why this letter can say you died, and were buried, and were raised, of things that occurred in Judea before you existed.

We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death. Baptism pictures burial: going under the water, as into the grave (Colossians 2:12). Immersion makes the picture vivid. And burial gets a mention, which otherwise looks like a decorative detail. Why mention being buried at all, when the death is the thing that matters? Because burial is what a society does to confirm that a death is real and final. A man in a coma may recover; a man in the ground has been formally and publicly given up on. The burial is the certificate. Paul includes it because he wants no possibility left open that the old life is merely convalescing somewhere.

In order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father. A strange phrase: raised by the glory of the Father. Not by the power of the Father, which is what we would have written. Glory is the weight and blazing reality of who God is, so the raising of Jesus was not merely an exercise of strength but an expression of the Father’s whole character, his verdict on his Son made visible. And the same glory stands behind your newness of life. The energy available for an ordinary Christian’s Tuesday is the energy that emptied the tomb.

We too might walk in newness of life. Rising from the water pictures rising with Christ. The purpose: a new kind of life. And notice what the purpose clause is not. Paul does not say we were raised in order to feel new, or to have new experiences. He says in order that we might walk. “Walk” is daily conduct, and it is the least dramatic verb available: ordinary, repetitive, unglamorous, and it gets you somewhere over time. “Newness” is a new quality of life, the life of the resurrection. Whatever the new life is, its natural expression is not an event but a gait.

A word before the debate. This is one of the passages where Christians divide, so a word about the subject first. Paul is not here chiefly settling how much water, or at what age. Those are real questions, but if you come to these verses looking only for ammunition you will miss what they are about. Paul’s subject is union with Christ, and baptism appears because it is the moment at which that union was publicly declared over you. It is the thing signified that this chapter is arguing from.

Where Christians differ: what does baptism do? Some see baptism as the moment when union with Christ actually happens (baptismal regeneration): Roman Catholic and Lutheran Christians say that in the rite God gives new birth and joins the person to Christ. Others, Martyn Lloyd-Jones among them, think Paul means not water baptism at all but the Spirit’s baptism into Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13). Verdict: Paul means water baptism, but as the sign and seal of a union God brings about by the Spirit through faith. Paul assumes that those he addresses are believers, for whom baptism expressed their faith. Union with Christ is by faith, wrought by the Spirit (Galatians 3:26–27; Ephesians 3:17); that is why Colossians says we were raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God (Colossians 2:12), and why Abraham’s sign followed his faith (4:11). Even when Peter says that baptism now saves you, he explains at once: not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience (1 Peter 3:21). The water does not save; Christ does. The reality is union with Christ; baptism is its God-given picture. Credobaptists see this as strong support for believers’ baptism by immersion, picturing death, burial and resurrection, and fitting a person who has already come to faith. Christians who baptise infants, many of them our dear brothers, see the sign as God’s promise to the children of believers (compare 4:11); but the dying and rising Paul describes here is something the baptised have entered by faith.

I was baptised as an infant, or I have never been baptised. What should I do? If you trust Christ and have never been baptised, be baptised: it is the Lord’s command for every disciple (Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38), and this passage shows how rich a gift it is. Speak to your church’s pastor. If you were baptised as an infant and have since come to faith, this app holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism belongs to those who profess faith, and so would encourage you to be baptised as a believer. Do it humbly, without contempt for the parents and church who brought you as a child in love and obedience as they understood it. Either way, the main thing is not the water but the union it declares: if you are in Christ, you have died and risen with him.

In a sentence. Do you not know that all who were baptised into Christ Jesus were baptised into his death, buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead by the Father’s glory, we too may live a new life?

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it uses Paul’s opening question. Take the sin you fight most often, and ask what you actually say to yourself in the moment of temptation. Most of us say some version of I must not, which is a fence, and fences are climbed. Paul’s argument supplies a different sentence: I am not that man any longer; that man is buried. It is not a stronger effort; it is a truer description. Notice which one comes to you unbidden. If it is always the first, you know the doctrine of this chapter and have not yet started using it. Remember your baptism today: you died and rose with Christ. Walk in newness of life.

For worship. The Christian life in this chapter does not run on resolutions. It runs on remembering what was done to us when we were put into Christ, and the water we went under was the public notice that a funeral had taken place. He went down into death first, alone, under the full weight of our sin; he lay in a borrowed grave; and he was raised by the glory of the Father, so that everyone joined to him might come up out of the water into a life that is his. We were buried with him. We walk with him. The glory that raised him is the glory that carries us.

parallels.desc: buried with him in baptism

verseByVerse.quote: For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his. We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his. We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.

For if we have been united with him in a death like his. The word Paul chooses for our union (symphytoi) is not a legal term at all. It means grown together, and the picture is organic, much as a graft grows when a shoot is cut into the stock of another tree and the two come to share one life. So this is not a partnership or an arrangement. What happens to the tree happens to the branch, because the branch is now living on sap it did not produce. His death is your death for the same reason that his life is your life.

We shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his. Both now, in new life, and at the last day, in a resurrection body. And notice the certainty Paul draws from the first clause: the second follows without any further condition. You cannot be grafted into a living tree and share only its dying. Nobody has ever been joined to Christ for the funeral and excluded from the resurrection.

We know that our old self was crucified with him. The “old self” (palaios anthrōpos, literally old man) is the person we were in Adam, before conversion (Ephesians 4:22; Colossians 3:9): the entire pre-conversion person, defined by solidarity with Adam and standing under that head. Crucified, put to death, with Christ (Galatians 2:20). Not being crucified gradually, but was crucified: a completed fact, an event that occurred when Christ died and was applied to you when you were joined to him.

If my old self was crucified, why does it keep getting up? The question every honest reader asks. Paul says the old man is dead. My experience says he was in the kitchen this morning, in a bad temper, saying something unkind. Either the doctrine is false or something has been misunderstood. Two distinctions clear it. The first is between the old self and remaining sin. The old self is not a part of you, like a compartment or a shadow self that survives alongside the new one. Paul’s phrase means the entire person you were, defined by Adam. That person is dead: the position is gone, the jurisdiction has ended, the man who belonged to Adam has been executed. What remains is not the old self but the habits, appetites and reflexes he trained into a body over many years, and those are a different thing. A country can change its government overnight; the officials who served the old regime are still in their offices on Monday morning, still know the procedures, and will carry on running things exactly as before unless somebody stops them. Their authority is gone. Their filing cabinets are not.

In order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing. The second distinction is in Paul’s own words. “Body of sin” is the person as controlled by sin. “Brought to nothing” (katargēthē) means rendered powerless, put out of action, put out of a job. Not annihilated, but stripped of its power. He is careful. He does not say sin is gone, or that its pull has ceased, or that you will not lose to it this week. He says it has been deposed. And a deposed power that still has adherents in the country is exactly what you experience every day: real fighting, genuine losses, and a war whose outcome is not in question.

The fight is evidence of life. This changes what the struggle means, and here lies the comfort for a reader discouraged by his own life. The presence of a fight is not evidence that the doctrine has failed; it is evidence that there are two parties. A man wholly under sin’s dominion does not fight it. He is not conflicted about it; he simply lives, and the accusations that trouble you would not trouble him. So the very thing that makes you doubt this passage, that you find yourself resisting, grieving, getting up again, is the thing the passage predicts. You are not failing to be dead. You are experiencing the resistance of a regime that has already lost.

So that we would no longer be enslaved to sin. The purpose: freedom from sin’s slavery. Freedom is the aim, not merely forgiveness. The verse is not describing a man who has been pardoned and left in the same condition. It is describing a man who has been taken out of service. And if you have ever wondered why the Christian life feels like a fight rather than a holiday, it is because you have been freed from an owner who has not yet accepted the verdict.

Will the struggle ever end? Yes. In this life it changes: battles that were fierce at the beginning often become quieter as the Spirit works and old habits are starved, though new ones appear, and some believers fight one besetting sin for decades. But the fight is not permanent. When a believer dies, his soul is made perfect in holiness and goes at once to be with Christ (Hebrews 12:23; Philippians 1:23), and at the resurrection his body is raised incorruptible (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Then the presence of sin will be gone as completely as its reign is gone now. Every resisted temptation today is the rehearsal of that freedom. The war you are in has an end date, and it is fixed by the God who has already won it.

In a sentence. If we have been united with him in a death like his, we will certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his, for we know our old self was crucified with him so that the body ruled by sin might be done away with, and we would no longer be slaves to sin.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it does not measure your success. Think about the last time you sinned in the way you most habitually sin. Ask what happened afterwards. Not whether you fell (you did) but what the falling produced: relief and no further thought, or a heaviness that would not settle until it had been dealt with? The second is not a sign of a weak Christian but of a live one. Corpses do not ache. The discomfort you feel about your own sin is one of the few pieces of evidence in the Christian life that cannot be manufactured. Then act on it: your old self was crucified, sin is no longer your master. Believe it, and say no to it.

For worship. The cross was not only where our debt was paid; it was where the man we used to be was put to death. Christ took our old self with him to Golgotha and did not bring it back. He grafted us into himself, so that we live on his life as a branch lives on the sap of the vine, and the One who shared our death will not withhold from us his resurrection. The tyrant has been deposed. The King has risen. And we are his.
verseByVerse.note: The “old self” (literally “old man”) is the person we were in Adam before union with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For one who has died has been set free from sin. Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For one who has died has been set free from sin. Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.

For one who has died has been set free from sin. “Set free” (dedikaiōtai) is literally has been justified, the court word of chapters 3 to 5. A dead man is released from all claims; the law has nothing more to say to him. And the principle was a commonplace, which is exactly why Paul uses it. Every legal system in the ancient world knew that death dissolves obligation; the rabbis said it, Roman law assumed it, and anyone in the room could have supplied an example. A creditor may pursue a debtor across three provinces and has no case against a corpse. The claim was perfectly valid yesterday. It is not that it has been forgiven; it is that the party it was filed against is no longer within the jurisdiction of the court. Having died with Christ, sin has no more legal claim on us.

Stronger than a debt written off. Set that beside the way most Christians actually think about their sin. We tend to imagine forgiveness as a debt written off by a generous creditor, which is true, and this letter has said so. But Paul is making a different point here, and it is stronger. The debtor has died. Sin is not standing at the counter having its claim graciously waived; it is standing at the counter discovering that the man it came for is not available, and never will be.

Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him. Union with his death guarantees union with his life. And verse 8 makes a move that ought to be noticed, because it changes the register. Everything up to this point has been argument: we know, do you not know, the reasoning from baptism and burial and grafting. Now Paul says we believe. He is not weakening the claim; he is being honest about how the second half of it is held. The death is behind us and can be argued from. The life with him is ahead of us and has to be trusted, because nobody has seen it yet. That names where faith is actually required. It is not usually difficult to believe that Christ died. The difficulty is believing that this arrangement ends well for you: that there is a life on the far side of your own grave, with him, in a body, and that the whole thing is not merely a sustaining story. Paul does not offer proof of that. He offers a link: if the first is true of you, the second follows, and the two cannot be separated because they are one union with one Person.

Dated and undated. Note the tense. The sentence is future, but it hangs on a past event that has already happened to you, which is why the New Testament can speak of the Christian’s future in the same breath as his history. Your death with Christ is dated. Your life with him is not yet dated, and is no less certain.

When will I live with him: now, at death, or at the resurrection? All three, in order. Now, you share his risen life by the Spirit (v. 4; Ephesians 2:5–6). At death, your soul goes immediately to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8); there is no sleep of the soul and no purgatory in between. And at his return, your body will be raised and you will live with him, body and soul, for ever in the new creation (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Paul’s we will also live with him reaches all the way to that last day, but it begins the moment you are joined to him. Death interrupts the body’s part in it; it never interrupts your being with him.

In a sentence. For anyone who has died has been set free from sin, and if we died with Christ, we believe we will also live with him.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it goes to which half of the verse you are actually resting on. Ask yourself what you think about, in a quiet moment, when you consider your own death. Not what you would say at a funeral: what arrives when it is your own. If the honest answer is a blank, or a vague hope, or a subject you steer away from, that is not necessarily unbelief. But notice that Paul, sitting in the same mortality as you, wrote we believe that we will also live with him, and treated it as the settled second half of something already begun. Say that sentence aloud about yourself today. The Christian’s confidence about the far side is not bravery. It is arithmetic done on a union already in force.

For worship. That is the shape of the whole chapter in two verses. Behind us, a death that has ended a jurisdiction; ahead of us, a life we have not yet seen. Both belong to the same Man, and we are in him, which means the only question about our future is one that was settled about his past. He died, and sin’s claim died with him. He lives, and he will not live without those he died for. You died with Christ, so you will live with him, now and for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him. For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him. For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.

Look at Christ. Observe where Paul has gone. He has been making claims about us, you died, you were buried, you will live, and a reader might reasonably ask how firm any of that is. So he stops talking about us altogether and spends two verses on Christ. Everything the chapter asserts about your security rests on facts about somebody else’s history, and that is deliberate. If you want to know how permanent your position is, do not examine your position. Examine his.

We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again. A fact with a date and no possibility of revision. That had never been true of anyone before. Lazarus came out of a tomb and was buried again later; the widow’s son at Nain died again in his time; every previous raising in Scripture was a reprieve, a postponement of an appointment that was eventually kept. The resurrection of Jesus is the only one in history that did not end in a second funeral. He has conquered death for ever, and holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). Death has been in charge of every human story ever told, and it lost one, permanently.

Death no longer has dominion over him. Death once had him; now never. Death exercised its authority over him for a fixed period, three days, and then lost it, and he walked out of its jurisdiction and has not been back.

For the death he died he died to sin, once for all. Be careful with the phrase died to sin, because it cannot mean for him exactly what it means for us. We die to sin as men leaving a dominion that owned us. He had never sinned and was never owned. Not that Christ had sin in himself, but he died to sin’s claim, its power and penalty, which he bore for us. He entered its territory voluntarily, bore its full penalty, and when it was paid, that transaction was complete and is now permanently behind him. Sin has no further business with him at all: nothing outstanding, no residual claim. And this is the key to the whole chapter: the same words, died to sin, are used of believers in verse 2. Since Christ had no sin, dying to sin cannot mean that sin was removed from inside him; it means that he passed out of the realm where sin and death had a claim. So it is with believers who died with him (see the note on vv. 1–2).

Once for all. Ephapax: a single, final act, never to be repeated (Hebrews 7:27; 9:12, 26; 10:10). It is one of the great words of the New Testament and the hinge of the letter to the Hebrews. It means once in a way that settles the matter and forbids repetition: not once so far, but once and therefore never again. And the argument it carries is this: a thing that must be repeated has not worked. The old sacrificial system ran on repetition precisely because nothing was ever finished; the same priest offered the same blood in the same room the following year, and the queue outside was made of the same people. This death ended the queue.

Why it matters for you. This is not Christological housekeeping. If you are in him, then sin’s claim on you was settled in the same transaction, and it cannot be reopened for the same reason it cannot be reopened against him. Your security is not that you have moved beyond sin’s reach by your own progress. It is that the account was closed on a Friday in Jerusalem and the receipt was issued on the Sunday, and neither can be recalled. Your sin was dealt with completely.

If Christ died once for all, what are we doing at the Lord’s Supper? Remembering and proclaiming that death, not repeating it. The Supper is not a fresh offering of Christ, as the Roman Catholic Mass teaches; Hebrews insists that he offered himself once, and that where there is forgiveness there is no longer any offering for sin (Hebrews 10:10–18). At the table the church proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26), and believers feed on Christ by faith, receiving afresh the benefits of a sacrifice already finished. The bread and cup do not add to the cross. They point to it, and the Spirit uses them to strengthen your hold on what it accomplished.

But the life he lives he lives to God. His risen life is wholly for God. Not to sin, not against sin, not in reaction to it: to God. The negative is finished and does not need revisiting; what remains is a life with a single direction. That is what Paul is about to ask of you, and it is why he has spent ten verses on what is true before issuing a single command.

In a sentence. We know that since Christ was raised from the dead, he cannot die again; death no longer rules him, for the death he died, he died to sin once for all, but the life he lives, he lives to God.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it will show you where your assurance actually sits. When you are anxious about your standing with God, notice what you instinctively go looking at. Almost all of us look inward: at the state of our faith, the quality of last week, whether we feel anything, whether the repentance was sincere enough. That is looking at a thing which genuinely does fluctuate, and the anxiety is therefore permanent. Paul in these two verses looks somewhere else entirely: at what happened to Christ, once, and cannot happen differently. Try it deliberately the next time the accusation comes. The question is not how am I doing? but is he still risen? There is only one possible answer, and it does not depend on your week. Then live to God.

For worship. Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again. Of all the sentences in this letter it is one to stand under longest. He died once, and the once was enough, and there is no circumstance in the future of the universe that will require him to do it a second time. He lives now wholly to his Father, and he lives for ever. The wounds are still on him. They are the only scars in existence that no longer mean anything is wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions.

So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin. The first command in Romans 6, and the first of the letter’s great commands to believers. Stop at the verb, because it has a history in this letter and the history is the whole point. “Consider” (logizesthe) is the accountant’s word: to reckon, count, enter in the books, the bookkeeping word of chapter 4. It first appeared as a word of crediting back at 2:26, where God credited an outsider with a standing he did not physically possess. It then dominated chapter 4, where Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness, eleven times in twenty-five verses. And now Paul takes the same verb and turns it round: God has been doing the reckoning all this time, and here he tells you to do some.

Not pretending, but counting on what is true. That settles what the command is not. It is not visualisation, and it is not talking yourself into a mood. An accountant who enters a sum that is not in the account is committing fraud; the entry is only honest if the money is there. So Paul is not asking you to pretend you are dead to sin. He is telling you to write down what is already the case, the same operation God performed when he credited righteousness that was genuinely Christ’s to people who genuinely had none. Reckoning never creates the fact. It aligns the books with it. You are dead to sin and alive to God, because you are in Christ. Believe it, and live from it.

The first imperative. Notice where the command comes. Ten verses of what is true of you, and only then something to do, and the something to do is not an action but an act of mind. Paul does not begin the practical section by telling you to fight harder or avoid more. He begins by telling you to believe something about yourself, on the grounds that a man who does not know who he is will fight the wrong war his whole life.

And alive to God in Christ Jesus. The two halves must be held together: dead to sin and alive to God. Most attempts at holiness are entirely negative, a list of things not done, a campaign of subtraction, and they fail predictably, because a life cannot be organised around an absence. You cannot make a room warm by removing the cold. Paul’s reckoning has a positive half: you are alive to God, which means available to him, responsive to him, in the room with him. The man who fights sin without cultivating that will find sin winning on ground he has left empty. And all of it is in Christ Jesus: not a state you hold by yourself, but what you are in him.

Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body. The sober half, which stops the chapter becoming a fantasy. That command would be pointless if sin were not making the attempt, so read the grammar honestly: Paul assumes an active, ongoing, daily campaign to restore a deposed regime. Sin still lives in us, and wants to reign again. Do not let it. And note precisely what is forbidden: not the presence of sin but its reign. He does not say let sin have no existence in you; he will spend chapter 7 on why that is not yet on offer. He says do not let it govern. The question is not whether sin is present, but whether it is giving orders that are being obeyed. A defeated army in the hills is a serious nuisance and a genuine danger. It is not the government. “Mortal body” means the body still subject to death and temptation, not yet glorified.

To make you obey its passions. Sinful desires. And Paul names the mechanism: sin reigns by making you obey its passions. It does not rule by force. It has no power to compel a Christian; what it has is persuasion, and its whole method is to present a desire as though it were an instruction. That is why temptation so rarely feels like a summons from an enemy and so often feels like simply wanting something. The lie is not usually about the thing desired. It is about your position: the suggestion that you have no real choice, that this is just how you are, that resistance is theoretical.

The pattern. First what God has done (the indicative), then what we must do (the imperative). Not become what you are not, but be what you are. The command presupposes freedom: sin cannot compel; it can only attempt to reign where it has been dethroned.

Is my body the problem? No. The body is God’s good creation, the Son of God took one, and it will be raised (8:11, 23). Paul is not teaching that the physical is evil, as some ancient philosophies did. He calls it the mortal body because it is still subject to death and is the arena where the daily battle is fought: sin works through bodily appetites, habits and senses. So the answer is not contempt for the body but rule over it, for God. Sleep, food, exercise and avoiding needless temptation are not unspiritual; they are part of keeping the battlefield in good order. Your body is not the enemy. It is the ground both sides want.

In a sentence. In the same way, count yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus, and do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey its evil desires.

On a Tuesday. Here is the practical form of the command. Next time you are tempted, do not begin by measuring how strong the pull is; that is a number that will always discourage you. Instead say two sentences to yourself, deliberately, in words: I am dead to this. I am alive to God in Christ. Then notice what happens to the temptation when it has been named as an ex-employer making a request rather than a master issuing an order. It may not evaporate; usually it does not. But it will have been correctly classified, and a great deal of the Christian fight is simply refusing to accept a false description of who you are. Then turn to God with the next thing you do.

For worship. The books have been correct in heaven since the cross. God reckoned our sin to his Son and his Son’s righteousness to us, and he has never had to alter an entry since. Paul’s first order is an accounting instruction rather than a moral one, because the work is already done: he is only telling us to bring our own copy into line with the Father’s. We are dead to sin and alive to God, in Christ Jesus, and the One who keeps the books has written our names beside his Son’s.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness. For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness. For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.

Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness. The two commands have different tenses in Greek, and the difference is the practical heart of the verse. The first is a standing prohibition: do not go on presenting your members to sin, describing a habit already in progress that must be broken. The second is a decisive act: present yourselves to God, definitely, as a thing done rather than a policy maintained. So Paul asks for two operations. One is the daily refusal of a groove already worn. The other is an act of handing over, of the sort a man can name and date.

Members. The word is not a vague term for the self; it means the parts of the body, and Paul means them literally: hands, eyes, tongue, feet, the physical equipment you actually sin and serve with. That is what saves the chapter from becoming interior and abstract. Holiness in Romans 6 is not primarily a state of mind. It is what your hands did this afternoon.

Instruments. The other word (hopla) can mean tools, but in Paul it more often means weapons: the equipment issued to a soldier. That fits everything the chapter has been saying about two regimes and a deposed power. Your body is not neutral territory in that conflict; it is equipment. It will be used by one side or the other today, and there is no third option in which it is used by nobody. Do not put it at sin’s service.

But present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life. Offer yourselves to God, as people raised from death (12:1). The reason given is not because you should, but because of what you are. It is a phrase about corpses. A man does not present a dead body to God for useful service; the thing has to be raised first, and it has been. So the surrender Paul asks for is not the desperate effort of somebody trying to be good enough. It is the natural act of somebody who has been given a life he did not have and is now deciding what to do with it.

And your members to God as instruments for righteousness. Your eyes, tongue and hands, used for God. The same body that sin once conscripted for unrighteousness is now offered to God as the tool of his purposes.

How do I actually present my members to God? Make it as concrete as Paul does, and go through them. Your eyes: what you choose to look at tonight, and what you refuse; whether you notice the lonely person at church. Your tongue: the conversation you will not join, the encouragement you will speak, the truth you will tell. Your hands: the work done honestly, the help given, the phone put down. Your feet: where you go and where you will not go. Begin the day by offering them to God in a sentence of prayer (12:1), and when you fail, offer them again rather than giving up. The act is renewed daily, but it is not complicated.

For sin will have no dominion over you. Read it slowly, because it is a promise and not an instruction. Paul has spent the chapter issuing commands, and here he stops commanding and simply states an outcome. He does not say sin ought not to have dominion, or that it will not if you are diligent. He says it will not. Sin will not be your master. You will still struggle with it (7:14–25), but it will not rule you. That is a sentence to take to bed on the evening of a bad failure.

Since you are not under law but under grace. The reason is the opposite of what any serious person would expect. Every instinct says that if you want a man to stop sinning, what he needs is more law: firmer rules, clearer boundaries, sharper accountability. Paul says law, as a way of standing with God, is precisely what keeps sin in power. It tells you what is right and supplies no ability to do it; it provokes what it forbids (5:20); and it leaves you under a condemnation that makes real repentance almost impossible, because a man who believes he is one failure away from being finished cannot afford to look honestly at himself. Sin thrives on that arrangement. Grace dismantles it. Not under the law as a way of acceptance with God, with its condemnation and its inability to change the heart. Under grace: God’s favour, which both forgives and empowers.

Where Christians differ: not under law? Antinomians take this to mean believers have no obligation to God’s moral law. Verdict: the very next verse asks, are we to sin because we are not under law? and answers, by no means! Not under law means not under its condemnation or as the means of justification. Believers are under the law of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:21) and fulfil the law by love (13:8–10). Paul has just given three commands in two verses, and he will give many more before the letter ends.

What it does not mean. Being under grace does not mean the commandments have no claim on you, and it certainly does not mean you will not sin, which is why verse 13 is written at all. What it means is that your standing does not depend on your performance, and therefore your failures cannot destroy you, and therefore you are finally free to fight them without terror, which is the only condition in which anybody has ever fought them successfully.

In a sentence. Do not offer any part of yourself to sin as a tool of wickedness, but offer yourselves to God as those brought from death to life, and your body parts to him as tools of righteousness, for sin shall no longer be your master, since you are not under law but under grace.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it comes straight out of the promise. When you fail badly, what do you reach for as the remedy? Most of us reach instinctively for law: a tightened rule, a new system, a resolution with more teeth, a private undertaking to be stricter. Notice how many times you have done that and how long each one lasted. Paul’s remedy runs the other way: go back to what is true of you, brought from death to life, not under law, and present the same members again today. It feels too easy because it costs you nothing in self-punishment, and self-punishment is the one payment sin is always happy to accept, since it keeps you looking at yourself. Give your eyes, tongue and hands to God today. Sin is not your master.

For worship. Sin lost its dominion not when we started keeping the rules better but when we changed kingdoms. The King who brought us from death to life does not stand over us with a list and a whip. He stands over us with grace, the favour that forgave us at the cross and now works in us by his Spirit, and he asks for our hands and eyes and tongues because he has already given us his own. Sin will have no dominion over us. He has said so, and his word is the most certain thing in the world.
verseByVerse.note: “Members” means the parts of the body — hands, eyes, tongue — used for good or evil.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Slaves of Righteousness: Freedom and Its Direction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The question of v. 15 replays the question of v. 1 in a new key: "Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace?" This is the libertarian version of the antinomian objection — if the law is not our master, then surely we are free to do anything. Paul's answer is again a flat denial, followed by a theological argument: freedom from sin does not mean freedom from all master; it means a change of master. Every human being serves either sin or righteousness — there is no neutral ground, no autonomous freedom that is subject to nothing.

The language of slavery runs throughout the passage and is deliberately shocking. Sin is a slave-master. Righteousness is a slave-master. The difference is in the direction: slavery to sin leads to death; slavery to righteousness leads to life and holiness. The Christian is not more free than the unbeliever in the sense of being subject to nothing; she is more free in the sense that she now serves the master whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light — the master whose service is perfect freedom.

The concluding verse is one of the most famous in the letter: "For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." The contrast between wages and gift is the contrast between law and gospel. Death is what sin earns — a wage paid in proportion to the work done. Eternal life is what God gives — a gift, free, unearned, proportionate not to the recipient's merit but to the giver's generosity. The entire letter is in this sentence.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace and the New Obedience

Romans 6:15–23 establishes that grace does not produce lawlessness but a new and deeper obedience — obedience that flows from a changed heart rather than a legal compulsion. The Reformers distinguished between the "old obedience" (driven by fear of punishment and desire for reward) and the "new obedience" (driven by love for God and gratitude for grace). Calvin was particularly insistent that the justified Christian is not released from obedience but liberated for it — the law now functions as a guide for the regenerate, not as a court that condemns. The third use of the law: the Christian, freed from condemnation, embraces the law as the expression of the will of the God she loves.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's slavery metaphor was immediately intelligible to a first-century audience in which slavery was the defining social institution. Every person knew what it meant to be owned by a master, to have their labour and their body subject to another's will. Paul's redeployment of this metaphor is arresting: you were a slave before, and you are a slave now — the only question is whose slave you are. The liberated Christian is not autonomous; she is re-owned, by a Master who purchased her with his own blood. Now: The modern West prizes autonomy above almost everything — the right to define oneself, to determine one's own values, to answer to no authority beyond the self. Romans 6 is a direct challenge to this: the autonomous self is a myth. Every person serves something — appetite, ambition, approval, comfort, identity. The gospel does not offer escape from all masters; it offers the only master worth serving.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means! Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then? Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means! Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?

Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means! A second form of the objection (v. 1), and the difference is worth marking. There the question was are we to continue in sin: shall we stay where we are? Here it is shall we sin: not keep on sinning, but commit acts of sin, a single act, an occasional liberty, the reasonable proposition that if the law is no longer my master then the odd indulgence costs nothing. It is the more plausible objection of the two, and most of us have made it without noticing, usually in the form this once will not matter. It receives the same categorical answer.

If you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey. Paul’s reply does not argue about the size of the act at all. He says: look at what obedience does. Present yourself to someone as an obedient slave and you are that person’s slave, not because a court has ruled it, but because that is what obedience is. Each act of yielding is a small act of enlistment. So the question can I get away with this once? is the wrong question entirely: the issue was never whether you would be caught but what you were becoming while you did it. And the principle is observable in ordinary life, which is why Paul assumes his readers will grant it immediately. Nobody decides to become an alcoholic; a man decides, several thousand times, to have a drink. Nobody chooses to become the sort of person who cannot be trusted with a confidence; he chooses to repeat one interesting thing. Habits are not formed by decisions about habits. They are formed by decisions about single occasions.

There is no third option. Everyone serves someone. There is no neutral freedom (Matthew 6:24; John 8:34). Paul offers two masters and no independent territory. The idea that a person could serve nothing, self-directed, autonomous, answerable to no authority beyond his own preferences, is not presented as a dangerous choice. It is not presented at all, because Paul does not regard it as a possibility. And on inspection he is right, which anyone can verify without leaving his own life. The man who has thrown off every external authority is not thereby unruled; he is ruled by his appetites, and appetites are the least merciful masters available, because they never say thank you and never say enough. Consider what actually governs a free modern person’s decisions: what he wants, what others will think, how he wishes to be seen, what he is afraid of losing. Those are not the absence of a master. They are four of them, and none was chosen deliberately, and none can be resigned from.

Either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness. Two masters, two destinations. And so the word freedom means something different in this chapter from what it means in ordinary speech. We use it to mean the absence of constraint. Paul uses it to mean being under the right authority: being owned by the one for whom you were made, which is the only condition in which any creature functions properly. A fish in a net is constrained; a fish on a riverbank is free of the water and dying of it.

Can a Christian give himself back to sin and so lose his salvation? Arminian Christians read the verse that way: a believer who keeps presenting himself to sin becomes its slave again, and the end of that road is death. But Paul is describing two kinds of people, not one person changing sides. He goes straight on: you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart (v. 17). A Christian still sins, sometimes badly, but sin is no longer his master (v. 14). Someone who gives himself to sin without struggle or repentance is not showing that he has lost his salvation; he is raising the question whether he ever had it (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and God uses it to keep his own, from whose love nothing can separate them (8:38–39).

In a sentence. Shall we sin because we are not under law but grace? By no means! Do you not know that when you offer yourselves to someone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one you obey, whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness?

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it is more revealing than asking what you believe. Over the last month, what actually decided your choices at the points where it cost you something? Not what you would have said governs you: what did. Trace three or four real decisions back to their reasons: the evening you spent as you did, the thing you did not say, the money, the way you handled the awkward conversation. Whatever turns up repeatedly at the end of those chains is a master, whether or not you would ever have used the word. Almost nobody finds only one, and almost nobody finds the one he would have named. Bring what you find to Christ, and give the next of those decisions to him.

For worship. If freedom meant self-rule, the Christian life would be a matter of achieving independence, and every failure would be evidence that you are not yet free enough. It does not. Your standing was never that you had become your own man. You were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:20), and the deed of sale names a Master who has already died for the slave: the one arrangement in the history of ownership where the property is safer than the owner. Everyone serves a master. Ours gave his life for us, and gives life to all who serve him.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, that you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart to the standard of teaching to which you were committed, and, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, that you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart to the standard of teaching to which you were committed, and, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness.

But thanks be to God. A spontaneous doxology in the middle of an argument. Look at what Paul does not say, because it is the most instructive thing in the verse. These Christians have turned from a genuinely wicked past and now obey from the heart. Any pastor would want to encourage that. Paul does not congratulate them. He thanks God, not them, and the grammatical result is that the only party commended in a sentence about their obedience is somebody else. That is not false modesty on their behalf. It follows from everything the chapter has argued: a slave does not transfer himself, and a dead man does not decide to be raised. Conversion is God’s work. If they are obeying from the heart, it is because they were given a different heart, and the right response to somebody else’s work is gratitude rather than applause. That is worth remembering the next time you catch yourself quietly pleased with your own spiritual progress. The progress may be entirely real. It is simply not yours to be pleased about.

You who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart. “From the heart”: not outward conformity, but inner obedience, the new covenant promised by the prophets, the law written on the heart and a new spirit within (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26–27). The phrase names the thing that distinguishes Christian obedience from every counterfeit. Slaves in the ancient world obeyed with their hands. Nobody expected a slave to agree; compliance was the whole transaction, and what he thought about it in the evening was his own affair. Paul says these slaves obey from the heart, which breaks the original metaphor and is exactly his point. The new Master has done something no owner has ever managed: he has changed what the servant wants.

To the standard of teaching to which you were committed. “Standard” (typos) is a pattern, a mould: the die into which molten metal is poured, or the stamp that leaves its shape on a coin. And note the direction, which is the reverse of what we would write. We would say the teaching was delivered to them. Paul says they were handed over to the teaching. The gospel is not a substance you take possession of and store; it is a shape you are poured into, and what comes out bears the impression of the mould. Christian teaching shapes the believer.

Doctrine as a mould. That explains something about doctrine that is easily missed by people who find it dry. If teaching is a mould, then what you steadily attend to will steadily form you, and this happens whether or not you are trying. Nobody sits under years of preaching and remains unshaped; the question is only what shape. That is also why a Christian cannot be indifferent to what is taught in the place he attends. You are not merely evaluating a message. You are standing in a mould.

And, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness. Freed from one master, bound to another. Christian freedom is not independence but a new, good slavery: slavery to the master who made us for himself, which is the paradoxical freedom of those who have found him.

What if my obedience feels mostly like duty? Almost nobody obeys from the heart perfectly or consistently; motives in this life come mixed, and a man who waits until his are pure before he acts will never act at all. Doing the right thing when you do not feel like it is not hypocrisy; it is often love choosing God over a mood. The right response to discovering mixed motives is not to stop obeying but to bring them, mixed, to the God who is changing them, and to ask him to make you love what he commands. And notice, as evidence, that you mind about the mixture at all. A slave who merely complies does not lie awake examining his sincerity.

In a sentence. But thanks be to God that, though you used to be slaves to sin, you have come to obey from the heart the pattern of teaching that has claimed your allegiance, and having been set free from sin, you have become slaves to righteousness.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it goes to the phrase from the heart. Take an area of obedience where you are currently doing the right thing, and ask what would happen if the external pressure came off: if nobody would ever know, if the person you would disappoint were not watching, if there were no consequence at all. Would you still do it? Obedience that survives the removal of the audience is obedience from the heart. Obedience that does not is compliance, and compliance is what the old master got. And look at what you are pouring yourself into each week: the teaching, the reading, the voices you listen to most. Let the gospel mould you. Obey it from the heart.

For worship. Something happened to these people that they did not do: they were slaves, and now they obey from the heart, and the change ran deeper than behaviour. The God who freed them did not merely change their circumstances; he changed their desires, writing his law on hearts that had been stone. If that has happened to you, the right response is the one Paul models: not satisfaction at how far you have come, but thanks to the One who moved you. Thanks be to God.

verseByVerse.quote: I am speaking in human terms, because of your natural limitations. For just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am speaking in human terms, because of your natural limitations. For just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.

I am speaking in human terms, because of your natural limitations. The apology tells you something about how Paul handles language. He has just built an entire argument on slavery, and now he half-withdraws it. Not because the metaphor is wrong, but because it is inadequate in one direction. Slavery was part of everyday life across the Roman world; many in the Roman church were slaves or former slaves, and Paul uses an image they knew. But no image drawn from a brutal human institution can carry what it is like to belong to God. Slavery communicates ownership, obligation and total claim, all of which are true. It cannot communicate that the Master is a Father, that the service is freedom, or that the slave is loved. So Paul uses it, and then tells you not to press it too far, since serving God is not oppressive. That is a useful rule for reading every biblical image: find what it was chosen to convey, and do not make it say what it was never built to say.

Because of your natural limitations. Literally, the weakness of your flesh. He is not insulting them. He means that we are creatures who think in pictures, who grasp ownership and obligation more readily than we grasp union, and who therefore need concrete images to get hold of spiritual realities. That is a description of everyone, and God has arranged his book accordingly: it is full of vineyards, sheep, courtrooms, marriages and slaves rather than definitions.

Just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to more lawlessness. This is a diagnosis of how sin actually works over time. You presented your members to impurity, and the result was not satisfaction but more lawlessness. Sin multiplies sin. It does not deliver and then rest. It escalates. What served last year does not serve this year; the dose that once produced an effect produces nothing, and the appetite that was fed has grown by being fed. Each sin makes the next easier. Anyone who has watched an addiction, in himself or somebody he loves, recognises the mechanism immediately, and Paul’s point is that it is not confined to the obvious vices. The man who begins by shading the truth in small ways finds it takes progressively larger departures to serve the same purpose. The habit of criticism does not fill up and stop; it needs fresh material. Pornography is the plainest modern example because the escalation is so measurable, and it is the same law that operates in a man’s ambition or his temper. Sin cannot be kept at a fixed level by an act of will, because increase is not an abuse of it. It is what it does.

So now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification. Then Paul does something quietly hopeful: he says the other direction has a slope too. The same escalating grammar, running upward. Now put the same energy into righteousness. Righteousness leads to sanctification: growing holiness, the progressive reorientation of the whole person toward God. Holiness also builds on itself. The thing you resisted with difficulty at thirty is not the same size at fifty, not because you have become impressive but because ten thousand small refusals have worn a channel. Neither slope is fast. Both are real.

For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness. One of the great ironies in the letter. He says it flatly, without comment, and the sarcasm is all the sharper for being unstated. Free from righteousness: it had no claim on you. That was the freedom on offer: free from any obligation to be good, free from the whole business of holiness, entirely at liberty in that department, and the previous verse has just described where that liberty was heading. A grim freedom. Remember it the next time freedom is presented as an escape from God’s claims. That freedom is genuinely available. Paul has just told you what it produces.

Is it demeaning to call ourselves slaves of God? It would be if the Master were like human masters. He is not. Human slavery, especially as it was practised in Rome and later in the Atlantic trade, was a terrible evil, and Paul knows its cruelty. He borrows only one thing from it: total belonging. Everything else the Bible says about this Master reverses the institution. He bought his slaves with his own blood, he calls them friends (John 15:15) and sons (8:15), he serves them at table (Luke 12:37), and his yoke is easy (Matthew 11:30). To be his is not to lose your dignity but to find it, because you were made for him. The only truly degrading slavery is the one Paul has just described.

In a sentence. Paul uses everyday terms because of human limitations: just as they used to offer themselves as slaves to impurity and ever-increasing wickedness, so now they should offer themselves as slaves to righteousness leading to holiness, for when they were slaves to sin, they were free from the control of righteousness.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it is about direction rather than position, which is the only fair way to measure a slope. Take something you struggle with and compare it not with last week but with five years ago. Is it costing you more to sin than it used to, or less? Does it take more to satisfy it, or less? And on the other side: is there anything that used to be a battle and is now largely settled, not because you gave up, but because it stopped being a live question? Those two answers together will tell you which slope you are standing on far more accurately than an audit of the last seven days. Then take one small step up the right slope today, and put into it the energy you once gave to sin.

For worship. The God who made us did not leave us on the downward slope where every sin made the next one easier and every appetite grew by being fed. He came down it himself, all the way to the bottom, and lifted us onto another road, where his grace compounds as surely as sin once did. The Master we serve now is a Father, his service is freedom, and the road he has set us on rises, step by small step, toward the holiness of his own Son.
verseByVerse.note: Slavery was part of everyday life across the Roman world; many in the church were slaves or former slaves.

verseByVerse.quote: But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life.

But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? Paul invites a backward look, and notice the form: he is not lecturing but asking, and the answer is meant to come from the reader. It is the question sin never invites you to ask, because sin lives entirely in the future tense. Its whole method is anticipation: what this will feel like, what it will settle, how much better the evening will be. It has nothing whatever to say about the morning after, and it never volunteers a retrospective. So Paul makes them look backwards, and the answer he expects is not a list of pleasures regretted but something more devastating: nothing. The Greek can be read so that the honest answer to what fruit did you get? is that there was none. Not bad fruit: no fruit. Sin is not an alternative crop; it is a season of work with an empty barn at the end of it, and the only thing left in the hand is the shame.

The honest inventory. Be concrete about it, because everyone reading this has the material. Think of something you did that you would not want said aloud. Now ask what it actually yielded. Not what it promised: what you have, now, as a result. Almost always the honest inventory reads the same way: an hour that no longer exists, a relationship altered by a degree nobody else noticed, a memory that arrives uninvited years later while you are doing something else. That is the harvest. Shame, regret, and death. It is why Paul does not need to argue the point; he only has to ask the question and wait.

Of which you are now ashamed. The word is chosen carefully, because shame has a particular character that guilt does not. Guilt says I did something bad; shame says I cannot look at it. It is the impulse to turn the face away, which is exactly what Adam did in the garden, and exactly why sin requires concealment to survive. A man does not hide what has done him good.

What it does not mean. A backward look can be turned into a weapon against the wrong person. Paul says of which you are now ashamed, and notice who is speaking: he is describing Christians looking back at a life they have left, and he does it in one sentence and moves on to the fruit they are bearing now. He does not have them dwell there. If you are a believer who cannot stop rehearsing an old sin, replaying it at night, unable to let it be finished, this verse is not asking that of you. The shame here has a purpose, and it is diagnostic, not punitive: it is meant to make the old master look like what he is, and then you are meant to look at the new one. Chapter 8 will say there is therefore now no condemnation, and it will not add except for that.

For the end of those things is death. The destination of sin. Not only where it finishes, but what it was always aiming at.

But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God. “Slaves of God”: the highest freedom. And see the great structural point of these two verses, which is easy to read past. The same four stages run in both directions: a master, a service, a fruit, and an end. Sin as master produced a service, whose fruit was shame, whose end is death. God as master produces a service, whose fruit is sanctification, whose end is eternal life. Nothing in the framework changes. Only the first term does, and everything downstream follows from it. That is why this chapter has spent twenty verses on ownership rather than on techniques for behaving better. Change the master and the rest of the chain reorganises itself.

The fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life. Two harvests: shame and death, or holiness and eternal life. Sanctification is the road; eternal life is the end. No one reaches the end without the road (Hebrews 12:14). And Paul has chosen an agricultural image rather than a mechanical one. Fruit is slow, it is seasonal, and it is not produced by the branch straining. Nobody ever grew an apple by effort. It appears because the tree is alive and attached and has been standing in the right place for long enough, which is the honest answer to any Christian discouraged by how gradual his own sanctification looks. You are not assembling something. You are growing, and growth is not visible on the timescale at which we tend to inspect ourselves.

Then is eternal life earned by holiness? No. Paul will say in the very next verse that eternal life is a gift. Holiness is not the price of heaven but the road that leads there, and God himself lays the road. Those he justifies he also sanctifies (8:29–30; Philippians 1:6), so that no one who is truly his arrives at the end without having been changed on the way. That is the point of Hebrews 12:14: not that we must become holy enough to deserve to see the Lord, but that the people who see him are people he has been making holy. If you are in Christ, the fruit is coming, slowly and surely, because the life in the branch is his.

In a sentence. What benefit did they reap then from things they are now ashamed of? Those things end in death. But now, freed from sin and enslaved to God, the benefit they reap leads to holiness, and the result is eternal life.

On a Tuesday. Look both ways, as Paul asks. Take the sin that tempts you most this week and, before you are in the moment, write down honestly what it yielded the last time: not what it promised, what it left. Keep the note where you will see it when the temptation comes, because sin will only ever tell you about tonight. Then write one fruit of the Spirit you have seen grow in you, however small, and thank God for it. Ask what sin has really given you. Then compare it with what God gives.

For worship. Behind us, a service that paid nothing and left us unable to look at the receipts. Ahead of us, an end we have not earned and cannot forfeit. And between them, the only thing that changed: not our capacity, not our resolve, but who owns us. The God who took us from the old master did not set us adrift; he planted us in his Son, and he is patient with fruit, as every good gardener is. The harvest he is growing in us ends in eternal life, and he has never lost a crop.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. — Romans 6:23
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

For the wages of sin is death. The word for wages (opsōnia) is not the general term for payment. It is the soldier’s word: the ration money paid out to troops, issued at intervals, the small regular allowance a man drew for his service. Wages were the regular pay of a soldier or labourer: what is earned. Sin pays, and its pay is death: physical, spiritual, eternal. You earn it. And the soldier’s word sharpens the picture in an unexpected direction. Sin does not pay its people in a single catastrophic settlement at the end. It pays them in instalments, on time, throughout the campaign.

Paid as you go. That corrects the way we usually hear this verse. We imagine death as the bill arriving at the end of a long life, the reckoning we shall have to face eventually. The soldier’s pay is drawn as he goes. Sin has been paying you all along, in the currency it deals in: the friendship that thinned and was never repaired, the capacity for wonder that dulled, the prayer that got harder to say, the person you can no longer be honest with. Those are not warnings of a future wage. They are the wage, being paid, in small coin, on schedule. The final payment is not a different currency. It is the same one, in full.

Is death really what every sin deserves, and does it mean hell? Yes, and the reason is not the size of the act but the greatness of the One sinned against. Every sin is treason against the infinitely holy God, the Fountain of all life, and turning from him is turning from life itself. So the death sin earns is not only the grave. It is the second death (Revelation 20:14), conscious and eternal separation from God’s goodness under his just wrath, which Jesus himself described more often than anyone (Matthew 25:46; Mark 9:48). That is sobering, and it should be. But Paul does not state the wage to crush you. He states it so that you will see the size of the gift beside it.

But the free gift of God is eternal life. Notice the grammar of the second half, because Paul deliberately breaks the parallel he has just built, as he did throughout chapter 5. The tidy version would be the wages of sin is death, but the wages of righteousness is eternal life. Nobody has ever earned the second wage, so he changes the noun. Not wages, but a gift (charisma, a gift of grace). Death is earned; life is given. You cannot earn eternal life, any more than you can avoid earning death apart from Christ. The two halves of the sentence do not balance, and the whole gospel is in the imbalance.

Hell is earned and heaven is not. That produces a curious asymmetry worth stating plainly. Nobody will be in hell who did not earn it, and nobody will be in heaven who did. That sentence offends most people the first time they meet it, but it is the only arrangement in which God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus, which is precisely what this letter has been arguing since 3:26.

In Christ Jesus our Lord. The gift comes only in him. The verse does not end with a benefit. It ends with a preposition and a name. Eternal life is not a free-floating spiritual commodity that God distributes, a substance he transfers to you at conversion and which you then possess independently, the way a man might be given a sum of money and go home with it. It is in a Person, the One who is himself the resurrection and the life (John 11:25). To receive eternal life is to receive Christ; whoever has the Son has life (1 John 5:12). That means it is not stored anywhere you could lose it, and it is not held in an account you could overdraw. To have it, you must have him; and if you have him, you cannot have less of it than he has.

Our Lord. The last word of the chapter is Lord, and it is not a flourish. Twenty-three verses about two masters, two slaveries, two harvests and two ends, and Paul finishes by naming the owner. He does not sign off with our Saviour, though he is that. The chapter has been about who you belong to, and it closes by saying so.

How do I receive the gift? The way any gift is received: by taking it, not by paying for it. Turn from trusting yourself, and trust Christ Jesus, who died for sinners and rose again, as your Saviour and your Lord. Tell him so, in your own words. You do not need to tidy your life first; a gift that required qualifications would be a wage. And if you have already received him, go on receiving: the gift is not a single transaction you once completed but a Person you live with, and every day you may come back to him and find that life in him is still yours.

In a sentence. For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

On a Tuesday. Here is the plainest test in the chapter. Ask which half of the verse you expect to receive, and then ask why. If your reason contains anything about yourself, that you have tried, that you believe the right things, that you are not as bad as some, you have answered from the first half of the sentence, where things are earned. The only answer the verse permits is a name that is not yours. And notice how ordinary this makes the people around you. There is no third category in the verse: everyone you meet today is drawing one of two things, a wage they have earned or a gift they have not. Pray for one of them by name, and be ready to tell them where the gift is found.

For worship. Wages and a gift, set against each other in one line, and the arithmetic is deliberately unbalanced. Sin pays, punctually and in full, and what it hands over is a grave. God does not pay at all. He gives, and what he gives is not merely a longer life or a better one but his own Son, and with him eternal life, the very life of God shared with the creature who had earned only death. Nobody has ever earned the second half of that verse. That is the entire reason it can be relied upon.
verseByVerse.note: Wages were the regular pay of a soldier or labourer — what is earned. A gift is not.

How can we who died to sin still live in it?<sup>3</sup>Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?<sup>4</sup>We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.<sup>5</sup>For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his.<sup>6</sup>We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.<sup>7</sup>For one who has died has been set free from sin.<sup>8</sup>Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.<sup>9</sup>We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him.<sup>10</sup>For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.<sup>11</sup>So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.<sup>12</sup>Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions.<sup>13</sup>Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness.<sup>14</sup>For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.<sup>15</sup>What then? 7.title: The Law, the Flesh, and the Struggle Within
7.overview:
Romans 7 is one of the most debated chapters in the New Testament. The first six verses use the analogy of marriage to explain the Christian's release from the law — just as death dissolves a marriage, so the death of the old self has dissolved the law's claim on the believer. Verses 7–25 then address the relationship between the law and sin in a passage of such raw psychological honesty that it has divided interpreters for centuries: is Paul describing his experience before or after his conversion?

The Reformed tradition, following Luther and Calvin, has generally argued that vv. 7–25 describe the experience of the regenerate person — not as the normal steady state of the mature Christian, but as the honest account of the ongoing struggle that even the believer has with indwelling sin. The person who says "I delight in the law of God in my inner being" (v. 22) is not an unregenerate person; the unregenerate person has no such delight. The chapter is not a counsel of despair but a radical honesty about the nature of the Christian struggle — which ends, in v. 25, with the triumphant answer: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Released from the Law to Bear Fruit for God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul uses the analogy of marriage to make a point about the law's jurisdiction. A woman is bound to her husband by law as long as he lives; if he dies, she is free to marry another. In the same way, the Christian has "died" to the law through her union with Christ's death — she is no longer bound to the law as a system of earning and condemnation. She is now married to another — to Christ who was raised from the dead — so that she might bear fruit for God.

The point is not that the law is bad (v. 7 will explicitly deny this) but that the law was never the instrument of life.
