Under the law's jurisdiction, the sinful passions "aroused by the law were at work in our members to bear fruit for death" (v. 5). This does not mean the law created those sinful passions; it means that the sinful nature, encountering prohibition, is provoked — not helped — by the law. The law reveals and aggravates what is already there; it cannot remove it.

But now — freed from the law, joined to Christ — the Christian serves "in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code" (v. 6). This is not antinomianism; it is the fulfilment of Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 — the new covenant in which the law is written on the heart by the Spirit, not merely imposed from without by the letter. The motive for obedience has changed: from fear of penalty to love of the God who has shown such grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Death to Law: Liberation for Obedience

The believer's death to the law (vv. 4, 6) has been the source of great misunderstanding. Paul is not teaching that the Christian is released from the moral content of the law — he will demonstrate in chapters 12–15 that the redeemed life is the life of love, which is the fulfilment of the law (13:8–10). He is teaching that the believer's relationship to the law has changed: no longer subject to it as a court that condemns, the Christian is now free to embrace its moral demands as the expression of the will of the God she loves. Calvin's third use of the law: a guide for the regenerate, not a goad for the condemned.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The marriage analogy was immediately accessible to Paul's Jewish readers, for whom marriage law was well understood. The death that dissolves the marriage — the death of the old self in union with Christ's death — was the theologically startling element. Paul is saying: you belong to a new husband now. The old master (law as condemning power) is dead to you; the new master (Christ) is alive to you. Serve him accordingly. Now: Many Christians live as though they are still married to the law — haunted by condemnation, driven by religious duty, exhausted by the performance of obligation. Romans 7:1–6 is the declaration of liberty: you have died to that system. You are joined to Christ. Serve him from love, not from fear.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know, brothers — for I am speaking to those who know the law — that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives? For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or do you not know, brothers — for I am speaking to those who know the law — that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives? For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.

Meaning first. Romans 7 explains the believer’s relationship to the law of Moses. First, believers have died to the law through Christ, as a widow is released from her marriage, so that they belong to Christ and serve in the new way of the Spirit (vv. 1–6). Second, the law is not sin; it is holy, righteous and good, but sin used it to provoke and kill (vv. 7–13). Third, Paul describes the painful struggle of one who loves God’s law but still finds sin at work in him: I do not do the good I want. The cry “Wretched man that I am!” is answered at once: Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord (vv. 14–25). The law can show sin, but cannot defeat it; only Christ and the Spirit can. And the chapter that goes deeper than any other into the misery of the human heart ends not with a technique but with a name.

For I am speaking to those who know the law. Jews, and God-fearing Gentiles familiar with Moses. Note who he says he is addressing. Paul is arguing from something his readers already grant, which is the strongest kind of argument and the most respectful. And that respect runs through the whole chapter. This is the passage in which he will insist that the law is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good (v. 12). Whatever he is about to say about being released from it, he is not disparaging it. He is doing something more delicate: explaining how a good thing can be the wrong thing to be married to.

That the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives. A basic legal principle, which every court in the ancient world and the modern one recognises: death ends legal obligations. A dead man cannot be sued, taxed or summoned. The binding force of the marriage covenant is real and serious, but it is dissolved by death. Paul is not allegorising marriage; he is establishing the principle of death as the end of legal obligation, a principle he will apply to the believer’s relationship to the law of Moses.

Why marriage? The choice of illustration is not incidental. Paul has debt and slavery available and has used both already in this letter. He picks marriage, and for a reader who knows the Old Testament that is not a random legal example but the covenant image. Israel is the wife; her idolatry is adultery; Hosea was told to marry a woman who would betray him so the nation could see what it had done. So the illustration carries what a lesson about debt could not: exclusive belonging, a covenant rather than a contract, and, as verse 4 will say, fruitfulness. Marriages are meant to produce something.

The pieces do not line up, and need not. Here is a difficulty a careful reader will have noticed, and it should be said out loud rather than smoothed over. In the illustration, the husband dies and the wife goes free. In the application, it is not the law that dies: Paul says you have died to the law (v. 4). The correspondence appears to swap round halfway through. Commentators have tied themselves in knots trying to make every element line up, and the honest answer is that Paul is not building an allegory in which each part maps onto another. He is establishing a single principle, that death dissolves legal obligation, and then applying it. Whoever does the dying, the bond is over. Pressing an illustration further than its author intended is one of the commonest ways to misread the Bible, and this passage catches people out with it.

What it does not mean. This is not a passage about divorce and remarriage. Paul is citing a commonplace everyone accepted in order to make a point about the law; he is not legislating for the woman whose marriage has ended. Anybody looking for teaching on that must go where it is actually given (Matthew 19; 1 Corinthians 7), and the next verse says more.

Married to the law. Then what the illustration is really for, which is where it stops being technical. A great many Christians are, in practice, still married to the law, and it is worth describing what that marriage is like, because people living in it rarely name it. It is life with a spouse who is never satisfied. He is not cruel and he is not wrong; his standards are perfectly reasonable and every criticism he makes is accurate. He simply notices everything you fail at and never once says well done. He offers no help: he tells you what is required and leaves you to it. And you cannot leave, because he is entirely in the right and you have nothing to plead. That is religion under law, and it produces exactly what you would expect: a conscientious person, permanently tired, who cannot enjoy God and cannot admit it.

The remedy. The remedy this passage offers is not that the spouse lowers his standards. He does not; the law is holy and stays holy. It is that the marriage has ended, by a death, and you are now joined to someone else. And Paul’s way of describing that new husband, in the next verses, is that he was raised from the dead. This one does not die, and this one is not waiting to be satisfied, because he has already satisfied everything the first husband required.

So do the Ten Commandments no longer apply to me? They still apply, but not as a husband you must satisfy to be accepted. Through Christ you died to the law as a covenant of works: its demand that you earn life by keeping it, and its sentence of condemnation when you do not. That relationship is over. But the moral law has not been abolished. It still shows what love for God and neighbour looks like, and Paul will quote the commandments to Christians as the shape of the life they now live (13:8–10). The difference is that you now keep them as a wife who is loved, by the Spirit’s help (8:4), and not as a debtor trying to stay in credit. The Reformers called this the third use of the law: a guide for the redeemed, not a ladder to heaven.

In a sentence. Don’t you know, brothers and sisters who know the law, that the law has authority over someone only while they live? For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he is alive, but if he dies, she is released from the law that bound her to him.

On a Tuesday. A woman long married to a severe man often goes on behaving as though he were watching, years after the funeral: checking herself, bracing, anticipating the criticism. So take an ordinary act of obedience this week, your praying, your giving, your Sunday, and ask honestly which husband it is being done for. Is it done to avoid a bad conscience, to keep something at bay, to stay in credit? Or is it done because you belong to somebody and want to be with him? The act is identical in both marriages. The person doing it is not. Death ends obligations, and in Christ you died to the law’s condemnation; the residue of the old marriage is worth noticing, and worth bringing to the new husband.

For worship. The law has not been abolished, weakened or found at fault. It is alive and perfectly holy and still says exactly what it always said. What has happened is that the person it had a claim on has died, in Christ, and the one now standing in her place is married to someone who has already met every demand the first husband ever made. Blessed be the Bridegroom who paid the dowry with his own life, and who will never once look at his bride with that tired, unsatisfied face.

parallels.desc: a wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.

She will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. Marriage is binding for life. And feel the force of the word Paul is willing to use. Adulteress: not an impropriety, not a technical irregularity, but the strongest word available for covenant betrayal. He is making the point that the bond is not a formality that lapses quietly. While the first husband lives, going to another is not merely disallowed; it is treachery, and everyone would call it that. The law’s claim is that serious.

But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress. Death frees her to remarry. And this is startling. The same act, belonging to another man, is treachery in one circumstance and entirely blameless in the other, and the only thing that has changed is a death. Nothing about the woman has altered. Her character is the same, her history is the same, and the man she goes to may be the very same man. What has changed is her standing, and standing is not a matter of degree. There is no partial adultery and no half-widow. She is either bound or she is free, and a funeral is what moves her from one category to the other.

A change of category. That is the whole reason Paul chose an illustration with such uncomfortable vocabulary. He needs a case where the transition is absolute rather than gradual, because that is precisely what he is claiming about the believer. Christians are not people whom the law is gradually letting off, whose obligations are slowly being reduced as they improve. The change is a change of category, effected by a death, complete on the day it happened.

Free to belong. And note who is free to do what. The woman is free from that law: not from all law, not from marriage as such, and certainly not free in the sense of belonging to nobody. She is free to be married again. Freedom in this passage is never freedom from attachment; it is freedom to be attached to someone new, which is exactly what verse 4 is about to say and exactly what chapter 6 spent twenty-three verses establishing.

Where Christians differ: divorce and remarriage. Some use these verses to say remarriage after divorce is never allowed while a former spouse lives. Verdict: Paul is using marriage as an illustration, not giving a full teaching on divorce. Marriage is meant to be for life. Elsewhere Scripture allows divorce for adultery (Matthew 19:9) and for desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15), and in those cases the innocent party may remarry. This is the Westminster position (Westminster 24.5–6). Divorce is always a tragedy, to be avoided where possible.

I am divorced and remarried, and not on those grounds. What now? Do not undo your present marriage. It is a real marriage, made with vows before God, and the way forward is to keep it faithfully, not to break a second covenant to atone for the first (compare Deuteronomy 24:1–4, where returning to a former spouse is forbidden). If there was sin in how the first marriage ended or the second began, name it to God plainly, put right what can still be put right, such as care for children or honesty with those you wronged, and then believe the gospel about it. The blood of Christ cleanses that sin as fully as any other (1 John 1:7). And speak with your pastor; you should not carry it alone.

Lawful, not tolerated. Here is the pastoral weight of the verse, and it is aimed at a particular reader. Some Christians carry a permanent, low-level sense that their happiness in Christ is somehow illegitimate: that they have got away with something, that a stricter accounting would find them out, that their peace is a little too easy for what they know about themselves. If that describes you, notice what this verse says about the woman in her second marriage. She is not living in a technically permitted irregularity. She is not being tolerated. She is not an adulteress: Paul says it flatly, and the word he chose is the one that would have accused her. Your standing with Christ is not a generous arrangement that would collapse under scrutiny. It is lawful. It would survive any court in the universe, because the death that made it lawful has already taken place.

Overlooked or resolved? That is the difference between two ways of holding the gospel. One says: God has kindly overlooked the problem. The other says: the problem has been legally resolved and there is nothing left to overlook. Only the second can be rested on at three in the morning, since a thing that has been overlooked can always be looked at again. This is why Paul will say that God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (3:26). The cross did not set justice aside. It satisfied it.

Widowed, not divorced. And it is worth saying what did not happen. The woman was not divorced from the first husband; nobody negotiated a release, and she did not walk out on an obligation she found burdensome. She was widowed. Which means she has no case to answer, nothing to justify, and no reason to avoid the neighbours. That is the position Paul is claiming for every Christian in relation to the law: not that you escaped it, but that the bond was ended in the only way it ever could be, and by somebody else’s death.

In a sentence. So if she has another man while her husband is alive, she is called an adulteress, but if he dies she is free from that law and not an adulteress if she marries another man.

On a Tuesday. Marriage is meant for life, so honour your own and pray by name for the marriages around you, especially the ones under strain. And if the low hum of illegitimacy follows you, the feeling that your peace with God is a little too easy, answer it with the word of this verse. Say it plainly when it comes: I am not tolerated; I am lawfully his, because a death has taken place. Then go and enjoy what he has given you without looking over your shoulder.

For worship. The God who could have overlooked our sin did something far more costly and far more glorious: he dealt with it. He did not dissolve the old bond by pretending it had never existed, or by lowering the law’s claim. He ended it by a death, his Son’s death, in which we died too, and he did it so thoroughly that no accuser in heaven or on earth can call the bride an adulteress. Our joy in him is not stolen. It was bought, lawfully, at the full price.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God. For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God. For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.

Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ. The application. In the illustration, the husband dies; here, we die. But the point is the same: death ends the old relationship. Through Christ’s death, his body on the cross, we died to the law as a way of salvation and as a condemning master. Death with Christ ended the believer’s obligation to the law as a covenant of works.

Through a body. Notice the instrument. You died to the law through the body of Christ: not through a decision, a ceremony, or a change of conviction, but through a body, which is to say through an execution that took place at a particular hour on a particular hill. Paul keeps the Christian life anchored to something physical and dated. Your release from the law is not a spiritual principle you have grasped; it is a consequence of what happened to somebody’s body, and you were in him when it happened (6:3–6).

So that you may belong to another. A new marriage. Freed from the law, we are married to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:25–32). The church is his bride. And this is the point of the death: not liberty, but a change of possession. Paul does not say you died to the law so that you might be free, full stop; a widow left alone is not what he is describing. The whole object of the exercise was a second marriage.

To him who has been raised from the dead. The new husband is identified by one characteristic, and it is not the one we would choose. Paul could have said the one who loved us, or died for us, or is the Son of God, and all are true. He names the resurrection because of what the illustration required. The first marriage ended by a death; the second cannot end the same way. This husband has been through death already and come out the other side, which means the wife is not going to be widowed twice. Christ being raised from the dead will never die again (6:9).

In order that we may bear fruit for God. Fruit of a marriage: children. Fruit of union with Christ: good works, holiness. This is what marriages were for in the ancient world, and it is what Paul has been driving at since verse 1. It changes what holiness is. A childless marriage is a grief; a fruitless one, in this metaphor, is a contradiction. But note where fruit comes from. It is not manufactured by the wife through effort. It is the natural consequence of a union, which is why the New Testament so rarely tells Christians simply to try harder and so often tells them to abide, remain, stay joined (John 15:4–5).

For while we were living in the flesh. “In the flesh” means in our unconverted state, before the Spirit: not merely having a body, but living as human nature organised without God. Paul uses the past tense. For a Christian, this is a condition left behind, and that matters when we come to verse 14.

Our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death. A strange and important sentence. The law did not restrain our sinful passions; it aroused them, like a sign saying do not touch that makes you want to touch. The chapter will unpack the mechanism in verses 7 to 13, and it has already been named at 5:20, but here the point is the outcome. The law, applied to a sinful nature, does not produce holiness. It produces provocation, then failure, then fruit for death. Both marriages are fertile. That is the horror of the first one: it was not barren, it was productive, and you have the children to prove it.

What does fruit for God actually look like? Paul names it elsewhere: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Galatians 5:22–23), and the righteous deeds that flow from them (Philippians 1:11). It is usually less dramatic than we expect. A temper that has become slower. A man who now gives quietly. A woman who can forgive a sister she once avoided. Repentance that comes sooner after a sin. Prayer that has become less a duty and more a conversation. It is also slow, like all fruit, and it is often seen more clearly by others than by yourself. If you want to know whether it is there, ask someone who has known you for years.

In a sentence. So, my brothers and sisters, you also died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might belong to another, to him who was raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit for God, for when we were in the realm of the flesh, the sinful passions aroused by the law were at work in us, bearing fruit for death.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test that tells the two marriages apart by what they yield rather than by how they feel. Take an area where you have made real moral effort: a habit fought, a temper managed, a discipline attempted. Ask what it actually produced over five years. Under the first husband the pattern is recognisable: a rule, a period of success, a collapse, a worse collapse, and then either despair or a quiet lowering of the standard so the failure stops showing. Under the second, the pattern is different and slower: something you did not particularly work at has quietly changed, and you noticed afterwards. The first produces effort and shame. The second produces fruit, which is a thing that grows while you are asleep. So spend this week less on the resolution and more on the union: time with Christ in his word, prayer, the Lord’s Table, the company of his people.

What it does not mean. This passage can be read as though obedience no longer matters. Paul has not said the new marriage is easier or that nothing is asked. He has said the wife now belongs to somebody who is alive and can help her, rather than to a husband who could only ever tell her what was required. The demands have not gone. The relationship in which they are met has entirely changed, which is what the last verse of this section is about to say.

For worship. The Son of God gave his body to be broken so that he could have a bride, and he rose so that she would never be widowed. He is the husband who is never tired of his wife, who does not merely command her to be fruitful but makes her so by his own life flowing into her. Everything good that will ever grow in the people of God is the fruit of that marriage, and every bit of it is fruit for God.

verseByVerse.quote: But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.

But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive. “But now” again, the same two words that opened the gospel at 3:21. Paul uses them at exactly the moments where the argument turns from what was to what is, and both times they follow a description of something inescapable. There the courtroom had fallen silent with every mouth stopped; here the first marriage has been described in all its fertility for death. And then: but now. “Released” is the same word used of the widow freed from the marriage law (v. 2), released like a prisoner freed.

That which held us captive. The phrase is the language of being gripped, held down, kept in custody. It is a striking thing to say about a good law, and it is why Paul spends the rest of the chapter clearing the law of blame. The law held us, not because it was bad, but because we were sinners under its condemnation. It was not the jailer by design. It became a prison because of what we brought to it, in the way that a mirror becomes unbearable to a man who cannot change his face.

So that we serve. Freed not to do nothing, but to serve. Both halves of the sentence have the same verb in them. Paul does not say we no longer serve. He says we serve differently. The question was never whether a Christian obeys, but out of what.

In the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code. This needs care, because it is the most misread sentence in this section. It is not a contrast between the Old Testament and the New, and it is certainly not a contrast between law as bad and Spirit as good. The written code is God’s own word. What Paul is contrasting is two ways of serving: by external rules written on stone, or by the Spirit, from a changed heart (2 Corinthians 3:6). This is the new covenant: the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33). Chapter 8 explains it.

A rule outside, a life inside. The difference between the two is the difference between a rule outside you and a life inside you. A written code can tell you what is required and can do nothing whatever to make you want it. That is not a defect in the code but a limit built into the medium; instructions pinned to a wall have never yet moved anybody. What the new covenant promised, and what this verse says has arrived, is not clearer instructions but a different interior. God said he would put his law within them and write it on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33), and put his Spirit within them and cause them to walk in his statutes (Ezekiel 36:27). Note what the statutes do in that promise. They do not change. The walking does.

Pushing the car. Most Christians default to the old way without ever deciding to. It is the natural language of the religious mind: I must, I should, I ought, I will try. And it produces a life that is genuinely disciplined and quietly joyless. The new way does not abolish the shoulds. It relocates the engine. The difference is not between a man who obeys and a man who does not, but between a man driving a car and a man pushing one, and from the outside on a flat road the two can look remarkably similar for quite a long way.

Does serving by the Spirit mean I wait until I feel like obeying? No. The Spirit does not usually work by replacing obedience with feelings; he works through your will, giving you both the desire and the strength to do what God says (Philippians 2:13). Often the desire follows the obedience rather than preceding it. So do the right thing on the dull days too, but do it as someone who belongs to Christ, asking his help, rather than as someone earning his place. The new way is not obedience minus effort. It is effort with a different source and a different motive: not to be accepted, but because you are.

In a sentence. But now, by dying to what once held us captive, we have been released from the law so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit, not in the old way of the written code.

On a Tuesday. This test is about fuel rather than performance. Take the last thing you did that you did not want to do: the visit, the apology, the money, the honest word. Trace why you did it. Was it because not doing it would have made you feel bad about yourself, or because someone would have noticed, or because you have a standard and standards must be kept? Or was it because you belong to Christ and it seemed like the thing that would please him? The action is identical either way; you cannot tell from outside; and the two are different marriages. Most of us will find a mixture, which is normal and not a crisis. What is worth noticing is which one is doing the heavier lifting when you are tired.

For worship. The law is not your husband and never was a good one for people in our condition, but you have not been released into having no master, no service and no obligation. You have been released into a house where the same things are asked and Somebody lives in you who wants them. This is the glory of the new covenant: God does not merely tell his people what is good, he comes to live in them and makes them love it. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation now broods over the human heart, and the law that once stood outside us accusing is written inside us by the hand of God.

parallels.desc: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–25 — The Law and the Ongoing Conflict
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means!" Paul's defence of the law is passionate and complete: the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good (v. 12). The problem is not the law; the problem is sin — which used the good commandment as a foothold for its own agenda. When the commandment "you shall not covet" entered Paul's consciousness, it awakened the very covetousness it forbade. Not because the commandment was defective, but because sin is so pervasive that even the confrontation with prohibition provokes the prohibited desire.

The famous passage beginning in v. 14 — "For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate" — is the most honest description of the experience of indwelling sin in all of Scripture. Whether Paul is describing pre-conversion or post-conversion experience has been debated exhaustively. The weight of the evidence — the delight in God's law (v. 22), the willing of the good (v. 18), the self-awareness of the conflict — points to the regenerate person, not the unregenerate.

The climax of the chapter is both a cry and a triumph: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!" (vv. 24–25). The cry of anguish is honest; the gratitude that follows is immediate. Paul does not wallow in the wretchedness. He knows the answer. He has the answer. The very struggle he describes is the evidence that the Spirit is at work — because the person without the Spirit does not experience this conflict; she simply does what sin desires. The one who hates what she does and loves the law of God in her inner being is alive in Christ, even while she wars against the flesh.

Two things in the middle of the chapter carry the argument and should not be lost. The first is Paul’s conclusion at v. 13, which is the point of the whole autobiographical section: the law did not kill him, sin did — working death in him through what is good, so that sin might be shown to be sin and might become sinful beyond measure. That is the purpose of the exercise. The law was given partly to provoke sin into the open, where its true character could be seen; a disease that is invisible cannot be treated, and sin’s worst feature is exactly its capacity to use a holy commandment as its instrument. The second is the image at v. 23, which supplies the vocabulary for everything Christians have said since about the inner conflict: another law waging war against the law of the mind, and taking the man captive. Paul does not describe an imbalance or a tension. He describes a campaign, with two sides, prisoners, and territory — which is why the chapter can end in a cry rather than a conclusion.
verseByVerse.theology:
Indwelling Sin and the Doctrine of Sanctification

Romans 7:14–25 is the biblical foundation for the Reformed doctrine that sanctification is a lifelong struggle, not a crisis experience of eradication. John Wesley and the Holiness tradition argued for the possibility of entire sanctification — the complete eradication of the sinful nature — in this life. The Reformed tradition, following Augustine, Luther, and Calvin, has insisted that indwelling sin remains until glorification. This is not defeatism but realism: the Christian who understands this will not be surprised or destroyed by the ongoing struggle. She will be equipped to fight it with the means God has provided — the Word, prayer, the sacraments, the community of believers — rather than pretending it does not exist or despairing when it does.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The experience Paul describes in vv. 14–25 had a parallel in the literature of the day — Ovid's famous line, spoken by Medea: "I see the better and approve it; I follow the worse." But the philosophers' solution (more reason, more discipline, more willpower) is precisely what Paul finds inadequate. The problem is not ignorance; it is the power of indwelling sin that reason alone cannot overcome. The solution is not philosophy; it is the liberating power of "Jesus Christ our Lord" (v. 25). Now: The Christian who has experienced Romans 7 — who has tried harder, prayed more, committed afresh, and still found the same sins returning — is not a failure. She is a normal Christian, living in the honest tension between the new self and the old, between the delight in God's law and the drag of indwelling sin. The answer is not more effort; it is more Christ. Chapter 8 is the answer to chapter 7.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, "You shall not covet." But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.” But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.

What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! If the law aroused sin, is the law itself evil? No. Paul is answering a question his own argument has created, and he knows it. He has just said the law arouses sinful passions (v. 5) and that we have been released from it (v. 6). Any fair reader will draw the obvious inference, that the law is the problem, and Paul reaches for his strongest denial and then spends nineteen verses defending the law he has just described as a captor. Very few writers are willing to state their opponent’s case that clearly before answering it.

Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. The law reveals sin (3:20). Like an X-ray: it shows the disease, but cannot cure it. Nobody blames the X-ray for the tumour.

For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.” The tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17). And it is not accidental. Of the ten he could have chosen, he takes the only one that nobody can be observed breaking. You can be seen stealing, or committing adultery, or dishonouring a parent; there are witnesses and there is evidence. Coveting happens entirely inside a man, an inward desire and not an outward act. As a Pharisee Paul could say that as to righteousness under the law he was blameless (Philippians 3:6), and he meant it. He had the other nine. It was the tenth that got in past his defences, because it is the one that asks what you want.

But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. “Opportunity” (aphormē) was a military term for a base of operations, the bridgehead from which a campaign is launched. So sin does not merely react to the commandment; it establishes a position on it and operates from there. That is a description of something everyone has experienced and few have named: the prohibition itself becomes the staging ground. A thing you had not thought about for months becomes interesting within an hour of being told it is off limits.

The wet-paint sign. The mechanism is so ordinary that it hardly needs arguing. A wet-paint sign creates an impulse to touch that did not exist a moment before. Tell a child not to put beans up his nose and you have introduced a possibility he had not previously entertained. Every parent knows the law of the forbidden shelf. It would be comfortable to conclude from this that prohibitions are unwise, until you notice what it actually reveals. The paint is not the problem. The child is not corrupted by the sign. What the sign does is bring into daylight something that was in him all along and had simply never been provoked into showing itself.

For apart from the law, sin lies dead. Dormant, not yet stirred up; not absent. And that is the most unsettling sentence in the paragraph, because it means that a quiet conscience is not necessarily evidence of a clean heart. It may only be evidence that nothing has yet come along to wake what is sleeping. Most of us have a high opinion of our own patience until we live with the right person, and of our own honesty until real money is involved.

So should I avoid giving rules to my children, or to myself? No. Paul is not against commandments; he is about to call this one holy and righteous and good (v. 12). Children need clear boundaries, and adults need them too. What this passage teaches is what rules can and cannot do. They can show what is right, restrain the worst outward evil, and expose what is in the heart. They cannot change the heart. So give the rule, and with it give the gospel: explain why God’s way is good, show the child that you also break rules and need forgiveness, and point to the Saviour who gives a new heart. A home with rules and no grace breeds either rebels or Pharisees. A home with grace and no rules breeds neither love nor wisdom.

In a sentence. Is the law sin? Certainly not! But Paul would not have known what sin was except through the law, for he would not have known coveting if the law had not said, “You shall not covet,” but sin, seizing the opportunity the commandment gave, produced in him every kind of covetous desire, for apart from the law, sin was dead.

On a Tuesday. Use the tenth commandment the way Paul used it. Do not audit your behaviour; you will pass. Audit your wanting. Over the last week, what did you find yourself wishing you had: not merely admiring, but wanting in a way that made your own life look thinner when you thought about it? Somebody’s marriage, their ease, their platform, their health, their children, the fact that things seem to work out for them. Nobody sees that and nobody can charge you with it. Which is precisely why it is the commandment Paul reached for when he wanted to explain how a blameless man discovered he was lost. When you find it, name it to God, and then thank him for one specific thing he has given you instead. Contentment is learned (Philippians 4:11), and gratitude is how it is learned.

For worship. The law stands entirely exonerated. It is holy, and it did not create the appetite; it walked into the house and turned the lights on. And the God who gave it did not give it to destroy us but to show us, with mercy, what we could not otherwise see, so that we would run to the only one who never coveted anything. Christ, who owned all things and was content with a manger and a cross, kept the tenth commandment in our place, in every desire of his heart, and now gives us his own contentment as a gift.
verseByVerse.note: Coveting is the one commandment that concerns only the heart.

parallels.desc: you shall not covet

verseByVerse.quote: I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died. The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died. The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.

I was once alive apart from the law. Who is the “I”? Perhaps Paul as a child before he understood the law; or Paul speaking for Adam, who lived before the command; or for Israel before Sinai. Probably Paul’s own experience, told in a way that echoes Adam and Israel. He felt alive, self-satisfied.

One story told three times. It is worth seeing why all three readings keep suggesting themselves, because the sentence has the shape of a story that has been told more than once. I was once alive apart from the law; the commandment came; I died. That is precisely the shape of Eden: a man in a garden with no prohibition in sight, then a single commandment, then death arriving exactly as promised. It is also the shape of Israel: a people brought out of Egypt on sheer mercy, then Sinai, then a golden calf before Moses was down the mountain. And it is the shape of a devout boy’s own life, secure in a religious home until the tenth commandment reached the place where he actually lived. Paul is not being vague. He is telling one story that has happened at every scale at which it could happen.

Alive? How could Paul, blameless as a Pharisee (Philippians 3:6), say he was once alive apart from the law? The “I” is too personal to be a mere figure of speech. Not because he had never heard the law, but because he had never felt its weight. He knew its outward demands and kept them. The commandment came to him when he saw that the law also forbids coveting (v. 7), a sin of the heart he could not stop. Then he died: his confidence in his own righteousness was finished. And the word alive should not be read as a claim that he was genuinely safe. He is describing how it felt, not how it was, which is exactly the condition of every unawakened person. Nobody who has not met the commandment in earnest believes himself to be in danger, not because he has examined the matter, but because the question has never been put to him with any force. There is a kind of peace which is simply the absence of information.

Does this mean children are innocent until they understand the law? No. Paul has already said that all die in Adam, even those who did not sin as Adam did (5:12–14); alive describes how things seemed, not his standing before God. Scripture gives no age of accountability. But it gives good ground for hope for those who die in infancy: David expected to go to his child (2 Samuel 12:23), and the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). Elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases.

But when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died. When the law’s demand pierced his conscience, sin revived, and he saw himself as spiritually dead, condemned. Two things swapped places. Sin had been lying dormant (v. 8) and now it is the living party; the man who thought himself alive turns out to be the corpse. The arrival of the commandment did not change the amount of sin in him. It changed which of the two was standing up.

The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me. The law promised life to those who keep it: keep my statutes and live (Leviticus 18:5). But to a sinner, it brings death. Not the law’s fault, but sin’s. Note the last two words. He does not say the commandment is death; he says it proved to be death to him, and the qualification is the whole defence of the law that this chapter is conducting. The same word that was life to a man who kept it is death to a man who cannot, not because it changed, but because he was what he was. It is the perfect tool in the hands of a broken workman.

Sunlight and water. The principle is not confined to religion. The same sunlight that ripens fruit blisters skin that cannot take it; the same water that a swimmer moves through drowns a man who cannot swim. Nothing is wrong with the light or the water. Something is wrong with what meets it. This is why every attempt to fix the human problem by improving the instruction has failed: the trouble was never the quality of the instruction.

Did anyone ever receive the life the law promised? One man did. Jesus Christ kept every statute, from the heart, every day of his life, and the life the law promised was rightly his. Then he went to the death the law threatens, not for any sin of his own but for ours (Galatians 3:13). So the promise of Leviticus 18:5 was not empty; it was kept by the only person who could keep it, and his life is credited to all who trust him (5:19). The law cannot give life to you. But Christ, who earned it under the law, gives it to you as a gift.

In a sentence. Once Paul was alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life and he died, and the very commandment that was meant to bring life brought death.

On a Tuesday. Here is the question this passage exists to ask. When did the commandment come to you? Not when did you first hear the Ten Commandments; most readers could recite several by nine years old. When did one of them find you: when did a sentence of God’s stop being a general statement about right and wrong and become an accusation with your name on it? Some people can date it. Others found it happening slowly over a year. But a churchgoer who cannot recall anything of the kind, who has always regarded himself as broadly all right and has never been genuinely alarmed by anything God has said, should consider whether he is standing in the first half of verse 9 rather than the second. That position feels considerably better and is the more dangerous of the two. Read one commandment slowly this week, and ask God to let it find you.

For worship. Take the strange comfort in the sequence, because it runs the opposite way to what we would design. In this verse, dying is progress. The man who is alive at the start is lost, and the man who is dead at the end is the one who will be writing about grace for the next nine chapters. God’s ordinary way of saving people is to let a commandment kill them first, and then to raise them with his Son. He wounds that he may heal; he kills that he may make alive (Deuteronomy 32:39). The law shows you are dead. Only Christ makes you alive, and he does it with a life that the law itself has pronounced righteous.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.

For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. “Deceived” echoes the serpent’s deception of Eve (Genesis 3:13; 2 Corinthians 11:3), and it is more exact than a general resemblance. Eve’s own account of what happened was that the serpent deceived her and she ate, and Paul uses the same verb. Sin lies: it says the forbidden thing will satisfy, that God is holding back good. It used God’s good command to kill.

The serpent’s method. Watch the method, since it has not changed in the intervening millennia. The serpent did not begin by denying the commandment; he began by misquoting it, asking whether God had really said not to eat of any tree, inflating the prohibition until God looked mean. Then he impugned the motive: God knows that when you eat you will be like him, which is to say, he is holding out on you. And only then the flat denial: you will not surely die (Genesis 3:1–5).

Still in service. Every one of those three moves is available today, and all three are still in use. The commandment is exaggerated until it sounds like deprivation for its own sake. The Giver’s motive is questioned: he is restrictive, he does not want you happy, other people manage this perfectly well. And the consequence is quietly denied: not that judgment is disproved, only that it recedes into the theoretical and stops being the sort of thing that will actually happen to you.

Sin misinforms. This locates the real damage precisely, and it is not where we usually look. Sin’s primary work is not to overpower you; it is to misinform you. Nobody sins while clear-sighted about what he is doing and what it will cost. The moment of temptation always contains a lie, and the lie is usually not about the thing itself but about the arithmetic: that this will satisfy, that it will not cost much, that you will be able to stop, that God is being unreasonable. Which is why the counter to temptation is so often simply telling yourself the truth, out loud if necessary, since what is being attacked is your information.

How do I actually fight sin’s lies? Do what Jesus did in the wilderness: answer the lie with what God has said (Matthew 4:1–11). That means having particular verses ready for particular temptations, learned in advance, not hunted for in the moment. Ask the arithmetic questions sin hopes you will not ask: what will this cost tomorrow, and who else will pay? Say the truth aloud: this will not satisfy; God is not holding out on me; he gave his Son, so he will not withhold any good thing (8:32). Tell a trusted Christian friend, because lies thrive in secret. And remember that being tempted is not sinning; Christ was tempted in every way, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).

So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good. The verdict. The law is not the problem. It reflects God’s holy character. The problem is sin. We must never despise God’s law. And this is a remarkable thing for Paul to write at this point. He has just spent five verses describing how the commandment was used to kill him. The obvious conclusion lies ready to hand, and he refuses it in the strongest terms he has: three adjectives where one would have done. He is not conceding the point grudgingly; he is defending the law with more warmth than he uses about almost anything else in the letter.

A wounded man’s verdict. That is worth pausing on, because it is a rare quality of mind. Paul has been genuinely damaged by his encounter with the commandment; he calls himself dead as a result. And he will not allow his own experience to be evidence against God. Most of us do the reverse instinctively: we take the thing that hurt us and conclude something about God from it, and the conclusion always flatters us. Here is a man who was wounded, who says so plainly, and who then says the instrument that wounded him was holy and righteous and good. The problem is not in the physician’s prescription but in the patient’s condition. To blame the law for producing death is to blame the mirror for the face it reflects.

In a sentence. For sin, seizing the opportunity the commandment gave, deceived him and through the commandment killed him, so the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous and good.

On a Tuesday. Sin lies to you; God’s law tells you the truth. So think of a commandment of God that has cost you something: the one that has stood in the way of what you wanted, or that you have failed at so often you have stopped hoping. Ask what you actually think of that commandment when you are honest. Is it holy, righteous and good? Or is there a quiet, unexamined sense that it is excessive, that God was asking too much, that a reasonable God would have made an exception for your case? That resentment is not usually stated even to oneself. But it is the serpent’s second move, still working, and it lives in a great many believers who would sign every doctrinal statement they were handed. Name it, and believe God instead.

For worship. The verdict of the passage is not that the law is dangerous but that we are. The commandment came into the world of a fallen man, and something in him took it, twisted it and used it as a weapon against him. Yet God was not defeated by the serpent’s lie. The woman’s offspring came, the second Adam, who in his own wilderness heard every one of the serpent’s moves and believed his Father instead. Where Eve was deceived and Adam fell, Christ stood, and the holy, righteous and good law that killed us found in him its perfect lover and its perfect keeper.
verseByVerse.note: “Deceived” echoes the serpent’s deception of Eve.

parallels.desc: the serpent deceived me

verseByVerse.quote: Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.

Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! The law did not kill; sin did. This verse is the conclusion the whole autobiographical section has been building toward, and it answers a question that ought to trouble a thoughtful reader. If God knew the law would provoke sin rather than restrain it, why give it? Paul does not say it was a miscalculation. He says it was the purpose.

It was sin, producing death in me through what is good. Sin used a good thing for evil. That shows how evil sin is. The law did not cause death; sin hijacked the law to produce death, and in doing so, exposed itself.

In order that sin might be shown to be sin. God’s purpose in the law: to unmask sin, to show it for what it truly is. The law was given, among other things, to make the disease declare itself. The reason is straightforward once stated. A sickness that produces no symptoms is not thereby harmless; it is merely untreated, because nobody goes to a physician for a condition he cannot feel. The cruellest illnesses are the silent ones. What the commandment did was force a hidden thing to produce symptoms, and the symptoms were violent, and that is why the patient finally went for help.

And through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure. “Sinful beyond measure” (kath’ hyperbolēn): utterly, hyperbolically sinful; the phrase is the one behind our word hyperbole, excessive, past all proportion. Notice how sin earns that description. Not by producing something spectacular; the passage has been about a man wanting things he should not want. Sin becomes sinful beyond measure by what it is willing to use. It took the holiest thing God had given, a good commandment from a good God designed for life, and turned it into an instrument of death. When we see that sin twists even God’s good law into an instrument of death, we see how terrible it is.

Sin has a strategy. This corrects the picture most people carry. We tend to imagine sin as weakness: appetite, lapse, the failure of a good intention. Paul is describing something with strategy. It waits, it seizes opportunities, it deceives, and it is prepared to take the best material available and repurpose it. Anything can be conscripted. Religion can be. Doctrine can be: a man may use accurate theology to avoid God, and many do. Even repentance can be, when it becomes a performance that manages guilt without ever reaching the thing that caused it.

Blindsided from the good side. This apparently technical verse is one of the most useful in the letter, because it explains why serious Christians are so often blindsided: why the man who has successfully fought an obvious sin for twenty years is taken from an angle he never watched. He was guarding the disreputable ground. The enemy was working through the commandment.

Do I need to feel terrible about my sin before I can come to Christ? No. The law shows us sin so that we will come, not so that we will first earn the right to come by feeling bad enough. Conviction is not measured by the depth of the misery but by where it sends you. Some people are brought to Christ through long terror of conscience; others through a quiet, clear seeing that they need him. Both are the Spirit’s work. If you see enough of your sin to know that you cannot save yourself, you see enough to come. Christ invites the weary and heavy-laden, not the sufficiently weary (Matthew 11:28).

In a sentence. Did what is good become death to him? By no means! It was sin, using what is good to bring death, so that sin might be shown for what it is, and through the commandment become utterly sinful.

On a Tuesday. Ask what good thing in your life is currently being used against you. Not a bad thing: a genuinely good one. Your work, which is a gift, and which has become the place you go to avoid a difficulty at home. Your theological knowledge, which is real, and which has become a way of being superior to other Christians. Your service, which helps people, and which has become how you avoid asking whether anybody knows you. Sin does not need bad material. It prefers good material, because good material is not inspected. Pick one good thing this week and inspect it, and ask God to show you how sinful sin is, so that you will treasure his grace.

For worship. The verse is not finally about how bad things are. God’s purpose in all this was revelation, not destruction. He let sin have the commandment and use it, precisely so that a man could see what was in him and stop negotiating with it. Nobody has ever been saved from a problem he did not believe he had. And the God who exposed sin beyond measure has answered it with grace beyond measure: where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (5:20). The chapter is about to end in a cry for rescue, and that cry is the whole point of the exercise, because it is the first thing this man has said that could be answered, and the answer is Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.

For we know that the law is spiritual. From the Spirit, reflecting God’s nature. Not that it is vague or only inward, but that it comes from the Spirit of God and carries his holiness. That is why a person of the flesh cannot keep it, and why those who walk by the Spirit begin to fulfil it (8:4).

But I am of the flesh, sold under sin. “Of the flesh” (sarkinos): made of flesh, human, weak. “Sold under sin”: as a slave sold to a master. And the tense changes here to the present. Paul is now describing his present experience, and the change opens one of the most debated and most comforting passages in Scripture.

For I do not understand my own actions. This is the most exact description of a common experience in all literature. Not I regret them; not I cannot justify them. He cannot make sense of them. That is the honest report of anybody who has fought a besetting sin: the strangest feature is not that it is powerful but that it is unintelligible. You did the thing you had genuinely resolved not to do, for reasons that seemed adequate at the time and evaporate on inspection, and afterwards you cannot reconstruct why. The man in this verse is not making excuses. He is baffled.

For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate. The universal experience of the struggling believer: wanting to do right, failing; hating sin, doing it. And notice the strange grammar of the desire. He does not do what he wants, which means he wants the right thing. That single word rules out a great deal. This is not a man making a show of reluctance while enjoying his sin; the wanting is real, and it is the source of the anguish. A man who wanted only the wrong thing would have no conflict and nothing to report.

Where Christians differ: who is the “I” of verses 14–25? Christians have long debated whether Paul here describes life before conversion or the ongoing struggle of a believer. Some (many early Greek fathers, Wesley, and many modern scholars) see an unbeliever under the law, or Paul before conversion. Verdict: with Augustine, Luther, Calvin and the Reformed tradition, this best describes a believer. The present tense; the delight in God’s law in the inner being (v. 22), which no unbeliever has (8:7); the hatred of sin (v. 15); the cry for deliverance and thanks for it (vv. 24–25): all fit a regenerate person who still has indwelling sin. It describes the struggle, not the whole Christian life; chapter 8 shows the victory by the Spirit. Mature believers often feel this struggle most keenly, because they love God’s law most.

The structural reality. Calvin, Luther, Owen and Sproul all read this as Paul’s ongoing Christian experience: not his worst moments or his spiritual low tide, but the structural reality of a believer who still lives in unredeemed flesh even while possessing a renewed heart. The unregenerate person simply lives in his sin without this distress; only the regenerate grieves over indwelling sin this way. And this is what gives the passage its staggering pastoral power. Anyone who has genuinely tried to live for God knows exactly what Paul is describing. The good news is that the chapter does not end with defeat; it ends, a breath later, in 8:1 with no condemnation. The struggle is real; the verdict is grace.

The case on the other side. Since a reading has been chosen here, honesty requires stating the strongest case against it, because a reader who consults other commentaries will meet it and should not be ambushed. There are two real difficulties. The first is the phrase sold under sin, which is very hard language for a man Paul has just described as set free from sin (6:18, 22). The second is the tense in this very chapter: while we were living in the flesh (v. 5), past tense, describing a condition left behind, and then verses 14 to 25 in the present tense describing what looks like exactly that condition. Those are not trivial. On the second, the present tenses run unbroken for twelve verses in a letter by a writer who has just used the past tense deliberately, which is difficult to explain if he has moved back to his pre-Christian life; and the delight of verse 22 remains the immovable obstacle for the other reading, since 8:7 says flatly that the unconverted mind does not and cannot submit to God’s law.

But how can a believer be “sold under sin”? This is the strongest objection to reading verses 14 to 25 as the experience of a Christian, and it deserves an honest answer. In 6:17–18 Paul says believers have been set free from sin; here he says I am sold under sin. Three things help. First, Paul carefully limits where this is true: nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh (v. 18); with my flesh I serve the law of sin (v. 25). He is describing what remains of the old nature, not the whole person, whose inner being delights in God’s law (v. 22). Second, he is describing the believer measured against the law alone, considered apart from the Spirit’s help: as far as the law’s power goes, even a believer cannot overcome sin; the law can command but not enable. That is why chapter 8, where the Spirit is named nineteen times, follows immediately. Third, the language of captivity describes real defeats in a real war (v. 23), not surrender: a soldier can be taken prisoner in a battle without changing sides.

A mediating view. Martyn Lloyd-Jones, in his great sermons on Romans, argued for a third option: that Paul describes a person awakened by the law to his sin, convinced and distressed, but not yet regenerate and not yet resting in Christ. Douglas Moo holds that Paul describes his own past experience as a Jew under the law, seen now with Christian eyes. These readings take seriously the strong language of verses 14 and 23. But the delight in God’s law in the inner being (v. 22), the hatred of sin (v. 15), and the thanksgiving for Christ’s deliverance (v. 25) are hard to fit any but a believer. The Reformed verdict above remains the most natural reading, and the most pastorally true to what believers actually experience.

The comfort survives either reading. Here is the thing that matters most pastorally, and it should be said plainly so that nobody is left hanging on a disputed point. If Paul is describing the Christian, then your experience of failure is normal and you are not disqualified. If he is describing life under law before Christ, then the passage is telling you what you have been rescued from and where to look instead of at yourself. The answer in both cases is the same, arrives in the same sentence, and is a Person rather than a technique. Nobody who takes either view is left without help.

What it does not mean. This passage has been misused in both directions. It is not a licence: a man who quotes Romans 7 to excuse a sin he has stopped fighting has taken a description of anguish and used it as a permission slip, and the anguish is precisely what he no longer has. And it is not a ceiling: Paul does not say the Christian life never improves. Chapter 6 has just insisted that it does, chapter 8 is about to describe the Spirit putting sin to death, and obedience compounds over years (6:19–22). This chapter describes the floor of Christian experience, the ground you may find yourself on at any point and are not thereby lost. It does not describe the ceiling.

Should I expect to feel like this all the time? No. The conflict is constant in the sense that indwelling sin is always present until glory, but the experience of it varies. There are seasons of real victory and quiet joy, when old sins have lost their grip and the war feels far away, and seasons when the struggle is fierce. What Paul describes here is what the believer finds when he measures himself honestly against the law: he never does the good as fully as he wants. Chapter 8 describes the same believer looking at Christ and the Spirit, and finding no condemnation, real power, and sure hope. A healthy Christian lives in both chapters at once, and spends more of his attention on the second.

In a sentence. We know the law is spiritual, but Paul is unspiritual, sold as a slave to sin, and he does not understand what he does, for what he wants to do he does not do, but what he hates he does.

On a Tuesday. If you feel this struggle, you are not alone; it is the mark of a heart that loves God’s law. So ask what your sin does to you afterwards. If it produces the bafflement of this verse, why did I do that, I did not even want it, then you are experiencing what Paul is describing, and the experience is evidence of two parties rather than one. There is someone in you who wanted otherwise. That someone did not exist before God put him there, and his presence is the reason the whole thing hurts. Let the hurt send you to Christ rather than into hiding.

For worship. The holy law, given by the Spirit, could only ever show us the gap between what we are and what we ought to be. But the Son of God came into that gap. He took flesh, our flesh, yet was never sold under sin; he always did the things that pleased his Father, and never once did what he hated. Then he gave himself up as the price of our redemption, so that the slaves sold to sin could be bought back by God. The one who knows our frame and remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14) is not ashamed to call such strugglers his brothers.
verseByVerse.note: Christians have long debated whether Paul here describes life before conversion or the ongoing struggle of a believer; many, following Augustine and the Reformers, read it as the believer’s experience.

parallels.desc: the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.

Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. His very unwillingness shows he sides with the law; his deepest self agrees with God. The argument is quietly brilliant and easy to walk past. Paul is still defending the law, and here is his final piece of evidence: my own failure proves the law is good. Because if I do what I do not want, then my wanting is on the law’s side. My conscience has cast its vote for the commandment even while my hands were voting against it. So even the sinner’s misery is testimony: the law is not condemned by the man who breaks it, it is endorsed by his shame.

Guilt as evidence. This is why guilt, uncomfortable as it is, is a form of evidence rather than merely a form of suffering. It is the sound of a moral order being acknowledged by somebody who has just contravened it. A man with no sense of the law’s goodness feels nothing after breaking it and has nothing to report.

So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. Not an excuse, but a diagnosis. Paul’s true self, the new self, does not want sin. Sin is an intruder, a squatter in the house. “Dwells” (oikousa): lives, makes its home. Sin is still present, though no longer the master. The believer is responsible for his sins, but they do not express who he truly is in Christ.

Not the oldest excuse in the world. Read carelessly, this verse is the oldest excuse in the world, and it is not one. But the guard needs stating in the strongest possible terms, because the verse has genuinely been used as a dodge. Paul is not saying it was not me. He has just spent a chapter accepting responsibility, I do, I practise, I keep on doing, and he never once asks to be excused. If you have ever caught yourself saying, in effect, that was not the real me, about something you did last Tuesday, you have not found this verse; you have found its counterfeit. The tell is simple. Paul’s sentence produces anguish and a cry for deliverance. The excuse produces relief and no cry at all.

A lodger with a room. What he is doing is making a distinction between what he is and what is in him, and the word he chooses for the latter is worth having: sin dwells in me. It is the word for taking up residence, having an address, being a settled inhabitant rather than a visitor. That is exactly right, and exactly uncomfortable. Sin in a Christian is not an occasional intruder who breaks a window and leaves. It has a room. It has been there for years, knows the layout, and is not paying rent. And the image explains something otherwise baffling: why sin in a believer so often looks like a habit rather than a decision. A lodger does not need to be invited each time. He simply moves about the house, and long after you have stopped wanting him there you will find that the arrangement carries on out of sheer familiarity.

Holding both. The pastoral use of the distinction is what it is actually for. It gives a Christian a way to hold two things that otherwise tear him apart: I did that, and that is not who I am. Most believers can only manage one at a time. Hold the first alone and you get despair: I did it, therefore that is what I am, therefore nothing has changed. Hold the second alone and you get evasion: that is not who I am, therefore it does not really count. Paul holds both in a single sentence: full responsibility, and an identity that is not defined by the failure. The first keeps you honest; the second keeps you standing.

How does this fit with John’s word that no one born of God makes a practice of sinning (1 John 3:9)? John is describing the settled direction of a life, not a sinless one; the same letter says that anyone who claims to have no sin deceives himself (1 John 1:8). Paul’s man hates the sin he does and fights it. What John rules out is the man who has made peace with it.

Will God punish me for the sins I commit as a Christian? Not with condemnation. Every sin you will ever commit was laid on Christ and paid for at the cross, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (8:1). But God does discipline his children, as a father and not as a judge (Hebrews 12:5–11). He may let you feel the bitterness of a sin, withdraw the felt sense of his nearness for a time, or allow consequences to stand, and he does it to make you share his holiness, not to make you pay. So confess your sins to him freely, as a child to a father who has already forgiven the debt (1 John 1:9), and expect his correction to be love.

In a sentence. If he does what he does not want to do, he agrees that the law is good, and so it is no longer he himself who does it, but sin living in him.

On a Tuesday. After your last serious failure, which sentence did you arrive at? That was not really me, so there is no need to make anything of it: that is the dodge, and it always ends the conversation. Or: that was me, and it is also not what I am, and I want it out of my house. That does not end the conversation but starts one, and the next thing it produces is a cry. Paul’s version of this doctrine has a prayer at the end of it. The counterfeit has a shrug. Fight the lodger in Christ’s strength, and refuse to let him tell you he owns the house.

For worship. Sin may dwell in a believer, but it does not own him. The deed of the house was bought with blood, and the Spirit of God has taken up residence in the same rooms where sin still lurks, and he is the stronger occupant. Glory to the Christ who did not wait for us to evict our own sin before he moved in, who came to live in a house he knew was haunted, and who has promised that one day not a trace of the old tenant will remain.

verseByVerse.quote: For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.

For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. Notice the correction Paul makes to himself mid-sentence, because it is the most careful thing in the chapter. He begins nothing good dwells in me, and then stops and adds a qualifier: that is, in my flesh. He will not let the first half stand alone. If he had stopped there he would have said something untrue about a Christian, because something good does dwell in a believer: the Spirit does (8:9), and the delight of verse 22 does. So he narrows it. The statement is about the flesh, and the flesh is not the whole of him.

Copy the correction. That correction is worth copying, because a great many Christians make the sentence Paul refused to make: there is nothing good in me at all. It sounds humble and it is not accurate, and the difference matters pastorally. A man who believes there is nothing good in him anywhere has no basis for hope, no evidence to reason from, and no explanation for the fact that he minds about his sin. Paul is precise: the flesh is unimproved and unimprovable; the man is not the flesh.

What is the flesh? “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, not the physical body. English misleads, because it suggests that physical appetites are the problem while the mind is clean. But the vice lists in this letter are full of pride, envy, gossip and malice, sins with no bodily component at all (1:29–31). Flesh means human nature organised without God: the whole self as it operated before grace arrived, and as its remnants still operate. That is why a thoroughly ascetic man can be entirely fleshly, and a man enjoying his dinner with thanksgiving need not be. The body is not the enemy. The body will be raised.

For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. Willing, but not able in his own strength. The flesh cannot do it; only the Spirit can (8:4, 13). Two things are true at once, and both need saying. The desire is real: this is not a man pretending to want holiness. And the ability is absent, which is the discovery that undoes every self-improvement scheme ever devised. Most moral advice assumes the missing ingredient is wanting, and therefore supplies motivation: consider the consequences, remember who you are, try harder. Paul has the motivation. He is drowning anyway.

Discovered on the fifth attempt. This is why the honest Christian recognises this verse instantly and the merely religious person does not. You have to have made the attempt in earnest to know that earnestness is not enough. Nobody discovers his own inability by reading about it; he discovers it on the fifth occasion of resolving the same thing with complete sincerity and failing by Thursday.

For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing. Not that he never does good, but that he never does it as fully as he wants, and evil keeps breaking through. The tense is continuous: this is a pattern, a returning, a thing with a history. Paul is not describing a bad week. He is describing the shape of a lifetime, which is why this passage is either the most depressing in the New Testament or the most liberating, depending entirely on what comes next.

No technique. Note what Paul does not do here, because it is the most important omission in the chapter. He does not offer a technique. There is no method, no seven steps, no promise that the ability will arrive if the desire is sufficiently sincere. He states the problem in its full hopelessness and lets it stand, for five more verses, because the answer to this condition is not a better strategy but a person, and he wants you to have exhausted every alternative before he names him.

If I cannot do it, why try at all? Because the ability Paul lacks in himself is given by the Spirit, and the Spirit works through your effort, not instead of it. Paul will say that by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body (8:13): you do it, and you do it by him. Work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). So you still fight: you pray, you flee, you confess, you form new habits. But you fight as someone who has given up on his own strength and is leaning his full weight on another. Despair of yourself is the beginning of victory, not the end of trying.
