In a sentence. Paul knows that good itself does not dwell in him, in his sinful nature, for he has the desire to do good but cannot carry it out, and he does not do the good he wants, but keeps doing the evil he does not want.

On a Tuesday. You cannot defeat sin in your own strength; depend on the Spirit, every hour. Take the sin you return to and ask which of these two is actually true of you: I do not really want to stop, or I want to stop and cannot. Be honest, because the two require different medicine. If it is the first, the problem is not ability but affection, and the answer is not more effort but repentance: you are enjoying it and have not yet decided otherwise. If it is the second, you are exactly where verse 18 is, and the news is better than you think. Your wanting is not nothing. It is the strongest evidence in this chapter that God has already been at work in you, because that desire was not there before and you did not manufacture it.

For worship. The God who saw that we had the desire but not the ability did not hand us a better method. He gave us himself. The Father sent the Son to do the good we could not do, and the Son sends the Spirit to do in us what we cannot do alone. Every holy desire in a Christian is the fingerprint of God, and he who began that good work will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6). He does not abandon a desire he has planted.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, not the body as such.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.

Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. Repeating verse 17, and the repetition is deliberate. Paul is driving the diagnosis home before he names the pattern.

So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand. “Law” here means principle, a fixed pattern. Whenever he wants to do good, evil is right there beside him. Temptation is always close; sin was crouching at the door for Cain (Genesis 4:7). In this letter the word law has mostly meant the law of Moses, and Paul now uses it in the sense we use when we speak of the law of gravity: a regularity you can count on, which operates whether or not you are attending to it, and which does not make exceptions for people who are trying hard.

Summoned by the good. Note the timing, because it is the whole observation. Not evil is always around, which is obvious and would hardly need saying. Evil arrives when the good is wanted. The intention and the opposition appear together, and the second is summoned by the first. Almost every Christian has experienced this and very few have been told to expect it. You resolve to pray more; the following week is the busiest in a year and you are more distracted at prayer than you have been in months. You determine to be patient with a particular person; that person becomes markedly more irritating within about thirty-six hours. You decide to take your marriage in hand, and the next fortnight supplies more friction than the previous six. Nobody warned you that the decision itself would be the trigger, so you conclude that the resolve was insincere, or that God is not helping, or that you imagined the whole thing.

The friction of moving. Paul says it is a law. It is what happens. The moment a man moves toward the good, something moves to meet him, and the fact that it happened is not evidence that the movement was false. It is evidence that it was real. Nothing opposes a resolution nobody intends to keep. If your Christian life were merely a matter of drifting, you would meet very little resistance; drifting is downhill and nothing contests it. The friction you feel is the friction of moving against something. A man walking with the current is not aware of the river.

What it does not mean. Not every difficulty that follows a good decision is a spiritual assault, and reading life that way makes people strange and frightened. Sometimes the week really was busy. Sometimes the person really is having a hard time and it has nothing to do with you. Paul is describing a pattern, not issuing a decoder for events, and a Christian who begins interpreting every inconvenience as warfare will exhaust himself and misjudge his neighbours.

So what do I do when the counter-attack comes? Keep going, and do the next small right thing. Expect resistance, so that it does not surprise you into quitting. Pray about it plainly, naming the resolve and the opposition to God. Shrink the resolution if necessary, from an hour of prayer to ten honest minutes, rather than abandoning it. Tell another Christian what you are attempting, because resolutions kept alone are easily dropped. And when you fail, start again the same day, not next Monday. The evil may lie close at hand, but the Lord is closer: he is at hand (Philippians 4:5), and he is the one who is able to keep you from stumbling (Jude 24).

In a sentence. If he does what he does not want, it is no longer he who does it, but sin living in him, so he finds this law at work: when he wants to do good, evil is right there with him.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last time you made a genuine resolve about something spiritual and it collapsed within a week or two. Ask what conclusion you drew. Most of us conclude something about ourselves: that we are not serious, that we never change, that there is no point starting again. Verse 21 offers a different reading of the same evidence: the collapse followed the resolve because that is what this law does, and the right response is not to stop resolving but to stop being surprised. A man who expects the counter-attack is not defeated by it. He is merely inconvenienced by something he was told about in advance. Expect temptation to stand close when you try to do good, and stand closer to Christ.

For worship. Evil lies close at hand, but it does not have the last word, and it is not the closest thing to a believer. Nearer than the sin that crouches at the door is the Saviour who stands at it and knocks, and nearer still the Spirit who already lives within. Christ walked the whole road of obedience with evil pressing on him at every step, from the wilderness to Gethsemane, and never once yielded. His was the resolve that no counter-attack could break, and he made it for us.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.

For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being. “Delight” (synēdomai): rejoice with, take pleasure in. Not I approve of it, not I concede that it is right, but I delight in it. That is the language of the psalmist (Psalm 1:2; 119:97), the vocabulary of a man who loves what God has said. And it is precisely what the next chapter says the unconverted cannot do: the mind set on the flesh is hostile to God and does not submit to God’s law, indeed it cannot (8:7). No unbeliever delights in God’s law. This is the new heart. Whatever else is disputed here, the man of verse 22 is not the man of 8:7. “Inner being” is the inner self, renewed by the Spirit (2 Corinthians 4:16; Ephesians 3:16).

But I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind. War. The believer is a battlefield: the flesh against the Spirit (Galatians 5:17). Not peace yet, but war. The verb describes a campaign, sustained, with strategy and objectives, not a series of accidents.

And making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members. Taken prisoner at times: not total defeat, but painful losses. The word is what happens to a soldier after a battle is lost: taken alive, bound, marched off in the direction the victor chooses. Paul does not say he is tempted. He says he is taken prisoner, which is a considerably more humiliating admission and a far more accurate one.

Where the battle is fought. Notice that the fighting is located in his members: hands, eyes, tongue, the body with its trained reflexes. The delight is in the inner being; the defeat happens where the habits live. That is exactly the shape of most Christian failure. Nobody sins because his theology collapsed that morning. The convictions were intact throughout, and were simply not where the battle was being fought.

Fortify the right position. If the war is fought in the members, then that is where the defences belong. This is why the New Testament so often tells people to do physical, unspiritual-sounding things: flee (1 Corinthians 6:18), cut it off (Matthew 5:30), make no provision for the flesh (13:14). Those are not commands about the inner life. They are commands about your hands, your feet and your evening. A man who prays earnestly about a temptation and takes no practical steps to make it harder has fortified the wrong position entirely. In practice that may mean the phone that stays out of the bedroom, the route home that does not pass the shop, the drink not poured, the account closed, the friend who has permission to ask.

Both real. A Christian who reads this passage and recognises himself in the captivity often concludes that the delight of verse 22 must therefore be false: that a man genuinely delighting in God’s law would not keep losing like this. Paul puts both in the same sentence and does not treat them as contradictory. The delight is real. The captivity is real. And the one does not cancel the other, because they are happening in different places: one in the inner being, one in the members. A prisoner of war has not changed sides. He is in enemy hands, and he is still loyal, and everything now depends on whether anybody is coming for him.

What should I do straight after I have lost a battle? Go to God at once, not after a decent interval of feeling bad. Confess the specific sin plainly; he is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9), because Christ’s blood has already paid for it. Do not try to earn your way back with extra devotion; you are received on the same ground as before, which is Christ. Put right anything you have damaged with others. Ask what made the defeat easier, and change that. Then get up and carry on, because the war is not lost when a battle is. The devil wants a fall to become a retreat. The gospel turns it into a return.

In a sentence. In his inner being he delights in God’s law, but he sees another law at work in his body, waging war against the law of his mind and making him a prisoner of the law of sin at work within him.

On a Tuesday. The war inside you is a sign of life; dead people do not fight sin. So if you suspect your own delight, do not ask whether you always obey; verse 23 has already answered that. Ask what you feel about the commandment you keep breaking. When you consider the standard you have failed, not the failure but the standard, is there anything in you that says that is good, and I wish I were like that? An unconverted man does not think that. He thinks the standard is unreasonable, or irrelevant, or somebody else’s business. If you find yourself agreeing with the very law that is currently defeating you, that agreement is not nothing. It is the deepest thing in you, and it was put there.

For worship. Somebody is coming for the prisoner. The Captain of our salvation has already fought the decisive battle and won it, disarming the rulers and authorities and triumphing over them in the cross (Colossians 2:15). The delight in God’s law that lives in the believer’s inner being is his work, the first fruit of a new creation; and the One who planted it there will not leave his soldier in enemy hands. The war is real, but the outcome was settled on a hill outside Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: his delight is in the law of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.

Wretched man that I am! A cry of anguish: not despair, but deep longing. The more you love God, the more your sin grieves you. The word translated wretched is worth having, because it is not self-pity. It describes a person worn out by hardship, battered, exhausted by a struggle that has gone on too long. The risen Christ uses it of the church at Laodicea, who did not know it applied to them (Revelation 3:17). Paul knows. And that is the difference between the man in this verse and almost everybody else: he has stopped explaining himself. Is this a Christian speaking? Yes, as the argument at verses 14 and 15 shows: an unbeliever does not delight in God’s law or cry out to be rid of his sin like this. This is a regenerate man, still in a body where sin lives, longing for the day it is gone.

Who will deliver me from this body of death? “Who,” not “what.” Not a technique, but a person. “This body of death”: this body subject to death and to sin’s pull. And the picture is more vivid than it looks. The Roman poet Virgil tells of the tyrant Mezentius, who punished men by binding the living to the dead, face to face and hand to hand, and leaving them to die in that embrace, and commentators have recalled the image here for centuries. Whether or not Paul had it in mind, it is exactly right for what he has described: something dead, strapped to a living man, which he cannot reach round to untie and cannot outrun. He does not ask to be improved. He asks to be delivered, which is what you ask when the problem is attached to you. He longs for full deliverance.

Who, not what. The interrogative is the whole thing. Not which discipline, which method, which conference, which resolution. By this point in the chapter every technique has been tried and reported on: he knows the law, he approves the law, he delights in the law, he wills the good, and he is still being carried off. There is nothing left to attempt. The only remaining category of answer is a rescuer.

Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! The answer bursts out at once. There is no interval. Paul does not describe a period of waiting, a dark night, a process of qualifying. Cry and answer are separated by a question mark. That tells you what the chapter is finally about: not the length of the misery but the nearness of the deliverer. Jesus Christ delivers: now in part, by the Spirit (8:2), and fully at the resurrection, when this body of death is changed (8:23; 1 Corinthians 15:57).

Thanks, not a request. Notice the form of the answer, because it is not what the question asked for. He asked who will deliver me, future tense, and the reply is thanks be to God: gratitude, in the present, for something already true. He does not say Jesus will rescue me one day. He gives thanks, which is what a man does when the rescue has happened and he is looking back at it, even while he waits for its completion.

So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin. A summary of the present tension. The believer, between conversion and glory, is both: not yet sinless, but no longer sin’s slave at heart. And this sentence keeps the passage honest. After the doxology Paul does not announce that the war is over. He restates it. That order matters. A lesser writer, having reached a triumphant note, would have stopped there and left the impression that the struggle was finished. Paul deliberately puts the tension after the thanksgiving, which is his way of saying that the deliverance is certain and not yet complete. You may be rescued and still be carrying the body. Chapter 8 opens on that same man, and its first word to him is that there is now no condemnation. Chapter 8 shows the Spirit’s power in this struggle.

Where Christians differ: sinless perfection. Some holiness teachers claim believers can reach a state of sinless perfection in this life; some in the Wesleyan and Holiness traditions teach that a believer can be so filled with love that he no longer sins deliberately, and often read 7:14–25 as life before conversion or before that second blessing. Verdict: Paul, an apostle, still struggled. John says that if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8). Believers grow in holiness and win real victories, but sinless perfection comes only at glorification (Philippians 3:12; 1 John 3:2). Sin’s rule is broken now; its presence ends only when we are glorified.

When will the struggle end? At death, for the soul, and at the resurrection, for the body. When a believer dies, his soul is made perfect in holiness and goes immediately into the presence of Christ (Westminster 32.1; Philippians 1:23; Hebrews 12:23). There is no purgatory to finish the job; Christ’s work has already finished it. And on the last day the body itself, the very place where this war has been fought, will be raised imperishable and glorious, with no law of sin left in its members (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). So the struggle is not for ever. It is the last chapter of the old life, not the first chapter of the endless one.

Is it right for a Christian to call himself wretched? As an honest cry about his remaining sin, yes; as his settled identity, no. Paul says wretched man that I am in the same breath as thanks be to God, and he calls every believer a saint, beloved, a child of God (1:7; 8:16). The cry is the voice of a man who sees his sin clearly and longs to be rid of it, and that clear sight is itself a gift. But it is not the whole truth about him, and he does not stop there. If you find yourself saying the first half of verse 24 and never the first half of verse 25, you have taken the lament without the answer.

In a sentence. What a wretched man he is! Who will rescue him from this body of death? Thanks be to God, who delivers him through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, with his mind he serves God’s law, but in his sinful nature he serves the law of sin.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you have been asking for. If your prayers about your besetting sin are essentially requests for assistance, help me to try harder, give me strength to keep the resolution, make me more disciplined, then you are still asking what. The prayer of this verse is different in kind. It is not a request for improved equipment; it is the cry of a man who has given up on himself entirely and wants a person to come and get him. Most Christians do not pray that prayer until they have exhausted the other kind, which is exactly why God so often lets them be exhausted. When you next cry wretched man that I am, answer at once with Paul: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

The design of the chapter. The chapter was never written merely to describe a problem. It was written to bring a man to the end of himself while he is still holding on to God, because the cry of verse 24 is the last thing a self-reliant man will say and the first thing a rescued man remembers saying. Wretched, bound to a corpse, and thanking God in the same sentence: that is not a contradiction. That is a Christian.

For worship. The cry goes up, who will deliver me, and the answer that comes back is not a method, or a discipline, or a programme of gradual improvement. It is a name. Paul does not answer his own question with what. He answers it with who, and the who is Jesus Christ our Lord, and that is the last word on the subject in the chapter and in the letter and in the world. Every other religion answers the question with an instruction. Christianity answers it with a Person, and then hands him over: the Son who took our body of death upon himself on the cross, carried it into the grave, and left it there, so that we might be raised with him into a life that sin can never touch. Thanks be to God.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>Or do you not know, brothers —for I am speaking to those who know the law—that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives?<sup>2</sup>For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.<sup>3</sup>Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.<sup>4</sup>Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God.<sup>5</sup>For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.<sup>6</sup>But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.<sup>7</sup>What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.”<sup>8</sup>But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.<sup>9</sup>I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died.<sup>10</sup>The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.<sup>11</sup>For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.<sup>12</sup>So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.<sup>13</sup>Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.<sup>14</sup>For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin.<sup>15</sup>For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.<sup>16</sup>Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good.<sup>17</sup>So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.<sup>18</sup>For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out.<sup>19</sup>For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.<sup>20</sup>Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.<sup>21</sup>So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.<sup>22</sup>For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being,<sup>23</sup>but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.<sup>24</sup>Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?<sup>25</sup>Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.

8.title: No Condemnation, All Glory
8.overview:
Romans 8 is the mountain peak of the New Testament. Commentators across twenty centuries have reached for superlatives and still found them inadequate. It begins with "no condemnation" and ends with "no separation" — and between those two impossibilities of loss, it contains the fullest and most glorious account of the Christian life available in Scripture: the Spirit, adoption, the groaning of creation, the golden chain of redemption, and the love of God from which nothing in the universe can separate us.

The movement of the chapter is from liberation (vv. 1–17) through present suffering (vv. 18–27) to eternal security (vv. 28–39). In each movement, the Spirit is central: He liberates (vv. 1–11), he adopts (vv. 14–17), he intercedes (vv. 26–27). And over all of it stands the sovereign love of a God who foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and will glorify — a chain that has never had a broken link and never will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — No Condemnation: Life in the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." One sentence — and the whole of the gospel's comfort is here. Not less condemnation. Not reduced condemnation. No condemnation. The verdict is absolute, unconditional, and permanent. It rests not on the quality of the believer's life on any given day but on the finished work of Christ and the irreversible union with him by faith.

The reason for the "no condemnation" is the "law of the Spirit of life" which has set the believer free from "the law of sin and death" (v. 2). This is not two different legal codes but two different powers — the power of the Spirit that gives life versus the power of sin that produces death. Christ condemned sin in the flesh (v. 3) — He bore its penalty, exhausted its power, stripped it of its right to condemn — so that the Spirit-empowered believer might fulfil the righteous requirement of the law (v. 4).

The contrast between "flesh" and "Spirit" in vv. 5–11 is not between body and soul — Paul is not a Gnostic. It is between life oriented around the self and its capacities (flesh) and life oriented around God and his Spirit (Spirit). The mind set on the flesh is death; the mind set on the Spirit is life and peace. The Christian is not defined by the flesh but by the Spirit — "you, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you" (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology:
Definitive Justification and Ongoing Assurance

Romans 8:1 is the permanent foundation of the Reformed doctrine of assurance. The condemnation that does not exist for those in Christ is not merely past (sins before conversion) but total: nothing from the past, present, or future can generate condemnation for the one who is in Christ. This is because justification is not a process but an event — a forensic declaration that has been made and cannot be unmade. The Christian may sin grievously; she is not beyond discipline, but she is not in danger of condemnation. The Spirit she has received is the guarantee (v. 11) that what began in justification will be completed in glorification.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jewish legal system that Paul's readers knew well had a concept of condemnation — the verdict of guilty rendered by a court against one who had violated the law. Paul takes this forensic language and applies it to the ultimate court: the tribunal of God. The verdict of "no condemnation" is the legal declaration of the divine Judge that the case is closed, the penalty has been paid, and the accused walks free — permanently. Now: Countless Christians live under a cloud of functional condemnation — not doubting their doctrinal justification but unable to feel free, perpetually haunted by past sins, unable to receive grace without qualifying it. Romans 8:1 is the word that cuts through all of this: not less condemnation, not reduced condemnation — none. Take it in. Live from it.

verseByVerse.quote: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death. — Romans 8:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death.

Meaning first. Romans 8 is the summit of the letter, and perhaps of the whole Bible. It begins with no condemnation and ends with no separation. In between: the Holy Spirit, mentioned nineteen times, who frees us from sin’s power, gives life, makes us God’s children, assures us of adoption, helps us pray, and guarantees our future glory. Present sufferings are nothing compared to the coming glory, when creation itself will be set free. God works all things for the good of those he has called, and his purpose runs unbroken from foreknowledge to glory. If God is for us, who can be against us? Nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Nothing against us at the beginning; nothing between us at the end.

There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. One of the most precious verses in Scripture. Before anything else, notice the first word, because it is the reason this verse is placed exactly here. Therefore: because of Christ’s work (3:21–5:21) and the believer’s deliverance (7:25). And what it reaches back to is not a triumphant paragraph about victory over sin. It reaches back to a man crying out that he is wretched and cannot do what he wants and keeps doing what he hates. That is the person to whom this sentence is addressed. Nothing has happened in between. He has not improved, resolved anything, or turned a corner. He has cried out, and the answer is: there is therefore now no condemnation.

Now. The little word should not be passed over. Already, not someday. Not when the struggle has been resolved, not at the end when the accounts are settled and it is safe to say such things. Now: in the middle of it, on the same page as the groaning, to a man who has just described his own life as captivity. If Paul had wanted to make this a reward for progress he had every opportunity, and he put the word now in instead. The verdict of the last day has been given in advance.

No condemnation. In the Greek the sentence opens with the negation: no (ouden) is the first word out of his mouth, in effect none, therefore, now, condemnation. The denial is fired before the subject arrives. None at all: not reduced, not probationary, but none. And the word itself is worth having. Katakrima is not merely the guilty verdict; it carries the sentence that follows from it, the penalty to be served. So Paul is not only saying the charge has been dropped. He is saying there is nothing left to serve. A man can be acquitted and still be ruined by the costs; this is an acquittal with no outstanding liability of any kind.

In Christ Jesus. United to him. His standing is ours. The location of the believer is the ground of freedom from condemnation. She is not in herself, where condemnation would be entirely appropriate. She is in Christ: hidden in him, clothed in his righteousness, sharing his verdict of righteous before the Father. The condemnation fell on Christ at the cross; it cannot fall again on those who are found in him.

For the law of the Spirit of life. “For” (gar): v. 2 explains why there is no condemnation. “Law” (nomos). This is the pivotal phrase of the chapter, and it raises a fair question: Paul usually means the law of Moses when he says law, so how can a reader be confident that here it means a power or a principle? There are four good reasons.

Why “law” here can mean a ruling power. First, Paul has just used the word this way, several times, in the paragraph immediately before. In 7:21 he says, I find it to be a law: that is, a regular pattern, a fixed principle, that when he wants to do right, evil lies close at hand. In 7:23 he sees another law in his members waging war against the law of his mind and making him captive to the law of sin. A law that wages war and takes prisoners is not a written code; it is a power that rules. The law of sin and death in 8:2 is plainly the same law of sin of 7:23 and 7:25. Second, Paul had already stretched the word the same way in 3:27, where boasting is excluded not by a law of works but by the law of faith: the principle or order of faith. Third, ordinary Greek, like ordinary English, used law for a fixed rule of how things work, as we speak of the law of gravity. Fourth, the two laws in v. 2 are set against each other as rival masters, one freeing from the other. The law of Moses is holy, righteous and good (7:12); it cannot be the law of sin and death in the sense of something evil. So the law of sin and death is the ruling power of sin, which always ends in death; and the law of the Spirit of life is the ruling power of the Holy Spirit, who gives life.

Where Christians differ: does “law” here still mean the law of Moses? Some scholars (for example James Dunn, and in his own way N. T. Wright) argue that both laws are the Mosaic law seen two ways: the law used by sin to produce death (7:8–11), and the same law, now empowered by the Spirit, leading to life. Verdict: there is a real play on words, and Paul is aware that he is using his key word in a surprising way. But the most natural reading, and that of most careful commentators (Calvin, Murray, Moo, Schreiner among them), is that law here means the governing power or authority under which a person lives. Two regimes, two rulers: the reign of sin leading to death, and the reign of the Spirit giving life. This also fits 5:21, where sin reigned in death but grace reigns through righteousness to eternal life.

Has set you free in Christ Jesus. “Set free” (ēleutherōsen, aorist tense: a decisive act, done once). Not a process that may or may not succeed, but a liberation that has happened. “In Christ Jesus”: the freedom is located in him. We are free because we are joined to him.

Two powers. Before conversion, the law of sin and death had total jurisdiction: sin indwelt, death reigned, condemnation was the only verdict possible. After conversion, in Christ and by the Spirit, a stronger power has entered and set the prisoner free. The chains are broken, not by the prisoner’s effort, but by the liberating power of the Spirit of God.

From the law of sin and death. Sin as a ruling power, and death as its wage and its end (6:23). The two belong together: where sin rules, death follows.

How did the one power set me free from the other? Paul answers in vv. 3–4, which begin with “For”. The liberation has two sides, and both matter. First, the legal side: sin’s claim on us was cancelled. Sin rules in death because the law’s sentence against the sinner stands; God condemned sin in the flesh of his Son (v. 3), so the sentence has been carried out and sin has no legal right left to hold us. This is why v. 2 can explain v. 1: no condemnation, because sin’s grip, which rested on our guilt, has been broken. Second, the living side: the Spirit, who is life, now lives in us (vv. 9–11). By uniting us to Christ in his death and resurrection, the Spirit has ended sin’s reign over us (6:6–7, 14: sin will have no dominion over you), and has given us a new heart with new desires (Ezekiel 36:26–27), so that we now want God and can resist sin. A useful picture, often used by preachers: the law of gravity is not repealed when an aircraft flies, but a stronger law, the lift of the wing, overcomes it, as long as the aircraft flies in that power. Sin still pulls; the Spirit is the stronger power.

What it does not mean. Set free from the law of sin does not mean that sin is no longer present, or that the believer no longer struggles. Romans 7:14–25 and Galatians 5:17 describe that struggle honestly. It means sin is no longer the master. We were slaves who had no choice; now we are free people who fight, and who are on the winning side. Nor does it mean freedom from God’s moral law as a guide for life (v. 4; 13:8–10).

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who walk not according to the flesh” to v. 1. This was probably copied from v. 4, and makes no condemnation sound conditional on our walk. The earliest manuscripts don’t have it. No condemnation rests on being in Christ, not on our performance. In v. 2, the manuscripts vary between “set you free” (singular, as in the ESV), “set me free” (as in the King James Version) and “set us free”. The singular “you” is probably original: Paul turns from the “I” of chapter 7 and speaks directly to each reader.

Living under a cloud. This verse has to be preached to Christians and not only to unbelievers, because a great many believers hold the doctrine and live underneath a cloud of something else. It shows in small ways. They cannot receive an assurance without immediately supplying a qualification: yes, but I do need to be more consistent. They approach God in prayer as though re-applying each time, with a short preamble establishing that they know they have no right to be there. They find it easier to believe they are forgiven than that they are welcome. And most tellingly, when something goes wrong, an illness, a setback, a door closing, their first instinct is to ask what they are being punished for. That last instinct is the one to catch, because it reads providence through a verdict that has been cancelled. If there is now no condemnation, then whatever the hard thing in your life is, it is not that. It may be discipline, it may be consequence, it may be the ordinary friction of living in a world that is groaning, but it is not God collecting on a debt, because there is no debt outstanding.

Three things often confused. Only one of them has been abolished. Condemnation is a judicial verdict, and for the Christian it is gone entirely. Discipline remains, and Scripture is emphatic that it is evidence of sonship rather than of wrath: the Lord disciplines the one he loves (Hebrews 12:6). And consequences remain, often in full. A man may be completely forgiven and still lose the marriage, still have the conviction on his record, still live with what he did. The forgiveness is not diminished by the wreckage; they are simply different things, and telling a man that his forgiveness must be doubtful because his circumstances are hard is one of the cruellest mistakes a Christian can make.

If there is no condemnation, why do I still feel guilty? Because feelings are slower than verdicts, and because a conscience trained for years under the old marriage keeps its habits for a while. Some guilt is the Spirit convicting you of a real sin you have not yet confessed: then confess it, plainly and specifically, and receive the forgiveness already bought (1 John 1:9). But much of what Christians feel is accusation, not conviction. Conviction is specific, leads to Christ and leaves you lighter; accusation is vague, drives you away from God and leaves you heavier. When the feeling persists after you have confessed, do not wait for it to lift before you believe. Answer it with this verse, out loud if necessary. God’s verdict is the fact; your feeling is weather.

In a sentence. Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, because through Christ Jesus the ruling power of the Spirit who gives life has set you free from the ruling power of sin that ends in death.

On a Tuesday. No condemnation. None. Whatever you did yesterday, if you are in Christ, God does not condemn you. And sin is no longer your master. When it pulls at you today, you are not a slave obeying a master but a free person resisting an enemy, with a stronger power living in you. Here is a test, and it takes about ten seconds. Say the sentence to yourself in the first person, there is no condemnation for me, and listen for what your mind supplies next. If a but arrives, or a qualification, or an instinct to add something about trying harder, that is the cloud. It is not unbelief; you may hold the doctrine perfectly. It is the residue of a marriage that has ended (see on 7:1–2), and it goes only the way residues go, by being noticed and contradicted, repeatedly, with this verse.

For worship. The last word of chapter 7 was a man tied to a corpse, asking whether anybody was coming for him. The first word of chapter 8 is no. No condemnation, because the condemnation has already fallen, on the Son of God, in full, on a hill outside Jerusalem. The Judge has spoken in advance of the last day, and he has spoken in our favour. Glory to the Christ in whom we are hidden, so that when the Father looks for the guilty, he finds us clothed in the righteousness of his beloved Son.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who walk not according to the flesh,” and that some read “me” for “you.”

verseByVerse.quote: For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. — Romans 8:3–4
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. “Could not do” (to adynaton tou nomou, the impossibility of the law). The law couldn’t save, not because it was bad, but because we were too weak to keep it (7:14–25). It could tell us what is right and condemn us for doing wrong, but it could not give us the power to obey or the forgiveness we need. God did what the law couldn’t.

Where the blame lies. Notice how carefully Paul assigns the blame, because he has been doing this since chapter 7 and here he does it in a single clause. The law was weakened by the flesh. The weakness was not in the instrument; it was in the material the instrument had to work with. A perfectly good set of instructions is powerless in front of a man who cannot follow them, and no improvement to the wording will help. The law failed the way a ladder fails a man with no legs, which is to say, it did not fail at all.

What Paul means by “the flesh”. This is the first time the word appears in Romans 8, and it runs through the whole first half of the chapter (vv. 3–13), so it is worth understanding well. “Flesh” (sarx) in Paul has a range of meanings. Sometimes it simply means the body’s tissue (2 Corinthians 12:7), or human descent (1:3, Jesus descended from David according to the flesh), or human beings in their frailty (3:20, no flesh will be justified). But in Romans 7–8 and Galatians 5 it carries a deeper, moral meaning: human nature as it is since the fall, living from itself and for itself, apart from God and turned away from him. Several things follow. It is not the body as such: Paul does not think the body is evil, or that sin lives in matter; Christ came in flesh, and our bodies will be raised (v. 11). The flesh includes the mind (v. 6, the mind of the flesh), the will and the desires. It is not only bodily appetites such as sex, food and drink; in Galatians 5:19–21 the works of the flesh include jealousy, rivalry, anger and divisions, which are sins of the spirit as much as of the body. It even includes religion done in our own strength: Paul calls his proud law-keeping confidence in the flesh (Philippians 3:3–6). The flesh is the whole self organised around self, trusting self, serving self and ruling self, instead of trusting and serving God. Paul also uses the word for a realm or era: the old age of Adam, under sin and death, in contrast with the new age of the Spirit that came with Christ. So to be in the flesh (vv. 8–9) is to belong to that old realm, unconverted; believers are no longer in the flesh (v. 9). Yet the flesh is still present in believers as a pull, a remaining inclination to sin, against which they fight by the Spirit (v. 13; Galatians 5:16–17). That is why the old NIV translated the word sinful nature: not a perfect translation, but it catches the point. When the flesh appears in vv. 4–13, this is what Paul means.

By sending his own Son. His own Son: pre-existent, sent from heaven.

In the likeness of sinful flesh. Carefully worded. Not in sinful flesh, since Jesus was sinless (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15). Not merely in the likeness of flesh, as if his body were unreal. In the likeness of sinful flesh: truly human, subject to weakness, temptation and death, yet without sin. He entered the very realm where sin ruled, in order to defeat it there.

One word out of place. This is the phrase the church has had to guard for two thousand years, and watch how precisely Paul places the word likeness. He does not write that Christ came in the likeness of flesh: that would make the incarnation a costume, and there were people teaching exactly that within a generation. Nor does he write that he came in sinful flesh, which would put sin in the Son. He writes likeness of sinful flesh: real flesh, genuinely ours, in the same condition of weakness and mortality that ours is in, and without the sin. One word out of place in either direction and the gospel collapses. If the flesh he took was not truly ours, he did not redeem ours; as the old Fathers said, what is not assumed is not healed. If it was sinful, he would have needed saving himself. He had to be near enough to be genuinely one of us and clean enough to be of use, and this clause holds both.

Was Jesus really tempted, if he never sinned? Yes, truly. He was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). He felt hunger in the wilderness, the pull of an easier road, and in Gethsemane the full horror of the cup. Sinlessness does not make temptation lighter; it makes it heavier. A man who gives way at the first push never learns how strong the pressure can become; only one who never yields feels its full weight to the end. So when you go to him with your temptations, you are not going to someone who cannot understand. You are going to the only person who has felt the whole force of temptation and stood, and who is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

And for sin. The ESV notes that this can also be rendered as a sin offering, like those laid down in Leviticus 4 and foretold in Isaiah 53:10.

He condemned sin in the flesh. “Condemned” (katekrinen), the verb of the noun in v. 1. Sin was condemned, sentenced and punished, in Christ’s flesh on the cross. That is why there is no condemnation for us: it fell on him. Penal substitution.

Where the condemnation went. Go back three verses. Chapter 8 opened by saying there is no condemnation for those in Christ, and here is where the condemnation went. It was not cancelled, waived, or quietly dropped. It was carried out. The same root stands in both verses, and that is the whole architecture of the passage: the condemnation that is not on you fell somewhere, and Paul names the place. The reason there is none in verse 1 is that there was some in verse 3.

On sin’s own ground. Note also in the flesh: the arena. Sin had made its home in human nature and had never been beaten there; every previous human being had lost on that ground. So God did not defeat sin from a distance by decree. He came into the territory sin had held since Eden, in the very material sin had always won in, and beat it there. This is the second Adam doing on our ground what the first Adam lost on it.

In order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us. “Righteous requirement” (to dikaiōma, singular: the just requirement, the righteous demand). Not the many commandments, but the law’s one total demand, the whole of what it requires. “Might be fulfilled” (plērōthē, passive: be fully met). Note that Paul does not say that we might fulfil it, but that it might be fulfilled in us. “In us” (en hēmin), not “by us”.

Where Christians differ: what does it mean that the law’s requirement is fulfilled in us? Readers have long wondered whether Paul means the law’s demand for punishment, carried out on Christ; or the law’s demand for a righteous life, now lived by believers; or both. There are three main views. The first is forensic: the law demanded perfect righteousness, and that demand is fully met for us in Christ, whose obedience and death are counted as ours. Calvin took it this way, and so does Douglas Moo: the passive verb, the singular “requirement”, the word “fulfilled”, and the link with no condemnation all point to something God does, completely, rather than our partial obedience. The second is ethical: the Spirit now enables believers to live the life the law always aimed at, love for God and neighbour. C. E. B. Cranfield and Thomas Schreiner take this view, pointing out that the verse ends by describing the walk of those in whom it is fulfilled, and that v. 4 explains why God sent his Son: not only to forgive us but to change us (Ezekiel 36:27; Jeremiah 31:33). The third holds both together. Notice that the requirement is not mainly punishment: the law’s real demand is righteousness, and the punishment falls on those who fail to give it. Christ met that demand both by his perfect obedience and by bearing the penalty for our disobedience. Verdict: the best reading holds the two together, with the forensic sense as the foundation. In Christ, the law’s whole requirement has been fully met for us, which is why Paul can say “fulfilled” without any qualification, and why it is passive and “in us”: we are in Christ, and what is true of him is counted true of us. And the same union with Christ brings the Spirit, who begins to produce in us the very righteousness the law requires. That is why the verse ends with how we walk. Justification and sanctification are never separated: no one has the first without beginning the second.

But how can it be fulfilled if my obedience is still imperfect? The forensic side answers most of this: in Christ the requirement is fully met now, and nothing can be added to it. But even the ethical side does not claim perfection. Paul says in 13:8–10 that the one who loves another has fulfilled the law, using the same verb, without suggesting that any believer loves perfectly. He means that love is the kind of life the law describes, and that a life of Spirit-produced love is genuinely, if not yet completely, the law’s fulfilment. It is real now, and growing; it will be perfect at glorification, when we are conformed to the image of the Son (v. 29; Philippians 1:6; 1 John 3:2). So Paul looks back to the cross, around at the Spirit’s present work, and forward to glory, all at once.

Who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. “Walk” (peripatousin): live, conduct one’s life step by step. This is not a condition we must meet in order for the requirement to be fulfilled; it is a description of the people in whom it is fulfilled. Everyone in Christ walks by the Spirit, imperfectly but truly. For the flesh, see above.

Not a technique. Do not turn this into a technique, because Paul does not, and this chapter will not describe the mechanism until verse 13. What he establishes here is only that the resources have changed. The man of chapter 7 was attempting the impossible with what he had; the man of chapter 8 has been given something he did not have, and the walking follows from the gift rather than producing it. That is the answer to chapter 7 in a phrase: the problem there was a man with the desire and not the ability, and here the ability arrives from outside him.

In a sentence. What the law could not do, because our sinful nature left it powerless, God has done: by sending his own Son, as a real human being like us but without sin, to be a sin offering, he passed sentence on sin in Christ’s own body, so that everything the law rightly requires would be fully met in us, who now live not by our sinful nature but by the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. This test goes to which of the two chapters you are actually living in. When you face a sin you have repeatedly lost to, what do you instinctively reach for? If the answer is your own determination, a firmer resolve, a better system, a promise to yourself, you are working with chapter 7 resources, and the outcome is on record. Paul’s question would be different: what has been given to me that I am not using? The Spirit is not a reserve to be summoned in emergencies. He is the standing condition of a Christian, and the reason the righteous requirement gets fulfilled at all. So begin today’s fight by remembering that sin has already been condemned in Christ, and ask the Spirit for the walking.

For worship. The paragraph turns on three words that ought to be read slowly: God has done. The law could not; the flesh could not; chapter 7 could not. And then the subject of the sentence changes, and everything after it is in a different tense: not what must be attempted, but what has been accomplished, in real flesh, on our ground, by somebody else. The Father sent his own Son; the Son took our flesh and bore our sentence; the Spirit now writes in us the very righteousness the law required. Sin was condemned in Christ’s body, so it cannot condemn us, and everything the law ever asked of us, Christ has given on our behalf.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “for sin” can also be rendered “as a sin offering.”

parallels.desc: the sin offering

verseByVerse.quote: For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.

For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh. Two kinds of people: those who live by the flesh (unconverted) and those who live by the Spirit (converted). For the meaning of the flesh, see on vv. 3–4. “Set their minds” (phronousin): think about, focus on, care about, have one’s outlook shaped by. It means more than thinking; it is the whole direction of a person’s concerns and desires. What you think about, value and pursue shows who you are.

A compass, not a moment. The phrase to get hold of is set the mind, because it is doing all the work and it is not what most readers assume. The Greek word covers more than thinking: it takes in what you are interested in, what you care about, what you are inclined toward, the whole disposition of a person. It is close to what we mean when we say a man’s mind is on something. It is not his opinion. It is where he goes when nothing is requiring him to be anywhere. So this is not about occasional thoughts. Nobody is judged by the stray notion that crossed his mind on a train. Paul is describing a compass rather than a moment: the direction the needle returns to when it is left alone.

Settings are visible in the gaps. This gives an unusually practical way of finding out where your mind is set. Not in what you do at church or at work, where the agenda is set for you, but in the unstructured minutes. What do you reach for when you wake in the night? What occupies the ten minutes in a queue, the drive with the radio off, the moment your hand goes to your phone before you have decided anything? Those intervals are not trivial; they are the readout. A man’s mind, when released, goes where it lives.

But those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. The Spirit-led mind cares about what God cares about (Colossians 3:1–2; Philippians 4:8): Christ, his word, holiness, his people, his kingdom.

For to set the mind on the flesh is death. “Death” (thanatos). Notice that Paul does not say it leads to death, but that it is death. In the Bible, death is first of all separation: physical death separates the soul from the body; spiritual death separates the person from God, the source of life. A mind set on the flesh is already in that state now: alive in the body, but dead toward God, unable to know, love or please him (Ephesians 2:1–3, dead in trespasses and sins, while walking in them; 1 Timothy 5:6, she is dead even while she lives). It is a kind of existence, but not the life human beings were made for. And unless God intervenes, this present death ends in physical death and finally in eternal death, the second death (6:23; Revelation 20:14). Paul sees the whole of it as one reality: what begins as separation from God now becomes separation from God for ever.

Not leads to, but is. The verdict is stated with startling flatness. Paul is not describing a penalty attached at the end but a condition already in effect. A life organised around the self is not awaiting a sentence; it is already the thing it will be judged for, in the same way that drowning is not the punishment for being underwater.

But to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace. “Life” (zōē). Not mere existence, but the life of God himself, shared with us: knowing God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (John 17:3). It is eternal life, begun now and completed in the resurrection (vv. 10–11). It is the life human beings were created for in Eden: life with God, from God and for God. “Peace” (eirēnē). First, peace with God: the war is over, and we are reconciled (5:1, 10), in contrast with the mind of the flesh, which is hostile to God (v. 7). Second, peace within, the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, rest, harmony, a life put right, at peace with God, with oneself and with others (Philippians 4:7). Like death, life and peace are present realities that grow into an eternal future.

Why peace? Note that second word, because it is not the one we would have chosen. We would have written life and holiness, or life and usefulness. Paul writes peace, and it is the exact answer to chapter 7. That was a chapter of war: a law waging war, a man taken captive, a self divided against itself. What ends the war is not a stronger will but a mind that has stopped being set on the thing that was fighting it.

The battle is decided upstream. If the setting of the mind determines everything downstream, then what a Christian feeds his attention on is not a minor matter of taste. It is the whole battle, decided in advance. We tend to think of the fight against sin as happening at the moment of temptation, and by then it is largely over; the mind arrives at that moment already set, and it was set during the hours that seemed to be about nothing.

What it does not mean. Paul is not saying that a Christian who has a worldly thought is spiritually dead, or that our minds are always perfectly set on the Spirit. He is describing two fundamentally different orientations of a whole life. Believers still struggle, but the basic direction of their minds has been changed.

A guard for the tender conscience. This verse can be turned into a whip for the wrong person. Paul is describing two categories of people, not grading Christians on their concentration. The believer whose mind wanders in prayer, who finds Scripture hard going this month, who is distractible and knows it, is not the man whose mind is set on the flesh. The proof is that he minds. A mind genuinely set on the flesh does not lie awake troubled by how little it wants God; it does not want God and is not troubled. Wanting to want him is already the needle pointing the right way, however unsteadily.

So how do I actually set my mind on the Spirit? By choosing what you look at, repeatedly, until the needle learns. Seek the things that are above, where Christ is (Colossians 3:1–2): give the first minutes of the day to his word rather than the news, even if only a psalm. Carry one verse with you and return to it in the gaps. Pray in sentences through the day. Think on whatever is true, honourable, just, pure, lovely and commendable (Philippians 4:8), which means also choosing what not to watch and read. Keep the Lord’s Day and gather with his people, because minds are set in company. And when you notice your mind has drifted, do not scold yourself; simply turn it back. Every turning is the Spirit at work.

In a sentence. Those who live by the sinful nature have their minds set on what it desires, but those who live by the Spirit have their minds set on what the Spirit desires; for a mind ruled by the sinful nature is already death, cut off from God, while a mind ruled by the Spirit is life with God and peace.

On a Tuesday. What do you think about most, and what do you want most? Look at where your attention actually went yesterday: not your duties, your attention, the reading, the watching, the scrolling, the conversations you sought out. Add up the hours honestly. Then ask what a stranger would conclude from that record about what you care about. This is not an invitation to guilt about entertainment, and Paul is not asking anybody to be joyless. He is pointing out that the needle settles where it has been trained to settle, and that nobody has ever set his mind on the Spirit by accident while setting his hours on everything else. Life and peace are not only the reward of heaven; they are what a Spirit-set mind begins to taste now.

For worship. The God who made the mind for himself has not abandoned it to the flesh. He has sent his Spirit to turn it, gently and persistently, back toward the things that are above, where Christ is seated. And what waits for the mind set on him is not a duty but a feast: life, which is God’s own life shared with us, and peace, which is the war ended and the soul at rest. The Prince of Peace made that peace by the blood of his cross, and the Spirit of peace now draws our wandering minds home to it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.

For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God. For the meaning of the flesh, see on vv. 3–4. Not neutral, but hostile. The unconverted mind is at war with God (5:10; Colossians 1:21).

Hostile, not merely indifferent. Take the word first, because it is stronger than most readers allow and it describes people who would be astonished to hear it. Paul is not saying that everyone outside Christ hates God consciously; a great many are perfectly polite about him, and some are religious. He is describing an orientation rather than an emotion. The flesh-mind is set against God in the way one magnet is set against another: not angrily, just constitutionally, so that the closer God comes the more it turns away. And you can see it in reactions people have no reason to fake. Notice what happens in an ordinary conversation when God stops being a topic and starts making a claim. Discussed as an idea, he is interesting; introduced as someone with rights over the person listening, the temperature changes. That shift is not rudeness and it is often unconscious. It is the thing Paul is naming.

For it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot. Not only does not, but cannot. Total inability. The natural person has no power to submit to God (1 Corinthians 2:14; John 6:44).

Cannot. This is the word the whole verse turns on, and it is the reason the passage carries such weight in the argument about chapter 7. Paul could have written that the flesh-mind does not submit, which would be a statement about behaviour. He writes that it cannot, which is a statement about capacity. That is a different claim entirely, and it is the claim that makes the Christian faith unlike every programme of moral improvement ever devised. The problem is not only that people will not do what God requires. It is that the natural man is not equipped to, in the way that a stone is not equipped to float.

Inability is not an excuse. This is easily misheard. Inability of this kind does not reduce guilt, because it is not a disability imposed from outside. It is the inability of a man who cannot bring himself to love someone he has decided to despise: real, total, and entirely his own fault. Nobody would accept I was constitutionally incapable of wanting to as a defence in any human relationship, and it is no defence here.

Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. Nothing an unconverted person does pleases God, because it doesn’t come from faith and love for him (Hebrews 11:6). Even their good deeds are not done for God’s glory.

Are the good deeds of unbelievers worthless, then? Not worthless to people: an unbelieving doctor who heals, a neighbour who is honest, a father who provides, all do things God commands and that bless others, and they are far better done than neglected. God restrains evil and gives such kindness through them by his common grace. But they cannot please God in the sense Paul means, because they do not come from a heart made right by faith, and are not done in love for him or for his glory (Hebrews 11:6). The Westminster Confession says this carefully: such works may be good things in themselves and useful to others, yet they cannot please God or make a person fit to receive grace (Westminster 16.7). So we honour the good we see in unbelievers, and we never tell them it will bring them to God.

Where Christians differ: free will. Arminians hold that God gives everyone enough grace (prevenient grace) to choose to believe. Verdict: Paul says the fleshly mind cannot submit to God. Only the Spirit’s regenerating work makes faith possible (John 3:3–8; Ephesians 2:4–5). This is why salvation is entirely God’s work: he must give new life before we can respond.

Why your arguments did not work. This explains something otherwise puzzling about evangelism and about praying for people you love. If unbelief were merely a shortage of information, the answer would be better arguments, and the intelligent would be converted at a higher rate than the rest, which they plainly are not. If it were a shortage of motivation, the answer would be more compelling appeals. Paul locates it in capacity, which is why conversion in the New Testament is described as new birth, resurrection, and the giving of a heart of flesh for a heart of stone. Those are not exaggerations for a change of mind. They are the right category of language for an inability being removed.

Praying for the one who will not believe. Take this where it is genuinely useful. You have explained it. You have lived it in front of them for years. You have answered the objections, and new ones arrived. Verse 7 tells you why, and it is not that you argued badly: what is required is a change nobody can produce by persuasion, in themselves or in anybody else. That is discouraging only until you notice what follows from it. The work is God’s, it is exactly the sort of thing he does, and the person you are praying for is not a harder case than you were. So keep praying, keep loving, and keep speaking; God gives new life through his word (James 1:18).

In a sentence. The mind governed by the flesh is hostile to God; it does not submit to God’s law, nor can it, and those in the realm of the flesh cannot please God.

On a Tuesday. Read verse 8, those who are in the flesh cannot please God, and ask why it does not describe you today, since it plainly did once. Nothing in your capacity changed by your own effort. Somebody made the stone float. If you love God’s law, it is because the Spirit changed you; you could not have done it yourself. Let that make you humble toward the unbeliever at work and patient with the one you pray for. Write down one name this week, and pray for that person as someone only God can raise.

For worship. This bleak paragraph stands immediately before the words you, however, and it is there so that you know what it cost to be able to read verse 9 and find yourself in it. The contrast is not there to frighten you. It is there to show you the glory of grace. When we were hostile, God loved us; when we could not submit, he submitted his Son to death for us; when we could not please him, he made us pleasing in the Beloved. Every Christian is a stone that God has made to float, and the praise belongs entirely to him.

verseByVerse.quote: You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness.

You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. Believers are no longer in the realm of the flesh (see on vv. 3–4), but in the realm of the Spirit, because the Spirit dwells in them. “Dwells” (oikei): lives at home, permanently. “If in fact” (eiper): not a doubt, but a reminder: since, as is the case.

Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. Every Christian has the Spirit. There is no Christian without the Spirit. No two classes of believers. Note: the Spirit of God (v. 9a) is the Spirit of Christ (v. 9b). The Spirit proceeds from both. Christ is God.

Three names in two verses. Notice how much Paul packs in. The Spirit of God dwells in you; anyone without the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him; and then, in the same breath, Christ is in you. He moves between them without pausing to explain, which is one of the ways the New Testament assumes the Trinity rather than arguing for it. And there is a pastoral consequence in the shorthand: to have the Spirit is to have Christ. You are not dealing with a lesser third party sent as a substitute while the Lord is elsewhere. The indwelling of the Spirit is how the risen Christ is present with his people.

Read by the wrong person. This sentence has troubled more consciences than almost any other in the chapter. It is stated without qualification, and it should be, because it is one of the great dividing lines. But it needs handling with care, because it is regularly read by exactly the wrong person: the anxious believer, who takes it as an examination he is probably failing, while the man who ought to be searched by it reads past it without a flicker. So be clear about what the verse does not say. It does not say anyone who does not feel the Spirit. It does not say anyone who has not had a particular experience, or spoken in a particular way, or reached a level of assurance, or can point to a datable moment. Paul is not describing a sensation. He is describing a possession, and possessions can be verified by their effects rather than by how vividly they are felt.

How would I know? Not by introspection, which mostly reports on your temperament and how you slept. Look for effects, and the New Testament names them plainly. Do you call God Father and mean it, not as a formula but as an address (v. 15)? Do you find yourself loving Christian people you have nothing else in common with (1 John 3:14)? Do you mind about your sin, and mind more than you used to (the whole of chapter 7)? Is Christ precious to you in a way he was not at twenty? Does Scripture speak, at least sometimes, as though someone were behind it? None of those is spectacular. All of them are supernatural, in the sense that nothing in the flesh produces them; verses 7 and 8 have just said so.

Is there a second experience of the Spirit that ordinary Christians lack? No. Every believer receives the Spirit at conversion: in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). There are no two classes of Christians, the ones who merely believe and the ones who have the Spirit. What Scripture does call for is being filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), a continual, repeated yielding to the one who already lives in you, shown in worship, thanksgiving and humble service, not in a single crisis experience. So if you trust Christ, do not go looking for the Spirit as though he had not yet arrived. Ask him to fill the rooms he already owns.

But if Christ is in you. The Spirit in you is Christ in you (Colossians 1:27). The Trinity dwells in the believer (John 14:23).

Although the body is dead because of sin. “Dead” (nekron). Not a corpse, but mortal: under the sentence of death, as good as dead, certain to die. Death entered the world through sin (5:12), and even the believer’s body still carries that sentence. Christians still grow old, fall ill and die.

An honest admission. Verse 10 makes an admission that is easy to skip and is one of the most honest sentences in the chapter. Paul does not pretend that the indwelling Spirit fixes everything now. Your body is still on the schedule; it is ageing as you read, and it will fail. Christians are not exempt from the mortality this letter has been describing since chapter 5, and any teaching which implies that enough faith should keep a believer well has not read this verse.

The Spirit is life because of righteousness. “The Spirit is life” (to pneuma zōē). Many readers find this phrase difficult, and translations differ. The King James Version and the 1984 NIV read it as the human spirit: “the spirit is life”, or “your spirit is alive”. The ESV, the 2011 NIV (“the Spirit gives life”) and the CSB read it as the Holy Spirit. Which is right?

Where Christians differ: the Holy Spirit, or the human spirit? The case for the human spirit: Paul contrasts body and spirit, two parts of the person, and the believer’s body is dead while their inner self is alive. Verdict: Paul means the Holy Spirit, for four reasons. First, he does not say the spirit is alive (zōn), which would suit the human spirit, but that the Spirit is life (zōē), a noun: the Spirit is life itself, its source. Second, the Spirit has just been called the Spirit of life (v. 2). Third, every other use of spirit in vv. 9–11 means the Holy Spirit, and v. 11, which continues the thought, says that the same Spirit will give life to your mortal bodies. Fourth, Paul’s contrast is not between two parts of a person, but between two powers: sin brings death, the Spirit brings life. So the meaning is: your body is still marked for death because of sin, but the Spirit who lives in you is life, and he gives you life now, which will reach even your body at the resurrection. The result is that the believer, as a whole person, is alive to God already (6:11). So the two readings meet in experience: we are alive inwardly because the Holy Spirit, who is life, lives in us.

Because of righteousness. “Because of righteousness” (dia dikaiosynēn), set in parallel with “because of sin”. As sin brought death, so righteousness brings life. Here this is mainly the righteousness of justification, God’s verdict that we are righteous in Christ (5:17–21: grace reigns through righteousness leading to eternal life). Because we are justified, the Spirit gives us life. The righteous life he then produces in us follows from this.

Decaying and being renewed. The two halves stand in the same sentence: the body dead, the Spirit life. Both true at once, which is the shape of the whole Christian experience: a man who is decaying and being renewed simultaneously, and who can feel both on the same afternoon (2 Corinthians 4:16). Which is why the next verse goes where it goes. Paul has just conceded the body to death; he is about to say what will happen to it afterwards.

In a sentence. You, however, belong not to the realm of the sinful nature but to the realm of the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God lives in you, and anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Christ; but if Christ is in you, then although your body is still subject to death because of sin, the Spirit, who is life itself, gives you life because you have been made righteous.

On a Tuesday. When your body is weak, ill or ageing, remember both halves of this verse. Your body is mortal because of sin; but the Spirit of life lives in you, and you are already alive to God. The decay is real, but it is not the end of the story (v. 11). And if you doubt that you have the Spirit, run the test the right way round. Do not ask whether you feel the Spirit. Ask where these things came from: a desire for God that you did not manufacture, that survives your worst weeks, and that you could not switch off if you decided to. The question then is not whether you have the Spirit but how else you propose to account for it.

For worship. The God who is one in three persons has come to live in the believer: the Father has sent the Spirit of his Son, and Christ himself dwells in us by that Spirit, the hope of glory (Colossians 1:27). The Lord of heaven has taken up residence in bodies that are wearing out, not because they are worthy of him, but because he has declared us righteous in his Son. He did not wait for a better house. He moved into this one, and he means to rebuild it.

verseByVerse.quote: If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.

If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you. The same Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you. Resurrection power, inside you.

The name God is given. Notice how Paul names God here, because he could have said anything and says this: him who raised Jesus from the dead. Not the Almighty, not the Creator, not the Father, but the one who did that particular thing on that particular morning. And he says it twice in one sentence, which is not elegant writing and is not meant to be. He is fixing the reader’s attention on a single historical act and then telling him that the same power is at this moment resident in his own body. The logic runs on that: if that Spirit dwells in you, and the previous verses have established that he does, for every Christian without exception, then the God who has already done the harder thing has stationed the means of doing the easier one inside you. The difficult case is behind us. What remains follows.

He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies. The promise of bodily resurrection. As Jesus rose bodily, so will we. Salvation includes the body (v. 23; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). Matter matters to God.

The body back, repaired. Then the word that should stop us: he will give life to your mortal bodies. Not to your souls, not to your spirits, not to some refined essence of you that survives the wreck. Paul is talking about the body that is currently reading this: the one with the bad knee and the thinning hair and the scan results, the one that gets tired at four in the afternoon.
