That is the object of the promise. Christianity does not offer escape from the body; it offers the body back, repaired.

Closer to Plato than to Paul. This is worth saying plainly, because many Christians have absorbed something closer to Plato than to Paul without ever deciding to. Ask a congregation what happens when a believer dies and you will hear about the soul going to be with the Lord, which is true and is not the main thing the New Testament says. The hope in this letter is not disembodied. It is a raised body, in a renewed creation, and this verse says the deposit on it is already lodged in the very flesh that is wearing out.

Your body now. This has something to say about how you regard your own body. If the thing you currently inhabit is destined to be raised, then it is not a shell to be endured, resented or despised, nor, at the other extreme, worshipped and defended against time. It is going somewhere. That is a steadier place to stand than either the contempt or the panic our culture offers.

Through his Spirit who dwells in you. The indwelling Spirit is the guarantee (Ephesians 1:14).

What happens to a believer between death and the resurrection? At death the believer’s body returns to the dust, but the soul does not sleep or wait in some shadowy place. It goes at once to be with Christ, conscious and at rest, which Paul calls far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Luke 23:43). The souls of the righteous are then made perfect in holiness and received into heaven, where they behold the face of God, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies (Westminster 32.1). There is no purgatory. And the waiting is not the end: on the last day the same Spirit who raised Jesus will raise their bodies, and soul and body will be joined again, glorious and imperishable.

Does it matter whether a Christian is buried or cremated? Not for the resurrection. The God who will raise bodies long since turned to dust, lost at sea or burned by martyrs’ fires is not hindered by the method of a funeral. Christians have historically preferred burial, because it pictures what we believe: the body laid down like a seed, waiting to be raised (1 Corinthians 15:42–44), and Jesus himself was buried. That is a good reason to choose it where you can, but it is not a command, and no believer should fear for a loved one who was cremated. The promise of this verse rests on the Spirit’s power, not on the condition of the remains.

In a sentence. If the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus from the dead lives in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who lives in you.

On a Tuesday. If you are ill, or ageing badly, or watching someone you love be dismantled by a disease with a name, this verse is not telling you that the body does not matter. It is telling you that it matters so much that God intends to raise it. The decline is real; Paul does not pretend otherwise, and calls the body mortal in the same breath as the promise. So treat your body with honour, as something that belongs to the Lord, and when you look in the mirror or sit in a waiting room, say what is true: this body is going to be raised.

For worship. The Spirit in you now is the same Spirit who was in the tomb on that Sunday, and he is not there as a comfort during the decline. He is there as a deposit against the reversal of it. That is why the promise is stated in the future and the guarantee in the present. Nothing in this verse asks you to hold on tightly enough to qualify. The one who raised Jesus has put his Spirit in your body, and a God who has gone to that trouble is not going to lose track of the address. Matter matters to God; he made it, his Son took it, and he will raise it in glory.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Heirs with Christ: The Spirit of Adoption
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Spirit does not merely set us free from condemnation; he establishes our identity as children of God. "For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'" (v. 15). The word Abba is the intimate Aramaic term for father — the word a child uses at the family table, in the moment of fear, in the unselfconscious familiarity of the parental relationship. Jesus used it in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). His Spirit now enables his adopted brothers and sisters to use it too.

The adoption of which Paul speaks is not merely a legal status (though it is that — full legal rights as sons and daughters, co-heirs with Christ). It is a relational reality experienced in the present: the Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. This inner witness — not our feelings but the Spirit's testimony — is the ground of Christian assurance at the deepest level. When we doubt our standing, when darkness presses in, when God feels distant — the Spirit within is still crying "Abba!" on our behalf.

"Heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ" (v. 17) — the inheritance is nothing less than God himself, shared with the Son. Everything that belongs to Christ by right of his eternal sonship is ours by right of our adoption. This is the logic behind Paul's bewildering statement in 1 Corinthians 3:21 — "all things are yours." The adopted child of God is heir to a universe, co-inheritor of a new creation. The suffering of the present age (v. 17 — "provided we suffer with him") is the path to that glory, not its obstacle.

The section does not begin there, however, and the two verses that open it are the hinge on which the rest turns. Paul first cancels an obligation: we are debtors — but not to the flesh. The old master has no further claim, which means every demand it still makes is made without authority. Then comes the one command in the passage, and it is not gentle: by the Spirit, put to death the deeds of the body (v. 13). This is the letter’s answer to the defeat of chapter 7, and it holds two things together that we habitually separate — the killing is genuinely ours to do, and the power to do it is not ours at all. And verse 14 then supplies the link to everything that follows: those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. The mortification of sin is not the price of sonship. It is the evidence of it, and the family likeness of people who are being led.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption and Assurance

The doctrine of adoption (huiothesia) is one of J.I. Packer's great themes in Knowing God: he argues that adoption is a higher privilege than justification, because justification changes our status before the court while adoption brings us into the family. Reformed writing on the Holy Spirit develops the same insight: the Spirit's primary work in the believer is to mediate the Trinitarian relationship — drawing the child into the love that the Father and the Son share, enabling her to cry "Abba" with the same intimacy that the eternal Son has always known. Assurance, at its deepest level, is not confidence in our own faith or our own experience; it is the Spirit-given knowledge that we are beloved children of the Father.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Roman adoption law in the first century was clear: an adopted son received full legal rights, the old debts were cancelled, the new family name was his, and the inheritance was secured. Paul's readers would have understood immediately the thoroughness of what adoption meant. No second-class status, no probationary period — full sonship, full inheritance, from the moment of adoption. Now: The "spirit of slavery" (v. 15) that produces fear is the functional religion of much nominal Christianity — the haunting sense that God is primarily a demanding judge to be appeased, that our standing depends on our performance, that we must earn our place at the table. Romans 8:15 is the antidote: not slaves, sons. Not fear, Abba. Not earning, inheriting.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. — Romans 8:12–13
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.

So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh. “Debtors” (opheiletai, people under obligation). We owe the flesh nothing (see on vv. 3–4 for its meaning). It has no claim on us. We owe everything to God, who has given us life by his Spirit.

The unfinished sentence. Notice that Paul never finishes it. We are debtors, not to the flesh, and then he stops. The construction sets up an obvious completion, but to the Spirit, and he does not write it. It is one of those places where the grammar breaks because the thought has run ahead of it, and the effect is that the reader has to supply the missing half himself. That is worth doing deliberately. You owe the flesh nothing. It is the old master whose debt has been cancelled by Christ. It still exerts a pull, and Paul has been painfully honest about that in chapter 7, but it has no legal standing, no rightful authority, no covenant claim on the person who is in Christ. Every demand it still makes on you is made without standing, by a creditor whose debt was settled and who is now simply hoping you have not read the paperwork.

For if you live according to the flesh you will die. A warning. A life ruled by the flesh shows a person is not truly in Christ, and leads to eternal death.

But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. “Put to death” (thanatoute, present tense: keep on putting to death). The old word for this is mortification, from the Latin for killing. “The deeds of the body” (tas praxeis tou sōmatos): the sinful practices carried out through the body, under the flesh’s rule, not the body itself. “By the Spirit” (pneumati): by means of the Spirit, as the power by which it is done. “You will live”: this is the life of v. 6, life with God now and eternal life.

A violent word, a continuous tense. This is the one command in the passage, and Paul chooses a violent word for it. Put to death: not manage, not moderate, not keep under review. And the tense is continuous: keep putting to death, as an ongoing occupation rather than a decisive event. That is honest about the Christian life in a way that our language for it often is not. There is no version of this in which the thing is dealt with once and never returns.

What does it mean to put sin to death by the Spirit? Many readers are unsure, and a common view is something like this: the Spirit shows me through God’s word that something is wrong; since the Spirit lives in me, it is now my job to say no; and by saying no I put the deed to death. That is right as far as it goes. There is real, active effort involved: Paul says you put to death, not that you wait for the Spirit to do it while you do nothing. And the Spirit does use his word to show us sin. But the great teachers on this verse add some important things.

John Owen. The fullest treatment of this verse in English is John Owen’s Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656), a short book written entirely on Romans 8:13. Owen made several points. Mortification is not merely stopping an outward act, hiding a sin, or exchanging one sin for another; it is a lifelong weakening of sin’s root, its inner desires, so that it loses its strength and its hold on the heart. It is not achieved by our own vows, rules and resolutions alone, which he said only drive sin underground. It is the Spirit’s work, and the Spirit does it by showing us the guilt and danger of the sin, by setting Christ crucified before us, by giving us faith to rely on Christ’s death and power, and by strengthening us with grace. Yet the Spirit does not do it without us: in Owen’s words, he works in us and with us, not against us or without us. So we must be active: hating the sin, watching for its approach, refusing its first motions, and above all, as Owen put it, setting faith to work on Christ for the killing of your sin. His most quoted line sums it up: be killing sin, or it will be killing you.

Other voices. Thomas Chalmers, in his famous sermon The Expulsive Power of a New Affection, argued that the heart cannot simply be emptied of a love; it can only be freed from one love by a greater love taking its place. Tim Keller often drew on Chalmers: since sin is at root idolatry, loving something more than God, it is put to death most deeply not by gritted teeth alone but by seeing and rejoicing in the greater beauty of Christ, so that the idol loses its attraction. Modern Reformed preachers in Owen’s line, such as John MacArthur and Alistair Begg, likewise stress that the Spirit’s main instrument is the word of God, the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17), and that mortification is daily, practical and never finished in this life.

The means the Spirit uses. Putting it together, the New Testament points to these means. Scripture: knowing God’s word, so that the Spirit can use it to expose and resist sin (Psalm 119:11; Hebrews 4:12). Faith in Christ’s death: reckoning yourself dead to sin and alive to God because you are united to him (6:6, 11). Prayer: asking for the Spirit’s strength, and confessing sin honestly (1 John 1:9). Refusing early: saying no to the first thought, not the last (James 1:14–15). Cutting off opportunities: make no provision for the flesh (13:14; Matthew 5:29–30). Replacing, not only removing: putting on the new self, its love, gratitude and service (Colossians 3:5–14; Ephesians 4:22–32). And fellowship: other believers who know your struggle and pray for you (Hebrews 3:13; James 5:16).

Map the chain. The how deserves more than a list of spiritual generalities, because put yourself in the way of the Spirit is exactly the sort of sentence a struggling man cannot act on at eleven at night. So be concrete. Most sin is not a decision; it is the last link in a chain, and by the time you reach the decision the outcome was settled several links earlier. That means the fight is not primarily at the moment of temptation, where you are weakest, but upstream of it, where you are still thinking clearly. Take the sin you keep returning to and ask what reliably precedes it: the hour of the day, the room, the device, the state you are in, tired, alone, resentful, unaccountable, having just been criticised, having just succeeded. Almost everyone can name the sin instantly and has never once mapped what comes before it, which is why the same battle is lost the same way for years.

Attack the chain, not the last link. That is what our Lord meant by the startlingly physical language of cutting off and tearing out (Matthew 5:29–30): not mutilation, but the removal of access, which is nearly always possible and nearly always inconvenient. And it is why the New Testament so often says flee rather than resist (1 Corinthians 6:18; 2 Timothy 2:22). There are temptations you are meant to stand and fight, and there are temptations where standing to fight is itself the mistake.

By the Spirit, not by willpower. This is what keeps all of that from being self-improvement with a religious vocabulary. The difference is not in the practical steps, which an unbeliever could also take, but in whether they are taken in dependence: whether you are praying while you do them, and whether the thing you actually want is not merely to stop failing but to please a Person. A man can lock his phone away in the strength of the flesh, and the flesh will find another route within a month. The same act, done in prayer, by a man asking God for the desire he does not yet have and looking to Christ crucified, is mortification. The Christian who fights sin only by clenching her teeth is working in the flesh to fight the flesh, a losing strategy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is earned by our success in killing sin; Paul is describing the life of those already justified, and those who belong to Christ will do this, imperfectly but truly. Nor does it mean harming the body, or rigid self-denial for its own sake (Colossians 2:20–23). And it does not mean waiting passively for the Spirit to take temptation away; by the Spirit, you put to death.

Can a Christian lose his salvation by living according to the flesh? No, but the warning is real and meant to be heeded. Verse 13 alarms people who ought not to be alarmed, so read it carefully. Paul describes a direction of life, not a tally of failures, and he has already settled the ground of standing in this letter. The question is not whether you have lost battles; the whole chapter assumes you have. It is which way you are facing. A man who is putting sin to death badly and repeatedly is doing the thing this verse describes. A man who has stopped, and made his peace with his sin, should be alarmed, because he shows no sign of belonging to Christ. God uses warnings like this one to keep his people (see on vv. 38–39), and those who are truly his will heed them.

In a sentence. So, brothers and sisters, we have an obligation, but not to our sinful nature, to live as it dictates; for if you live by the sinful nature you will die, but if, by the power of the Spirit, you keep putting to death the sinful practices of the body, you will live.

On a Tuesday. Name the sin you most need to put to death. Then write down the four things that usually happen before it. Choose one of those four and make it harder this week: not the sin, the link before it. Ask the Spirit for strength, look at Christ crucified for that very sin, and do not negotiate with it. That is what it looks like to put something to death rather than to resolve about it, and most Christians have never once tried it, which is why the resolutions have such a poor record.

Both halves stand. Neither may be dropped. If you attempt this in your own strength you will fail, as chapter 7 has already demonstrated at length. And if you wait to be delivered without lifting a hand, nothing will happen either, because the verb in this verse is addressed to you. The Spirit does not do it instead of you. He does it through you, and the hands are yours.

For worship. We owe the flesh nothing because we owe Christ everything. He took the sin we fight and bore its death on the cross, so that we would not have to die for it; and he sends his Spirit to kill in us what he has already condemned in himself. The war we wage is a mopping-up operation after a victory already won. And the promise at the end of the verse is pure grace: you will live, with the life of God himself, now and for ever.

parallels.desc: put to death what is earthly in you

verseByVerse.quote: For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, "Abba! Father!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”

For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. “For” (gar): v. 14 explains v. 13. Those who by the Spirit put to death the deeds of the body are those who are led by the Spirit. “Led” (agontai, present passive: are being led, continually). The Spirit is the one who leads; we are led. “All”: every believer, not a spiritual elite. In context, being led by the Spirit means being led in holiness: away from the flesh, toward obedience to God and the putting to death of sin. The same is true in Galatians 5:16–25, where being led by the Spirit is set against the works of the flesh and shows itself in the fruit of the Spirit. This is the mark of God’s children.

Evidence, not a threshold. The direction of verse 14 is nearly always read backwards. Paul does not say that those who are led by the Spirit become sons. He says those who are led by the Spirit are sons: the leading is the symptom, and the sonship is the condition producing it. That matters, because read the other way it becomes a treadmill: am I being led enough to count? Paul is offering evidence, not a threshold. A Christian who has never had a strong impression about a career move and who has been slowly and unglamorously turning away from the same sin for ten years is precisely the person this verse is describing.

What it does not mean. Being led by the Spirit here does not mean receiving detailed inner guidance for life’s decisions: which job to take, which house to buy, which person to marry. Many believers read it that way, and then worry that they are not hearing the Spirit, or treat their feelings and impressions as the Spirit’s voice. But that is not Paul’s subject. He is describing what every child of God already experiences: the Spirit drawing them, through his word, to trust Christ, to hate sin, to fight it, and to live for God. God does guide our lives, by his providence, and he gives wisdom to those who ask (James 1:5; Proverbs 3:5–6). But the way Scripture teaches us to make decisions is by knowing and obeying his revealed word, praying for wisdom, seeking good counsel, and then choosing freely within his will, trusting him with the outcome. A believer who is unsure which car to buy is not therefore unsure whether he is a child of God. Nor does being led mean that the Spirit bypasses Scripture with new revelations; the Spirit leads by the word he inspired, applying it to our hearts, convicting, encouraging and changing our desires.

For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear. Not the fear of a slave before a master, or of a criminal before a judge, which is how people relate to God under the law without grace.

Back. Note the word. Paul is describing a relapse, a return to a former condition, and it is the standing temptation of the Christian life. Nobody consciously decides to relate to God as a slave. It happens by drift, and it has a recognisable feel: the sense that you are on probation; that God is broadly disappointed; that the relationship is under review and this week’s performance is the evidence. That is the spirit of slavery, the constant anxiety of a slave who never knows whether today brings punishment, and this verse says it is not what you received.

But you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons. “Adoption” (huiothesia). In Roman law an adopted son received full rights and inheritance, his old debts cancelled, his status changed for ever. Adopted by God: brought into his family, given his name, made his heirs. “Sons”: in the ancient world, sons inherited. Women believers too are “sons” in this sense: full heirs (Galatians 3:26–28).

What does adoption add to being justified? Justification is the courtroom: God the Judge declares the guilty righteous for Christ’s sake. Adoption is the family: God the Father takes those he has acquitted into his household as his own children. A judge can acquit a man and never see him again; this Judge takes the acquitted man home. Adoption brings the Father’s name, his love, his access, his care, his discipline and his inheritance (Westminster 12.1). That is why Paul moves from no condemnation to Abba. The first tells you that you will not be punished. The second tells you that you are wanted.

By whom we cry, Abba! Father! “Cry” (krazomen, call out, often with deep feeling). “Abba”: Aramaic for Father, the intimate word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). Not formal, but warm and close. The Spirit enables us to call God what Jesus called him. The cry of a child running to its father.

A word left untranslated. Abba is not a piece of devotional decoration. It is domestic Aramaic, the word used in a house, at a table, by a child who has not yet learned to be careful. It is not baby-talk, as is sometimes said; grown men used it of their fathers all their lives. What it is, is unguarded. And its presence here tells you something remarkable about the early church. Paul is writing in Greek, to Greek-speakers in Rome, and he leaves this one word untranslated, because they were already using it. Somebody had taught these Gentile converts an Aramaic word they had no other use for, and the reason is not hard to find.

The word he used in the dark. Jesus used it. In Gethsemane, face down, with the cup in front of him, our Lord prayed Abba, Father (Mark 14:36). That is the only place in the Gospels where the Aramaic word itself is recorded on his lips, and it is at the worst hour of his life. So the word the church inherited is the word he used when everything was going wrong, which means it was never a term for the good days. It is what the Son said in the dark, and the Spirit puts it in your mouth in the same conditions. And notice the verb: we cry. Not a recitation but something closer to a shout, the sound a person makes involuntarily. The evidence of adoption Paul points to is not a doctrine you affirm calmly. It is what comes out of you when you are frightened.

What if my own father makes this word hard to say? The word father is not neutral for everybody. If your own father was frightening, absent or cruel, then this verse asks you to use the warmest word in the language and hands you a cold one. Two things. First, Scripture knows: it is God who is called the father of the fatherless (Psalm 68:5), which is not a metaphor borrowed from good fathers but a claim made in the absence of them. Second, the direction of the comparison is the reverse of what we assume. Your father was not the original of which God is a copy. God is the original, and every human father is a more or less faithful attempt at him. Yours may have been a poor likeness. That tells you nothing whatever about the original, and this verse is an invitation to meet him.

In a sentence. Everyone who is led by the Spirit of God is a child of God, for the Spirit you received does not make you slaves who live in fear again; he is the Spirit who makes you God’s adopted children, and by him we cry, Abba, Father.

On a Tuesday. Here is one of the surest tests in the letter. What comes out of you at the moment of real fear? Not what you would say in a Bible study: what actually surfaces when the phone rings at two in the morning, when the scan result arrives, when the child is late home and not answering. If the reflex is toward God rather than away from him, if the instinct, even a wordless one, is to reach for a Father rather than to brace for a Judge, then that reflex was put there. No unconverted man produces it under pressure. Fear strips away everything learned and leaves what is actually there. So call God Father today, in plain words, and mean it; and if you are fighting sin and longing to please him, take that as the sign that his Spirit is leading you.

For worship. The eternal Son, who has called God Abba from before the foundation of the world, has shared his own word with us. He was forsaken so that we might be welcomed; he cried out in the dark so that we might cry Abba in ours and be heard. The Spirit of the Son has been sent into our hearts, and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ now turns to every adopted child with the same face he turns to his only begotten Son. We are not slaves on probation. We are sons and daughters at home.
verseByVerse.note: In Roman law an adopted son received full rights and inheritance, as if born into the family. “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used within the family.

parallels.desc: sons of the living God

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God,

Setting and background. In Roman law, adoption was a formal legal act performed before witnesses, so that if the adoption were ever challenged, for example after the father’s death, the witnesses could testify that it had really taken place. Paul has just spoken of the Spirit of adoption (v. 15), and in the law of Moses a matter was established by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). So here are two witnesses to our adoption.

The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit. “Bears witness with” (symmartyrei, testifies together with). Two witnesses: the Holy Spirit, and our own spirit, our inner self. “Himself” (auto): the Spirit in person.

A second witness. The two-witness point is not a happy coincidence of grammar; it is the law of Israel. A charge was established by two or three witnesses and never by one (Deuteronomy 19:15), and Paul has been writing in courtroom terms since chapter 1. So when he says the Spirit bears witness with our spirit, he is describing testimony that meets the legal standard. Your own sense of being God’s child would not be sufficient evidence on its own; you are, after all, an interested party. A second witness has been called, and he is not.

That we are children of God. “Children” (tekna). This is the content of the testimony.

Where Christians differ: to whom does the Spirit testify? Many Christians struggle with this verse because they are not sure they hear or feel anything, and wonder whether they lack the Spirit’s witness. One suggested way out is to read it as the Spirit testifying to God the Father that we are his children, rather than testifying to us. It is a thoughtful suggestion, and it has a real foothold: a few verses later the Spirit does speak to the Father on our behalf, interceding for us (vv. 26–27). Verdict: in this verse, though, the witness is given to us. First, the verb means to testify together with: the Spirit’s testimony joins our spirit’s testimony, which only makes sense if our own spirit is also hearing and confessing the truth. Even if the Greek is read as the Spirit testifying to our spirit, the hearer is still us, not the Father. Second, the Father does not need to be told who his children are; the Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19), since he chose them (v. 29). Third, the context is about our fear and assurance: the Spirit of slavery led to fear, but the Spirit of adoption leads us to cry Abba (v. 15). The witness is for our sake.

What does this feel like? Every honest reader asks, and it is better asked than left sitting: how would I know if it had happened to me? A great many faithful Christians read a verse like this and conclude that whatever Paul is describing has evidently passed them by. So be clear about what is not being claimed. Paul does not describe a voice, or an experience with a date attached, or an event you could arrange in a meeting. And the tense is worth noticing: the Spirit bears witness, present and continuous, not bore witness at some crisis you ought to be able to point to. It is a testimony that has been going on quietly underneath your Christian life, most of it below the level at which you notice anything.

How does the Spirit’s witness work? This is the most helpful answer for those who struggle. The witness is not usually a voice, a vision or a special feeling. Look at v. 15: by the Spirit we cry, Abba, Father. Galatians 4:6 says the same: God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father. The Spirit’s witness is mainly the cry he produces in us: a real, if sometimes weak, trust in God as our Father, a desire to come to him, and confidence that he will receive us for Christ’s sake. When you pray, Father, forgive me for Jesus’ sake, and you mean it, the Spirit is bearing witness with your spirit. He works through the gospel promises, giving us faith to believe them (1 John 5:10–13), and through the new life he produces: love for God’s people (1 John 3:14), obedience (1 John 2:3), and hatred of sin (v. 13). The Westminster Confession puts it this way (Westminster 18.2): assurance rests on the divine truth of the promises of salvation, the inward evidence of the graces those promises speak of, and the testimony of the Spirit of adoption witnessing with our spirits that we are the children of God.

A settledness. What the witness produces, more often than not, is not a feeling but a settledness: the ability to read a promise of God addressed to his children and find that it does not bounce off, that you take it as meant for you, without having to argue yourself into it. The instinct, noted a verse earlier, to reach for a Father under pressure. The peculiar fact, if you stop and consider it, that you care whether God is pleased with you at all. None of that announces itself as a witness. All of it is one. And if you have been anxiously looking for the experience and finding nothing, grasp this: the Spirit’s witness is not usually heard as a separate voice alongside your own thoughts. It is heard in them. When you pray Father and mean it, that is not you working up a conviction and hoping the Spirit will confirm it. That prayer is the confirmation. You have been looking for a second witness while the second witness was speaking with your mouth.

Where Christians differ: a direct witness? Some teachers, including the Puritan Thomas Goodwin, John Wesley and Martyn Lloyd-Jones, held that besides this ordinary witness the Spirit sometimes gives a direct, immediate assurance, an overwhelming sense of God’s love, and they encouraged believers to seek it. Verdict: God may give seasons of special joy and assurance, and believers may thank him for them. But the verse does not make such experiences the test of whether we are God’s children. The normal witness of the Spirit is the one every believer has: faith in Christ’s promises, the cry of Abba, and the fruit of the new life. Do not wait for a feeling before you believe you are God’s child; believe God’s promise, and the Spirit will witness through it.

Where Christians differ: can we be sure? Roman Catholic teaching (Council of Trent) holds that, apart from special revelation, no one can be certain of being in grace. Verdict: the Spirit himself testifies that we are God’s children. Assurance is the birthright of believers (1 John 5:13; Westminster 18.1). It may be shaken or weak at times, but it is God’s will that his children know they are his.

Two guards. They run in opposite directions. The first: this cannot be manufactured, and it should not be simulated. There is a kind of teaching that presses people to claim an inner assurance they do not have, and it produces either despair or pretence. Assurance in Scripture is something God gives, and he gives it in his own time, often to people who have walked with him a long while. The second: the witness of the Spirit is not a licence to ignore evidence. John wrote a whole letter supplying tests, do you love the brothers, do you keep his commandments, do you confess the Son, and he wrote them so that people might know (1 John 5:13). The inner witness and the outward fruit are not rivals; they are the two witnesses agreeing. A man who claims a deep inner assurance and whose life shows nothing of Christ has one witness, and it is the interested party.

What if I have no assurance at all? Then you are not the first, and you are not thereby lost. The Westminster Confession says plainly that assurance is not of the essence of faith, so that a true believer may wait long and struggle hard before he has it, and may have it shaken by sin, temptation or God’s seeming withdrawal (Westminster 18.3–4). Faith that rests on Christ saves, even when it is too weak to feel sure of itself. So do not look first at your assurance; look at Christ, and keep looking. Keep hearing the word, coming to the Lord’s Table, praying, confessing sin, and walking in obedience, because these are the ordinary means by which God strengthens assurance. Talk to a pastor. And keep calling God Father, even when the word feels thin.

In a sentence. The Spirit himself joins his testimony to the testimony of our own hearts that we are God’s children.

On a Tuesday. If you are unsure whether you hear the Spirit’s witness, ask a simpler question: do I, however weakly, turn to God as my Father, trusting Jesus to bring me to him? If you do, that cry is the Spirit’s own witness in you. Believe it. Then notice what you already do. Do you call him Father when nobody is listening? Does your sin trouble you as an offence against someone rather than a breach of a rule? When you are told that God loves his children, does some part of you quietly include yourself in the sentence? Those are not achievements you have produced. They are the second witness, testifying, and he has been doing it for years, mostly while you were not attending.

For worship. The verse says children rather than repeating the legal word for sons from the verse before. Paul has established the adoption as a matter of standing and rights; here he uses the word of birth and family. The court has ruled, and the house has accepted you, and it is the second of those that the Spirit spends his time telling you about. The Holy Spirit of God, who searches the depths of God, stoops to whisper to anxious children that they belong. The Father does not merely tolerate us; he wants us to know that we are his.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and if children, then heirs — heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him. — Romans 8:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
and if children, then heirs — heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him.

And if children, then heirs. Children inherit.

Heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. Heirs of God: we inherit God himself, and all he has. Fellow heirs with Christ: we share his inheritance, the whole world (4:13), the new creation. Everything that belongs to Christ is ours (1 Corinthians 3:21–23).

Heirs of God. Stay with the phrase, because it is stranger than it looks and we tend to read past it. An heir normally inherits what the deceased owned: the estate, the property, the holdings. Paul does not say we are heirs to God’s possessions. He says heirs of God. The inheritance is not a portfolio; it is the person himself.

All Levites now. This is not a new arrangement, and Israel had a picture of it. When the land was divided, eleven tribes walked away holding a map: this valley, that ridge, the olive terraces, the well. Levi was handed nothing at all: no acres, no boundary stones, no deed. And the reason given was not a slight but the highest honour in the book: the LORD is their inheritance (Deuteronomy 18:2). The other tribes were given things God had made. Levi was given God. What Paul is telling every adopted child in Rome is that they are all Levites now. And take the comfort on the reverse side of that. Everything else you possess can be taken from you, by a diagnosis, a market, a war, or simply by time, which takes everything eventually and is never in a hurry. An inheritance that is God cannot be repossessed.

Fellow heirs. This is the more staggering half. Paul does not say we inherit alongside Christ in some junior capacity, a smaller share appropriate to newcomers. The word is one of his “with” compounds: joint-heirs. Which means the measure of what you will receive is not calibrated to your service, your maturity, or how well your Christian life has gone. It is calibrated to his. Everything the Son inherits by right of being the Son, the adopted receive by right of adoption, and there is no clause anywhere reducing the portion of the ones who came in late or did badly.

If we are all fellow heirs, are there still rewards? Yes, and both truths stand. Every believer receives the whole inheritance, because it is Christ’s and we have it in him. Scripture also speaks of rewards for faithful service (1 Corinthians 3:12–15; Matthew 25:21; 2 Corinthians 5:10). But these are not wages earned alongside grace; they are God crowning his own gifts in us, and there will be no envy in that kingdom, only joy. A thimble and a bucket can both be full. So serve faithfully, knowing that nothing done for him is forgotten, but never imagine that your place at the table depends on it.

Provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him. “Provided” (eiper, if indeed, since). “Suffer with him” (sympaschomen). The road to glory goes through suffering, as it did for Christ (Luke 24:26; 2 Timothy 2:12; 1 Peter 4:13). Does this make the inheritance depend on how much we suffer? No. Paul is not setting a price, but describing the family path: the children share their brother’s road. Suffering with him does not mean that every believer will be martyred, or that suffering earns anything. It covers all that comes to believers because they belong to Christ: opposition, the cost of obedience, and the groaning of living in a fallen world while waiting for glory (vv. 18–23). Every true child of God shares in it in some measure; it is a mark of belonging, not a payment for the inheritance.

With him. The clause has frightened people it was never aimed at. The reader who is frightened by it is nearly always the one currently suffering, and what he hears is a demand for more. So notice what Paul actually writes. Not provided you suffer enough, and not provided your suffering is of a religious kind. He writes suffer with him, and the whole weight is in the last word. It is not the quantity that qualifies anything; it is the company. The question is not how much you are bearing but who is bearing it alongside you, and the answer this chapter gives is that he is not observing your suffering from a distance. He is in it, and he has been in worse. We do not earn glory by suffering; suffering is the road that leads to it, not the price that purchases it, and the fellow heir follows the same path as the Heir.

What it does not mean. This verse is sometimes used to sanctify things that ought to be resisted. Suffering with Christ does not mean accepting every affliction as sent and staying where you are. It does not mean a woman should remain in a house where she is being harmed: abuse is never to be tolerated, and she should seek safety and help at once. It does not mean an illness should not be treated, or that an injustice should be borne quietly when it could be addressed. Paul himself avoided danger repeatedly, appealed to Caesar, and was lowered over a wall in a basket. The verse describes the shape of the road, not a duty to seek out wounds.

In a sentence. If we are children, then we are heirs, heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, if indeed we share in his sufferings so that we may also share in his glory.

On a Tuesday. This test is about what your suffering has been doing to you rather than about how much of it there has been. Think of the hardest thing you have carried in the last five years. Has it driven you toward God or away from him? Not whether it felt good; it did not, and Paul does not ask that. Whether, over time, you have found yourself praying more honestly, holding this world more loosely, and wanting the day of glory in a way you did not before. That movement is what suffering with him looks like from the inside, and it is not a sign that you are being punished. It is a sign that you are on the road the Heir himself walked.

For worship. Glory is the last word of the sentence and not the first. Everyone would take the inheritance today if it were offered without the road. The Son was not offered it that way either: he endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2), and now he shares the joy with those who share the road. The heir of all things has made us his fellow heirs, and the inheritance he shares is God himself, who cannot fade, be stolen, or wear out. Blessed be the Father who gives himself, and the Son who would not inherit without his brothers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–30 — Future Glory: Groaning, Intercession, and the Golden Chain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The present sufferings are real — Paul does not minimise them — but they are not worth comparing to the glory that is to be revealed (v. 18). The entire creation groans, longing for the liberation that the resurrection of the children of God will bring. The believer groans too, in the Spirit, longing for the full redemption of the body. And the Spirit himself groans on behalf of believers with groanings too deep for words, interceding according to the will of God. Three levels of groaning: creation, believer, Spirit — all pointed toward the same consummation: the full glory of the children of God in the new creation.

"And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (v. 28). This verse has comforted more afflicted souls than almost any other in Scripture — and it has been more abused by careless application than almost any other. Paul is not promising that everything that happens to Christians will feel good or produce obvious benefit. He is promising that the God who is sovereign over all things is working in all things — the good and the bad, the joyful and the painful — toward a single end: the good of those he has called. The suffering is not outside his purposes; it is within them.

The "golden chain" of vv. 29–30 is the most concise summary of the Reformed ordo salutis in Scripture: foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified. Five links, each leading inevitably to the next, with no link missing and none reversible. The glorification is in the past tense — "he also glorified" — because it is as certain as if it had already happened. The God who foreknew in eternity past will glorify in eternity future, and nothing can interrupt the chain.
verseByVerse.theology:
Effectual Calling and the Golden Chain

Romans 8:29–30 is the biblical foundation for the Reformed doctrine of election and effectual calling. Foreknowledge here is not merely prior knowledge but prior relational knowing — the same sense in which God "knew" Israel (Amos 3:2) or the Shepherd knows his sheep (John 10:14). Those whom God foreknew with this special, electing love he predestined; those he predestined he called (effectually, inwardly, irresistibly); those he called he justified; those he justified he glorified. The chain is unbreakable. Every link is divine. The reason no one finally falls from grace is not that believers are strong enough to hold on, but that the God who foreknew and called them is powerful enough to keep what he has started.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The groaning of creation in vv. 19–22 draws on the Jewish understanding that the natural world was affected by human sin (Genesis 3:17–18) and will be renewed in the messianic age. Paul extends this vision: not just Israel but the whole creation waits for the redemption of God's children. The gospel is not merely the rescue of souls; it is the renewal of all things. Now: Romans 8:28 is one of the most misused verses in the Christian repertoire — invoked as a quick comfort for minor inconveniences and sometimes grotesquely applied to genuine catastrophe. Used rightly, it is not a promise that things will work out the way we hope; it is the promise of a sovereign God who is working toward his purpose in all things — and his purpose is better than our preferences.

verseByVerse.quote: For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.

For I consider. “Consider” (logizomai): calculate, the bookkeeping word again, the accountant’s word that has run through this letter: reckoned, credited, entered in a book. So Paul is not saying he feels that the sufferings are light. He is saying he has done the sum. This is a man writing from inside the arithmetic, not above it: beaten five times with thirty-nine lashes, three times with rods, stoned and left for dead, shipwrecked three times (2 Corinthians 11:23–28), and not many years from a Roman execution. Nobody can accuse him of setting a low value on suffering because he has not met any.

That the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us. Put them on the scales: sufferings on one side, glory on the other. The glory far outweighs. An eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). “Revealed to us”: or “in us.” We will share it.

Not worth comparing. The word is doing something precise. Paul does not say the sufferings are small; he says they are not in the same category as the glory: the two cannot usefully be set side by side, the way you cannot weigh a colour against a sound. That is a different consolation from the one we usually offer each other. We tend to say that the good will eventually outweigh the bad, which is a promise about a balance sheet, and a grieving person can feel the falseness of it immediately: no quantity of future pleasantness makes a dead child worth it. Paul is not proposing a trade. He is saying the coming thing is of an order that makes the comparison itself break down.

This present time. Two further things in the sentence are easily missed. First, the sufferings are of this present time, a phrase with a boundary in it. Paul is not describing suffering as a permanent feature of the universe but as belonging to an age that is ending. Second, the glory is to be revealed, which is the word for drawing back a covering. It is not being manufactured somewhere and shipped in later. It exists now, in Christ, and is presently out of sight, which is exactly what this chapter says about the whole Christian hope, and why the honest thing to say about the present is not that it is fine but that the curtain is still down.

Revealed to us. What is coming is not merely a better world that you get to look at. Paul will say in a few verses that we are to be conformed to the image of the Son (v. 29). It is a transformation of the person doing the looking.

What it does not mean. A verse like this can be used as a stick. It is possible to quote Romans 8:18 at a woman who has just buried her husband in a way that is genuinely cruel, as though the right response to grief were to stop making so much of it. That is not what the verse does, and the surrounding paragraph proves it: within eight verses Paul has creation groaning, believers groaning, and the Spirit himself groaning. He is not asking anyone to minimise. He is putting something on the other side. And the timing is everything. This verse is not a reply to somebody’s pain in the first week. It is ammunition to be stored in advance and used later, by the sufferer himself, on the days when the thing threatens to become the whole horizon. Paul writes it in the first person: I consider. He is telling them the conclusion he has reached about his own troubles, which is a considerably more usable thing to hand to someone.

Is it wrong to grieve, if the glory is so great? No. Jesus wept at the tomb of a friend he was about to raise (John 11:35). Paul tells the Thessalonians not that they should not grieve, but that they should not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is the right response to real loss in a fallen world, and the glory to come does not make the loss less real; it makes it not final. Christian grief and Christian hope live in the same heart at the same time. Weep, and hope while you weep.

What exactly is the glory? Not a vague brightness. Scripture names it. We will see Christ as he is and be like him (1 John 3:2). We will have bodies raised imperishable and glorious, like his (Philippians 3:21). We will be free of sin for ever, not only its guilt but its presence. We will live with God in a renewed creation, where he wipes away every tear and death is no more (Revelation 21:3–4). We will know him, worship him, serve him and reign with him, with the whole family of God from every nation. And at the centre of it all is not a place but a Person: the Lamb who was slain, whose face we shall see (Revelation 22:3–4).

In a sentence. Paul considers that our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us.

On a Tuesday. Take the heaviest thing you are currently carrying and try to complete this sentence honestly: compared with what is coming, this is... Most of us cannot finish it, and the reason is instructive. It is not that we doubt the glory. It is that we have never spent any time on it: we could describe our trouble in considerable detail and could not say four specific things about what we are promised. The sum Paul has done requires both figures, and most Christians have only one. Which is why the comparison feels hollow when we reach for it: we are weighing a vague word against a vivid ache, and the ache wins every time. So this week, read one passage about the glory (Revelation 21–22 or 1 Corinthians 15), and let it fill in the other side of the scales.

For worship. The glory that will be revealed is the glory of the Son himself, who went down into the deepest suffering this world contains and came up crowned. He did not ask us to walk a road he had not walked; he walked it first, and he walked it further. And the God who weighs our sufferings knows their exact weight, for he has counted every tear (Psalm 56:8). He has promised an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison (2 Corinthians 4:17), and he has never once promised more than he gave.

verseByVerse.quote: For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope

For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God. “Eager longing” (apokaradokia): watching with outstretched neck, craning to see. The whole universe is waiting on tiptoe for the day when God’s children are revealed in glory.

Craning its neck. The word is a picture rather than a concept. Apokaradokia is built from the word for a head: it describes someone craning, a person at the front of a crowd on a station platform, leaning out past the others, watching the point where the train will appear. That is what Paul says the physical universe is doing. Not decaying quietly. Waiting, with its neck out. And waiting for what, exactly? Not for its own repair, which is the surprise. Creation is craning for the revealing of the sons of God: it is watching for us. That reverses the usual arrangement, in which we are the ones waiting for the world to improve. Paul says the world is waiting on the disclosure of who God’s children turn out to be, because its own liberation is attached to ours. It went down when we did, and it comes up the same way.

Does creation really long for anything? No. Rocks, rivers and stars do not have minds or feelings. Paul is using personification: a figure of speech that speaks of non-human things as if they were people, to help us feel a truth. The Bible does this often. The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1). The earth mourns (Isaiah 24:4). The mountains and hills break into singing, and the trees clap their hands (Isaiah 55:12). The sea roars and the fields exult because the Lord is coming to judge the earth (Psalm 96:11–13), which is the very hope Paul has in view here. And Jesus said that if his disciples were silent, the stones would cry out (Luke 19:40).

Poetic, but not unreal. The picture describes something true. Creation really is not yet what God means it to be. It is in bondage to decay (v. 21): things wear out, die and break down. And its future is really tied to ours: it will be set free when God’s children are revealed in glory. We say a dry field is crying out for rain; the field feels nothing, but the need is real. So here: the whole created order is unfinished, pointing beyond itself. Paul lends it human longing so that we will feel how much is at stake, and so that we will long too (v. 23).

What it does not mean. Not that nature has a soul, or that the earth is a goddess to be honoured; that is the error Paul condemned in 1:25, worshipping the creature rather than the Creator. But also not that the physical world does not matter. God will not scrap his creation; he will renew it and set it free (v. 21; Revelation 21:1–5).

For the creation was subjected to futility. The creation was subjected to futility when God cursed the ground after Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:17–19). “Futility” (mataiotēti): frustration, emptiness, the word of Ecclesiastes (“vanity of vanities”). Creation can’t fulfil its purpose: decay, disaster, death.

The thing that will not hold still. Futility is exactly the right word for what we actually experience. It is the very word the Greek Old Testament uses again and again in Ecclesiastes for vanity: breath, vapour, the thing that will not hold still. It is why every human achievement has a slightly hollow centre, why the beautiful thing decays and the building needs repointing and the body that was strong at thirty is not at seventy. Nothing here stays. Paul is not being pessimistic; he is describing the condition of a world under sentence, and everybody knows it whether or not they have a theology for it.

Not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope. Who is him who subjected it? Not Adam, who had no power to subject creation to anything, nor Satan, who could not do it in hope. It is God, who pronounced the curse on the ground because of Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:17–19). Creation did not choose its frustration; it was bound up with humanity’s fall, because humanity was meant to rule it. And God subjected it in hope, with its liberation already planned. The curse was never meant to be final.

A hard sentence, and a mercy in it. This should not be softened. The thorns of Genesis 3, the decay, the earthquakes, the diseases that kill children in countries that did nothing in particular to deserve them: Paul does not attribute any of that to blind chance or to the devil. He traces it to a judicial act of God following Adam’s rebellion. It is one of the hardest sentences in the letter, and the honest thing is to let it stand. But notice what it saves you from. If the disorder of the world is an act of God, then it is meaningful and it is bounded. A universe damaged by accident has nobody to appeal to and no reason to expect a repair. A universe placed under futility by a Judge can be released by the same Judge, and the sentence has an end date. That is precisely why Paul adds the last two words: in hope. The subjection was never punitive only. It was passed with a view to the release.

Your ache is agreement. This yields something worth having about your own experience of the world. The sense that something is wrong with the way things are, the grief at a landscape ruined, the anger at a disease that should not exist, the refusal to be reconciled to the fact that everything you love is temporary, is not immaturity, and it is not a failure to be spiritual. It is agreement with the apostle. Creation is groaning; you are supposed to hear it.

In a sentence. The creation waits in eager expectation for God’s children to be revealed, for creation was subjected to frustration, not by its own choice, but by the will of the one who subjected it, in hope...

On a Tuesday. This test goes to whether your hope is actually Christian or only vaguely religious. When you imagine what God has promised, does the physical world appear in the picture at all? Most people, asked what they are looking forward to, describe a departure: souls somewhere else, this world left behind and presumably discarded. Paul describes an arrival, and a world craning its neck for it. If matter has no place in your hope, your hope is smaller than the one this chapter is describing, and considerably less interesting. The rivers and the mountains and the animals are not scenery to be struck at the end of the play. They are waiting to be included. Next time you walk outside, look at it that way.

For worship. The whole world is waiting for what God will do, and the God who subjected it did so in hope. He never once lost sight of the morning when the curse would be lifted. The Son through whom all things were made entered his own creation, wore its thorns as a crown, and rose as the first piece of the world made new. The cosmos stands on tiptoe because its Maker has promised to come back for it, and he always keeps his word.
verseByVerse.note: The creation was subjected to futility when God cursed the ground after Adam’s sin.

parallels.desc: cursed is the ground because of you

verseByVerse.quote: that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

That the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption. Creation itself will be liberated. Not destroyed and replaced, but renewed (Acts 3:21; Revelation 21:1–5; Isaiah 65:17). Decay, death and disorder will end.

Bondage to corruption. Corruption here is not moral wickedness but decay: the process by which things come apart. Everything you have ever loved is subject to it. The apple browns, the iron rusts, the paint flakes, the photograph fades, the memory blurs, the strong man weakens, and every living thing on this planet is on a schedule it did not choose and cannot appeal. Paul calls that a slavery, which is exactly the right word: it is not an occasional misfortune but a condition nothing here can escape.

What is abolished. What is promised is not that decay will be slowed or managed but that it will be ended, and this is the point at which the Christian hope becomes concrete rather than sentimental. Hold the promise against what is actually broken. No more funerals, because there will be nothing left to bury. No more scans, no waiting rooms, no results delivered by a doctor who has learned how to arrange his face. No more of the particular grief of watching a mind go while the body remains, or a body go while the mind remains. No more photographs of people you cannot ring. The thing this verse abolishes is not unpleasantness in general. It is the specific machinery by which everything good is taken away from you.

And obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God. Creation’s destiny is tied to ours. When God’s children are glorified, creation will be set free with them. This will happen when Christ returns, at the same time as the resurrection of the dead (1 Corinthians 15:23, 51–54). Then God will make the new heavens and the new earth (2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 21:1).

The family estate restored. The phrase Paul uses for the destination is odder than the translations make it sound. Creation is not given a freedom like ours, granted separately in a parallel arrangement. It is brought into the very liberty that belongs to God’s glorified children, as though the family estate were being restored along with the family. That is the Genesis arrangement running backwards: the ground was cursed because of a man (Genesis 3:17), and it is released because of men, and both times the creature and its habitat go together.

What are the new heavens and the new earth? The phrase comes from Isaiah (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22) and is taken up by Peter and John (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1). “The heavens and the earth” is the Bible’s way of saying the whole universe, as in Genesis 1:1: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. So the promise is a whole renewed creation, not just a better place for souls.

New in what sense? The Greek word for “new” here (kainos) usually means new in kind or quality, rather than brand-new from nothing. Our resurrection bodies are the best guide. They will be our bodies, raised and transformed: sown perishable, raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). The risen Jesus still bore the marks of the nails (John 20:27). In the same way, the new creation will be this creation, set free (v. 21), and yet so changed that it is truly new. Peter speaks of fire (2 Peter 3:10–12), but he also compares it with the flood, when the world of that time perished (2 Peter 3:6), yet the earth itself remained. The fire purifies and remakes; it does not simply erase.

What will it be like? Scripture gives us glimpses, not a map. God himself will dwell with his people: heaven and earth joined (Revelation 21:3). There will be no more death, mourning, crying or pain (Revelation 21:4), and no more curse (Revelation 22:3). It will be a home of righteousness (2 Peter 3:13). We will have real, resurrected bodies, and eat at the feast of the kingdom (Matthew 8:11; 26:29). God’s servants will serve him and reign (Revelation 22:3–5). The river and the tree of life are there (Revelation 22:1–2): Eden restored, and more than restored, because it is now a city full of the nations, who bring their glory into it (Revelation 21:24–26).

A garden at both ends. This explains something about the shape of the Bible that is easy to miss. It opens in a garden and closes in a garden city, with a river and a tree and leaves for the healing of the nations (Revelation 22:1–2). It does not open in a garden and close in a cloud. Whatever else the end of the story is, it is physical, and any version of the Christian hope in which believers finally leave the material world behind has got the last chapter wrong.

What it does not mean. Not that our final hope is to float on clouds as spirits for ever. When believers die, they go to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8), but that is not the end of the story. The final hope is the resurrection of the body in a renewed creation. Nor do we know the details: Revelation’s gold and jewels are pictures of glory, not a building plan. And it is not something we build by our own efforts. God says, I am making all things new (Revelation 21:5). Yet nothing done in the Lord is wasted (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Where Christians differ: the future of creation. Some believe the earth will be annihilated and believers will live in a purely spiritual heaven; others (premillennialists) expect a renewed earth in a thousand-year kingdom before the final state. Verdict: Scripture promises that this creation will be set free and renewed at Christ’s return: new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). Not escape from the material world, but its redemption. The amillennial view sees this as the final state, following Christ’s single return.

Work on material things. This is where the doctrine touches the way you live now. If God intends to redeem the material creation rather than discard it, then work done on material things is not a lower kind of work. The farmer, the surgeon, the engineer, the conservationist, the man who repairs things properly instead of badly: none of them is doing something merely temporal while the spiritual people do the real work. They are, in a small way, doing to a corner of creation what God intends to do to all of it. That does not make their labour permanent; the building will still fall down eventually. It makes it a signpost, which is a serious thing to be.

Will animals be there? Scripture pictures the new creation with animals in it: The wolf shall dwell with the lamb (Isaiah 11:6). Whether a particular pet will be raised, Scripture does not say, and we should not claim more than it does. But the hope of renewal shapes how we treat the world now. God put man in the garden to work it and keep it (Genesis 2:15), and that rules out both worshipping the earth and wasting it carelessly.

In a sentence. ...that the creation itself will be liberated from its bondage to decay and brought into the freedom and glory of the children of God.

On a Tuesday. God will renew this world; care for it now, as a sign of what he will do. And next time you are genuinely stopped by something in the created world, a sky, a piece of music, the face of someone asleep, notice the ache that comes with it, the one that wishes it would hold still. That ache is not a fault in you and it is not greed. It is the correct response to something beautiful under sentence, and this verse is the answer to it: the sentence is being lifted. What you love is not going to be taken from you permanently. It is going to be given back, without the decay attached.

For worship. The God who called creation very good in Genesis will vindicate that verdict in the new creation. He does not abandon what he has made; he redeems it. The One who sits on the throne says, I am making all things new (Revelation 21:5), and the Lamb who was slain has paid for the liberty of the whole cosmos with his blood. Every leaf that falls this autumn falls in a world that has been promised its spring.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.

For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. Not death throes, but birth pains. The groaning of creation, earthquakes, storms, disease, is not meaningless. It is labour, leading to new birth (Matthew 24:8).

Two kinds of screaming. The metaphor is chosen with great care, and it changes the character of the noise. There are two kinds of screaming in a hospital, and they can sound alike to somebody in the corridor. One is coming from a ward where something is ending; the other from a delivery room where something is beginning. Nothing in the sound itself tells you which is which. Paul says the groan of this world is the second kind, and that is a claim about meaning, not about volume. Labour pains are not less painful for being productive. And the image does not hurry anyone. It does not say the pain is small, or brief, or that a woman in the middle of it should be cheerful. It says the pain is going somewhere. There is a further honesty in it that we tend to skip: labour gets worse before it ends. Nobody in Scripture promises that the groaning of this age will taper off gently.

Does creation really groan? Not literally. Creation is not a person: the earth has no mind, and it does not feel pain as a mother in labour does. As in verse 19, Paul is using poetic language, personification, speaking of creation as if it were a person to help us feel a truth (see the note on v. 19). The picture of childbirth says two true things at once. The pain is real: creation really is broken, subject to decay, disease and disaster. And the pain is not pointless: like labour, it is leading somewhere, to the birth of a new creation (v. 21). Then the poetry turns to us: we, who really do feel, groan too (v. 23).

And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly. The firstfruits were the first part of the harvest, given to God as a pledge that the rest would follow (Leviticus 23:10). The Spirit is the first instalment of our full salvation (Ephesians 1:14). We groan too: not in despair, but longing.

Groaning because of the Spirit. Paul does something that ought to stop us: he puts Christians in the same sentence as the earthquakes and the decay. We groan too, and note who he says is doing it: not the immature, not the weak in faith, but those who have the firstfruits of the Spirit. The groaning is not evidence that something has gone wrong with your Christianity. It is evidence that the Spirit is in you. Firstfruits is a harvest word: the first sheaf, brought in before the rest, which is both genuinely the harvest and unmistakably not all of it. A man who has never tasted anything does not know what he is missing; the taste is what creates the hunger. So the Spirit’s presence does not settle you into contentment with the present world. He makes you less at home in it. The longing you feel is not a defect in your discipleship; it is the appetite the first course produced.

Homesick saints. That is why the ache goes up rather than down as a Christian matures, and why the most godly people you have known were often the most homesick. If you have found that the older you get in the faith the less this world satisfies you, you have not lost ground. You have been given more of the firstfruits.

As we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies. We are adopted now (v. 15), but the full adoption awaits: the resurrection of our bodies. Already, and not yet. The body will be redeemed, bought back from decay.

The paperwork is signed. This is odd at first, because Paul said in verse 15 that we have received the Spirit of adoption. Both are true, and the tension is the whole shape of the Christian life. The adoption is legally complete and experientially partial: you are a son now, and you are still living in a body that is failing. The paperwork is signed. The child has not yet come home. And the last words are the ones to hold. Not the redemption of our souls, which is what most Christians would have predicted. Our bodies. The thing being waited for is the one part of you that is visibly losing, and there is a reason Paul specifies it. Your soul is not the part of you that has a diagnosis.

Does this groaning mean I should not seek help for depression? No. The groaning of this verse is the longing of every believer for the redemption of the body, and it is healthy. Depression is something else: an illness of a body and mind that are part of this groaning creation, and like any illness it may need a doctor, medicine or counselling as well as prayer. Seeking that help is not a lack of faith, any more than setting a broken leg is. Elijah under the broom tree was given sleep and food before he was given a word (1 Kings 19:4–8). Tell your pastor and a trusted friend, see your doctor, keep coming to Christ, and if you ever think of ending your life, tell someone today.

In a sentence. We know that the whole creation has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth right up to now, and not only creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption, the redemption of our bodies.

On a Tuesday. When you feel the groan, the flat Sunday evening, the sense that nothing here is quite it, the grief that arrives without a specific cause, what do you conclude about yourself? Most of us treat it as a fault to be fixed: ingratitude, or a failure to count blessings, or something to be medicated with distraction. Paul treats it as the Spirit’s own work in you, running in the same direction as the groaning of the entire universe. You are not malfunctioning. You are in labour, along with everything else God has made. Turn the ache into a prayer: come, Lord Jesus.

For worship. Our groaning is not hopeless. It is labour before the birth of a new world, and the One who will deliver it has already passed through death and come out the other side as its firstborn. The Spirit who groans in us is the down payment of everything we long for; the Son whose body was redeemed from the grave on the third day is the pledge that ours will follow. The God who began the harvest with one sheaf has never yet left a field ungathered.
verseByVerse.note: The firstfruits were the first part of the harvest, given to God as a pledge of the whole harvest to come.

verseByVerse.quote: For in this hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in this hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience.

For in this hope we were saved. Salvation has a future dimension. We were saved, and saved with a hope of what is still to come.

Saved into hope. Take the first clause on its own, because it is easily read past and it settles something. The verb is past tense, completed. Salvation is not the thing being hoped for; it is the thing that has happened, and hope is the element it was delivered into. A Christian is not someone who hopes he will be saved. He is someone who has been saved into a situation that is not yet finished. The fullness of what we are saved into lies ahead, not behind.

Hope is a strong word. It is worth rescuing the word from the way we use it. In ordinary English hope is the weakest word we have for the future: I hope it does not rain, meaning I have no idea and no control. In Scripture it is one of the strongest: a settled expectation of something certain that has not yet arrived. The uncertainty is entirely in the timing and entirely absent from the outcome. A man waiting at an airport for a plane that has already taken off is not hoping in the English sense. He does not know the minute; he knows the plane is in the air.

Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? Hope by definition is about what we don’t yet have.

Invisibility is the arrangement. The logic of verse 24 is almost comically obvious once stated: nobody hopes for what he sees. So the invisibility of the thing is not an objection to the hope but a condition of it. If you could see it, this would not be hope; it would be sight, and Paul would have to find another word. The very feature of the Christian life that most troubles us, that the promises are not visible, that God does not produce evidence on demand, is not a flaw in the arrangement. It is the arrangement. You are not failing because you cannot see it. You would be failing if you needed to.

But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience. “Patience” (hypomonēs): endurance, steadfastness. Christian hope produces patient endurance. Not passive waiting, but steadfast living (5:3–4).

Remaining under. The word is the one from chapter 5, and it is not patience in the mild English sense of not being irritable in a queue. It is built from remaining under: the capacity to stay put beneath a weight that is not lifting. It is a soldier’s word, not a saint’s. And notice that Paul assumes there is a weight; he does not say we wait with serenity, or with enthusiasm, but with the sort of endurance you only need when the waiting costs something. So the honest shape of the Christian life in this passage is this: saved, certainly; groaning, genuinely; seeing nothing, at present; and staying put. That is a considerably less triumphant account than the one often preached, and it is a great relief to anybody whose experience has not matched the advertised version.

What if I find it hard even to want heaven? Then say so to God, and ask him for the longing; it is a prayer he delights to answer. Desire for glory grows the way appetite grows: by tasting.
