Spend time with what Scripture says about the age to come, and especially with Christ himself, because heaven is wanted most by those who want him most. Notice too that many Christians do not want heaven because they picture it wrongly, as a thin and ghostly place; the real promise is a raised body in a renewed world with the Lord. And do not despise the small longing you already have. The firstfruits of the Spirit are small by definition.

In a sentence. In this hope we were saved, but hope that is seen is no hope at all, for who hopes for what they already have? But if we hope for what we do not yet have, we wait for it patiently.

On a Tuesday. This test distinguishes hope from optimism, which are constantly confused. Optimism is a temperament: some people have it and some do not, it rises and falls with sleep and circumstance, and it collapses when the facts turn against it. Hope is a conviction about an outcome guaranteed by somebody else, and it is entirely compatible with feeling terrible. So ask: if you were told today that the thing you are waiting for will not come in your lifetime, the prodigal will not return before you die, the illness will not lift, the marriage will not mend, would you still be a Christian on Sunday? An optimist could not survive that sentence. Hope can, because hope was never resting on the timetable. What you hope for is not yet seen; wait for it with patience, for it is certain.

For worship. Paul can put waiting and salvation in the same breath without embarrassment. The waiting is not the interval before the Christian life begins. It is the Christian life, conducted in the dark, by people who have been given every reason to believe the lights are about to come on. And the One we wait for is not a vague future but a faithful Lord who has already come once, exactly as promised, and has said, Surely I am coming soon (Revelation 22:20). The God of hope has never yet disappointed anyone who waited for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.

Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. “Helps” (synantilambanetai): takes hold together with, shares the load. Like someone grabbing the other end of a heavy log.

The other end of the load. The word for helps is one of Paul’s compounds and it repays unpacking, because it is a picture of two people and a load. It means to take hold of something together with somebody, from the other side. It occurs only once more in the New Testament: Martha, complaining that Mary has left her to serve alone, asks the Lord to tell her sister to help her (Luke 10:40). Same word. So this is not general assistance from a distance. It is somebody coming to the other end of a thing too heavy for one person and lifting. And notice precisely where the help is applied. Not to our circumstances, in the first instance, and not to our understanding. To our weakness, and Paul names the particular weakness he has in mind, which is not the one we would have chosen.

For we do not know what to pray for as we ought. An honest admission. Even Paul didn’t always know what to pray. In suffering especially, we don’t know what is best.

We do not know. That is an extraordinary admission to find in Scripture, and it is worth letting it land before rushing to the comfort. The apostle includes himself. Not the immature, not the new believer, not the poorly taught. The problem is not technique; it is that we genuinely cannot see far enough to know what is good. You pray for the illness to be lifted, and it may be the illness that saves your life in a way you cannot yet imagine. You pray for the door to open, and you do not know what is behind it. Paul himself prayed three times for a thorn to be removed and was told no, and the no turned out to be the better answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–9).

But the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. The Spirit prays for us, from within. Creation groans (v. 22), we groan (v. 23), and now the Spirit is said to groan too.

The third groan. So the Spirit does not merely improve our praying. He prays. This is the third and deepest groan in a passage that has already given us creation groaning and believers groaning. The Trinity is not a spectator of the ache of the world.

What does “too deep for words” mean? The Greek is two words: stenagmois alalētois, “groanings” that are alalētos, literally “not spoken”. It can mean wordless, never put into speech, or unutterable, too deep to be put into speech. Either way, the point is not that God cannot understand them, or that the Spirit is short of words. The point is that this praying happens below the level of our words. Our words fail; his intercession does not. And it is perfectly understood: the Father, who searches hearts, knows the mind of the Spirit (v. 27).

Whose groanings are they? Paul says the Spirit himself intercedes. But he has just said that we groan inwardly (v. 23), and the Spirit is the Spirit who lives in us (vv. 9–11). So many, including Calvin, understand it this way: the Spirit stirs up in our hearts the deep, wordless longings that we cannot express, and takes them up as his own intercession before the Father. Others stress that the Spirit intercedes for us in a way hidden from us altogether. Both agree on the heart of it: the Spirit is praying for us, within us, in line with God’s will. Groaning is also a word borrowed from our experience. It speaks of deep, earnest desire, not of the Spirit being in distress or unable to cope.

What it means in real life. You sit by a hospital bed and cannot find a single sentence to pray. You wake at night with a weight you cannot name, and all you can say is, O God. Your grief over a child, a marriage or your own sin comes out as a sigh or tears. That is not failed prayer. The Spirit takes that wordless longing, and before the Father it becomes a prayer that is exactly right, because the Spirit always asks according to the will of God. You do not have to find the right words to be heard.

What it does not mean. Not that words in prayer do not matter: Jesus gave us words to pray (Matthew 6:9–13), and the Psalms are full of them. Not a secret prayer language that only some believers have (see below). And not that we can stop praying because the Spirit prays instead. He helps us in our weakness (v. 26): he takes the other end of the load, and we keep carrying it with him.

And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit. God the Father knows what the Spirit means. Perfect communication within the Trinity.

Because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God. His prayers are always in line with God’s will, so they are always answered. Two intercessors: Christ at God’s right hand (v. 34), and the Spirit in our hearts.

The whole circuit. See the architecture, because it is astonishing. The Father searches hearts and reads what the Spirit is saying in you. The Spirit intercedes according to the will of God. So a prayer that begins as an inarticulate ache in a believer is taken up by God the Spirit, presented to God the Father, in perfect accordance with the will of God, and Christ is at the right hand interceding as well (v. 34). Every person of the Trinity is engaged in getting your prayer answered rightly, and the only weak link in the chain is the part you were worried about.

The praying has changed hands. This is exactly the comfort the verse was written to give, and it is aimed at a specific reader. If you are in a season where prayer has become almost impossible, where you sit down to pray and produce nothing, or where the grief is so heavy that the words do not assemble, or where you have prayed so long about one thing that you cannot bear to raise it again, this verse says the praying has not stopped. It has changed hands. The groan you cannot articulate is itself being carried, and it arrives at the Father in perfect condition. And this is not a technique or a special category of spiritual person. Paul describes what the Spirit does for ordinary Christians in ordinary weakness, most of it happening below the level at which you would notice anything. You do not need to feel this for it to be true. It is not an experience to be attained; it is a fact to be leaned on.

Where Christians differ: are these groanings tongues? Some see these groanings as speaking in tongues; many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians read them as a private prayer language given by the Spirit. Verdict: no. They are “too deep for words”, not spoken in any language, and they belong to every believer, since Paul is speaking of all who have the Spirit (vv. 9, 14). Tongues were a spoken gift given to some, not to all (1 Corinthians 12:30). Paul says it is the Spirit who intercedes, and that his groanings are too deep for words, which is the opposite of an utterance. This is the Spirit’s hidden intercession for all God’s children, and the comfort is meant for every believer who cannot find words to pray.

In a sentence. In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness, for we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us through wordless groans, and he who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for God’s people in accordance with God’s will.

On a Tuesday. The test is not about the quality of your prayer life but about what you do when it fails. When you cannot pray, do you stay away until you can, waiting until you have something worth saying, or the composure to say it? Most of us do, and it is exactly backwards. The verse says the moment you have nothing is the moment the Spirit is doing his particular work. Go and sit down with nothing. Say so. That inarticulate sitting, with a heart that cannot form a sentence, is not the absence of prayer. On the authority of this verse, it may be the truest praying you have done all year.

For worship. When we do not know how to pray, the Spirit prays for us, and we are never alone in prayer. The Holy Spirit, who is God, kneels, as it were, beside the weakest believer and takes the other end of the load. The Father who searches hearts hears every groan and understands it perfectly. The Son at his right hand pleads his finished work. No prayer of the believer is too broken, too incoherent or too wordless to reach the throne, because the whole Godhead is at work to carry it there.

parallels.desc: you have searched me and known me

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. — Romans 8:28
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.

And we know. Not hope or guess, but knowledge. Certain.

Apostolic certainty. This is not optimistic hope but apostolic certainty. Paul is not encouraging a cheerful mindset; he is stating a fact about the way God operates in the world. The sovereignty of God over all things, including suffering, loss, betrayal, disease and death, means that nothing is random for the child of God. And because this is the most quoted verse in the chapter and very nearly the most abused, it is worth being exact about what it does not say before enjoying what it does.

That for those who love God all things work together for good. All things: not just good things, but suffering, loss, failure, even sin. Not that all things are good, but that God works them together for good. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God works all things together for good.” Either way, God is the one at work. “Good”: defined by v. 29, being made like Christ. Not necessarily comfort, but Christlikeness.

For those who are called according to his purpose. The promise is for those who love God, and they love him because he called them. His purpose comes first. God’s calling here is effectual: it brings people to faith (v. 30).

What it does not mean. It does not mean everything will turn out the way we want, or that bad things aren’t truly bad. It means that God, in his wisdom, weaves even the worst things into his good purpose for his people. Joseph said it: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20).

Not that all things are good. Paul has just spent ten verses on futility, bondage, decay and groaning; he is not now going to tell you that the groaning was fine all along. The cancer is not good. The betrayal is not good. The child’s death is not good, and God does not call it good: he calls death an enemy, and the last enemy at that (1 Corinthians 15:26). What the verse says is that God works in all things, which presupposes material that needs working on.

Not on our timetable. Nor does it say that all things work together for what you would recognise as good, or that the good will be visible on any particular timetable, or that a reason will be supplied. Joseph waited more than twenty years to be able to say what God had been doing (Genesis 50:20), and most of the people in Scripture who suffered were never told anything at all. Job never learned about the conversation in chapter 1.

Not of everyone. Twice in one sentence Paul draws the circle: for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose. This is a promise made to a family, not a general observation about how the universe treats people. To offer it to somebody outside that circle is not comfort; it is a false assurance, and they will find out. The right thing to offer them is the gospel, which invites them into the circle.

Not for the hospital corridor. A great deal of damage is done with this verse by people who mean well. It is not a sentence to be deployed at a funeral, or in a hospital corridor, or in the first weeks after a marriage ends. Not because it is untrue then; it is precisely as true then as at any other moment. But in the mouth of the sufferer it is a handhold, while in the mouth of a bystander it sounds like an instruction to stop making a fuss, as though the pain has already been accounted for and can therefore be set down. Paul writes it in the first person plural: we know. It belongs to the people inside the trouble, and the right thing to do with someone in fresh grief is what Job’s friends did for seven days before they opened their mouths and ruined everything.

All means all. Having cleared that away, see how much is actually here, because the verse is stronger than the version we usually preach. Paul chooses the widest word available. It includes the things done to you by other people’s malice, which is the hardest category, and Genesis says so without flinching: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). Both clauses stand. The brothers’ intention was evil and is not reclassified. God’s intention ran through the same event in the opposite direction. It also includes your own sins and stupidities: not that they were good, but that they are not outside the working. And it includes the wasted years, which is the item most people privately assume is excluded: the decade in the wrong job, the friendship that cost you and produced nothing, the season you were too ill or too lost to be of use to anyone.

Work together. This is the right image, because it is not a claim that each item is individually beneficial. Ingredients are not individually pleasant; nobody eats flour, raw egg is unappetising, and salt on its own is unbearable. The promise is not that every element tastes good but that the baker knows what he is doing and there will be a cake.

What good? The very next verse supplies the definition, and it changes everything. The good in view is not comfort, or resolution, or the outcome you asked for. It is being conformed to the image of his Son (v. 29). That is a considerably higher good than the one we would have chosen, and it explains why so many prayers get answered sideways: you asked for the circumstance to change and God is at work on the person in the circumstance.

If God works even my sins for good, why should I not sin? Because God works good out of sin in spite of what sin is, not because it is any less evil. Paul has already rejected this exact argument: shall we sin that grace may abound? By no means (6:1–2). Sin still grieves the Father, wounds others and scars you, and David’s forgiven adultery still cost him a child and a divided house. A son who wrecks his father’s car is not entitled to call it good because his father later teaches him through it. What this verse gives you after a fall is hope, that God has not abandoned you to your worst decisions. It never gives you permission for the next one.

In a sentence. We know that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, who have been called according to his purpose.

On a Tuesday. Whatever is happening to you, God is working it for good, the good of making you like Christ. So take the worst thing that has happened to you and ask, not whether you can see the good, because you very often cannot, but whether you are more like Christ than you were before it. More patient with people who are struggling. Less confident in yourself. Quicker to pray. Harder to impress with things that do not matter. Kinder to those in the same trouble. If any of that is true, you have found the good, and it did not look like good at the time and never does.

For worship. Where none of that is visible yet, the verse still stands, because it does not say we see. It says we know: exactly the word for a thing held on to in the dark, on the authority of somebody who can see the whole of it. The God who turned the worst deed ever done, the murder of his Son, into the salvation of the world is the God who holds every thread of our lives. If he could work Calvary for good, there is nothing in your story he cannot work.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God works all things together for good.”

verseByVerse.quote: For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son... And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified. — Romans 8:29–30
verseByVerse.commentary:
For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified.

For those whom he foreknew. “Foreknew” means more than knowing ahead of time: God set his love on them beforehand. In Scripture, “know” often means to love, to choose (Amos 3:2; Jeremiah 1:5; Matthew 7:23). Notice: “those whom” he foreknew, not “what” he foreknew. He foreknew persons, not their faith.

Foreknowledge as love. “Foreknew” carries the full biblical weight of the word know as God uses it: not mere awareness or prediction, but intimate, prior love. When God says to Israel in Amos 3:2 that he has known them only, of all the families of the earth, he does not mean he was unaware of the other nations; he means he chose Israel with covenant love. When Jeremiah hears that God knew him before he was formed in the womb (Jeremiah 1:5), it means more than that God was aware of him in advance; God had already set his love on Jeremiah before he drew his first breath. That is the sense here. Foreknowledge is not God looking down the corridor of time and selecting those he predicts will believe; it is God’s prior sovereign love that is the very ground of their believing.

He also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. The goal of predestination: likeness to Christ. God’s plan is to make his children like his Son.

Predestined to a likeness. Notice what the predestining is actually to, because this is where most discussion of the doctrine goes wrong before it starts. Paul does not say predestined to be saved, or predestined to heaven, or predestined to be on a list. He says predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. The destination is not primarily a place; it is a likeness. And that is the good the previous verse was reaching for. God’s settled intention concerning you, formed before the world existed, is that you should end up like Jesus Christ.

In order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Christ the eldest brother, with a vast family like him.

A family for the Son. Firstborn here is not about origin; it is the language of rank and inheritance, the pre-eminent one in a family. So the whole vast work of election, calling, justification and glory exists to produce a family for the Son. God was not merely rescuing individuals from a fire. He was gathering brothers and sisters for his Son, and the reason you are being made like Christ is that you are being made a member of his household. Family resemblance is not a metaphor here. It is the goal.

And those whom he predestined he also called. Effectual calling: the call that brings people to faith.

And those whom he called he also justified. Declared righteous, by faith.

And those whom he justified he also glorified. The golden chain: foreknown, predestined, called, justified, glorified. Five links, unbroken. Every person in the first link is in the last. No one drops out. And “glorified” is in the past tense, though future for us: so certain that God speaks of it as done.

Every verb is God’s. The chain is remarkable for its relentless divine agency: every verb has God as its subject. He foreknew, he predestined, he called, he justified, he glorified. The human person appears only as the object of each action, never as its subject. This is not passive fatalism; it is the most glorious news in Scripture: active divine faithfulness that begins in eternity, works through history, and ends in eternity with the human person glorified in the likeness of the Son. If foreknowledge merely meant foreseen faith, then God would be responding to what we do, and the whole golden chain would hang on us. Paul’s point is precisely the opposite: the chain holds because every link is God’s work, not ours.

The missing link. Look at what is missing from the chain, because it is the most comforting thing in the sentence and almost nobody notices it. Foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and then straight to glorified. There is no link for sanctified. Not because sanctification is unimportant; the whole chapter has been about it. But if progress in holiness were a link in this chain, the chain would be exactly as strong as your last six months, and every believer would have grounds for terror. Paul’s chain contains no link that depends on you. Your sanctification is the content of what God is doing between the fourth link and the fifth, not a condition to be met between them, and because he does it, it will be done.

Where Christians differ: foreknowledge and predestination. Arminians teach that God foreknew who would believe and predestined them on that basis. Verdict: Paul says God foreknew persons, not their choices; “foreknew” in biblical usage means to set one’s love on beforehand. And the chain is unbroken: all who are called are justified, so the call must be effectual, not merely an invitation many refuse. God’s choice is the cause of faith, not its result (Ephesians 1:4–5; 2 Timothy 1:9). This is unconditional election, and it is the ground of perfect assurance: if God began it in eternity, he will finish it in glory.

The Arminian case, heard fairly. Many Christians in the Arminian tradition read foreknew as God knowing in advance who would believe. They point to the ordinary sense of the word, and to Peter’s description of believers as elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father (1 Peter 1:2). But Paul says God foreknew people, those whom he foreknew, not facts about them. He uses the same verb in 11:2, of his people whom he foreknew, where it means God’s choosing love for Israel. And faith itself is God’s gift: it has been granted to you to believe (Philippians 1:29). If God chose us because he saw we would believe, the chain would begin with us.

Is it unfair? It would be unfair only if anyone deserved to be chosen. No one is condemned who did not deserve it, and everyone who is saved owes it to mercy (9:14–16). The question is not why God does not save everyone, which Scripture leaves in his wisdom, but why he saves anyone, which Scripture answers: because he loved them, freely, in Christ. Election does not make heaven smaller than it would have been; without it, heaven would be empty.

How do I know I am in this? The question should be asked out loud rather than left to trouble people privately. The first link is in eternity past and you cannot read it. Nobody has ever been given access to the decrees of God, and every attempt to peer into them ends either in presumption or despair. So do not start there. Of the five links, the first two and the last are out of sight, but the middle two are visible. Have you been called: not merely invited by a preacher, but drawn, so that there came a point at which Christ mattered to you in a way he had not before? Are you justified: when you consider standing before God, are you resting on Christ rather than on your record? Those are answerable questions. And a chain does not have a middle without both ends. If you can find yourself at link three or four, links one and five are settled, and they were settled without consulting you.

What if I am afraid I am not elect? Notice that the anxiety itself is a kind of answer. Nobody who is indifferent to God lies awake worrying about this. The desire is not the qualification, but it is evidence of the drawing, and the door has never been shut on anyone who came: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). You are never asked to find your name in eternity past before you come to Christ. You are asked to come, and those who come find they were expected.

If God has chosen, why evangelise or pray? Because the God who chose the end also chose the means. Those he predestined he called, and he calls through the gospel preached by people like you: how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard (10:14)? Election is not a reason to stay silent; it is the reason evangelism will not fail. Paul kept going in Corinth because the Lord told him he had many people in that city (Acts 18:10). You do not know who the elect are, so offer Christ freely to everyone, and pray, because prayer is one of the ways God brings about what he has purposed.

What it does not mean. A doctrine this strong is regularly turned into passivity. Nothing here suggests that effort is pointless or that a Christian may now sit still; Paul has already commanded you to put sin to death (v. 13) and will spend four chapters on obedience. The chain does not tell you what to do. It tells you why what you do will not finally fail, which is a different thing entirely and a far better one.

In a sentence. Those God foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he would be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters, and those he predestined he also called, those he called he also justified, and those he justified he also glorified.

On a Tuesday. You will not find your name in eternity past. You will find it in what you want on a Tuesday. So look at your own hands and find what you are holding. Do you trust Christ, and want him? Then thank God, this morning, for loving you before you existed, and get on with the work he has given you, knowing that he who began it will finish it.

For worship. Here is a chain forged before the world was made, whose first link is in eternity past and whose last is in eternity to come, and only the middle of it happens where you can see. And glorified is in the past tense, though it is future for us: the God who stands outside time speaks of it as already done. Your glorification is not a possibility but a certainty, not because you are strong but because he is faithful. From eternity past to eternity future, the Father holds his children in an unbreakable chain, and every link of it was forged by love.
verseByVerse.note: “Foreknew” means more than knowing ahead of time: God set his love on them beforehand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–39 — Nothing Can Separate Us from the Love of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter ends with a doxology of certainty — a sustained rhetorical climax in which Paul asks a rapid series of questions, answers each in triumph, and then piles up a list of everything in the universe that might be imagined to separate the Christian from the love of God — only to declare that none of it can. This is not wishful thinking; it is the logical conclusion of everything Paul has argued since 1:16. The gospel that justifies the ungodly will not ultimately abandon the justified; the God who did not spare his own Son will certainly spare those for whom his Son died.

"If God is for us, who can be against us?" (v. 31). The answer is not that no one will be against us — Paul has just described tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, and sword (v. 35). The enemies are real. But no enemy, however powerful, can ultimately prevail against those for whom God himself has declared himself as advocate and champion. The "who" of the question is not answered with "no one" but with "it doesn't matter" — because God's being for us outweighs any opposition.

The concluding list — death, life, angels, rulers, things present, things to come, powers, height, depth, anything else in all creation — is Paul's way of saying: I have tried to think of everything, and I cannot think of anything that can separate you from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. The love of God is not a feeling that fluctuates with our spiritual temperature; it is the settled, sovereign, covenant commitment of the God who gave his Son for us. That love will not let us go — because it has never been dependent on us to begin with.

Two of the questions in between deserve naming, because they are the ones a troubled conscience actually asks. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? and Who is to condemn? (vv. 33–34). Paul does not answer by denying that there is anything to charge — the first three chapters of this letter were the charge sheet. He answers by naming who occupies the two seats that matter: it is God who justifies, and the one who might condemn is the one who died, was raised, is at the right hand, and is at this moment interceding. The prosecution may say what it likes; the bench and the counsel for the defence are already taken. And then v. 37, which is not a claim that the hardships are avoided: in all these things — the tribulation, the famine, the sword — we are more than conquerors, which means the victory is won inside the trouble rather than by escaping it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Perseverance of the Saints

Romans 8:31–39 is the biblical anchor of the Reformed doctrine of the perseverance (or preservation) of the saints. The saints do not persevere because they are strong; they persevere because God keeps them. The question is not whether we can hold on to God but whether God will hold on to us — and Paul's answer is thunderous. The God who predestined, called, and justified will glorify. Nothing in the universe — not even our own faithlessness — can sever the love that chose us before we existed and purchased us at the cost of the Son. Perseverance is not a human achievement; it is a divine gift, the last link in the golden chain.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's list of hardships in v. 35 — tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, sword — was not hypothetical for his original readers. The Roman church would face Nero's persecution within a decade. Some of them would be burned as torches in Nero's gardens; some would be torn by dogs. Paul writes these verses for people who will need them when the persecution comes. Now: The Christian in the comfortable West reads Romans 8:35–39 as comfort for ordinary difficulties. The Christian in the persecuted church reads it as the word they need to die well. Both readings are valid, and the comfortable Christian is unwise to forget that what sustained the martyrs is the same grace that sustains her — and the same grace may yet be tested in ways she has not anticipated.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?

What then shall we say to these things? Paul draws the conclusion of everything he has said, and the question is looking further back than we usually notice. These things are not merely the golden chain of the previous verse. The phrase reaches back through the whole letter: the wrath revealed, every mouth stopped, the propitiation set forth in public, the ungodly justified, peace with God, the reign of grace, no condemnation, the Spirit given, the groaning, the chain. Paul has finished arguing. What follows is not another proof but a challenge thrown out to the universe.

If God is for us, who can be against us? Not that no one opposes us, since many do, but that no opposition can succeed against those God is for.

Since, not if. The if is not tentative. In Greek it is the sort of conditional that assumes the thing is true: better heard as since God is for us. Paul is not raising a possibility. He is stating the established fact of eight chapters and asking what could possibly follow from it. And for us does not mean on our side, as though God were choosing between two teams. It means that God himself is our advocate, our champion, our protector.

He who did not spare his own Son. An echo of Abraham, who did not withhold Isaac (Genesis 22:12, 16). But God went further: he did not spare his Son.

Abraham’s sentence, spoken of God. The words Paul chooses here are not his own. That verb, in that construction, comes from one place in the Greek Old Testament, and every reader who knew the Scriptures would have heard it instantly. On the mountain, with the knife raised over Isaac, the voice from heaven says to Abraham that now he knows Abraham fears God, seeing he has not withheld his son, his only son (Genesis 22:12, 16). Paul takes the sentence God spoke to Abraham and applies it to God.

No ram in the thicket. Sit with that for a moment, because the whole verse rests on it. Abraham was stopped. There was a voice, and a hand caught before it fell, and a ram in the thicket: a substitute provided so that the son could walk down the mountain alive. At Calvary there was no voice. Nobody called from heaven; the hand was not caught; there was no ram in the thicket, because this time the Son was the ram. God asked Abraham for something he did not in the end require of him, and then did it himself.

But gave him up for us all. “Gave him up” (paredōken): handed over, to death. “For us all”: all God’s people, those foreknown and called (vv. 29–30).

The same verb. The word for what he did is the one that has been running through this letter like a dark thread: gave him up, the same word used three times in chapter 1 of God handing sinners over to what they had chosen (1:24, 26, 28). The letter’s most terrible verb and its most merciful one are the same verb, and here it reaches its destination. The Father handed over the Son so that he would never have to hand us over.

How will he not also with him graciously give us all things? The argument from greater to lesser. If God gave the greatest gift, his Son, he will not withhold anything lesser that we need. Every good thing comes with Christ.

The arithmetic is settled. Paul does not say God will give us all things; he asks how it could conceivably be otherwise. If the account has already borne the largest possible debit, no later request puts it under strain. The point is not that God is generous in general: the question of his generosity was answered publicly, on a hill, at a cost that cannot be exceeded. Everything else is a smaller ask than the one already granted. Note also the verb for the giving: not simply give but graciously give, built on the word for grace. It is not a transfer of goods but the disposition of a giver. And all things is the same phrase as in verse 28: the all things that work together for good are the all things he will freely give. The two verses describe one arrangement from two sides.

What it does not mean. This verse has been made into a blank cheque. It does not promise that God will give you whatever you ask for. All things here is bounded by what has just been defined as the good, conformity to the image of his Son (v. 29), and the chapter has already admitted that we often do not know what to pray for (v. 26). So the promise is not that you will get the outcome you want. It is that nothing you truly need will be withheld, and that the God supplying you is the one who has already proved he does not hold back the things that cost him.

Then why do I lack things I ask for? Because a good Father gives what is good, which is not always what is asked, and because he sees further than we do. Sometimes he withholds a thing because it would harm us, sometimes because something better is coming, and sometimes for reasons we will not learn in this life. What you can be sure of is the direction of his heart. Ask freely and specifically; Jesus tells you to (Matthew 7:7–11). But when the answer is no or not yet, do not read it as stinginess. A God who gave his Son is not saving money on you.

In a sentence. What then shall we say in response? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also, along with him, graciously give us all things?

On a Tuesday. This test is about evidence rather than feeling. Name something good that you want and have quietly concluded God is not willing to give you: the healing, the child, the work, the release from the thing that has you. Now set out the evidence on both sides. On the side of his unwillingness you will generally find a long silence and a feeling. On the side of his willingness you have an execution, publicly conducted, of his own Son, on your behalf, while you were his enemy. That is not a close-run comparison, and the reason it does not feel decisive is that we weigh the evidence we can see against the evidence we can feel, and the feeling is nearer. God gave you his Son; he will not hold back anything you truly need.

For worship. Abraham climbed a mountain with his son and came down with him. God climbed the same kind of hill and came down alone, and the whole security of every Christian rests on the fact that nobody stopped him. The Father who did not spare his own Son has nothing left to prove about his love. Every lesser gift comes to us wrapped in that greatest one, and with Christ, all things are ours.

parallels.desc: the LORD is on my side; I will not fear
you have not withheld your son

verseByVerse.quote: Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died — more than that, who was raised — who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died — more than that, who was raised — who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us.

Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? A courtroom scene. “God’s elect”: those chosen by God. Satan accuses (Revelation 12:10), conscience accuses, others accuse. Can any charge stand?

It is God who justifies. The judge himself has declared them righteous. Who can overturn the Supreme Court?

Outranked, not denied. Notice how Paul answers, because it is not the way we would. Asked who shall bring any charge, the natural reply is nobody: there is nothing to charge. Paul does not say that, and he could not: the first three chapters of this letter were the charge sheet, and every word of it stands. He answers a question about the prosecution by naming the judge. The charges may be entirely accurate. They have already been heard by the only bench with jurisdiction, and the verdict is in. So the accusation is not being denied but outranked. A great deal of Christian anxiety comes from trying to fight on the wrong ground. When the accusation arrives, you are a fraud, you have done that same thing again, a real Christian would not think this, the instinct is to argue the facts, and the facts are often against you. This verse does not ask you to win that argument. It asks who is sitting on the bench.

Who is to condemn? No one, because:

Christ Jesus is the one who died. He paid the penalty.

More than that, who was raised. Proof the payment was accepted.

Who is at the right hand of God. Reigning, in the place of power.

Who indeed is interceding for us. Four reasons no one can condemn us: his death, resurrection, exaltation, intercession. He pleads his finished work for us continually (Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2:1). Our defence attorney is the judge’s Son, and the one who paid our fine.

A compressed creed. The answer to the second question is a creed in four clauses, each one raising the ground higher. He died: the penalty has been carried. He was raised: the payment was accepted, publicly receipted. He is at the right hand: the one competent to condemn is the one already seated as sovereign. He is interceding: and he is using that position, at this moment, on your behalf.

The most neglected doctrine. Stay with the last clause, because it is doing enormous work here. Christians think a great deal about what Christ did and almost nothing about what he is doing. Paul says he is interceding: present tense, continuous, now. Not that he is pleading with a reluctant Father, as though the Father needed persuading; the Father is the one who gave him. It means the case is permanently before the court with counsel permanently present. John puts it in the plainest possible terms for people who have just failed: if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1).

Who sits where. Consider who is on which side of the room, because Paul has arranged this deliberately. The Judge is the one who justifies. The counsel for the defence is the one who might have condemned. There is no seat left for the prosecution that carries any weight, which is why Scripture can call the enemy the accuser of our brothers, who accuses them day and night before our God (Revelation 12:10), and still treat him as thrown down. He is not necessarily lying about you. He simply has no standing in this court.

What do I do when my conscience accuses me of something true? Agree with it about the sin, and disagree with it about the verdict. If the charge is true, confess it to God plainly; do not argue, minimise or blame. Then take your stand where this verse stands: it is God who justifies, and Christ has died for this very sin. Even when our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything (1 John 3:20). If you have wronged someone, put it right. But do not let a true charge become a false sentence. The sin was real; so was the payment.

What it does not mean. This cannot be turned into indifference about sin. Nothing here suggests that the charges do not matter: the Advocate is also the one who died for them, which is a considerably more serious view of your sin than the accuser has. And John says if anyone does sin, not since everyone does and it hardly signifies. The point is not that sin is trivial. It is that it has already been answered, by someone still speaking.

In a sentence. Who will bring any charge against those God has chosen? It is God who justifies. Who then can condemn? No one, for Christ Jesus who died, and more than that, was raised to life, is at the right hand of God interceding for us.

On a Tuesday. When the accusation comes, and it will come, usually at night and usually after a failure, listen to your own reply. If it begins with but I, in any form at all, but I am trying, but I have repented, but I am not as bad as that, but I did well last week, you have accepted the prosecution’s framing and are attempting to conduct your own defence. You will lose, because your record cannot bear the weight and you know it. The reply this passage gives contains no information about you whatever: it is God who justifies; Christ Jesus died, was raised, is at the right hand, and is speaking for me now. Four facts, none of them about your week.

For worship. Every seat that matters in that courtroom is occupied by someone on your side. The accusations may be perfectly accurate; the Judge has ruled; the only person qualified to condemn you is at this moment on his feet, speaking in your favour, and he is not doing it out of sentiment, but because he has the receipts. Each of the four clauses is a door closing on the accuser. There has not been a moment since that Easter morning in which the Son of God was not speaking to his Father about people who do not deserve to be mentioned.

parallels.desc: he who vindicates me is near; who will contend with me?

verseByVerse.quote: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? As it is written, "For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? As it is written, “For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered.”

Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? The final question. Can anything break Christ’s love for us?

The thing under guarantee. Notice the exact form of the question, because Paul has narrowed it and the narrowing is the comfort. He does not ask whether these things can separate us from a sense of God’s nearness, or from peace of mind, or from comfort, any of which suffering demonstrably can disturb. He asks whether they can separate us from the love of Christ. That is the thing under guarantee. Your feelings about God will be knocked about badly by famine and danger and the sword; his love for you is not among the casualties.

Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? Seven trials, most of which Paul himself endured (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). The sword: Paul was later beheaded.

Reading out his diary. The list is not rhetorical. Every item on it had a face for Paul: a man who had been flogged, stoned, shipwrecked, gone hungry and cold, and who would in a few years meet the last item on the list personally. He is not compiling worst cases. He is reading out his diary. Nor was it hypothetical for the people receiving the letter. Within about a decade of this being read aloud in Rome, Nero would be using Christians as entertainment, some torn by dogs, some crucified, some set alight in the imperial gardens. Paul was writing these sentences for people who would need them. That is worth remembering when the verse is used, as it usually is, for far smaller troubles. It is not too grand for your difficulties. It was simply built to bear a great deal more.

For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered. From Psalm 44:22. Suffering is not a sign that God has abandoned us. It has always been the lot of God’s people. Believers are not spared suffering, but they are never separated from Christ’s love in it.

A psalm of complaint. This is the strangest thing in the passage, and it is usually skated over. At the very summit of his argument for the security of the believer, Paul quotes a psalm, and not a psalm of triumph. Psalm 44 is a complaint. The nation is being slaughtered and cannot understand why: all this has come upon them, though they have not forgotten God; and it ends by crying out to heaven, Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? (Psalm 44:17, 23). That is the psalm Paul reaches for, deliberately, in the middle of the most confident paragraph he ever wrote. It tells you something about Christian assurance that a hundred cheerful sermons will not. Paul is not claiming that the Christian life will look like victory from the outside. It will often look exactly like abandonment, sheep in a queue at the slaughterhouse, and he says so by quoting the complaint rather than answering it. The security he is describing is not visible in the circumstances. If it were, he would not have needed the psalm.

For your sake. The appearances are wrong. Regarded as sheep to be slaughtered is how it looks and not how it is, and the thing you cannot see is the only thing that has not moved. Notice, too, the three words the psalm gives for why: for your sake. This is not meaningless attrition. Even at the slaughterhouse the sheep belong to somebody, and their being there has to do with him.

Is it wrong to ask God why? No. Paul has just quoted a whole psalm that asks him, and God put it in the Bible. Lament is not unbelief; it is faith that talks to God when it does not understand him, rather than turning away. The psalmist asks why and still calls God his own, and still appeals to his steadfast love (Psalm 44:26). Jesus himself cried out from the cross, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matthew 27:46). So bring your questions to God, not away from him. What you must not do is turn the unanswered why into a verdict against his love. The cross has already settled that.

In a sentence. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble, hardship, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger or sword? As Scripture says: for your sake we face death all day long; we are considered sheep to be slaughtered.

On a Tuesday. When you are in the middle of something hard, what conclusion do you draw about God’s love for you? Nearly all of us reason from the circumstance: if he loved me, this would not be happening, or at least it would be lifting by now. Paul reasons the other way round, and he is entitled to, because he has already produced the evidence in verse 32. The measure of Christ’s love for you is not the state of your life this year. It is a cross, which is fixed, dated, and unaffected by anything currently happening to you. Suffering does not mean Christ has stopped loving you. And remember those who are being killed for his sake today; pray for them by name and region this week (Hebrews 13:3).

For worship. The question at the head of these verses can be asked boldly. Paul is not daring the universe to try. He has been through the list, in his own body, and is reporting back: none of it reached the thing that mattered. The Good Shepherd himself became the sheep led to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7), so that no sheep of his would ever face the slaughter alone. His love went through tribulation, distress, persecution, nakedness and the sword, and came out the other side with nail-scarred hands still holding his own.

parallels.desc: for your sake we are killed all the day long

verseByVerse.quote: No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.

No, in all these things we are more than conquerors. “More than conquerors” (hypernikōmen): super-conquerors, overwhelmingly victorious. Not by escaping trials, but in them. The trials themselves become servants of our good (v. 28).

A word Paul had to build. The word looks as though Paul made it up, and he may well have. To conquer is nikaō, and he has put hyper on the front of it: over-conquer, hyper-conquer. English has no single equivalent, which is why the translators reached for a phrase. He needed something that did not exist, so he built one. And the first words are the ones to hold: in all these things. Not out of them, not after them, and not instead of them. The tribulation is still tribulation, the famine is not cancelled, and the sword of verse 35 is not confiscated before it falls. Paul is describing a victory that happens with the sword still in the room.

Through him who loved us. Past tense: who loved us, at the cross. The victory is his, shared with us.

Living on a finished act. This is the phrase that keeps the whole thing from becoming a boast about Christian resilience. Note the tense: loved, past, pointing at a completed act rather than a passing sentiment. The strength you are conquering by is not being generated in you now; it was expended at a particular moment in history, on a hill, and you are living on it. That is a great relief to anyone who has ever read a verse like this and quietly concluded that real Christians must be stronger than they are.

What do we conquer? Not people. Paul will soon tell us to bless those who persecute us (12:14), and our enemies are to be loved, not defeated (12:20–21). What we conquer are “all these things”: the list in verse 35 (tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, sword) and the list in verses 38–39 (death and life, angels and rulers, present and future, powers, height and depth). Behind them stands the accusation of verses 33–34: who shall bring any charge, who is to condemn? Each of these threatens to do one thing: to separate us from the love of Christ, to break our faith, or to prove that God has abandoned us. To conquer them is for them to fail at that.

In what way do we conquer? Not in the way the world means. Verse 36 has just quoted Psalm 44: for your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered. Sheep led to slaughter do not look like conquerors. Yet that is exactly who Paul calls conquerors. We win, not by escaping these things, but in them. Three things happen.

1. They cannot separate us from God’s love. A persecutor can take your freedom, your health or your life, but not your Saviour (vv. 38–39). The thing these enemies were trying to do, they cannot do.

2. They are made to serve us. God works all things together for good (v. 28). Suffering produces endurance, character and hope (5:3–5), and our light, momentary affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). The enemy is turned into a servant.

3. Even death becomes gain. For Paul, to die was to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:21–23). The last enemy, which seems to win, opens the door home (1 Corinthians 15:54–57).

Why “more than” conquerors? An ordinary conqueror wins the battle but is often wounded by it, and loses something. The believer loses nothing that finally matters, and gains from the very battle: the enemy ends up serving him. And the victory is secure before the battle even starts, because Christ has already won it: take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33; Colossians 2:15). Revelation gives the same picture: the saints conquered the accuser by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death (Revelation 12:11). They conquered by dying faithful.

The lion did not make them let go. This is not a rhetorical flourish; it is the chapter’s own argument arriving. Verse 28 said all things work together for good; verse 29 defined that good as being made like the Son. So the mechanism is already on the table. Adversity that would have destroyed you is conscripted into making you like Christ, which was the point of your existence. The enemy is not merely defeated. He is put to work. That is why the martyrs are not tragic figures in the New Testament. The lion did not defeat them; the lion did not even manage to make them let go, and in the attempt it sent them home.

What it looks like. A Christian with cancer whose body weakens while her trust in Christ grows deeper. Believers in prison for their faith who sing, as Paul and Silas did at midnight (Acts 16:25). A grieving father who still says, the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord (Job 1:21). Paul himself, chained in Rome, writing the most joyful of his letters. None of them escaped. All of them conquered.

What it does not mean. Not triumphalism: that Christians will be healthy, wealthy and successful, or that the church will win every battle in society. Not that we will always feel victorious: Paul once despaired of life itself (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). Our feelings may say defeat while the fact is victory. And not that the victory is our own strength or courage. It is through him who loved us. Christ’s love holds us; we do not hold ourselves.

In a sentence. In every hardship we do more than survive: through Christ, who loved us, none of these things can separate us from him, and God turns them to our good.

On a Tuesday. Do not ask whether you feel victorious; almost nobody in genuine trouble does, and Paul has just quoted a psalm of complaint precisely to make room for that. Ask instead a question about direction. Through the hardest thing you have carried, did you end up further from Christ or nearer? Not happier: nearer. If, on the far side of it, you pray more honestly than you used to, hold this world more loosely, and find Christ more necessary than you once did, then the thing was sent to separate you and did the reverse. That is the whole of what more than conquerors means, and you may have been doing it for years without giving it a name. And this is not a demand that you perform triumph, nor a rebuke to anybody who is currently losing. A Christian weeping in a hospital corridor is not failing this verse. He is standing inside it, in the dark, being carried by a love that does not require him to notice it in order to hold.

For worship. The victory is his, and he shares it with us. The Lamb who was slain is the Lion who has conquered (Revelation 5:5–6), and he conquered by being slain. Every trial that was sent to tear us from him has been made to bind us closer, every enemy has been put to work for our good, and even death has been turned into a door. In our trials we are more than conquerors, not because we are strong, but because he loved us, and that love was finished on the cross and can never be undone.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. — Romans 8:38–39
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

For I am sure. “Sure” (pepeismai): persuaded, convinced. A settled conviction.

A man who has tested the rope. Paul ends his great chapter with a personal declaration. This is not abstract theology; it is the confession of a man who has been through the catalogue of verse 35 personally (2 Corinthians 11:24–28 is his autobiography) and has found the love of God holding through every item on the list. The certainty is not presumption. It is the certainty of a man who has tested the rope and found it holds.

That neither death nor life. Paul names every kind of power, time and place, whether seen or unseen. Death can’t; it brings us to Christ. Life can’t, with all its trials and temptations.

Nor angels nor rulers. Spiritual powers, good or evil.

Nor things present nor things to come. Nothing in the present or the future.

Nor powers, nor height nor depth. Perhaps astrological terms, the stars thought to rule human fate. Or simply: nothing above, nothing below.

Every field covered. Look at how the list is built, because it is not a heap of words. It comes in pairs, and each pair is chosen to cover a whole field by taking its two extremes. Death nor life: every possible state a creature can be in; there is no third option. Angels nor rulers nor powers: the entire unseen order, whatever ranks it holds. Things present nor things to come: all of time, in both directions. Height nor depth: the whole of space; and these were terms an astrologer would recognise, for the highest and lowest points of a star’s course, the moments when its influence over a life was thought to be greatest. Paul is going through the ancient world’s inventory of powers that determine a human fate and crossing them off.

Nor anything else in all creation. Everything that is not God is created. Nothing created can overpower the Creator’s love. Including ourselves: we are part of creation too.

Whatever you were about to raise. Having covered states, spirits, time and space, Paul adds the clause that closes every remaining door. It is the sentence of a man who has stopped to think whether he has missed anything and has decided to make it impossible to name one. That is worth doing personally: whatever you were about to raise, your own temperament, your family history, a sin you have not mentioned to anybody, the thing you are most afraid will one day undo you, is in that clause. If it is part of creation, it is on the list of things that cannot.

The one thing not on the list. Note also what he does not include, because it is the most important omission in the chapter. There is one being in the universe who is not part of creation, and that is God himself. Paul has listed everything that cannot separate you from the love of God, and the only possible remaining threat would be God changing his mind, which is precisely what the whole letter has been arguing he will not and cannot do, because the love was fixed before you existed and secured at the cost of his Son.

Will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. The love of God is found in Christ. As long as we are in him, we are in that love, for ever.

Love in a Person. The very last words locate it exactly: the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Not the love of God in general, a benevolence in the sky which we hope covers us. It is love in a Person, held for you in someone who died and was raised and is at the right hand interceding. Which means the question could I lose it? is really the question could he be dislodged? And that is a considerably easier question to answer.

But could I not separate myself? It is the question every honest reader asks at this point, and it deserves a straight answer. Two things. First, you are part of creation, and Paul’s catch-all does not make an exception for the reader. Second, and better: the whole chapter has already answered it, because the chain of verses 29 and 30 contains no link that depends on you. If your remaining in the love of God rested on your grip, the honest verdict on every one of us would be that we will let go, probably before Friday. The security here is not that we hold on well. It is that the holding is being done from the other end.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be lost? Some hold that, though nothing outside us can separate us, we can separate ourselves by turning away. Verdict: “nor anything else in all creation” includes us. And the chain of vv. 29–30 ensures that all who are justified are glorified. This is the perseverance of the saints: God keeps his own, and they persevere because he keeps them (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29; 1 Peter 1:5). It is not a licence for carelessness, but the ground of joyful, confident obedience.

The warnings of Hebrews. Arminian Christians answer differently. Paul lists outside powers, they say, but a believer may still turn away by his own choice, and they point to the warnings of Hebrews (Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26–29). The warnings are real and must be heard. But they are among the means by which God keeps his people, not evidence that he may fail to. Those who finally fall away show that they were never truly his: they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). And Paul’s chain has no missing link: those God justified, he glorified.

What of a Christian who takes his own life? Suicide is a grave sin, and no one should read this verse as making it light. But it is not the unforgivable sin, and Scripture never says it is. A believer’s safety rests on Christ’s grip, not on the state of his mind in his last hour, and death heads Paul’s list. Those who mourn a believer who died this way may grieve with hope. And anyone tempted to it should tell someone today, a friend, a pastor or a doctor, and hold on to the love that will not let him go.

In a sentence. For Paul is convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

On a Tuesday. Nothing in all creation can separate you from the love of God in Christ. Nothing. Rest in it. And here is the test the whole chapter has been building toward. Say the sentence with your own name and the thing you fear most in it: neither death, nor the diagnosis, nor what I did all those years ago, nor my father’s illness in me, nor the years I wasted, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate me from the love of God in Christ Jesus my Lord. Notice where it sticks. Whatever makes that sentence hard to say is the thing you have been treating as stronger than the cross, and Paul has just spent thirty-nine verses establishing that there is no such thing.

No condemnation, no separation. Notice how the chapter began, and what has happened between. It opened with no condemnation and it ends with no separation, and everything in between explains how one leads to the other. Nothing against you at the beginning; nothing between you at the end. And the whole letter turned at chapter 3 on the fact that a Judge who is just could also justify, so that the last word of the greatest chapter in Scripture is not a sentiment but a verdict, entered in a court, and unappealable.

For worship. Read the list again slowly and notice that nothing was left off it. Death, which takes everyone. Life, which wears everyone down. Angels and rulers and powers, whatever they are and whatever they intend. Things present, which press hardest, and things to come, which are the ones that frighten. Height and depth, the whole vertical extent of creation. And then, in case anything had slipped the net, nor anything else in all creation. The apostle went looking for something in the universe strong enough to break the grip of God on one of his children, and came back having found nothing at all. The love that chose us before creation cannot be overcome by anything within it. This is where the gospel argument ends, and where faith comes to rest: in the love of God, in Christ Jesus our Lord.

By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh,<sup>4</sup>in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.<sup>5</sup>For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit.<sup>6</sup>For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.<sup>7</sup>For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot.<sup>8</sup>Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.<sup>9</sup>You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. Father!”<sup>16</sup>The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God,<sup>17</sup>and if children, then heirs—heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him.<sup>18</sup>For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.<sup>19</sup>For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God.<sup>20</sup>For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope<sup>21</sup>that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God.<sup>22</sup>For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now.<sup>23</sup>And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.<sup>24</sup>For in this hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees?<sup>25</sup>But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience.<sup>26</sup>Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words.<sup>27</sup>And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.<sup>28</sup>And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.<sup>29</sup>For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.<sup>30</sup>And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified.<sup>31</sup>What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?<sup>32</sup>He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?<sup>33</sup>Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies.<sup>34</sup>Who is to condemn? 9.title: The Sovereignty of God in Election
9.overview:
Romans 9 is one of the most contested chapters in the Bible — and one of the most important. Having concluded chapter 8 with the ringing assurance that nothing can separate the called from the love of God, Paul faces an obvious and agonising question: what about Israel? If God's purposes cannot fail, why has the covenant people largely rejected their Messiah? Has the word of God failed (v. 6)? The question is not merely theological; it is personal — Paul carries a great sorrow and unceasing anguish for his kinsmen (v. 2).

Paul's answer operates at two levels. At the level of Israel's history, he demonstrates that God has always worked through election within the covenant community — not all of Abraham's descendants, but Isaac; not both of Isaac's sons, but Jacob. The principle of sovereign election is not new to the new covenant; it has always been God's method. At the level of theological principle, Paul defends the justice and freedom of God in election with arguments from Exodus and from the potter-and-clay image of Jeremiah — arguments that have made comfortable readers deeply uncomfortable for twenty centuries, and that are meant to.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before Paul addresses the theological question, he opens his heart. "I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh." This is not rhetoric; this is the visceral grief of a man who loves his people with a love that has been intensified, not diminished, by his encounter with Jesus Christ. The apostle who will argue the sovereignty of divine election without flinching is also the apostle who weeps for the lost.

The catalogue of Israel's privileges in vv. 4–5 is breathtaking in its scope: adoption, glory, covenants, law, worship, promises, patriarchs, and — the climax — the Christ himself, who is God over all, blessed forever. Israel's advantages are not nothing; they are everything. The tragedy Paul mourns is not that Israel never had the gospel; it is that the Messiah came from Israel and was rejected by Israel. The most profound privilege in history became the most profound irony in history.

The emotional weight of this opening is deliberate. Paul is not a cold Calvinist dispensing doctrinal tablets from a safe distance. He is a broken-hearted evangelist who would, if it were possible, exchange his own eternal security for the salvation of his kinsmen. That passion drives the theological argument that follows — the question is not academic but is drenched in tears.
verseByVerse.theology:
Evangelistic Passion and Doctrinal Conviction

Romans 9:1–3 demonstrates that a robust doctrine of divine sovereignty in election does not produce indifference toward the lost. Paul believed in unconditional election (v. 11) and still ached for the salvation of those he loved. The Reformed tradition has always insisted that election is the encouragement of mission, not its enemy: we preach because God has people everywhere (Acts 18:10), and because the means he uses to call the elect is the preaching of the gospel. Paul's tears and Paul's theology belong together.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's list of Israel's covenant privileges was designed to prevent any glib dismissal of Jewish unbelief — as though Israel had simply missed something obvious. The privileges were real, the access was extraordinary, and the rejection of the Messiah was therefore the greater tragedy. Now: The Christian who has grown up in a church family, heard the gospel from childhood, been surrounded by every means of grace, and yet has never personally trusted Christ is in a position analogous to the Israel Paul mourns. Privilege does not save; it only deepens accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit— — Romans 9:1
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit—

Meaning first. Romans 9–11 answers the question that chapter 8 raises. If nothing can separate God’s elect from his love, what about Israel? God made promises to Israel, yet most Jews have rejected their Messiah. Has God’s word failed? If it failed for them, how can we trust it for us? Paul answers in three steps. In chapter 9, God’s word has not failed, because his promise was never to every physical descendant of Abraham but to the children of promise, chosen by his free mercy: Isaac, not Ishmael; Jacob, not Esau (vv. 6–13). God is not unjust in choosing, for mercy is his to give, and no one has a claim on it (vv. 14–24). The Old Testament itself foretold both the calling of Gentiles and the saving of only a remnant of Israel (vv. 25–29). In chapter 10, Israel is responsible for its unbelief: it sought righteousness by works and stumbled over Christ, the stumbling stone (9:30–10:21). In chapter 11, God has not rejected his people: there is a remnant now, and a future fullness, and all of it ends in praise of the unsearchable wisdom of God. Chapter 9 is the Bible’s fullest teaching on God’s sovereign election, and Paul writes it with tears.

The setting. Paul was a Jew, a Pharisee, and the apostle to the Gentiles. Some Jews accused him of abandoning his people and teaching against the law (Acts 21:21, 28). The Roman church had Jewish and Gentile believers, and Gentiles were tempted to look down on Jews (11:18–20). So Paul opens with a solemn oath of love for Israel before he says hard things.

I am speaking the truth in Christ, I am not lying. A double oath, positive and negative. “In Christ” means as one united to Christ, speaking in his presence. And ask the obvious question first: why does a man need witnesses in order to say that he is sad? Nobody swears an oath about an uncontroversial feeling. Paul swears because he knows exactly how this sentence will be heard. In every synagogue from Antioch to Corinth he is the man who went over to the other side: the promising student of the rabbis who now eats with Gentiles, who tells circumcised men they stand no better before God than Greeks, who has just spent eight chapters explaining that the law cannot save anybody. To his own people he is not a grieving brother; he is a defector, and a defector’s tears are cheap. So before he says one word about election he raises his hand in court.

My conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit. Conscience (syneidēsis, co-knowledge) is the faculty that knows along with you (2:15), the inner witness that can be called but never sits as judge. It is a second witness, and it speaks under the Spirit’s guidance. The law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15); Paul brings Christ, his conscience and the Holy Spirit, three witnesses for one sentence about sorrow, because he fully expects not to be believed.

No step down from the summit. Notice where this sentence falls. There is no paragraph of transition between chapter 8 and chapter 9. The previous line is the highest in the letter: nothing in all creation will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. And the very next words from the same pen are great sorrow and unceasing anguish. Paul does not climb down off the summit to write this. He writes it standing on the summit. The assurance of chapter 8 and the grief of chapter 9 are in one man’s chest at the same hour, and neither is pretending. A great deal of Christian unhappiness comes from assuming the two cannot live together: that if you were really certain of God you would not be this sad, or that if you are this sad you cannot really be certain of God. Paul is both, on the same page, without apology.

The Spirit who groans. Do not hurry past the third witness. Paul calls the Holy Spirit to testify to a grief. A chapter ago that same Spirit was interceding with groanings too deep for words (8:26); here the groan has surfaced and has names attached to it: brothers, kinsmen, a whole people. The wordless groan of chapter 8 and the spoken anguish of chapter 9 are the one Spirit doing the one work. Chapter 8 ended by telling you that nothing can separate you from the love of God. Chapter 9 opens by showing you what that love does to a man once it has hold of him. It does not seal him up, safe and unbothered, at a distance from the lost. It puts him in tears over people who would gladly see him dead.
