What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul turned against his people when he preached to Gentiles. And the doctrine of election that follows is not spoken coldly or from a height. It comes from a heart breaking for the lost, and it must be heard that way, or it will be heard wrongly.

Why does Paul need to say this before teaching election? Because doctrine heard from someone who does not love you sounds like contempt, and Paul is about to say the hardest things in the letter about his own people. If he began with the potter and the clay, his Jewish readers would assume he was gloating, and his Gentile readers might be tempted to gloat themselves (11:18–20). So he shows his heart first. There is a lesson in the order. The truth of election is not softened by love, but it can only be rightly heard where love is plainly present. Whoever teaches it with a shrug has not been taught it by Paul.

In a sentence. Paul solemnly swears in Christ, with his conscience confirming it by the Holy Spirit, that what he is about to say about his love for Israel is true.

On a Tuesday. Hard truths should be spoken by people who love those they speak to. Before you correct anyone, make sure your heart is grieved, not proud. And run a test before you read another line of this chapter. Bring to mind the person you most want saved and have most nearly given up on. Now ask what your doctrine of God’s sovereignty does to that name when you hold it there. Does it send you back to praying, or does it quietly excuse you from praying at all? Paul held the highest view of election in the New Testament, and it did not produce a shrug. It produced this. Any account of divine sovereignty that leaves you calmer about the perishing than Paul was is not the account Paul is about to teach.

For worship. The Lord who holds his people so fast that nothing in all creation can separate them from his love is the same Lord whose Spirit fills them with tears for those still outside. His sovereignty never makes his servants cold; it sets them on fire. Blessed be the God whose love, once it takes hold of a man, will not let him be at peace while his brothers perish, and blessed be the Spirit who groans in us for them.

verseByVerse.quote: that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh.

That I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. Sorrow (lypē) and anguish (odynē, pain like a wound) that never stop. The sorrow is great (megalē), no passing grief. The anguish is unceasing (adialeiptos), and the only other place Paul uses that word in this letter is 1:9, where it describes his praying: without ceasing I mention you always in my prayers. One word, used twice, for two things, which tells you that in Paul they are not two things. His grief is the shape his prayer life takes. He does not grieve on Tuesday and pray on Wednesday; the ache is itself the intercession, running underneath the letters and the journeys and the trials. If you have prayed the same name every morning for thirty years, a son, a sister, a husband who will not come, and you have wondered whether the fact that it still hurts means your faith is thin, this verse says the reverse. That hurt is what unceasing prayer feels like from the inside. The man who has just sung that nothing can separate him from God’s love (8:39) carries a constant grief. Joy in God and grief for the lost live together in a healthy Christian heart.

For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ. “Accursed” is anathema, something devoted to God for destruction, the thing under the ban that Israel was forbidden to keep back (the Old Testament ḥerem, Joshua 6:17). Paul is not saying he would be embarrassed or inconvenienced for their sake. He is saying he would take the sentence himself. And measure that against the page he has just written. A few verses ago he piled up everything in the universe that cannot separate him from the love of God: death, life, angels, rulers, height, depth, anything else in all creation. Now, with the ink barely dry, the man who wrote that list volunteers to be its one exception. He would sooner be the thing chapter 8 says cannot happen than watch his people perish.

I could wish. The verb is doing careful work. Paul does not write I wish, but I could wish (ēuchomēn, imperfect): the tense of a wish stated and withdrawn in the same breath, a thing he would ask for if it could be asked for. He knows better than anyone in the New Testament that it is not on offer, since he has just said nothing can separate him from Christ. That is not a weakening of the sentence; it is what makes it believable. A man in the grip of feeling says impossible things and means them for an afternoon. Paul says an impossible thing, tells you in the grammar that he knows it is impossible, and says it anyway, because it is the only measure he has for how much this costs him.

For the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh. Fellow Jews, his own flesh and blood. In chapters 7 and 8 the phrase according to the flesh has been almost a curse word: the flesh that cannot please God, that sets its mind on death. Here it means nothing worse than family. Blood. The people whose kitchens he grew up in. Grace did not dissolve those ties or promote him past them; it set them on fire. If you have ever been made to feel that your desperation over your own household is a lower, fleshly sort of love that a mature Christian should have risen above, Paul puts the most intense sentence in this letter on exactly that ground: my brothers, my kinsmen, my own flesh.

Moses before him. Moses made the same offer at Sinai, after the golden calf: blot me out of your book that you have written (Exodus 32:32). The answer was no. Paul’s offer is refused too, and for the same reason. A sinner cannot be accursed on behalf of sinners; he has nothing to spare. There is exactly one man in history whose being cut off could save anybody, and he has already been cut off. Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), the same idea, the same ban, and the darkness at noon and the cry my God, my God, why have you forsaken me? are what Paul’s wish looks like when it is granted to someone who could carry it. So the deepest thing this verse tells you is not how much Paul loves Israel. It is that his love, at full stretch and offering everything, is a shadow of a love that actually went through with it.

Grief, doctrine, prayer, hope. You may be about to read a chapter on election with a name in your throat: a child who walked away, a husband who is kind and unbelieving, a friend who has heard it all and closed the door. Do not read verses 6 to 23 first. Read verse 3 first, and read it as your own permission. The man who is about to say that God has mercy on whomever he wills is weeping while he says it, and he does not treat the two as rivals. He does not console himself with sovereignty and stop caring. He does not stop caring and call it submission. He grieves in chapter 9, argues in chapter 9, and in chapter 10 he is still praying: my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved (10:1). In chapter 11 he is saying God has the power to graft them in again (11:23). Same man, same argument, no contradiction.

Two guards. This is the ground where a true doctrine is most easily turned into a cruelty. First, election is never a diagnosis you are permitted to run on another person. Nowhere does Scripture allow you to conclude that because someone has not come yet, they were never going to. Paul’s own kinsmen are the unbelievers in question, and he spends three chapters refusing to write them off. You do not know who is elect. You know who to pray for. Those are different pieces of information, and only one of them has been given to you. Second, the guard runs the other way: this is not a guarantee that everyone you love will be saved in the end, and pretending otherwise would be a comfort that breaks when tested. What you are given is not a prediction. It is a warrant to keep asking, from a God who is free, which is exactly why the asking is worth anything at all.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that one person can be damned in place of another, or that Paul’s salvation was uncertain. Only Christ could bear the curse for others, and he did. Paul is expressing the depth of his love, not offering a real exchange.

Is it wrong to grieve this much if I trust God’s sovereignty? No. Paul held God’s sovereignty more firmly than anyone, and he grieved without ceasing. Jesus, who knew the Father’s plan perfectly, wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). Grief for the lost is not unbelief; it is love agreeing with God that perishing is terrible. What sovereignty adds is not numbness but hope: because salvation depends on God and not on the sinner, no one you pray for is beyond his reach. Grieve, and let the grief drive you to prayer rather than to despair. The two belong together in a healthy heart.

In a sentence. Paul has great sorrow and constant pain in his heart, so much that, if it were possible, he would be willing to be cursed and cut off from Christ if it would save his fellow Jews.

On a Tuesday. The test is simply whether verse 3 embarrasses you. Read it as a description of your own heart toward the people nearest you who do not know Christ, and see how far short it falls. Most of us find we have quietly settled: not renounced them, just filed them, with an occasional prayer and a resigned sentence about how it is in God’s hands. Paul never got that far. He had the strongest possible doctrine of God’s hands, and it left him unable to rest. So ask God for a heart like this for those you love who do not know Christ, and pray for them today by name. If the sovereignty of God has made you peaceful about the perishing rather than desperate for them, you have not yet been taught it by Paul.

For worship. Moses offered to be blotted out and was refused. Paul could wish himself accursed and knew it could not be. But the Son of God did not merely wish it. He was made a curse for us, cut off in the darkness so that people who deserved the ban could be brought near. Every tear Paul shed for Israel was a small reflection of the love that went all the way to the cross. Blessed be the Christ who became anathema, so that nothing could ever make us anathema again.
verseByVerse.note: “Accursed” is anathema — devoted to destruction.

parallels.desc: Moses: blot me out of your book

verseByVerse.quote: They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.

They are Israelites. Not just Jews, the word Paul used all through chapter 2, but Israelites, the honoured covenant name. It is what a man is called after God has met him in the dark and refused to let him go without giving him a new name (Genesis 32:28). Paul chooses that word deliberately, because in two verses he is going to take it apart: not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel (v. 6). The whole chapter is an argument about who actually bears this name, and Paul opens it by laying the name on the table with everything that came with it. He lists eight privileges (vv. 4–5), which make their unbelief all the more tragic. He does not belittle them; he catalogues them in wonder, and the grief he feels is proportioned to the size of the gift.

The adoption. Israel was God’s firstborn son (Exodus 4:22; Hosea 11:1). This national sonship was a privilege and a picture, pointing to the full adoption of all believers in Christ (8:15).

The glory. The Shekinah, God’s visible glorious presence, in the cloud and fire, the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus 40:34). And these are not ideas. Every item on the list has a date and eyewitnesses. The glory is the day the cloud filled the house of the LORD so heavily that the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10–11), and the night the fire stood over the camp so that a child could wake in the desert and see by it.

The covenants. Plural: with Abraham, at Sinai, with David, and the promised new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31). Some early manuscripts read the singular, the covenant, but the plural is well supported and fits the list.

The giving of the law. One Greek word, nomothesia: the event at Sinai when God spoke his law to them. No other nation had statutes and rules so righteous (Deuteronomy 4:8).

The worship. Latreia: the priestly service of tabernacle and temple, the sacrifices God himself had appointed. Not religious feeling, but a specific altar, a specific priest, a specific animal, on a specific morning, with the blood still warm.

And the promises. Above all, the promises of the Messiah and of salvation. They were not optimism; they were sentences with names in them, spoken to particular men in particular fields. Whatever else Israel lacked, they were never guessing. They had the address.

The words of chapter 8. Now the sting, and it is what makes this list unbearable rather than merely impressive. Read the words again with chapter 8 open beside them. Adoption: the word Paul has just used for the Spirit-given cry of sons (8:15, 23). Glory: the thing we rejoice in hope of and are being conformed to (5:2; 8:18, 30). Covenants and promises: the whole argument of chapter 4. Paul is not saying Israel had a lesser, preliminary version of what Christians have. He is using the vocabulary of the summit of his own letter and handing every word of it to people who have refused the Messiah. That is why he cannot be comforted by their privileges. It is the privileges that are breaking his heart.

To them belong. Check the tense, because it is the quietest and most important word in the verse. Present: not belonged. Paul writes around AD 57, a generation after the crucifixion, about a nation that has largely and publicly said no, and he does not put one item of the list into the past tense. Nothing has been repossessed. That one present-tense verb is the seed of chapter 11, where it grows into a sentence: the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (11:29). Paul is grieving, but he is not writing an obituary.

What it does not mean. This verse is not written to frighten the person who has been in church all his life into concluding that his case is now worse than a stranger’s and probably hopeless. Paul’s point is not that privilege damns; it is that privilege does not save, which is a different sentence entirely. What condemned Israel was not having the covenants but refusing the Christ the covenants pointed to, and the invitation was open to every one of them the moment they stopped refusing, which is what Paul spends chapter 10 saying. If you are the churched reader reading this with a cold hand on your chest, that alarm is not the verdict. It is the kindness of God still doing what 2:4 said it was for.

If privileges do not save, why are they called privileges? Because they are real gifts that bring you near to the truth. Paul says the Jews’ advantage was much in every way, chiefly that they were entrusted with the words of God (3:1–2). A Christian upbringing, a Bible, a faithful church: these put the gospel within reach, and God often uses them to bring people to faith. But they are means, not the thing itself. A map is a great privilege to a lost traveller; it does him no good if he never follows it. The privilege is meant to lead you to Christ, and it becomes a greater responsibility if you refuse him.

In a sentence. They are Israelites; theirs were the sonship as God’s people, the glory of his presence, the covenants, the law given at Sinai, the temple worship and the promises.

On a Tuesday. Make your own list of six. A Christian home, perhaps. A baptism. Thirty years of sermons. A Bible with your name printed on the front. Friends who pray for you. A church that has known you since you were small. Every one of those is a real mercy from a real God, and Paul refuses to sneer at Israel’s list, so do not sneer at yours. But the question this verse asks is not how long the list is. If all six were removed tomorrow, what would be left? Israel had more religious advantage than you will ever have, and when the Messiah stood in front of them the advantages did not turn most heads. Privilege puts you in the room. It does not put you in the family. Do not trust in your privileges; trust in the Christ they point to.

For worship. God gave Israel his name, his presence, his covenants, his law, his worship and his promises, and he has not taken them back. Such is the faithfulness of the God who gives. And every gift on the list was a finger pointing to one man, in whom the adoption, the glory and the promises are all yes (2 Corinthians 1:20). The list in front of you was never a bill being presented. It is a door that has been standing open in your house so long that you may have stopped noticing it was a door, and the one who holds it open is Christ.
verseByVerse.note: “The glory” is God’s glorious presence among his people, as in the tabernacle and temple.

parallels.desc: Israel is my firstborn son

verseByVerse.quote: To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen. — Romans 9:5
verseByVerse.commentary:
To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.

To them belong the patriarchs. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the fathers to whom God made the promises, and with whom the rest of this chapter is about to deal.

And from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ. The greatest privilege. The Messiah was a Jew. “According to the flesh” means by his human descent (1:3). The phrase implies there is more to him than his human descent, and Paul now says what. And notice what the verse does to genealogy. God over all has a family tree. He has ancestors with names and reputations and awkward histories, a line running back through kings and shepherds to the patriarchs. Of all the privileges on the list, this is the one that cannot be revoked or repeated: one nation, out of every nation on earth, supplied the human nature of God. The blood is Jewish blood. Whatever the church has said about Israel in its uglier centuries, it has had to say it about the relatives of its own Lord.

Who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen. A clear statement that Christ is God. Having said what Christ is according to the flesh, Paul says what he is beyond the flesh: God over all. The incarnation does not diminish his deity; it expresses it in the most unexpected way, the God over all taking the flesh of the covenant people he came to save. This is the ultimate privilege and the ultimate tragedy: the God of Israel came to Israel, and Israel largely did not receive him. And Paul does not stop to defend the statement. Nine chapters into the most closely argued letter ever written, the argument simply gives out and turns into praise. He states it, blesses Christ for it, and signs it with an Amen.

Textual note: the punctuation. The earliest manuscripts had no punctuation, so the sentence can be divided in more than one way. The ESV text reads it as referring to Christ. Its footnote gives alternatives that make it a separate praise of God the Father, such as: Christ. God who is over all be blessed forever. This is a real grammatical possibility, not an invention by people avoiding the deity of Christ, and it should be admitted honestly. Verdict: The ESV text is right. The natural flow of the Greek joins “who is” to the Christ just named. “According to the flesh” is a limiting phrase that calls for its counterpart, exactly as in 1:3–4, where descended from David according to the flesh is answered by Son of God in power; cut the sentence in half and the limitation dangles with nothing to limit. Paul’s separate blessings of God normally put “blessed” first (2 Corinthians 1:3; Ephesians 1:3; compare Luke 1:68), which here it does not. And a sudden burst of praise to the Father sits oddly in the middle of a lament, whereas a final and highest item at the end of a list of privileges sits perfectly. Most of the church fathers read it this way. It fits the New Testament’s plain teaching that Jesus is God (John 1:1; 20:28; Titus 2:13; Hebrews 1:8). The traditional reading is not merely the pious one; it is the natural one.

Whose hands are these? Now see where Paul has put this sentence, because it is not decoration. He is about to spend twenty verses defending the freedom of God: mercy on whomever he wills, a potter with rights over the clay, Pharaoh raised up for a purpose. That argument frightens people, and it should not be softened. But Paul establishes who this sovereign is before he shows what this sovereign may do. So when the potter’s hands appear in verse 21, you already know whose hands they are. They are not the hands of raw power, or fate, or a will with no character behind it. They are the hands of the one who took the flesh of the very people he chooses among, who came into the world through a womb in his own creation, and who, when he finally held the clay, did it with the nails still in. The doctrine of election is only unbearable while God is anonymous. Verse 5 makes sure he is not.

Amen. At the end of the worst grief in the letter, one word. Paul has just said he could wish himself accursed. He has listed everything his people were given and what they have done with it. And in the same breath he stops and blesses God forever. He is not being brave and he is not changing the subject. He will do it again at the end of the argument, when chapter 11 closes with to him be glory forever. The grief is bracketed by worship at both ends. That is the shape Paul gives to unresolved sorrow: not resolved, not explained away, but held inside praise.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Son replaces the Father, or that the Father and the Son are the same person. The Son is God over all together with the Father and the Spirit, one God in three persons. Nor does “according to the flesh” mean his humanity was a costume. He is truly man, of David’s line, and truly God, one person for ever.

How can Jesus be a man descended from Israel and also God over all? Because the eternal Son, who is God, took a full human nature to himself when he was conceived by the Spirit in Mary (John 1:14; Galatians 4:4). He did not stop being God, and he did not merely appear to be human. He is one person with two natures, as the church confessed at Chalcedon: truly God, truly man, without confusion and without division. So the baby in Bethlehem was God over all, and the man on the cross was the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). That is why his death can save: a man died, and the one who died was God.

In a sentence. Theirs are the patriarchs, and from them, as far as his human descent goes, comes the Messiah, who is God over all, forever praised. Amen.

On a Tuesday. God over all is a phrase with no exceptions in it. Over all includes the diagnosis you are waiting on, the child who will not speak to you, and the years you have prayed into what looks like an empty room. If the sovereign were merely over all, that would be a fact to submit to and nothing more. But John says of this same person that he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11), which means the one who is over all has already been on the receiving end of the exact refusal you are grieving. Here is the test: when you think of the God who decides, whose face do you see? If it is a face, and a face that has wept, you are reading Romans 9 with Paul. If it is a blank, the next twenty verses will feel like a threat.

For worship. The highest privilege in Israel’s list was not a covenant or a law. It was a man they could have touched, who was God over all. The kinsman according to the flesh is God over all, and both halves of that sentence are true; the church has spent two thousand years learning not to drop either one. Blessed forever be the Son who is over all, who stooped to be born of a Jewish mother, who wept over the city that would refuse him, and who rules every sorrow of his people with pierced hands. Amen.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes alternative punctuations, such as “Christ. God who is over all be blessed forever”; the ESV text calls Christ God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–29 — God's Sovereign Choice: Election and the Potter's Right
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"But it is not as though the word of God has failed" (v. 6). Paul's answer to the crisis of Israel's unbelief begins here, and it begins with a bold reframing: the apparent failure of Israel is not evidence that God's word has failed, but evidence that God's word always operated by election within the covenant people. "Not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel." Physical descent never automatically conferred covenant membership; God's sovereign choice always determined the true Israel within the physical Israel.

The examples cascade: Isaac, not Ishmael. Jacob, not Esau — chosen before either had done anything, "in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls" (vv. 11–12). The principle is starkly stated: election is unconditional — it precedes any human act or merit. It rests on God's sovereign call, not on human lineage, religious achievement, or anticipated faithfulness. The citation of Malachi 1:2–3 — "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated" — is the Old Testament's own statement of the unconditional nature of God's electing love.

The potter-and-clay image of vv. 19–23 (drawn from Jeremiah 18 and Isaiah 29, 45) is Paul's defence of God's sovereign right to do as he wills with his own creation. The objection — "Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?" — is met not with a philosophical solution to the problem of compatibilism but with a reminder of creaturely status: who are you, O man, to answer back to God? This is not a retreat from argument; it is the recognition that the creature's moral expectations of the Creator reveal a confusion about the fundamental relationship between the two. God does not owe explanation to clay.

Between the patriarchs and the potter stand two verses this section cannot be understood without. Paul raises the objection himself — Is there injustice on God’s part? (v. 14) — and answers it not with a theory but with a quotation: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy (v. 15, from Exodus 33:19). Those words were spoken to Moses at the golden calf, when Israel had just forfeited everything and Moses asked to see God’s glory. What God showed him was his freedom to be merciful. So the sentence that sounds coldest here was originally God’s answer to a plea for a nation that deserved destruction, and it was good news.

Then Pharaoh (vv. 17–18), who cannot be passed over. God tells him, For this very purpose I have raised you up, and Paul draws the conclusion at its hardest: he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. Two things must be said and both are in the text. Exodus says God hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and Exodus also says Pharaoh hardened his own heart, repeatedly and deliberately, and Paul is not unaware of either.

And v. 16 has already ruled out the comfortable escape: it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy. Nobody is saved by wanting it hard enough or trying hard enough. That sentence closes a door on self-salvation, which is the only door it was ever meant to close.

The vessels of vv. 22–23 repay close reading, because Paul breaks the symmetry on purpose. The vessels of mercy he has prepared beforehand for glory — God is named as the one who did it. The vessels of wrath are simply prepared for destruction, with no agent named at all. Paul had the grammar available to say God prepared them, and he did not use it. Alongside that stands the strangest word in the sentence: God has endured with much patience the vessels of wrath. Whatever else this passage teaches, it does not describe a God impatient to destroy.

And the section does not end with the potter; it ends with four quotations, which is where its whole emotional direction turns. Verse 24 finally names the point of the argument — even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles. Then Hosea, twice (vv. 25–26): those called not my people will be called sons of the living God — words originally spoken about Israel’s own rejection and restoration, now stretched to take in outsiders.

Then Isaiah, on the remnant (vv. 27–28). And finally Isaiah 1:9 (v. 29), which does not say what a modern reader expects: not only a remnant was left, as though God were rationing, but that if the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom. The survival of anyone at all is the mercy. Read the chapter from that last verse backwards and the question changes shape — it stops being why are some passed over, and becomes why is anybody here.
verseByVerse.theology:
Unconditional Election

Romans 9:6–29 is the primary New Testament text for the Reformed doctrine of unconditional election — God's sovereign choice of individuals for salvation, made before the foundation of the world, based not on foreseen faith or merit but on his own good pleasure and purpose. Calvin devoted extensive treatment to this chapter in the Institutes (III.21–24), arguing that to make election conditional on foreseen faith is to make the grace of God a reward for human initiative, which contradicts the very nature of grace. The alternative — that God elects on the basis of his own sovereign love, working through human responsibility — is the only framework that gives glory entirely to God and hope entirely from God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The examples of Isaac/Ishmael and Jacob/Esau were drawn from Israel's founding narratives — stories every Jewish reader knew by heart. Paul was not importing foreign principles; he was showing that the principle of sovereign election was embedded in Israel's own origin story. The God who chose Jacob over Esau before either was born is the same God who has, in Christ, gathered a people from both Jews and Gentiles by the same sovereign grace. Now: The doctrine of unconditional election produces, in those who receive it, either rebellion ("that's not fair") or worship ("why me, Lord?"). The second response is the correct one. The person who asks "Why was I chosen?" and finds no answer in herself has understood the doctrine — and is on her knees.

verseByVerse.quote: But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel, and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but "Through Isaac shall your offspring be named."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel, and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”

But it is not as though the word of God has failed. The theme of chapters 9–11. Understand why this question had to be asked here and not somewhere else. Paul has just finished the highest paragraph in the letter: nothing in all creation can separate the called from the love of God. And a reader who knows the Old Testament has an obvious reply ready. God said things like that to Israel too. He bound himself to them with oaths and signs and centuries of patience, and look at them now. So Israel is not a side issue Paul is tidying up before he moves on. Israel is the test case for chapter 8. If God’s word to them fell over, then no promise of his is worth the weight you are putting on it, and your assurance is a sentiment. Paul is not writing an appendix about somebody else’s family. He is defending the only ground you have for believing anything he told you in the previous chapter.

Failed. The verb is ekpiptō, used of a ship driven off its course and onto the rocks (Acts 27:17, 26, 29) and of a flower falling from its stem. It is not the word for a plan that was defeated; it is the word for something that has come adrift from where it was heading. And the tense is perfect: it has not fallen off course and it is not lying wrecked now. Paul is answering a reader who stands on the shoreline looking at what appears to be wreckage, and telling him he is looking at a ship still under way.

For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel. The answer. Paul uses the word Israel in two senses in one sentence: the physical nation descended from Jacob, and within it an Israel in the full sense of the promise, those chosen and called by God. The promise was always to the second. It is deliberate wordplay, the same name twice in one breath meaning two different things. Paul made a similar move at 2:28–29, where he distinguished the outward Jew from the one whose circumcision is of the heart. There it was about a sign. Here it is about a bloodline. Same knife, deeper cut.

How do we know this is true? This is a big claim, and Paul does not simply assert it. He proves it, and the Old Testament had been saying it all along. Five lines of evidence:

1. The sentence itself. Literally: not all who are from Israel are Israel. The same word cannot mean the same thing both times, or the sentence would contradict itself. The first Israel is the man Jacob and his physical descendants; the second must be something narrower. Paul defines it two verses later: it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring (v. 8).

2. The first generations of the family. Paul’s proof comes straight from Genesis (vv. 7–13). Abraham had two sons, Ishmael and Isaac. Both were his physical offspring, yet God said the line of promise would come through Isaac (Genesis 17:19–21; 21:12). Then Isaac’s wife Rebekah had twins: same father, same mother, conceived together. Before they were born, God chose Jacob, not Esau (Genesis 25:23). So from the very beginning, being born into the family did not by itself make someone an heir of the promise. If that was true of Abraham’s own sons and grandsons, it was true of their descendants.

3. The remnant. The prophets repeatedly spoke of a faithful remnant within the nation. Paul quotes Isaiah in this chapter: though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved (v. 27; Isaiah 10:22; also Isaiah 1:9 in v. 29). In Elijah’s day, when the nation had turned to Baal, God kept seven thousand who had not bowed the knee (1 Kings 19:18), and Paul says, so too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace (11:2–5). The idea of an Israel within Israel is not Paul’s invention; it is the prophets’ teaching.

4. The circumcision of the heart. Moses himself told Israel to circumcise their hearts, and promised that God would one day do it (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6). Jeremiah said that the whole house of Israel was uncircumcised in heart (Jeremiah 9:25–26). So the Old Testament already distinguished outward membership, marked by circumcision, from inward reality, a heart given to God. That is exactly Paul’s point in 2:28–29.

5. John the Baptist and Jesus. John warned his hearers not to presume to say, We have Abraham as our father (Matthew 3:9). Jesus told some who claimed Abraham as their father that if they were his children, they would do what Abraham did (John 8:39–44). And he called Nathanael an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit (John 1:47): an Israelite in the true sense, not only by birth.

Who belongs to this true Israel? In this verse Paul is speaking of Jews: the believing remnant chosen within the nation (v. 27; 11:5), such as Paul himself (11:1). Elsewhere he teaches that believing Gentiles also become Abraham’s offspring and are grafted into Israel’s olive tree (Galatians 3:7, 29; Romans 4:11–12; 11:17), and in verse 24 he goes on to say that God has called his people not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles. Whether Paul ever calls the church as a whole “Israel” is debated (Galatians 6:16). But the principle is the same: membership in God’s true people comes by promise and faith, not by birth alone.

Where Christians differ: the two Israels. Dispensationalists hold that “Israel” in Scripture always refers to ethnic Israel, so the true Israel here is believing Jews only, and God’s promises to the nation remain separate from his purposes for the church. Covenant theologians see in this verse the principle that runs through the whole Bible: the true people of God are the chosen and believing, Jew and Gentile together in Christ. Verdict: in Romans 9:6 itself, both sides largely agree: the true Israel is the elect, believing remnant within the Jewish nation. The wider truth, that believing Gentiles share fully in Abraham’s family, is taught clearly elsewhere (Galatians 3:29; Ephesians 2:11–22), and makes one people of God, not two. But Paul does not therefore write off ethnic Israel. He keeps calling the nation Israel (9:31; 10:21; 11:7), says they are still beloved for the sake of their forefathers (11:28–29), and looks forward to a future turning of Israel to Christ (11:25–26).

And not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring. Physical descent from Abraham did not make someone a child of the promise. Abraham had two sons in Genesis, Ishmael and Isaac (and later more by Keturah), but only one carried the promise. And put the verse where it belongs, in a room with two people in it. Abraham has a son: not a hypothetical son, but Ishmael, years in the house by now, the boy he has raised and taught and loved. When God comes to promise a son by Sarah, Abraham’s response is not gratitude. It is a plea for the child he already has: Oh that Ishmael might live before you! (Genesis 17:18). It is one of the most human sentences in the Bible. Let it be this one. I already love this one.

Not cursed, not discarded. God’s answer is no, and in the same breath he promises to bless Ishmael, make him fruitful and multiply him greatly (Genesis 17:20). The boy is not cursed and not thrown away. He is simply not the one the promise runs through. Election language in Scripture is very often like this, and it is worth noticing early in a chapter that will get much harder: being outside the line of promise is not the same as being outside God’s kindness.

But “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.” Paul quotes Genesis 21:12, and it comes from a hard page. It was spoken on the morning Abraham had to send Hagar and the boy away, when the text says the thing was very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son. Paul does not sweeten that. He quotes the sentence at its actual address, in a household in tears. Ishmael was Abraham’s son and was blessed, but he was not the heir of the covenant. And Paul’s claim is not that God changed his mind about Israel. It is that God’s promise was always narrower and more particular than descent: from the first generation it ran through one named son and not the other, and everyone reading had always known it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s promise to Israel was a trick. It does not mean that being a physical Jew counts for nothing (3:1–2; 11:28–29). Nor does it mean that the church has simply replaced Israel, so that the Jewish people no longer matter to God (11:1–2). The narrowing is not something new that happened to Israel from outside; it is the principle that was operating inside Israel from Abraham onward, and in chapter 11 Paul insists it is still the same tree with the same root. It means that God never promised to save every descendant of Abraham, and so the unbelief of many Jews does not cancel his word. Nor is this a tool for sorting your congregation. Paul applies it to his own people with tears; he never hands it to a reader as a means of deciding which of the people in the next pew are the real Israel.

Does this apply to people who grew up in the church? Yes, the principle does. Being born into a Christian family, baptised and brought up in church does not by itself make a person a child of God, any more than being born a Jew did. Each person must be born again (John 3:3) and come to Christ in faith. That is not a reason for alarm for those who trust him, nor a reason to despise a Christian upbringing, which God often uses to bring children to faith. It is a reason never to assume. Parents should pray for and speak to their children as people who need Christ, not as people who already have him because of their family.

In a sentence. It is not that God’s word has failed: not everyone descended from Israel is true Israel, and not all Abraham’s descendants are his true children; rather, as God said, his offspring would be counted through Isaac.

On a Tuesday. When it looks as if God’s promises have failed, look again at what he actually promised. He always keeps his word, though not always in the way we expected. Name a promise of God you have quietly stopped expecting him to keep, for yourself or for someone you have prayed over for years. Now ask which of two things you actually believe: that the promise has failed, or that it is more precise than you assumed and is doing something whose shape you cannot yet see. Israel’s neighbours read the second as the first. It is the commonest mistake in the Christian life, and it is made by people who are genuinely looking at the evidence.

For worship. Abraham’s promise never ran through the son he already had. It ran through the son who did not exist yet, born to two people long past the age of producing him. The word of God cannot fall off course, because it was never travelling on what Abraham had available. It was travelling on what God had said he would do. Blessed be the God whose word has never once run aground, who keeps his promise by his own power through every century of human failure, and who has brought it safe to harbour in Christ, the true seed of Abraham, in whom all the promises are kept.

parallels.desc: through Isaac shall your offspring be named

verseByVerse.quote: This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring. For this is what the promise said: "About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring. For this is what the promise said: “About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son.”

This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God. Ishmael was a child of the flesh: born by ordinary human means, when Abraham and Sarah tried to obtain the promised son by their own plan through Hagar (Genesis 16). Natural birth does not make a child of God. And “flesh” here is not contempt for natural family, and certainly not contempt for Jewish descent: Paul has just spent three verses calling these people his brothers and weeping over them. Flesh means what human capacity can produce on its own. The category is not about ethnicity. It is about ability.

But the children of the promise are counted as offspring. Isaac was born by God’s promise and power, to a barren woman past age (Galatians 4:23, 28). His birth was impossible by natural means: Sarah was barren and Abraham’s body was as good as dead (4:19), which is precisely what marks it as a birth of promise. And do not walk past the verb, because it is an old friend. “Counted” is logizomai, the accountant’s word, the verb the whole of chapter 4 was built on, where Paul leant on it again and again to say that righteousness was not earned by Abraham but entered on his account from outside. Watch what has changed. In chapter 4 the thing reckoned was a verdict: righteousness credited to a man. Here the thing reckoned is a person: someone entered into a family. Same verb, same direction of travel, from outside, in. You did not qualify for this household on the strength of your paperwork. You were counted into it. And reckoning is not pretending. God is not agreeing to overlook the fact that you are not really related. He is stating what is now the case. The register is not a polite fiction; it is the register.

For this is what the promise said. Paul quotes from Genesis 18:10 and 14: About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son. God named the time and the son before Isaac was conceived. Notice first that it has a date on it. Not one day, not in my own good time. About this time next year. God put a deadline on his own word, in a house where the deadline was the entire problem: the one thing that had run out was time. Notice second what he promises to do about it: I will return. The promise is not merely that a child will appear. It is that God will come back. He does not post the miracle from a distance; he says he will be there, in person, at the tent, in a year. The promises of God keep turning out to have God himself inside them.

Is anything too hard for the LORD? Attached to that date is the question the whole of Genesis 18 turns on (Genesis 18:14). It is put as a question, not an announcement. God invites the arithmetic. He is not asking Abraham and Sarah to stop counting; he is asking them to finish the sum and see who is on the other side of it. The pattern set in Isaac points forward to the new birth itself: the children of God are those born of divine initiative, not natural capability (John 1:12–13).

What it does not mean. Someone might object: Ishmael was the son of a slave, so of course Isaac was chosen; the difference lay in the mothers. Paul answers that in the next example, where the sons have the same mother and father, and are even twins. Nor does birth by divine initiative make you a piece of furniture that things were done to. Isaac was genuinely born. There was a pregnancy, a labour, a baby who cried and fed and grew. Abraham genuinely believed, and Sarah genuinely carried him. Divine initiative does not cancel human reality; it is what human reality was waiting on. And Isaac is not a guarantee that God will do the particular impossible thing you have in mind, the marriage restored, the diagnosis reversed, the son home by Christmas. Sarah was given a son; plenty of faithful women in Scripture were not. What Isaac establishes is not a promise about your circumstances but evidence about your God: this is the kind of God who acts where there is nothing to act with.

My conversion was ordinary. Am I really a child of promise? Very likely, yes. Isaac’s birth was a miracle, and it still took nine months. No lightning, no voice, no visible interruption of the world: just a woman growing larger through a winter and a baby in the spring. So if you came to Christ with no drama at all, a friend who kept asking, a hard year, a sermon you barely remember, and one day you noticed you believed it, do not conclude you are a child of the flesh because the wiring did not show. The most supernatural birth in the Old Testament looked, from outside the tent, like an ordinary confinement. The question is not how dramatic your beginning was but whether you now trust Christ.

In a sentence. So it is not the children born naturally who are God’s children, but the children born by God’s promise who are counted as Abraham’s offspring, for God’s promise was that at this time next year he would come back and Sarah would have a son.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test you can actually run. Trace your Christian life backwards as far as it goes. Past the decision, past the church you happened to walk into, past the person who would not leave you alone about it, past the household you were born into. Keep going, and mark the point where the chain stops consisting of things you arranged. Everyone who does this honestly arrives somewhere they did not put themselves. And remember the sharpest point of all: the flesh did produce a son. Ishmael was real, healthy and Abraham’s, and he grew into a nation. The flesh is not incapable; it can produce plenty. What it could not produce was the one the promise had already named. So when you plan, work and strive, do it gladly, but do not mistake what your own strength produces for what only God’s word can create.

For worship. If you are a child of God, you were born by his promise and power, not by your own effort. He set the date, he came back to the tent, he opened a dead womb and laughed with Sarah when the boy was born. And he has done the same in you: he spoke, and a heart that could produce nothing living began to believe. Blessed be the God for whom nothing is too hard, whose word makes children where there were none, and who counts us into his family by the same promise that gave Abraham his son.

parallels.desc: Sarah shall have a son

verseByVerse.quote: And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac, though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad — in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls —
verseByVerse.commentary:
And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac, though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls—

And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac. A stronger example. It is worth naming the loophole this second example exists to close. In the first case there were two mothers, and one of them was a slave. A reader can always say the real difference was Hagar: a different woman, a different standing, a different household. So Paul reaches for the one pairing where no such explanation is available. One father, one mother, one conception, one womb, one pregnancy: twins (Genesis 25:21–26). Every variable that could be offered as the hidden reason has been removed, and the difference between the two boys remains. That is why he says not only so: the second case is not a repetition, it is the airtight version.

A frightened mother. Put the scene where Genesis puts it, because it is not a seminar. Rebekah is pregnant and in pain. The children struggle together within her until she says, If it is thus, why is this happening to me? and goes to inquire of the LORD (Genesis 25:22). The most contested doctrine in the Bible arrives as an answer to a frightened woman asking why her pregnancy hurts.

Though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad. God spoke before their birth, before either had done anything. So his choice cannot have been based on their deeds. Before the boys had a character, a history, a temperament or a single act to their name, the distinction was set.

In order that God’s purpose of election might continue. “Purpose” (prothesis, as in 8:28) and “election” (eklogē, choosing out) together: God’s purpose that works by choosing. “Might continue” (menō, remain, stand). And look at the small phrase carrying the argument: in order that. Paul does not say the choice happened to be made early. He says it was made early on purpose. The timing is not a detail of the story; the timing is the demonstration. God arranged for this decision to be announced at the one moment when nobody could mistake what it rested on. If you wanted to make the basis of election unmistakable, this is exactly how you would stage it.

Not because of works but because of him who calls. The basis of election is not anything in the person, but God who calls. Calling here is God’s effective summons, as in 8:30. The sentence has two columns, works and the caller, and everything about the person is in the first.

Where Christians differ: election based on foreseen faith. Arminian teachers say God chose people because he foresaw that they would believe; others say election here is only about nations or roles in history, not individual salvation. The first view deserves a straight answer rather than a dismissal, because faith is not a work, and so not because of works does not by itself settle it. Verdict: Paul’s point excludes foreseen faith. If God had chosen Jacob because he foresaw Jacob’s faith, Paul would simply say so, and the objection of verse 14 (is God unjust?) would never arise. Paul says the choice was made before they had done anything, good or bad, and not by works but by him who calls; his alternative to works is not foreseen faith but the caller. Five verses later he says it flatly: it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy (v. 16). Foreseen willing is still willing. Faith is not the cause of election but its fruit (Acts 13:48; Ephesians 2:8). And though Jacob and Esau stand at the head of nations, Paul uses them to answer a question about individual salvation: why some Jews are saved and others are not (vv. 1–6, 24, 27). This is unconditional election (Westminster 3.5; Canons of Dort 1.7–10).

The comfort on the underside. Now turn the verse over, because its comfort is on the underside and many readers never get there. The choice was made before Jacob had done anything good. Then ask the obvious consequence: if nothing good you did was ever the reason, then nothing bad you do can be the disqualification. The basis was never in that column, and it cannot be withdrawn from a column it was never in. That is why this doctrine, which frightens people at first hearing, has been the deathbed comfort of so many Christians. It is the only ground of assurance that your own performance is unable to erode.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God is arbitrary or that his choice is random. His reasons are hidden in his own wisdom and love (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). It does not mean human choices do not matter; Esau truly despised his birthright (Hebrews 12:16). And it is not a licence to sin. Paul heard that objection coming and answered it at 6:1–2: grace is not permission, and a man who uses the security to excuse the sin has misunderstood what he was secured for. The point is not that behaviour is irrelevant. It is that behaviour was never the foundation, and a house is not held up by its curtains.

If election is unconditional, how can I know I am elect? Not by peering into God’s secret decree, which is not revealed, but by looking where God has pointed you: to Christ and to his promise. Do you trust Christ? Then you have been called, and those he called he predestined (8:30). Faith is the fruit of election, so the fruit tells you about the root. Peter tells believers to make their calling and election sure by growing in godliness (2 Peter 1:10), not as the ground of acceptance but as its evidence. Look first to Christ, not to yourself. Assurance grows as you rest on his promise and see his work in you.

In a sentence. And there is more: Rebekah’s twins had the same father, our ancestor Isaac, yet before they were born or had done anything good or bad, so that God’s purpose in choosing might stand, based not on works but on God who calls,

On a Tuesday. Your salvation does not rest on your record. It rests on God’s purpose, which was settled before you did anything. That is humbling, and it is a firm place to stand. So the next time you set about deciding whether you are really a Christian by reviewing the last month, the prayers you skipped, the temper you lost, the coldness you cannot account for, notice what you are doing. You are examining evidence that postdates the decision by your whole life. That is not a reason to stop caring how you live. It is a reason to stop treating the audit as the verdict. The month is real and worth attending to, and it is not the ground you are standing on.

For worship. Two boys, not yet born, indistinguishable in every respect a human being could measure, and a difference between them that came from outside them both. Whatever else the doctrine of election is, it is the news that the most important thing ever decided about you was settled before you were in a position to spoil it. Blessed be the God whose purpose stands, who chose in love before we had done anything good or bad, and whose call reached us not because of us but because of him.

verseByVerse.quote: she was told, "The older will serve the younger." As it is written, "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated."
verseByVerse.commentary:
she was told, “The older will serve the younger.” As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

She was told, “The older will serve the younger.” From Genesis 25:23. God reversed the normal order, in which the firstborn has the leading place. Esau was born first, but Jacob received the blessing. And one honest detail cuts both ways: this never came true between the two men in their lifetimes. When they finally meet, it is Jacob who bows to the ground seven times and calls his brother my lord (Genesis 33:3). The oracle was fulfilled at the level of nations, centuries later, when Edom became subject to David (2 Samuel 8:14).

As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” Paul quotes Malachi 1:2–3, written more than a thousand years after Rebekah’s pregnancy, when God pointed to his covenant love for Israel (Jacob’s descendants) and his judgment on Edom (Esau’s descendants). Paul uses it to confirm that God’s choice of Jacob over Esau was his free, sovereign love.

Hated. In Hebrew idiom, “love” and “hate” in a comparison can mean choosing one and not the other, loving one and loving the other less. The ESV note says so. This is not special pleading invented to get God off a hook; Genesis supplies the parallel in the same family. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, says Genesis 29:30, and the next verse says the LORD saw that Leah was hated. Nobody imagines Jacob felt malice toward Leah. Jesus speaks the same way when he says a disciple must hate his own father and mother (Luke 14:26), demanding a preference so decisive that everything beside it looks like its opposite. So “hated” here means first of all that God did not choose Esau for covenant love.

But not merely neutral. The softening must not be allowed to run all the way. Read on in Malachi and the sentence does not stay mild: I have laid waste his hill country and left his heritage to jackals; they may build, but I will tear down (Malachi 1:3–4). That is opposition, stated by God, against a nation. And Malachi’s verdict lands on a real record. Edom stood at the roadside and watched Jerusalem burn, and did more than watch: gloating over the ruin, cutting off the fugitives, handing over survivors (Obadiah 10–14). It is Edom that Psalm 137 remembers shouting, Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations! So two sentences are stacked here, doing different work. Verse 12 is the oracle over the womb, before either boy had done anything. Verse 13 is the verdict on a nation with a long history of wickedness behind it. Paul puts them together because both are true. Nobody should be told that God announced hatred over a foetus, because that is not what the text he is quoting says.

Where Christians differ: individuals or nations. Some say verses 10–13 speak only of nations (Israel and Edom) and earthly roles, not eternal salvation. The case is stronger than it is usually given credit for: Genesis 25:23 says in so many words two nations are in your womb, and Malachi means Israel and Edom, not two men. What that reading gets right is a needed corrective: Paul is arguing about how God constitutes a people, and he never hands anybody a device for sorting the individuals around him. Verdict: The original prophecies did concern the nations that came from the two brothers. But Paul applies the principle to individuals and to salvation, because that is his question: why some Israelites are saved and others are not (vv. 3, 6, 22–24). And nations are made up of individuals. Jacob and Esau themselves illustrate God’s choice of persons. Within a few verses Paul moves to two named individuals, Moses and Pharaoh, and then to even us whom he has called (v. 24). The objection that follows (v. 14) only makes sense if Paul is teaching unconditional individual election.

The man God chose. Now the point that settles it, best made concrete. Look at what we are told about Jacob. He bought his brother’s birthright with a bowl of stew from a man who came in from the field exhausted. He put goatskins on his arms and his brother’s clothes on his back and lied to his blind father’s face to steal a blessing. He spent twenty years outmanoeuvring an uncle who was outmanoeuvring him. And when he finally had to face Esau, he sent his wives and children ahead of him toward the four hundred men in order of how much he valued them. Then look at the brother God passed over, in the one scene where we see them as grown men. Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept (Genesis 33:4). If election were a reward for character, this verdict is upside down. That is exactly why Paul chose the example. He is not asking you to admire Jacob. He is showing you a case where the evidence runs so obviously the wrong way that no one can pretend the choice was made on merit.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God hates people as a cruel tyrant, or that Esau was condemned for no reason. All are sinners, and none deserve mercy. God’s choosing of some is pure grace; his passing over of others leaves them to their own just deserts. And it is not a licence to write anyone else off: not the relative who has gone cold, not the friend who argues. Paul refused to do that with the very people this chapter is about, and he did it in tears.

What if I am an Esau? Look at what actually marks Esau, because Genesis is not vague. I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me? (Genesis 25:32), and the narrator’s summary: Esau despised his birthright (25:34). The defining thing about him is not that he longed for God and was shut out. It is that he did not want it. He had it, and sold it for one hot meal, because the future was less interesting than his appetite. So do not ask whether you feel chosen. Ask what you actually want. A man terrified of being Esau is showing the opposite of Esau’s defining trait. Contempt is not anxious. Nobody ever lay awake grieving over a birthright he despised. If you want Christ, come to him; he turns no one away (John 6:37).

In a sentence. Rebekah was told the older would serve the younger, just as Scripture says that God loved Jacob but rejected Esau.

On a Tuesday. When you catch yourself thinking that God chose you because you were the better sort, remember Jacob at the cooking pot and at his blind father’s bedside. And when you are tempted to despair because you are no better than Jacob, remember that God’s love has always rested on heel-grabbers. Then turn the lesson outward: treat the Esaus around you, the irreligious, the kind unbeliever, the brother who walked away, with the warmth Esau showed Jacob, and keep praying for them. You do not know God’s secret choices. You know his command to love and his promise to hear.

For worship. The two boys were indistinguishable before they were born. By the night they met again, one was a wealthy chieftain who ran and forgave, and the other a limping exile who had cheated almost everyone who ever trusted him, and who had spent the previous night wrestling until daybreak, refusing to let go without a blessing. And the word of God stands over the one who limped, who went into that night called Jacob, the heel-grabber, and came out of it called Israel, which is the name this chapter is arguing about. Blessed be the God of Jacob, whose love is not drawn by our worth but freely given to the unworthy, who wounds and renames and will not let his chosen go.
verseByVerse.note: “Hated” in Hebrew idiom can mean “loved less” or “passed over” — here, not chosen.

parallels.desc: the older shall serve the younger
I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God's part? By no means! For he says to Moses, "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God’s part? By no means! For he says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”

What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God’s part? The natural objection. If God chooses one twin and not the other, before either has done anything, isn’t that unfair? The fact that Paul raises this objection shows he is teaching unconditional election. No one would accuse God of injustice for choosing those he foresaw would believe. And notice who is asking. Paul raises the objection himself. Nobody forced it on him, no opponent is quoted, and he does not treat it as an impertinence. He states it in its sharpest form and then answers it. If the argument of verses 11–13 did not raise the question of God’s fairness in your mind, you were not following it closely enough. A version of election that has never made anybody ask whether it is fair is milder than the one Paul is teaching. The question is evidence that you have understood, not evidence that you are resisting.

By no means! Mē genoito, Paul’s strongest denial (as in 3:4; 6:2). God cannot be unjust. The denial is fired at the conclusion, not at the person who reached it.

For he says to Moses. Paul answers from God’s own words in Exodus 33:19, and the shape of his answer is the answer. He does not construct a defence or explain how sovereignty and responsibility fit together. He quotes a sentence, and the sentence is not about justice at all. It is about mercy. That switch is the argument. Injustice would mean somebody received less than he was owed. So ask what is owed. At the foot of the mountain where these words were spoken, what was owed was destruction, and everybody knew it. The question is not whether God is unjust. It is whether God is obliged. And notice the tense: he says, not said. The declaration has not been withdrawn or spent; it is standing.

The scene at Sinai. Put the quotation back in its own place, because it is almost never read where it stands. Moses is on the mountain receiving the law. At the bottom, the people are dancing round a metal calf, a few months after watching the sea open. Moses comes down, breaks the tablets, and three thousand men die that day. The covenant is in pieces before the ink is dry. Then God tells Moses to go up to the land but says he will not go with them himself, lest I consume you on the way. Moses will not accept it: if your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here. Better no promised land than a promised land without God. And then, with the nation still smelling of the fire, he asks for something no one had ever asked for: Please show me your glory.

“I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” Here is what God answered: I will make all my goodness pass before you and will proclaim before you my name. And then the sentence Paul quotes. A man asks to see the glory of God, and what God shows him is his freedom to be merciful. Not power or the fire on the mountain; those had been on display for months. When God defines his own glory to the one man who asked to see it, he defines it as mercy that answers to nothing outside itself. So the hardest-sounding sentence in Romans 9 is, in its own place, the definition of divine glory. The grammar loops back on itself exactly like I am who I am at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14): once about his being, once about his mercy, and both times nothing outside God determines it. Mercy by its nature is undeserved. If it were owed, it would be justice, not mercy. So God is not unjust when he gives mercy to some and not to others. No one is treated worse than he deserves; some are treated far better.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God has no reasons, or that he enjoys the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). It means the reason for his mercy lies in himself, not in us. And nothing here entitles anyone, least of all to a frightened person, to say the words, perhaps he has not chosen you. That sentence appears nowhere in this chapter. The first time God spoke Exodus 33:19, its effect was that a nation which had earned annihilation was not destroyed. The sentence entered the Bible as a reprieve. If you hear it as a door swinging shut, that says more about what you expect of God than about what the verse says.

Then is God fair? Is it fair that some receive mercy and others do not? If fair means everyone gets what he deserves, God is perfectly fair to all who are lost: no one in hell will be punished beyond his sin. But no one in heaven will be there because it was fair. They will be there because God was merciful, and mercy cannot be demanded. Think of a judge who pays the fine of one guilty man out of his own pocket. The others have not been wronged; they received justice. The one has received a gift. Grace is not a matter of being fair, and that is the best news there is, because fairness would condemn us all.

In a sentence. What should we say then? Is God unjust? Absolutely not! For he says to Moses that he will have mercy on whoever he chooses to have mercy on, and compassion on whoever he chooses to have compassion on.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to say God is unfair, remember: you do not want fairness. Fairness is judgment. You need mercy, and it is his to give. Here is a test to run on paper. Try writing the rule by which God would be obliged to be merciful to you, the condition that would make mercy something he owes. Then read your rule back and ask honestly whether you meet it. Anything that obliges God to be merciful is a standard, and a standard that lets you in on your performance can also shut you out on your performance. A mercy answerable to nothing but God’s own freedom is the only kind that cannot be revoked when you fail.

For worship. Justice is what the calf deserved. Everything after the calf is mercy. Paul is not defending God against the charge of giving somebody too little. He is answering people who have not yet grasped that the whole story, from the mountain onward, is God giving somebody far too much. Blessed be the LORD, who when asked to show his glory showed his mercy, who is gracious to whom he will be gracious, and whose freedom to have mercy is the only hope of sinners and the sure hope of all who come to him in Christ.

parallels.desc: I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious

verseByVerse.quote: So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God who has mercy. For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, "For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy. For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”

So then it depends not on human will or exertion. The conclusion. “Will” (thelō, desire, choice) and “exertion” (trechō, running, the image of a race): literally, not of him who wills, nor of him who runs. Ask almost anyone how a person gets right with God and the answer will be some version of wanting it enough or trying hard enough. Those are the two: desire and effort. Paul excludes both in one clause, and there is no third thing left that a human being brings. Esau wanted the blessing and ran to hunt game for it (Genesis 27), but did not get it.

But on God, who has mercy. Salvation rests finally on God’s mercy. We do will and run, but only because God has first worked in us both to will and to work (Philippians 2:13). Paul ran hard and said so: I do not run aimlessly (1 Corinthians 9:26). What he denies is that willing and running are the cause. He put both halves in one sentence once: I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own (Philippians 3:12). The pressing on is real, and it is downstream. You do not run in order to be laid hold of. You run because you were.

Relief for the exhausted. There is relief in this that tired people miss. If salvation did depend on will and exertion, the honest follow-up question would be: how much? How much wanting counts as enough, how much effort clears the bar? Nobody could ever answer that, and nobody could ever rest. Verse 16 does not remove your hope. It removes a measurement no one has ever passed.

For the Scripture says to Pharaoh. The other side: hardening. Paul quotes Exodus 9:16. Notice “the Scripture says”: what Scripture says, God says. And put the quotation back where Exodus has it, because much turns on that. Read Exodus 9:15–16 whole: by now God could have put out his hand and struck Pharaoh and his people with pestilence, and they would have been cut off from the earth, but for this purpose he raised him up. So the verse is God explaining to Pharaoh why he is still alive. It is spoken to a man who by every reckoning should already be dead, six plagues into a contest he has lost, and it accounts for his continued existence. It belongs with the same chapter’s account of God enduring with much patience (v. 22).

For this very purpose I have raised you up. God brought Pharaoh onto the stage of history, made him king, and kept him standing through the plagues. Pharaoh’s whole career was ordered by God’s purpose: not as approval of his wickedness, but as the stage on which God’s power would be displayed to the nations.

That I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth. God’s purpose was to display his power and glory through Pharaoh’s defeat. It is not a boast; it is a statement of what actually happened, and the evidence can be traced. Forty years later, in Jericho, a Canaanite prostitute told two Israelite spies why she had hidden them: we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you, and our hearts melted (Joshua 2:10–11). The news had crossed a desert and a border and got into a brothel in a doomed city. The Philistines had heard of it too (1 Samuel 4:8). And it saved Rahab. She and her household came out of Jericho alive, and her name stands in the first chapter of Matthew, in the genealogy of Jesus Christ. The display of God’s power against a king who would not yield became the report that reached a woman with no standing at all, and she became an ancestor of the Messiah.

What it does not mean. It does not mean human choices are fake or that we should not repent and believe. The gospel commands everyone to believe (10:9–13). It does not mean willing and running are worthless. It means that when anyone does believe, the credit goes to God’s mercy, not to his own wisdom or effort.

If it does not depend on my will, should I just wait for God to act? No. God’s mercy does not bypass your will; it renews it, so that you willingly come. The gospel calls you to repent and believe now (Acts 17:30; 2 Corinthians 6:2), and Paul will say in the next chapter that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (10:13). If you want Christ, that desire is already the sign of God’s mercy at work. Do not sit waiting for a feeling. Call on him, read his word, go where it is preached, and pray, Lord, have mercy on me. No one who ever came to him was refused.

In a sentence. So it does not depend on human desire or effort, but on God’s mercy. For Scripture says to Pharaoh that God raised him up for this purpose: to show his power through him and to make his name known throughout the world.

On a Tuesday. Take stock of how you are trying to hold on to God. If your peace rises and falls with how hard you prayed this week, you are measuring the wrong thing. Keep running, because Christ has laid hold of you, but rest your weight on his mercy rather than on your stride. And when you share the gospel, remember Rahab: the news of what God has done travels further than you think, and reaches people you would never have picked.

For worship. Run the two verses together and see what Paul has built. Not of him who wills or runs: Pharaoh willed and ran harder than anyone in the story, and it moved nothing. But of God who has mercy: and the mercy reached the last person in the region anyone would have picked, by way of the hardest heart in it. Blessed be the God who makes his name known through the defeat of tyrants and the rescue of outcasts, and whose mercy, not our running, carries every one of his children home. If you have run to Christ, praise the mercy that made you run.

parallels.desc: for this purpose I have raised you up

verseByVerse.quote: So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. You will say to me then, "Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?”

So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. The two sides of God’s sovereignty, drawn from the two quotations: mercy (Moses) and hardening (Pharaoh). To harden (sklērynō) is to make stubborn, unresponsive. And notice that the two halves do not rest on the same kind of evidence, and Paul does not pretend they do. He has mercy on whomever he wills summarises God’s own self-declaration at Exodus 33:19. He hardens whomever he wills is Paul’s conclusion from the Pharaoh narrative. Nowhere does God announce himself as the one who hardens in the way he announces himself as the one who is merciful. Scripture is not even-handed between the two, and neither is this chapter; that comes back with force at verses 22–23.

How God hardens. Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15, 32) and that God hardened it (Exodus 9:12; 10:20), and God foretold it before any plague (Exodus 4:21). Both are true. The order in the story is worth noticing. Through the first five plagues it is Pharaoh who hardens himself. The first time the account says the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart is at the sixth (9:12), after Pharaoh had done it to himself repeatedly and had promised to let the people go and gone back on it. That does not soften the doctrine, since God announced the hardening in advance. What it shows is the shape of the thing. God does not put evil into a good heart. He hardens by withholding the softening grace that would melt the heart, and by giving sinners over to the sin they already love (1:24, 26, 28). Pharaoh is Romans 1 in a single man. He freely chose his stubbornness and was fully guilty; God judicially confirmed him in it. The Westminster Confession says that God, for sinners already sinful, withholds his grace and gives them over to their own lusts (5.6).
