I ask, then, has God rejected his people? Notice first that this is not an academic question Paul has invented in order to answer it. It is the question his own argument has just forced. Chapter 10 ended with God holding out his hands all day long to a disobedient and contrary people (10:21), and any reader who has followed the argument that far is already forming the sentence: then that is the end of them. Paul asks it aloud before anyone else can, which is what an honest teacher does with the conclusion his last paragraph invites. The word “rejected” (apōtheomai) means to thrust away, to push off. And Paul’s wording deliberately echoes an old promise: the LORD will not forsake his people, for his great name’s sake (1 Samuel 12:22; Psalm 94:14). The very form of the question in Greek expects the answer no.

By no means! And the recoil is violent. Mē genoito is the strongest negative Paul has, and he keeps it for conclusions that would wreck the gospel if they were allowed to stand: shall we sin that grace may abound (6:1–2), is there injustice with God (9:14), does faith overthrow the law (3:31). It is worth being clear about what the phrase is. It is not yet an argument. It is a man flinching. The argument follows in the next breath, and its first instalment is startling.

For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. He points at himself. Not at the thousands of Jewish believers in Jerusalem (Acts 21:20), which would have made a statistically stronger case, but at one man, named, in the first person. And of all the specimens available he selects the one with the worst history in the room: the young man at whose feet the witnesses laid their coats while Stephen was stoned, who approved of his execution (Acts 7:58; 8:1), and who then went from house to house dragging believers off to prison. He is a Jew by birth, of a known tribe (Philippians 3:5), once an enemy of Christ, and God saved him. The proof that God has not finished with Israel is a Jew who had done his level best to finish the church. If God had rejected Israel, he would not have saved Paul.

The least of the tribes. The genealogy is doing work too, and the third item is the sharpest. Benjamin was the smallest tribe in Israel, small enough that Saul, its most famous son and Paul’s namesake, protested his own anointing by asking whether he was not a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel (1 Samuel 9:21). It was also the tribe that stayed with Judah and the house of David when the kingdom split (1 Kings 12:21). Paul opens a section about a remnant by naming himself out of a tribe that was itself a kind of remnant. Smallness has never been evidence that God has left the building.

God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. This is the clause the whole sentence rests on. It does not mean that God knew in advance how they would turn out; on that reading the verse would be cold comfort, since how they have turned out is exactly the problem. To know, in the Bible’s vocabulary, is to set your regard on someone: before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jeremiah 1:5). It is the same verb (proginōskō) that opened the golden chain in 8:29, and it carries the same weight here: God set his love on them beforehand. His people here are the nation he chose in love; within it, as the next verses show, is the elect remnant. The relationship did not begin with them, so it does not end with them either. God’s foreknowing love cannot be cancelled by the people it was set upon.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that every Jew is saved, or that God has two ways of salvation, one for Jews and one for Gentiles. There is one way, faith in Christ, for all, for there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is Lord of all (10:12). And Paul is precise about what he establishes here. God has not rejected his people, and the proof offered is Jewish people who believe in Jesus. It is a remnant argument. He is not yet making the larger claim about Israel’s future, which comes at v. 26 and should be argued there, and he is making no claim about territory or politics at all. Taking less than he says empties the chapter; taking more than he says borrows his authority for something he did not write.

Why does a chapter about Israel matter to an ordinary Gentile Christian? Because your own salvation hangs on the same question. Romans 8 ended with promises that nothing can separate God’s people from his love. If God could make promises to Abraham’s children, set his love on them, and then quietly walk away when they failed, the promises of Romans 8 would be worth nothing either. Chapters 9 to 11 are Paul’s answer to the question of whether God keeps his word. Every Gentile believer has an interest in the answer being yes. And there is a family interest too: your Bible, your Saviour and your promises all came to you through Israel, and Paul will shortly tell you that you are a branch on their tree.

So what if I feel that God has finished with me? Watch how Paul answers this question, because the method is transferable even though the subject is not. He does not go inward. He does not take the temperature of Israel’s devotion, or of his own, and he offers no reassurance about anyone’s feelings. He points to a Person and a history: something God did, at a date, to a man who was not looking for it. When the fear comes that you are finished, most of us go and look at our feelings, which is like checking the weather to find out whether you are married. Look instead at what God has done: the promise he made, the Son he gave, the call that reached you. Those do not move when you do.

In a sentence. Paul asks, then: did God reject his people? Not at all! He himself is an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin. God did not reject his people, whom he foreknew.

On a Tuesday. If God has not given up on Israel after centuries of unbelief, he has not given up on you, or on the people you pray for. So do a small thing on the back of an envelope. Write down one thing God has done in your life that you could testify to in a court: an event, not a mood. A day. A change you did not manufacture. A sin that lost its grip. The evidence Paul reaches for is of that kind, and it is the kind to reach for when the old fear returns. Then pray, by name, for the person you had privately concluded was finished.

For worship. The chapter that has to answer whether God abandons people opens by producing a man who had abandoned God with both hands, and who is now writing the letter. Whatever holds Israel, it is plainly not Israel’s grip. It is the grip of the God who set his love on a people before they had done anything, kept it through the wilderness, the judges, the kings and the exile, and kept it still while they handed his Son to the Romans. He foreknew, and so he does not let go. Blessed be the God whose faithfulness is not a reaction to ours, and whose love, once set, outlasts everything we do to deserve its withdrawal.

parallels.desc: the LORD will not forsake his people

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel? "Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life." But what is God's reply to him? "I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel? “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.” But what is God’s reply to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”

Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah. Paul turns to 1 Kings 19, and the scene is worth putting back, because where this cry falls in Elijah’s life is the most useful thing about it. He has just come off the greatest public victory in the Old Testament. Carmel, the whole nation watching, four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal calling on a god who did not answer, and then fire out of a clear sky onto a soaked altar. Then a single messenger arrives from Jezebel with a threat, and the man who faced down a nation runs for his life, goes a day’s journey into the wilderness, sits under a broom tree and asks God to let him die.

After the triumph. Take the timing seriously, because it is not what anyone expects. The collapse comes after the triumph, not after a defeat. Whatever it is that empties a person out, it is evidently not only failure. The dangerous ground is the week after the thing went well, when the adrenaline drains, there is nothing left in the tank, and one small piece of bad news arrives. Anyone who has crashed on a Monday after a Sunday that went beautifully has sat under that tree.

A nap and a meal. And notice what God does first, because it is not what a religious instinct would predict. He does not correct the theology. He lets him sleep, sends food, lets him sleep again, and sends food again (1 Kings 19:5–8). Only later, after forty days of walking to Horeb, comes the low whisper and the number. The answer to I alone am left began with a nap and a meal. Some of what presents itself as a crisis of faith is a body that has not been fed or rested, and God treats it accordingly before he treats anything else.

How he appeals to God against Israel. Paul’s verb is pointed. “Appeals” (entynchanō) is the word used of the Spirit’s intercession for the saints (8:27). Here Elijah uses it against Israel, not for it. That is intercession running backwards. The prophet’s whole office was to stand between God and the people and plead for them; here he stands in the same place and prosecutes. Despair rarely stays private. Given long enough it starts building a case, and the people it builds the case against are usually the very ones you were called to serve.

Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life. From 1 Kings 19:10, 14. Elijah thought he was the only faithful one left. And here is a detail that ought to stop us, because it is checkable. I alone am left was not merely an overstatement. One chapter earlier Obadiah had told Elijah to his face that he had hidden a hundred prophets of the LORD in caves, fifty to a cave, and fed them with bread and water (1 Kings 18:13). Elijah knew. He had been told, by the man who did it. And standing on the mountain he says he is the only one left. Despair does not merely misread the evidence; it edits the file.

But what is God’s reply to him? “Reply” is chrēmatismos, a divine answer, an oracle. Elijah has spoken his complaint; God speaks his verdict, and it is the only word in the exchange that is entirely accurate.

I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal. From 1 Kings 19:18. God’s reply puts the verb where it belongs. He does not say seven thousand have stood firm, or seven thousand have kept themselves pure. He says I have kept for myself. Both halves matter: they were kept, and they were kept for him. Their survival is not a report on their stamina; it is a statement about his grip. The remnant exists because of God, not because of their strength. That is exactly the point Paul needs, since the remnant of his own day is about to be defined by grace and not by works.

Faithfulness in the negative. Consider what these seven thousand had actually done. Nothing, visibly. Their faithfulness is described entirely in the negative: they had not bowed the knee to Baal. No movement, no platform, no public stand that made the history books. Just seven thousand people who, at the moment when everyone else bent, did not. If your own obedience feels like nothing more than a series of things you did not do, the gossip you did not pass on, the compromise you did not make, you are in the register God chose to count.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the seven thousand were the only ones God cared about. The point is that God always keeps a people, even when it looks as though faith has died out. And the remnant doctrine has a smug cousin. Elijah’s error was self-pity, and the error next door to it is self-congratulation: the small faithful group that has quietly begun to enjoy being small, and reads the seven thousand as a compliment. It is not a compliment. Nobody in that seven thousand knew they were being counted, and the man who was sure he had the roll call was the one who had it wrong.

What if I really am the only Christian at work, or in my family? Then you are in the place where Elijah felt he was, and God’s answer still holds: you can see far less of the board than you think. There are almost certainly believers nearer than you know, and God has never felt obliged to introduce you to all of them. Ask him to show you one. Meanwhile, do not try to stand alone: be faithfully joined to a local church, so that the isolation of Monday is answered by the fellowship of Sunday. And remember that even where you are visibly alone, you are not unaccompanied. The one who kept the seven thousand for himself is keeping you, and he is in the room.

In a sentence. Don’t you know what Scripture says about Elijah, how he complained to God about Israel: “Lord, they have killed your prophets and torn down your altars; I am the only one left, and they are trying to kill me”? And what was God’s answer? “I have kept for myself seven thousand who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”

On a Tuesday. When the cause looks lost, the statistics grim, the culture running the other way and your own church greying, the Elijah reflex is not that you conclude things are hard. It is that you conclude you can see the whole picture. You cannot. The church is always smaller than it should be and considerably larger than it appears. So think of the last time you said some version of there is nobody left, and then go and count. Name the people you actually know who have not bowed: not the impressive ones, the quiet ones. The colleague who will not join in. The woman who has visited the same housebound member for nine years. The teenager who is embarrassed and goes anyway. Almost everyone who does this honestly is surprised. And if you are worn out, eat something and get some sleep before you decide anything about the state of the kingdom.

For worship. God’s answer did not end with the number. In the same breath he sent Elijah back down the mountain with three errands: a king to anoint, another king to anoint, and a successor to call (1 Kings 19:15–16). The cure for a man who wanted to die was food, a fact, and a list of things to do on Thursday. That is the tenderness of our God: he feeds the body before he corrects the mind, he answers despair with truth rather than scolding, and he gives the broken servant work again. He has always been keeping more people than his prophets could count, and he keeps them for himself. Blessed be the Shepherd who never loses a sheep he has kept, and who keeps his own when even the prophet thinks they are gone.

seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal

verseByVerse.quote: So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace. — Romans 11:5–6
verseByVerse.commentary:
So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.

So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. Do not hurry past the first phrase. Paul is not offering Elijah as a pleasant parallel from long ago. He is saying that what was true on that mountain is still happening, now, in his own decade. “Remnant” (leimma) means what is left over. The thousands of Jews who believed in Jerusalem (Acts 2:41; 21:20) were this remnant. And the remnant is not an emergency measure God resorts to when a generation goes wrong. It is the ordinary shape of how he has always saved: never the whole nation by birth, always a kept people within it.

Chosen by grace. The phrase behind it is worth having in full, because English softens it. It reads literally: according to the election (eklogē) of grace. There is a choosing underneath the remnant, and the choosing has a character: it is of a piece with grace, made of the same material. God chose them freely, not for merit. The remnant is not the group that turned out to be better. It is the group that was chosen, by a God whose choosing is gift all the way down.

But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works. Grace and works are opposites as the basis of God’s choice. If God chose because of works, it would be wages, and wages are a debt, not a gift (4:4). Paul is closing off a compromise that every religious person reaches for: that it is mostly grace, with some contribution of our own. He denies that the two can be mixed at all. Not because a little effort would be too much, but because they are rival accounts of where the outcome came from, and only one of them can be true of the same thing.

Otherwise grace would no longer be grace. Grace (charis) is free, undeserved favour. Mix in merit and it stops being grace. Think of the difference between being given a house and being sold one at a discount. Make the discount as steep as you like; take it to ninety-nine per cent. The deed still says sold, the buyer still completed, and he can still say what he paid. That last sentence is the whole issue. Grace is not a very large discount. It is a different kind of transaction, and the moment anything is owed the paperwork changes. A textual note: some later manuscripts add a further sentence, that if it is by works it is no longer grace, otherwise work is no longer work. The ESV rightly follows the shorter, earlier reading; the meaning is the same.

Why say something so obvious? It is fair to ask why an apostle needs to state this to people who already believe it. Because the instinct is inexhaustible. Grace is the one doctrine that will not stay where you put it: agreed to on Sunday, quietly renegotiated by Wednesday, and the renegotiation almost never announces itself. It comes disguised as seriousness. And it usually surfaces where people do not look for it. Listen to how you explain other people’s faith. She was always a seeker. He had a good upbringing. They were the sort who would respond. Every one of those sentences is a small denial of verse 6, an attempt to locate something in the person that accounts for the outcome. The same instinct running the other way explains those who have not come: he was always hard, that family was never going to. This is the seed of the arrogance Paul will confront twelve verses from now, when the Gentile reader starts explaining why the branches were broken off.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the remnant are passive. They believe and obey. But their faith is the fruit of grace, not its cause. None of this makes obedience optional: the man who writes verse 6 writes chapter 12 a page later. Works are the evidence and never the ground, as Paul showed at 2:7–8. What verse 6 forbids is not effort. It is invoicing.

If God chooses by grace, how can I know whether I am chosen? Not by trying to read God’s secret decree, which is not given to you, but by doing what the gospel commands: believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. Election is never revealed in advance as a list; it is discovered from the inside, as faith. Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (10:13), and no one who comes to Christ is turned away (John 6:37). So if you are coming, trusting him, you have your answer, because nobody comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). Election is meant to be a comfort to those who believe, not a riddle that keeps people from believing. Make your calling and election sure by looking at Christ, not by looking for your name.

Is it unfair that God chooses some and not others? Paul has already faced that question head-on in 9:14–24, and his answer begins with the fact that no one is owed mercy. If God gave everyone what they asked for by their works, no one would be saved. That anyone is chosen is astonishing; that grace is free means it cannot be claimed. And notice that in this verse election is the reason there is hope at all in a dark time. In Elijah’s day, and in Paul’s, the nation as a whole had turned away. Left to themselves, none would have remained. The remnant exists because God chose to keep one.

In a sentence. So in the same way, at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace. And if it is by grace, it is not by works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.

On a Tuesday. Grace is free or it is not grace. Stop trying to earn what God gives, and stop measuring others by what they have earned. Here is a way to catch yourself. Take the last two or three people you know of who came to faith, and notice the explanation you reached for. If it was a fact about them, you have just told yourself the version of the story verse 6 rules out. Then think of the person you have quietly filed as unreachable, and notice that the same verse removes your reason. And when you are tempted, after a good week, to feel that God must be pleased with you now, or after a bad week to feel he must be finished with you, say the verse aloud. Both feelings are invoices.

For worship. The remnant is an odd sort of company. Nobody in it is there for a reason that anybody in it could name. That is what makes it a remnant rather than an elite, and it is the only reason anyone reading this has any business being in it either. Before the world was made, God set his free favour on people who would bring him nothing, so that the glory of their salvation would belong entirely to him. He did not discount salvation; he gave it. He did not meet us halfway; he came all the way, in his Son, to people who were not coming. Grace that is grace all the way down, from the choosing to the keeping to the glory: that is the gift, and that is the God.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened, as it is written, "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened, as it is written, “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day.”

What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. Sit with the first clause before the hard one, because it carries the grief of the whole section. Seeking. This is not a description of a nation that had stopped caring, drifted into comfort and let religion lapse. These were the people still at it, still in the synagogue, still keeping the calendar, still possessed, as Paul put it a chapter ago, of a zeal for God (10:2). Israel was seeking righteousness before God (9:31; 10:3), and did not get it. And set that beside the words Paul quoted from Isaiah a few verses earlier, where God says he was found by those who did not seek him (10:20). The two sentences make one of the bleakest ironies in Scripture. The party that was searching missed it; the party that was not searching was found.

Where the failure happened. That is not an argument that seeking is pointless. It is an argument that seeking is not the same as receiving, and that a person can look very hard in a direction where he has already decided the answer must lie. Paul has said twice where the failure actually happened: not that they sought too little, but that they pursued it as if it were based on works (9:32), and would not submit to a righteousness that came as a gift (10:3). The thing they wanted arrived in a form they had ruled out in advance, and so it went past them.

The elect obtained it. The elect (literally “the election”) are the remnant chosen by grace. They obtained righteousness, through faith in Christ. Notice that Paul does not say the elect sought better. He says they obtained. The difference between the two groups is not found in the quality of their searching but in the grace that chose and gave.

But the rest were hardened. Then the sentence nobody wants. “Hardened” (pōroō) means to make callous, like the hard skin that forms over a wound, and it is passive, implying that God did it, as he hardened Pharaoh (9:18). Paul writes it with no agent named, the same reticence he showed at 9:22, and that should be respected. But he does not hide behind the grammar for long, because the very next line quotes Scripture saying God gave them a spirit of stupor. He is not squeamish, and we should not be tidier than he is. It is a judicial act: God gives over to blindness those who refuse the light, the same pattern of giving over that the letter set out at 1:24–28.

As it is written, God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day. A blend of Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 29:10. A “spirit of stupor” (katanyxis) is numbness, deep sleep, spiritual insensibility. The picture behind Isaiah is worth seeing: people who stagger and cannot say why, drunk but not with wine, because the LORD has poured on them a spirit of deep sleep (Isaiah 29:9–10). Not a blindness that knows itself, but a stupor: the fog of a man who is certain he is thinking clearly, and whose gait tells everyone else in the room that he is not. Jesus quoted similar words from Isaiah 6 about those who would not understand his parables (Matthew 13:14–15).

A heart that has to be given. The other half of the citation, from Moses, says the same thing from the opposite side: to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand, or eyes to see, or ears to hear (Deuteronomy 29:4). What is described there is not something added but something withheld. A heart that understands is a thing that has to be given, which means it was always a gift and not standard equipment, and the judgment, at its most terrible, is God declining to supply what was never owed. And there is a small marvel in down to this very day. Paul is quoting a line that in Deuteronomy already said to this day. The phrase has now been accurate on two days about fourteen centuries apart: Moses using it of the wilderness generation, Paul of his own. Some things about the human heart do not date.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God hardens innocent people who want to see. The hardening is a judgment on persistent unbelief. And it does not mean the hardening is total or final, as verse 25 will show. Paul does not treat hardening as a sentence beyond appeal. He unhardens the category with his own pen sixteen verses later: if they do not continue in their unbelief, they will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again (v. 23).

Could I be hardened without knowing it? The person who asks that question with real anxiety is showing the opposite of the stupor Paul describes. Hardening, as Scripture paints it, is comfortable: it does not lie awake worrying about God. If you are troubled about your heart, the trouble itself is a sign that God is at work in you, and the remedy is not to analyse yourself but to come to Christ now, today, while it is called today (Hebrews 3:13). The real danger is the opposite: hearing the gospel again and again and quietly deciding there is no hurry. So whatever you do with this verse, do not postpone. The door Paul describes is open to anyone who will stop continuing in unbelief.

Is it fair for God to harden people? God never hardens an innocent heart that wants him. He hands people over to what they have chosen. Pharaoh hardened his own heart before we read that God hardened it, and Israel had resisted the prophets for centuries before Paul quotes this verse. Hardening is God giving people the thing they insisted on: a life without the light they refused. That is just. What is not owed to anyone is the softening, and every softened heart is a mercy. So the right response to this verse is not to accuse God, but to thank him if your eyes have been opened and to pray for those whose eyes are still shut.

In a sentence. What then? What Israel sought so earnestly it did not obtain. The elect among them did, but the others were hardened, as Scripture says: “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that could not see and ears that could not hear, to this very day.”

On a Tuesday. Name something you are currently asking God for. Now name the form you have privately decided the answer must take, the exact shape you would accept it in. Most of us have one and have never said it aloud. Then ask what would have to be true for you to recognise the answer if it came in a different shape entirely: slower, smaller, through a person you do not much like, or as a door closing. Israel’s tragedy was not indifference. It was a specification. And if you are tempted to file someone under hardened and stop praying for him, remember who wrote this verse. Nobody in Jerusalem watching Saul of Tarsus collect his warrants would have put him anywhere but in the second column. He is the one holding the pen.

For worship. If you see Christ, it is because God opened your eyes. You did not have better eyesight than the people around you; you were given sight, as surely as the man born blind was given it on the road out of the temple. The same God who could justly leave the whole race in its stupor has chosen to speak light into hearts that loved the dark, saying, as at creation, let light shine out of darkness (2 Corinthians 4:6). Every believer is a miracle of opened eyes. Thank him, and pray with hope for those who are still blind, because the God who unhardened you is not short of power.

parallels.desc: the LORD has not given you eyes to see
a spirit of deep sleep

verseByVerse.quote: And David says, "Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them; let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And David says, “Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them; let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever.”

And David says. Paul quotes Psalm 69:22–23, a psalm of the suffering righteous man. Something has to be said first about the kind of prayer this is, because a modern reader hits it and flinches. David asks God to darken people’s eyes and bend their backs, and an apostle quotes it with approval. It is fair to find that hard, and the difficulty is not answered by pretending the psalm says something gentler than it does.

Three things make it bearable. They are all in the text. First, the man praying is not nursing a private grudge; he says earlier in the psalm that it is for God’s sake he has borne reproach (Psalm 69:7, 9). The hostility he is under is aimed past him at God. Second, an imprecation is the opposite of vengeance: it is a refusal to act, a man handing the case to the one Judge entitled to hear it and then doing nothing himself. Third, Paul is not issuing a prayer for us to aim at our neighbours. He is producing a text as evidence: this is what Scripture already said would happen, and it is happening.

The psalm of the cross. The choice of psalm is not incidental. The New Testament applies Psalm 69 to Christ again and again: zeal for your house will consume me (John 2:17), the reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me (15:3), and the sour wine handed up on a sponge to a thirsty man (John 19:28–29; Matthew 27:34, 48). The psalm that supplied the vinegar at Golgotha supplies the verdict here. The sufferer and the rejected are the same figure, and the judgment falls on those who rejected God’s anointed.

Let their table become a snare and a trap. Look at what is asked to become a trap, because the image is sharper than it sounds. A snare is not set out in open country. It is set where the animal habitually feeds, on the path it takes without thinking, at the place it has learned is safe. The table here is their feasts, their comforts, and especially their religious privileges and the law in which they trusted: the sacrifices, the Passover, the whole apparatus by which God had fed them for centuries. What should have been blessing becomes a trap. The trap is in the dining room.

A stumbling block and a retribution for them. “Retribution” (antapodoma) is payback, a just recompense for rejecting God’s anointed. The greatest blessings, when they are refused, become the occasion of the greatest judgment. The same privileges that were meant to lead to Christ have become the stones people trip on.

Let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever. Blindness and bondage. Bend their backs is the shape of a man under a load he cannot put down: the back of a slave. That is a bitter thing to say about the law, since the law was given to a people God had just brought out of the house of slavery, and it opens by saying so (Exodus 20:2). The same commandments that were a rescue have become a weight, not because they changed but because of what men made them carry. “Forever” (dia pantos) here means continually, constantly, not necessarily eternally. Paul is quoting a lament, not announcing a verdict on Israel’s last day, and he knows what he will write fourteen verses later: that they can be grafted in again, that God has the power to do it, and that mercy is the destination. Verses 9–10 describe a condition, not a docket that has been closed.

Who noticed the bent back. It is worth remembering who saw that back and offered to do something about it. Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest; take my yoke upon you, for my yoke is easy and my burden is light (Matthew 11:28–30). That is not a general invitation to tired people. It is addressed to exactly the posture this psalm describes, by the very one the psalm was about.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may curse Jews or anyone else. David’s prayer is a cry for God’s justice against those who persecuted his anointed king, fulfilled in God’s judgment on those who rejected Christ. Christians are told to bless those who persecute them (12:14). And it does not justify the shameful history of Christian hatred of Jews, which this chapter, read to its end, condemns.

May a Christian pray the cursing psalms today? Yes, in the way the psalms themselves teach, though with care. They are part of God’s word, and they give voice to a longing for justice that is right: that evil will not have the last word. When a Christian prays them, he hands vengeance to God rather than taking it himself (12:19), and he prays first against the powers of evil, sin and Satan, and against unrepentant cruelty, rather than against personal enemies. Above all, he prays them at the foot of the cross, where Christ bore the curse for those who would believe (Galatians 3:13), and so he joins to his cry for justice a prayer for his enemies’ repentance, as Jesus did from the cross (Luke 23:34). What he must never do is use them to bless his own grudges.

In a sentence. David says, “May their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a payback for them. May their eyes be darkened so they cannot see, and their backs be bent continually.”

On a Tuesday. The good things God gives can become a trap if they replace him. What traps a settled Christian is almost never the thing he already knows is dangerous. It is the privilege: the Bible knowledge that has quietly made him unteachable, the role at church that has become the name he answers to, the doctrinal precision that began as reverence and now runs mostly on contempt. All of it good; all of it his table. So do not only audit your sins this week, which is the guarded ground anyway. Ask which part of your religious life you have never once examined because it is so obviously good. That is where nobody is watching, and it is where the snare in this psalm is set.

For worship. There is a mercy hidden in the bleakness. A trap laid at a table is only a danger to those who keep sitting at it. The man who gets up and follows the one who was offered the vinegar has left the room. And the one who drank the sour wine went further than offering rest to bent backs: he took the curse onto his own back, was darkened under it at noon, and carried it into the grave, so that the table could become a feast again. Now there is a table spread by him, where the bread is his body and the cup is his blood, and it is no snare to anyone who comes in faith. Praise the Christ who turned the curse of Psalm 69 into the invitation of Matthew 11.

parallels.desc: let their own table before them become a snare

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–24 — The Olive Tree: Gentiles Grafted In, Israel Recoverable
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The section does not begin at the tree. It begins with a question about the difference between two ways of going down: did they stumble in order that they might fall? (v. 11). The distinction is the whole argument. A stumble is what happens on the way somewhere — you go down, and you get up. A fall, in the sense Paul is denying, is terminal. His answer is the same violent negative that opened the chapter.

What follows is the mechanism, and it is stranger than a consolation. Their trespass has meant salvation for the Gentiles, and that Gentile salvation is aimed back at Israel — so as to make Israel jealous, which is Moses’ own word from Deuteronomy 32:21, quoted a chapter earlier (10:19). Then the arithmetic of v. 12: if their failure has meant riches for the world, how much more their full inclusion. Paul is reasoning from the lesser to the greater, and the reasoning only works if there is a fullness still to come.

Verses 13–14 are more startling than they look, and they are addressed to Gentiles explicitly. Paul says he makes much of his Gentile ministry precisely in order to provoke his own people and save some of them. The apostle to the Gentiles is running a strategy whose second target is Israel; the two ministries are not in competition, and the Gentile church is, without knowing it, part of how God intends to reach the synagogue.

Then two images before the tree. If their rejection meant reconciliation for the world, their acceptance will mean life from the dead (v. 15) — a phrase Paul does not explain, and which readers have taken either as the general resurrection at the end or as a quickening of such magnitude that no smaller word would do. And v. 16: if the firstfruits of the dough are holy, so is the whole lump; if the root is holy, so are the branches. That is the offering of Numbers 15:20–21, where a consecrated portion makes the batch consecrated — a part standing for a whole, which is exactly what a remnant is and exactly what the tree is about to illustrate.

The olive tree is one of the most evocative images in the letter. The cultivated olive tree is Israel — the covenant people, rooted in the patriarchs, sustained by the promises of God. Natural branches (unbelieving Jews) have been broken off — not because God has given up on the tree, but because of unbelief. Wild branches (believing Gentiles) have been grafted in — not because of their natural superiority but purely by grace, "grafted in contrary to nature" (v. 24). The tree itself, its root and its sap, remains unchanged; what changes is which branches are bearing fruit on it.

Paul's warning to the Gentile believers is sharp and pointed: "Do not be arrogant toward the branches" (v. 18). The Gentile who imagines that the Jewish people have been permanently and finally replaced, that God has transferred his covenant purposes entirely and irreversibly to the Gentile church, has not been paying attention to chapters 9–11. God is able to graft the natural branches back in (v. 23). Indeed, he has said he will. The mercy shown to Gentiles is not a reversal of God's purposes for Israel; it is part of the very mechanism by which those purposes will ultimately be fulfilled.

The warning against Gentile pride is not merely a pastoral nicety; it is a theological corrective to supersessionism — the view that God has permanently replaced Israel with the church, that the covenant promises to Abraham and his physical descendants are entirely and exhaustively fulfilled in the Gentile church. Romans 11 will not allow this. The natural branches can be grafted back in; the God of the olive tree has not changed his mind about the tree.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Olive Tree and the Question of Supersessionism

Romans 11:17–24 is the central text in the debate between supersessionism (the church has entirely replaced Israel as the covenant people) and its alternatives. The text resists the supersessionist reading: unbelieving Jews are broken off branches — not dead stumps — and can be grafted back in. The root and richness of the olive tree (the Abrahamic covenant and its promises) remain; what changes is which branches are currently bearing fruit. The Reformed tradition has generally held to a form of "fulfilment theology" — the church is the continuation and fulfilment of Israel — while resisting the conclusion that God's purposes for ethnic Israel are entirely exhausted. Romans 11:25–29 will make this explicit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Gentile believers in Rome were apparently in danger of looking down on Jewish unbelief with a degree of spiritual smugness. Paul's corrective is immediate: you stand only by faith; the one who broke off natural branches can break off wild ones too. The Gentile's security in the olive tree rests on the same grace that brought him in — and that grace is not a possession he holds, but a gift he receives. Now: Two thousand years of church history have produced exactly the Gentile arrogance Paul warned against — anti-Semitism often wrapped in theological language, the assumption that God has finished with the Jewish people. Romans 11 stands against this permanently. God has not and will not abandon the people he foreknew.

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous. Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous. Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!

So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? The question is built on two verbs, and the whole hope of the chapter sits in the gap between them. A stumble happens on the way somewhere; it is an interruption in a journey, and the man who trips is still going where he was going. A fall, in the sense being denied here, is going down and not getting up, the end of the travelling. And note the little words in order that. Paul is not denying that the stumble had a purpose. He is denying that the purpose was the fall. What they tripped over has already been named: the stone laid in Zion, which is sanctuary or obstacle depending entirely on how you come at it (9:32–33).

By no means! The second mē genoito of the chapter. The stumble is not the end of the story.

Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles. God brought good out of Israel’s sin. And this is not a theory. It is what had been happening, city by city, for a decade. Paul goes to the synagogue first, is thrown out, and says he is turning to the Gentiles: at Pisidian Antioch, at Corinth, and later in Rome itself (Acts 13:46; 18:6; 28:28). The mechanism in this verse has street names. Israel’s no became the world’s opportunity.

So as to make Israel jealous. The purpose, from Deuteronomy 32:21, already quoted at 10:19. When Israel sees Gentiles enjoying the blessings promised to Israel, God means it to stir them to come back. And there is something in that word worth stopping for. Jealousy is not an emotion you can feel about a stranger. Nobody is jealous over a thing he never wanted. For the provocation to work at all, the affection has to still be there underneath, buried under centuries of refusal but not extinguished. So the very emotion God intends to stir is evidence of a bond that was never cut. You cannot make someone jealous of a house he was glad to leave.

Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles. “Failure” (hēttēma) is defeat, loss, a diminishing. Their loss has become the Gentiles’ gain. And notice that Paul does not soften the noun. The thing God used is still called a trespass in the same sentence in which its results are called riches. No relabelling, no suggestion that it was secretly fine all along.

How much more will their full inclusion mean! “Full inclusion” is plērōma, fullness, and Paul will use the word once more at v. 25, there of the Gentiles, here of Israel: two fullnesses, one at each end of the mystery. If their loss brought such blessing, their fullness, a great turning of Israel to Christ, will bring far more. The argument is the lesser-to-greater reasoning he used at 5:9–10: if the accident produced this much, wait for the intention. Paul looks forward to this in verses 25–26.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God caused their sin as a mere tool. Israel’s rejection was truly their trespass, and they were responsible for it. But God overruled it for good, as he did with Joseph’s brothers, who meant evil while God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20), and with the cross itself, where wicked hands carried out the definite plan of God (Acts 2:23).

If God brings good out of sin, does that make the sin less bad? No, and Paul’s grammar refuses that conclusion. He calls it trespass and riches in one breath. Almost everyone has an episode they have become unable to name honestly precisely because good came out of it: the marriage that ended, the betrayal, the failure that redirected a life. Because God used it, we start calling it a blessing in disguise, and something in us knows that is not true and quietly stops trusting the whole account. The biblical way is to say both sentences, in that order: that was wrong; God brought this out of it. That is the guard that Romans 8:28 needs and is rarely given. God working all things for good never turns evil into good. It means evil does not get the last word.

In a sentence. So Paul asks: did they stumble so as to fall beyond recovery? Not at all! Rather, because of their transgression, salvation has come to the Gentiles to make Israel envious. And if their transgression means riches for the world, and their loss means riches for the Gentiles, how much greater riches will their full inclusion bring!

On a Tuesday. Take the episode in your life you have found hardest to name honestly, and say both of Paul’s sentences about it aloud, to God: that was wrong; you brought this out of it. Do not let the second sentence cancel the first, and do not let the first make you doubt the second. Then look at your own life as a Gentile believer and remember what it is for. If you are part of the riches that came to the world, your life is meant to be the kind of thing that makes others jealous, in the good sense: hungry for the God you know.

For worship. Notice where the arithmetic points. If God can get the salvation of the nations out of a trespass, the question is no longer whether he can work with the wreckage. It is what he intends to do when he finally has something to work with. This is the God who took the worst sin ever committed, the rejection and murder of his Son, and made it the salvation of the world. No sin outwits him. No refusal of his people has ever left him without a plan. He turns the stumbling of the few into riches for the many, and he is not finished turning. Praise him for a wisdom that no sin can defeat and a mercy that keeps finding new roads.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.

Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Paul turns his head. He stops addressing the room in general and faces one part of it, and there was a reason. The emperor Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome some years earlier (Acts 18:2), and when the edict lapsed they came back to a church that had carried on without them and had become largely Gentile in the meantime. That seam probably runs under much of this letter, and it helps explain why chapters 9 to 11 are here at all. Paul is not lecturing an abstract audience about Israel. He is speaking to Gentile believers who needed to understand that Israel’s story is their story too, and who were in danger of despising the Jewish believers sitting near them.

Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles. Paul’s special calling, given on the Damascus road and confirmed by the apostles in Jerusalem (1:5; 15:16; Galatians 2:7–8; Acts 9:15).

I magnify my ministry. “Magnify” (doxazō) is glorify: he honours and gives himself fully to his work among the Gentiles. It should sound stranger than it does. Paul makes much of his own work, deliberately, and says so in writing. He is not being modest and he is not pretending to be. But he immediately tells you what the immodesty is for. He wants his work to look like something worth having, because there are people watching it whom no argument will reach.

In order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them. “My fellow Jews” is literally my flesh. Paul’s Gentile ministry had a Jewish goal. As Gentiles came to faith, he hoped some Jews would be stirred to seek their Messiah. “Save” here means to be God’s instrument in saving them, as when he says he has become all things to all people, that by all means he might save some (1 Corinthians 9:22). And then the most quietly moving word in the two verses: some. This is the man who a chapter and a half ago wished himself accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of his people (9:3), and his working expectation is a few. Hold those together, because both belong to a healthy servant of God: a hope with no ceiling on it, and an estimate with no fantasy in it. He is not managing his disappointment in advance. He is simply not lying to himself about next year.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul neglected the Gentiles or saw them as mere bait. He loved them, laboured for them and suffered for them. But his love for Israel ran through all he did, and he did not separate his Gentile mission from his Jewish hope; each served the other.

Should Christians still share the gospel with Jewish people? Yes, gladly and humbly, as Paul did. Some today say it is unkind or even anti-Jewish to evangelise Jewish people, because they have their own covenant. Paul, a Jew, says the opposite: his heart’s desire and prayer was that they might be saved (10:1), and here he shapes his whole ministry around that hope. It would be a strange love that kept from Jewish friends the Messiah who came from their own people. But it must be done in Paul’s spirit: with grief over the church’s history of contempt, with respect, with patience, and above all with lives that make the gospel look like the fulfilment of their Scriptures rather than a foreign religion.

In a sentence. Paul is talking to you Gentiles. Since he is the apostle to the Gentiles, he takes pride in his ministry, in the hope that he may somehow stir his own people to envy and save some of them.

On a Tuesday. Do your work in such a way that it draws others to Christ. A faithful Christian in an ordinary job can make others hungry for God. Paul’s hardest audience was not people who had never heard; it was people who had heard, grown up inside it, and concluded they knew exactly what it was. Every church has them: the one raised in it who is finished with it, the minister’s son, the woman who can quote more of it than you can and has no intention of going back. You do not argue those people in. They have had the arguments, usually from someone who loved them, sometimes at volume. What Paul reaches for is a spectacle: people visibly better off for the thing they walked away from. Not a performance of happiness, which they will detect at once, but something duller and harder: being demonstrably changed, over years, in the parts of life they can actually see. So think of the person you know who has heard it all and is done with it, and recall what has passed between you recently. Was it argument, or evidence?

For worship. The apostle to the nations carried his own people in his heart wherever he went, and that is a small picture of a greater love. The Lord Jesus wept over Jerusalem as he came down the Mount of Olives (Luke 19:41), and from the cross prayed for those who put him there. His ministry to the world never cancelled his love for the people of his flesh; it was the long road by which he would bring them home. Praise the Saviour whose heart is wide enough for the nations and faithful enough for Israel, and who uses even ordinary lives, gladly lived, to make the hardest hearts hungry for him.

verseByVerse.quote: For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead? If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead? If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.

For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world. Their rejection (apobolē, casting away) is God’s setting aside of Israel for unbelief. Through it the gospel went to the nations, and the world was reconciled to God, who in Christ was reconciling the world to himself (5:10; 2 Corinthians 5:19). The setting aside of one people became the bringing near of every people.

What will their acceptance mean but life from the dead? Their acceptance (proslēmpsis, being received back) will mean life from the dead. It is worth admitting that Paul does not explain the phrase, and careful readers have taken it two ways. Some take it as the final resurrection: Israel’s turning stands so close to the end that the general resurrection follows it. Others take it as the strongest figure available for a great spiritual revival in the world, a quickening so far beyond ordinary revival that no smaller word would carry it, like the dry bones of Ezekiel 37 standing up in a valley. In favour of the second, Paul does not use his usual phrase for the resurrection of the dead, and the riches for the world of v. 12 suggest an outpouring of new life among the nations. In favour of the first, the phrase is very strong, and Paul links Israel’s salvation closely with the Deliverer’s coming (v. 26). Hold the question with an open hand. Either way, Israel’s return will be wonderful.

The note of the phrase. What is not in doubt is its register, and there is one other place the idea is used of a person that settles the feel of it. A father, explaining to a resentful elder son why there is music coming from the house: it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found (Luke 15:32). That is the note. Not a chart of the last things so much as a door opening on a feast that somebody had stopped expecting.

If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump. From Numbers 15:17–21, and the picture is domestic. A woman making bread from the new harvest takes a cake from the first batch and gives it to God before any of it is eaten. From that moment the whole batch is holy, set apart to him: not because each loaf was separately consecrated, but because the first piece was, and it stood for the rest. The offering is made at the beginning, and it settles what the whole thing is. The firstfruits are probably the patriarchs, or perhaps the believing remnant. Because God consecrated them, Israel as a whole remains set apart in his purpose.

And if the root is holy, so are the branches. The root is the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to whom the promises were made, and the strongest proof is the one Paul gives himself twelve verses later, when he says Israel is beloved for the sake of their forefathers (v. 28). The root is the fathers and the promises made to them, and behind both the God who swore by himself because there was nobody greater to swear by (Hebrews 6:13). The image prepares for the olive tree, and the change of metaphor matters. A lump of dough is inert; a root is alive and doing something. What flows through it is not merely a status but sap. That is why Paul reaches for the tree next instead of staying with the bread. Bread cannot be broken off and grafted back.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Jew is personally holy or saved. “Holy” here means set apart by God’s covenant purpose, in the way the children of a believer are called holy in 1 Corinthians 7:14: belonging to a sphere marked out by God’s dealings, not personally regenerated. Each branch must still be joined by faith, as the next verses show.

I came to faith late, with no Christian family. Is my faith second-hand? No. The holiness in view never came up out of any branch. It comes through the root. A branch attached last Tuesday is drawing on exactly the same sap as one that has been there sixty years. Some believers carry a quiet sense that their faith is not quite the real thing: no heritage, converted out of nothing much, always aware of others who have had it since childhood and seem to hold it more naturally. But nobody in God’s family is there by pedigree, and nobody draws life from his own history. Everyone draws it from Christ and the promise. Your family tree does not hold you up. His tree does.

In a sentence. For if their rejection brought reconciliation to the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead? If the part of the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole batch; and if the root is holy, so are the branches.

On a Tuesday. Ask what your assurance is currently resting on, and notice whether the answer is a fact about the root or a fact about your branch: the promise God made, or the health of your own attachment to it. Both feel like faith from the inside. Only one of them holds in a bad month. Then let the phrase life from the dead shape the way you pray for your church and for Jewish people. Pray big, not because you can see it coming, but because God has told you what he can do with the dead.

For worship. God’s purposes for his people are not finished, and the music of Luke 15 is still to be heard from the house. The God who brought a whole world back to himself through Israel’s setting aside will do something even greater when he receives them back: nothing less than life from the dead. This is the God who calls into existence the things that do not exist and gives life to the dead (4:17). He keeps a root alive through centuries of winter, and he has never yet failed to bring spring. Look forward with joy to what he will yet do, and praise him for the sap that flows from his promise into every branch he has grafted in.
verseByVerse.note: The first portion of dough was offered to God, and it made the whole batch holy. The “root” is the patriarchs.

parallels.desc: a loaf from the first of your dough

verseByVerse.quote: But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree, do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you. — Romans 11:17–18
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree, do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you.

The olive tree. Israel is often pictured as God’s olive tree, green and beautiful with good fruit (Jeremiah 11:16; Hosea 14:6). There is one tree: the one people of God, rooted in the promises to the patriarchs. It is not that Israel is one tree and the church another.

But if some of the branches were broken off. Unbelieving Jews. And notice the restraint: some. Not the tree felled, not the branches, but some of them. It is the same care Paul showed at v. 14 in hoping to save some, and the same care he will show at v. 25 in calling the hardening partial. He is exact about quantities in a chapter where every reader on both sides reaches for totals.

And you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others. Gentile believers, wild by nature, outside the covenant, once strangers to the promises and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:11–12), now grafted in by faith among the believing Jews. And the oddity of the horticulture is deliberate. Ordinary practice ran the other way: you joined a cultivated cutting onto hardy wild stock, so that the good fruit came from the cultivated side. What is described here is the reverse, and at v. 24 Paul labels it contrary to nature. He is not making a mistake about farming. He is pointing at the one feature of the picture that nobody would have done on purpose, which is the feature that makes it grace.

And now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree. Literally the root of fatness, the rich sap of the tree. Gentiles share in the blessings promised to Abraham, so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles (Galatians 3:14, 29). The Gentile believer draws nourishment from roots he did not plant: the covenant with Abraham, the promises to Israel, the Scriptures of the Old Testament. He is a latecomer to a tree whose roots go down to the very call of God to Abraham.

Do not be arrogant toward the branches. “Arrogant” (katakauchaomai) is to boast against, to crow over. Some Gentile believers in Rome were looking down on Jews. And the tense is worth catching: it is a present imperative, stop doing it, do not carry on. Paul is not warning a church about a danger on the horizon; he is interrupting something already under way in the room he is writing to. The broken-off branches are not enemies to be despised but kinsmen to be mourned and prayed for, and Paul’s own posture at the start of chapter 9 is the model: grief, not gloating. The Gentile Christian who looks at Jewish unbelief with satisfaction has forgotten where he came from and what he was when grace found him.

If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you. This is the clause the command rests on. The church owes its life to Israel’s root: salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22). Put the picture back and it is faintly absurd, which is the point. A branch is congratulating itself on the tree. A thing that is held six feet off the ground by something it did not make, cannot see, and could not survive ten minutes without, has formed a view about its own contribution.

An inventory. Everything the branch has arrives through a join it did not make, and that is worth turning into a list, because it takes a minute and it is hard to argue with. Name something in your faith that you invented. The Scriptures came through Israel. The God you pray to introduced himself to Abraham, Moses and the prophets. The words you use when you have no words of your own are usually a psalm written by a Jewish king. The Messiah you belong to was a son of David, circumcised on the eighth day. Nothing on the list is yours; all of it arrived down the trunk.

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Dispensationalists teach that God has two distinct peoples with two programmes, Israel and the church. Others teach that the church has simply replaced Israel, so ethnic Israel has no further place. Verdict: The olive tree shows one people of God across both testaments, rooted in the promises to the patriarchs. Gentiles do not form a new tree; they are grafted into the old one, and they do not grow beside it either. So there are not two peoples. But neither has God finished with ethnic Israel: the natural branches can be, and will be, grafted back into their own tree (vv. 23–26). The church is the continuation and fulfilment of Israel, not a separate plan, which is how Paul can tell Gentile believers that they are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Ephesians 2:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Gentiles must become Jews or keep the ceremonial law. They are grafted in by faith alone.

Should Gentile Christians keep Jewish feasts or customs, then? They are free to learn from them, but they are not required to keep them, and must never make them a badge of a higher Christianity. The feasts and food laws were a shadow of things to come, and the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). Christ is our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), and the Lord’s Supper, not the Seder, is the meal he commanded his church to keep. Studying the feasts can deepen your grasp of the gospel; celebrating a Passover meal to understand the Last Supper can be a fine way to teach children. But Paul fought hard against Gentiles being told they must take on the law to be full members (Galatians 5:1–6). Honour the root by trusting the Messiah it bore, not by adopting its shadows.

The church did not heed this. It has to be said plainly. The specific sin Paul forbids here, Gentile Christians holding Jewish people in contempt, became over the centuries a settled habit of Christendom, dressed in theological language and eventually in far worse than language: expulsions, forced baptisms, massacres, and the ground prepared for the horrors of the twentieth century. Whatever else Romans 11 is, it is a warning given early, in writing, by an apostle, and disregarded. A commentary that expounds the metaphor and passes over that in silence has not really read the verse.

In a sentence. If some of the branches have been broken off, and you, though a wild olive shoot, have been grafted in among the others and now share in the rich root of the olive tree, do not boast over those branches. If you do, remember: you do not support the root; the root supports you.

On a Tuesday. Never speak of the Jewish people with contempt, and do not laugh along when others do. Your faith grows from their root. Pray for them by name if you know any, and love them. And make the inventory personal: next time you open your Bible, sing a psalm or pray the Lord’s Prayer, notice that you are drawing on Israel’s sap, and give thanks for it.

For worship. God did not plant a new tree for us; he grafted us into the old one, wild shoots cut from a barren hillside and set, against all good gardening, into the richest root on earth. Everything we live on came down that trunk: the promise to Abraham, the law and the prophets, the psalms, the covenant, and at the last the Son of David himself, the root and the descendant of David (Revelation 22:16). He is the true Israel, the vine and the root in one, and every branch lives because it is joined to him. Praise the Gardener whose grafting goes against nature because it goes according to grace.
verseByVerse.note: Israel is often pictured as God’s olive tree.

parallels.desc: a green olive tree

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will say, "Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in." That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then you will say, “Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.” That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but fear.

Then you will say, “Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.” Watch the move Paul makes here, because it is the most instructive sentence in the paragraph and it is easy to read straight over. He puts the boast into the Gentile’s mouth for him. The proud Gentile says: they were removed to make room for me. I must be special.

That is true. And instead of denying it, Paul concedes the fact. The doctrine in the boast is correct. What he refuses is the inference. Everything in the sentence is accurate except the posture it produced. That is a warning of a very particular kind, because it means orthodoxy is not a defence. A man can have the mechanism of election exactly right, be able to defend it from the text, and still be drawing from it a conclusion that Paul answers with the word fear.

They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. The real reason was unbelief, not ethnicity. And you stand only by faith, not by merit. The two halves are not symmetrical in the way the boast assumed. Not because of your faith, as though faith were the qualification that replaced their lineage, but through it. Faith is not a possession that entitles you to the position; it is the manner of holding on. Faith is the empty hand that receives, and it gives no ground for boasting (3:27). Nobody stands on his own grip. He stands because of what he is gripping.

So do not become proud, but fear. Literally, do not think high thoughts. Fear here is reverent awe and humble watchfulness (Philippians 2:12; Proverbs 3:7). And the command is startling in this letter of all letters. Three chapters ago Paul told these same readers they had not received a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear (8:15). He is not contradicting himself, and the difference is worth naming, because a great deal of pastoral damage lives in the confusion. The fear he forbade is the fear of a slave who does not know whether he is owned. The fear he commands is the alertness of someone standing somewhere high who has understood exactly what is holding him up.

Two kinds of fear. They feel different in practice. One makes you check the rope; the other makes you refuse to climb, or pretend you are not on a cliff at all. The first is what Paul means when he tells another church to work out its salvation with fear and trembling, immediately adding that it is God who works in them (Philippians 2:12–13). Fear of that sort is not the opposite of assurance. It is what assurance looks like in someone who is paying attention.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should live in terror of God. It means a humble, reverent dependence that never takes grace for granted.

How can I fear God and still be sure of my salvation? Because the fear Paul commands is aimed at pride, not at God’s promises. The one who stands by faith looks away from himself to Christ, and that is exactly where assurance comes from. What Paul wants you to fear is the thought that you are standing in your own strength, or that you are better than those who fell. A child holding his father’s hand near a cliff edge is both perfectly safe and very careful, and the carefulness is part of the safety. If your fear drives you to Christ, it is the right kind. If it drives you away from him into anxious self-inspection, it is the wrong kind, and the answer is to look at his grip, not yours (John 10:28–29).

In a sentence. You will say then, “Branches were broken off so that I could be grafted in.” Granted. But they were broken off because of unbelief, and you stand by faith. So do not be arrogant, but tremble.

On a Tuesday. Take a position you hold and are confident is biblically right: about who is in and who is out, about a group that has gone wrong, about the tradition you left. Now ask what it makes you feel toward the people it excludes. If the honest answer is anything in the family of satisfaction, you are the man in verse 19, and Paul’s reply to you is the same as his reply to him: yes, that is true, and now be afraid. Then let the fear do its proper work: turn it into prayer for those people, and into thanksgiving that you stand at all.

For worship. You stand only by faith, and faith is a gift (Ephesians 2:8). The hand that holds is itself held. Everything that keeps you on the tree was given: the grafting, the sap, the faith that clings, the God who is at work in you to will and to work for his good pleasure. So the right posture before him is not the swagger of a branch that thinks it chose the tree, but the awe of a branch that knows it was chosen, cut and joined by a hand that did not have to reach for it. Bow low, and stand in awe of the grace that holds you up.

parallels.desc: let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed

verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God's kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God’s kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.

For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. If God did not spare Israel, with all its privileges, when it fell into unbelief, he will not spare Gentile churches that do the same. Many once-flourishing churches have been cut off: think of the churches of North Africa, home of Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine, and of Asia Minor, where all seven churches of Revelation stood. The risen Christ warned Ephesus that he would remove its lampstand unless it repented (Revelation 2:5), and in time there was no lampstand there.

Note then the kindness and the severity of God. Paul opens with an imperative that is usually read as a connective. Note then is literally look. He is not inviting a reflection; he is turning the reader’s head and holding it there. Look at both of these things, and do not look away from either. They are two sides of God’s character, held together. Kindness (chrēstotēs, goodness, generosity) is the word Paul used at 2:4 of the kindness meant to lead a man to repentance. Severity (apotomia) is rare and has been chosen. It comes from the verb to cut off sharply; it is the word for a sheer face of rock, an edge with nothing gradual about it. Paul uses it in a paragraph about branches being cut off. The vocabulary and the metaphor are the same thing. Both are real.

A God who is only one of them. Most of us, if honest, have a God who is one of these and not the other. The one whose God is all kindness has a religion that cannot account for a cross: there was no crisis grave enough to require it. The one whose God is all severity has a religion that cannot account for his own continued existence, and usually knows it, and lives braced. Paul puts the two words side by side in one sentence and tells you to look at both, because a God who is only one of them is not the God who is there. And the place where you see both at once, at full strength, is Calvary: severity toward sin, poured out on the Son; kindness toward sinners, poured out from him.

Severity toward those who have fallen, but God’s kindness to you. Israel’s unbelief brought severity; the Gentiles’ faith received kindness. Neither group earned the outcome it received from God’s hand, for kindness by definition is not earned, and severity fell on a refusal that was entirely their own.

Provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off. A conditional warning. Continuing (epimenō, remain, persevere) in God’s kindness means continuing to trust it, not trusting yourself. And the warning is against the very unbelief that broke the natural branches. Note that the you is singular, as throughout the olive tree: Paul addresses the Gentile reader as one representative branch, so that the warning reaches each person who reads it and should not be blunted.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be cut off? Some take this verse to show that a truly saved person can lose salvation. Verdict: Paul speaks here mainly of Gentiles as a group, a branch of the tree, not of each individual’s election. And the warning is one of God’s means of keeping his elect. Those who are truly in Christ will continue, because God keeps them (8:30, 38–39; John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6). Those who fall away show that they were not truly of us, for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and true believers heed it. This is the perseverance of the saints (Westminster 17.1). Nobody has ever been frightened out of the kingdom by Romans 11:22. A good many have been woken up by it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation depends on our own effort to keep ourselves. It depends on God’s kindness, which keeps us continuing in it.

How do I know I am continuing in his kindness? Not by a perfect record, but by where you keep returning. Continuing means that, through falls and dry seasons, you keep coming back to God’s mercy in Christ as your only hope, rather than drifting into either self-trust or indifference. Signs of it are simple: you still want him; you still grieve over sin and confess it; you still hold to the gospel when you are tempted to rest on something else; you stay among his people and under his word. A believer may be weak in all of these and still be continuing. The danger sign is not struggle but settled carelessness, the life that has stopped caring whether it is near God at all.

Could my own church be cut off? A local church or a whole denomination can lose the gospel and cease, in any real sense, to be a church of Christ, and history is full of them. It rarely happens with a dramatic decision. It happens when the church starts to stand on something other than faith in God’s kindness: its tradition, its respectability, its size, its culture, its moral campaigns. The remedy is not panic but the same one Christ gave Ephesus: remember, repent, and do the works you did at first (Revelation 2:5). Pray for your church’s leaders, love the gospel at the centre of its life, and do not assume that a past of faithfulness guarantees a future.

In a sentence. For if God did not spare the natural branches, he will not spare you either. Consider therefore the kindness and sternness of God: sternness to those who fell, but kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you also will be cut off.

On a Tuesday. Take God’s warnings seriously. They are not threats against his children but loving fences that keep them safe. Here is a way to find out which half of verse 22 you are short of.
