Read it twice and notice which clause you had to make yourself slow down for. Almost everyone glides over one of them. If severity is the word your eye skips, the God you are picturing is smaller and safer than the one who cut branches out of his own tree. If kindness is the word that feels as if it must have conditions attached, you have been living under a sentence Christ has already served.

For worship. Look, says Paul, and when we look we see a God more glorious than either half alone could show: severe enough to cut off his own branches, kind enough to graft in wild ones; holy enough that sin must be judged, loving enough to bear the judgment himself. At the cross the edge of the rock and the generosity of his heart met in one place, and the kindness we are told to continue in was bought by the severity he endured. Praise the God whose kindness is not soft and whose severity is not cruel, and who keeps every branch that rests in his kindness to the end.

verseByVerse.quote: And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again. For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again. For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree.

And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in. The way back is open. Their unbelief, not their ancestry, cut them off, and faith will graft them back in. And the condition is doing something merciful that is easy to miss. If they do not continue in their unbelief: that is the only thing named as keeping anyone out. Not the years, not the history, not the accumulated weight of a life spent elsewhere. One thing, and it is the one thing that can stop.

For God has the power to graft them in again. Humanly, a broken branch cannot be put back. But God can do it. Israel’s salvation depends on his power, as everyone’s does. And notice where Paul locates the obstacle, because it is not where anyone expects. The question was never capacity. In every discussion of a hardened person, ours included, the unspoken assumption is that the case has become difficult: too many years, too much said, too settled a refusal. Paul answers a question nobody asked aloud by stating that God is able, which tells you exactly what the doubt had really been about.

For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree. Growers normally grafted a cultivated branch onto wild stock, not a wild branch onto a cultivated tree. Paul knows this. “Contrary to nature”: God did something unnatural, a miracle of grace, in bringing Gentiles in. And it is a quiet demolition of Gentile confidence. The Gentile believer accepts that he himself was cut out of a wild tree and grafted, against nature, into a cultivated one. Then he has already granted the harder of the two miracles. Putting a branch back onto the tree it grew on is not the astonishing operation. His own presence there is.

How much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree. If God did the unnatural thing, how much easier the natural one. Paul’s will be looks forward with confidence. And there is a phrase here that ought to be read slowly by anyone inclined to arrogance: their own olive tree. After all these verses about grafting and standing and being warned, the tree is still described as belonging to them. The guest has been given a great deal; he has not been given the deeds.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jews can be saved apart from faith in Christ. Grafting in happens when they do not continue in unbelief.

Someone I love was raised in the faith and has left it. May I hope? Yes, and this verse gives you good reason. Almost everyone reading it has someone in mind who grew up inside the faith and is now outside it, and about whom a quiet verdict has been reached: too far in, too long out. Read verse 24 again with that person in view. The branch that once grew on the tree is the case Paul calls easier. He is not promising you an outcome, and it would be cruel to pretend he is; some never return. But he tells you which column the case belongs in, and he tells you God is able. So keep praying, keep loving, keep the door open without nagging, and let your own life be the kind of evidence that makes them jealous.

If they must believe, what does God’s power have to do with it? Everything, because the faith that grafts them in is itself God’s gift. A branch cannot graft itself back. When someone who has long resisted Christ comes to believe, it is because God has given him new eyes and a new heart, as he did for Paul on the Damascus road. That is why we pray for unbelievers and do not merely argue with them. Their coming to faith is real and personal, and they will be fully responsible and fully willing in it, but it is God who makes the dead branch willing. Prayer for the hardest case is therefore never wasted: it is addressed to the only one with the power.

In a sentence. And if they do not persist in unbelief, they will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again. After all, if you were cut out of an olive tree that is wild by nature and, contrary to nature, grafted into a cultivated olive tree, how much more readily will these natural branches be grafted back into their own tree!

On a Tuesday. Name the thing you have privately filed as impossible: a person, a relative, a friend who walked away. Write their name down and pray for them today, not with a sigh but with confidence in God’s power. Then notice that the verse does not merely say God could manage it. It says this is the less remarkable of the two graftings, and that the more remarkable one has already happened, to you.

For worship. No one is too far gone for God. He grafted wild branches into a tree they had no right to, and he can graft natural branches back into a tree that was always theirs. The gardener of this passage is not a man coaxing reluctant wood; he is the God who raises the dead and calls things that are not as though they were. He did it for you when you were wild. He has done it for Jewish men and women in every century since Pentecost. He will do it yet. Pray with confidence for Jewish friends and for all who seem cut off, and praise the God whose power makes every hopeless case only a matter of time and grace.
verseByVerse.note: Growers normally grafted a cultivated branch onto wild stock; grafting a wild branch into a cultivated tree is, as Paul says, “contrary to nature.”

parallels.desc: when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–36 — The Mystery, the Promise, and the Doxology
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reveals a mystery so that the Gentile believers will not become proud: a partial hardening has come on Israel until the full number of Gentiles has come in, and in this way all Israel will be saved, as the prophets foretold of a Deliverer from Zion who will remove ungodliness from Jacob. As regards the gospel, Israel is at present opposed to it for the Gentiles’ sake; as regards God’s choice, they are loved because of the patriarchs, for God does not take back his gifts and call. Just as Gentiles once disobeyed and now have received mercy, so Israel has disobeyed so that they too may receive mercy; God has shut everyone up in disobedience in order to have mercy on all. Paul ends in wonder at the depth of God’s riches, wisdom and knowledge, whose ways no one can trace or advise: all things are from him, through him and to him, and to him be glory for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Irrevocability of God's Covenant Purposes

Romans 11:29 — "the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable" — is the theological capstone of chapters 9–11 and one of the most important statements about God's faithfulness in Scripture. The word translated "irrevocable" (ametamelēta) means without repentance — God does not change his mind about what he has given and whom he has called. Applied to Israel: whatever the full meaning of "all Israel will be saved" (v. 26), it means at minimum that God has not and will not permanently and finally abandon the people he chose. Applied to the individual Christian: the calling and justification God has effected in her life will not be revoked. The golden chain of 8:29–30 and the irrevocability of 11:29 are two sides of the same coin.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The doxology of vv. 33–36 was Paul's own response to the argument he had just made. Having argued through three chapters about divine sovereignty, human responsibility, the mystery of Israel, and the purposes of God — he does not end with a systematic summary. He ends with worship. This is the correct response to the depth of God: not the mastery of a doctrine but the surrender of a doxology. Now: In an age that demands that every theological mystery be resolved into a satisfying rational system, the doxology of Romans 11:33–36 is the necessary reminder: we are not God. The depths of his wisdom and knowledge exceed our categories. The only posture that is finally appropriate before the mystery of divine election and human salvation is the posture Paul strikes: "From him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever."

verseByVerse.quote: Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written, "The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob"; — Romans 11:25–26
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written, “The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob”;

Lest you be wise in your own sight. The phrase comes from Proverbs 3:7, and before anything else, notice why Paul says he is telling them this. The greatest disclosure about the future in the whole letter is handed over for a stated pastoral reason: to stop a group of Christians thinking too well of themselves. The doctrine is administered as medicine, and the complaint it is prescribed for is conceit. That ought to govern how it is used. A reader who comes away from these verses with a firmer grip on a timetable and no change in how he regards anybody has taken the medicine and kept the disease. Paul is not satisfying curiosity here. He is treating a church.

I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers. A “mystery” (mystērion) in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God (16:25; Ephesians 3:3–6). Not a puzzle to be solved by clever readers, but a secret God has chosen to tell. Nobody could have worked it out from the headlines of Paul’s day; it had to be disclosed.

A partial hardening has come upon Israel. Partial: not every Jew is hardened, for the remnant believes. The phrase is literally in part, and by now Paul’s precision is a habit worth noticing. He hopes to save some (v. 14). Some of the branches were broken off (v. 17). The hardening is in part. In a chapter where every reader reaches instinctively for totals, the apostle keeps writing fractions. And the hardening is also limited in time.

Until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. The single most important word in the sentence is until. It is a word of time, and it has an end point. Whatever the hardening is, it has an expiry condition written into the same clause that announces it, which is exactly what a permanent rejection would not have. The fullness (plērōma) of the Gentiles is the full number of elect Gentiles that God intends to save. “Come in” means into the kingdom, into the people of God. The hardening lasts until then.

And in this way all Israel will be saved. “In this way” (houtōs) means in this manner, by this process: through the hardening of part of Israel, the coming in of the Gentiles, and the jealousy that provokes Israel to faith.

As it is written, The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob. From Isaiah 59:20–21, with words from Isaiah 27:9. The Deliverer is Christ. Israel’s salvation, like everyone’s, comes through him, by turning ungodliness away from Jacob: forgiveness and new hearts. Paul has adapted Isaiah’s wording, as he did openly at 10:6–8, but the point to hold is the content. When Paul says how Israel will be saved, he says a Deliverer comes, ungodliness is banished, and sins are taken away (v. 27). That closes off a reading that has become popular and that the text will not carry: that Israel might be saved on a separate track, without Christ, by covenant alone. Paul has spent chapter 10 insisting there is one name to call on and one message that has to be brought. He does not now provide a second door. The hope in v. 26 is enormous, and it is the same hope by the same means as everybody else’s.

Where Christians differ: who is all Israel? Three main views are held among Reformed Christians. First, all Israel is the whole church, Jew and Gentile, the Israel of God (Galatians 6:16); this was Calvin’s view. Those who hold it point also to 9:6, not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel, and to the words in this way, which describe how Israel is saved rather than when. Second, all Israel is the total of elect Jews saved throughout history, the remnant in every generation, as in vv. 1–10. Third, all Israel is the Jewish people as a whole, who will turn to Christ in large numbers in the future, before his return. Dispensationalists add a separate future plan for national Israel in a thousand-year kingdom. Verdict: The third view fits the passage best. In verse 25, Israel means ethnic Israel, distinguished from the Gentiles; it would be strange for the word to change meaning in the next sentence. The contrast of now and then (vv. 12, 15, 23–24, 30–31) points to a future turning, and the full inclusion of v. 12 looks for something greater than a remnant. So Paul expects a great conversion of the Jewish people to Christ. But this happens through the gospel, by faith in Christ, into the one olive tree, the church. It is not a separate plan of salvation, and it does not require a rebuilt temple or a thousand-year earthly kingdom. It fits the amillennial view: the church age ends with the return of Christ, the resurrection and the judgment, and no secret rapture. All Israel need not mean every individual Jew; in Scripture it often means Israel as a whole (1 Samuel 7:5; 2 Chronicles 12:1). The Westminster Larger Catechism teaches us to pray for the calling of the Jews (Q. 191).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jews can be saved without Christ, and it gives no ground whatever for anti-Jewish hatred. Nor does it mean any modern political state fulfils this prophecy; Paul speaks of conversion to Christ. What he promises is forgiveness: when I take away their sins (v. 27). He says nothing of territory, a rebuilt temple or a thousand-year reign. Christians may pray for the Jewish people and judge the policies of the modern state as they would any other nation’s. What Paul teaches us to long for is that they come to their Messiah.

When will this happen, and should we watch for signs? Scripture gives no date, and Paul gives none. He says until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and only God knows when that number is complete. So we should not try to read it off the news, or treat events in the Middle East as a countdown. Our task is the one Paul gives in this chapter: to preach the gospel to the nations, to love and pray for Jewish people, and to stay humble. The Lord will return visibly, at a day and hour no one knows (Matthew 24:36), and his people will be ready by being faithful, not by being well informed about a timetable.

Does all Israel mean every Jewish person who has ever lived? No. In the Old Testament the phrase usually means Israel as a whole, the nation as a body, without implying every single person (1 Samuel 7:5; 2 Chronicles 12:1). When the nation gathered at Mizpah, it was all Israel, though not every individual was present. So Paul’s hope is that the Jewish people as a people, in great numbers, will turn to Christ. It does not mean that Jews who die rejecting him are saved, any more than Gentiles who reject him are. There is one Saviour for all, and the way of salvation for Jew and Gentile alike is faith in him.

In a sentence. Paul does not want you to be ignorant of this mystery, brothers and sisters, so that you may not be conceited: Israel has experienced a hardening in part until the full number of the Gentiles has come in, and in this way all Israel will be saved. As it is written: “The deliverer will come from Zion; he will turn godlessness away from Jacob.”

On a Tuesday. God is working out a plan that spans the whole of history. Your part in it is to pray, to witness, and to stay humble. So take a doctrine you hold firmly, election, or the last things, or whatever your tradition has taught you to be certain about, and ask what holding it has done to you. Has it made you gentler with people who have it wrong? Slower to write anyone off? If the honest answer is that it has mostly made you more sure you are right, you are holding it in exactly the posture the first clause of v. 25 was written to prevent. Then pray this week, by name if you can, for the calling of Jewish people to their Messiah.

For worship. The God of this mystery is the Lord of history. He ordered the stumbling of Israel and the coming in of the nations, the hardening and its end, so that every part of the human story serves his purpose of mercy. He sent the Deliverer out of Zion once, to die and rise; he will send him again from the heavenly Zion, and Jacob will not be forgotten. Nothing is random, nothing is lost, and the hardening that seemed final has an until written into it by the hand that wrote the promise. Praise the God whose plans are older than the nations and kinder than our fears.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God. Interpreters differ over whether “all Israel” means the Jewish people as a whole before the end, or the whole company of God’s people, Jew and Gentile. The more natural reading in context is the first: a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ.

parallels.desc: a Redeemer will come to Zion

verseByVerse.quote: "and this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins." As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“and this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins.” As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers.

And this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins. Isaiah 59:21 joined with Isaiah 27:9, echoing the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:33–34. Take this clause first, because it tells you what the promise is actually made of. Not a territory, not a restored monarchy, not a political settlement. The content of the guarantee is forgiveness. Israel’s salvation will be by forgiveness of sins in Christ, the heart of the new covenant (Hebrews 8:8–12), the same thing Paul has been offering to everybody since chapter 3.

As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. In relation to the gospel, unbelieving Israel stands as God’s enemy, opposed to the message and under his displeasure. Their rejection opened the door for the Gentiles: for your sake. And that phrase ought to stop a proud Gentile reader. Not merely enemies, whom you may therefore look down on, but enemies in a way that has worked to your advantage. The hostility he might have felt superior to is the hostility that opened the door he walked through. There is no posture left to him but gratitude, and gratitude is the one posture that cannot be combined with contempt.

But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers. Yet in relation to God’s choice, Israel as a people is still loved, because of his promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. God loved the fathers and chose their offspring after them (Deuteronomy 4:37; 7:8). And this is stranger than it looks. They are loved on somebody else’s account: not for anything in the present generation, since Paul has just spent two chapters describing what is in the present generation, but because of promises made to men who had been dead for nearly two thousand years.

Loved for another’s sake. Before anyone finds that arbitrary, notice that it is the only way anyone in this letter is loved. Nobody is accepted on his own account. The Gentile reader standing in the tree is there for the sake of another, and so is every Christian who has ever lived: loved because of someone else’s obedience, held because of promises made before he was born. Israel’s case is not an exception to the gospel’s logic. It is the gospel’s logic applied to a nation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they are saved because of their ancestors. No one is saved by family merit. It means God’s love for the patriarchs guarantees his continued purpose for their descendants, which will be fulfilled when they turn to Christ.

How can people be God’s enemies and beloved at the same time? Because God’s relation to people has more than one side, and Scripture speaks of both honestly. As long as someone rejects Christ, he stands under God’s displeasure; that is the enemy side. Yet God may at the same time have purposes of love toward him that he has not yet carried out, as he had toward every believer before conversion: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (5:10). Every Christian was once both. So this verse should keep us from two errors: pretending unbelief does not matter, and writing off those who are presently against the gospel. God has not written them off.

In a sentence. “And this is my covenant with them when I take away their sins.” As far as the gospel is concerned, they are enemies for your sake; but as far as election is concerned, they are loved on account of the patriarchs.

On a Tuesday. What is hardest here is practical. Paul holds two entirely true things about the same people in one sentence and refuses to let either cancel the other. Most of us cannot do it for one afternoon about one relative. The person who has genuinely wronged us becomes simply the person who wronged us; the person we love becomes someone whose faults we have to shrink in order to keep loving them. Verse 28 does neither. So try writing the sentence. Take the person you are most tangled with and put both halves down in one line, joined by and rather than but: what is actually wrong, and what is actually true of them and of your bond. If you cannot get both onto the page without one of them softening, you have found the work. Paul managed it about people who had tried to have him killed.

For worship. God remembers his promises across thousands of years. Abraham had been in the grave for two millennia, and God was still loving his children for his sake. The same faithfulness holds you: you are loved for the sake of Christ, whose obedience will never be forgotten by his Father, and whose name is the reason you are welcome. Our God does not lose track of a promise, does not let a covenant lapse, and does not stop loving those he has set his heart on because their present generation has disappointed him. Praise the God who keeps faith with the dead and the living, and who takes away sins as the very content of his covenant.

parallels.desc: when he takes away his sin

verseByVerse.quote: For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. For just as you were at one time disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. For just as you were at one time disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,

For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. “Irrevocable” (ametamelētos) is built on the verb to regret, with the negative in front: without regret, never taken back. English makes it sound legal, and it is not. It does not chiefly say that God is unable to take a thing back. It says he has no second thoughts about having given it. God does not change his mind about what he has given and to whom he has called. The gifts are the privileges of 9:4–5, the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the promises; the calling is God’s choosing of Israel as his people.

No regret in God. Everyone knows the other experience from the inside. The reference you wrote for someone who then embarrassed you. The trust you extended and watched being spent. The money you handed over telling yourself it was a gift, and the small cold feeling months later when you understood how it had been used. There is a kind of regret that attaches itself to generosity after the fact, and it is one of the most ordinary emotions there is. Paul says there is none of it in God.

A comfort for every believer. Be exact about what the sentence is answering. In context it is a statement about Israel. Extending it to the individual believer is legitimate, because it is the same God and the same logic that produced the chain of 8:29–30, in which those he called, he also justified and glorified, and God never revokes his saving call. But it is an extension, and it should be named as one. Named as one, it is enormous.

For just as you were at one time disobedient to God. The Gentiles, before conversion, were disobedient (1:18–32; Ephesians 2:1–3). Paul will not let his Gentile readers forget where they started.

But now have received mercy because of their disobedience. Israel’s disobedience opened the door of mercy to the Gentiles. Your mercy came to you through someone else’s refusal, which leaves no room at all for looking down on them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God’s calling of Israel guarantees salvation without faith. It means God’s purpose for Israel stands and will be fulfilled.

Does irrevocable mean a minister who falls into serious sin keeps his calling to office? No, this verse is not about that. Paul is speaking of God’s covenant choice of Israel and, by extension, of his saving call to his people. He is not saying that anyone who once held church office or had a gift for ministry must always be allowed to exercise it. Scripture sets qualifications for elders (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9), and a man who disqualifies himself must step down, whatever his gifts. God may restore such a man to fellowship and use him again, but the church must not quote Romans 11:29 to shield a leader from discipline or to protect the institution at the expense of those he has wronged.

In a sentence. For God’s gifts and his call can never be revoked. Just as you who were at one time disobedient to God have now received mercy as a result of their disobedience,

On a Tuesday. When you doubt whether God still wants you, remember: his calling is irrevocable. He does not regret calling you. Almost every Christian carries a private theory about what would finally exhaust God’s patience: a specific thing, usually unnamed, that they suspect would be the end of it. Say what yours is. Then notice that verse 29 does not answer by assessing whether your particular item would qualify. It denies that the category exists. God does not sit down afterwards and wish he had chosen differently. Bring the thing to him in confession, and leave it with the God who has no regrets about you.

For worship. Here is a God without second thoughts. Before the foundation of the world he knew everything his people would do, every failure and every betrayal, and he chose them anyway, gave them his gifts anyway, and called them anyway. Nothing they did later took him by surprise, so nothing they did later could make him wish he had not. He did not regret Abraham, or Jacob, or David, or Peter, or you. His Son went to the cross knowing exactly whom he was dying for, and he does not look back on it with regret. Praise the unchanging God whose gifts are never recalled and whose calling never wavers.

parallels.desc: God is not man, that he should lie

verseByVerse.quote: so they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy. For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
so they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy. For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.

So they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy. The pattern reverses. Jewish disobedience brought mercy to Gentiles; mercy to Gentiles will bring mercy to Jews. You were disobedient and received mercy; they are disobedient and will receive mercy; and the two groups reach it by roads of exactly equal dignity, which is to say none. There is no senior partner in this room. A textual note: some manuscripts omit the second now, as the ESV notes. If it stands, it means that the time of mercy for Israel is the present gospel age, and it can come at any time.

For God has consigned all to disobedience. “Consigned” (synkleiō) is a prison word, and the picture should not be lost. It means to shut up together, to lock in with no way out, the same word Paul uses when he says the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin (Galatians 3:22). The image is not a courtroom but a cell with the whole human race in it, Jew and Gentile together, every exit tried and found locked. God has shut up everyone in the prison of their disobedience, so that no one can escape by his own merit.

That he may have mercy on all. And then the reason, which is the most surprising clause in the chapter: he locked them in so that he might have mercy. The confinement is not the end of the story and never was; it is the means. God closed every other door so that the only one left would be the one that opens from outside. Nobody in that cell can be told he took the second-best way out, because there was no other way out for anyone. The purpose is that all who are saved are saved by mercy alone. “All” here means all kinds, Jew and Gentile alike, both groups. No one gets in except by mercy.

Where Christians differ: universal salvation. Some read “mercy on all” as meaning that every human being will finally be saved. Verdict: The context is about two groups, Jews and Gentiles, not every individual. Paul has just spoken of branches cut off and of God’s severity (v. 22), and elsewhere of eternal destruction (2 Thessalonians 1:9). He hopes to save some of his countrymen (v. 14), and he opened chapter 9 in anguish over people he expects to be lost. The two alls are the same width, and the whole argument since chapter 9 has told us what that width is: two categories, not every person. God shows mercy on both groups without distinction, but not all individuals are saved. Hell is real and conscious and eternal (Matthew 25:46).

Did God make people disobey? No. God is never the author of sin, and no one is forced to disobey against his will (James 1:13). The disobedience was entirely ours, freely chosen, as chapter 1 showed. What God did was to shut the doors: he gave the law, which exposed sin; he let both Jew and Gentile go their own way and prove what was in them; and he closed off every route to salvation by merit, so that the only door left is mercy. It is the way a doctor might let a patient see the full results of the tests before he offers the cure, not because he caused the disease, but so that the cure is received as a cure.

In a sentence. So they too have now become disobedient, in order that they too may now receive mercy as a result of God’s mercy to you. For God has bound everyone over to disobedience so that he may have mercy on them all.

On a Tuesday. No one is saved except by mercy. Neither are you. What verse 32 destroys is the idea that anybody is a special case. Every argument about who is too far gone assumes there is a scale, with some people further down it. Verse 32 says the door was locked on all of us at the same time, from the same side, by someone who had already decided how the story ends. So this week, think of the person you find hardest to imagine receiving mercy, and pray for them. Then think of the person you find hardest to show mercy to, and do one kind thing for them. Let mercy make you humble, grateful and merciful.

For worship. This is the God who locks the prison so that he can open it. He let the whole race prove its rebellion, Jew and Gentile alike, and then sent his Son into the cell to carry the sentence and walk out with the key. Not one prisoner comes out by his own merit, and so not one can boast; every one comes out by mercy, and so every one can sing. The design that looked like a sentence was a rescue all along. Praise the God whose purpose in shutting us up was to have mercy, and whose mercy is wide enough for both Jew and Gentile.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the second “now.”

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!

The doxology. After eleven chapters of the deepest theology in Scripture, on sin, justification, union with Christ, the Spirit, election and Israel, Paul does not end with a conclusion but with worship. Doctrine is meant to lead to doxology, from doxa, glory. Having argued for three chapters through the mystery of God’s purposes with Israel and the nations, he does not land with a formula. He lands with an open mouth and a bowed head.

Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! Three depths. The riches of his grace and mercy (2:4; 9:23; 10:12). The wisdom of his plan, which uses even sin and hardening to bring salvation to the world, for Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). The knowledge by which he foreknew his people and sees all things. And let the argument stop here, because Paul stops it here. Eleven chapters of the tightest reasoning in Scripture, the wrath, the law, the faith of Abraham, the two Adams, the grave, the Spirit, the potter, the olive tree, and it does not end in a conclusion. It ends with a man running out of language in front of God and saying so.

How unsearchable are his judgments. “Unsearchable” (anexeraunētos) means what cannot be fully investigated. His decisions and decrees go beyond our understanding. You can follow them a long way, as Paul has just done, but you will not reach the bottom.

And how inscrutable his ways! “Inscrutable” (anexichniastos) carries a picture that English hides. It is built on ichnos, a footprint: literally, his ways cannot be tracked, like footprints that cannot be followed (the same word in Ephesians 3:8). You can see where he has been, and you cannot reconstruct the route. Israel’s own hymnbook had already put it exactly there, and about the greatest thing God ever did for them: your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters, yet your footprints were unseen (Psalm 77:19). The deliverance at the Red Sea was the least deniable act in the nation’s history, and it left no tracks. That is the sort of God Paul has been describing for three chapters.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is irrational or that we can know nothing about him. He has revealed much, as Romans shows. But what he has revealed opens onto a depth no creature can fathom. Mystery is not an excuse to stop thinking, but the place where thinking turns to worship. This verse is regularly conscripted to end conversations, and Paul has just disproved that use at length: nobody reasons harder than the man who wrote chapters 9 to 11. The doxology stands at the end of the argument, not instead of it. Anyone who reaches for verse 33 at the start, to avoid the work, is quoting Paul’s conclusion while refusing his method.

A depth, not a muddle. Notice what Paul does with the questions he never resolved. He leaves some standing: why these and not those, how the hardening and human responsibility fit together, what exactly life from the dead means. He does not apologise for them and he does not paper over them. He looks at the unexplained remainder and calls it depth, which is a word of praise. That is the difference between a mystery and a muddle. A muddle is something you have failed to sort out; a depth is something you have come to the edge of.

Is it wrong to be troubled by chapters 9 to 11? No. Paul himself was troubled; he began this section with great sorrow and unceasing anguish (9:2). Hard questions about election, hardening and Israel are not a sign of unbelief, and you should not pretend to feel no difficulty. But notice the direction Paul’s troubled mind travelled. He took the questions to Scripture, reasoned through them as far as God had revealed, and then, at the edge of what he could see, he worshipped rather than accused. The same road is open to you. Ask your questions honestly, study, talk to mature believers, and when you reach the limit, let the remaining mystery make God bigger in your eyes, not smaller.

In a sentence. Oh, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable his judgements, and his paths beyond tracing out!

On a Tuesday. When you reach the end of what you can understand about God, do not complain. Worship. Take the question about God’s ways that troubles you most at present, perhaps a prayer unanswered, a loss unexplained, a friend who has not believed. Bring it to him honestly. Then read these four verses aloud, slowly, and let them be your answer for today. You do not have to resolve the question to trust the One who knows the answer.

For worship. The riches were always going to be deeper than the reasoning. That is not the failure of the argument; it is what the argument was for. Here is a God whose mercy outruns our sin, whose wisdom outruns our plans, and whose knowledge outruns our questions. He made a path through the sea and left no footprints, and he made a path to the cross that no one could have predicted and no one can now undo. We do not reach the bottom of him and we never will, and that is our joy: we will spend eternity discovering that he is more than we thought. Oh, the depth.

parallels.desc: my thoughts are not your thoughts

verseByVerse.quote: "For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?”

For who has known the mind of the Lord. From Isaiah 40:13, in the great chapter on God’s incomparable greatness. No creature fully knows God’s thoughts. God knows himself fully; we know only what he reveals (1 Corinthians 2:11, 16). And it is worth recovering to whom Isaiah said this, because the usual application is the reverse of the original. Isaiah 40 is addressed to exiles, a beaten, deported people whose complaint is quoted a few verses later: my way is hidden from the LORD, and my right is disregarded by my God (Isaiah 40:27). They are not complaining that God is too free. They are afraid he has lost track of them.

Or who has been his counselor? No one advised God when he planned salvation. He did not need help or input. His plan comes from his own wisdom alone (Job 15:8; Jeremiah 23:18). And to those exiles the news that nobody has ever instructed God is comfort, not rebuke. It means his handling of their case has not been delegated, or advised, or worked out from partial information. It has a quieter mercy in it still: if nobody has ever been God’s counsellor, then nobody has ever successfully briefed him against you. No one got to him first. There is no version of your file that he has been given by someone else.

Built, not blurted. The three questions of vv. 34–35 are not a random pile. They answer the three nouns of v. 33 in reverse order: his knowledge (who has known his mind), his wisdom (who has been his counsellor), his riches (who has given to him). Even Paul’s astonishment is built rather than blurted, which tells you something about the man: he is no less careful in worship than he was in argument.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should not pray or bring our requests to God. He invites prayer. But we do not instruct him; we trust him.

If no one advises God, why pray? Because God has ordained prayer as one of the means by which he carries out his plans, and he delights to hear his children. When you pray, you are not informing God of something he did not know, or persuading him to be kinder than he was. You are a child bringing his needs to a Father who has promised to act through the prayers of his people (James 5:16; Matthew 7:7–11). Prayer changes things because God has decided that it will; and it changes the one who prays, bringing his will into line with God’s. Pray boldly, and leave the counsel to him.

In a sentence. Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his adviser?

On a Tuesday. You do not need to understand everything God is doing in your life. He needs no adviser. Trust his wisdom. When you notice yourself privately drafting the plan you think God should follow, and growing resentful that he has not followed it, stop and say this verse to him. Then tell him the need, plainly, and hand the plan back.

For worship. Who has known the mind of the Lord? Nobody. Not one creature, in any age. He has never been advised. He has never revised a decision in the light of information that reached him late. There was no consultation before the foundation of the earth and none since, and there is no counsellor anywhere whose absence from the room has ever left him at a disadvantage. And this is the mind that decided, without anyone needing to suggest it, to save the ungodly at the cost of his own Son. No one could have advised it; no one would have dared. Praise the all-wise God whose counsel needs nothing from us and gives everything to us.

parallels.desc: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: "Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?”

Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid? From Job 41:11 (see also Job 35:7). The setting of the quotation gives it its weight. Job 41 is God speaking out of the whirlwind, near the end of the longest and least comfortable answer in Scripture, and the line runs: who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Whatever is under the whole heaven is mine. It is said to a man who wanted an accounting, and who was, by the book’s own verdict, more nearly in the right than his friends. Even to him the answer is that there is no ledger between them in which he could ever be the creditor. No one has ever put God in debt. No one can claim that God owes him salvation. Everything we have, including the faith we give him, he first gave us: what do you have that you did not receive? (1 Corinthians 4:7). This sums up the message of Romans: salvation is by grace, not earned.

The background hum. The instinct this verse kills is a persistent one, and it is rarely admitted aloud. It shows up as the faint sense, after a stretch of obedience, that something is now owed: that the year of faithful service has bought a measure of protection, that God should not let this particular thing happen to someone who has been doing what you have been doing. It is not usually a belief. It is a background hum, and it becomes audible the moment life goes wrong.

What if God did owe you? Turn the question round and let it land. You would have a claim, and enforceable claims are excellent things to have. But a debt paid is not a gift given, and a God who was settling an account with you would not be loving you. Think of the difference between the friend who visits because he owes you and the friend who visits because he wanted to see you. Everything that makes the second visit worth anything is the absence of obligation. That is what verse 35 protects. It is not only a statement about God’s independence, though it is that. It is the guarantee that nothing you have ever received from him was a payment.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God does not reward his people. He does, but all his rewards are grace, crowning his own gifts.

But do we not give to God when we give money, time or service? We do, and he receives it gladly; but every gift we bring was his before it was ours. David said it when Israel gave lavishly for the temple: all things come from you, and of your own have we given you (1 Chronicles 29:14). Giving to God is not making a deposit that puts him in our debt; it is returning a small part of what he lent us, as an act of thanks and love. That is why Christian giving should be cheerful, not calculating (2 Corinthians 9:7). We give because he first gave, and we can never out-give him.

In a sentence. Who has ever given to God, that God should repay them?

On a Tuesday. Listen this week for the background hum: the moment you feel that God owes you something because of how faithful you have been. When you catch it, do not merely suppress it. Replace it with thanks. Name three things you have received from him today that you did nothing to earn, starting with breath and ending with the cross. Then give something away, freely, to someone who cannot repay you, and taste a little of the joy of giving without a ledger.

For worship. The one who owes nothing to anyone is the one who gives everything to everyone who comes to him. He was never in our debt, and yet he paid our debt. He needed nothing from us, and yet he gave us his Son, his Spirit, his kingdom and himself. No one has ever given to God first; he has always got there before us, with more than we could ask. You have never given God anything that was not first his. Give him everything, thank him for everything, and praise the God whose every gift is free.

verseByVerse.quote: For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.

For from him and through him and to him are all things. The whole of reality in one sentence. From him: he is the source of all things, the Creator. Through him: all things exist and are carried along by his power, the Sustainer and Ruler. To him: all things exist for his glory, the Goal. This includes salvation: planned by him, carried out through him, and ending in his praise (1 Corinthians 8:6; Colossians 1:16). Weigh the three prepositions separately, because each one closes a door. From him: nothing that exists brought itself. Through him: nothing that exists is keeping itself going. To him: nothing that exists is its own point. Between them they leave no room for the one claim the whole letter has been dismantling since 1:21, that a creature might be the origin, the sustainer or the end of anything.

The frame of three chapters. There is a frame around chapters 9 to 11 that is easy to miss and worth seeing whole. Chapter 9 opened with Paul in grief over his own people, and he broke off in the middle of it to bless the God of whom he spoke: God over all, blessed forever. Amen (9:5). Here at the far end, having argued the whole thing out, he says Amen again. The section begins with worship over a sorrow and ends with worship over a resolution, and the same word closes both. Paul does not arrive at praise because his difficulties dissolved; several of them still stand on the page. He arrives at praise because the God he could not fully trace turned out, when the argument was finished, to be more merciful than the argument had made him fear: a God who shut everyone in so that he could let everyone out, and who has not taken back a single thing he ever gave.

To him be glory forever. Amen. The right response to all of this. Glory (doxa) is honour, praise, weight. The Westminster Shorter Catechism begins here: our chief end is to glorify God and enjoy him forever (Q. 1). Amen: so be it, truly. The chapter that began by asking whether God had rejected his people ends with everything in existence going home to him. Nothing has been lost on the way, and the Amen is not the end of a prayer. It is a signature under a verdict.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God needs our glory to be complete. It means he deserves it, and our joy is found in giving it.

Does all things include evil and suffering? Yes, in the sense that nothing happens outside God’s rule and purpose, but not in the sense that he does evil. Scripture teaches that God ordains whatever comes to pass, yet in such a way that he is not the author of sin, and the responsibility of creatures is not taken away (Westminster 3.1). Joseph’s brothers sold him, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). The cross was the greatest evil ever done, and it was through him and to his glory. So when suffering comes, you are not in the hands of chance or of the devil. You are in the hands of the God from whom, through whom and to whom all things are, who is working even this toward his glory and your good.

In a sentence. For from him and through him and for him are all things. To him be the glory forever! Amen.

On a Tuesday. Everything is from him, through him and to him, including you, your work, your rest, and the ordinary errands of today. Before you start the day, take one routine task, the washing-up, the commute, the email you dread, and say over it: from him, through him, to him. Then do it as for the Lord. And at the end of the day, look back and give him the glory for whatever was good in it, for it came from him and was carried by him.

For worship. From him, and through him, and to him, are all things. Every galaxy and every atom of it. Every angel. Every kingdom that ever rose and every one that fell. Every hour of every life that has ever been lived, including the ones nobody recorded. The election of Abraham, the hardening of Pharaoh, the seven thousand, the remnant, the olive tree, the cross and the empty tomb, the fullness of the Gentiles and the salvation of all Israel. It began in him, it is being carried by him, and it is going home to him, and there is no fourth preposition, and nothing anywhere that falls outside the three. To him be glory forever. Amen.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin.<sup>2</sup>God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel?<sup>3</sup>“Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.”<sup>4</sup>But what is God’s reply to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”<sup>5</sup>So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace.<sup>6</sup>But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.<sup>7</sup>What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened,<sup>8</sup>as it is written, “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day.”<sup>9</sup>And David says, “Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them;<sup>10</sup>let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever.”<sup>11</sup>So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous.<sup>12</sup>Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!<sup>13</sup>Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry<sup>14</sup>in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.<sup>15</sup>For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead?<sup>16</sup>If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.<sup>17</sup>But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree,<sup>18</sup>do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you.<sup>19</sup>Then you will say, “Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.”<sup>20</sup>That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but fear.<sup>21</sup>For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.<sup>22</sup>Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God’s kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.<sup>23</sup>And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again.<sup>24</sup>For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree.<sup>25</sup>Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in.<sup>26</sup>And in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written, “The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob”;<sup>27</sup>“and this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins.”<sup>28</sup>As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers.<sup>29</sup>For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.<sup>30</sup>For just as you were at one time disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,<sup>31</sup>so they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy.<sup>32</sup>For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.<sup>33</sup>Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!<sup>34</sup>“For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?”<sup>35</sup>“Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?”<sup>36</sup>For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.

12.title: The Transformed Life
12.overview:
"Therefore" — with this word, chapters 12–16 are connected to everything that has gone before. The mercies of God described in chapters 1–11 are the foundation; the transformed life of chapters 12–16 is the superstructure. Paul does not move from theology to ethics because theology is the theoretical part and ethics is the practical part; he moves from theology to ethics because the ethics are the fruit of the theology. The mercies of God are not merely things to be believed; they are the motive force of a whole new way of living.

Chapter 12 opens with one of the most celebrated calls to consecration in the entire New Testament: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship" (v. 1). The language is deliberately sacrificial — the life of the justified Christian is offered to God in its entirety, not merely its "spiritual" dimension. And then the renewal of the mind (v. 2), which makes possible the discernment of God's will — the good, acceptable, and perfect. The rest of the chapter is the practical outworking of these two verses across the life of the Christian community.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The Living Sacrifice and the Renewed Mind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God" — the ethical appeal is grounded entirely in the indicative of grace. Paul does not say "in view of your obligations" or "in view of the moral law." He says: in view of the mercies of God — the whole sweep of justification, adoption, the Spirit, the love that cannot be separated from, the glory that is coming. It is the mercies that create the motivation; the obligation flows from the gift, not from duty alone.

"Present your bodies" — not just your souls or your religious activities, but your bodies: the physical, concrete, embodied reality of your daily existence. The body that gets up in the morning and goes to work. The hands that type the email. The mouth that speaks in the meeting. The feet that walk into the neighbour's house. Paul insists on the bodily nature of Christian worship because God insists on it: the gospel is not a recipe for spiritual escapism but for the consecration of the whole life — body and soul, private and public, sacred and secular — to God.

"Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind" (v. 2) — the passive voice is significant: be transformed, not transform yourself. The transformation is something that happens to you, from the inside, through the renewal of your mind by the Spirit and the Word. The Christian does not achieve transformation by heroic effort; she submits to it by attending to the means through which God renews the mind — Scripture, prayer, worship, community, suffering. And the evidence of transformation is discernment: the ability to prove what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body as Instrument of Worship

Romans 12:1 demolishes the sacred-secular distinction that has plagued Christian thinking since the patristic era. The body — presented to God as a living sacrifice — is itself the site of worship. This means that the Christian's daily work, physical rest, sexual life, eating and drinking, financial decisions, and embodied relationships are all, in principle, acts of worship when offered to God in faith and obedience. The Reformers' insistence on the holiness of ordinary life is grounded here. John Calvin saw the entire creation as the theatre of God's glory; Paul grounds that vision in the consecrated body of the believer. Your body is not a vehicle for your soul; it is the instrument of your worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The language of sacrifice was immediately understood by both Jewish and Gentile readers. In the Jewish tradition, sacrifice was the central act of worship — the presentation of an offering to God. Paul is saying that the entire life of the Christian is now the sacrifice: not an animal brought to an altar, but a person brought to God in the totality of their daily existence. The temple has been interiorised; the altar is everywhere; the offering is ongoing. Now: The call to "not be conformed to this world" is perpetually urgent because the world perpetually presses in. Every culture — including Christian subculture — has its conforming pressures, its assumed values, its default ways of measuring worth, success, and meaning. The renewal of the mind is the counter-pressure: learning to see all of life through the lens of Scripture, of the gospel, of the mercies of God, until the world's categories no longer have automatic authority over us.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. — Romans 12:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.

Meaning first. Romans 12 begins the practical part of the letter (chapters 12–16): how people who have received God’s mercy should live. Paul does not leave doctrine behind and turn to ethics as a separate subject; the therefore of verse 1 ties the whole Christian life to the mercies of chapters 1–11. First, the foundation: give your whole self to God as a living sacrifice, and be transformed by a renewed mind, not squeezed into the world’s shape (vv. 1–2). Second, life in the church: think of yourself soberly, for we are one body with many members, and each must use the gift God’s grace has given (vv. 3–8). Third, a string of short commands describing genuine love: love within the church, love toward outsiders, and love toward enemies, ending with the call to overcome evil with good (vv. 9–21). Gospel grace produces a new kind of person and a new kind of community. The chapter that opens by asking for a body on an altar closes by asking for a body that does not hit back, and both requests are made by the mercies of God.

I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God. Everything in this chapter hangs on a word that is easy to step over. Chapter 12 is not where Romans stops being doctrine and starts being practical, as though the first half were the theory and the second the application. It is one argument with a hinge in it, and the hinge is that little word therefore. “Appeal” (parakaleō: urge, exhort, encourage) is a pastor’s pleading, not a cold order. And Paul says what the therefore points back to: by the mercies of God. Not by the law, not by your obligations, not by what you owe. He has eleven chapters behind him and he gestures at all of it: wrath deserved and revealed (1:18), justified freely as a gift (3:24), peace with God (5:1), no condemnation now (8:1), nothing in all creation able to separate you from his love (8:39), and mercy as the only door out of a locked room (11:32). That is the pile he stands on to ask for anything at all.

The mercies. The plural is deliberate. “Mercies” (oiktirmoi) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God’s compassions, translating a Hebrew family of words related to the word for a womb: the ache of a parent over a child. It is not one act of clemency. It is a disposition, and Paul has been cataloguing its instalments since chapter 3: justification, adoption, the Spirit, election, his faithfulness to Israel. And it tells you the order in which Christian obedience actually works, which is the order most of us reverse. Almost nothing in this letter is asked of anyone until chapter 12, and even the commands of chapter 6 come after five chapters of what God has done. The mercies of God come first, and obedience follows as a response, never as a way to earn them. Any version of the Christian life that begins with the appeal and treats the mercies as background music has the engine and the fuel the wrong way round, and it will run for about eighteen months.

To present your bodies as a living sacrifice. “Present” (paristēmi) is a technical word, for bringing an offering forward and setting it down at the altar. Paul has used it before, at 6:13, 19, where he told these readers to present their members to God as instruments of righteousness. This is the same instruction with the whole letter now behind it, which is why it can be an appeal rather than a command. And what is brought forward is your bodies: not just your soul, but your whole self as you live in the world, with your eyes, hands, tongue and time. That is the least evasive word Paul could have chosen. A person can offer God his intentions from an armchair; intentions cost nothing and go nowhere. Your body is the one part of you that cannot be in two places, that has to actually turn up, that leaves a record.

A living sacrifice. In the Old Testament, sacrifices were killed. Christ made the one atoning sacrifice for sin, once for all (Hebrews 10:10–14). Now believers offer themselves as living sacrifices, not to atone, but in thanksgiving. And the paradox is worth pressing. A dead sacrifice has one great advantage: it stays where it is put. Nobody ever had to go back to the altar and look for it. A living one has legs. That is the whole difficulty of the Christian life in a sentence: not that the offering is hard to make, but that it is made by something that can get up afterwards and walk off, usually without any conscious decision to. So the offering is not one moment but a daily presenting, in the living of an ordinary life.

Holy and acceptable to God. Holy: set apart for God, like an offering without blemish. Acceptable: well-pleasing to him. And here is the wonder in the phrase. Our offerings are never without blemish; they are mixed with self and weakness. Yet through Christ they please God, for we are a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5). The Father receives the gift of a stammering, half-hearted life because it comes to him through his Son.

Which is your spiritual worship. “Spiritual” is logikos, which can mean rational, reasonable, fitting; the ESV note mentions the rendering rational. “Worship” is latreia, the priestly service of the temple (9:4). In view of God’s mercies, giving your whole life to him is not extreme devotion; it is the only reasonable response. To receive so much and offer so little in return would be the irrational thing. Worship is not just what we do on Sunday; it is the whole of life given to God.

Do not be conformed to this world. “Conformed” (syschēmatizō) means pressed into the shape of, like dough in a mould. And “this world” is literally this age (aiōn), the present evil age with its values, opposed to God (Galatians 1:4). That matters. You cannot get away from an age by moving house, leaving the city or joining a smaller church; it is not somewhere else, it is now. The pressure is not at the border. It is in the water.

But be transformed by the renewal of your mind. “Transformed” is metamorphoō, the word the Gospels use of Jesus on the mountain, when he was transfigured before them and his face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2), and the word Paul uses of believers being changed into Christ’s image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). Paul takes the word for what happened to the Lord in front of three terrified disciples and applies it to what is meant to be happening to an ordinary believer’s mind. Not improvement. A change of form. Both verbs are present tense and passive: keep on being transformed, by God’s work in you. But passive does not mean idle. You cannot transform yourself, and you can decide what you put your mind under: what you read, what you listen to, whose company you keep, what you rehearse while driving. The means is the renewing of the mind, a new way of thinking shaped by God’s word. Nobody drifts into a renewed mind. They drift into the other thing.

That by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. “Testing” (dokimazō) means to prove, to approve after testing; it is the word used of assaying metal. And it closes a circle opened in the first chapter. There Paul wrote that because people did not see fit, did not on testing approve, to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind, a mind that was itself adokimos, failed, rejected metal (1:28). The faculty that refused to test God properly was the faculty that was surrendered. Here that is reversed. What was lost at 1:28 is handed back at 12:2, and the whole letter stands between the two. The will of God here is his moral will, revealed in Scripture, not secret guidance. It is good (morally right), acceptable (pleasing to God) and perfect (complete, lacking nothing).

A competence, not a signal. This corrects the way most people go looking for God’s will. The verse does not promise a signal, an impression or a door that opens at the right moment. It promises a competence: a mind so remade that it can weigh a situation and recognise what is good in it. God’s more usual answer to what should I do? is not an instruction. It is a different person doing the deciding.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must withdraw from the world; Jesus prayed not that his Father would take us out of the world but that he would keep us from the evil one (John 17:15). It does not mean the body is bad. It means the believer’s whole life belongs to God and is being changed from the inside.

How do I make a big decision, like a job, a move or whom to marry? Begin with what God has already revealed. Many decisions are settled by his moral will: marry only in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39), do not take a job that requires you to sin, keep your promises. Within those bounds, God usually gives freedom, and he expects you to use the renewed mind this verse describes. Pray for wisdom (James 1:5). Ask which option will help you love God and others better, use your gifts, and keep you under good teaching in a faithful church. Take counsel from mature believers who know you (Proverbs 15:22). Then decide, and trust God with the outcome. You do not need a sign to obey; and if you have honestly sought to please him, you have not missed his will.

What does renewing my mind look like in practice? It is slow and ordinary. Read Scripture regularly, not only for information but to let it reshape what you love and how you see. Sit under faithful preaching each Lord’s Day, and let one truth from it go with you into the week. Memorise a few verses and turn to them when anxious or tempted. Notice which voices shape your thinking most hours of the week, from your phone, the news, entertainment and friends, and change the balance. Pray Scripture back to God. And expect change to be gradual: like the growth of a tree, you rarely see it happen, but you see it has happened.

In a sentence. Therefore, brothers and sisters, in view of God’s mercy, Paul urges you to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God; this is your true and fitting worship. Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what God’s will is: his good, pleasing and perfect will.

On a Tuesday. Start the day by offering yourself to God: your body, your work, your words. Then feed your mind on his word, so that the world does not shape your thinking more than Scripture does. If you want to know what you have actually presented to God this month, the honest evidence is not your sense of devotion. It is your diary and your bank statement, which between them describe where your body went and what it did when it got there. And try a backwards test. Think of a decision you made five years ago and would now make differently: not a sin, just a judgement that looks poor today. What changed? If only your circumstances changed, nothing has happened. If you can now see something in it you could not see then, that is this verse at work, so slowly you never once caught it in the act.

For worship. By the mercies of God. Not by the logic of it, or the duty of it, or the reasonableness of the arrangement, but by the mercies, and Paul has spent eleven chapters piling them up before he asks for anything at all. No condemnation. A righteousness apart from the law. Peace with God. An inheritance with Christ. A Spirit who prays when praying is beyond us. A love that death cannot reach. The Son of God laid himself on the altar as a dying sacrifice so that we could lay ourselves there as living ones, and the Father receives our poor offerings because they come through him. That is the pile the appeal stands on. He does not ask for a single thing until there is nothing left for him to give.
verseByVerse.note: “Therefore” builds on chapters 1–11: the mercies of God come first, then the response. The ESV notes that “spiritual worship” can also be rendered “rational service.”

parallels.desc: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–8 — Gifts of Grace: Sober Self-Assessment in the Body
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The renewed mind produces, first, a sober assessment of oneself — neither inflated pride nor false modesty, but honest recognition of the measure of faith God has given and the gifts he has distributed. The image Paul uses is the body: one body, many members, each with a different function. No member of the body of Christ is the whole body; no gift given to one member is given to all; the diversity is not a deficiency but the design.

Paul's list of gifts in vv. 6–8 — prophecy, service, teaching, exhortation, giving, leading, showing mercy — is not exhaustive but representative. Each gift comes with a manner: prophesy in proportion to your faith, serve in your serving, teach in your teaching, exhort in your exhorting, give with generosity, lead with zeal, show mercy with cheerfulness. The gifts are not to be displayed but exercised — put to work in the service of the body for the benefit of all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Charismata: Gifts of the Spirit for the Common Good

The gifts listed in Romans 12 are what Paul elsewhere calls charismata — graces, gifts of the Spirit. The Reformed tradition has emphasised that every gift is given for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7), not for the personal spiritual enhancement of the recipient. The gift of teaching is not given so that the teacher can be admired; it is given so that the body can be built up. The gift of mercy is not given as an ornament of personal piety; it is given to be exercised toward those in need. Gift and function are inseparable; the gift that is not exercised in service is a lamp hidden under a bowl.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The early church was a remarkable mixture of social classes, ethnic backgrounds, and educational levels. The gifts distributed by the Spirit crossed every human boundary: the slave might have the gift of teaching; the educated Greek might have the gift of service. The body-of-Christ framework was the theological revolution that made sense of this diversity. Now: The contemporary church regularly struggles with two opposite errors in the theology of gifts: the inflation of spectacular gifts (leading to unhealthy spiritual hierarchy and competition) and the dismissal of ordinary gifts (leading to the impression that only the "up-front" gifts matter). Romans 12:6–8 keeps the balance: every gift, faithfully exercised in its proper sphere, is a grace from God and a service to the body.

verseByVerse.quote: For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned. — Romans 12:3
verseByVerse.commentary:
For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned.

For by the grace given to me. Paul speaks with apostolic authority, which itself was a gift of grace (1:5; 15:15). He does not command from a position of earned superiority; he speaks from the same posture of received grace that he is commending. He speaks humbly as he calls them to humility.

I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think. The verse is built on a pun that English cannot quite carry. Paul uses the verb think (phroneō) four times in one line, twice with prefixes: do not over-think (hyperphroneō) yourself beyond what you ought to think, but think so as to be sound-minded (sōphroneō). The first fruit of a renewed mind is a right view of yourself. And note who it is addressed to: everyone among you. Not the leaders, not the gifted, not the ones with a platform. It is issued to every person in the room without exception, which tells you what Paul expects to find in every person in the room.

Why this comes first. The renewed mind could have produced any number of first fruits, and the one Paul names is an accurate self-estimate. Partly because pride is the last thing in a person to be renewed and the first thing to corrupt everything else. But mostly because of what is coming in the next verse: he is about to describe a body, and a body cannot function if every member has privately concluded it is the head. Pride divides the body; humility builds it.

But to think with sober judgment. Sober is literally unintoxicated: not solemn, but sensible and realistic, neither inflated nor falsely humble. Paul is describing a man whose estimate of himself is not under the influence of anything. And the most useful thing in the verse is what sober does not mean. It does not mean thinking badly of yourself. The man who says he is no good at anything is not being humble; he is being inaccurate, and often he is fishing, and everyone in the conversation knows it. False modesty is simply pride that has learned it gets a better reception upside down. Humility is not pretending you have no gifts; it is seeing your gifts as God’s gifts. Sober judgment can say I am good at this in a level voice, because the sentence is a fact about a gift rather than a claim about a person.

Each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned. “Measure” (metron) is portion, allotment. God gives each believer faith and gifts in varying measure. Some take the measure of faith as the standard of faith, the same for all: the gospel itself. Others take it as the amount of faith or gifting given to each. Either way, what you have was given, so there is no room for boasting: what do you have that you did not receive? (1 Corinthians 4:7). And it is not comparison. The moment the standard becomes another believer, the exercise has already failed, whichever way the comparison comes out. Paul tells another church the same thing with the testing verb of v. 2: let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbour (Galatians 6:4). The measure was assigned to you. Nobody else was issued yours.

What it does not mean. It does not mean self-hatred or refusing to serve. Sober thinking includes recognising your gifts so that you can use them.
