Does God give different amounts of saving faith? No. Saving faith is not graded; the weakest faith in Christ saves as surely as the strongest, because it is Christ who saves, not the strength of your grip on him. A trembling hand receives the gift as truly as a steady one. The measure of faith here is the portion God has given each believer for the service he has called him to, which is why Paul goes straight on to the different gifts (vv. 4–8; 1 Corinthians 12:11). So never conclude that because your faith feels small, you are less saved than someone else. You may be less mature, and you should want to grow; but you are not less justified.

How can I tell healthy confidence from pride? Pride needs to be noticed and compared; sober confidence does not. Ask a few honest questions. When someone else is praised for the thing you do well, are you glad or stung? When you are corrected, do you listen or defend? Do you use your gift to serve others, or to be seen? Can you thank God for your ability without needing anyone else to mention it? Healthy confidence knows its gift, uses it, and is happy for others to have greater ones. Pride is restless until it is ranked. The cure for both pride and false modesty is the same: look at what you have as given, and at the Giver as worthy.

In a sentence. For by the grace given to Paul, he says to every one of you: do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but rather think of yourself with sober judgement, in keeping with the faith God has distributed to each of you.

On a Tuesday. Measure yourself by what God has given you, not by comparison with others. That cures both pride and envy. And try a test that almost nobody passes first time. Say your strongest gift out loud, in one plain sentence, with no disclaimer in front of it and no boast behind it. Most people cannot do it. Either it will not come out at all, or it arrives wrapped in apologies, or it comes out slightly too large. The wobble in either direction is the measurement. Then thank God for the gift, and ask him where to use it this week.

For worship. Every capacity you have was handed to you by a God who owed you nothing. The mind that thinks, the hand that serves, the faith that trusts: all of it is grace, measured out by a wise Father who knows exactly what each child needs for the work he has given. He did not make us all the same, and he did not make any of us self-made. And the One who had every gift in full did not think of himself more highly than he ought; though he was in the form of God, he humbled himself to the cross (Philippians 2:6–8). Praise the generous God who gives every gift, and the humble Son who shows us how to carry them.
verseByVerse.note: A play on the verb “think” (phroneō): not to think too highly (hyperphronein) but to think with sober judgment (sōphronein).

verseByVerse.quote: For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.

For as in one body we have many members. Paul’s favourite picture of the church (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 4:15–16). A human body is one, yet has many parts. And the metaphor carries a bluntness we tend to soften. Parts of a body are not detachable. A hand that leaves the arm does not become an independent hand with its own plans; it becomes a dead hand, quite quickly, and the arm does not do well either. Paul chose an image in which separation is not a lifestyle option but an injury to two parties.

And the members do not all have the same function. “Function” (praxis) is activity, work. An eye sees; a hand works. Difference is not a problem but the design. That is worth saying to the person who has quietly concluded he is peripheral. Consider how much of your own body you could actually name: a handful of parts, mostly the ones you can see. Almost everything keeping you alive at this moment is something you have never thought about, could not point to, and would not miss until it stopped.

So we, though many, are one body in Christ. Our unity is in Christ: we are joined to him, and so to one another. The unity is not organisational but real, because we are all in the same Christ. The church is not a club of individuals who happen to share beliefs, but an organism in which every part exists for the whole.

And individually members one of another. The last phrase is stranger than it usually sounds. Paul does not say that we are members of the body, which would be tidy. He says we are members of one another. The belonging is not routed through an institution; it runs directly between people. You are not attached to the church and therefore adjacent to the others. You are attached to them. Each believer belongs to every other believer. You need them, and they need you. A Christian without a local church is like a hand cut off from the body.

What it does not mean. It does not mean everyone must be the same. Nor does it mean that differences in gifts mean differences in worth.

Do I really need to join a local church? Yes, if you can. The New Testament knows nothing of Christians who belong to Christ but to no congregation. Believers were baptised and added to a church (Acts 2:41–42), they had elders who watched over them (Hebrews 13:17), and they met together, which Hebrews tells us not to neglect (Hebrews 10:24–25). Online sermons can feed you, but they cannot know you, visit you, correct you, or receive your gifts. Commit to a faithful local church where the gospel is preached, the ordinances are kept, and members care for one another. If illness or circumstances keep you housebound, ask the church to bring its fellowship to you.

What if a church has hurt me? Then you are not alone, and your pain is real. Some churches have wounded people badly, and where there was abuse it must be named, reported where it is a crime, and never covered up. But the answer to a sick body is not to live as a severed hand; it is, in time, to find a healthy body. Take your time, pray, and look for a church where the gospel is clear, leaders are accountable, and people are gentle. Tell a pastor there what happened. Christ has not given up on his church, and he has not given up on healing you within it.

In a sentence. Just as each of us has one body with many members, and these members do not all have the same function, so in Christ we, though many, form one body, and each member belongs to all the others.

On a Tuesday. The useful question is not whether you are one of the parts people can name. It is whether anything would stop if you did. In most congregations there are two or three people about whom nobody thinks and without whom nothing would happen by Thursday. Find out who they are in your church and thank them this week. And if you are one of them, take heart: the body knows what it would lose, even if it never says so.

For worship. Thank God for the other members of your church, even the ones very different from you. You belong to them, and they to you, because every one of you belongs to Christ. He is the head from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint, grows and builds itself up in love (Ephesians 4:16). He did not save us one by one and leave us to find our own way; he made us a body, his body, with his life running through every member. Praise the Christ who gathers the scattered into one, and who gives each of us a place in a body no one could have designed but him.

verseByVerse.quote: Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;

Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us. “Gifts” (charismata) come from “grace” (charis). The word itself makes the argument. Charisma is charis with an ending that names a particular instance of the thing, so a gift is not something grace produces alongside itself. It is a piece of grace, made specific and handed to a named person. A spiritual gift is grace in action, an ability given by God for building up the body. Not earned, and not chosen by us, for the Spirit apportions to each one individually as he wills (1 Corinthians 12:11). The ability you have is not a reward for the grace you received. It is more of it.

Gifts that differ. And the emphasis falls on differ. Paul does not begin by celebrating that everyone has a gift; he begins by insisting that the gifts are unlike each other. The church that is uneasy with difference has not achieved unity. It has achieved a body made entirely of one organ, which is not a picture of health in any anatomy.

Let us use them. The Greek has no verb, but the sense is clear. Gifts are for using, not admiring. Possessing a gift without exercising it is a failure of stewardship, like a servant burying his master’s money in the ground (Matthew 25:25).

If prophecy, in proportion to our faith. Prophecy (prophēteia) in the New Testament was speaking a message revealed by God for the church (1 Corinthians 14:3, 29–31). In proportion to our faith is literally according to the analogy (analogia) of the faith. It may mean according to the measure of faith given to the prophet (v. 3), or in agreement with the faith, the body of truth already revealed. The second has a long history, and from it Reformed interpreters drew the principle of the analogy of faith: Scripture interprets Scripture, and no teaching may contradict the rest of God’s word. Both readings keep the gift under an authority outside the gifted person.

Where Christians differ: does prophecy continue today? Continuationists believe the gift of prophecy continues in the church, giving new messages from God, usually understood as words prompted by the Spirit, to be weighed by the church (1 Corinthians 14:29) and never equal to Scripture. Verdict: The gift of prophecy, in the sense of new revelation from God, belonged to the foundation period of the church, laid by apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20). With the completion of Scripture, the canon is closed, and no new revelation is to be added (Hebrews 1:1–2; Westminster 1.1, 1.6). A word from God cannot be fallible, and a church that receives new words alongside Scripture will soon be ruled by them. Today the prophetic function continues in a secondary sense through faithful preaching, which applies Scripture to the church with power, as one who speaks oracles of God (1 Peter 4:11). This view is held charitably: many continuationist brothers and sisters love Christ, and everyone agrees that any claimed word must be tested by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that only some Christians have gifts. Every believer has been given grace to serve.

How do I find my gift? Not chiefly by a questionnaire, but by serving. Begin where there is need: the crèche rota, the welcome team, visiting the sick, the washing-up after church. Notice what bears fruit and what others in the church recognise in you, and keep going. Gifts are given to serve one another as good stewards of God’s varied grace (1 Peter 4:10), so they are found in the serving, not before it. And notice what is not on Paul’s list. There is no gift of being impressive, and nothing here that would look like much from a distance. Serving, teaching, encouraging, giving, leading, being kind to people in trouble: that is the inventory, and most of it happens where nobody is watching. If you have concluded you have no gift, check whether you have been searching the wrong list.

Are natural talents spiritual gifts? Often God uses the abilities he gave you at birth, for he is the Creator as well as the Redeemer; a gifted organiser or a natural carer may find that the Spirit takes up those abilities for the church. But a talent becomes a gift to the body when it is given over to Christ and used in love to build others up. Some abilities appear only after conversion, and some natural talents are never meant for church use at all. The test is not where the ability came from, but whether it is being used to serve the body by grace, in humility.

In a sentence. We have different gifts, according to the grace given to each of us. If your gift is prophesying, then prophesy in accordance with the faith;

On a Tuesday. Ask: what has God given me to serve others with? Then use it this week, in your church. If you do not know, offer yourself to one practical need, and ask a mature believer what he sees in you. And if you know your gift but have let it lie unused, pick it up again: there is someone in your church waiting, without knowing it, for exactly what God gave you to give.

For worship. Every gift in the church is a piece of the grace of God, cut to fit a particular person and handed over for the good of others. The risen Christ, ascending on high, gave gifts to men (Ephesians 4:8), and he goes on giving them, so that no congregation is ever left without what it needs to be built up. He gives his word, and gives men to preach it; he gives hands to serve and hearts to comfort. Praise the generous Lord of the church, whose grace takes a thousand shapes and never runs out.

verseByVerse.quote: ...if service, in our serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching; the one who exhorts, in his exhortation; the one who contributes, in generosity; the one who leads, with zeal; the one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness. — Romans 12:7–8
verseByVerse.commentary:
if service, in our serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching; the one who exhorts, in his exhortation; the one who contributes, in generosity; the one who leads, with zeal; the one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness.

If service, in our serving. “Service” (diakonia) is practical help, the root of our word deacon. Whoever has this gift should give himself to it. And the list changes shape halfway through, which is instructive. The first items simply repeat themselves: the one who serves, in his serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching. That looks like a tautology and is in fact a correction. There is a great deal of activity available around a gift that is not the gift: meeting about the serving, recruiting for the serving, having views about how the serving should be done. Paul’s instruction is to be found in the thing itself.

The one who teaches, in his teaching. Explaining and applying God’s truth (1 Timothy 4:13; 2 Timothy 2:2). The teacher is called to teach, not to perform or to be admired for teaching.

The one who exhorts, in his exhortation. “Exhorts” is parakaleō, the same word as v. 1: urging, encouraging, comforting. Teaching informs the mind; exhortation moves the will. The church needs both: the one who explains what is true and the one who comes alongside and says, now do it, and I will help you.

The one who contributes, in generosity. Giving to others’ needs. “Generosity” (haplotēs) means simplicity, single-mindedness: a gift with one motive in it and no second agenda folded underneath, giving without hidden motives or holding back (2 Corinthians 8:2; 9:11).

The one who leads, with zeal. “Leads” (proistēmi, stands before, presides) is used of elders (1 Thessalonians 5:12; 1 Timothy 5:17). Lead with diligence and earnestness, not laziness. The leader who leads without energy or conviction is failing the body.

The one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness. Caring for the sick, poor and suffering. “Cheerfulness” (hilarotēs, from which we get hilarity) is a glad heart, not a grudging one, and Paul uses its cousin when he says God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). Mercy done with a martyr’s air does more harm than good; the face of mercy should be the face of joy.

The manner can cancel the gift. The last three items take a manner rather than a repetition, generosity, zeal, cheerfulness, and this is where gifts most often go wrong. It is entirely possible to exercise the right gift in a way that damages the person receiving it. Everyone has met the merciful helper who leaves you feeling like a case, the giver whose gift arrives with strings you discover later, the leader who is technically present and visibly elsewhere. The gift was real in all three. The manner cancelled it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean this is a complete list of gifts (compare 1 Corinthians 12; Ephesians 4:11; 1 Peter 4:10–11). Nor does it mean that those without a particular gift are excused from the duty. All must serve, give and show mercy. The gifted do so in a special way.

What if I serve but feel no cheerfulness? Do not stop serving; ask God to change the heart behind the hands. Cheerfulness is not a mood you can switch on, but it grows from remembering why you serve: Christ came not to be served but to serve and to give his life (Mark 10:45), and he served you first. Sometimes the lack of joy is a sign of tiredness, and you need rest or to share the load; sometimes it is a sign that you are serving to be noticed, and the remedy is to serve somewhere no one will see. Pray before you serve, think of the person rather than the task, and give thanks afterwards. Joy often follows obedience rather than preceding it.

In a sentence. If it is serving, then serve; if it is teaching, then teach; if it is encouraging, then encourage; if it is giving, give generously; if it is leading, lead diligently; if it is showing mercy, do it cheerfully.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it requires somebody else. Ask a person who has actually received your gift what it was like to be on the receiving end of it. Not whether it helped; they will say yes. Whether they felt like a person or a project. Most of us have never asked, and the manner is the half of this that we cannot assess from inside. Then, this week, do one act of service, teaching, encouragement, giving, leadership or mercy, and do it in the manner Paul names.

For worship. Put the whole list together and the striking thing is how ordinary it is. Nothing here requires a stage. What it requires is that the thing actually gets done, by the person it was given to, in a manner that makes the recipient glad it was them who did it. And every one of these gifts is a small reflection of Christ, who has them all in perfection: the Servant who washed his disciples’ feet, the Teacher who spoke as no man spoke, the Comforter of the weary, the Giver of himself, the Shepherd who leads his flock, and the merciful High Priest who sympathises with our weaknesses. Every gift in your church comes from the same grace and points to the same Lord. Thank God for your teachers, servers, givers, leaders and those who show mercy, and thank him most for the One they all resemble.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–21 — Love in Action: The Ethics of the Transformed Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9–21 form a rapid-fire sequence of practical exhortations that read almost like headings from a sermon on the Christian life — compressed, vivid, and comprehensive. Love without hypocrisy. Abhorring evil, holding fast to what is good. Outdoing one another in showing honour. Fervent in spirit. Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, constant in prayer. Contributing to the needs of the saints. Blessing those who persecute. Weeping with those who weep. Not being haughty. Repaying no one evil for evil. Living at peace with everyone. Not taking revenge. Overcoming evil with good.

The section begins and ends with love: "Let love be genuine" (v. 9) and "overcome evil with good" (v. 21). Everything between is the anatomy of genuine love in practice. Paul is not describing an achievable moral programme; he is describing the shape of a Spirit-renewed life — what grace looks like when it has taken hold of a person and begun the long work of conforming her to Christ.

The command to bless persecutors (v. 14) and to overcome evil with good (v. 21) are among the most demanding in the entire New Testament. They presuppose a radical reorientation of the instinct for self-protection and retaliation — an instinct that the Spirit does not suppress but redirects. The Christian who blesses her persecutor is not pretending the persecution is acceptable; she is entrusting the righting of wrongs to the God who says "vengeance is mine" (v. 19, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35) and acting from the love that wishes even the enemy's good.

Two things in the section deserve naming. The first is a piece of wordplay in v. 13. The command is not merely to show hospitality but to pursue it — and the verb is the one Paul uses in the very next line of those who persecute you. The same word, one sentence apart, running in opposite directions: some people are chasing you, and you are to go chasing after strangers.

The second is v. 20, which is the sharpest instruction here and the most misread: if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink. Paul takes it from Proverbs 25:21–22, and the burning coals are not a promise that your kindness will make him suffer in some superior way. The image is most naturally read as the burning of shame that leads to repentance. The aim of the exercise is not a defeated enemy. It is an enemy who has stopped being one.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ethic of the Cross in Daily Life

The ethics of Romans 12:9–21 are the daily practical form of the theology of the cross. The crucified Christ did not retaliate; he blessed those who cursed him; he overcame evil with the supreme good of his self-offering. The Christian who lives by this ethic is not simply following rules but is embodying the pattern of the One who died for his enemies. This is why Paul can ground the command to bless persecutors in the experience of God's mercy (v. 1): the person who knows she was God's enemy and has been loved into sonship has the deepest possible motivation for loving her enemies. She is doing to them what was done to her.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman church included people from across the social spectrum — slaves, freedmen, members of Caesar's household (Philippians 4:22), wealthy patrons, poor migrants. The potential for social friction, hierarchy, and mutual contempt was enormous. Paul's commands — "outdo one another in showing honour" (v. 10), "do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly" (v. 16) — were written for a community in which these things were concrete daily challenges, not abstract ethical principles. Now: The contemporary church is no less stratified by income, education, race, and social status. Romans 12:9–21 is still the practical charter of a community that crosses every human division by the power of a love that is genuinely without hypocrisy. The test is not whether the church affirms diversity in principle but whether its members weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice — across every line that the world uses to divide.

verseByVerse.quote: Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor. — Romans 12:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor.

Let love be genuine. The heading of verses 9–21. “Love” is agapē, self-giving love. “Genuine” (anypokritos) is built out of the theatre. A hypokritēs was an actor, a man who spoke his lines from behind a mask, so that the face the audience saw was not the face that was there. Love that is anypokritos is love with the mask off. Not love that is always warm, which no one can manage, but love that is not performing a warmth it does not have. A community in which people perform love for approval while privately indifferent to one another’s good is not a church in any meaningful sense; it is a religious social club.

Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. This is usually skipped, and it should not be, because it is what keeps love from turning into a mood. Love is not soft on evil. Both verbs are violent. “Abhor” (apostygeō) is a strong word: loathe, shudder at, find repellent. “Hold fast” (kollaō) is the word for gluing two things together so that they tear if you separate them. So genuine love is not neutral about anything. The sentimental version, which treats love as universal acceptance, has no capacity for abhorrence at all, and so it has nothing to glue itself to either. Real love hates what harms the beloved. Paul puts a hatred and an adhesive in the same breath as the command to love, because a love with no hatreds in it is not deep enough to hold anybody.

Love one another with brotherly affection. Verse 10 stacks two family words on top of each other: philadelphia, love of brothers and sisters, and philostorgos, built on storgē, the particular word for the love that runs between members of a household, the unchosen affection of people who belong to each other by birth. The church is a family, and its love should be warm. It is not being asked to be a pleasant society. It is being asked to have the texture of a family, including the part where you did not pick them.

Outdo one another in showing honor. A competition in honouring others: try to be first to show respect. The verb can also mean to go first, to lead the way, and some take it as prefer one another in honour, putting others ahead of yourself (Philippians 2:3). Either way the striving is real. In a culture of social competition and status-seeking, this turns the instinct inside out. Paul does not tell a status-conscious church to stop competing. He tells them to change the event. It is the only competition the New Testament permits: to be the one who moves first, before anyone has earned it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love is just a feeling. It means active, sincere goodwill that shows itself in actions.

How can I love people in church I do not naturally like? Begin with what love does, not with what you feel. Agapē is not liking; it is willing and doing someone’s good. You can pray for him by name, speak well of him, greet him warmly, ask about his week, and help him when he needs it, all while your feelings lag behind. Very often feelings follow. Remember too that you belong to him and he to you, by the same blood of Christ, and that God chose you both knowing exactly what you are like. If there is a real wrong between you, deal with it honestly (Matthew 18:15). If it is simply that he grates on you, he is probably one of God’s chosen tools for making you more like Christ.

Does hating evil mean hating people who do evil? No. Paul says hate what is evil, not who. A Christian hates sin most of all in himself, and he hates what sin does to those he loves. But he is to love his neighbour, and even his enemy, as this chapter goes on to say (vv. 14, 20). Think of a doctor who hates cancer precisely because he loves his patient. In the same way, the more you love someone, the more you hate the lies, the addictions and the cruelties that are destroying him. Love that refuses to hate evil cannot help anyone, and hatred of evil without love becomes a kind of evil itself.

In a sentence. Love must be sincere. Hate what is evil; cling to what is good. Be devoted to one another in love. Honour one another above yourselves.

On a Tuesday. Find someone in your church today and honour them: a word of thanks, a note, a meal, a real compliment. Try to get there first. And here is a test that takes ten seconds and is unpleasant. Think of the last time you were in a room where somebody was praised for doing well the thing that you also do. Not a rival, a friend. What happened inside you before you had time to arrange your face? Whatever that was, it is the honest reading on this verse, and the mask Paul is talking about is the one that went on immediately afterwards. Confess it, and then go and honour that person.

For worship. There was once a love entirely without a mask. The Son of God came among us and never performed a warmth he did not have: every word to the leper, every look at Peter, every tear at Lazarus’ tomb was real. He hated evil with a holy hatred, overturning the tables in the temple, and he clung to what is good with his whole life. And he went first in honour, laying aside his glory and taking the lowest place, so that we who had no honour might share his. Praise the Christ whose love is genuine to the bone, and who is making us a family that loves like him.

parallels.desc: hate evil, and love good

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord. Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord. Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.

Do not be slothful in zeal. Start with the odd one. It puts two words together that ought not to fit. “Slothful” (oknēros: hesitant, sluggish) is the word Proverbs uses of the sluggard, the man who will not get out of bed, and “zeal” (spoudē) is diligence, eagerness. How is a person lazy at zeal? Very easily, and it is the commonest condition in a long-standing Christian. Nothing has been renounced and no doctrine has been abandoned; the effort has simply stopped, gradually, in a way that required no decision. From outside it is hard to tell apart from having lost your faith, and from inside it feels like being tired. Christian love works hard.

Be fervent in spirit. “Fervent” (zeō) means to boil, to be hot. The ESV notes that this can also be read as fervent in the Spirit, that is, set on fire by the Holy Spirit. Both are true: a warm spirit comes from the Spirit. Luke uses the same word of Apollos, who was fervent in spirit and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus (Acts 18:25), and the picture is worth keeping literal: something with heat under it, moving, audible. The opposite is not coldness. Most people who need this command are not cold. They are lukewarm, which is a temperature that takes no energy to maintain, and which the risen Christ finds sickening (Revelation 3:16).

Serve the Lord. As slaves (douleuō) of the Lord Jesus. All our zeal must be directed to him, not to our own projects. Zeal without this direction can be dangerous; Paul himself had once been zealous for God in persecuting the church (Philippians 3:6). A few manuscripts read serve the time, but serve the Lord is the better reading.

Rejoice in hope. The hope of glory (5:2; 8:24–25). Joy now, because of what is coming. And the three that follow are not three separate topics but one situation handled three ways, and the situation is trouble. Rejoice in hope looks forward to how it ends.

Be patient in tribulation. “Patient” (hypomenō) is to endure, to remain under the load, and there is a great difference between remaining under something and merely waiting for it to pass. Tribulation (thlipsis: pressure, affliction) is expected, for Paul has already said that suffering produces endurance (5:3). Be patient stays under the weight of it now.

Be constant in prayer. “Constant” (proskartereō) is to persist, to devote yourself to, with the sense of stubbornly not letting go. It is the word Luke uses of the first church devoting itself to the apostles’ teaching and to the prayers (Acts 2:42; Colossians 4:2). Prayer talks to God about the trouble throughout, and it is how hope and patience are kept alive.

What it does not mean. It does not mean frantic busyness. Zeal is directed toward the Lord and sustained by prayer.

What do I do when my zeal has gone cold? Do not wait to feel fervent before you return. Go back to the means God uses to light the fire: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, and the fellowship of warm believers. Remember the mercies of verse 1; zeal is fed by grace, not by guilt. Ask whether something has crept in to cool you, an unconfessed sin, an idol, exhaustion, or a grievance, and deal with it. Ask the Spirit to set your heart alight again, as he did at the first; Christ told a cooling church to remember from where it had fallen, repent, and do the works it did at first (Revelation 2:5). And be patient: embers can be fanned into flame (2 Timothy 1:6).

What if prayer feels dead? Keep praying anyway, because constancy, not feeling, is the command. Use the Psalms, which give words to every state of soul, including the dry ones (Psalm 42; 63). Pray short, honest prayers through the day rather than waiting for a perfect hour. Pray with others, for their warmth can carry you. And remember that prayer is not measured by how it feels to you but by who hears it: your Father hears, the Son intercedes for you (8:34), and the Spirit helps you in your weakness when you do not know what to pray (8:26).

In a sentence. Never be lacking in zeal, but keep your spiritual fervour, serving the Lord. Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, faithful in prayer.

On a Tuesday. Take the trouble you are currently in and ask which of the three you have quietly dropped: rejoicing in hope, enduring under it, or praying about it. Almost nobody loses all three at once. Most people keep two running and abandon the one they find hardest, and which one that is turns out to be a fairly exact description of them. Pick it up again today, starting with five minutes of honest prayer.

For worship. Pray now, and as you do, look at the One who never once grew lukewarm. Zeal for his Father’s house consumed him (John 2:17). He rejoiced in hope, for the joy set before him enduring the cross (Hebrews 12:2). He was patient in tribulation as no one has ever been, and he was constant in prayer, rising early in the dark and spending whole nights with his Father. Now he gives his Spirit to warm our cold hearts and lives to pray for us. Praise the fervent Saviour who sets his people on fire, and ask him to fill you again with hope, with patience in what you are going through, and with prayer.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “fervent in spirit” can also be read “fervent in the Spirit.”

verseByVerse.quote: Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality. Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality. Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them.

Contribute to the needs of the saints. “Contribute” (koinōneō) is to share, to have fellowship. The saints are fellow believers, God’s holy people. Christians share their goods with Christians in need (Acts 2:44–45; Galatians 6:10). Paul himself was collecting for the poor believers in Jerusalem as he wrote (15:25–26). The movement from the inward life of vv. 11–12 to the outward life is immediate: a boiling spirit shows itself in an open purse.

And seek to show hospitality. “Seek” (diōkō) is to pursue, to chase, and Paul plainly enjoyed the word. It appears again in the very next clause for the people who persecute you: same word, one line apart. Some are hunting you; you are to be out hunting for strangers to feed. It is a small joke with a serious edge, and it settles whether hospitality is something that happens when someone turns up. It is something you go looking for. Hospitality (philoxenia) is literally love of strangers, not of friends. A meal for people you enjoy is a good thing and is not what this word means. The stranger is the test. In a world of poor and dangerous inns, opening your home to travelling believers was vital and costly (Hebrews 13:2; 3 John 5–8). Do not just wait for chances; go after them.

Bless those who persecute you. A turn toward outsiders, and Paul is not the first to say it. This is his Master’s sentence: bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you (Luke 6:28; Matthew 5:44). It is one of the clearest places in the letters where you can hear Paul repeating the Sermon on the Mount, and it should be heard that way: not an apostolic policy but a quotation. To bless (eulogeō) is to speak well of, and to ask God’s good for.

Bless and do not curse them. Paul repeats it for emphasis. Do not call down harm on enemies. Jesus prayed for his executioners (Luke 23:34); Stephen did the same as the stones fell (Acts 7:60). And there is mercy in the particular verb. Because to bless is to speak well, the command is not first about what you feel. It is about what you say, and what you say is something you can do this afternoon while feeling nothing appropriate whatsoever. Say something true and good about them to God. Decline the sentence you were going to say about them to somebody else. That command is open even to a person whose feelings have not caught up and may not for years.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring injustice or refusing to seek legal protection. It means our hearts and words toward persecutors are filled with goodwill, not revenge. And this verse has been used to keep people in harm, so the guard must be plain. Blessing a persecutor is something you do with your mouth about a person. It is not a requirement to stay within his reach, to keep supplying him with access, or to describe what was done as acceptable. Paul is about to put two escape clauses into the peace command four verses from now, and to hand justice to a magistrate with a sword a few verses after that (13:4). He is not asking anyone to be defenceless.

How does this fit with the psalms that call down curses on enemies? Those prayers hand the enemy over to God’s justice rather than taking revenge, which is exactly what Paul commands a few verses later (v. 19; see on 11:9–10). The Christian may still pray that God will stop the wicked and do right, and cry out for justice for the oppressed. What he may not do is wish evil on a person in his own name. His word to and about his persecutor is blessing, and his deepest prayer for him is that he will repent and be saved, as Saul the persecutor was.

Does hospitality need a big house or a lot of money? No. Hospitality is a matter of an open heart, not a large kitchen. A pot of soup, a cup of tea, a lift to church, a seat beside you after the service, or an invitation to join your family’s ordinary meal can all be hospitality. Many of the best hosts in the early church were poor. Start small and simple: invite the newcomer, the international student, the widow, the single person who goes home alone. The aim is not to impress, which turns hospitality into entertaining, but to welcome, as Christ has welcomed you (15:7).

In a sentence. Share with the Lord’s people who are in need. Practise hospitality. Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse.

On a Tuesday. Invite someone into your home this week, ideally someone you do not already know well. And pray by name for someone who has treated you badly: ask God for his good, and say one true and kind thing about him to someone else, or at least decline to say the unkind one.

For worship. This is the hospitality of God. We were strangers and enemies, and he did not wait for us to turn up; he came looking for us, pursued us, and set a table for us in his house. When we persecuted his Son, he answered with blessing; from the cross came the prayer Father, forgive them. Every believer is a stranger who has been welcomed and an enemy who has been blessed. Praise the God who chases sinners down with kindness and opens his home to those who had shut him out, and let his welcome become yours.
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to travelling believers was vital in a world of poor, unsafe inns.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight.

Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Sympathy: feeling with others. It is often said that weeping with the weeping is the harder half, and it costs something to enter another’s pain without rushing to offer solutions. But there is a strong case for the other order. Grief invites sympathy, and sympathy is an emotion we are practised at; there is even a quiet satisfaction in being the one who sat with someone. Another person’s good news offers nothing of the kind. It invites comparison, and it usually arrives in the exact area where you wanted news of your own: the pregnancy, the job, the child doing well. Envy gets in the way. Rejoicing with the rejoicing can be the harder half, and it is certainly the less admired one, because nobody notices you doing it. Love does both, for if one member suffers, all suffer together, and if one member is honoured, all rejoice together (1 Corinthians 12:26).

Taking your cue from someone else. Either way, notice that both commands ask you to take your emotional cue from somebody else’s life rather than your own. That is the actual instruction, and it is a strange one. Paul does not tell the Roman Christians here what to feel about their own circumstances. He tells them to be governed, for the moment, by what is happening to the person in front of them.

Live in harmony with one another. Literally, think the same thing toward one another: be of one mind, not in every opinion, but in shared purpose and care.

Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. “Haughty” is literally thinking high things. “Associate with” (synapagō) means to be carried along with, the same word used of Barnabas being carried away by others’ hypocrisy (Galatians 2:13): a word for losing your own footing and going where the current goes. Paul turns it into a virtue and points it downward. “The lowly” can mean lowly people or lowly tasks. The instruction is not to be kind to people beneath you, which leaves the arrangement intact. It is to let yourself be carried into their company and their concerns until the phrase beneath you stops meaning anything. Spend time with ordinary, poor, unimportant people. Jesus did.

Never be wise in your own sight. From Proverbs 3:7, and it is a quotation with a history in this letter. It is the phrase Paul used a chapter ago when he revealed the mystery of Israel precisely so that Gentile believers would not be wise in their own sight (11:25). There it guarded the church against contempt for outsiders. Here the same words guard it against contempt for the people in the next seat. Do not be conceited about your own opinions.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faking emotion. It means caring enough to enter into others’ lives.

What do I say to someone who is grieving? Often very little. Job’s friends did best in the first seven days, when they sat with him in silence (Job 2:13), and worst when they began to explain. Go, sit, listen, and let them talk about the one they have lost. Say you are sorry and that you love them. Do not rush to explain the loss, compare it with your own, or tell them how they should feel. Weep if you weep; Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus though he was about to raise him (John 11:35). Then keep coming back, weeks and months later, when everyone else has moved on. Practical help, a meal, a lift, a note on the anniversary, often speaks more than words.

What if I cannot feel glad about someone else’s good news? Be honest with God about it; envy confessed is already losing its grip. Then act in love before the feeling arrives: congratulate them sincerely, thank God aloud for their blessing, and pray for them. Remind yourself that their blessing was not taken from you; God is not poorer for giving to them, and his plans for you are not smaller. And look at what envy is: a quiet complaint against God’s generosity (Matthew 20:15). The more you rest in Christ as your treasure, the freer you become to be glad when others receive good things.

In a sentence. Rejoice with those who rejoice; mourn with those who mourn. Live in harmony with one another. Do not be proud, but be willing to associate with people of low position. Do not be conceited.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for someone else’s blessing today, sincerely. And sit with someone who is grieving. Then a piece of recent history: name the last time someone told you good news that you had wanted for yourself. Recall what you said, and then recall the half-second before you said it. Almost everyone can do this exercise, which is itself the finding: we remember those half-seconds because something in us knows they are the real answer. Bring that half-second to God, and ask him for a heart that is glad when others are blessed.

For worship. Our Lord Jesus came into the joys and griefs of ordinary people. He went to a wedding and made the wine flow, and he stood at a grave and wept. He did not think high things; he associated with the lowly, fishermen, tax collectors, lepers, children, and was carried along into their company until he was called the friend of sinners. He is the high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), who rejoices over us with singing and grieves with us in our sorrow. Praise the Son of God who stooped so low, and who is making his people into a family that feels with one another.

parallels.desc: be not wise in your own eyes

verseByVerse.quote: Repay no one evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repay no one evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.

Repay no one evil for evil. The instinct to pay back is strong; the Christian breaks the cycle (Matthew 5:38–39; 1 Thessalonians 5:15; 1 Peter 3:9). And notice what exactly is forbidden: repayment, evil for evil, not the pursuit of justice. That distinction is about to be made explicit when Paul describes the magistrate as God’s servant who does not bear the sword in vain (13:4). The ban is on the private settling of accounts, and it is worth keeping the two apart, because collapsing them has done real harm to people who were told that reporting a crime was unchristian.

But give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all. “Give thought” (pronoeō) is a verb of forward planning: to plan ahead, to consider in advance. Honourable means what even unbelievers recognise as good and noble (Proverbs 3:4; 2 Corinthians 8:21). Our conduct should commend the gospel. And honourable conduct in the sight of outsiders is not what happens when a Christian is at his best by accident. It is arranged beforehand, usually before the situation arrives, by someone who has decided in a calm hour what he will do in a hot one.

If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all. Look at how carefully that command is fenced, because the care is unusual and it is pastoral. Paul could have written live peaceably with all and left it there. Instead he puts two realistic qualifications in front of it. If possible: sometimes peace is impossible without betraying truth. So far as it depends on you: you cannot control others, only yourself. He is conceding, in writing, that there are relationships which cannot be at peace, and that this will sometimes not be your fault. That concession matters enormously to the sort of person who takes the whole weight of every broken relationship onto himself. Paul has already set the limit for you. Your responsibility ends where your conduct ends. It does not extend to producing an outcome that requires another person’s cooperation. Make sure that, if there is no peace, it is not your fault.

The other edge. And this cuts both ways, and the other edge is sharper. If peace fails, the question is whether it failed on the far side of everything that depended on you. Most of us know quite precisely where our own contribution stopped, and it is usually a little earlier than we tell people.

What it does not mean. It does not mean peace at any price. We do not give up the truth of the gospel to keep peace.

Does living at peace mean I must reconcile with someone who abused me? No, not in the sense of restoring closeness or trust. Forgiveness, letting go of revenge and handing the case to God, is commanded of every Christian. Reconciliation, the rebuilding of a relationship, takes two, and it requires real repentance and changed behaviour on the other side. With someone who has abused you, safety comes first, and it may be right to keep your distance permanently, to report what happened, and to involve the authorities. As far as it depends on you means you do not seek his harm and you do not stir up conflict; it never means you must put yourself or others back in harm’s way. Abuse is never to be tolerated in the name of peace.

What about conflicts in church, especially over truth? Seek peace earnestly, but never by abandoning the gospel. Paul, who wrote this verse, opposed Peter to his face when the gospel was at stake (Galatians 2:11–14). Most church conflicts, though, are not about the gospel. They are about preferences, personalities, money and hurt pride, and these call for humility, patience, speaking directly to the person rather than about him (Matthew 18:15), and a readiness to give way. Ask before any conflict: is this a matter of Scripture, or of my preference? Hold firmly to the first, and hold the second lightly.

In a sentence. Do not repay anyone evil for evil. Be careful to do what is right in the eyes of everyone. If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you are at odds with? Do your part to make peace. Apologise for your share, plainly, without adding a but. Leave the rest to God. And decide now, in a calm hour, what you will do the next time a particular person provokes you: the honourable thing, chosen in advance.

For worship. God is the God of peace, and he made peace with us at his own cost. We were the ones who broke the relationship, and he did not wait for us to mend it; he did everything that depended on him, and more, making peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). He did not repay evil for evil; he repaid our evil with the good of his Son. Praise the God of peace, who has reconciled his enemies to himself, and who makes his children peacemakers in a world at war.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord." To the contrary, "if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.” To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head.”

Beloved, never avenge yourselves. Paul chooses this moment, of all the moments in the chapter, to call them beloved. It is the only place in these thirteen verses where he stops commanding and uses a word of affection, and it lands immediately before the hardest thing he asks. People are not argued out of revenge. The tone is doing work the argument cannot. A tender address as he gives a hard command: personal revenge is forbidden.

But leave it to the wrath of God. Literally, give place to wrath: step aside and make room. The picture is of someone standing in a doorway. You are not being told there is nothing to be done about what was done to you. You are being told to move, because something else is coming through. This is not because evil does not matter, but because justice belongs to God, and he will do it perfectly. That distinction is the whole pastoral weight of the verse, and it is constantly lost. This is not let it go, and it is not a suggestion that the wrong was small enough to absorb. It says the opposite. The matter is too serious to be left in the hands of the injured party, who is the one person in the case guaranteed to judge it badly: either far too harshly, or just as often far too leniently, because he wants the whole thing to stop. It is not being dropped. It is being moved to a competent court. God also acts through the governing authorities (13:4).

For it is written, Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord. From Deuteronomy 32:35, the Song of Moses, which is the third time in three chapters Paul has reached into that song: he took the jealousy line from it at 10:19 and again in chapter 11. It is the song God gave Israel to sing about their own future, and it turns out to contain both the mercy that provokes and the vengeance that reassures. God will judge all evil, either at the cross or at the last judgment. So we can let go.

To the contrary, if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink. From Proverbs 25:21–22, and this is where most people quietly stop reading. Not merely refrain from revenge: actively do good to your enemy. And notice how concrete the instruction is: food and drink, the two things a body needs today. Paul does not ask for a change of heart toward the man before you act. He asks for a meal, which is a thing you can do while your heart is still exactly where it was.

For by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head. Heaping burning coals probably means bringing the enemy to shame and repentance through unexpected kindness: the burning pain of conscience. Some connect it with an Egyptian ritual in which a penitent carried a pan of coals on his head as a sign of remorse. Both point the same way, and Proverbs itself ends the couplet not with the enemy’s ruin but with the promise that the LORD will reward you. It does not mean kindness is a clever way to hurt your enemy more. The goal in view is not an enemy who has been outmanoeuvred by your virtue. It is an enemy who stops being one.

What it does not mean. It does not mean crime should go unpunished, or that victims may not report wrongs to the authorities. Chapter 13 gives the state the sword. What is forbidden is personal revenge. In Paul’s own mind, going to the authorities is not a failure of this verse but one of the ways God answers it. Reporting a crime is not vengeance. Leaving a dangerous house is not vengeance. This verse has been quoted at frightened people to keep them still, and that use of it is a plain abuse.

Where Christians differ: does this forbid self-defence? Some Christians, from the Anabaptists to modern pacifists, hold that a follower of Jesus must never use force, and they cite our Lord’s command to turn to him the other also (Matthew 5:39). Verdict: Vengeance comes after the harm, to pay it back; defence comes during it, to stop it. The law allowed a householder to strike a thief breaking in at night (Exodus 22:2), and Scripture commands us to rescue those who are being taken away to death (Proverbs 24:11). In Matthew 5 Jesus speaks of an insult, a slap on the cheek, not an attack on life. So Christians may use proportionate force to protect themselves and especially others, and the state may wield the sword. What they may not do is retaliate. Christians who hold the pacifist view are to be respected as brothers who are trying to follow Christ’s word.

Must I forgive someone who has not said sorry? In your heart, yes; in the full sense of restored relationship, that waits on his repentance. Even before he repents you must lay down revenge, hand the case to God, refuse bitterness, and wish him good, as Jesus prayed for those who were crucifying him (Luke 23:34). That is what this verse commands. But full reconciliation, where the wrong is named, confessed and the relationship restored, needs his repentance too (Luke 17:3). So you can be ready to forgive, and free from hatred, while still waiting, and while still keeping wise boundaries or pursuing justice through proper channels. Forgiving is not pretending it did not happen.

In a sentence. Do not take revenge, dear friends, but leave room for God’s wrath, for it is written, “It is mine to avenge; I will repay,” says the Lord. On the contrary: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink. In doing this, you will heap burning coals on his head.”

On a Tuesday. Name the person you most want to see paid back. Then, in prayer, step out of the doorway: tell God what was done, plainly, and hand him the case. If a crime was committed, it may be right to report it; that is not revenge. And then do one concrete good for that person or, if contact is not safe, pray for his repentance. Expect your feelings to lag behind. Do it anyway.

For worship. Hand your desire for revenge to God. He is just, and he will repay, and that is a comfort, not a threat, to everyone who has been wronged. But see what he has done with his own vengeance toward us. We were his enemies, hungry and thirsty and without excuse, and he fed us with the bread of life and gave us living water to drink. The burning coals of his kindness have been heaped on our heads until we were ashamed and turned to him. Where his justice had to fall on our sin, it fell on his Son. Praise the God who keeps vengeance in his own hands, and who has used his hands to save his enemies.
verseByVerse.note: Heaping burning coals probably means bringing the enemy to shame and a change of heart through kindness.
