verseByVerse.quote: Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

Do not be overcome by evil. “Overcome” is nikaō, conquer, win the victory, and it is used twice in one line. The first half of the verse is passive, and everything turns on that. The danger named first is not that you will do something wrong; it is that something will be done to you and will not stop when the doing stopped. Evil is described here as an opponent that can win a match inside a person long after the original injury is over. If evil makes you bitter and vengeful, it has won. Being wronged is not defeat; becoming like the wrongdoer is.

A familiar condition renamed. This is the most useful thing in the verse, because it renames something we all recognise. The man who was genuinely wronged, who was right about it, and who is now permanently harder than he used to be, sharper with his family, quicker to assume the worst, unable to speak about a whole category of people without an edge, has not been defeated by an argument. He has been overcome, in exactly Paul’s sense. The thing that was done to him has gone on to do a second thing.

But overcome evil with good. Goodness is the weapon that defeats evil. Paul is not describing a retreat into niceness. He is describing a battle with a weapon the other side cannot match, because good is the one move to which evil has no reply. Return evil and you have agreed to fight on ground the enemy chose and has held since Eden. This is how Christ conquered: by suffering, forgiving, and doing good to his enemies. God did not overcome the world’s evil with mere force but with sacrificial love, for while we were still sinners, while we were enemies, Christ died for us (5:8, 10). The cross is the supreme example.

What it does not mean. It does not mean being passive or naive. It is active, strategic goodness.

What if the evil keeps going and good seems to change nothing? Then keep doing good, and remember that the outcome belongs to God. Overcoming evil with good does not always change the other person; sometimes it only keeps evil from changing you, and that is already a victory. The cross looked like defeat on Friday. Joseph waited years before he saw what God had done with his brothers’ evil. Do not grow weary of doing good, for in due season you will reap, if you do not give up (Galatians 6:9). Where the evil is ongoing harm, doing good may mean protecting the vulnerable, telling the truth and calling in the authorities. Good is not the same as giving in.

In a sentence. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

On a Tuesday. When someone does you wrong today, ask: what good can I do in return? That is how you win. And here is the closing test of the chapter, the honest one. Take the worst thing that has been done to you and ask, not whether you have forgiven it, since that question is too large for an afternoon, but this: name one way you are different now because of it. Then ask whether that difference is a wound you are carrying or a victory the thing has won. The two feel the same from inside, and they are not the same at all. Bring the answer to Christ, who heals wounds and breaks the hold of what has overcome us.

For worship. The chapter that opened by asking for a body on an altar closes by asking for a body that does not hit back. Both are the same request, and both are made by the mercies of God, which is to say by someone who has already been on the receiving end of exactly this treatment from God himself. We did evil to him, and he did good to us. We nailed his Son to a cross, and the Son prayed for us and died for us and rose to give us life. Evil threw everything it had at Christ and was overcome, not by a greater violence but by a greater love. Praise the conquering Lamb, who overcame evil with good, and whose enemies, by his grace, stopped being his enemies.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship.<sup>2</sup>Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.<sup>3</sup>For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned.<sup>4</sup>For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function,<sup>5</sup>so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.<sup>6</sup>Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;<sup>7</sup>if service, in our serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching;<sup>8</sup>the one who exhorts, in his exhortation; the one who contributes, in generosity; the one who leads, with zeal; the one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness.<sup>9</sup>Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good.<sup>10</sup>Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor.<sup>11</sup>Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord.<sup>12</sup>Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.<sup>13</sup>Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality.<sup>14</sup>Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them.<sup>15</sup>Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep.<sup>16</sup>Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight.<sup>17</sup>Repay no one evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all.<sup>18</sup>If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.<sup>19</sup>Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.”<sup>20</sup>To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head.”<sup>21</sup>Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

13.title: Citizens of Two Kingdoms
13.overview:
Romans 13 addresses two dimensions of the Christian's life in the world that might seem unrelated but are theologically connected: the relationship to governing authorities (vv. 1–7) and the debt of love that fulfils the whole law (vv. 8–14). Both passages apply the gospel-transformed mind of 12:2 to concrete social realities. The Christian is not a free agent owing nothing to anyone; she is embedded in a created order (civil government) and a moral order (the law of love) that place real obligations on her life.

The passage on governing authorities is one of the most important and most abused in the New Testament — used to justify passive submission to every form of political power, and also to justify every form of political resistance. Paul's point is neither absolutist submission nor automatic resistance; it is the theological grounding of civil authority in God's own ordering of human society, combined with the practical obligation to honour, obey, and pay taxes to those who wield legitimate authority.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Governing Authorities: God's Servant for Good
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God" (v. 1). The theological foundation is clear: civil government is not a human invention that God tolerates; it is an ordering of human society that God has established for the good of human beings. The magistrate, the soldier, the tax official — in their legitimate exercise of authority, they are God's servants (diakonos — the same word used for church deacons) for the maintenance of order, the punishment of evil, and the commendation of good.

The context matters: Paul is writing to Rome under the early Nero, before the persecutions of the 60s. The Roman state, for all its paganism, provided the remarkable infrastructure of law, roads, and relative peace (the Pax Romana) that enabled the gospel to spread across the empire. Paul is not asking the Roman Christians to endorse every policy of the emperor; he is asking them not to be revolutionaries — not to treat their citizenship in the kingdom of God as a license to ignore or undermine the civil order that God has established.

The limits of this submission are implied by the rest of Scripture (Acts 5:29 — "We must obey God rather than men") and by Paul's own record of civil disobedience. When the governing authority commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, the Christian must obey God. But the default posture is submission, because the default function of civil government — even imperfect civil government — is the ordering of human life in a fallen world for the common good.

Three things in the passage should not be passed over. The first is v. 2, which supplies the sanction: whoever resists the authority resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment. Paul is not merely recommending civic good manners. He is saying that the ordering itself has God behind it, so that contempt for it is not a neutral act.

The second is the second half of v. 4, and it is the hinge on which the previous chapter turns. The magistrate does not bear the sword in vain; he is an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer. A few verses earlier Paul forbade the Christian to avenge himself and told him to give place to the wrath (12:19). He now names the office through which some of that wrath is administered in the present. Vengeance was not abolished when it was taken out of your hands. It was relocated.

The third is v. 5, which gives the motive: submission is owed not only to avoid God’s wrath but also for the sake of conscience. That distinguishes the Christian citizen from the merely prudent one. Fear of penalty produces compliance wherever penalties are likely; conscience produces the same behaviour where no one is watching and nothing would follow.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Kingdoms and Civil Authority

The Reformation developed the doctrine of the two kingdoms — the kingdom of God's left hand (civil government) and the kingdom of his right hand (the church) — as the theological framework for understanding passages like Romans 13. God governs the civil sphere through natural law and common grace, using even unbelieving rulers to maintain order and restrain evil. God governs the church through Word and Spirit. The two kingdoms are distinct but not separate; the Christian citizen participates in both, with different modes of loyalty appropriate to each. Luther and Calvin both insisted on the legitimacy and dignity of civil authority while limiting its scope: Caesar has his domain; Christ has his; and the two must never be confused.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman Christians were tempted, for obvious reasons, to view the imperial state with suspicion or hostility — an institution that had crucified their Lord and would eventually persecute them. Paul's command to submit was not politically naive; it was theologically grounded. God uses even imperfect and eventually hostile governments to structure human life. The Christian who refuses all civil order in the name of heavenly citizenship has not understood the two-kingdom distinction. Now: In democracies, Romans 13 applies to the obligation of citizens to participate in civil society — paying taxes, respecting legitimate authority, working through legal channels to promote justice. It does not require silent compliance with injustice; the Christian who uses the legitimate tools of civil society to oppose evil is not violating v. 1 but fulfilling v. 4's vision of government as a servant of good.

verseByVerse.quote: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.

Meaning first. Romans 13 carries on the theme of how believers live in the world. Chapter 12 forbade personal revenge and told the wronged Christian to leave it to the wrath of God; chapter 13 shows one way God carries out that wrath in this age: through the governing authorities. First, Christians submit to the government, because God appointed it to reward good and punish evil, and so they pay taxes and give honour where it is due (vv. 1–7). Second, the only debt Christians should always carry is love, for love fulfils the law (vv. 8–10). Third, the hour is late and the day of Christ’s return is near, so believers wake up, throw off the deeds of darkness, and put on the Lord Jesus Christ (vv. 11–14). The Christian is a good citizen, a loving neighbour, and a person dressed for the coming day. And the chapter that begins with Caesar on his throne ends with Christ as the believer’s clothing: every throne in it is under God, and the last word belongs to the King who is coming.

The setting. Paul wrote under the emperor Nero, in the early, better years of his reign, before his persecution of Christians in AD 64. A few years earlier Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome after disturbances (Acts 18:2), and some of the Christians who received this letter had been among the exiles. There was unrest over taxes in the capital around this time. A small congregation that confessed Jesus, not Caesar, as Lord could easily be seen as a nest of rebels. Paul makes clear that the gospel does not make Christians revolutionaries, and he does it without flattering Rome for a moment: his whole argument rests on God, not on the emperor.

Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. “Every person” is literally every soul: no exceptions, apostles included, and Paul includes himself. And before anything else, notice the verb. Be subject is not the ordinary word for obey. Paul had hypakouō available and uses it elsewhere of children and slaves; here he writes hypotassō, a word about rank and arrangement, to place yourself under an ordering. The difference is not a technicality. A person can be genuinely subject to an arrangement and still decline a particular command inside it, which is precisely what the Christian martyrs did when they refused to offer incense to the emperor and then declined to run away. They did not resist the arrest, the court or the sentence. They simply would not sin. The governing authorities (exousiai hyperechousai, the authorities that are over you) are the rulers of the state, from the emperor down to the local magistrate and, today, the council officer and the traffic warden.

For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. Here is the root of the whole passage. “Instituted” (tassō, appointed, set in order) is the same root as the verb for be subject: God orders the ranks, and the Christian takes his place in the order God has made. Government is God’s idea before it is anyone’s policy. Human authority is borrowed authority. Jesus told Pilate, who boasted of his power to release or crucify, that he would have no authority over him at all unless it had been given him from above (John 19:11). Nebuchadnezzar had to eat grass for seven years to learn that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will (Daniel 4:17, 32), and the king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD (Proverbs 21:1). So Paul’s command is not naive about Rome. It is principled about God. The state’s proper work, order, justice and protection, serves God’s purposes even when the state itself does not acknowledge him. That is common grace: the kindness by which God restrains evil and makes ordinary life possible for believer and unbeliever alike.

Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed. “Resists” (antitassō) is a military word: to range yourself in battle order against something. It is the opposite of the ordering in verse 1. Paul is not describing a citizen who thinks the government is wrong, or who campaigns, petitions, votes against it, or refuses one specific unjust demand. He is describing settled hostility to the existence of ordered authority itself, on the grounds that a person who now belongs to another kingdom has been released from this one. That was a live temptation in Rome, and it is a live temptation still, in two opposite political costumes, one of the right and one of the left. The reasoning is identical either way: my citizenship is in heaven, so these arrangements have no claim on me. Paul’s answer is that they have a claim on you because they have an Author, and that the alternative to imperfect order is not freedom but the strong doing as they please with the weak.

And those who resist will incur judgment. Judgement (krima) here comes in two ways: from God, whose order has been opposed, and through the state’s own punishment, which is one of the means God uses. Rebellion against lawful authority is not a private political opinion. It is a quarrel with the One who appointed it.

What it does not mean. It is worth saying plainly what this passage does not say, because it has been made to say all of it. It does not say every ruler is good, or that every action of a government is approved by God. It does not say every command must be carried out, or that rulers are above God’s law. It does not say a government may not be criticised, voted out, or taken to court, or that Christians may not vote, speak out, protest lawfully, or work to change laws. And it does not say that whatever a state does is thereby God’s will. Paul grounds the whole argument in the next two verses on what government is for, and an argument from function does not cover a government that has turned its function upside down.

Scripture refuses the absolutist reading. And it does so repeatedly. The Hebrew midwives disobeyed a direct royal order to kill baby boys, and the text says God dealt well with them (Exodus 1:17–20). Three young men declined to bow to a state-erected image and said so to the king’s face (Daniel 3:18). Daniel went on praying with his windows open toward Jerusalem against an explicit statute (Daniel 6:10). The apostles told the supreme council of their own nation, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). None of these is treated as a lapse. Several are held up as the very point of the story. And the canon puts the matter beyond doubt by describing the same empire twice. In Romans 13 Rome is God’s servant for good. In Revelation 13 the same imperial power is a beast rising out of the sea, making war on the saints (Revelation 13:7). Both are Scripture, and neither cancels the other. A state is an ordinance of God and can become a monster, and the Christian is required to know which one he is looking at.

Where Christians differ: obedience and resistance. Some say Christians must obey the state in everything. Others say Christians may overthrow any unjust government. Verdict: Christians must submit to the governing authorities in all lawful things, even when rulers are unbelievers or unjust (1 Peter 2:13–18). But no human authority can command what God forbids or forbid what God commands, and then we must obey God rather than men (Acts 4:19; 5:29; Daniel 3; 6). Such disobedience should be open, peaceful, and willing to accept the consequences, as the apostles accepted their beating and went away rejoicing (Acts 5:40–41). Reformed tradition has also taught that when rulers become tyrants who destroy the very purpose for which God gave them authority, lesser lawful magistrates may lead lawful resistance. Calvin allowed that lower magistrates, such as estates and parliaments, have a duty to restrain a king who savagely oppresses his people (Institutes 4.20.31), and later Reformed writers such as Samuel Rutherford built on that to justify resistance led by lawful authorities. Private Christians are not to take up arms against their government on their own authority. But where lawful authorities resist a ruler who has turned against the good he exists to serve (v. 4), they are not resisting God’s ordinance but upholding it. Such cases are rare and grave, a last resort, and never a private person’s revenge (Westminster 23.4). Paul wrote these words under Nero, and his point here is the normal duty: submission.

Even wicked rulers? A reader naturally asks: was Nero instituted by God? Was a tyrant? Paul is speaking of two things at once. First, the office: government as such is God’s ordinance, his gift to restrain evil in a fallen world; anarchy is never his will. Second, God’s providence: no ruler comes to power apart from God’s sovereign rule, which sets up kings and removes them (Daniel 2:21; 4:17). Sometimes he gives a nation a wicked ruler as a judgement, as he used Assyria and Babylon (Isaiah 10:5; Jeremiah 27:6). That a ruler holds power by God’s providence does not mean God approves of what he does with it, any more than God approved of Pilate condemning Jesus (John 19:11). The ruler is accountable to God for every abuse, and will answer for it.

A guard that must be said aloud. This passage has been used by slaveholders against abolitionists, by governments against the people they were crushing, and, closer to home and more often, by individuals telling someone under their power that resistance is a sin. That is a misuse, and the text itself supplies the refutation. Verse 4 defines authority by its service to your good, and the ordering Paul tells you to submit to is one whose own laws forbid what is being done to you. A husband, a pastor or an employer who abuses is not the governing authority of Romans 13; he is the wrongdoer of Romans 13. Reporting a crime is not resisting the ordinance of God. It is using it.

How do I know whether a law actually requires me to sin? Ask whether it commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands, not merely whether it is foolish, costly or unfair. Being made to pay a tax you think wasteful does not require sin. Being ordered to sign a false statement, to stop telling people about Christ, to deny him, to take part in harming the innocent, or to abandon the gathering of God’s people altogether would. Most cases are easy; the hard ones are rarer than our rhetoric suggests. When you are unsure, search the Scriptures, talk to your elders, and pray before you act. And if you must refuse, refuse respectfully and openly, without contempt, and be ready to bear the cost as Daniel was.

Does this still apply in a democracy, where the people choose the government? Yes, and in some ways it is easier to keep. In a democracy the governing authority is the whole lawful order: the constitution, the courts, the parliament and the officials it appoints. When you vote, write to your representative, campaign or take a case to court, you are not resisting that order; you are using the means it gives you. What Paul forbids is the attitude that treats the order itself as having no claim on you, whether that shows itself in quiet law-breaking, in contempt for those elected, or in refusing to accept a lawful result because your side lost.

In a sentence. Let everyone submit to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except what God has established; the authorities that exist have been established by God. So whoever rebels against the authority is rebelling against what God has instituted, and those who do so will bring judgement on themselves.

On a Tuesday. Obey the speed limit, file your taxes honestly, and speak respectfully of your leaders; your citizenship is part of your worship. Then try a sorting exercise, because most of our complaints fail it in one direction or the other. Take the thing you are angriest at your government about and ask which of three it is: something you dislike, something that is unjust, or something that requires you personally to sin. The first is politics, and Paul says nothing about it here. The second calls for every lawful means you have. Only the third is the martyr’s question, and it is rarer than we think. That is worth knowing, because a Christian who treats the first as though it were the third has spent the credibility he will need if the third ever arrives.

For worship. Every throne in Rome stood by permission. Nero did not know it, and neither did the senate, but the God of Israel had set every one of them in its place, and would remove each one in his time. That same God has now given all authority in heaven and on earth to his Son (Matthew 28:18). The Lord who told Pilate that his power came from above did not use his own power to escape Pilate. He submitted to an unjust court, a corrupt governor and a Roman cross, so that rebels against the throne of heaven could be pardoned. Now he reigns, King of kings and Lord of lords (Revelation 19:16), and the government is upon his shoulder (Isaiah 9:6). Every president, prime minister and magistrate holds office under him and will give account to him. So the Christian can be the calmest citizen in the land: not because the rulers are good, but because the King is.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote under the emperor Nero, in the early, better years of his rule. Jesus had said, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.”

verseByVerse.quote: For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval, for he is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval, for he is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer.

For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Paul now says what government is for: to restrain evil and protect good. He describes what rulers are meant to be, and what they generally are even when they are imperfect, since even a bad government usually punishes theft and murder. And notice that he argues from function throughout. Rulers are a terror to bad conduct: that is a description of what authority is for, and the whole case rests on it. When a ruler becomes a terror to good conduct, he is not exercising the thing being described here; he is doing the opposite of it, and Paul’s argument, which runs entirely on function, cannot be stretched to bless him. The passage grounds authority. It does not immunise it.

Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval. The way to live without fear of the police is to do right. And the small word approval deserves its moment, because it is the half nobody quotes. “Approval” (epainos) is praise. The state is not described here only as a punisher. It is also expected to commend what is good: the magistrate as an institution that notices decency and honours it, the award for bravery, the citizen thanked for handing in what he found. Any account of government drawn from this passage that produces only fear has read one of its two halves.

For he is God’s servant for your good. “Servant” is diakonos, minister, the same word used of deacons in the church and of Paul himself (1 Corinthians 3:5). The ruler is God’s minister whether he knows it or not, as the pagan Cyrus was called the LORD’s anointed and used to send Israel home (Isaiah 45:1). The state, even in its pagan form, is conscripted into God’s service. And its work is for your good: peace, order and justice, the safe street and the honest market, the conditions in which families can be raised and the gospel can be preached (1 Timothy 2:1–2).

But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. The sword stood for the government’s power to punish, including the power of death (Genesis 9:6; Acts 25:11). In vain means for no purpose: God gave it real authority to use force, and it is not decoration. And the author’s own circumstances make the point sharper than any argument could. Paul wrote this sentence about the government that, by the church’s consistent tradition, later executed him with that very sword, on no just charge, under the same emperor. He knew what Rome was. He wrote it anyway, which tells you the sentence was never a compliment paid to Rome. It was a claim about God.

For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer. Now the thing this passage exists to do, and it repays a debt from a few verses ago. In 12:19 Paul told the wronged Christian never to avenge himself but to leave it to the wrath of God. Here he calls the magistrate an avenger (ekdikos) who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer. In Greek it is the same word family, and the same wrath. The avenging Paul forbids you in 12:19 is the avenging he assigns to the officer in 13:4. So the state may do what the individual may not.

Where the wrath went. That resolves the thing that makes 12:19 so hard to swallow. Wrath was never cancelled when it was taken out of your hands, and you were never being asked to pretend the wrong did not happen. You were being asked to stop being the one who settles it, and here, immediately, Paul tells you where some of it has gone. The wrath you were told to leave the matter to has an address, a payroll and an office in your own city. That is why the two verses have to be read together, and why reading either alone does damage. On its own, 12:19 sounds like the abolition of justice. On its own, 13:4 sounds like the sanctifying of state force. Together they say something precise: justice is real, it matters enormously, and you personally are not the one authorised to administer it.

If I have forgiven someone, should I still go to the police? Yes, if a crime has been committed. Going to the police is not a failure of Romans 12 and not a lapse in forgiveness. Paul has just called that officer God’s servant. Forgiveness means you give up your own right to repay, hate or punish; it does not mean you shield the wrongdoer from the authority God has appointed, still less that you leave others in danger. This is especially true where there has been abuse of a child or of a spouse: the church must never hide it, and the victim must never be told that silence is the Christian thing. You are not taking the matter into your own hands; you are handing it to the hands appointed for it.

Where Christians differ: capital punishment. Some Christians believe the death penalty is always wrong, reading the sword more generally as the state’s power to punish, and pointing out that courts make mistakes and that Christ calls us to mercy. Verdict: Scripture gives the state the right to use the sword, including the death penalty for the gravest crimes such as murder (Genesis 9:6; Acts 25:11). Behind it stands God’s word to Noah, given before Moses and to the whole human race: whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. The penalty rests on the dignity of the human made in God’s image, not on contempt for it. Christians may disagree on whether, in a given country with its legal system, the death penalty should be used, given the risk of error and injustice; Scripture permits it rather than requiring it in every case, and it requires that it be done justly. But it is not wrong in principle. This is not personal revenge, which is forbidden; it is God’s justice carried out by lawful authority.

May a Christian serve as a soldier or police officer? Yes. If the ruler is God’s servant in bearing the sword, a believer may serve in that office. When soldiers asked John the Baptist what to do, he did not tell them to leave the army but to stop extorting and be content with their wages (Luke 3:14), and Jesus praised the faith of a centurion above anything he had found in Israel (Matthew 8:10). Christian pacifists cite the saying that all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52), but that was a rebuke to Peter for using it to resist God’s plan, not a ruling on lawful office. The same principle underlies the long Christian teaching on just war: force may be used by lawful authority, for a just cause, as a last resort. A Christian in uniform must still refuse an unjust order, and serve with the restraint of a man who knows whose servant he is.

What if the police or the courts themselves are corrupt? Then they are failing at the very thing Paul says they exist for, and Christians may say so and work to put it right by lawful means: complaint, appeal, the press, the ballot, the higher court. Corruption in an office does not abolish the office; it calls for its reform. Meanwhile, keep doing good, keep your own hands clean, and remember that every corrupt judge has a Judge. The psalmist pictures God standing in the assembly of the rulers and holding judgement among them (Psalm 82:1). No injustice done under colour of law escapes him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the state may use the sword to compel faith or to punish true worship. Its sphere is civil justice, not the conscience before God. The magistrate may punish the thief; he has no authority to tell the church what to believe or whom to worship, and the long history of Christians persecuting Christians in the name of this verse is a history of the sword used in vain.

In a sentence. For rulers hold no terror for those who do right, but for those who do wrong. Do you want to be free from fear of the one in authority? Then do what is right and you will be commended. For the one in authority is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for rulers do not bear the sword for no reason. They are God’s servants, agents of wrath to bring punishment on the wrongdoer.

On a Tuesday. The next time you pass a police car, a court building or a town hall, read it as Paul would: God’s servant for my good, under God, answerable to God. Thank him for the order you enjoy without thinking about it, the locked door that stays locked and the contract that is honoured. Pray by name for someone who serves in law and justice. And if you are carrying a wrong done to you, ask whether it belongs with the authorities rather than in your own heart, where it has been quietly demanding its sentence.

For worship. There was one day when the servant of God bore the sword against the only innocent man who ever stood in his court. Pilate found no fault in him and sentenced him anyway. And yet under that injustice God was carrying out a justice deeper than Rome could see. The wrath of God against sin, which the magistrate carries out only in part and only imperfectly, fell in full on his own Son, so that it would never fall on those who trust him (3:25–26; 8:1). The cross is where the sword of earthly justice and the wrath of heaven met in one body, and both were turned into mercy. God is just, and he is the justifier. Every court on earth is a small and broken sign of a Judge who will one day judge in perfect righteousness, and who has already borne the judgement himself for his people.
verseByVerse.note: The sword stood for the government’s power to punish, including capital punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience. — Romans 13:5
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God’s wrath but also for the sake of conscience.

Therefore one must be in subjection. “Must” (anankē) is necessity: it is required, not optional. And Paul gives two reasons, ranked in order of depth.

Not only to avoid God’s wrath. Wrath here is the punishment the state carries out on God’s behalf, described in verse 4. Fear of consequence is a real motive, and Paul does not sneer at it; he lists it first. A sensible person does not want a fine, a criminal record or a prison cell. But it produces a citizen who is dependable in proportion to the likelihood of being caught, which is not so much a citizen as a calculation.

But also for the sake of conscience. A higher reason. The word is syneidēsis, the co-knowing faculty Paul described back at 2:14–15 as an inner courtroom where thoughts accuse and sometimes excuse. It is the same faculty, now applied to the traffic of ordinary civic life, and the conscience of a Christian knows that government is God’s ordinance. So believers obey the law even when no one is watching and they could get away with breaking it. Obedience comes from the inside, not only from fear. A Christian is not law-abiding for the reason most people are.

The empty junction. The difference shows up wherever the penalty disappears. An empty road at three in the morning, a red light, no cameras and no other car within a mile. Nothing whatever will happen if you go. Almost everybody knows exactly what they do at that junction, and it is one of the few completely honest facts a person has about himself, because there is nobody to perform for. Conscience produces the same conduct at the empty junction as at the busy one. That is the whole distinction in verse 5.

The same conscience sets the limit. This verse and Acts 5:29 are not in tension; they are the same principle. A conscience that can be overruled by a statute is not a conscience; it is a licence. The reason Peter could refuse the council is the same reason Paul can tell you to pay your taxes without being watched: in both cases the man is answering to Somebody who is not in the room. Conscience, informed by Scripture, is not the servant of the state but of God, and that is exactly why it makes both the best citizen and the one citizen who cannot be bought or bullied into sin.

What it does not mean. It does not mean conscience must obey a law that requires sin. Conscience bound to God may need to disobey such a law (Acts 5:29). Nor does it mean that every law is wise or just, or that the conscience must rubber-stamp every government action. The same conscience that recognises the legitimacy of civil authority also recognises its limits.

Is it really a sin to break a small law, like going a little over the speed limit? In principle, yes, because Paul ties obedience to conscience, not to the size of the penalty. The question is not whether anyone will mind but whether God has placed you under this order, and he has. That does not mean you should live in anxious scrupulosity over every unclear regulation, or treat a genuine accident as a crime. It means you do not make a private exception for laws you find inconvenient. If you have been careless here, confess it simply, receive his forgiveness, and start keeping the rule cheerfully, as a small daily act of worship.

What if my conscience objects to something other Christians think is fine? Do not act against your conscience, but do bring it to Scripture. Conscience is not infallible; it can be too tight or too loose, and it needs to be taught by God’s Word. Where a matter is a genuine question of sin, obey God. Where it is a matter of personal scruple, follow your conscience without condemning brothers who see it differently, which is exactly the subject Paul turns to in the next chapter (14:5, 22–23). Talk it through with a wise older Christian or an elder.

In a sentence. Therefore it is necessary to submit to the authorities, not only because of possible punishment but also as a matter of conscience.

On a Tuesday. Find your empty junction: the place where you keep a rule only because someone might see. The expense claim, the parking, the hours on the timesheet, the small print on the insurance form. Keep it there today, unwatched, for the Lord’s sake. A good conscience before God is worth more than anything you could get away with.

For worship. There is a Witness at every empty junction. He sees the three in the morning as clearly as the noon, and darkness is not dark to him (Psalm 139:12). That is a terror to the man who lives for appearances, and an immense rest to the Christian, because the One who sees everything is not a spy collecting evidence but a Father who has already forgiven everything in his Son. The blood of Christ purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). So the believer’s quiet obedience on an empty road is not fear of being caught. It is a cleansed conscience, glad to please the God who loved him first, in a place where no one else will ever know.

verseByVerse.quote: For because of this you also pay taxes, for the authorities are ministers of God, attending to this very thing. Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed. — Romans 13:6–7
verseByVerse.commentary:
For because of this you also pay taxes, for the authorities are ministers of God, attending to this very thing. Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed.

For because of this you also pay taxes. Because government is God’s servant, it has a right to be funded. Jesus had already said it, when his enemies tried to trap him with a coin: render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s (Mark 12:17; Matthew 22:21). Paul applies the principle. Civil life requires contribution, and the Christian is not exempt from the obligations of the community he lives in.

For the authorities are ministers of God. Verse 6 uses a word for the authorities that ought to stop the reader. In verse 4 they were diakonoi, servants. Here they are leitourgoi, the term for those who perform a public religious duty, the word behind our liturgy, used in the Greek Old Testament of priests serving at the altar. Paul later uses it of himself, ministering the gospel like a priest (15:16). He has just described the tax office as a kind of liturgical order. The clerk processing a tax return is doing, without knowing it, a species of the thing a priest does: a service rendered to God.

Attending to this very thing. The verb (proskartereō, to devote yourself to, to persist at) is one Paul used a chapter earlier in 12:12, where the Christian is to be constant in prayer. The official at his desk persists at his post with the same word used of the believer at his prayers. Governing is full-time work. It is an extraordinarily high view of an extraordinarily dull job, and it ought to change how we think of the civil servant, the tax inspector and the planning officer.

The setting of the command. None of this was written in comfortable circumstances. The Roman historian Tacitus records serious public complaint over indirect taxes in AD 58, with Nero considering abolishing them outright, and Romans was written within a year or so of it. Paul is not offering a general principle in a calm season. He is telling a small, suspect congregation in the capital to keep paying, on time, into a treasury that funded the games, the temples of the gods, and eventually the machinery that would kill them.

Pay to all what is owed to them. “Pay” (apodidōmi) means to give back, to render what is due. It is not a gift but a debt. But notice the limit sitting inside the command. Pay what is owed: which concedes that not everything demanded is owed. The saying of Jesus behind it has the same shape and is usually quoted only halfway. Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s is not the whole sentence; the second clause, and to God the things that are God’s, is a boundary drawn round the first. Caesar may have the coin with his image on it. He may not have the man made in the image of God.

Taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed. “Taxes” (phoros) were direct taxes, on land and persons, the tribute paid by subject peoples; “revenue” (telos) meant customs, tolls and duties on goods. Pay both honestly, the visible and the hidden, the income tax and the duty at the border.

Respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed. “Respect” is phobos, literally fear, reverence; “honour” is timē, esteem, the regard due to a person’s position. The fourfold list is worth reading slowly for what it costs. Taxes and revenue are money, and money is the easy half: it leaves the account and the matter ends. Respect and honour are harder, because they are owed to a person, sometimes to a person you did not vote for and do not admire. Peter, writing under the same emperor, said it in four words: honour the emperor (1 Peter 2:17). Paul does not say honour the ones who deserve it. He says pay what is owed to the office.

What it does not mean. It does not mean tax money is always spent well, or that we cannot argue for lower or fairer taxes. It means we pay what the law requires. And honouring a ruler does not mean pretending he is good, or keeping silent about real wrongs; John the Baptist rebuked Herod, and the prophets confronted kings to their faces.

Must I pay taxes that fund things I believe are wrong? Yes. Jesus and Paul both told believers to pay taxes to Rome, knowing that Rome funded idol temples, gladiatorial games and the persecution of the church. When you pay what is owed, the responsibility for how it is spent rests on those who spend it, not on you. You remain free, and often obliged, to speak, vote and campaign against what is wrong. But withholding a lawful tax is not one of the means Scripture gives you.

Is it wrong to reduce my tax bill? Not if you do it honestly. Using the allowances and reliefs the law itself provides is not cheating; the lawmaker meant them to be used. What is wrong is evasion: hiding income, inventing expenses, taking cash to keep it off the books, or bending the truth on a form because no one will check. A useful test is whether you could explain what you did, plainly, to the tax inspector and to your Lord. If you would rather not, you probably already know the answer.

How can I honour a leader I believe is doing real harm? Honour the office and treat the person with basic dignity, while telling the truth about his actions. You may disagree firmly, criticise policies, and vote him out. What you may not do is mock, sneer, invent, or speak of him with contempt, because he bears God’s image and holds God’s appointment. Above all, pray for him by name, as Paul told Timothy to pray for kings under Nero (1 Timothy 2:1–2). It is very hard to go on despising someone you are honestly praying for.

In a sentence. This is also why you pay taxes, for the authorities are God’s servants, who give their full time to governing. Give to everyone what you owe them: if you owe taxes, pay taxes; if customs, then customs; if respect, then respect; if honour, then honour.

On a Tuesday. Be honest on your tax return, even with the small things. Then take the practical edge of this verse, which lands close to home. How do you speak about the people currently in power when you are among people who agree with you: in the car, at the meal table, in the group chat? That is where this verse is actually kept or broken, and almost nobody thinks of it as a Romans 13 question at all.

For worship. Once, collectors came to Peter asking whether his Master paid the temple tax. Jesus said that the sons of a king are free; the tax was for his Father’s house, and he was the Son. Then, so as not to give offence, he paid it anyway, with a coin from a fish’s mouth, for himself and for Peter (Matthew 17:24–27). The One to whom everything is owed paid what he did not owe. And he went on to pay the debt we could never pay, the debt of sin owed to the justice of God, in full and at the cross. So there is one to whom all honour is truly due, without reserve and without qualification. Every coin we hand to Caesar and every word of respect we give the office is a small acknowledgement that God orders the world; but the honour we give to Christ is of another kind. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honour and glory and blessing (Revelation 5:12).
verseByVerse.note: “Taxes” were direct taxes; “revenue” meant customs and tolls.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Love Fulfils the Law: Put on Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law" (v. 8). The transition from taxes and respect to love is sudden but logical: both are obligations owed to those among whom we live. But the debt of love is unique — it is a debt that is perpetually owed and perpetually paid but never fully discharged. You can pay a tax and be done with it; you can never be done with the obligation to love, because the opportunities to love are inexhaustible and the command is perpetual.

Paul's claim is audacious: love fulfils the entire law. The specific commandments — do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not covet — are all "summed up" in this word: love your neighbour as yourself (quoting Leviticus 19:18). This does not make the specific commandments irrelevant; it establishes their theological root. Love is the soil from which all the particular expressions of right conduct grow. The person who truly loves her neighbour will not steal from him, will not lie to him, will not commit adultery against him. Love is not a substitute for the law's specific demands; it is the power that fulfils them from within.

The passage closes with the urgency of eschatological time: "the night is far gone; the day is at hand" (v. 12). The Christian lives in the interim between the first coming of Christ (which inaugurated the day of salvation) and his return (which will complete it). This is not time to sleep; it is time to wake, to lay aside the works of darkness, to put on the armour of light — and supremely to "put on the Lord Jesus Christ" (v. 14). The Christian life is not moral self-improvement; it is the clothing of oneself in Christ, day by day, until the transformation is complete.

Between the dawn and the clothing stands v. 13, which supplies the specifics: let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. Three pairs, and the order of them is the sting. The list begins where anyone would expect a vice list to begin and ends somewhere entirely respectable — with arguing and envy, which are set down in the same sentence, under the same heading, as the drunken procession through the streets.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law

Romans 13:8–10 gives the summary of the second table of the law: love your neighbour as yourself. This is not a replacement of the law with an undefined sentiment; it is the identification of the animating principle from which all the law's specific demands flow. The Reformed tradition has insisted that love and law are not opposites — love is the motive; the law is the guide. The renewed person who loves God supremely and her neighbour genuinely will want to know concretely what that love requires in specific situations, and the law provides exactly that: the concrete shape of love in action.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's command to "put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh" (v. 14) was the verse that Augustine read in the garden in Milan in 386 AD, at the moment of his conversion. He had been struggling with the inability to break free from sexual sin; these words fell on him with the weight of divine command and divine grace simultaneously. The verse is still doing what it did to Augustine: convicting, commanding, and empowering. Now: The urgency of vv. 11–14 is the urgency of the gospel in every age: the window of this life is short; the return of Christ is certain; the works of darkness are not appropriate wear for people who are children of light. Every day lived in unrepentant sin is a wasted day; every day lived in Christ is a day that will outlast the sun.

verseByVerse.quote: Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. For the commandments, "You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet," and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. For the commandments, “You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet,” and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

Owe no one anything. The move from taxes to love is not the change of subject it appears to be, because Paul is still using the same word. Verse 7 said pay to all what is owed; verse 8 opens owe no one anything. Same root, consecutive sentences. He has been talking about debts all along: leave no debt unpaid, whether taxes, respect or money. And now he names the one item on the account that never clears.

Except to love each other. That is the strange and rather beautiful thing about the exception clause. Every other obligation in this passage can be discharged. You can pay the tax, settle the bill, return the borrowed tool, and the matter is closed; there is a real satisfaction in owing nobody anything. Nobody has ever reached that position with this debt. It is charged again every morning, to the same people, at the same rate. Augustine called it the debt we always pay and always owe. And the reason it never clears is that it is measured by a love that never ran out: we love because he first loved us, and if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another (1 John 4:11, 19). Every day we owe more love, because every day we have received more.

For the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. Love fulfils (plēroō, fills full, brings to completion) the law: it does what the law requires toward others. The law is like the outline of a building; love is the building itself, standing in the shape the plans described.

For the commandments. Paul lists the second table of the Ten Commandments, our duties to our neighbour: the seventh, sixth, eighth and tenth (Exodus 20:13–17; Deuteronomy 5:17–21). That is worth noticing before anyone concludes Paul has replaced religion with ethics. He is not summarising the whole law here; he is summarising the half of it that deals with the person next to you. The first table, love for God, is not in view because it is not in dispute, and Jesus called that the first and great commandment (Matthew 22:37–38).

You shall not covet. He ends the list with coveting, the one commandment nobody can see you break, the commandment that undid Paul himself back in chapter 7 (7:7–8). It sits here as the proof that this is not a code of external conduct. You can satisfy the other three by simply not doing things. You cannot satisfy that one without something happening inside. Love, like coveting, lives in the heart before it reaches the hands.

And any other commandment, are summed up in this word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” “Summed up” (anakephalaioō) means brought together under one head, the very word Paul uses in Ephesians 1:10 of God uniting all things in Christ. Every duty to your neighbour has one heading. The words come from Leviticus 19:18, hidden in a chapter of practical laws about harvests and wages and the deaf and the blind. Jesus lifted them out and called them the second great commandment, on which, with the first, hang all the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 22:39–40; Galatians 5:14).

Does “as yourself” command us to love ourselves first? No. It assumes the care for ourselves that everyone already has: no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it (Ephesians 5:29). We feed ourselves when hungry, defend our own reputation, excuse our own faults and want the best for our own future. That care becomes the measure of what we owe our neighbour. The command is not to build up self-love but to give others what we naturally give ourselves, which is the golden rule turned into a single word (Matthew 7:12).

Where Christians differ: is borrowing wrong? Some take owe no one anything to forbid all borrowing, including mortgages and loans. Verdict: Scripture does not forbid borrowing as such; it regulates it (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–8; Psalm 37:21; Matthew 5:42). Jesus told his disciples not to refuse the one who would borrow from them, which would be strange if borrowing were sin. The context here is paying what is due, and the command is to pay what you owe when it is due and not leave debts unpaid. What Scripture condemns is failing to repay: the wicked borrows but does not pay back (Psalm 37:21). It also warns that the borrower is the slave of the lender (Proverbs 22:7), so wisdom avoids unnecessary debt. A Christian may take a mortgage or a loan he can repay, should keep its terms exactly, and should be slow to borrow for what he cannot afford.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love replaces the commandments, so that we can decide for ourselves what love requires. Love is defined by the commandments; it fulfils them, it does not ignore them. Whenever someone says love permits what God’s law forbids, Paul’s list answers him: love does not commit adultery, does not take a life, does not steal, does not covet. The commandments tell love where to go, and love supplies the power to go there.

Who is my neighbour? Jesus answered that question with a story, and turned it round (Luke 10:25–37). The neighbour is not only the person who lives next door, or who is like you, or who deserves it; it is anyone whose need God puts in your path, including the stranger and the enemy. In practice it begins with the nearest: your family, the people you work with, your church, the actual house next door. Then it widens to whoever is lying wounded on your road this week.

Does loving my neighbour mean I must always say yes? No. Love seeks the other person’s real good, and sometimes that means saying no: refusing to fund an addiction, to cover up a lie, or to go on enabling sin. Love does not require you to stay in danger. A person suffering abuse is not failing to love by getting safe and seeking help; the abuser is the one breaking the law of love. What love rules out is the cold no that protects only my comfort. Ask: which answer genuinely serves this person before God?

In a sentence. Let no debt remain outstanding, except the continuing debt to love one another, for whoever loves others has fulfilled the law. The commandments against adultery, murder, theft and coveting, and whatever other command there may be, are summed up in this one command: love your neighbour as yourself.

On a Tuesday. Pay your bills on time; then turn to the debt you can never pay off. And make it uncomfortably specific. Bring to mind the person in your church you find hardest: not an enemy, just the one you would rather not sit near. The debt is owed to him this week at exactly the same rate as to the people you like, and unlike a tax it cannot be paid by anyone else on your behalf. Most of us are not refusing to pay it. We have simply arranged our lives so the invoice rarely arrives. Arrange this week so that it does: a call, a meal, a word of thanks.

For worship. There was one man who owed no one anything. He had no debts to God, no unpaid duties to his neighbour, no account in arrears. And he chose to become the greatest debtor in history: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). He took on himself the debt of sin we owed to the justice of God and paid it to the last coin. He loved his neighbour as himself, and more than himself, laying down his life for people who were his enemies (5:8–10). In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10). Every time we love a difficult brother, we are paying out of a fortune that was given to us. The debt of love never clears, because the love we draw from is without bottom.

parallels.desc: love your neighbour as yourself

verseByVerse.quote: Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.

Love does no wrong to a neighbor. The commandments listed in verse 9 are negative: do not harm. Love never harms. It does not steal a neighbour’s spouse, life, goods or reputation. And the negative form of the definition is a mercy, which is worth seeing. Positive definitions of love are hard to check. Ask whether you loved your wife enough this week and there is no clean answer, only a mood, and the answer you give will depend mostly on how tired you are. Paul’s version can be checked. Have I done this person wrong? That is a question with a yes or a no, and it can be asked about a specific Tuesday. It makes this the most usable sentence in the chapter for anyone trying to examine himself without either flattery or despair. It gives you a floor you can stand on and measure from.

A floor, not a ceiling. But a floor is what it is, and the guard matters. This verse must never be turned into: as long as I have harmed nobody, I have loved. A man can go a whole year wronging no one and loving nobody; the coldest people most of us know are perfectly innocent of this list. Paul has already set the ceiling one chapter earlier, where love blesses the persecutor and feeds the hungry enemy (12:14, 20), which is a great deal more than not wronging him. Love does far more than avoid harm; it is patient and kind, it bears and believes and hopes and endures (1 Corinthians 13:4–7). Verse 10 tells you where love starts. It does not tell you where it stops.

Therefore love is the fulfilling of the law. “Fulfilling” (plērōma) is fullness, the complete expression of a thing. Love is what the law looks like when it is lived from the heart. This is the new covenant promise come true: not the outward constraint of a code written on stone, but the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33), so that a renewed person does from within what the law demanded from without. The fulfilment of the law is not its abolition but its achievement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a feeling of love is enough. Love shows itself in keeping God’s commandments (John 14:15). Nor does it mean that we can earn God’s favour by loving well; Paul has spent eleven chapters showing that we are justified freely by grace through faith. Love is the fruit of that justification, not its root.

How can I love someone I feel no affection for? Begin with what love does, not with what it feels. Scripture commands love, and a feeling cannot be commanded, but actions can: do this person no wrong, speak well of him, pray for him by name, and do him one concrete good. Feelings very often follow obedience rather than leading it. And you are not left to manufacture this alone. God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (5:5). Ask him for it, honestly, about this particular person.

In a sentence. Love does no harm to a neighbour. Therefore love is the fulfilment of the law.

On a Tuesday. At the end of the day, ask the floor question about three specific people: my spouse or closest friend, a colleague, and someone at church. Have I wronged any of them today, in word, deed, or the private thought that I let settle? If so, put it right tomorrow morning. Then ask the ceiling question about one of them: what good could I do him this week that he would never think to ask for?

For worship. There has been one perfect fulfilment of the law of love on the earth. Christ never did his neighbour wrong: in thirty years he never took what was not his, never coveted, never spoke a word that was not both true and loving. And he did not stop at the floor. He went to the ceiling and beyond it, touching lepers, eating with sinners, washing the feet of the man who would betray him, praying for the soldiers driving the nails. He is the fulfilling of the law. What he fulfilled, he credits to everyone who believes (10:4), and what he credits, his Spirit begins to work out in them. So the love asked of us here is not a ladder to God. It is his own love, coming down, living again in his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Besides this you know the time, that the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed. The night is far gone; the day is at hand. So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. — Romans 13:11–12
verseByVerse.commentary:
Besides this you know the time, that the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed. The night is far gone; the day is at hand. So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light.

Besides this you know the time. “Time” is kairos: not clock time but the decisive season, the hour that has a character to it, the age between Christ’s first coming and his return. And Paul says you know it. His argument is not that his readers need new information. It is that they already possess it and are living as though they did not, which is the ordinary condition of most Christians most of the time.

That the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. Sleep here is spiritual drowsiness: carelessness, being at ease in the world, drifting with the culture (1 Thessalonians 5:6–7; Ephesians 5:14). And keep the picture of waking literal for a moment, because it is exact. Nothing in the room changes when a person wakes. The furniture is where it was, the light is what it was; the only difference is that someone is now present to it. Paul is not asking for new circumstances. He is asking for someone to be awake inside the ones already there.

For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed. Salvation here is its completion: the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body and final glory (8:23–24). Every day brings it closer. The Christian does not walk away from his salvation as the years pass; he walks toward it.

What “salvation is nearer” does not mean. It does not mean believers are not yet saved, or that their salvation is still in doubt. Scripture speaks of salvation in three tenses: we have been saved from sin’s penalty (justified, 5:1; Ephesians 2:8); we are being saved from sin’s power (sanctified, 6:22); and we shall be saved from sin’s presence, when Christ returns and our bodies are raised (8:23; Philippians 3:20–21). Here Paul means the third. Every day brings that final rescue a day nearer. It is as certain as the first, since those he justified he also glorified (8:30).

The night is far gone; the day is at hand. The night is this present evil age; the day is the day of the Lord, Christ’s return. The night is nearly over. “At hand” (engizō) means has drawn near. The Christian lives in the overlap of the ages: the old age of darkness and death is passing away, and the new age of light and life has already broken in with the resurrection of Christ. To live in the works of darkness is to dress for a night that is already ending.

So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Both verbs are clothing verbs, strip off and put on, like taking off night clothes in the morning, or a soldier arming for the day’s battle (Ephesians 6:11–17; 1 Thessalonians 5:8). And the second is the very verb Paul will use two verses later of putting on Christ himself. Verses 12 and 14 are one picture, not two. The word rendered armour (hopla) is simply the word for weapons or equipment, and Paul has used it in this letter before: present your members to God as instruments for righteousness (6:13). Same word. What was handed over as equipment in chapter 6 is what you get dressed in here. The Christian is not issued a costume for the daylight. He is issued kit. The works of darkness are named in the next verse.

Where Christians differ: was Paul wrong about the timing? Some say Paul expected Christ to return within his lifetime and was mistaken. Verdict: Paul taught that the day is near, meaning that it is the next great event in God’s plan and could come at any time, not that he knew the date (1 Thessalonians 5:1–2). Since Christ’s first coming, we have been in the last days (Hebrews 1:2). The time is short whether Christ returns tomorrow or in a thousand years, since with the Lord a thousand years are as a day (2 Peter 3:8). And notice that the sentence is not a calculation but a comparison, and it is true every time it is read: salvation is nearer now than when we first believed. It was true for Paul. It is truer for you than it was for him. And for each of us the day arrives at our own death if it has not arrived before, which no one has ever had grounds to think was far off. His return will be one visible, public event, not a secret rapture, followed by the resurrection of all the dead and the last judgement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should set dates, or stop working and wait. Paul told the Thessalonians who did that to get back to work (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12). It means live every day ready.

Should I be afraid of the day? Not if you are in Christ. For the unbeliever the day is judgement; for the believer it is dawn. Paul calls it salvation, the morning after a long night, the moment the Bridegroom comes for his bride. The fear that is right is the sober fear of being found asleep, which drives us to wake up; the fear that is wrong is the dread of rejection, which Christ has removed (8:1). If you are trusting him, the day that is drawing near is the best day of your life.

So what do I actually do differently because the day is near? Three things. Keep short accounts: do not leave sin unconfessed or quarrels unreconciled, as if there were all the time in the world. Spend your life on what will last: people, the gospel, faithfulness in your calling, rather than things that will burn. And hold everything else loosely: possessions, ambitions and grievances look very different in the light of morning. Nearness is not a reason for panic but for wakefulness and for joy.

In a sentence. And do this, understanding the present time: the hour has already come for you to wake up from your slumber, because our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed. The night is nearly over; the day is almost here. So let us put aside the deeds of darkness and put on the armour of light.

On a Tuesday. Live today as if Christ could return tonight. What would you stop doing? What would you start? Then look at two stretches of the day nobody plans and nobody sees: the last hour before you sleep and the first fifteen minutes after you wake. We arrange our public hours carefully. Those two are where the actual dressing happens, and most of us have never once considered them a spiritual question. Tomorrow, give the first minutes of the day to the Lord who is coming, before the phone gets them.

For worship. The night has been long. It began in a garden when the first man hid from God, and it has been dark ever since: dark with war and grief, with graves and tears. But there has been a light on the horizon since another garden, where a tomb was found empty at early dawn. The sun of righteousness has risen with healing in its wings (Malachi 4:2), and the morning he began cannot be stopped. Christ is the bright morning star (Revelation 22:16), the herald of a day that will have no night in it, when God himself will be our light (Revelation 22:5). Every sunrise is a small rehearsal. Every day is a day nearer. And the One we are waiting for is not coming to find out whether we are good enough to be saved; he is coming to finish what he has already begun.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires. — Romans 13:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.

Let us walk properly as in the daytime. “Properly” (euschēmonōs) means decently, becomingly, in a way that fits. Live in a way that is fit to be seen in daylight, with nothing to hide. That is the test in a phrase: behave now as you would if it were already light. Everyone understands it instinctively, because there is a whole category of things people do at one in the morning that the same people would not do at eleven, in the same street, in front of the same neighbours. The Christian is a person for whom it is always, in effect, eleven in the morning.

Not in orgies and drunkenness. Then three pairs of night sins, and the arrangement is the sting. First, sins of excess: “orgies” (kōmoi), the wild parties and drunken processions through the streets that were a familiar feature of Roman nights, and drunkenness.

Not in sexual immorality and sensuality. Second, sexual sins. “Sexual immorality” is koitai, literally beds: sexual sin. “Sensuality” (aselgeia) is unrestrained lust, shamelessness, the point at which a person no longer even bothers to hide.

Not in quarreling and jealousy. Third, sins of relationship: strife and envy. The list begins exactly where a first century reader would expect a vice list to begin, and then, without any change of tone, ends with arguing and envy. Sit with that for a moment, because it is aimed at the respectable. The man who has never been drunk in his life, whose sexual conduct is beyond reproach, and who cannot let a disagreement go, who keeps score, who needs to be right, who has a running commentary about someone in the church, is named in this verse, in the same breath and under the same condemnation as the drunk in the street. Paul does not grade them. We do.

Unpaid love on a Friday night. And these are pointedly social sins, every one. Drunkenness and revelry are things done in company; sensuality involves somebody else; quarrelling and jealousy require a second party by definition. This is still the argument that began at verse 8 with the debt of love. The vice list is not a change of subject. It is what unpaid love looks like on a Friday night: using people for pleasure, or resenting them for what they have.

But put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Believers have already put on Christ, once for all, at their conversion, signed in their baptism: as many of you as were baptised into Christ have put on Christ (Galatians 3:27). Now they must put him on daily: take on his character, live consciously in union with him, and let him be the clothing others see (Colossians 3:10–14). This is not pretence but identity, choosing to act from the new self rather than the old. And notice the full title, the Lord Jesus Christ. You do not put on a set of values. You put on a Person: the Lord who rules you, Jesus who saves you, the Christ promised from of old.

Wearing another man. There is no higher instruction in the New Testament, and no stranger one: that a man should wear another man, and be seen in him, and be recognised by him rather than by anything of his own. The garment is not a set of qualities extracted from Christ and copied. It is Christ. And it is how the chapter that began with Caesar ends. Paul has moved from the empire to the tax office to the neighbour to a man’s own evening, and the last instruction is the smallest and the most total.

And make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires. “Provision” (pronoia) is forethought, planning ahead, from the same root as the verb Paul used at 12:17, give thought to do what is honourable. The same faculty is in view both times. You plan for good in a calm hour, and you plan for the flesh in a calm hour too, usually without admitting that is what you are doing: the route home that passes the place, the app left installed, the second bottle bought just in case, the evening arranged so that being alone is inevitable. Nobody falls at the moment of temptation. They fall at the moment of provisioning, which happened days earlier and felt like nothing at all. “The flesh” here is not the body as such but our fallen human nature with its sinful desires, which still pulls at the believer (for the fuller explanation, see the note on 8:3–4). The strategy of holiness is not only to resist temptation in the moment, but to arrange life so that temptation has less foothold.

Augustine in the garden. The scene deserves to be told properly, because it is the most famous thing that ever happened to these two verses. In the late summer of AD 386 a North African professor of rhetoric sat weeping in a garden in Milan, thirty-one years old, intellectually convinced of Christianity for some time and unable to break with a sexual habit. As a young man he had prayed in the notorious form: give me chastity and self-control, but not yet. He heard a child’s voice from a neighbouring house, chanting what sounded like a game: tolle lege, take up and read, take up and read. He went back to where he had left a book of Paul’s letters, opened it, and read the first passage his eye fell on. It was this one: not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarrelling and jealousy, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh. Augustine writes in his Confessions (8.12) that he neither wished nor needed to read further. At the end of the sentence, it was as if a light of certainty flooded his heart, and all the darkness of doubt vanished.

Which clause did it. What is worth noticing is that it was not a promise or a doctrine but a plain prohibition followed by a plain command. He had known the doctrine for years. What he had never done was obey the sentence. Augustine had been saying not yet; Romans 13:14 is God’s answer: now. And behind the child’s voice, and the open book, and the eye falling on that page, was the sovereign grace of God, which does not wait for a man to be ready but makes him ready, and which would turn that weeping professor into the greatest teacher of grace the church had known since Paul.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all celebration or wine is sinful. Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding (John 2:1–11), and Scripture speaks of wine that gladdens the heart of man (Psalm 104:15). It forbids excess, drunkenness, and the loss of self-control.
