Nor does make no provision mean the body or its desires are evil in themselves; God made them good. It means refusing to plan for their misuse.

How do I actually put on Christ, day by day? Begin each day by remembering who you are: united to Christ, forgiven, clothed in his righteousness. Then fill your mind with him in his Word, so that you know what he is like and can recognise his ways. Pray, asking him for his patience, purity and kindness for the particular situations of the day ahead. When a temptation comes, ask, what does the Lord Jesus look like here, and do that, by his strength. Meet with his people and come to his table, where he feeds his church with himself by faith. Putting on Christ is not a technique but a relationship lived in the open.

What if I have removed the provisions and still fall? Then come back to Christ at once. Removing provisions is wise, but it is not what saves you; Christ is. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). Then look honestly at what led to the fall, because there is often another provision you had not noticed, and tell a trusted Christian friend, because sin grows in secret and weakens in the light. Falling again does not mean you are not a Christian. Making peace with the sin and no longer fighting it would be the danger sign.

In a sentence. Let us behave decently, as in the daytime, not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy. Rather, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not think about how to gratify the desires of the flesh.

On a Tuesday. Go looking for your own provisions, not only your own sins. Name one arrangement in your life whose only real function is to keep a door open: an app, a habit, a place, a route home, a friendship that always ends the same way. Then close that one thing, not the sin itself but the arrangement. It is a far smaller act, it can be done this evening, and it is what this verse actually asks for. Then put on Christ: begin tomorrow with him before anyone else has your attention.

For worship. He was stripped so that there would be something for the guilty to wear. At the foot of the cross the soldiers gambled for the last thing he owned, while he was in the act of clothing the world. The Son of God hung naked in the daylight, bearing the shame of every work of darkness ever done in the night, so that sinners could be dressed in his righteousness and stand unashamed in the light of God. He has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness (Isaiah 61:10). The chapter began with the emperor and ends with a garment, because in the end the only thing that matters about any of us is whether we are wearing Christ. And the One we put on is the very One who is coming, so that on the day of his appearing he will find his people already dressed in himself.
verseByVerse.note: Augustine was converted on reading these verses in a garden in Milan in AD 386.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God.<sup>2</sup>Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.<sup>3</sup>For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval,<sup>4</sup>for he is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer.<sup>5</sup>Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God’s wrath but also for the sake of conscience.<sup>6</sup>For because of this you also pay taxes, for the authorities are ministers of God, attending to this very thing.<sup>7</sup>Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed.<sup>8</sup>Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law.<sup>9</sup>For the commandments, “You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet,” and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”<sup>10</sup>Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.<sup>11</sup>Besides this you know the time, that the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed.<sup>12</sup>The night is far gone; the day is at hand. So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light.<sup>13</sup>Let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy.<sup>14</sup>But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.

14.title: The Weak and the Strong: Liberty and Love
14.overview:
Romans 14–15 address a specific pastoral conflict in the Roman church: tension between Jewish Christians who maintained food laws and Sabbath observances ("the weak in faith") and Gentile Christians who felt free from such regulations ("the strong"). But Paul's treatment of this specific conflict generates principles that apply to every generation's version of the same tension: the conflict between Christian liberty and Christian love, between what I am free to do and what love requires me to do for the sake of my brother.

The governing principle is not the extension of legal restriction to those who are free, nor the dismissal of sensitive consciences as mere scrupulosity. It is love — the willingness to limit one's own legitimate freedom for the sake of the weaker brother's conscience and the unity of the body. Paul himself is clearly among "the strong" (15:1 — "we who are strong"), but his pastoral concern is to protect the weak while educating them toward greater freedom, without allowing either group to destroy the other with contempt or judgment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Welcome the Weak: Do Not Judge or Despise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions" (v. 1). The command is striking in both its positive and its negative dimensions. Positively: welcome him — bring him into the full fellowship of the community, do not treat his scruples as a reason for exclusion. Negatively: not to quarrel over opinions — do not make his welcome the occasion for pressuring him to adopt your view or defend your freedom. The welcome is genuine; the agenda of the welcome is his good, not your point-scoring.

The specific examples Paul uses — one person eats only vegetables, another observes certain days as special — are illustrations of a broader principle. The particulars may be first-century Jewish food laws and Sabbath observances; the principle is the obligation of both the strong and the weak to refrain from the two characteristic sins their positions generate: the strong's temptation to despise the scrupulous (treating their sensitivity as weakness or intellectual failure), and the weak's temptation to judge the free (condemning as sinful what God has declared clean).

"Each of us will give an account of himself to God" (v. 12) — the eschatological horizon is the great leveller. Neither the strong nor the weak will stand before God and be assessed on the basis of whether they were free in matters of food and days. They will give an account of themselves — whether they served Christ, whether they loved their brother, whether they built up the body. The things that divide them now will be irrelevant then; what will matter then should be what governs them now.

Four things in the section are worth adding, because the ground between the opening command and v. 12 is where the argument is actually made. The first is v. 4, which supplies the reason judging is out of order: Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? The picture is a domestic household. You do not discipline another man’s staff, however sure you are that they are doing it wrong, because they were not hired by you and do not answer to you.

And that verse ends in a promise rather than a rebuke — he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand. Paul’s confidence is not that the disputed practice does not matter but that the disputed brother is being personally held up by someone competent. God is already at work on the person you were about to correct.

The second is v. 6, and it is the criterion the whole section turns on. Both parties — the one who observes the day and the one who does not, the one who eats and the one who abstains — are described as acting in honour of the Lord, and both are said to give thanks to God. Paul is not calling the difference trivial. He is pointing out that the same thanksgiving is going up from both sides of the table.

The third is v. 9, which grounds the whole thing in the gospel rather than in tolerance: to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living. The purpose of the cross and resurrection is stated here as lordship — which settles who is entitled to rule another believer’s conscience, and the answer is the one who paid for it. And the fourth is vv. 10–11, where the argument is sealed with Isaiah 45:23: every knee bowing, every tongue confessing, the strong and the weak side by side at the same tribunal, neither of them presiding.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adiaphora and the Conscience

The Reformed tradition uses the term adiaphora (things indifferent) for matters that Scripture neither commands nor prohibits — the territory of Romans 14. In these matters, Christian liberty is real: what God has declared clean is clean; what the gospel has freed the conscience from need not be re-enslaved. But liberty is not the highest value; love is. Calvin insisted that in matters of adiaphora, the strong must exercise their freedom with sensitivity to the weaker conscience — not capitulating to every scruple indefinitely, but never using freedom as a weapon against the brother Christ died for.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific tensions in Rome were between Jewish and Gentile believers over Torah food laws and calendar observances — real, living issues that threatened the unity of a church in which both groups worshipped together. Paul does not resolve the tension by declaring one group right and the other wrong; he transcends it by pointing both groups to a standard higher than their own position: the lordship of Christ (v. 8) and the coming judgment (v. 12). Now: Every generation of the church has its equivalent of the Romans 14 debate: alcohol, entertainment, dress, worship style, political engagement. The principles are the same: welcome the brother with differing scruples; do not quarrel over opinions; do not despise; do not judge; remember that each will give account to God and not to you.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions. One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions. One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.

Meaning first. Romans 14:1–15:13 deals with a problem in the Roman church: believers disagreed over matters that Scripture leaves free, such as foods and special days. Paul calls those with tender scruples the weak and those who are free in conscience the strong, and he counts himself among the strong (15:1). He gives each side its duty. The strong must not despise the weak; the weak must not judge the strong; God has welcomed both, and each answers to the Lord, before whose judgement seat we will all stand (vv. 1–12). Then he presses the strong especially: do not use your freedom in a way that makes a brother stumble or destroys him, for the kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (vv. 13–21). Finally: keep your faith between you and God, and do not act against your conscience, for whatever does not come from faith is sin (vv. 22–23). The chapter teaches Christian liberty and Christian love together. And to settle a quarrel about menus and calendars, Paul reaches for the largest things he knows: that God has welcomed us, that Christ died and rose to be our Lord, and that every knee will bow to him.

The setting. The weak probably include Jewish believers who kept the food laws and holy days of the law of Moses, and perhaps some Gentiles who avoided meat for fear it had been offered to idols (as in 1 Corinthians 8 and 10). Meat sold in the markets of Rome often came from pagan temples. Some, unable to be sure, ate only vegetables, as Daniel did in Babylon (Daniel 1:8–12). The church in Rome had been through upheaval: the Jewish believers expelled under Claudius had returned to find congregations that were now largely Gentile, with different habits at the table. A shared meal, which was at the heart of early Christian fellowship, had become a place of tension.

As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him. Everything in this chapter depends on getting one thing straight at the start, and modern readers almost always get it backwards. “Weak in faith” does not mean weak in trusting Christ for salvation, and it does not mean lax, doubting or half-hearted. It means not yet fully persuaded of the freedom the gospel gives in such matters. It is the man with more rules, not fewer: the one who cannot eat the meat, cannot ignore the day, cannot do the permitted thing without his conscience objecting. That inverts the way the words are normally used in church. We instinctively call the strict Christian the strong one and the relaxed Christian the weak one, the serious brother against the compromiser. Paul’s labels run the other way. If the chapter is read with the usual assumption in place, every instruction in it lands on the wrong person.

The weight of the word welcome. “Welcome” (proslambanō, receive, take to oneself) means accept fully into fellowship, not merely tolerate. Paul uses it three times in this section, and the other two settle its weight. Here the strong are to welcome the weak; in verse 3 the reason is that God has welcomed him; and at 15:7 the standard becomes welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you. Same verb. The hospitality being asked for is not politeness at the edge of the room. It is the kind God has already shown to the person you find difficult.

But not to quarrel over opinions. “Opinions” (dialogismoi) are reasonings, debatable thoughts. Do not welcome someone in order to argue him out of his scruples. Paul anticipates the manoeuvre exactly. It is entirely possible to receive someone warmly with the settled intention of working on him, to be hospitable at him. The welcome that comes with a project attached is not the welcome commanded here, and the person on the receiving end can always tell.

One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables. The strong believe all foods are clean (v. 14; Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). The weak avoid meat altogether to be safe. The concrete situation explains the vegetables, which otherwise look eccentric. A scrupulous Jewish believer in Rome could not easily verify how an animal had been slaughtered or whether the meat in the market had come through a temple. He was not making a case for a diet. He had simply found that the only way to be certain was to eat no meat at all, which is what a tender conscience usually does. It over-corrects, because it cannot bear the risk.

Where Christians differ: what counts as a disputable matter? Some apply this chapter to every disagreement, including doctrine and morality. Verdict: Romans 14 concerns things that Scripture does not command or forbid, matters indifferent in themselves (the Greek term is adiaphora). It does not cover the gospel itself, which Paul defends fiercely (Galatians 1:8–9), or clear moral commands, such as sexual purity (13:13). Where God has spoken plainly, we do not treat it as an opinion. Where he has not, we give liberty, for God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster 20.2).

How do I tell a disputable matter from a real sin? Three questions sort them. Does Scripture command it or forbid it? Is the gospel itself at stake? Is anyone being told that he must do this to be right with God? Where the answer to all three is no, this chapter governs, and the strong bear with the weak. But where Scripture calls something sin, no appeal to liberty or conscience can make it a disputable matter. And where the gospel is at stake, the strong must not yield: when false brothers wanted Titus circumcised as a condition of acceptance, Paul says he did not yield in submission even for a moment (Galatians 2:5). Bearing with a weak conscience is love; letting it rule the church is not.

What are the disputable matters today? Rarely meat sold in temples. Today they are more likely to be alcohol, the keeping of Christmas and Easter, styles of music in worship, which Bible translation to use, schooling choices for children, dress, diet, films and novels, social media, or how strictly to keep Sunday. On all of these, sincere believers who love the Lord reach different conclusions. The list will change from generation to generation; the principle does not. Where God has not spoken, no Christian has the right to speak as though he had.

I think I am the weak brother. Is that an insult? No. The term names one thing only: a conscience not yet free in a matter where God has in fact granted freedom. It says nothing about your sincerity, your salvation or your love for Christ. The man Paul describes is scrupulous precisely because he is afraid of displeasing God, which is not a contemptible reason for anything. And notice whom this chapter is written to protect. Nearly every command in it is aimed at the strong, on your behalf. Paul does not spend a single verse telling you to hurry up.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the weak are second-class Christians. It does not mean that strong opinions are always wrong; Paul has one, and states it (v. 14). It means that in matters God has left free, love must rule.

In a sentence. Accept the one whose faith is weak, without quarrelling over disputable matters. One person’s faith allows him to eat anything, but another, whose faith is weak, eats only vegetables.

On a Tuesday. Think of a fellow Christian who has scruples you do not share. Welcome him warmly: invite him, sit with him, and let your conversation be about Christ, not about the scruple. Do not try to argue him out of it. And if you are the one with the scruple, think of the brother who is freer than you, and receive him with the same warmth.

For worship. Before there was any question of whom we would welcome, God welcomed us. We came with nothing in our hands but the wrong opinions, the wrong history and a great deal of sin, and he did not receive us on condition that we first agree with him about everything. He took us to himself in Christ, and he has gone on bearing with our slowness ever since. The Lord who receives sinners and eats with them (Luke 15:2) has set a table where the scrupulous and the free sit side by side, both of them there for one reason only: he wanted them. The welcome of God is wider than our opinions, and warmer than our hearts.
verseByVerse.note: The “weak” probably include Jewish believers who kept the food laws, and others who avoided meat that might have been offered to idols.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.

Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains. The temptation of the strong is to look down on the weak as narrow and legalistic. “Despise” (exoutheneō) is to count as nothing, to treat as of no account. And notice how precisely the two sins are assigned. Paul does not warn both parties about both dangers. The one who eats is told not to despise; the one who abstains is told not to judge. Each temptation is matched to the position that produces it. Freedom does not tempt a person to condemn; it tempts him to find the other man faintly ridiculous: the amused dismissal, the raised eyebrow, the anecdote told later about how strict so-and-so is.

And let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats. The temptation of the weak is to condemn the strong as worldly or compromising. “Pass judgement” (krinō) here means condemn. Scruple does not tempt a person to sneer; it tempts him to convict. Neither party is usually in any danger of the other’s sin, which is why each so easily believes himself innocent.

For God has welcomed him. If God has accepted him in Christ, who are you to reject him? Our fellowship must be as wide as God’s welcome. This is the ground of all Christian unity: not agreement on secondary matters but shared reception by the same God. The brother you are tempted to despise or condemn sits at your table because God himself pulled out the chair.

Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? The household image is domestic rather than abstract. “Servant” (oiketēs) is a household servant. You may think another family’s arrangements peculiar; you do not walk into their kitchen and start correcting their staff. Not because standards do not matter, but because it is not your household and they did not take instruction from you. Every believer is Christ’s servant, not yours.

It is before his own master that he stands or falls. His master decides whether his service pleases him. The verdict on another believer’s practice in these matters is not yours to give, because the approval that matters is not yours to give.

And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand. The verse ends somewhere unexpected. Having asked who you think you are, Paul does not finish by saying the servant may well fall and that will be his own affair. He says he will be upheld. The strong person you think is falling will in fact stand, because the Lord holds him up. The apostle’s confidence runs toward the very person you were worried about. Somebody competent already has hold of him. It is a word of assurance in the middle of an ethical argument: Christ keeps his servants (Jude 24).

The relief hidden in this verse. A great deal of the anxiety Christians carry about other Christians is really a quiet doubt about whether God is managing them properly. Paul’s answer is that he is, and that your supervision was never part of the arrangement. You may pray for your brother, love him, and talk with him. You do not have to hold him up. The Lord is able.

Does this mean Christians must never judge? No. Paul forbids condemning a brother over matters God has left open. Elsewhere he commands the church to judge sin among its members (1 Corinthians 5:12–13), pronounces a curse on those who preach another gospel (Galatians 1:8–9), and at the end of this letter tells the Romans to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine they have been taught (16:17). The question is not whether to judge but what: sin and false teaching, yes; another believer’s conscience on a disputable matter, no.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can never correct a brother in sin (Galatians 6:1; Matthew 18:15). It means we do not condemn others over matters God has left free.

In a sentence. The one who eats everything must not treat with contempt the one who does not, and the one who does not eat everything must not judge the one who does, for God has accepted him. Who are you to judge someone else’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls. And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.

On a Tuesday. A test, and it sorts the two sins neatly. Think of a believer whose practice differs from yours on something Scripture does not settle. Now notice which reflex arrives first: the urge to laugh, or the urge to convict. Whichever it is tells you which of the two groups you are actually in, whatever you would have said about yourself. Then confess it to God, and say something kind about that brother to someone else this week.

For worship. The Lord is able to make him stand. He is able to make you stand. Every believer on earth is upheld, at this moment, by hands that do not tire and do not let go. He is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24). Not one of his servants is left to stand by his own strength, not the strong with all his knowledge nor the weak with all his scruples. The Master of the house holds every one of them, and he has never yet dropped a servant he took into his house. To him be glory, who keeps what he has welcomed.

verseByVerse.quote: One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.

One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. The days in question were probably the Sabbath and the Jewish feasts and fasts (Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16). Some believers still kept them as special; others considered all days alike.

Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. “Fully convinced” (plērophoreō) means filled up to full assurance. Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say the matter is unimportant, and he does not say do as you please. Both the freedom and the scruple are required to have been thought about. That rules out the position most people actually occupy, which is neither conviction nor liberty but inheritance. A great many Christian practices are held for no reason anyone can now state: it is how we were raised, it is what our church does, it is what the people we admire do. Paul is not asking everyone to reach the same conclusion. He is asking everyone to have reached his own, which is a more demanding request than it sounds and falls equally on both parties.

Paul’s restraint. It is worth registering how remarkable this is coming from Paul. He is not neutral on the question; he says plainly nine verses later that he is persuaded nothing is unclean, and he is one of the strong. Yet here he defends the right of a man to reach the opposite practical conclusion and act on it before God. He will argue for his view. He will not legislate it. That is apostolic authority used with great gentleness, and it is a model for every pastor and parent.

The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. Both sides can act for Christ. The motive matters. The criterion Paul offers is not practice but orientation: is it done for the Lord?

The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God. Then the common ground, and it is not agreement. It is thanksgiving. The eater thanks God for the food; the abstainer thanks God too. Two men do opposite things at the same table and both of them say grace over it, and Paul treats that as the decisive fact about both. Both honour the Lord.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day. Some say this verse proves no day is special for Christians. Others hold that the fourth commandment, given at creation (Genesis 2:3) and part of the moral law, binds Christians to a strict Sabbath observance, now on Sunday, and that this verse speaks only of Jewish ceremonial days. Verdict: the Old Testament Sabbath was a shadow fulfilled in Christ, who is our true rest (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10; Matthew 11:28). Christians are not bound by the Sabbath laws of Moses, and Paul here leaves Jewish days to conscience. But the first day of the week, the Lord’s Day, the day of Christ’s resurrection, was the day the early church gathered for worship (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10). Gathering with God’s people on that day, resting from ordinary work where possible, and giving it to worship, is a great privilege and a wise rhythm, not a heavy burden. Those who keep a stricter Sunday observance, as in the Westminster tradition, do so in honour of the Lord, and should be welcomed, not despised.

What about Christmas and Easter? They belong to this chapter. A church may keep them gladly, as days to rejoice in the birth and resurrection of the Lord, and many believers find them a rich help to worship. Others, especially in some Reformed traditions, have declined to keep any holy day beyond the Lord’s Day, wanting nothing in worship that Scripture does not command. Both can do it in honour of the Lord. What no one may do is bind another’s conscience: neither by treating the man who keeps Christmas as compromised, nor by treating the man who does not as a killjoy.

How do I become fully convinced? Not by waiting for a feeling. Read what Scripture actually says on the matter, and what it does not say. Ask why you do what you do, and whether you could give a reason from God’s Word. Talk it through with mature believers, including some who disagree with you. Pray for wisdom (James 1:5). Then reach a conclusion you can thank God for, and live by it with a clear conscience, while remaining teachable. Being fully convinced does not mean you can never change your mind. It means you are acting from conviction now, not from pressure or confusion.

What it does not mean. It does not mean regular gathering for worship is optional (Hebrews 10:25). The day may be a matter of conscience; meeting with the Lord’s people is not.

In a sentence. One person considers one day more sacred than another; another considers every day alike. Each of them should be fully convinced in his own mind. Whoever regards one day as special does so to the Lord. Whoever eats meat does so to the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and whoever abstains does so to the Lord and gives thanks to God.

On a Tuesday. Before any choice in a disputed area, ask: can I do this for the Lord, and thank God for it? Not can I defend it, not can I find someone who agrees, but can I actually thank God for this specific thing, out loud, without the sentence going strange in my mouth? If so, go ahead with a clear conscience. Liberty that cannot say grace over what it is doing has stopped being liberty somewhere, and scruple that cannot thank God for the freedom it is declining has become something other than conscience.

For worship. Every day is the Lord’s, and the first day of the week is his in a special way, because on it he rose. The Sabbath that Israel kept for fifteen centuries was a picture, and the picture has come true: there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, and it is found in the One who said, come to me, all who labour, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). He finished his work on the cross and rested in the tomb, and on the first day he rose to give rest to the weary. So the believer who keeps a day and the believer who does not are both resting in the same Saviour, both saying grace to the same Father. All our days are gifts, and all our thanks go to one Giver.
verseByVerse.note: The days in question were probably the Sabbath and Jewish festivals.

verseByVerse.quote: For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.

For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. The principle beneath all of this. No Christian is his own master. We are not self-owned. Every choice, what to eat and what day to observe, but also every life decision, is made in the presence of the Lord to whom we belong.

For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. All of life, and death itself, is lived toward Christ: for him, in his service, under his eye. The Christian does not even die for himself. He dies into the arms of the One who owns him. And the repetition carries it: to the Lord, to the Lord, the Lord’s, three times in a single verse. Both parties keep claiming to be right; Paul keeps answering that neither of them is his own. And ownership is the one fact that settles a dispute between equals, because it does not decide who is correct. It decides who has standing to rule.

So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s. We belong to him. This is our great comfort. The Heidelberg Catechism begins with this verse and its truth: my only comfort in life and in death is that I am not my own, but belong, body and soul, to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ (Question 1).

Where this sentence has ended up. It is worth stopping to notice, because almost every reader meets this verse somewhere other than here. Whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s is read at gravesides. It is carved on stones. It is said quietly to people in hospital rooms at three in the morning. And Paul wrote it about a disagreement over vegetables. That is not a deflation of the verse; it is the point of it. Faced with a squabble about menus and calendars, Paul does not reach for a rule of thumb or a compromise. He reaches for the largest thing he knows, that a Christian is owned in life and in death, and he puts it underneath the smallest possible quarrel. The size of the argument he brings is a measure of how seriously he takes the damage the quarrel can do.

What does it look like to live to the Lord on an ordinary day? It means asking, about the ordinary things, whom am I doing this for? Work done for him is done honestly and well even when no one checks (Colossians 3:23). Money is spent as a steward, not an owner. Time, including rest, is received as his gift. Relationships are handled as his business, because the people are his. It does not mean thinking religious thoughts every minute. It means that nothing in your life is a private zone where he has no say, and that is not a burden but a freedom: you no longer have to be your own god.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we have no responsibility to others. Because we belong to the Lord, we must care for those who are also his (v. 15).

In a sentence. For none of us lives for himself alone, and none of us dies for himself alone. If we live, we live for the Lord; and if we die, we die for the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Take the decision in front of you this week, large or small, and ask it plainly: Lord, this is yours; what do you want? Then, if you face something frightening, an illness, a diagnosis, the death of someone you love, say this verse aloud, slowly, and let it be the floor you stand on.

For worship. We are not our own; we were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). The One who owns us did not acquire us cheaply. He paid for us with his own blood, and having paid, he will not lose what he bought. In life we are his: every breath, every meal, every Tuesday. In death we are his: the last breath and the grave itself. There is no moment of a believer’s existence, from new birth to resurrection, when he is not held by his Lord. This is the comfort that has carried the dying for twenty centuries. Whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s, and he is ours.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.

For to this end Christ died and lived again. Consider what Paul has just done to settle a dispute about dinner. He has gone to the death and resurrection of the Son of God. Not as an illustration, and not as a general appeal to take things seriously, but as the actual argument. To this end: this was what it was for. Among the great purposes of the cross and the empty tomb was this: to establish Christ’s lordship over his people. He died to purchase those who had been enslaved to sin and death; he rose to rule them as the living, reigning King.

That he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living. Christ’s rule reaches beyond the grave. Believers who have died are still his (1 Thessalonians 4:14–16), and believers alive now are his. Death cannot remove us from his ownership. By dying and rising he won the right to rule over all (Philippians 2:8–11; Acts 2:36). And notice the order: the dead first, then the living. The believers you have buried have not passed out of his jurisdiction into some neutral territory. They are still his, under the same lordship, on the same terms, which is why Paul can say a verse earlier that we die to the Lord and mean something more than a pious figure of speech.

Both sides disqualified. If the purpose of the cross was that Christ should be Lord, then every attempt by one believer to take charge of another’s conscience in a matter God has left open is an encroachment on the very thing Calvary was transacted to secure. The strong man imposing his freedom and the weak man imposing his scruple are making the same mistake, from opposite ends. Both are trying to sit on a throne that was bought with blood for someone else.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Christ became Lord only at his resurrection, as if he were not God before. He was always God the Son. But as the God-man and Redeemer, he received the lordship he won by his death and resurrection.

Where are believers who have died? With Christ, consciously, now. They are not asleep in the sense of being unaware, and they are not in some place of further cleansing. Paul says that to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Their bodies rest in the grave awaiting the resurrection; their souls are with him, under his rule and in his joy. Scripture describes their death as sleep because it is temporary and peaceful, not because they have ceased to know.

In a sentence. For this very reason Christ died and returned to life, so that he might be the Lord of both the dead and the living.

On a Tuesday. When someone you love dies in Christ, remember: he is still their Lord. They are safe with him. And when you are tempted to rule another believer’s conscience, remember what it cost to make Christ Lord, and leave the throne to him.

For worship. He went into the one country from which no ruler had ever returned, and he came back, and he came back holding the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). The dead are not outside his jurisdiction. They are not lost, or filed away, or waiting in some neutral territory beyond his reach. Every believer who has ever been buried is at this moment under the same Lord as every believer still drawing breath. He rules both countries, because he has lived in both. And the throne he occupies was not seized but earned, by a death and a rising, so that his people would belong to a Master who loves them enough to have died for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God; for it is written, "As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God; for it is written, “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.”

Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? To the weak: why judge? To the strong: why despise? The Greek puts a weight the English cannot: both questions begin with an emphatic you. He is turning to each party in the room by name, and the effect is of a man pointing. And note the word brother, twice. You are not arguing with an opponent. You are family.

For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God. The judgement seat is the bēma, and it was a piece of ordinary civic furniture: the raised stone platform in a Greek city from which a magistrate gave his ruling. Paul had stood on the wrong side of one himself, in Corinth, when Gallio heard the case against him and dismissed it (Acts 18:12–16). He is not reaching for a vague image of accountability. He is describing a place where you are the one standing and someone else is seated. In 2 Corinthians 5:10 Paul calls it the judgement seat of Christ, for God judges through Christ (John 5:22; Acts 17:31). We will not be judges there; we will be judged. So we should not take the judge’s seat now. At the judgement seat the strong and the weak stand exactly level.

For it is written, “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.” The words come from Isaiah 45:23 (with as I live from Isaiah 49:18). Everyone will bow before God. And the quotation is doing more than proving that everyone is accountable. Isaiah 45:23 is spoken by the God who has just said there is no other, and Paul elsewhere takes the same verse and applies it to Jesus, at whose name every knee bows (Philippians 2:10–11): further proof that Jesus is God. So the scene at the end is not a courtroom with an unknown judge. It is the One before whom you will bow beside the brother you were correcting.

The seat is occupied. And that is the argument. Not that judgement is unpleasant, but that the seat is taken. Every act of judging another believer over an open question is an attempt to sit somewhere that already has someone in it.

Will believers be judged? Yes: we must all appear before the judgement seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). But not to decide whether they are saved. That was settled when they believed: whoever believes does not come into judgement, but has passed from death to life (John 5:24; 8:1). What is examined is their life and service. Some will receive reward, and others will suffer loss, though they themselves are saved (1 Corinthians 3:12–15).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will be condemned at the judgement. There is no condemnation for those in Christ (8:1). Nor does every knee bowing mean that all will be saved. Believers will bow in worship and joy; the rest will bow because they must, acknowledging too late the Lord they refused, and will go away into eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46). The bowing is universal; the salvation is not.

In a sentence. You, then, why do you judge your brother? Or why do you treat him with contempt? For we will all stand before God’s judgement seat. It is written that the Lord swears by his own life that every knee will bow before him and every tongue will acknowledge God.

On a Tuesday. The next time you catch yourself rehearsing a verdict on another Christian over a matter Scripture leaves open, picture the two of you standing side by side before the throne. Say, in your heart: Lord, you are his judge and mine. Then pray for him instead of judging him.

For worship. Every knee shall bow. The day is fixed, and nothing in heaven or on earth or under the earth will be missing from it. The proud will bow, and the emperors, and every tongue that ever mocked him, and his own people, who will bow first and gladly, because the Judge on the throne is the Saviour who was judged in their place. The same Lord who will sit on the judgement seat once stood before Pilate’s, silent, condemned for us. The One we will bow to is the One who bowed his head on the cross and gave up his spirit. Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

parallels.desc: to me every knee shall bow

verseByVerse.quote: So then each of us will give an account of himself to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then each of us will give an account of himself to God.

So then each of us will give an account of himself to God. “Account” (logos) is a reckoning, like an account book. Each of us: personally, individually. Of himself: not of others. The Greek presses the reflexive hard: each of us will give an account concerning himself. Whatever else is asked, you will not be asked about him. You will not be asked to account for your brother’s choices in matters of conscience, but for your own life (Matthew 12:36; Hebrews 4:13).

No comparisons in court. This removes at a stroke the defence most of us have quietly prepared. Nearly every account we give of ourselves is comparative: I am not as strict as him, I am not as careless as her, at least I have never. It works well in conversation, because there is always someone available to be worse. It will not be admissible, because the other party will be busy giving his own account, about himself, at the same moment.

If I am justified, why should the account concern me? Because it is real, and because your Father cares how his children live. The account is not a trial to decide whether you will be condemned; that was settled at the cross. It is more like a son showing his father what he did with what he was given. It should make you serious about how you live, not afraid of rejection. And it should free you from comparison, because you are not being measured against your brother, only seen by your Lord, who knows your weakness and remembers that you are dust (Psalm 103:14).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we must fear the judgement as unbelievers do. In Christ we are justified. But it gives a sober seriousness to how we live.

In a sentence. So then, each of us will give an account of himself to God.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it takes a minute. Try describing your own spiritual condition to God without mentioning another Christian, a church you left, a movement you disagree with, or a generation you think has gone wrong. Just yourself, to God. Most of us discover how much of our self-assessment was actually about somebody else, and that is precisely the material that will not be there to lean on. Spend less time evaluating other Christians, and more time preparing your own account.

For worship. There is One who knows every line of your account, and he is not an auditor hoping to find fault. He is the Lord who wrote your name in the book of life before the foundation of the world, and who has already paid every debt the account could show (Colossians 2:14). When you stand before him, it will be as one whose sins are forgiven, whose works, however small, he has been watching with love, and who will not lose the reward of a cup of cold water given in his name (Matthew 10:42). No one else could be trusted with such an account. He can, because he is both perfectly just and perfectly kind.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Do Not Cause a Brother to Stumble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother" (v. 13). The second half of chapter 14 moves from the mutual prohibition of judging and despising to the positive obligation of the strong: limit your freedom in cases where exercising it would damage your brother's conscience and lead him into sin. The governing concern is his welfare, not your rights.

Paul's theological grounding of this obligation is striking: "By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died" (v. 15). Christ died for the weak brother. The price paid for his soul is the blood of the Son of God. The strong believer who uses her freedom to demolish someone Christ purchased at infinite cost has committed something far more serious than poor table manners. She has treated as worthless what God treated as worth his Son.

The kingdom of God principle of v. 17 is the positive vision behind the self-limitation: "For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." The things that matter most — right standing before God, harmony in the body, Spirit-given joy — are not determined by what we eat. The strong person who surrenders her food freedom for the sake of a brother's peace and joy has not lost anything that matters; she has demonstrated something that matters supremely: she cares more about his joy in the Holy Spirit than about her right to eat what she pleases.

Verses 13, 15 and 17 carry the section, and the rest of it carries the argument. Verse 14 is the pivot, and it is the boldest sentence in the chapter: I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. Both halves are asserted. The thing really is clean, and it really is defiling for the man whose conscience says otherwise — which is why the answer to his scruple is teaching rather than pressure.

Verses 16 and 19–21 then supply the working rules. Do not let the good thing you possess — your liberty — get itself a bad name (v. 16). Pursue what makes for peace and for building up (v. 19). And the counterpart: do not, for the sake of food, demolish the work of God (v. 20). Paul is running a construction metaphor across these verses, and the choice he puts to the strong is whether their freedom is putting walls up or taking them down.

Verse 22 turns to the free man personally: the faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Not conceal your convictions, but stop parading a liberty — and then a beatitude for the man who can act without a backward glance at himself.

And v. 23 closes the chapter with the sentence that has travelled furthest from it: whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. In context it is about a specific man doing a specific thing while divided in his own mind. It has been made to carry a great deal more than that.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christian Liberty and the Law of Love

Romans 14:13–23 establishes the fundamental principle of Christian ethics in matters of liberty: freedom is real, but love is higher. The freedom the gospel gives is not a license to do everything the law permits without regard to others; it is the freedom to serve. The one who is free in Christ is freed from the bondage of sin and law — freed for the service of God and neighbour. To use freedom as a weapon against a brother's conscience is a misuse of freedom as fundamental as legalism; it is just as self-centred, only differently oriented.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific issue of meat offered to idols (closely related to the Romans 14 situation, developed more fully in 1 Corinthians 8–10) was a genuine and daily challenge in the first-century city. Much of the meat available in the marketplace had passed through a pagan temple. The strong knew the idol was nothing; the weak felt defiled. Paul's principle: your knowledge does not give you the right to wound your brother's conscience. Now: The strong Christian in every age is tempted to treat her freedom as a badge of theological maturity to be displayed rather than a gift to be managed with care. The test of genuine maturity is not the willingness to exercise freedom but the willingness to limit it out of love — to choose the brother's conscience over personal preference, his joy over your rights.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother. I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. — Romans 14:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother. I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean.

Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer. The conclusion of verses 1–12. Paul now turns from the judgement seat to the dinner table, and from the weak to the strong. The transition is crucial: he is not merely telling the two sides to live and let live. He is asking the strong to take active responsibility for the spiritual welfare of the weak.

But rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother. Verse 13 turns on a pun that the English hides. Paul writes, in effect, let us no longer judge one another, but judge this instead: the same verb (krinō) twice, in opposite directions. He does not tell the Roman Christians to stop making judgements. He tells them to make one, and to make it about themselves: decide, settle it, resolve never to put an obstacle in a brother’s path. The verdict-passing energy is not to be switched off. It is to be turned round.

What a stumbling block is. The obstacle in view is specific. A proskomma is the thing your foot catches on; a skandalon was the trigger of a trap, the stick that springs the snare. Neither word means giving offence in the modern sense. The damage described is not that the weak brother is annoyed by your steak. It is that he eats one, against his own conscience, because you made it awkward not to, and something inside him gives way. A stumbling block is anything in your conduct that draws a brother into doing what he believes is sin.

I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself. Paul sides with the strong, and states where he got his view. That is an unusual formula and it is doing real work. He is not offering a personal preference or the conclusion of his own reasoning; he speaks by Jesus’ authority and teaching. Behind it very probably stands his Master’s own ruling on the question, the day Jesus told the crowd that nothing entering a man from outside can defile him, which Mark glosses in a famous aside: thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). Paul is not innovating. He is agreeing. The food laws, which had marked Israel out as holy for centuries, were fulfilled in Christ. “Unclean” (koinos) means common, ritually impure.

But it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. Look at the second half of the verse, because everything pastoral depends on it. Paul asserts both things at once and does not soften either. The food is objectively clean. It is genuinely defiling for that man. He does not say the weak brother is imagining his problem. If someone believes something is wrong, it is wrong for him to do it, because he would be going against his conscience. The object is not unclean, but acting against conscience is sin.

Conscience creates obligation, not reality. That distinction is worth holding carefully, because it is the whole logic of conscience. Conscience does not create reality: believing meat unclean does not make it so, and Paul says as much in the same breath. But conscience does create obligation. It is not an infallible guide, and it is a binding one, and a man who acts against it has done wrong even when the act itself was harmless.

So how do I help a brother with a weak conscience? Never by pressure. If the problem is that he thinks it unclean, the only real remedy is that he should come to think otherwise, and that is done by teaching, time and the example of people he trusts. Getting him to do the thing while he still believes it wrong does not free him. It just damages the instrument. So be patient, open the Scriptures with him when he wants to, live your own freedom gently, and leave the timing to the Spirit. Some people never change their mind on the matter, and that is all right; Paul never says the weak must become strong before they are welcome.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that sin is whatever someone thinks it is, so that morality is relative. Paul speaks only of matters indifferent, like food. Murder is unclean whatever anyone thinks.

In a sentence. Therefore let us stop passing judgement on one another. Instead, make up your mind not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in the way of a brother. Paul is convinced, being fully persuaded in the Lord Jesus, that nothing is unclean in itself. But if anyone regards something as unclean, then for that person it is unclean.

On a Tuesday. Before you use your freedom in front of someone, ask: could this trip him up? Love may mean holding back. And here is a test for the strong reader, a question about method rather than doctrine. On the matter where you are confident you are right and a fellow believer is wrong: are you trying to change his mind, or trying to change his behaviour? The first is what this verse asks for. The second is what most of us actually attempt, because it is quicker.

For worship. The Lord Jesus spoke one sentence, and the menus of the world were opened. Every food was made clean, every table made a place where Jew and Gentile could sit together, because the One who fulfilled the law had come. All the old boundaries of clean and unclean pointed to a holiness that only he could give, and he gives it, not through what goes into the mouth but through what he does in the heart. He has made the unclean clean: lepers, sinners, Gentiles, us. And the One who sets his people free is the same One who teaches them to use their freedom tenderly, for he never once used his own power to crush a bruised reed (Isaiah 42:3).

verseByVerse.quote: For if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died.

For if your brother is grieved by what you eat. “Grieved” (lypeō) means pained, hurt. This is more than being annoyed. It means his conscience is wounded, perhaps because he is drawn into doing what he thinks is wrong, or perhaps because he watches a brother he loves do what he believes dishonours God.

You are no longer walking in love. Note the phrase that decides the matter. Not: you have broken a rule. The strong man in this scene has done nothing forbidden; his theology is correct and his dinner is lawful. He has simply stopped walking in love somewhere between being right and being at the table, and Paul treats that as the thing that has gone wrong. You may be right about food, but you are wrong about love. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up (1 Corinthians 8:1).

By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died. A shocking contrast. Christ gave his life for this brother; will you not give up a meal for him? The weight is immense: Christ’s life on one side of the scale, your dinner on the other. And the verb is worth naming because Paul reached for the largest one available. “Destroy” (apollymi) is the word used across the New Testament for ruin and perishing, the opposite of being saved. He could have said upset, or discourage, or set back. He chose the word for wreckage, and he attached it to a plate of food.

What destruction looks like. In practice it is less dramatic than the word suggests and more serious than it feels. It is not usually a single catastrophe. It is a man persuaded to act against his conscience once, in company, to avoid looking foolish, and a conscience overridden once is a good deal easier to override the second time. What has been damaged is not his opinion about meat. It is the instrument by which he says no to anything.

Where Christians differ: can someone for whom Christ died be destroyed? Some use this verse to argue that Christ died for people who will finally perish, and that a true believer can be lost. Verdict: Paul is warning the strong about the real tendency of their actions: what they do could lead a brother into sin and spiritual ruin. The warning is real and must be taken seriously. But God uses such warnings to keep his people. Elsewhere Paul is clear that those for whom Christ died will certainly be saved (5:8–10; 8:32–34). Christ died effectively for his sheep, and none of them will be snatched from his hand (John 10:11, 28). This is definite atonement and the perseverance of the saints. The man who wrote that nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God (8:39) is not contradicting himself over dinner. He is doing what Scripture consistently does with real dangers: naming them at full strength, to people who are in a position to cause them. The point here is ethical: treat your brother as someone precious to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the weak can control the strong by complaining about everything. The concern is a brother who might be led to sin against his conscience, not one who simply disapproves. A Christian who uses his scruples to rule the church, or who demands that his preferences become everyone’s law, is no longer the weak brother of this chapter. He is closer to the false brothers to whom Paul would not yield for a moment (Galatians 2:5).

How do I know whether my freedom is actually hurting someone? Watch and ask. Is there a believer in the room whose conscience forbids this, and who might follow your example against it? Is he a new Christian, or someone fighting a particular battle, perhaps with alcohol or gambling, for whom your freedom could reopen an old door? Has he told you it troubles him? If you are unsure, you can simply ask him privately and gently. Most of the time the answer is clear, and the cost of restraint is small: an evening, a meal, a glass. The brother is worth far more.

In a sentence. If your brother is distressed because of what you eat, you are no longer acting in love. Do not by your eating destroy someone for whom Christ died.

On a Tuesday. Bring to mind the brother whose scruple you find most tiresome. Then say to yourself, deliberately, the phrase Paul uses: the one for whom Christ died. Christ thought him worth a cross. Let that change how you see him today, and what you are willing to give up for him.

For worship. Christ died for that difficult brother. He died for the scrupulous believer with his long list of things he cannot do, and for the free believer who finds him tiresome. He died for each of them by name, and he will lose neither. And the Lord who gave his life for them both did not count his own rights as something to be held on to; he set them aside, all of them, and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). The strong Son of God made himself weak for the weak. Every time a Christian lays down a freedom for a brother, he is tracing, in a very small way, the outline of the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil. The good that is in danger of being spoken ill of is the liberty itself: your Christian freedom, a true gift of the gospel. If you use it carelessly, it will be criticised, literally blasphemed. That is the sting of verse 16, and it is easy to miss. Paul is not warning the strong that they will get a bad name. He is warning them that Christian freedom will. A right thing, handled without love, becomes the very thing people point at as evidence that the doctrine produces bad men. A good freedom gets a bad name.

For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking. The kingdom of God is his rule, present now in Christ and coming in fullness. Its heart is not food. To fight over food is to miss what really matters.

But of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. Righteousness: right standing with God and right living. Peace: with God and with one another. Joy: delight in God. All three are given and produced by the Holy Spirit (Galatians 5:22). And read them in the argument they sit in, because they are not only the private inward states we usually take them for. Peace here is peace between the two parties at the table. Joy is the joy of a brother who has not been trampled. Even righteousness is being contrasted with a menu: right standing and right dealing rather than dietary correctness. Paul is describing what a room looks like, not only what a soul feels like.

Our longer lists. This is where the verse becomes uncomfortable, because every generation keeps a list of things the kingdom is not made of, and every generation’s list is longer than Paul’s. His was food and drink. Ours runs to music, translations, schooling, dress, politics, and the precise vocabulary a person uses about matters on which we already agree.

What it does not mean. It does not mean bodily things do not matter to God. It means the kingdom’s essence lies in spiritual realities, not external rules.

Does this mean our freedom does not matter? No. Christian liberty is precious; Christ bought it, and Paul fought for it all his life (Galatians 5:1). But it is a means, not the goal. Freedom exists for love, worship and joy, and the moment it is used to wound a brother or to win an argument, it has forgotten what it is for. Prize your freedom enough to protect its good name.

In a sentence. Therefore do not let what you know is good be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. If you are arguing with a Christian about something that is not central, stop and ask: is this serving righteousness, peace and joy? Then run a test that is external and easy. Suppose someone observed your congregation for a month with no access to its statement of faith. What would he conclude the thing was about, from the conversations after the service, from what generates heat, from what people are known for? If the answer is not somewhere near righteousness, peace and joy, the answer is somewhere near food and drink, whatever the modern equivalent has turned out to be.

For worship. The kingdom of God has come, and it is not a matter of menus. It is the reign of the King who gives his righteousness to sinners, who made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and who pours the joy of the Holy Spirit into hearts that were once dead. This is the kingdom Jesus preached and brought, the kingdom that a thief entered on the day he died, the kingdom that is wider than every quarrel and will outlast every empire. Its King is righteous, its peace is unbreakable, and its joy no one will take from us (John 16:22). Blessed be the God who has brought us into it.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men. So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men. So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding.

Whoever thus serves Christ. Thus: by living for righteousness, peace and joy rather than for food. This is how we serve (douleuō, to serve as a slave) Christ. Every disputed meal is, in the end, a question of whom we are serving.

Is acceptable to God and approved by men. Pleasing to God, and recognised as good even by people (12:17). “Approved” (dokimos) means tested and found genuine, like a coin that has been weighed. A believer who lays down his rights for others is pleasing to God, and even the watching world, which understands very little of our doctrine, recognises that kind of love when it sees it.

So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding. “Pursue” (diōkō) is a chase word, the same verb Paul used twice in back-to-back verses two chapters ago: seek to show hospitality, and bless those who persecute you (12:13–14). Peace is not something you refrain your way into. It is hunted down, which implies it moves. And upbuilding (oikodomē) is a builder’s noun. Paul thinks of a congregation as a site with work going on, where every action either adds a course of bricks or removes one (1 Corinthians 14:12; Ephesians 4:29). That is the picture he will complete a verse later with its opposite, when he tells them not to demolish.

The better question. This reframes the question the strong believer is actually asking. The instinctive question about a disputed freedom is: am I allowed? And in this chapter the answer is usually yes, which is exactly why the question is useless. Paul substitutes a different one: what will this build? A thing can be entirely permitted and still take a wall down, and the permission is no help at all in that situation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean peace at the expense of truth. The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable (James 3:17).

Does pursuing peace mean I should never disagree? No. Paul himself has just told the strong that he agrees with them (v. 14). Pursuing peace means disagreeing in a way that builds: speaking the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), choosing the right time and place, listening before answering, refusing to caricature the other view, and never letting a difference on a secondary matter turn into a break in fellowship. Some peace is false, bought by silence about sin or the gospel. But most quarrels in churches are not about the gospel, and on those, the person who makes peace is called a son of God (Matthew 5:9).

In a sentence. Anyone who serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and receives human approval. Let us therefore make every effort to do what leads to peace and to mutual edification.

On a Tuesday. Before you speak about a disputed matter this week, at church, at home or online, ask: what will this build? Then do one deliberate thing that builds someone up: a word of encouragement, a note, an hour of help. Pray for your church’s peace by name, the people and the elders.

For worship. The God of peace is a builder. He is building a house out of living stones, Jew and Gentile, strong and weak, fitted together into a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:20–22), and Christ himself is the cornerstone. He has been at the work for two thousand years and has never laid a stone in the wrong place. And he has made peace with us at the greatest cost a peace was ever made: the blood of his Son. A church that pursues peace is only echoing the God who pursued it first, and who came looking for us when we were his enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.

Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. The work of God is your brother, God’s workmanship (Ephesians 2:10), or the church God is building in him and around him. “Destroy” (katalyō) is the builder’s opposite of verse 19: to tear down, demolish, pull down what has been put up. Paul has now set the two side by side: build up (v. 19), demolish (v. 20). And what is being demolished is not the weak brother’s opinion or his comfort. It is called the work of God. Someone else has been building in that man, patiently, for years, and the warning is about walking onto that site with a hammer over a question of lunch. Do not demolish God’s building for a plate of meat.

Everything is indeed clean. Paul repeats that the strong are right in principle. He never retracts his view to keep the peace.

But it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats. Literally, it is evil for the person who eats with offence. Being right is not enough. How you use your rights matters.

It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble. Love may mean giving up a right altogether, at least in certain company. Wine is mentioned perhaps because it too was used in pagan offerings. And this verse needs handling carefully, because it has been made to do work Paul did not give it. It has been quoted for two centuries as a standing rule about alcohol, and read that way it turns the chapter upside down. Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say wine is unclean; he has just insisted that everything is indeed clean (v. 20), and that nothing is unclean in itself (v. 14). What he says is that abstaining is good where it prevents a brother stumbling. The abstinence is voluntary, situational, and adopted for somebody else’s sake.

Why the restraint cannot become a law. That is precisely why it cannot be turned into a rule for everyone. The moment the strong man’s self-limitation is made a law binding every believer, it has stopped being an act of love and become the very thing this chapter forbids: a scruple imposed on another man’s conscience. The chapter asks the free to restrain themselves. It never asks them to legislate the restraint.

Where Christians differ: alcohol. Some say this verse requires total abstinence from alcohol for all Christians. Others say Christians can drink freely regardless of others. Verdict: Scripture presents wine as a gift of God (Psalm 104:15; John 2:1–11) and forbids drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18; 13:13). Drinking in moderation is a matter of Christian liberty. But love will gladly give it up where it would cause a brother to stumble, for instance around someone struggling with alcohol. Those who choose to abstain may do so for the Lord, and should not judge those who drink moderately.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the strong must give up their liberty forever and everywhere because someone somewhere disapproves. Paul speaks of situations where a real brother might be led into sin.

Should I tell people that I am holding back for their sake? Usually not. The practical form of this verse is smaller and harder than a policy. It is the decision, made quietly and usually noticed by nobody, that at this table, with this person, on this evening, you will not have the thing you are perfectly entitled to have. And you will not announce that you are not having it, which is the part most of us fail. A sacrifice that is advertised turns into a rebuke, and makes the weak brother feel like a burden. If he asks, answer simply and kindly. Otherwise let love work in silence.

What if a friend is fighting an addiction? Then this verse applies with full force. If someone near you is recovering from alcohol, gambling, or any other bondage, your freedom in that area should be laid down gladly whenever you are with him, and probably for longer and more widely than you think necessary. Do not make him the one who has to ask. Ask yourself what would make it easiest for him to stand, and do that, without fuss. That is not legalism. It is love carrying a brother’s burden (Galatians 6:2).

In a sentence. Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. All food is clean, but it is wrong for a person to eat anything that causes someone else to stumble. It is better not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything else that will cause your brother to fall.

On a Tuesday. Is there a freedom you enjoy that someone near you finds hard? Consider laying it down when you are with him, quietly, for love. Then thank God that you have something to lay down, and someone worth laying it down for.

For worship. The brother at your table is the work of God. The Father chose him before the world began, the Son died for him, and the Spirit has been at work in him for years, patiently, laying stone on stone. What God has begun in him, God will finish (Philippians 1:6). Think what it means that the Almighty should spend such care on a single weak believer: no detail of his life too small for God’s attention, no scruple too slight for God’s patience. And the God who builds is the God who gave up more than wine and meat. He gave up his only Son, so that the work of grace in his people would never be demolished.

verseByVerse.quote: The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves.

The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. The faith here is your conviction about liberty: that all foods are clean. You do not need to flaunt it. Enjoy it before God, privately, without making it a test of fellowship. And it is worth being clear about what this is not. Paul is not telling the strong to hide their convictions, be evasive, or pretend to scruples they do not have; he has just stated his own position in the plainest terms (v. 14). What he is forbidding is the display. There is a kind of liberty that is not enjoyed so much as exhibited, and needs an audience of the scrupulous to be fully satisfying.

Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves. “Blessed” means happy, in God’s favour. The happy person is one whose conscience does not condemn him for what he does. A clear conscience is a great gift (Acts 24:16). It is one of the most quietly attractive sentences in the letter. The happy man is the one who can do the thing and then simply get on with the evening: no small internal argument afterwards, no rehearsing of the justification, no wondering at midnight whether it was all right.

A mercy for the scrupulous. That is a real and underrated mercy, and it is worth naming for the scrupulous reader who has never had it. A great many sincere Christians conduct a running trial of themselves over things God has not forbidden, and the verdict is always appealed.
