Paul calls the man free of that blessed, which tells you that God regards a settled conscience as a gift and not as laxity.

Can a quiet conscience be wrong? Yes, and the guard matters, because the sentence can be misread as: if you feel fine, you are fine. Paul is speaking of a conscience taught by the gospel, not of one that has simply gone quiet. Scripture knows the other kind: the conscience that stops objecting because it has been ignored for long enough, consciences that are seared (1 Timothy 4:2). The absence of self-accusation is a blessing when it comes from clarity. It is a symptom when it comes from numbness, and the difference is usually visible to everyone except the man himself. The safeguard is to keep your conscience under the Word, and to listen when wise friends raise a concern.

Isn’t keeping my convictions private a kind of hypocrisy? No. Hypocrisy is pretending to be what you are not. Paul is not asking you to pretend to scruples you do not have, or to deny your view when asked. He is asking you not to parade your freedom where it would wound. A man who does not order a drink at a meal with a brother who struggles is not lying; he is loving. Your convictions remain yours, openly held before God, and you can explain them gently to anyone who sincerely wants to know.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith in Christ should be kept private. Paul speaks only of convictions about matters indifferent. The gospel itself is to be confessed with the mouth before the world (10:9–10).

In a sentence. So whatever you believe about these things, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves.

On a Tuesday. Notice whether there is any freedom you enjoy more when someone disapproving is watching. If so, that pleasure is the sign Paul is warning about; quietly drop the display. And if you are the scrupulous one who keeps trying yourself at midnight over things God has not forbidden, take one such matter to Scripture and to a wise friend this week, settle it, and then receive the blessing of this verse: stop appealing the verdict.

For worship. The blessing of a clear conscience is not something we could ever have given ourselves. Our consciences had every reason to condemn us, and they did. Then the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleansed our consciences from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). Now there is no condemnation (8:1), and the believer can lie down at night in peace, not because he is innocent but because he is forgiven. Thank God for the freedom bought for us in Christ, and for the quiet heart that knows it is at peace with God.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because the eating is not from faith. For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. — Romans 14:23
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because the eating is not from faith. For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.

But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats. The word behind has doubts (diakrinō) is worth seeing, because it describes the man exactly. It means to waver, to be divided in mind: the same root Paul used for judging in verse 13, here turned inward on a person at war with himself. He is not uncertain in the abstract. He is eating the thing while one half of him objects, and Paul says the verdict on that is already in. If someone is unsure whether something is right but does it anyway, he is condemned, by his own conscience and before God. He acted against what he believed was God’s will.

Because the eating is not from faith. Faith here is a settled conviction before God that this is right. And the reason given is precise. Not because the food was wrong; Paul has said twice in this chapter that it is not (vv. 14, 20). The condemnation attaches to the division, not to the dinner.

For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. A general principle. If you cannot do something in confidence that it pleases God, do not do it. Acting against conscience trains you to ignore God’s voice. It is the sentence that has travelled further than any other in this chapter. It has done enormous work in Christian theology: Augustine used it against the idea that the virtues of unbelievers are truly virtuous, and the Reformers took it up as proof that no act, however decent, pleases God apart from faith in Christ (Hebrews 11:6; Westminster 16.7). That use is not a distortion; the principle really does reach that far. Without faith it is impossible to please him.

Does this mean I am sinning whenever I am unsure? No. The verse terrifies people, and the terror is usually caused by reading it out of the room it was written in. It does not mean that every action not preceded by a conscious act of faith is damnable, or you would sin every time you changed gear. It does not mean you must feel certain before you may act; feelings of certainty are not faith and often accompany foolishness. It does not mean that being unsure about a hard question is itself sinful; Paul has just spent a chapter making room for people who are unsure. What it does mean, in context, is this: do not do the disputed thing while you believe it to be wrong. A man eats what he thinks is unclean, because the company made it awkward not to, and the eating is a small act of unbelief: he has acted on the pressure of the room rather than on his conviction before God.

The cure is not paralysis. Verse 5 already gave it: each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. The answer to doubt is not to stop acting; it is to stop being divided: to go and find out, to be taught, to reach a settled position and then act from it. Paul is not asking the doubting man to do less. He is asking him to come to a conviction, which is more work than either abstaining or complying. Freedom that bypasses the conscience is not liberation but another kind of bondage. Real growth moves the conscience forward through teaching, example and patient fellowship, not through the bulldozer of a confident majority.

Textual note: the doxology. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert 16:25–27 here, at the end of chapter 14. Others place it after 15:33, and most at the end of chapter 16. The best evidence places it at the end of chapter 16, where the ESV prints it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean conscience is infallible. Conscience can be wrongly trained and needs to be taught by Scripture. But until it is better taught, do not go against it.

How do I train my conscience? By putting it under God’s Word. Read Scripture widely, so that you know both what God commands and what he leaves free; many tender consciences are bound by rules that came from a family, a church culture or a past fear rather than from the Bible. Ask, of each scruple: where does God say this? Learn from mature Christians, past and present. Pray for understanding. And be patient: a conscience grows the way a person grows, slowly. Never force it to go faster than conviction, and never let it fall asleep.

In a sentence. But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because his eating is not from faith; and everything that does not come from faith is sin.

On a Tuesday. When in doubt, don’t. Then go to Scripture, so that your conscience can be better taught, and come to a settled conviction you can act on with thanksgiving.

For worship. Notice where the chapter has arrived. It opened with a command to welcome a man whose conscience was tighter than yours, and it closes by insisting that his conscience must not be violated, not even by a truth. Paul has spent twenty-three verses defending the right of a brother he disagrees with to go on disagreeing with him until he is genuinely persuaded. That is what he means by strength, and it is a reflection of God’s own patience. The Lord does not drive his children; he leads them. He is gentle with the doubting, and he does not break the bruised reed or quench the smouldering wick. He teaches the conscience he has cleansed, and he is willing to take years over it. And everything that pleases him begins with faith: faith that he himself gives, in a Saviour he himself provided. From first to last, our acceptable obedience is his gift. To him be the glory for ever.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert 16:25–27 here, at the end of chapter 14. Others place it after 15:33, and a few omit it. The variation probably shows that the letter circulated in more than one form in the early church; but the doxology is found in almost all manuscripts, and its natural place is at the close of the letter, where the ESV prints it.

14.text: <sup>1</sup>As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions.<sup>2</sup>One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.<sup>3</sup>Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him.<sup>4</sup>Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.<sup>5</sup>One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind.<sup>6</sup>The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.<sup>7</sup>For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself.<sup>8</sup>For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.<sup>9</sup>For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.<sup>10</sup>Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God;<sup>11</sup>for it is written, “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.”<sup>12</sup>So then each of us will give an account of himself to God.<sup>13</sup>Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother.<sup>14</sup>I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean.<sup>15</sup>For if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. 15.title: Unity, Hope, and the Mission of Paul
15.overview:
Romans 15 brings together three threads: the conclusion of the weak/strong argument (vv. 1–13), the personal explanation of Paul's apostolic mission (vv. 14–21), and his travel plans and prayer requests (vv. 22–33). The chapter is held together by the theme of the worldwide scope of the gospel — Christ's own example of self-giving (vv. 1–3), the Gentile mission as the fulfilment of Old Testament prophecy (vv. 9–12), and Paul's ambition to preach where Christ has not yet been named (vv. 20–21).

The opening section (vv. 1–13) concludes the argument of chapter 14 by pointing to Christ as the model of the strong bearing with the failings of the weak. Christ did not please himself (v. 3) — He endured the reproaches of others for their sake. The strong who follow his example are not making a heroic sacrifice; they are imitating their Lord. And the doxological prayer of vv. 5–6 and 13 frames the whole argument in worship: the God of endurance, encouragement, hope, and peace is the one who enables the unity for which Paul prays.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Example of Christ and the God of Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves" (v. 1). Paul has waited until now to identify himself with the strong — and he identifies himself only to place the obligation of the strong front and centre. The strong do not have the right to demand that the weak keep up with them; they have the obligation to bear with the weak, to build them up, to serve their good. "Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up" (v. 2).

The model is Christ: "For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, 'The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me'" (v. 3, quoting Psalm 69:9). The Son of God did not come to be served but to serve — to bear not only the sins of the weak but their reproaches, their insults, the consequences of their failure. The one who is most perfectly strong became the servant of all. The Christian who follows this pattern — bearing the burdens of others rather than asserting the rights of the free — is walking in the footsteps of the one who bore our ultimate burden at Calvary.

The doxological climax of the section (vv. 5–6, 13) frames the whole practical argument in prayer and worship. Paul's wish is not merely that the Roman Christians be nice to each other; it is that they glorify God together with one voice (v. 6) — the strong and the weak, Jew and Gentile, all singing the same praise to the same God. And the God of hope fills with all joy and peace in believing (v. 13) — not the meagre joy of people who have resolved their differences, but the overflowing joy of people who have been given hope by the Spirit.

Between the example of Christ and that benediction stand four more things, and they carry the argument to its conclusion. The first is v. 4, which explains why Paul has just settled a first-century dispute about food by quoting a psalm: whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. The Old Testament was written for the benefit of readers who did not yet exist, and its stated product is not information but hope.

The second is v. 7, and it is the summit of everything since 14:1: welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God. The same verb Paul used in 14:1 for receiving the weak, and in 14:3 of God receiving him, now appears a third time with Christ himself as the measure. The strong were told to welcome; here everyone is told to welcome everyone, on the pattern of a welcome none of them deserved.

The third is vv. 8–9, where Paul states how one Christ serves two peoples. He became a servant to the circumcised to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs — that is, to demonstrate God’s truthfulness — and he did it so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. The two halves are not symmetrical, and the asymmetry is the point: Israel receives a kept promise, the nations receive sheer mercy, and neither group has grounds to look down on the other.

The fourth is the chain of quotations in vv. 9–12, drawn deliberately from every part of the Hebrew Bible — the Law (Deuteronomy 32:43), the Writings (Psalm 18:49; Psalm 117:1) and the Prophets (Isaiah 11:10). Paul is not producing a proof text. He is showing that the inclusion of the nations was the settled expectation of the whole canon, and the chain ends on the word the benediction will pick up: in him will the Gentiles hope.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ as the Model of Solidarity with the Weak

The Christological grounding of the strong's obligation in Romans 15:3 is one of Paul's most important ethical moves. Ethics derived from the example of Christ is not mere imitation-of-a-good-man moralism; it is participation in the pattern of the one who is Lord, whose servanthood was the shape of his sovereignty, whose self-giving is the source of the Christian's capacity for self-giving. When Paul says "bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2), the law of Christ is precisely this: the pattern of the one who bore what he did not owe so that we might be released from what we could not pay.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The unity Paul prays for in vv. 5–6 — "that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" — was not an abstract aspiration. The Roman church had real divisions: Jewish and Gentile believers, strong and weak, people from different social classes and national backgrounds. The one voice of praise was the visible, social miracle that would demonstrate to the watching city of Rome that something genuinely new had entered the world. Now: The unity of diverse believers in genuine, cross-cultural, cross-social worship is still the most powerful apologetic the church has available. A community of people who have every reason to be divided — by race, class, culture, education, politics — worshipping together with one voice glorifies the God whose gospel is the only power that creates such unity.

verseByVerse.quote: We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up.

Meaning first. Romans 15 has two parts. In verses 1–13, Paul finishes the argument about the strong and the weak that began in 14:1. The strong must bear with the weak, as Christ did not please himself (vv. 1–6); and all must welcome one another as Christ welcomed them, for Christ came to serve the Jews and to bring the Gentiles to praise God, as the Scriptures foretold (vv. 7–12). He ends with a prayer that the God of hope will fill them with joy and peace (v. 13). In verses 14–33, Paul begins to close the letter. He explains why he wrote so boldly: his priestly calling to offer the Gentiles to God (vv. 14–21). Then he shares his travel plans: first Jerusalem with the gift from the Gentile churches, then Rome, then Spain, and he asks them to pray for him (vv. 22–33). Theology and mission, love and plans, all serve one end: the glory of God among the nations. And the chapter that settles a quarrel about dinner ends up in the throne room, with every nation on earth singing.

Who are the strong and the weak? Chapter 14 has introduced them. The weak are believers, most likely many of them Jewish Christians and those influenced by them, whose consciences would not yet let them eat certain foods or ignore certain holy days (14:2, 5). The strong are those who understand that in Christ nothing is unclean in itself (14:14) and feel free. Paul is not describing weak faith in Christ against strong faith in Christ; both are trusting the same Saviour. He is describing how much freedom a conscience has grasped on matters God has left free. And notice that the weak are not the people with the worst morals. They are often the most careful people in the room.

We who are strong have an obligation. Paul counts himself among the strong, and then immediately turns the identification into a duty rather than a privilege. The strong do not have the right to lord their freedom over the weak; they have an obligation to them. The word (opheilō) is a debt word, and it completes a thread that runs the length of the letter. Paul opened by calling himself a debtor to Greeks and to barbarians (1:14); he told this church two chapters ago to owe no one anything except to love one another (13:8); and here the strong are said to owe the weak. Three times the language of the ledger, and every time the balance runs the wrong way round from what the strong would expect. They thought their knowledge made them creditors. It makes them debtors.

To bear with the failings of the weak. And “bear with” is too polite for the verb. Bastazō means to pick up and carry. It is the word for shouldering a load, the same one Paul uses when he tells the Galatians to carry one another’s burdens and so fulfil the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2), and the same one John uses of Jesus going out carrying his own cross (John 19:17). Not tolerate. Not endure with a fixed expression. Carry. The strong are not to put up with the weak grudgingly, sighing at the inconvenience; they are to get underneath them and take the weight.

Their failings, not their convictions. Then notice what Paul calls the thing being carried: not their views but their failings (asthenēmata), their weaknesses, their scruples and tender consciences. Paul does not soften his opinion in order to be kind. He has already said plainly that nothing is unclean in itself (14:14), and he says here that the weak brother’s scruple is a weakness. He simply refuses to let being right function as permission. That is the whole difficult art of this passage, and it is rarer than either of its counterfeits. One counterfeit pretends the other man is right in order to keep the peace. The other tells him he is wrong and treats that as the end of its responsibility. Paul does neither. He thinks the weak brother mistaken and picks him up anyway.

And not to please ourselves. Strength is for serving others, not for doing whatever we like. This is the organising principle of the Christian life, and it overturns the instinct of the whole world: not self-gratification but the neighbour’s good. The gospel produces people whose first question in any situation is not what do I get, but what does my neighbour need. Every gift God gives, whether knowledge, maturity, health, money or a robust conscience, comes with a direction attached, and the direction is outward.

Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up. Pleasing the neighbour does not mean flattering him or giving in to every demand, but seeking his real good: “to build him up” (oikodomē, edification, the word for putting up a house). And one guard is needed, because please your neighbour is one step away from a disaster. Paul is not commending the anxious accommodation that shapes itself to whatever the room requires. The man who told the Galatians that if he were still trying to please people he would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10) is not now recommending it. The qualifier does the work: please him for his good, to build him up. Pleasing aimed at his growth is love. Pleasing aimed at his approval is fear, and the two are almost indistinguishable from outside and never confused on the inside.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the strong must give up the truth about Christian liberty. It means they use their liberty for love. Paul has not withdrawn a single word of 14:14. The strong man is still right; he is simply no longer allowed to make his rightness the most important thing in the room.

What if the weak brother is using his scruple to run everyone else? This is a real situation, and Paul himself faced it. Bearing with a tender conscience is different from surrendering to a man who turns his scruple into a rule for the church or a test of salvation. When false brothers demanded that Titus be circumcised, Paul did not yield for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved (Galatians 2:3–5). The difference lies in what is being claimed. A weak brother says, I cannot do this with a clear conscience. A legalist says, you cannot be right with God unless you live as I do. The first you carry gently, often for years. The second you resist, kindly and firmly, because the gospel itself is at stake. And both are to be loved.

Does this mean I can never use my freedom? No. Paul’s point is not that the strong must live permanently by the weakest conscience in the church, but that they must never use their freedom in a way that wounds a brother or draws him into sinning against his conscience (14:15, 20–21). Most of the time your liberty harms no one, and you may enjoy God’s gifts with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4). The question is not whether this is allowed, but who is at the table and what it will do to him. Keep your freedom between yourself and God (14:22) when using it would hurt someone, and use it freely when it would not.

In a sentence. We who are strong ought to bear with the failings of the weak and not to please ourselves. Each of us should please our neighbours for their good, to build them up.

On a Tuesday. The test is about direction rather than behaviour. Take the last time you gave way to another Christian. Did you do it because it would help him, or because it would stop him being difficult with you? The action is identical either way. Only one of them is in this verse. Then think of the person in your church whose conscience is tighter than yours, the one whose rules you privately find tiresome. Ask what it would look like this week to carry him rather than manage him: a meal planned around what he can eat with a clear conscience, a joke about his scruples left unmade, a kindness he will never know you gave. Use your strength today, whether in knowledge, maturity or resources, to carry someone weaker, not to please yourself.

For worship. There is only one truly strong one in the universe, and he did not use his strength to please himself. The Lord who needs nothing from anyone stooped to carry the weakest people who ever lived, and we are those people. He has been bearing our failings, not tolerating them but shouldering them, since the day he first took us up, and he has never once put us down. Every strong believer in Rome was himself a weak thing carried. That is the glory of God in Christ: omnipotence that bends low, and owes us nothing, and carries us anyway.

parallels.desc: bear one another’s burdens

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, "The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.”

For Christ did not please himself. The supreme example, and Paul reaches for it without warning, in the middle of a discussion about vegetables. That is the way his mind works: no question is too small to be settled at the cross. Christ, who had every right, gave them all up. He came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45); though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:5–8). If he did not please himself, how can we insist on our rights over food? The cross is both the motive and the measure of Christian self-giving.

A whole life of interruptions. And Christ did not please himself is a startling piece of understatement when you put flesh on it. It meant crowds arriving when he had gone away to be alone, and his having compassion on them anyway (Mark 6:31–34). It meant a conversation with a woman at a well when he was tired and thirsty (John 4:6–7). It meant no reliable place to lay his head, for years (Luke 9:58). It meant washing the feet of men who would run away that same night (John 13:5). The phrase covers a whole life in which the interruption was never treated as an interruption, because the people who caused it were the reason he had come.

But as it is written, The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me. Paul quotes Psalm 69:9, a psalm of the suffering righteous one, which the New Testament applies to Christ again and again (John 2:17; 15:25; 19:28–29; Romans 11:9–10). Look at the line he chose, because it is stranger than it first appears. The you is God. The me is Christ. The insults were aimed at the Father, and they landed on the Son. That is the mechanism of the cross stated in a single line: hostility directed at God arriving somewhere else, absorbed by someone who was not its target. He bore the scorn and hatred the world aims at God, and at Calvary he bore far more: the curse that our sin deserved (Galatians 3:13). He carried a burden infinitely heavier than any the strong are asked to carry.

The same psalm twice. Psalm 69 has already appeared in this letter, back in chapter 11, where its words of judgment were turned on those who rejected the sufferer it describes (11:9–10). Paul goes to the same psalm for both: the psalm of the righteous man crushed by hostility that was not his own supplies both the judgment on those who refuse him and the example for those who follow him. The one who bore the reproach is either your pattern or your judge.

How can a psalm of David be about Christ? David wrote Psalm 69 out of his own suffering, as a king hated without cause. But David was more than a private man; he was the anointed king, the one through whom God had promised a greater Son (2 Samuel 7:12–16). His sufferings were a sketch, and Jesus is the finished portrait. The disciples saw it the day he cleared the temple and remembered that it was written, zeal for your house will consume me (John 2:17), the first half of the very verse Paul quotes here. The Spirit who spoke through David knew whose voice would finally fill the psalm (Acts 2:30–31; 1 Peter 1:11). So when Paul reads the psalm as the words of Christ, he is not spiritualising it. He is reading it the way its Author meant.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ never enjoyed anything, or had no joy. He went to weddings and dinners, and for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). He did the Father’s will with delight. But he never put his own comfort first. Nor does it mean Christians must say yes to every request. Jesus withdrew to pray, refused to be made king by a crowd (John 6:15), and would not do miracles on demand for Herod. He did not please himself, but neither did he please everyone. He pleased his Father, and the good of others was always in view.

In a sentence. For even Christ did not please himself, but, as it is written: “The insults of those who insult you have fallen on me.”

On a Tuesday. Where the argument lands is not primarily a demand. The strong believer being asked to give up a lawful dinner is being invited into something the Son of God has already done at a scale that makes the request look small, and the invitation is the honour, not the imposition. So take the thing you are being asked to give up this week for someone else’s sake, the evening, the preference, the right to have the last word, and say it plainly to yourself: this is a very small portion of the road he walked for me. Then walk it gladly.

For worship. The insults were aimed at the Father, and the Son stepped into their path. He did not merely tolerate the reproach; he received it, all of it, in his own body, and let it stop there. The mockery at the foot of the cross, the spitting, the crown of thorns: every one of them was meant for God, and every one fell on Christ. And beneath the visible reproach lay the invisible one, the wrath that our sin had earned, which fell on him too, so that it would never fall on us. Blessed be the Son who did not please himself, who pleased the Father by bearing what we deserved, and who still calls it joy.

parallels.desc: the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me

verseByVerse.quote: For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus,

For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction. Notice where this sentence sits. Paul has just settled a live pastoral dispute by quoting a psalm, and verse 4 is his justification for having done so. It is a footnote to his own method, and it tells you what he thinks he is doing every time he reaches back into the Old Testament. “Instruction” (didaskalia) is teaching. The whole Old Testament was written for Christians too. It is not just ancient history but God’s word to us (1 Corinthians 10:11; 2 Timothy 3:16). And the claim is a large one: those texts were written for the benefit of readers who did not exist when the ink was wet. The man who wrote Psalm 69 was describing his own misery. Paul says he was also, without knowing it, writing for a mixed congregation in Rome arguing about meat a thousand years later.

That through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. “Endurance” (hypomonē) is steadfastness under weight; “encouragement” (paraklēsis) is comfort and exhortation together, the voice of one who comes alongside. Both come through the Scriptures, and their goal is hope. That is not the chain we expect. Paul does not say the Scriptures were given to produce knowledge, or even obedience. He says the output is hope. That is a strange thing to say about a library of ancient documents, and it is only true because of what they are a record of: a long series of occasions on which God did what he said he would do, generally later and stranger than anyone wanted. Abraham waited twenty-five years for a son. Joseph spent years in a pit and a prison. Israel waited four centuries in Egypt and seventy years in Babylon. Every time, God kept his word.

Why endurance comes before hope. You do not read the Bible and instantly feel hopeful. You read it, find that the waiting in it is nearly always longer than seems reasonable, and slowly become the kind of person who can wait. The hope is on the far side of that. Scripture trains endurance by showing you the God who has never once failed a waiting people, and endurance trained in that school grows into hope (5:3–5).

May the God of endurance and encouragement. A prayer, and it does something quiet with the two words. Having said that Scripture gives endurance and encouragement, Paul immediately calls God the God of endurance and encouragement. The book hands over what its Author is. God is the source of the endurance and comfort that Scripture brings, because Scripture is his voice. Which is also a caution: a person can read the words and acquire the information without ever meeting the one whose character they are (John 5:39–40).

Grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus. Harmony is literally to think the same thing, as in 12:16. In accord with Christ Jesus: according to his example and his will. Unity is not uniformity of opinion on food, but one mind about Christ. The strong and the weak will go on disagreeing about the menu; what Paul prays for is that they will be of one mind about the Lord who welcomed them both, and that this will be loud enough to drown out the menu.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament is only about us. It is first about God and his Christ (Luke 24:27, 44). But because it is about him, it gives us hope.

If the Old Testament was written for us, do all its laws still bind us? Not in the same way. Everything in the Old Testament is for our instruction, but not everything in it is a command addressed to us. The ceremonial laws, the sacrifices, food laws and festivals, were shadows fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1), which is exactly why the strong in Rome were right that foods are clean. The civil laws governed Israel as a nation and teach us their underlying justice. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still shows us God’s will for every person (13:8–10; Westminster 19.3–5). So read every page asking what it shows you of God, of Christ and of his promises, and you will find instruction even in Leviticus.

What if I read the Bible and still do not feel hopeful? Keep reading, and change what you are looking for. Hope in this verse is not a feeling you get from a passage on a good morning; it is a settled expectation that grows as you watch God keep his promises page after page. Read the long stories, not only the comforting verses: Joseph, Ruth, the exile and return, and above all the Gospels, where the darkest Friday is followed by Sunday. Pray the psalms of lament, which are in the Bible precisely for people who cannot feel hope yet (Psalm 42; 88). And read with others, because encouragement often reaches us through a brother’s voice reading the same words.

In a sentence. For everything that was written in the past was written to teach us, so that through the endurance taught in the Scriptures and the encouragement they provide we might have hope. May the God who gives endurance and encouragement give you the same attitude of mind toward each other that Christ Jesus had,

On a Tuesday. The test is a plain question about motive. Why do you open the Bible? To find out what it says, to check a position you already hold, to have something to give somebody else, or because you need to be able to keep going? The last of those is what this verse says it is for, and most of us would have to admit it is not usually why we went. So this week, read the Old Testament not as a dusty record but as God’s word for you. Choose one story of waiting, and ask how long it took God to keep his word, what the people thought in the middle, and how it ended. Look for his faithfulness, and take hope.

For worship. God is not only the giver of endurance; he is the God of endurance, patient beyond all our imagining, who carried his promise through Abraham’s old age, through Egypt and the wilderness, through the fall of David’s house and the long silence before Bethlehem, and never once let it drop. He is the God of encouragement, who comes alongside his people in their grief and speaks. And he wrote all of it down, centuries in advance, for us: for readers he already knew by name, who would need on some ordinary morning to be told that he keeps his word. The Bible is the record of a faithfulness that has never failed, and its Author has not changed.

verseByVerse.quote: that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.

That together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. The goal of unity is worship. “Together” (homothymadon) means with one passion, the word Luke uses of the first believers praying and breaking bread (Acts 1:14; 2:46), and “with one voice” is literally with one mouth. A divided church cannot praise God with one voice. When strong and weak, Jew and Gentile, sing together, God is glorified. That is a striking place for two chapters of conflict resolution to end. Not in a settlement, not in agreement, not even in mutual respect. In a room full of people who still disagree about the disputed thing, making one sound.

The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Paul names God by his relation to the Son. The God the Roman Christians worship is not a general deity to whom Jews and Gentiles bring their separate religions; he is the Father of Jesus, and he is known through Jesus. The one thing the strong and the weak share is the thing that matters most: the same Father, through the same Son.

Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you. Verse 7 is the summit of an argument that has been climbing since 14:1, and the way to see it is to follow one verb. “Welcome” (proslambanō) means to receive someone into your company, into your home and your table. In 14:1 the strong were told to welcome the man whose conscience was tighter than theirs. In 14:3 the reason given was that God has welcomed him. Here the same word arrives a third time, and now it runs in every direction at once, welcome one another, with Christ himself as the standard.

As Christ has welcomed you. And that standard is not vague, because this letter has already specified it. Christ welcomed you while you were ungodly (4:5), while you were still weak (5:6), while you were still a sinner (5:8), while you were an enemy (5:10). That is the measure now laid against your dealings with the believer whose views on a secondary matter irritate you. The comparison is not flattering to anybody. He did not welcome the promising, or the nearly persuaded, or those who had come most of the way and needed a hand over the last stretch. He welcomed the ungodly, the weak, the enemy, and he did it while the welcome was still being refused. Which quietly removes the last available excuse. Nobody in Rome was being asked to welcome someone worse than they had been when they were welcomed. Nobody since has been.

For the glory of God. Then the purpose clause, which is easy to read past. Christ welcomed us for God’s glory; and when we welcome one another, God is glorified again. The welcome is not primarily for the comfort of the person received, useful as that is. It is for God’s reputation. A church where people who would never otherwise sit together eat together is a living advertisement for the grace that brought them there.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we welcome unrepentant sin into the church (1 Corinthians 5). It means we welcome all whom Christ has welcomed.

Does unity mean we have to agree about everything? No. Paul is describing a church that still disagrees about food and days, and he prays for one voice, not one opinion on every question. Christians must agree on the gospel itself: who Christ is, what he has done, and how a sinner is made right with God (Galatians 1:8–9). On secondary matters, such as the matters of conscience in chapter 14, or how to school children, or styles of music, or whether to drink wine, believers can hold different convictions and still worship side by side. Even on weightier differences, such as baptism, where churches must decide their own practice, we can honour brothers who differ as true brothers in Christ. The mark of maturity is not that you have no convictions, but that your convictions do not stop you singing with someone who holds different ones.

Who counts as someone Christ has welcomed? Anyone who credibly confesses Jesus as Lord, trusts him alone for salvation, and is not living in open, unrepentant sin. You do not have to see into his heart; you receive what he professes and how he lives. That includes the believer who is socially awkward, the one from a very different background, the new convert whose life is still a mess but who is fighting, and the one whose politics you find hard to bear. If Christ has received him, the table belongs to Christ, and you are not its doorkeeper.

In a sentence. so that with one mind and one voice you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you, in order to bring praise to God.

On a Tuesday. Think of the Christian you find hardest to welcome: not an enemy of the gospel, but a brother whose habits, opinions or manner grate on you. Ask the question this verse puts to you: was I easier to welcome when Christ welcomed me? Then do one concrete thing this week that a welcome would do: invite him to eat, sit beside him on Sunday, ask him a real question and listen to the answer. And when you sing in church, look around: Christ welcomed every one of these people.

For worship. There is nobody in any congregation on earth who is a harder case than the one Christ has already taken in. He opened the door to us when we were barring it from the inside, and he did not wait for us to become presentable. He welcomed us at the cost of his own blood, for the glory of his Father, and he has never once regretted it. Every time a church sings with one voice, the strong and the weak and the people who will never agree about the menu, heaven hears the sound the cross was meant to make: one family, praising one Father, through one Son.

verseByVerse.quote: For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God's truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, "Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God’s truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, “Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name.”

For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised. Weigh the word Paul uses for what Christ became. Not a teacher of the circumcised, not a Messiah for them, but a servant (diakonos), the ordinary word for someone who waits on others at table. Christ came first to the Jews, born under the law, ministering in Israel (Matthew 15:24; Galatians 4:4). And Paul is writing to a congregation with a Gentile majority that has already needed warning against arrogance toward Jewish believers (11:18). He tells them that the Lord they worship took the role of a servant to the very people they are inclined to look down on.

To show God’s truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs. Truthfulness (alētheia) is God’s faithfulness to his word. By coming to Israel, Christ proved God true to his promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. All the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). The God who swore an oath two thousand years before Bethlehem kept it to the letter, in a manger, in the land he had named, from the tribe he had named, in the line of the king he had named.

And in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. Then the asymmetry, which is exact and worth slowing down for. To the circumcised, Christ came to confirm promises. To the Gentiles he came so that they might glorify God for his mercy. Two different words because two different situations: Israel had promises to be kept, and the nations had none. Nothing had been sworn to the Gentiles in the way it had been sworn to Israel. They were strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12). Though the oath to Abraham that all nations would be blessed in his offspring (Genesis 22:18) meant that mercy to the nations was always the plan, the Gentiles themselves receive on the only basis available to people with no claim.

A rebuke and a comfort. Which is a rebuke and a comfort in the same sentence, depending on who is reading. For the Gentile believer tempted to feel like the main story: you are here on mercy, and mercy by definition was not owed. For the Jewish believer watching his people’s privileges apparently pass to strangers: the promises were not cancelled, they were confirmed, and Christ took the servant’s place to do it. Both have reason to praise, and neither has reason to boast.

As it is written, Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name. Paul quotes Psalm 18:49 (also 2 Samuel 22:50), David’s song of victory after the LORD delivered him from all his enemies. David, the king, praises God among the nations. And in Christ, the Son of David, the line becomes his own: the Messiah stands among the Gentiles and leads their praise of the Father. Hebrews puts the same thought in Christ’s mouth: in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise (Hebrews 2:12). When a Gentile church sings, it is not starting a song of its own. It is joining one its King is already singing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Gentiles were an afterthought. God’s plan always included them (Genesis 12:3), as the following quotations show.

Were the Jews not saved by mercy too? Yes. Paul’s contrast is about the route, not the ground. Every Jew who was ever saved was saved by mercy; the promises themselves were mercy, given to a people who did not deserve them (Deuteronomy 7:7–8), and Paul has spent chapters 9 to 11 insisting that Israel’s salvation rests on God’s gracious choice (11:5–6). The difference is that Israel had been given the promise in advance, so Christ’s coming showed God keeping his word. The Gentiles had been given no such word to hold, so his coming to them could only look like sheer kindness. Both are mercy. One is mercy keeping a promise; the other is mercy with nothing to keep.

In a sentence. For Paul tells you that Christ has become a servant of the Jews on behalf of God’s truth, so that the promises made to the patriarchs might be confirmed and, moreover, that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written: “Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles; I will sing the praises of your name.”

On a Tuesday. God keeps his promises. The same Christ who confirmed the promises to Abraham will keep every promise he has made to you. So take one promise you are struggling to believe this week, that he will never leave you (Hebrews 13:5), that he works all things for good to those who love him (8:28), that he will finish what he began (Philippians 1:6), and set it beside the promise to Abraham that waited two thousand years and was kept to the letter. And if you are a Gentile believer, let one prayer this week be nothing but thanks that you were shown mercy you had no claim to.

For worship. The Lord of glory became a servant at table. He took the lowest place in Israel to prove that God’s word is true, and in doing so he threw the doors open to nations who had never been promised anything. The patriarchs saw it from far off and greeted it (Hebrews 11:13); we have seen it arrive. God is truthful, for he kept every word he swore. God is merciful, for he gave what he never swore. And Christ is the place where both meet: the faithfulness of God to Israel and the mercy of God to the world, joined in one servant, who now leads every nation in praise of his Father.

parallels.desc: I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations

verseByVerse.quote: And again it says, "Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people." And again, "Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And again it says, “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people.” And again, “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him.”

And again it says, Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people. From Deuteronomy 32:43 in the Greek translation, at the end of the Song of Moses. Gentiles rejoicing together with Israel: exactly the unity Paul wants in Rome. And the Song of Moses has a history in this letter. This is its third appearance. Paul took the jealousy line from it at 10:19 and the vengeance line at 12:19, and here he takes its closing summons to the nations. The song God gave Israel to sing about their own future, a song mostly about their unfaithfulness and his faithfulness, turns out to contain the Gentiles as well.

With his people. Above all, watch the preposition. Not instead of them. Not in a separate room, not in a successor arrangement. Alongside, in the same congregation, singing the same thing: which is precisely the picture Paul has been trying to produce in Rome for two chapters, and it turns out Moses got there first.

And again, Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him. From Psalm 117:1, and Psalm 117 is a small joke of providence. It is the shortest chapter in the Bible, two verses long, and the whole of it is a call for the nations to praise the God of Israel, for his steadfast love toward us is great, and his faithfulness endures for ever. Something the size of a sentence has been sitting in the middle of the Hebrew hymnbook for centuries, saying exactly this. And note the reason it gives: God’s love toward us, Israel, is the reason the nations should praise. What God does for his people is meant to set the whole world singing.

The whole Old Testament agrees. The four quotations are not a pile. Paul has taken one from the Law (Deuteronomy 32), two from the Writings (Psalms 18 and 117) and one from the Prophets (Isaiah 11, in v. 12): every division of the Hebrew Bible. He is not producing a text that happens to support his case. He is demonstrating that his case is what the whole book was always saying. The nations praising Israel’s God is not a Christian innovation laid over the Old Testament. It is the Old Testament’s own hope, finally coming true.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Gentiles replace Israel. They rejoice with his people.

Does with his people mean there are two peoples of God? No. There is one olive tree, rooted in the promises to the patriarchs, into which believing Gentiles are grafted alongside believing Jews (11:17–24), and in Christ there is one new man where once there were two (Ephesians 2:14–16). Gentiles do not get a separate covenant or a separate hope. They join Israel’s worship, praising Israel’s God through Israel’s Messiah. What God will yet do for the Jewish people as a whole is a question Christians answer in different ways from chapter 11, and Paul leaves room for a future mercy to Israel (11:25–32). But there is only ever one family of faith, and one song.

In a sentence. Again, it says, “Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people.” And again, “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles; let all the peoples extol him.”

On a Tuesday. Pray Psalm 117 today, slowly; it will take you less than a minute. Then pray for a nation where Christ is not yet praised: look up one people group or one country where the church is small, learn one fact about it, and ask God to raise up a church that sings Psalm 117 in its own language. And notice the people in your own congregation from backgrounds unlike yours. Their voices in your church are the answer to a song Moses sang.

For worship. From the beginning, God has been gathering a choir from every nation. He announced it in the Law, sang it in the Psalms and promised it in the Prophets, and for centuries it was a hope held by a single nation on a strip of land between the desert and the sea. Now it is being sung on every continent, in thousands of languages, by people whose ancestors bowed to idols of wood and stone. His steadfast love is great toward us, and his faithfulness endures for ever. Praise the LORD, all you nations: he has done exactly what he said.
verseByVerse.note: Paul cites the Law, the Psalms and the Prophets to show God always intended Gentiles to praise him.

parallels.desc: rejoice with him, O heavens
praise the LORD, all nations

verseByVerse.quote: And again Isaiah says, "The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And again Isaiah says, “The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope.”

And again Isaiah says. From Isaiah 11:10 in the Greek translation, the last of Paul’s four witnesses and the one on which the others converge. All four quotations point to Christ as the one through whom the Gentiles enter the praise and hope of Israel’s God.

The root of Jesse will come. Jesse was David’s father; the root of Jesse is the promised king from David’s line (Isaiah 11:1). The phrase carries a picture that is lost if you hear it as a synonym for the family of David. Isaiah wrote it about a stump. His image was a dynasty felled like a tree, cut off at ground level, with nothing above the soil worth looking at, and a green shoot coming up out of the dead wood. That was written to people watching the house of David being reduced to a ruin. The promise was not that the tree would be spared. It was that something would grow out of the part that was left after everything visible had been taken away. Jesus is that root and offspring of David (Revelation 5:5; 22:16).

Life out of a stump. Which is worth holding onto, because it is the shape of a great deal of God’s work and almost never the shape we would have chosen. A shoot out of a stump is not a rescue of the tree. It is life on the other side of the loss, from the same root, and unrecognisable to anyone who was hoping the old thing would simply be repaired. By the time Jesus was born, David’s line had dwindled to a carpenter in Nazareth. Nobody looking at Joseph’s workshop would have seen a throne.

Even he who arises to rule the Gentiles. “Arises” (anistamai) is the word the New Testament uses for resurrection. Paul surely heard it: the shoot from the stump rose from the dead, and the risen Christ rules the nations. The Greek translation of Isaiah gave Paul a word that the empty tomb had filled with meaning.

In him will the Gentiles hope. The nations will put their hope in Israel’s Messiah. And Paul ends the chain on the word he is about to build his benediction from. Isaiah says the Gentiles will hope in him; the very next verse addresses the God of hope. The quotation is not a full stop. It is the handover.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s rule over the nations is only future. He reigns now, at God’s right hand, and the nations are coming to him through the gospel (Matthew 28:18–19).

Why is Jesus called the root of Jesse, not just a branch? Both are true, and Scripture uses both. Isaiah 11:1 calls the coming king a shoot from the stump of Jesse and a branch from his roots: he grows out of David’s family as its descendant. But Isaiah 11:10 calls him the root of Jesse, and Jesus himself says, I am the root and the descendant of David (Revelation 22:16). He is David’s offspring according to the flesh (1:3), and David’s source and Lord as the eternal Son (Matthew 22:41–45). The family tree that produced him was itself kept alive by him. He comes from David, and David came from him.

How can Christ rule the nations now, when the world looks so godless? His rule is real now, but it is mostly hidden, like a seed in the ground or yeast in dough (Matthew 13:31–33). He reigns over all things for the sake of his church (Ephesians 1:20–22), restraining evil, overruling the plans of rulers, and gathering his people from every nation through the preaching of the gospel. Every new believer in a closed country is a sign of his rule. One day it will be visible to everyone, when he returns in glory and every knee bows (Philippians 2:10–11). Until then, we trust what we cannot always see, and the headlines are not the measure of his reign.

In a sentence. And again, Isaiah says, “The Root of Jesse will spring up, one who will arise to rule over the nations; in him the Gentiles will hope.”

On a Tuesday. Put your hope in the risen king who rules the nations. The news headlines do not have the last word; he does. And look at the stump in your own life: the thing that has been cut down, the plan that failed, the family line or the ministry that seems finished. God’s way has often been to bring a shoot out of exactly that kind of dead wood. Do not demand that he repair the old tree. Ask him for life from the root.

For worship. When David’s house lay felled and the stump looked dead, God was not finished. Out of the roots came a shoot, a carpenter’s son, despised and rejected, cut down again on a cross and laid in a tomb. And from that death he arose, to rule the nations and to be their hope. The root of Jesse is the risen Lord, and every Gentile who trusts him is the fulfilment of a promise written seven centuries before he came. The tree that God plants out of a stump will never be cut down again.
verseByVerse.note: Jesse was David’s father; the “root of Jesse” is the promised king from David’s line.

parallels.desc: the root of Jesse, of him shall the nations inquire

verseByVerse.quote: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope. — Romans 15:13
verseByVerse.commentary:
May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope.

May the God of hope. A benediction to close the whole argument of the letter, and one of the most complete prayers in the New Testament. God is the source and object of hope. He gives it, and it rests in him. This is the last thing Paul says to the Roman church as argument. What follows is travel plans and greetings; the case that began at 1:16 with a gospel that is the power of God for salvation ends here, and it ends not in a conclusion but in a prayer.

Not the God who recommends hope. The God of hope: not the God who recommends it, or requires it, or is disappointed by its absence, but the God whose own name it is, and out of whom it comes, and who has never yet run short of it. Hope is not a mood he asks his people to work up. It is something he has, in himself, in quantities the situation is not consulted about.

Fill you with all joy and peace in believing. Joy and peace are two of the marks of the kingdom (14:17), and the verb is fill: not trickle, not portion out, but fill. All joy: not qualified, not conditional. And note the small phrase “in believing”. The joy and peace arrive in the act of trusting, not after it as a reward for having trusted well enough. The phrase means while believing, in the believing itself. Not a payment for faith, but the weather inside it. They come not by trying to feel joy, but by looking to Christ and resting the weight of your life on what God has said.

A mercy to a particular reader. Notice that Paul does not command them to abound in hope. He asks God to do it to them. Nobody in this verse is being told to cheer up, and nobody is being held responsible for producing a feeling they cannot presently locate. For the believer in a dark season, that matters enormously. The verse is not a standard you are failing to meet. It is a prayer someone is praying for you.

So that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope. “Abound” (perisseuō) means overflow. Not enough hope to get by. Not sufficient hope to endure. Abounding hope: more hope than circumstances justify, a flood rather than a trickle, and it comes by the Spirit’s power, not human optimism (5:5; 8:24–25). And the hope is not optimism, which is a temperament some people are born with and others are not. It is expectation grounded in what has been argued for fourteen chapters: a verdict already passed, a Spirit already given, a Son already raised, a love that nothing in creation can reach (8:38–39). That is why it can abound past what circumstances justify. It was never taking its measurements from the circumstances.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians never feel sorrow or anxiety. It means that God can fill a believer with joy and peace even in sorrow: sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10).

How is Christian hope different from wishful thinking? Wishful thinking says, I hope it will turn out well, with no particular reason to think it will. Christian hope says, I know how it will turn out, because God has promised it and Christ has already risen. In the New Testament, hope is certainty about something not yet seen (8:24–25). Its object is definite: the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body, the glory of God, the new creation (5:2; 8:18–23). Its ground is definite: the character of God and the finished work of his Son. It may not tell you how next month will go. It tells you, with full assurance, how everything will end, and that you will be there.

What if I believe but do not feel joy and peace? Then you are in the company of many faithful saints, and this verse is still for you. Feelings can be dimmed by illness, grief, exhaustion, depression or long trial, and none of those mean your faith is false. Keep doing the believing: keep looking to Christ, keep hearing his word, keep praying even when the words are thin. Joy and peace come in believing, but they do not always come on our schedule. Ask God for them plainly, as Paul did. If darkness lingers, speak to a pastor or a trusted believer, and do not be ashamed to seek medical help where it is needed. The Spirit’s work is often deeper than our feelings can register.

In a sentence. May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you trust in him, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Pray this verse for yourself and for someone you love, today, by name. Then do the thing the verse says hope comes through: believing. Write down one fact from Romans that is true of you whether you feel it or not: no condemnation (8:1), nothing can separate (8:39), all things for good (8:28). Read it aloud when the day gets hard. You are not manufacturing hope; you are standing where the Spirit pours it.

For worship. The letter’s last word of argument is not a demand but a benediction: that the God who is himself the source of hope would fill people who cannot manufacture it, by a power that is not theirs, until they have more of it than their situation can account for. Hope is his name. He has never yet run short of it, and he gives it without measure. The grave was the strongest argument against hope that has ever been made. He answered it on a Sunday morning and has not needed to argue since.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–33 — Paul's Priestly Ministry and His Plans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now turns from theology and pastoral exhortation to autobiography and travel plans — and the transition is less abrupt than it appears. His account of his apostolic ministry is itself a miniature theology of mission. He describes himself as a minister (leitourgos — a cultic, priestly term) of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, performing the priestly service of the gospel of God, offering the Gentiles as an acceptable offering, sanctified by the Holy Spirit (v. 16). The mission to the Gentiles is not merely evangelistic strategy; it is priestly worship — the bringing of the nations as an offering to God.

The scope of Paul's completed mission (vv. 19–21) is staggering: from Jerusalem to Illyricum (modern-day Croatia), he has "fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ." Not because every person has heard it but because he has planted the gospel in strategic centres throughout the eastern Mediterranean, from which the word can spread into every surrounding region. His ambition going forward is equally characteristic: not to build on another man's foundation, but to preach where Christ has not yet been named. The pioneer missionary impulse is written into the logic of the commission.

The prayer request of vv. 30–33 is one of the most moving passages in Paul's letters. He asks the Roman church to "strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf" — the word for "strive together" (sunagōnizomai) is an athletic term, contending alongside someone in a contest. Prayer is work, and Paul wants co-labourers in it. He asks for three things: deliverance from unbelievers in Judea, acceptance of his offering by the Jerusalem church, and the joy of reaching Rome. All three will be granted, none in the form he pictured; the Rome visit will happen, but in chains.

Two stretches of the section deserve adding. The first is how it opens (vv. 14–15). Having written the most demanding letter in the New Testament, Paul tells its recipients that he is satisfied about them — full of goodness, filled with knowledge, able to instruct one another — and that what he has written is offered by way of reminder. He does not present a word of it as news.

The second is vv. 22–29, which contains the two most concrete things in the chapter. One is Spain (v. 24): Paul is not looking for another province but for the western edge of the known world, and he is asking Rome to become the base that sends him there. This is why the letter exists in the form it does.

The other is the Jerusalem collection (vv. 25–28), a relief fund gathered from the Gentile churches of Macedonia and Achaia for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Paul is in Corinth, he intends to go west, and he is about to travel east instead — at real personal risk — to deliver money. And he does not call it charity. He says the Gentiles owe it to them (v. 27): having shared in Israel’s spiritual blessings, they owe material ones back. The collection is the argument of chapters 9–11 converted into currency and carried some eight hundred miles in the wrong direction.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mission as Priestly Worship

Romans 15:16 is one of the most theologically rich descriptions of apostolic mission in the New Testament. Paul images his Gentile mission as priestly service — the offering of the nations to God as a sacrifice acceptable and sanctified by the Holy Spirit. This means that evangelism is not merely a strategy for church growth or a duty to be discharged; it is an act of worship, the gathering of the nations to lay them as a living offering before the God who created and redeemed them. This priestly vision of mission has sustained every great missionary movement in the Reformed tradition, from Calvin's Geneva sending missionaries to France, to William Carey going to India, to the countless sent ones who have carried the gospel to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's completed mission from Jerusalem to Illyricum represents perhaps fifteen years of gruelling apostolic labour — multiple missionary journeys, imprisonments, beatings, shipwrecks, cold and hunger. The nonchalance with which he refers to having "fulfilled the ministry of the gospel" in this vast region is the confidence of a man who has done what he was sent to do and is already looking at the next frontier. Now: The pioneer missionary impulse of v. 20 — to preach where Christ has not been named — remains the highest calling in the church's mission. There are still places, peoples, and communities where the name of Christ has not been proclaimed. The obligation Paul felt is the obligation the church still carries, until all nations have heard.

verseByVerse.quote: I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another. But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God
verseByVerse.commentary:
I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another. But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God

I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers. “Satisfied” (peithō) means persuaded, confident. After strong words, Paul reassures them. He did not write because he thought they were a bad church. And weigh what has just happened. Paul has written fourteen chapters of dense argument, told this church not to be arrogant (11:18), not to think too highly of itself (12:3), not to despise or judge one another (14:3), and not to please itself (15:1). He now says he is persuaded about them, and that they are competent to instruct each other without him.

That you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another. Goodness (agathōsynē) is moral excellence and kindness. Knowledge is knowledge of the gospel. And able to instruct (noutheteō) means to admonish, to counsel, to set someone’s mind right by warning and teaching. Ordinary church members are able to counsel each other from God’s word (Colossians 3:16). Paul is not writing to a congregation that needs him to do all its thinking. He is writing to people who already have the Spirit, the Scriptures and one another.

But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder. “Very boldly”: Paul admits he has been direct. By way of reminder: much of what he wrote, they already knew. He calls the whole letter a reminder. Not instruction, not correction, but a reminder, which claims that nothing in it should be news to them. Whether or not that is literally true of chapters 9 to 11, it is the posture he chooses, and the posture is the point: he addresses them as people who already know, being called back to what they have. Christians need to be reminded of truths they know (2 Peter 1:12–13). We do not usually drift because we have never heard the truth, but because we have stopped hearing it.

Because of the grace given me by God. His apostleship is a gift of grace, and it gives him the right to write this way (1:5; 12:3). The boldness of the letter is not superiority but apostolic responsibility: the commission creates an obligation to speak even to those who already know, because the gospel is too important to assume and never needs to be restated too often.

The hard thing, and then the honest praise. Which is worth stealing as a practice. Most of us, having said the hard thing, either apologise for it afterwards or say nothing and let it stand. Paul does neither. He says the hard thing at full strength and then tells them plainly what he thinks of them, and it is not a technique for softening the blow. He means it, or the sentence would be worth nothing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that teaching is only for experts. All believers can and should instruct one another.

If members can instruct one another, why do we need pastors? Because God gives both, and they do different work. Christ gives pastors and teachers to the church to equip the saints for the work of ministry (Ephesians 4:11–12), and elders are charged with teaching, guarding the flock and answering for souls (Acts 20:28; Hebrews 13:17). But the goal of their teaching is a church in which everyone can speak the truth in love to everyone else (Ephesians 4:15–16). A healthy church is not one where the pastor does all the counselling. It is one where a believer struggling on Wednesday is helped by a friend who opens the Bible with him, long before the problem reaches the pastor’s study.

I do not feel able to counsel anyone. Where do I start? Start smaller than you think. Instructing one another in this verse is not delivering lectures; it is bringing God’s word to bear on a friend’s life with goodness and knowledge. Know the gospel well enough to remind someone of it. Listen first, and ask what is really going on. Point to a promise or a command that fits. Pray with them there and then. Be honest about your own struggles. And know when to say, this is beyond me, let us ask the elders together. Most faithful counsel in the history of the church has been given over kitchen tables by people who would never have called themselves counsellors.

In a sentence. Paul himself is convinced, brothers and sisters, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with knowledge and competent to instruct one another. Yet he has written to you quite boldly on some points to remind you of them again, because of the grace God gave him

On a Tuesday. The test is a simple one, and it is uncomfortable for anyone who has ever had to correct somebody. Think of the last time you told a fellow Christian something difficult. Could you, that same day, have named three genuine strengths in them out loud? If not, the correction may still have been true, but it was not coming from where Paul’s came from. And you are able to encourage and counsel a fellow believer from Scripture. Do it this week: one text, one friend, one honest conversation.

For worship. The God who gave Paul his boldness is the God who fills ordinary believers with goodness and knowledge. He does not keep his truth for a professional class. He pours his Spirit on the whole church, writes his word on the hearts of his people, and then sets them to speak it to one another. And he is patient enough to remind us, again and again, of what we already know, because he knows how quickly we forget. Every reminder of the gospel is grace repeated, from a God who never tires of telling his children the same good news.

verseByVerse.quote: to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God.

To be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles. “Minister” here is leitourgos, a word for priestly or public service (the same word used of rulers in 13:6, and of priests in the temple). Paul stacks three sanctuary words into one sentence. He is a leitourgos; he is in priestly service; and what he brings is an offering. There is no ordinary missionary vocabulary here at all. The whole verse is written in the language of the altar.

The man who could never be a priest. Which is a remarkable thing for this man to claim, since he could never have served as a priest in Israel. He has told us his tribe twice: Benjamin (11:1; Philippians 3:5), not Levi. The one role in Israel closed to him by birth is the one he now uses to describe his life’s work, and the sanctuary he serves in is the Gentile world.

In the priestly service of the gospel of God. “Priestly service” (hierourgeō) means to act as a priest, to perform sacred service. Paul pictures his mission as priestly work, offering the believing Gentiles to God. His altar is the gospel; his offering is people. And notice what is on the altar. Not his preaching, not his sufferings, not the churches he founded: the offering of the Gentiles. The converts are the sacrifice. Which connects directly to what he asked of them three chapters ago: present your bodies as a living sacrifice (12:1). Paul’s job description is to bring to God the very offering he told them to make of themselves.

So that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. The offering is the Gentiles themselves, as Isaiah foresaw when he saw the nations brought as an offering to the LORD from every land (Isaiah 66:20). Once unclean in Jewish eyes, they are now made holy, not by circumcision, but by the Spirit. Then the clause keeps it from being a boast about results: what makes the offering fit to present is not its quality. Under the old arrangement an offering had to be without blemish; here the offering is a collection of former idolaters, and what qualifies them is that the Spirit has made them holy. This is also a powerful argument against the scruples of the weak: if God accepts the Gentiles as a holy offering, no Christian may treat them as unclean.

In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God. “Proud” (kauchēsis) is boasting, glorying. The pride Paul expresses is not personal vanity but the joy of a craftsman whose work has been effective, and it is grounded entirely in Christ Jesus. He boasts not in himself but in what Christ did through him: by the grace of God I am what I am (1 Corinthians 15:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that ministers are priests offering sacrifices of atonement, as in Roman Catholic teaching on the Mass. Christ’s sacrifice was once for all (Hebrews 10:10–14). Paul’s priestly language is a picture of evangelism. All believers are a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices (1 Peter 2:5).

Is evangelism only for missionaries and pastors?
