No. Paul had a unique apostolic calling, but every believer belongs to the royal priesthood that proclaims the excellencies of him who called us out of darkness into his marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9). Not everyone is a preacher, but everyone is a witness: ready to give a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). For most Christians that means the neighbour, the colleague, the relative and the friend, prayed for by name, loved patiently, and told the gospel plainly when the door opens. And everyone can support those who are sent, by prayer and giving, as Paul is about to ask the Romans to do.

Is it wrong to feel proud of something God has done through me? Not if the pride is the kind Paul has here: glad, grateful and pointed at Christ. There is a sinful pride that says, look what I did, and a holy gladness that says, look what Christ did, and he let me be there. The test is where the credit goes, and how you feel when someone else gets it. If you can rejoice as much over fruit in another person’s ministry as in your own, your boasting is in Christ Jesus.

In a sentence. to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles. He has the priestly duty of proclaiming the gospel of God, so that the Gentiles might become an offering acceptable to God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. Therefore he glories in Christ Jesus in his service to God.

On a Tuesday. All of this changes what evangelism is. If bringing people to Christ is a duty, it competes with other duties and loses to most of them. If it is priestly work, carrying an offering to God, then it belongs in the same category as worship, and the question stops being whether you have time for it. So name one person this week you long to see brought to God. Pray for them as a priest would pray, and look for one opening to speak of Christ.

For worship. God accepts people who were once far off, idolaters with nothing clean to bring, and he makes them holy by his own Spirit. That is how you came to be standing before him. You were not presented because you were without blemish; you were presented because the Spirit had washed you, and because the one great sacrifice, the Lamb without blemish, had already been offered once for all. Christ is the priest who offered himself; the Spirit is the fire that sanctifies the offering; the Father receives it with delight. And every converted sinner on earth is a sacrifice of praise laid on that altar.
verseByVerse.note: Paul pictures his mission as priestly work, offering the believing Gentiles to God.

parallels.desc: they shall bring your brothers as an offering

verseByVerse.quote: For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience — by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God — so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience—by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God—so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ.

For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me. The grammar is the first thing to notice, because Paul has arranged the sentence so that he cannot be its subject. Christ acts; Paul is the preposition. Paul was the instrument; Christ was the worker. That is a usable rule and a hard one. It is not false modesty, which declines to mention the work at all: Paul reports his in detail, with a map. It is the discipline of reporting the work with the right subject at the front of the sentence.

To bring the Gentiles to obedience. The obedience of faith (1:5; 16:26): believing the gospel and living under Christ’s lordship. The letter opened and closes with the same phrase, and it describes the goal of all mission. Not decisions recorded, but nations brought to bow to Christ in trust and obedience.

By word and deed. Preaching and actions: both proclaimed the gospel. Paul’s message was spoken, and his life and labour embodied it: working with his own hands, caring for the churches, loving the people he served.

By the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God. Signs point to something beyond themselves; wonders cause amazement. Paul did miracles that confirmed his message (Acts 14:3; 19:11–12; 2 Corinthians 12:12). But notice the final phrase: the power of the Spirit of God. That is the power behind word, deed and sign alike. It is the Spirit who makes the preaching effective, opens hearts, and brings the nations to obedience.

So that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ. Illyricum lay along the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, north-west of Macedonia (modern Albania, Croatia and nearby). Paul had preached in a great arc from Jerusalem through Syria, Asia Minor and Greece. The map deserves a moment. Jerusalem to Illyricum is the whole eastern Mediterranean, well over a thousand miles as the roads ran, and Paul covered it on foot and by ship over many years, the years that also contain the beatings, the shipwrecks, the night and a day adrift at sea and the sleepless nights he lists elsewhere (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). None of that appears here. He gives the coordinates and moves on.

Fulfilled. And fulfilled the ministry of the gospel needs reading carefully, because it plainly does not mean that everyone in that arc had believed. It means he had fully preached the gospel, planting churches in key cities from which it would spread, with churches left behind that can reach their own territory. Paul’s definition of a finished job is not a converted population. It is a living church in place, doing what he would otherwise have stayed to do.

Where Christians differ: signs and wonders today. Some teach that signs and wonders like those of the apostles should accompany all gospel preaching today. Verdict: Paul calls signs and wonders the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12). They confirmed the apostolic message as Scripture was being given (Hebrews 2:3–4). With the apostles gone and the canon complete, the miraculous sign gifts have ceased as a regular part of ministry. God still answers prayer and can heal and work wonders as he pleases, but the gospel is now confirmed by the written word. This is held charitably toward continuationist brothers and sisters.

What it does not mean. It does not mean miracles are the main way the gospel spreads. Paul puts word first.

Does God still heal today, then? Yes, and Christians should ask him to. What has ceased is the apostolic gift by which particular people worked signs at will to confirm a new revelation. What has not ceased is God himself, who hears the prayers of his people. James tells the sick to call the elders, who are to pray over them and anoint them, and the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick (James 5:14–15). Sometimes God heals, quickly or slowly, with or without medicine, which is also his gift. Sometimes he does not, and gives grace to bear the weakness instead, as he did for Paul (2 Corinthians 12:7–10). Either way, pray boldly and leave the answer with him.

In a sentence. Paul will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through him in leading the Gentiles to obey God by what he has said and done, by the power of signs and wonders, through the power of the Spirit of God. So from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum, he has fully proclaimed the gospel of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Speak only of what Christ has done through you. Let your stories of ministry glorify him, not you. It is easily tested: listen to yourself this week describing something that went well in your church, your work or your family, and notice who is doing the verbs. If it is mostly I, try telling it again with Christ as the subject, and see how much more true it sounds.

For worship. Christ is the worker in every work of God. He walked those Roman roads in his servant, he spoke through his servant’s mouth, he opened hearts in Lystra and Philippi and Corinth that no preacher could open. And he is still working by his Spirit through the same gospel, from Jerusalem round to the ends of the earth, in villages Paul never heard of and languages he never spoke. The gospel advances because the risen Christ is building his church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
verseByVerse.note: Illyricum lay along the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, north-west of Macedonia.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else's foundation, but as it is written, 'Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand.' — Romans 15:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else’s foundation, but as it is written, “Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand.”

And thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel. “Ambition” (philotimeomai) is built from the words for love and honour: to aspire, to make something your aim and point of pride, as in 2 Corinthians 5:9. Paul does not apologise for having an ambition or convert it into something more modest. He simply points it somewhere: at the places where the name of Christ has never been said out loud. Ambition is not the problem in a Christian; ambition pointed at the wrong thing is.

Not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else’s foundation. Paul’s pioneer calling was to go where no church yet existed. Others could water where he planted (1 Corinthians 3:6, 10). His specific gift was pioneer evangelism: breaking new ground, planting the gospel in soil that had never received it, and leaving behind a church that would then reach its own region.

Those who have never been told of him will see. Paul quotes Isaiah 52:15, from the great servant song, and the text he reaches for is worth locating. Isaiah 52:15 is the last verse before Isaiah 53. It belongs to the passage about the one despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions, by whose stripes we are healed. The servant’s message would reach kings and nations who had never heard. Paul lifts his mission statement out of the paragraph about the suffering servant, and takes the part where the nations who were never told finally see. Every faithful missionary sent to unreached peoples is doing what Paul did and fulfilling what Isaiah foresaw.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that building up existing churches is less important. Paul spent years teaching established churches. But some are called to pioneer. A guard is needed here, because this verse has been used to make settled ministry look second-rate. Paul is describing his own calling, not issuing a universal rule. He himself stayed in Ephesus for three years (Acts 20:31). Somebody had to be Timothy at the unglamorous end of a long pastorate, and Paul’s letters to him are not consolation prizes for a man who failed to be a pioneer. The ambition commended here is that the unreached should be reached, not that every Christian should be restless.

What are unreached peoples, and what can I do from here? An unreached people is a group, usually defined by language and culture, among whom there is no church strong enough to evangelise the rest without help from outside. Many of them have no Bible in their language and have never met a Christian. Most of us will not go to them, but every one of us can share Paul’s ambition. Learn about one such people and pray for them by name. Give to missionaries working among them. Welcome internationals in your own town, since many come from places where the gospel is hard to hear. Encourage the young people in your church who sense a call. And ask God whether he might be calling you.

In a sentence. It has always been Paul’s ambition to preach the gospel where Christ was not known, so that he would not be building on someone else’s foundation. Rather, as it is written: “Those who were not told about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”

On a Tuesday. Ask what your ambition is. Not your plan for the week, but the thing you would most love to see happen before you die. If the name of Christ is nowhere in it, ask God to reshape it. Then pray this week for the unreached peoples of the world, and for one missionary you know who has gone where Christ has not been named.

For worship. The Servant was despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, and because he poured out his soul to death, the nations who were never told of him have seen. Kings shut their mouths before him. That is the God we worship: one who does not wait for the nations to seek him, but sends his word to the ends of the earth, to people who had no idea anyone was looking for them. Every day, somewhere, someone hears the name of Jesus for the first time, and understands. The promise of Isaiah is still coming true, and it will go on coming true until every tribe and tongue is gathered.

parallels.desc: that which has not been told them they see

verseByVerse.quote: This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you. But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you. But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you,

This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you. His pioneer work kept him busy elsewhere (1:13). The verb for “hindered” (enkoptō) is a road-builder’s word: to cut into a road, to break up the surface so that no one can pass. It is not the language of a man whose plans slipped. Something has been across the road, repeatedly, for years. And Paul does not treat that as bad luck. He names it as the reason, without complaint and without suggesting anything went wrong, which is a small thing to notice and a hard one to imitate. He told them at the very start of the letter that he had planned to come and had been prevented until now (1:13). Between that sentence and this one lies most of his working life.

But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions. A sentence that would be absurd from anybody else. The eastern Mediterranean is finished. Not converted, but finished, in the sense that churches now exist which can do the rest. He has planted churches across the region; the foundation is laid, and local believers can carry on. Nobody else in the New Testament talks like this, and it explains everything about the man’s restlessness.

And since I have longed for many years to come to you. Paul had wanted to see Rome for a long time (1:10–11; Acts 19:21). His long-deferred visit is not indifference. It is the discipline of a pioneer missionary who will not plant where others have already sown (v. 20). Rome is now within reach, not only as a destination but as a staging post for the westward advance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every person in those regions was now a Christian. It means the strategic churches were planted.

How do I know whether God is hindering me, or I am just giving up? Ask what is actually across the road. Paul was hindered not by fear or idleness but by faithfulness: there was gospel work in front of him that had to be done first. So look at your own delay honestly. If what keeps you from the thing you long for is a real duty God has placed in front of you, then the delay is his, and you can wait without guilt. If what keeps you is fear, comfort or sin, then call it by its name and repent. And in either case, keep the desire alive in prayer, as Paul kept praying for Rome for years (1:10). God often brings a long-held desire to pass at the moment it can do the most good.

In a sentence. This is why he has often been hindered from coming to you. But now that there is no more place for him to work in these regions, and since he has been longing for many years to visit you,

On a Tuesday. Your plans may be hindered for years by God’s work elsewhere. Wait patiently. His timing is good. Think of one longing that has been delayed for a long time: a ministry, a reconciliation, a door you have prayed to see open. Ask what faithful work God has given you to do in the meantime, and do it with your whole heart.

For worship. God’s timing is never careless. For years he kept Paul from Rome, not because he had forgotten Rome, but because there were churches to be planted in Galatia and Macedonia and Achaia first, and people in them whose names are written in heaven. Every hindrance in Paul’s road was a door somewhere else. The Lord of the harvest knows the order in which the fields are to be reaped, and he does not waste a single year of a servant’s life.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be helped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be helped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a while.

I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain. Spain is the detail to stop on, because it is easy to read as just another destination. It was not. Spain was the far western end of the Roman world: beyond it the map ran out and the Atlantic began. When Paul says Spain, he is naming the end of the earth as his generation understood the phrase, and he says it in the same breath as a request for travelling expenses. Paul’s vision was to take the gospel to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8).

And to be helped on my journey there by you. “Helped on my journey” (propempō, send forward) was a technical term for missionary support: supplies, money, companions, perhaps letters of introduction (Acts 15:3; 1 Corinthians 16:6; Titus 3:13; 3 John 6). Part of Paul’s purpose in writing Romans was to win their support for the Spanish mission. Which puts this whole letter in its practical setting. The most sustained piece of theology ever written was composed, among other things, as an introduction from a man asking a church he had never visited to fund his next expedition. Paul evidently thought that the way to raise support for a mission was to explain the gospel at length. Very few people have thought so since.

Once I have enjoyed your company for a while. Paul looks forward to fellowship, to being filled up (empiplēmi) by them. He does not see the Roman church only as a supply base. He expects to be fed by them.

Did Paul ever reach Spain? We do not know. Acts leaves him under house arrest in Rome and stops. Clement of Rome, writing about AD 96, says he reached the limits of the west, which many have taken to mean Spain, and it may. The honest position is that the last plan recorded in the letter is the one plan whose outcome the New Testament never reports. And there is something worth sitting with in that. A man lays out an ambition at the end of his greatest work, and the record simply does not say whether he got there. Most faithful lives end that way: with the last thing unresolved on the page, and the accounting done somewhere else.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul saw Rome as just a stopover. He loved them and wanted to share spiritual gifts with them (1:11–12).

Is it right for missionaries to ask for money? Yes, when it is done openly and for the sake of the gospel. Paul asks plainly here, and the New Testament commends churches that send gospel workers on their way in a manner worthy of God, since they go out for the sake of the name (3 John 6–8). Paul sometimes refused support where it would have hindered the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:12, 15–18), but he never thought supporting missionaries was second-class work. Those who give become partners in the mission (Philippians 1:5; 4:15–17). So when a missionary asks for help, do not hear it as begging. Hear it as an invitation to share in the work.

In a sentence. Paul plans to do so when he goes to Spain. He hopes to see you while passing through and to have you assist him on his journey there, after he has enjoyed your company for a while.

On a Tuesday. Ask how your church can send others forward on gospel journeys. Give and pray for missionaries. If you support one, write to them this week, not with a request but with encouragement. If you do not, ask your church who it sends, and begin.

For worship. The gospel has always been heading for the ends of the earth, because the God who sent it intends to be worshipped there. Paul looked west to Spain, the edge of his map; the gospel has since gone far beyond it, to continents he never imagined, carried by people who were helped on their journey by churches that loved them. Whether or not Paul reached Spain, Christ did. And the Lord of the harvest records every faithful plan, finished or unfinished, in a book that will be opened on the last day.
verseByVerse.note: Spain was the western edge of the known world. Whether Paul ever reached it is uncertain; early tradition says he did.

verseByVerse.quote: At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem.

At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints. “Bringing aid” (diakoneō) is serving. Before Rome, Paul must make a long trip back east. Put this on a map and it becomes strange. Paul is writing from Corinth. He intends to go west, to Rome and beyond it to Spain. And the first thing he is going to do is travel some eight hundred miles in the opposite direction, to Jerusalem, carrying money. He also knows what is waiting there. A few verses later he will ask them to pray that he is delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, so this is not a man who has failed to consider the risk. He is postponing the mission of his life and walking toward the city where he is most likely to be killed, in order to hand over a relief fund.

For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem. The collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem took years to gather (1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9). Macedonia (Philippi, Thessalonica) and Achaia (Corinth) were in Greece. “Contribution” is koinōnia, fellowship, sharing: the gift was an expression of unity between Gentile and Jewish believers. The Jerusalem church was poor, a community that had been through famine (Acts 11:28–30) and was largely cut off from the wider society it had left, and Gentile congregations that owed it everything were sending help. The unity Paul has argued for across eleven chapters was about to arrive in Jerusalem in a bag, carried by representatives of the very nations chapter 11 said had been grafted in.

Have been pleased. And “have been pleased” is his word for the givers, twice in two verses. The Macedonians in particular he describes elsewhere as giving out of extreme poverty, beyond their means, and begging for the privilege (2 Corinthians 8:1–4). Nobody in this transaction is being squeezed. The gospel had made poor Greeks glad to give to poorer Jews.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul cared only for spiritual needs. The gospel produces concern for the poor (Galatians 2:10).

Should Christians help poor believers first, or the poor in general? Both, with a particular care for the church. Paul says, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith (Galatians 6:10). A family looks after its own members first, not because it does not care about the neighbours, but because they are family. So churches should make sure no believer among them, or in poorer churches elsewhere, goes without, as this collection did. And Christians should also be known for mercy to the poor around them, whoever they are, as the good Samaritan was (Luke 10:29–37). The order is especially, not only.

In a sentence. Now, however, Paul is on his way to Jerusalem in the service of the Lord’s people there. For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the Lord’s people in Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. Generosity across cultural lines builds unity. Give this week to help poor believers somewhere else, perhaps through your church or a trustworthy agency serving persecuted or impoverished Christians. And ask the question the Macedonians answered: is my giving something I am squeezed into, or something I would beg for the privilege of doing?

For worship. Our Lord Jesus Christ, though he was rich, for our sakes became poor, so that we through his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). That is the fountain from which the whole collection flowed. Greek believers who had never seen Jerusalem gave gladly to Jewish believers they would never meet, because they had been made rich by a Jewish Saviour who gave everything. The grace of God is never only words. It reached down into our poverty in a body, on a cross, and it goes on reaching through the open hands of his people.
verseByVerse.note: The collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem was a major project of Paul’s later ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.

For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. Glad giving, and also a debt. Both are true at once. The word Paul uses is owe, and with it he closes a thread that has run the length of the letter. He called himself a debtor to Greeks and barbarians in the first chapter (1:14). He told them to owe no one anything except to love (13:8). He said the strong owe the weak (15:1). And here the Gentile churches are debtors to Jerusalem. Four times, and never once is the debt owed in the direction the debtor would have chosen.

For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings. The gospel, the promises, the Messiah, the Scriptures: all came to the Gentiles from the Jews (9:4–5; 11:17–18). “Share” is koinōneō. Notice what this does to Gentile self-importance, which has been Paul’s target since chapter 11. The nations did not generate their own faith. The Scriptures came through Israel, the promises were made to Israel, the Messiah was born an Israelite. Salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22). A Gentile church sending relief to Jerusalem is a congregation admitting in public where it got what it has.

They ought also to be of service to them in material blessings. Literally, in fleshly things: money, food. “Be of service” is leitourgeō, priestly service, the same family of words Paul used of his own ministry in verse 16. Giving money is a form of worship (Philippians 4:18). And the exchange he describes is deliberately uneven. They received spiritual things and are repaying in material ones, which is not a fair swap and is not meant to be. You cannot return a gospel. What you can do is send money, and Paul treats that as the appropriate response to having been given something that cannot be repaid.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation can be paid for. It means gratitude for spiritual gifts shows itself in material generosity (1 Corinthians 9:11; Galatians 6:6). And one caution, since the verse is sometimes made into a general rule that those who teach should be paid by those taught. Paul does argue that elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:11–14; Galatians 6:6), and it is fair enough. But here he is describing something narrower and stranger: a debt owed by the whole Gentile church to the mother congregation, paid as a statement about what the church is.

Do Gentile Christians today owe something to the Jewish people? A debt of gratitude, certainly. Every Gentile believer worships Israel’s God, reads Israel’s Scriptures and trusts Israel’s Messiah. That should rule out every trace of contempt for Jewish people, which has disgraced the church too often in its history (11:18–20). It should move us to love, to pray for their salvation as Paul did (10:1), and to share Christ with them humbly. The particular debt in this verse was owed to Jewish believers in need, so its closest application is generous care for Jewish Christians and for the poor among God’s people. Christians differ on how this relates to modern politics, and the verse does not settle those questions.

In a sentence. They were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have shared in the Jews’ spiritual blessings, they owe it to the Jews to share with them their material blessings.

On a Tuesday. You have received spiritual riches from others: the people who taught you the gospel, the church that baptised you, the preachers and writers and saints of history who carried it down to you. Name three of them. Then ask what you could give in return, whether money to a ministry like theirs, a letter of thanks to one still living, or time given to pass on what they gave you. Give generously, and give gladly.

For worship. Every Gentile who has ever trusted Christ is living on an inheritance he did not earn. God chose Abraham, kept his family through famine and slavery and exile, gave them his law and his prophets and his psalms, and out of them, according to the flesh, came the Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever (9:5). Then he opened that whole inheritance to the nations. We are debtors to mercy alone, and the debt can never be repaid. It can only be answered with joyful giving and with praise to the God who made strangers into heirs.

verseByVerse.quote: When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected, I will leave for Spain by way of you. I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected, I will leave for Spain by way of you. I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.

When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected. Literally, having sealed to them this fruit. The verb is a commercial one: to seal, the mark pressed into wax to certify that a consignment has arrived intact and is what it claims to be. Paul intends to sign for the delivery personally. It is the language of a man closing a transaction he has been conducting for years. And the gift is called fruit: the fruit of the gospel among the Gentiles, grown in Greek soil and brought home to the root.

I will leave for Spain by way of you. The plan: Jerusalem, then Rome, then Spain.

I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ. Paul is confident that his visit, whenever it happens, will be full of Christ’s blessing. Not his own blessing, not the church’s, but Christ’s: the riches of the gospel brought by an apostle who carries them. He is right, and he has no idea what it will cost. He did reach Rome. He was arrested in Jerusalem within days of arriving with the money (Acts 21), spent two years in custody at Caesarea, appealed to Caesar, was shipwrecked off Malta, and came into the city at last under guard, in chains, at imperial expense, some three years after writing this sentence (Acts 28:16). Every word of the prediction held. None of the arrangements did. Even as a prisoner, he came in the fullness of Christ’s blessing: the gospel advanced (Philippians 1:12–13).

Unhindered. And there is one detail that reads like a deliberate answer. In the first chapter of this letter Paul said he had often planned to come and had been prevented (1:13); here he says he has been hindered again (v. 22). Luke ends the book of Acts with Paul in Rome, under house arrest, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, and the last word of the whole narrative in Greek is unhindered (Acts 28:31). The obstruction was to the man, never to the message, and Luke closes the account on the very word Paul had been unable to use about himself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul knew exactly how things would go. He planned, and God directed his steps differently (Proverbs 16:9; James 4:13–15).

Is it a lack of faith to make plans? No. Paul planned carefully: routes, timing, support, even a three-stage itinerary across the whole Mediterranean. Scripture commends forethought (Proverbs 21:5; Luke 14:28). What it forbids is the arrogance that plans as though tomorrow belongs to us. Instead you ought to say, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (James 4:15). So plan as well as you can, pray over the plans, hold them with open hands, and when God changes them, trust that his route is better than the one you drew. Paul’s confidence was not in the itinerary. It was in Christ’s blessing, which no change of route could remove.

In a sentence. So after he has completed this task and has made sure that they have received this contribution, he will go to Spain and visit you on the way. He knows that when he comes to you, he will come in the full measure of the blessing of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Make your plans, and hold them loosely. If God reroutes you, his blessing can still be full. Think of a plan of yours that went wrong in the last few years and ask honestly: what came through it anyway? Not everything that went wrong was secretly good. But the blessing of Christ was not one of the things you lost.

For worship. The plans of a man can be overturned in a single afternoon in the temple courts, and the purpose of God cannot be overturned at all. Paul came to Rome in chains, and the chains became a pulpit to the whole praetorian guard. The Lord who holds the hearts of kings and the winds over the sea brought his servant to the very city he had prayed for, by a route no one would have chosen, and the gospel ran ahead of him unhindered. The fullness of the blessing of Christ does not depend on our arrangements. It depends on Christ, and he does not fail.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,

I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit. A solemn request. The love of the Spirit is the love the Spirit produces in believers, which binds them together across the miles. Notice the Trinity in verse 30: the Lord Jesus, the Spirit, and God the Father, to whom the prayers are made. Christian prayer is drawn into the life of the triune God: to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit.

A frightened apostle. Take the request at face value first, because it is easy to admire the vocabulary and miss the man. The apostle who wrote chapter 8 is frightened. He is about to walk into a city where people want to kill him, and he writes to a church he has never met to ask them to get into the struggle with him. This is not a rhetorical flourish. It is a man arranging support before something he is dreading. And it means that the great apostle, the man who wrote this letter, believed he needed the prayers of ordinary believers he had never seen.

To strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf. “Strive together” (synagōnizomai) means wrestle together, contend alongside. The root is agōn, the word for a contest, from which we get agony. Paul uses its relatives of Epaphras, who was always struggling on behalf of his church in his prayers (Colossians 4:12). Prayer in this vocabulary is not a mood or a discipline of quietness. It is exertion, done alongside somebody, on their behalf, at a distance.

That I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea. Paul knew Jerusalem was dangerous for him; many there hated him as a traitor to the law (Acts 20:22–23; 21:10–14).

And that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints. He also feared the Jewish believers might reject a gift from Gentiles, because of suspicion about his ministry (Acts 21:20–21). It is a striking fear: that the very gift meant to show unity might be refused by the people it was meant to bless.

How God answered. These prayers were answered in unexpected ways: Paul was arrested in Jerusalem, but his life was spared; the believers received him gladly (Acts 21:17); he was protected by the Romans from a plot to kill him (Acts 23:12–35); and he reached Rome at the empire’s expense, as a prisoner (Acts 27–28). Hold the requests against what happened, because this is where the passage does its deepest pastoral work. He asked to be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea. He was seized in the temple and would have been beaten to death had Roman soldiers not run down and taken him into custody (Acts 21:30–33). He was delivered, into arrest. He asked that his service be acceptable to the saints. Luke says the brothers received him gladly, and then mentions the money only once more, in passing, in Paul’s defence before Felix (Acts 24:17). And he asked to come to Rome with joy and be refreshed. He came in chains, and the last picture Luke gives us is of him welcoming all who came to him, preaching for two years. He got the joy. He did not get it in the shape he asked for.

Not a glib answer. Which needs saying carefully, because it is one step from a cruelty. This is not the cheap assurance that every unanswered prayer is secretly a better answer. Paul lost years to that arrest, and the man asking here for a safe journey did not get one. What the passage shows is narrower and more honest: that God answered every one of these petitions, and answered none of them in the manner requested, and that Paul’s ministry was not diminished by the difference. Several of his letters are traditionally dated to his imprisonment.

What it does not mean. It does not mean prayer is a way to control God. We pray, and God answers in his wisdom, sometimes better than we asked.

If God has already planned everything, why pray? Because God has planned the prayers too. He ordains not only what will happen but the means by which it happens, and prayer is one of his chosen means (Westminster 5.3). Paul believed God was sovereign over every step of his journey, and he still begged the Romans to wrestle in prayer, because he knew God works through the prayers of his people. Prayer does not change God’s mind; it is the way God has chosen to bring his good purposes to pass, and the way he draws us into his work. When you pray for a missionary’s safety, you are not interfering with providence. You are one of the means providence is using.

In a sentence. Paul urges you, brothers and sisters, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to join him in his struggle by praying to God for him. Pray that he may be kept safe from the unbelievers in Judea and that the contribution he takes to Jerusalem may be favourably received by the Lord’s people there,

On a Tuesday. Wrestle in prayer today for a missionary or pastor by name. Ask specifically, as Paul did, for their safety and for the fruitfulness of their work. Then take a prayer of your own that you consider unanswered, and instead of asking whether God said no, ask what actually happened next: not to your circumstances, but to you and to the people around you. Sometimes the honest answer is still that it was a loss and you are waiting. Paul would not have argued with that; he wrote chapter 8 about groaning. But sometimes the answer arrived under a different name and was not recognised because it was not carrying the right paperwork.

For worship. The Father hears, the Son intercedes, and the Spirit pours his love into the hearts of people who have never met, so that a church in Rome can wrestle in prayer for a man walking toward Jerusalem. That is the communion of saints, and it is the work of the triune God. He heard every one of those prayers. He kept Paul alive through mobs and plots and shipwreck, and brought him to Rome by his own road. He is the God who answers prayer, always wisely, often surprisingly, never carelessly, and he holds his servants in his hand when every human plan has failed.
verseByVerse.note: These prayers were answered in unexpected ways: Paul was arrested in Jerusalem and reached Rome as a prisoner.

verseByVerse.quote: so that by God's will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company. May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
so that by God’s will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company. May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

So that by God’s will I may come to you with joy. By God’s will: all Paul’s plans depend on it (1:10). He did come, though not as he had planned. By God’s will is a phrase that costs Paul something here, and he cannot have known how much. He wanted to arrive rested, in good company, on his way to Spain. The will of God in this instance included a riot, a conspiracy, two years in custody at Caesarea, a shipwreck and a chain. He wrote the words anyway, and the words held. He holds even his own travel plans with open hands.

And be refreshed in your company. “Refreshed” (synanapauomai) means to rest together, to be refreshed alongside. Even apostles need rest and the encouragement of fellow believers. The man who has carried the churches on his heart for twenty years wants nothing more from Rome than to sit down with them and be renewed.

May the God of peace be with you all. Amen. A benediction. The God of peace is the God who made peace with us through Christ (5:1), through the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and who gives peace within the church, between strong and weak, Jew and Gentile (14:19; 16:20). His peace surpasses all understanding (Philippians 4:7).

The names of God in this chapter. It is worth collecting the titles this chapter has given God, because they form a pattern. The God of endurance and encouragement (v. 5). The God of hope (v. 13). The God of peace (v. 33). Three times Paul names God by the exact thing the people he is writing to need: a divided and weary church needs the God of endurance and encouragement, a discouraged one the God of hope, an anxious one the God of peace. That is not a literary habit. It is how Paul prays: he does not merely tell God what to provide; he addresses him as the one who already is what the situation lacks. And it means the last thing the argument of Romans leaves in the room is not a doctrine but a presence.

Peace is the right last word. The letter began with a courtroom: wrath revealed from heaven, every mouth stopped, the whole world accountable to God (1:18; 3:19). It arrives here at the God of peace be with you all, and the all is doing quiet work: the strong and the weak, Jew and Gentile, the ones who eat and the ones who do not. The hostility the letter opened with has been dealt with in both directions, between God and man, and now between the people sitting in the same room.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the letter ends here. Chapter 16 adds greetings and a final doxology.

What if church drains me rather than refreshes me? Then you are not alone, and the verse still shows the goal. Paul expected to be refreshed by Christians, and God means his people to be that for one another (Philemon 7, 20). But churches are made of forgiven sinners, and some seasons are hard. Look for refreshment where it can be found: one or two believers you can pray with honestly, a small group, a friendship around the Bible. Ask whether you come expecting only to give, or only to receive; both starve a soul. And if something in your church is genuinely harmful, speak to the elders. But do not give up meeting together (Hebrews 10:24–25), because the God of peace usually sends his refreshment through his people.

In a sentence. so that he may come to you with joy, by God’s will, and in your company be refreshed. The God of peace be with you all. Amen.

On a Tuesday. Be someone others are refreshed to be with. Think of one weary believer you know, a pastor, a parent, a missionary on home leave, and do something this week that would leave them rested rather than more tired: a meal, a listening ear, a note that asks nothing in return. And let the God of peace be with you as you go.

For worship. The God of peace made peace at the cost of his Son’s blood. He took the courtroom of Romans 1, with its wrath and its silenced mouths, and turned it into a family table where enemies are reconciled and the strong and the weak eat side by side. He is not the God who demands peace from people who cannot make it. He is the God of peace, who is peace in himself, who gives it through the cross, and who comes to be with his people, all of them. Amen: so it is, and so it will be.

16.title: Greetings, Warnings, and the Final Doxology
16.overview:
Romans 16 is sometimes treated as an appendix — a list of greetings to be skimmed before putting the letter down. It is far more than that. The twenty-six people Paul greets in vv. 3–15 (twenty-four of them by name), with several households besides, constitute a remarkable social portrait of the early Roman church: women who worked hard in the Lord, co-workers who risked their necks for Paul, households that may have belonged to powerful men, and many names common among slaves and freedmen. The community Paul is writing to and for is not an abstraction; it is these people, in this city, with these names and these stories.

The chapter also contains a sharp warning against those who create division and cause obstacles contrary to the doctrine (vv. 17–20) — a reminder that the unity and the gospel Paul has laboured to establish require vigilance as well as love. And then the letter ends where it began: with the gospel. The doxology of vv. 25–27 is one of the most comprehensive summaries of Paul's gospel in the New Testament — the mystery kept secret for long ages, now disclosed through the prophetic Scriptures, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith, to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — A Network of Saints: The Social World of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The list of greetings in Romans 16 is the most extensive in Paul's letters and has rightly been treated as a window into the earliest church. Twenty-six individuals are greeted, twenty-four of them by name, along with several households and groups. The social diversity is remarkable: Phoebe, a deacon and patron from Cenchreae; Priscilla and Aquila, tentmakers and theological teachers; Andronicus and Junia, "well known to the apostles" and Christians before Paul; Epaenetus, the first convert in Asia; Mary, who worked very hard. Slaves and free, women and men, Jews and Gentiles — all members of the same body.

Phoebe (vv. 1–2) deserves special notice: Paul commends her as a deacon (diakonos — the same word used of male church officers) of the church in Cenchreae, and as a patron (prostatis) who has been of help to many, including Paul himself. She was almost certainly the letter-carrier — the person who bore the manuscript of Romans from Corinth to Rome and, as was customary for letter-carriers in antiquity, would have read and explained the letter to its recipients. The greatest theological letter ever written was entrusted to a woman for its first public delivery.

The greeting "holy kiss" (v. 16) — appearing in four of Paul's letters — was the physical expression of the family bond that the gospel created. In the ancient world, the kiss of greeting belonged chiefly to family. The church that greeted one another with a holy kiss was declaring, physically and publicly, that these people — strangers by blood, foreigners by origin, divided by every social category — were family. The gospel had done what nothing else could do: created a new human community that crossed every boundary the ancient world had erected.

Between the famous names and the holy kiss lies the bulk of the list, and it is worth not skipping. Verses 8–15 greet Ampliatus, Urbanus, Stachys, Apelles, the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus, Herodion, Tryphaena and Tryphosa, Persis, Rufus and his mother, then Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas.

Several of those are ordinary slave names, and three of them — Ampliatus, Stachys and Persis — Paul calls beloved. Two are greeted not as individuals but as households — and in one of them only those in the Lord. Three of the workers named in this stretch are women, and one man is remembered chiefly through his mother, who Paul says has been a mother to him as well (v. 13).

And the last two clusters are given no description at all — nine names and an unnamed sister, with nothing attached, followed by the brothers who are with them and all the saints who are with them, who are not named at all. That proportion is the honest shape of the church in every century: a few remembered for something, most remembered only for being there, and the majority not written down.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as the New Humanity

Romans 16:1–16 is the embodiment in flesh-and-blood names of Paul's theological argument in chapters 1–15. The "no distinction between Jew and Greek" of 10:12, the olive tree of Jew and Gentile grafted together of 11:17–24, the "welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you" of 15:7 — all of these are visible in the list of names. This is what the gospel looks like when it has done its work: Phoebe and Priscilla and Andronicus and Junia, the patron and the tentmaker, the first convert and the former persecutor's associates, all belonging to each other in Christ. The doctrine of justification by faith produces a sociology.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The social mixing of Romans 16 was, by the standards of the first-century world, radical to the point of scandalous. Social boundaries in Rome were enforced with rigour; meals with social inferiors were a form of self-humiliation. The church that gathered Phoebe the patron and the slaves of great households and the Jewish tentmakers for common worship and common greeting was an institution the Roman world had no category for. Now: The contemporary church's ability or inability to embody the social diversity of Romans 16 is one of the most important tests of its gospel fidelity. A church that is racially, socially, or economically homogeneous by design has stopped short of what the gospel creates. The greetings of Romans 16 are not an antiquarian curiosity; they are the template for the new humanity the gospel is building.

verseByVerse.quote: I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well. — Romans 16:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well.

Meaning first. Romans 16 closes the letter. It may look like a list of names to skip, but it shows what the gospel of chapters 1–15 produces: a real family of men and women, Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, rich and poor, who love and serve one another. First, Paul commends Phoebe, who probably carried the letter (vv. 1–2). Then he greets twenty-six people by name in Rome, many with a word of warm praise (vv. 3–16). Then he warns against those who cause divisions with false teaching, and promises that the God of peace will soon crush Satan (vv. 17–20). Then his companions send greetings, including the scribe Tertius (vv. 21–23). Finally, a great doxology sums up the whole letter: glory to the only wise God, who strengthens us by the gospel of Jesus Christ, the mystery now revealed to all nations to bring about the obedience of faith (vv. 25–27). The letter that began with God’s wrath against all ungodliness ends with a room full of forgiven people, greeting one another by name, and a sentence that breaks off into worship.

Why should I read a list of names? Because this is where the doctrine becomes visible. Paul has spent fifteen chapters arguing that God justifies the ungodly, shows no partiality, and makes Jew and Gentile one family in Christ. Chapter 16 is what that looks like on the ground: a wealthy patroness, a tentmaking couple, slaves with common names, a member of Herod’s circle, a city treasurer and a man called Fourth, all greeted as brothers and sisters. Read the names slowly and you are looking at the church Romans 1–15 creates. You will also find that God remembers people the world forgets, and that is a doctrine too.

I commend to you our sister Phoebe. A letter of commendation (synistēmi, to recommend, introduce): a common practice so that travelling believers could be trusted and received (2 Corinthians 3:1). Phoebe was probably carrying this letter to Rome. “Our sister”: a member of God’s family. And begin with the physical fact, because it is easy to lose. Somebody had to carry this letter. There was no post for private correspondence; a document travelled because a person carried it. Cenchreae was Corinth’s eastern harbour, and the roll containing Romans went from there to Rome in the luggage of the woman being introduced in these two verses.

The voice in the room. And carrying was not the whole job. In the ancient world the bearer of a letter commonly read it aloud to the recipients and answered for it: the sender’s voice in the room. Romans takes something over an hour to read at a steady pace. When the congregations of Rome first heard about the potter and the clay, about the olive tree, about nothing being able to separate them from the love of God, they very possibly heard it in Phoebe’s voice, and when somebody asked what Paul meant, it may well have been Phoebe who explained what she knew of his mind. The church’s copies of Romans very probably descend from a manuscript that was placed in a woman’s hands and carried across the sea.

A servant of the church at Cenchreae. Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth, where Paul was writing (Acts 18:18). “Servant” is diakonos; the ESV notes that it can be rendered deaconess. It may mean she served in a general way, or that she held a recognised office of service. The word can mean servant in a general sense, but here it is attached to a particular congregation, of the church at Cenchreae, which points toward a recognised role rather than a general description.

That you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints. Receive her as a fellow believer should be received: with love, hospitality and honour. Phoebe is coming to a city where she may know almost no one; the Roman church is being instructed to treat her as one of their own, which, in Christ, she is. This is the hospitality of the ancient church made concrete.

And help her in whatever she may need from you. Perhaps she had business in Rome, legal or commercial, and needed help. Paul does not say, and he does not need to. Whatever she needs, they are to supply.

For she has been a patron of many and of myself as well. “Patron” (prostatis) means benefactor, protector, helper: probably a woman of some means who used her wealth and influence to support Paul and others, perhaps opening her home and helping travellers. The word is rare and in some ways startling. In Roman society a patron was the person of standing who supplied money, housing, protection and introductions to those who depended on him. It is the only appearance of the noun in the New Testament, and Paul says she has been a patron of many and of myself as well. The apostle to the Gentiles is on record as having been somebody’s dependent, and he is not embarrassed to say so.

Where Christians differ: Phoebe and women in church office. Some argue from Phoebe that women may hold any office in the church, including elder or pastor. Others deny that Phoebe held any office at all. Among those who agree on the eldership, some take her title in its general sense, others see her as a deaconess serving especially among women, and others as a deacon in the same office as 1 Timothy 3:8–13, reading 1 Timothy 3:11 as speaking of women deacons. Verdict: Phoebe was an honoured servant of her church, and she may well have held a recognised role of service, which some Reformed churches call deaconess (compare 1 Timothy 3:11). The office of deacon is one of practical service and mercy, not of governing or teaching the church with authority. The New Testament reserves the office of elder or pastor, with its authority to teach and rule, for qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). This is the complementarian view: men and women are equal in worth and in Christ (Galatians 3:28), with different callings in the church and home. Phoebe’s example shows how highly Paul valued women’s ministry, and churches should honour and use women’s gifts fully within Scripture’s pattern.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women’s service is second-class. Paul begins his greetings by commending a woman. Whatever view one takes of her title, the facts are plain: a woman held a recognised place of service in her congregation, funded the apostle, and was trusted with the delivery of the most important letter he ever wrote.

What do deacons actually do? Deacons care for the practical needs of the church so that the elders can give themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. The pattern begins in Acts 6:1–6, where seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom were appointed to ensure that widows were not neglected in the daily distribution of food. Today that means things like caring for the poor and sick, organising practical help, looking after buildings and finances, welcoming newcomers and coordinating mercy. Their qualifications are mostly about character (1 Timothy 3:8–13). It is not a lesser calling: those who serve well gain a good standing and great confidence in the faith (1 Timothy 3:13).

So how can women serve in my church? In more ways than most churches use. Women in the New Testament host churches (Lydia, Acts 16:15), fund the mission (Luke 8:1–3), carry apostolic letters (Phoebe), labour in the gospel alongside Paul (Philippians 4:2–3), explain the faith privately to men and women alike (Acts 18:26), teach and train younger women (Titus 2:3–5), and pass the faith to children (2 Timothy 1:5). In a complementarian church, women can lead ministries of mercy, teach women and children, counsel, organise, show hospitality, pray in the gathering, and serve in recognised roles of service. What is reserved for qualified men is the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church. A church that keeps that boundary but leaves its women’s gifts unused has obeyed half the chapter.

In a sentence. Paul commends to you our sister Phoebe, a deacon of the church in Cenchreae. He asks you to receive her in the Lord in a way worthy of his people and to give her any help she may need from you, for she has been the benefactor of many people, including him.

On a Tuesday. Use what you have, whether home, money or influence, to help those who serve the gospel, as Phoebe did. Think of one missionary, pastor or gospel worker who is a stranger somewhere, or who carries a heavy load, and ask what a patron would do: a room, a meal, a gift, a phone call, an introduction. And when a visiting believer comes to your church, receive them in a way worthy of the saints: learn their name, find out what they need, and help.

For worship. The God who wrote the greatest letter in the world did not send it by angel. He sent it in the hands of a sister from a harbour town, who had used her money to support his servants, and he has kept her name in his book ever since. That is how he works: through ordinary saints, carried along by his providence, so that the glory is his. He saw every coin she gave and every traveller she sheltered, and he honoured her before the whole church for two thousand years. He is a God who notices, and who remembers, and who delights to use what his people offer him.
verseByVerse.note: Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. The ESV notes that “servant” can also be rendered “deaconess.” Phoebe probably carried this letter to Rome. A patron was a benefactor who supported others with her resources.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.

Greet Prisca and Aquila. Prisca is a form of Priscilla. She and Aquila had returned to Rome after Claudius’ expulsion of the Jews (Acts 18:2) was lifted. They were a married couple, tentmakers like Paul. Paul met them in Corinth, worked with them, and took them to Ephesus, where they taught Apollos the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:2–3, 18–26). They also hosted a church in Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:19).

The order of the names. Paul writes Prisca and Aquila, the wife before the husband, and he does so in most of the places where the couple appears. In a world that ordered such things carefully, that is not an accident, and the usual explanation is the simplest one: she was the more prominent of the two, perhaps by social standing, perhaps by gift and zeal. Paul notices, and does not mind.

Back in the city that expelled them. Then notice where they are standing when this greeting arrives. They are in Rome, and Paul met them in Corinth because they had been thrown out of Rome, when Claudius expelled the Jews from the city (Acts 18:2). They rebuilt in Corinth, moved on to Ephesus, and have now gone back to the city that had once evicted them. The tension between Jewish and Gentile believers that stands behind so much of chapters 9 to 11 and 14 runs straight through this one household. They have been refugees for the faith, and they have gone back.

My fellow workers in Christ Jesus. “Fellow workers” (synergoi): partners in gospel ministry. Paul does not call them his helpers or his supporters. He calls them co-workers, people who share the same labour.

Who risked their necks for my life. Literally, laid down their own necks: the posture of a man on an executioner’s block. Whatever happened, they put their heads where his was going to be. We do not know the event, perhaps the riot in Ephesus (Acts 19:23–41). Paul does not tell us the incident, which suggests everyone concerned already knew it.

To whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well. By saving Paul, they served all the churches he founded. Their courage at one particular moment may have preserved the ministry that carried the gospel across the Gentile world. Every Gentile believer reading Romans owes something to a couple who were willing to die for the man who wrote it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Priscilla held the office of elder because she helped teach Apollos. She and her husband explained the gospel to him privately, in their home, which is the kind of instruction every believer may give.

How does Priscilla teaching Apollos fit with 1 Timothy 2:12? Egalitarian Christians see her as proof that Paul placed no limit on women’s teaching. But look at what Luke says she did. With her husband she took Apollos aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:26). That was private instruction by a couple, not the authoritative teaching of the gathered church that 1 Timothy 2 reserves for qualified men. The complementarian reading honours both texts. Women may and should teach the faith: to other women (Titus 2:3–5), to children (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), and in private conversation like this with men too. The office of elder and the preaching of the church belong to men. And Paul’s greeting shows how highly he valued her.

What does it look like for a married couple to serve together? Priscilla and Aquila worked the same trade, opened the same home, taught the same young preacher and risked the same danger. Their marriage was not a retreat from ministry but a base for it. For couples today that might mean opening your home to a Bible study, having students or lonely people at your table, mentoring a younger couple, or working side by side in a church ministry. It means praying together for the church, not only for yourselves. And it means a husband who leads with self-giving love and a wife who is honoured as his fellow worker, both of them looking outward together.

In a sentence. Greet Priscilla and Aquila, Paul’s co-workers in Christ Jesus. They risked their lives for him. Not only he but all the churches of the Gentiles are grateful to them.

On a Tuesday. If you are married, ask your spouse this week: what could we do together for the church that neither of us could do alone? If you are single, think of a couple whose home has been a blessing to you, and thank them. And ask whose neck you would put on the block: whose good, whose safety, whose ministry matters more to you than your own comfort?

For worship. The gospel moves through specific, costly, named human lives, and behind every one of them is the God who gives such courage. He gave Priscilla and Aquila a home in exile, a trade to work, a church to host, and a love for his servant strong enough to risk death. And they were only following their Lord, who did not merely risk his neck for us but laid down his life, and took it up again. Thank God for Christian couples who serve together, open their home, and risk much for the gospel, for every one of them is a gift from his hand.
verseByVerse.note: Prisca is a form of Priscilla. She and Aquila had returned to Rome after Claudius’s expulsion of Jews ended.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.

Greet also the church in their house. Churches met in homes; there were no purpose-built church buildings for a long time, until the third century. Rome probably had several house churches (vv. 5, 14, 15). The church (ekklēsia) is the people, not the building. It is worth noticing that a whole congregation is meeting in someone’s front room. No building, no sign, no address anybody would recognise: a house with more people in it than usual on a particular day. For the first two hundred years or so, that is what the church looked like everywhere, and from those rooms the gospel conquered the empire.

Greet my beloved Epaenetus. “Beloved”: Paul’s warm affection for individuals. He does not greet a congregation in the abstract. He greets a man he loves.

Who was the first convert to Christ in Asia. Literally the firstfruits (aparchē) of Asia for Christ. Asia was the Roman province in western Turkey, with Ephesus as its capital. Firstfruits is a sacrificial term: the first of the harvest brought to God as the pledge that the rest is coming. Paul has used it already in this letter of the patriarchs (11:16) and of the Spirit we have been given as the first instalment of our redemption (8:23). Here he attaches it to one man. Which fits what he said about his ministry only a chapter ago: that his work is priestly service, and the offering he brings is the Gentiles themselves (15:16). Epaenetus is the first handful of that harvest. He may have been converted through Priscilla and Aquila’s ministry in Ephesus, which would explain why he is greeted next to them.

The loneliness of being first. Somebody in every place has to be the first, and being first is a lonely business. The first believer in a province has no church to join, no one who understands, and nobody who has done it before him. Epaenetus was that man in Asia, and the region became one of the great centres of early Christianity: the seven churches of Revelation were all in it. One convert was the pledge of thousands.

What it does not mean. It does not mean house churches are the only biblical model. They were the practical form in that time. The essentials are the word, the sacraments, prayer and fellowship (Acts 2:42).

Is a small church meeting in a home a real church? Yes, if it has what makes a church a church. A church is not defined by its building or its size but by its marks: the gospel truly preached, the ordinances of baptism and the Lord’s Supper rightly administered, and a people under the care of qualified elders, gathering regularly for worship and holding one another to account in love (Acts 2:42; 14:23; Hebrews 10:24–25). A dozen people in a living room with these things are a church. A thousand people in an auditorium without them are not. Whatever its size, a church should be connected in fellowship with other faithful churches, as the house churches of Rome were connected to each other and to Paul.

In a sentence. Greet also the church that meets at their house. Greet Paul’s dear friend Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in the province of Asia.

On a Tuesday. Your home can be a place of church life: Bible study, prayer, hospitality. Open it. And if you are the only believer in your family, your street or your workplace, remember Epaenetus. The first is never the last if God has planted him there. Pray for the harvest of which you might be the firstfruits.

For worship. When God begins a work, he does not stop at the first. Epaenetus in Asia was a pledge, and God kept it: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea, and churches beyond counting. The Spirit in our hearts is the same kind of pledge, the first instalment of a glory that will certainly come. Our God is the Lord of the harvest. He sows a single seed in a pagan province, and he means the whole field.
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes; there were no church buildings.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me.

Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you. “Worked hard” (kopiaō) means toiled to the point of weariness. We know nothing else of her, but God knows all her labour. Mary is easily lost between Prisca and Junia, and the verb Paul uses of her is worth noticing: it is the word he uses of his own apostolic work (1 Corinthians 15:10; Galatians 4:11). It appears three times in this chapter, and every time it is attached to women: Mary here, and Tryphaena and Tryphosa, and Persis, in verse 12.

He noticed. Paul does not say what any of them did. He says how hard they did it, and that he noticed, and that he wanted a church on the other side of the Mediterranean to know their names. That is not nothing to a person whose work is invisible by nature and unrecorded by default.

Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen. “Kinsmen”: fellow Jews (9:3). They were probably a husband and wife. The ESV notes that the name may be read Junias, a man’s name, but Junia, a common Roman woman’s name, is more likely. The early church read it as a woman’s name almost without exception. John Chrysostom, preaching in the fourth century, took it as female and marvelled at the devotion of this woman. The masculine form Junias has not been found in any ancient inscription or writing, and most modern scholars agree that Junia is correct.

And my fellow prisoners. They had been in prison with Paul at some point, or for the same cause (2 Corinthians 11:23). They had shared his chains for Christ, a bond forged in suffering.

They are well known to the apostles. The Greek phrase can mean “well known to the apostles” (ESV) or “outstanding among the apostles” (ESV note). Either way they were held in high regard by the church’s founding leaders.

And they were in Christ before me. They became Christians before Paul’s conversion, around AD 33–34, so they were among the very first believers, perhaps from Pentecost (Acts 2:10 mentions visitors from Rome). Think of it: when Paul was still breathing threats against the church, these two were already in it, and may well have been among the people he was hunting. Now he calls them kinsmen, fellow prisoners, and those who were in Christ before him.

Where Christians differ: was Junia an apostle? Some say Junia was a female apostle, and so women may hold any office. Others insist the name must be male, or the phrase must mean only “known to the apostles.” Verdict: The ESV reading, well known to the apostles, is grammatically well supported. But even if the phrase means outstanding among the apostles, the word apostle is used in the New Testament in two senses: the unique apostles of Christ (the Twelve and Paul), who had seen the risen Lord and laid the church’s foundation; and messengers or missionaries sent by churches (2 Corinthians 8:23; Philippians 2:25). Andronicus and Junia could only be apostles in the second sense, as travelling missionaries, as Barnabas is called an apostle in Acts 14:14. This does not overturn the New Testament’s teaching on eldership (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), nor does it reopen the apostolic office, whose foundational work ended with the apostles of Christ (Ephesians 2:20). What it does show is a woman who shared Paul’s chains for Christ and was honoured by name for it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean their faithfulness was small. They suffered for Christ and were highly regarded by the church’s leaders.

What if my service goes unnoticed? Then you are in the company of Mary, and of most of the faithful people who have ever lived. Paul noticed Mary, but notice that we still know nothing about what she did, only that she worked hard. God does not need your work to be seen in order to reward it. Your Father who sees in secret will reward you (Matthew 6:4), and God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love you have shown for his name in serving the saints (Hebrews 6:10). Serve for his eye, not for applause. And make it your habit to do what Paul did here: notice the hidden labourers in your church and thank them by name.

In a sentence. Greet Mary, who worked very hard for you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, Paul’s fellow Jews who have been in prison with him. They are well known among the apostles, and they were in Christ before he was.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone in your church whose work is unseen: the person who sets out the chairs, cleans after the meal, prays for the missionaries, visits the housebound. Thank them this week by name, and tell them specifically what you have noticed. And think of the believers who were in Christ before you, the people who prayed for you before you prayed, and thank God for them.

For worship. The Lord keeps a record of every weary hour spent in his service. Mary’s toil, Junia’s chains, the long years of the first believers who were in Christ before the apostle himself: none of it was lost. He saw them, and he wrote their names into the Scripture of his church. And behind every believer who came to Christ before us stands the same sovereign grace that brought us: the grace that turned Saul the persecutor into Paul the prisoner, and made him the brother of those he once hunted. Thank God for the believers who came to Christ before you, who prayed and suffered for the church you now enjoy, and for the grace that put you among them.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the name may be read Junias (a man’s name). Andronicus and Junia had become believers before Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.

Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Several of these names were common among slaves and freedmen in Rome. Ampliatus is found in inscriptions in the imperial household. Sit with what that means for a moment. Ampliatus is a slave’s name: common, unremarkable, the sort of name that appears in household records. In the Roman world such a man had no standing and no expectation that anyone of consequence would know he existed. Paul calls him my beloved in the Lord, and puts him in a letter that has been read aloud in every century since.

A tomb in the catacombs. A tomb in one of Rome’s oldest Christian catacombs bears this name, cut in unusually careful lettering for so ordinary a name. Whether it is this man cannot be shown, but somebody clearly thought an Ampliatus worth honouring.

Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ. “Our”: he had worked with Paul and others in the gospel. Urbanus (from urbs, city) was a common Roman slave name.

And my beloved Stachys. Stachys means ear of grain. Again, Paul’s love for individuals. Three names in two verses, and two of them carry the word beloved.

The sociology the doctrine produces. This is the reason the chapter is not an appendix. Paul has spent fifteen chapters arguing that God justifies the ungodly and shows no partiality (2:11). Here is what that looks like when it has finished arguing: an apostle listing a slave among the people he loves, by name, in writing, for the record.

What it does not mean. It does not mean slaves were second-class in the church. In Christ there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28). Some of the most honoured members of the Roman church were probably slaves or former slaves.
