How can a church make people of low status truly belong? By treating them the way Paul treats Ampliatus: by name, with affection, as co-workers. That means more than being polite on Sunday. It means asking the cleaner, the refugee or the man with no job to serve alongside the professionals, not only to be served. It means eating in each other’s homes. It means choosing leaders for godliness, not for wealth or polish (James 2:1–5). It means praying for and visiting the people who will never be able to repay the visit. A church where everyone in leadership looks the same, earns the same and lives in the same streets should ask whether the gospel has finished its work there.

In a sentence. Greet Ampliatus, whom Paul loves in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our co-worker in Christ, and his dear friend Stachys.

On a Tuesday. In the church, social status means nothing before God. Treat everyone in your church as beloved in the Lord. This week, learn the name of someone in your congregation whose life is very different from yours, and use it next Sunday. Ask how you can pray for them. Then pray.

For worship. God has chosen what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in his presence (1 Corinthians 1:28–29). Ampliatus had no standing in Rome, and he has a name in Scripture. That is the grace of God: he passes by the great houses and calls their slaves his beloved. He looked on us in our lowliness too, and made us his own. Blessed be the God who shows no partiality, and whose love is not drawn by rank but given freely to the least.
verseByVerse.note: Several of these names were common among slaves and freedmen in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus. Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus. Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.

Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. “Approved” (dokimos) means tested and proved genuine, the word for metal that has been through the fire and come out true. Apelles had been through some trial and stood firm. His faith was tested and found real. Paul gives him only one phrase, and it is perhaps the best one a Christian can receive.

Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus. The households of Aristobulus and Narcissus probably include slaves and freedmen belonging to important men. Aristobulus may have been the grandson of Herod the Great, who lived in Rome as a private citizen. When such a man died, his household did not disperse; the slaves passed as property to the emperor while keeping their old master’s name. His household slaves would remain known by his name after his death, which would explain why Paul greets those who belong to the family of each man rather than the men themselves.

Greet my kinsman Herodion. A fellow Jew. His name suggests a link with the Herod family, fitting the mention of Aristobulus. The name means belonging to Herod. If the connection is what it appears to be, a member of the household of the family that killed John the Baptist and mocked Christ is being greeted as a kinsman and a brother, a few lines from a slave and a woman who works too hard.

Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus. Narcissus may be the powerful freedman of the emperor Claudius, who was forced to commit suicide in AD 54. His slaves would have passed into the emperor’s household. “Those in the Lord”: only some in that household were believers. Not all of them. Some. Which is a very exact picture of how the faith actually spread through that city: not by converting a great house but by taking root among its servants, a few at a time, in the quarters below. The gospel had reached into the imperial palace (Philippians 4:22).

What it does not mean. It does not mean a whole household had to believe for some members to be saved. Individuals came to Christ even in pagan households.

What if I am the only Christian in my home or workplace? Then you stand where these believers stood, and Paul thought you worth greeting. Live as one approved in Christ: faithful, honest, hard-working and kind, so that you adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in everything (Titus 2:10). Do not hide your faith, but let your life speak before your words do, as Peter tells believing wives with unbelieving husbands (1 Peter 3:1–2). Pray daily for the people around you by name. Find fellowship elsewhere, in a church where you are known and fed, because you cannot be the only light in a dark house without being refuelled. And remember that God has often begun his work in a household or an office through one believer who simply stayed faithful.

In a sentence. Greet Apelles, whose fidelity to Christ has stood the test. Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus. Greet Herodion, Paul’s fellow Jew. Greet those in the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Pray for believers who are the only Christians in their homes or workplaces. Think of one by name and send them a word of encouragement this week. And if your faith is being tested now, take Apelles’ title as your hope: the fire does not destroy true faith. It proves it.

For worship. The gospel cannot be kept out of any house, not even the house of Herod, not even the household of Caesar. It went down the stairs into the slaves’ quarters of the most powerful men in Rome and took root there. The grace that saved a Herodion is grace that can reach anyone. And the God who tests his people does so not to destroy them but to show them true, like gold from the furnace. He kept Apelles through his trial, and he will keep every one of his own until the day they are approved before his face.
verseByVerse.note: The households of Aristobulus and Narcissus probably included their slaves and freedmen.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.

Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Probably sisters, perhaps twins. Their names mean dainty and delicate, yet they were hard workers (kopiaō) in the Lord. Paul may be smiling as he writes it: the dainty ones are labouring to exhaustion for Christ.

Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord. Persis means Persian woman, perhaps a former slave. Paul notes her past labour: she has worked hard, perhaps now elderly. The past tense may mean that her years of strength are behind her, and Paul has not forgotten them. Women are prominent among Paul’s named co-workers throughout his letters, a pattern that reflects the genuine place of women in the mission of the early church.

Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord. Rufus may be the son of Simon of Cyrene, whom Mark mentions (Mark 15:21). Mark wrote his Gospel probably for the church in Rome, and names Simon’s sons, Alexander and Rufus, as people his readers knew, a detail that only makes sense if they knew who those two were. If so, the man who carried Jesus’ cross had a son in the Roman church. It cannot be proved. But it is entirely possible that the woman who mothered Paul was the wife of the man who carried the cross of Christ, and that her son was sitting in one of these house churches when the letter was read out. “Chosen” (eklektos): elect, or perhaps choice, outstanding.

Also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well. She had cared for Paul like a mother, perhaps in Antioch, where men from Cyrene were among the church’s leaders (Acts 11:20; 13:1). This clause deserves more than a passing mention, because it is one of the warmest things Paul ever wrote and it is over in a moment. Consider the man writing it. Paul had no wife and no household. He had been flogged five times, beaten with rods three times, stoned once and left for dead (Acts 14:19), shipwrecked, hungry, cold and short of clothing (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). And somewhere in all that, a woman took him in and treated him as her own: fed him, presumably made him rest, possibly told him off.

She is not named. He never gives her name. He identifies her only as somebody’s mother, and that is evidently how he thinks of her. It is worth saying plainly to anyone who has quietly done that for a Christian worker and assumed it counted for little: the apostle put it in Scripture. Spiritual motherhood is a precious ministry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Rufus was more elect than others. All believers are chosen in Christ (Ephesians 1:4).

What does chosen in the Lord mean, if every believer is chosen? Paul may mean simply that Rufus is one of God’s elect, as every believer is, and is saying it of him warmly. Or he may use the word in its other sense, choice or outstanding, as we speak of choice fruit. Either way, it rests on the truth Paul has taught in this letter: that God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world, not because of anything in them, but in love (8:29–30; 9:11; Ephesians 1:4–5). That is not a cold doctrine. Here it is a term of affection. To be chosen in the Lord is to be loved by God from eternity, and every believer may say it of himself with wonder.

Can I be a spiritual mother or father if I have no children? Yes, and the church badly needs you to be. Rufus’s mother was a mother to a man who was not her son. Paul called Timothy his true child in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2), and Jesus promised that those who leave family for his sake will receive mothers and brothers and children a hundredfold in this age (Mark 10:29–30). Single and childless believers can be the steadiest spiritual parents a young Christian ever has. Have someone younger to your table regularly. Pray for them by name. Ask how they are really doing, and listen. Teach them what you have learned of Christ, and let them see your faith in hard days.

In a sentence. Greet Tryphena and Tryphosa, those women who work hard in the Lord. Greet his dear friend Persis, another woman who has worked very hard in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has been a mother to Paul too.

On a Tuesday. Be a spiritual mother or father to someone younger in the faith. Feed them, pray for them, open your home. And if you are older and your days of hard labour are past, like Persis, do not think your service has ended. Your prayers, your counsel and your example are still labour in the Lord.

For worship. Perhaps the man who carried the cross of Jesus up the hill had a son in this church and a wife who mothered the apostle. If so, the cross he was forced to carry became the cross that saved his family. That is how God works: the heaviest burden of one day becomes the means of grace for generations. And the God who chose Rufus before the world began is the God who sets the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6), who gave a homeless apostle a mother in the faith, and who has promised that none who leave anything for his sake will go without. He is the Father of the fatherless, and he makes his church a home.
verseByVerse.note: Rufus may be the son of Simon of Cyrene, whom Mark mentions as if known to his readers.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.

Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Probably a house church, or a group of believers who lived or worked together. Most of these names are typical of slaves and freedmen. And these two verses are different from everything before them, and the difference is the point. The names arrive with nothing attached. No my beloved, no who worked hard, no who risked their necks, no approved in Christ. Just the names.

Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them. Another group, perhaps another house church. Philologus and Julia may have been husband and wife, with Nereus and his sister as their children. We know nothing else about a single one of them. Nereus has a sister whose name was not thought necessary. And behind both clusters stand the ones who are not named at all, the brothers who are with them, all the saints who are with them: rooms full of people reduced to a phrase.

The names. Paul greets twenty-six people by name, about a third of them women, a mix of Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free. He knew so many people in a city he had never visited because believers travelled, and many had met him elsewhere. The church in Rome was a network of house churches, held together by love.

The real proportion of the church. That is the actual proportion of the Christian church, in the first century and in this one. A handful of people are remembered for something. Rather more are remembered only as having been present. The overwhelming majority are not written down anywhere, and every one of them got up on ordinary mornings and believed and was faithful and died. Paul wrote the names down anyway. He had no way of knowing that in doing so he was putting Patrobas and Olympas into the permanent Scripture of the church, still being read aloud two thousand years later by people who know nothing about them but their names. Which is a fair picture of what God does with obscurity. The register that matters is being kept somewhere else, and it is not short of space.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul greeted only important people. Most were ordinary. All were precious.

Among so many believers, does God really know me personally? Yes. The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3). He knows the number of the hairs on your head (Matthew 10:30) and has engraved his people on the palms of his hands (Isaiah 49:16). Paul’s list of unknown names is a small picture of a great truth: God does not love his church in bulk. He chose each one, Christ died for each one, and the Spirit dwells in each one. On the last day you will not be lost in the crowd; you will be known, and welcomed by name. Rejoice that your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20).

In a sentence. Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas and the other brothers and sisters with them. Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas and all the Lord’s people who are with them.

On a Tuesday. Take your church directory, or simply picture the faces, and pray for five people you rarely speak to, by name. And if you feel like one of the unnamed, one of all the saints who are with them, take heart: you are exactly the kind of person the church has always mostly been made of, and God has not lost track of you.

For worship. God knows each of his people by name. Before the world was made he wrote their names in the book of life of the Lamb, and not one of them will be forgotten. Patrobas and Olympas are unknown to history and known to God, and the same is true of most of the saints who have ever lived. He keeps the register. He counts the stars and calls them all by name (Psalm 147:4), and he counts his children with even greater care. Thank him that your name is known to him and written in his book.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends in that culture, on the cheek. Holy: pure, set apart, expressing the love of brothers and sisters in Christ (1 Corinthians 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:26; 1 Peter 5:14). In the early church it became part of the worship service, before the Lord’s Supper. And the command has a small word in it that does all the work: greet one another. Not greet the people you would naturally greet. In a congregation that has spent two chapters arguing about food and days, and that contains a member of Herod’s circle, several slaves, a wealthy patroness and an unknown number of people who find each other difficult, one another is a considerably more demanding instruction than it looks. The gesture of family, extended across every barrier the ancient world had built.

All the churches of Christ greet you. The churches Paul had planted, or those he was representing, send their love. The church is worldwide. And the line does something quietly generous. Congregations in Corinth and Philippi and Ephesus, most of whom have never met a single person on this list, send their greetings to strangers. Paul is telling a church he has never visited that it is already being thought about by people it will never meet.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians today must greet with a literal kiss. The principle is warm, pure, family affection, expressed in a way fitting for each culture: a handshake, an embrace.

Must Christians greet each other with a kiss today? The command is repeated (1 Corinthians 16:20; 1 Peter 5:14), but what it commands is the warmth, not the form. In Paul’s world a kiss was an ordinary family greeting; Paul makes it holy, a greeting between brothers and sisters in Christ. Where a kiss carries that meaning it may still be used; where it does not, a handshake or an embrace obeys the command. What is not optional is greeting one another as family, and always in a way that is holy: pure, appropriate, and safe for everyone, especially children and the vulnerable.

What if I find greeting people at church hard? Many believers do, whether from shyness, anxiety or past hurt, and Paul is not commanding you to become the loudest person in the room. Start small. Learn three names and use them. Greet the person sitting nearest you before or after the service. Look for the newcomer standing alone, because they are probably more nervous than you. If conversation is hard, a warm handshake and a simple word, it is good to see you, obeys this verse. Ask God to help you, and remember that the people you greet are your family in Christ, not an audience judging you.

In a sentence. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ send greetings.

On a Tuesday. Greet your fellow believers warmly on Sunday. Learn names. Look people in the eye. Make a point of greeting one person you would not naturally greet: someone older or younger, someone from a different background, someone you have had a disagreement with. And pray this week for a church in another country, because all the churches of Christ are your family too.

For worship. Christ has made one family out of strangers. A slave and a city treasurer, a Jew and a Gentile, an apostle and a woman who mothered him: all of them exchange the greeting of brothers and sisters, because they share one Father and one elder Brother. And the family is worldwide. Every Sunday, in every time zone, the churches of Christ greet one another across oceans, one people of every tongue, held together by the love of God. That is no human achievement. It is the work of the Son who was not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11).
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–27 — Final Warning and the Doxology of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before the closing doxology, Paul inserts a sharp warning (vv. 17–20) against those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine the Romans have been taught. The letter has been, among other things, a sustained argument for the unity of the body across the strong/weak divide; it would be a bitter irony if the letter itself became a tool of division. Paul's instruction is clear: watch them, avoid them. The divisive person — whatever their theological credentials — is not serving Christ but their own appetites, and they deceive the naive with smooth talk and flattery.

The closing doxology (vv. 25–27) returns to the letter's great themes for one final, comprehensive statement. God is able to strengthen — the power of the gospel is not an argument but a strengthening. According to Paul's gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ — these are identified: Paul's gospel is the gospel of Jesus Christ, not a human theological construct. According to the revelation of the mystery kept secret for long ages — the gospel is not a new invention; it is the disclosure of what God planned from before time began. Now made known to all the nations — the universality Paul has argued throughout. For the obedience of faith — the phrase that bracketed the letter in 1:5 now closes it. To the only wise God — the doxology of chapter 11 returns, now applied to the whole letter's argument. Through Jesus Christ — the mediator of all grace and all glory. To whom be glory forever. Amen.

The letter that began with Paul introducing himself as a slave of Christ and set apart for the gospel ends with everything returning to God — from him, through him, and to him. The argument is complete. The doxology is the only adequate conclusion. Amen.

Two stretches sit between the warning and the doxology and should not be passed over. The first is v. 19, where Paul softens nothing but changes his tone: their obedience is known everywhere and he is glad of them, and what he wants is that they be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. It is the counterpart to the warning — the way to be undeceived is not to become worldly-wise about corruption but to know goodness well.

The second is vv. 21–24, a second greeting list, this time from Paul’s end of the journey: Timothy and three Jewish co-workers; Gaius, in whose house both Paul and the whole Corinthian church are lodged; Erastus, the city treasurer, whose name has plausibly been found on a paving inscription at Corinth; and Quartus. Between them stands v. 22, where Tertius, who wrote this letter, adds a greeting of his own — the only place in the New Testament where the man holding the pen speaks in his own voice.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery Revealed: Gospel and Old Testament Unity

Romans 16:25–27 returns to the theme announced in 1:1–4: the gospel was promised beforehand through the prophets; the Old Testament is the gospel in anticipation; the New Testament is the gospel in fulfilment. The "mystery" kept secret for long ages is not something the Old Testament was ignorant of but something it was pregnant with — the inclusion of the Gentiles in the covenant people, the extension of the Abrahamic blessing to all nations, the righteousness of God given through faith in Jesus Christ. Calvin's canon of interpretation applies: the two testaments are one Bible, one gospel, one covenant of grace, administered differently but pointing to the same Saviour.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The warning of vv. 17–20 against divisive teachers was written into the most doctrinally comprehensive letter Paul ever wrote. The letter's very depth makes it susceptible to misuse: its teachings on election, freedom, and grace can all be distorted into weapons of division. Paul's warning is therefore structurally appropriate — the deeper the theology, the greater the need for vigilance against those who weaponise it. Now: Every generation produces its version of the smooth-talking divisive teacher who uses theological language to advance personal agendas and create factions. Paul's three-fold response is the standing instruction: watch them carefully; avoid them; trust the God of peace who will soon crush Satan under your feet (v. 20).

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them. For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive. — Romans 16:17–18
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them. For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive.

I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions. A sudden warning, after all the warmth. “Watch out” (skopeō) means keep an eye on, mark, the word from which we get scope. Divisions (dichostasiai, standing apart) means splitting the church into parties. The command is pointed and practical: watch and avoid. The divisive teacher is not to be engaged endlessly in debate or accommodated indefinitely in the hope that he will improve. He is to be identified and avoided, not with contempt, but with the clear sight of people who know what they have been taught and can recognise a deviation when they see it.

And create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught. “Obstacles” (skandala) are traps, snares that trip people up. Contrary to the doctrine: the teaching of the apostles, which Paul has set out in this letter. The problem is not differences over food (chapter 14), but false teaching that undermines the gospel. The standard of judgment is not novelty against tradition, or majority against minority opinion. It is the apostolic teaching, the gospel Paul has spent sixteen chapters expounding. The community that has this letter has the measuring rod. Apply it.

Avoid them. “Avoid” (ekklinō) means turn away from. Do not give them a platform or follow them (2 Thessalonians 3:6, 14; Titus 3:10).

For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites. Literally, their own belly, the organ of appetite. They serve their own desires: money, pleasure, influence (Philippians 3:19). Verse 18 tells you how to recognise them, and the marks are not doctrinal so much as personal. Whatever is being said at the front, something is being fed at the back: money, or a following, or the pleasure of being the one who sees what others have missed.

And by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive. “Smooth talk” (chrēstologia, fine words) and “flattery” (eulogia, nice speech). False teachers are often charming. And the method named is not argument. The divisive man in Paul’s description does not begin by attacking the church; he begins by being remarkably nice to you. He tells you that you are more discerning than the others, that you have noticed what they have not. Flattery is the tool because it recruits: you cannot build a faction out of people you have insulted. His targets are named too. “Naive” (akakoi) means innocent, unsuspecting, without guile. Not fools. Good-hearted people who assume others mean what they say, which is why the very next verse asks for a particular kind of shrewdness.

What it does not mean. It does not mean avoiding every Christian you disagree with. Paul distinguishes between disputable matters (chapter 14) and teaching contrary to the gospel. The first calls for patience; the second for watchfulness. A guard is essential here, because this verse is one of the most abused in the letter and the abuse is easy. Paul has just spent two chapters commanding these same people not to separate over disputed matters: not to judge, not to despise, to welcome the man whose conscience differs (14:1–15:7). He cannot be undoing that a chapter later. Romans 16:17 is not a licence to avoid the Christian who disagrees with you.

How do I tell a false teacher from a Christian who simply disagrees with me? Look for all three marks Paul gives, together. First, the teaching is contrary to what the apostles taught: it denies or distorts the gospel itself, who Christ is, his atoning death and resurrection, justification by faith, the authority of Scripture, or the call to holiness. Second, the man is serving himself: his teaching keeps leading back to his money, his following or his importance. Third, he works by flattery and private recruiting rather than by open argument. Someone who holds a different view of a disputed matter and says so plainly is the person chapter 14 told you to welcome. Someone who is quietly assembling a party around himself is the person this verse tells you to walk away from. The difference is not how strongly he disagrees. It is what he is building.

What does avoid them actually mean? Do I cut them off? It means refusing them influence. Do not sit under their teaching, buy their books, follow their channels, invite them to speak, or let them recruit you or others. If such a person is in your church, the elders must deal with it, warning him and, if he will not repent, removing him from fellowship (Titus 3:10–11; Matthew 18:15–17). You should not run your own private campaign. But avoiding is not hating. Paul tells another church not to regard such a person as an enemy, but to warn him as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:15). Pray for him, speak the truth to him when it is right, and long for his repentance. The door to his return should always stand open.

In a sentence. Paul urges you, brothers and sisters, to watch out for those who cause divisions and put obstacles in your way that are contrary to the teaching you have learned. Keep away from them. For such people are not serving our Lord Christ, but their own appetites. By smooth talk and flattery they deceive the minds of naive people.

On a Tuesday. Test teachers, books, podcasts and preachers by Scripture, not by how pleasant they sound. Take the voice that has most influenced your thinking this year and ask three questions: does what he teaches match the gospel of Romans? Whose kingdom does it build? And does it work by making me feel more discerning than my church? Then notice when you are being flattered, by anyone. It is one of the surest signals that somebody wants something from you.

For worship. Christ guards his church. He gave apostles to lay down the truth once for all, he gave Scripture to keep it, and he gives pastors and ordinary believers the discernment to recognise a counterfeit. Teachers who serve their bellies come and go, and their factions crumble; the church built on the apostles’ doctrine still stands after two thousand years, because the Lord Christ is its master and it serves him. Blessed be the faithful Shepherd who knows his sheep, who will not let them be snatched out of his hand, and whose voice they know from the voice of a stranger (John 10:4–5, 28).

verseByVerse.quote: For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you. Their faith was famous (1:8). Paul is not accusing them but protecting them. He warns because he loves what he sees, and he wants it kept.

But I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. Wise in good: knowing it and doing it well. Innocent (akeraios, unmixed, pure) in evil: inexperienced, simple about it. The positive and the negative of the same counsel. In a world of sophisticated evil and manipulation, the Christian is to be genuinely knowledgeable about goodness, not naive, and genuinely innocent of evil, not worldly-wise in wickedness. Jesus said to be wise as serpents and innocent as doves (Matthew 10:16; 1 Corinthians 14:20). You do not need to taste evil to understand it.

The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The promise echoes God’s word to the serpent in Eden: the offspring of the woman would crush its head (Genesis 3:15). This is the first gospel promise in the Bible, and here it is in the last chapter of Romans. Christ has already won the decisive victory at the cross (Colossians 2:15). Now God will crush Satan under the feet of his people, as they share in Christ’s victory, finally at his return. The false teachers are Satan’s agents (2 Corinthians 11:13–15); their defeat is certain.

The God of peace who crushes. Hold the two halves together, because the combination is startling. The God of peace will crush Satan. The verb is violent, to break in pieces, to grind, and it is attached to the title Paul has just used at the end of the previous chapter for the God he commends to them (15:33). That is not a contradiction, and the letter has been explaining why for sixteen chapters. Peace is not made by leaving the hostility in place. It is made by dealing with what caused it, which is why this letter opened with wrath and arrived at reconciliation. A God of peace who could not crush anything would have no peace to offer.

Under your feet. And the promise is put in a strange place. Not under Christ’s feet, though Genesis 3:15 said the serpent would bruise the heel of the woman’s offspring and be crushed by him, and that was settled at the cross. Paul hands the victory out to a mixed, quarrelling congregation of slaves and patrons and former idolaters, and tells them the last act will happen under their shoes. They share in the victory because they are united to the Victor.

Soon. “Soon” (en tachei, quickly, without delay). Soon does not set a date. Some of it came quickly: the false teachers at Rome would be exposed and the church preserved, a foretaste of Satan’s defeat. The final crushing comes at Christ’s return, which is always near, the next great event in God’s plan (see the note on 13:11–12). The point is certainty: the outcome is fixed, and the wait will seem short in the light of eternity (8:18; 2 Corinthians 4:17). It has been two thousand years, and that has to be faced honestly rather than hurried past. The honest reading is not that Paul miscalculated but that he is describing a decisive outcome that is fixed and imminent in the sense that matters: the next thing on God’s agenda, whatever the interval turns out to be. With the Lord one day is as a thousand years (2 Peter 3:8–9).

A word for the tired. Which is a word for the reader who is tired of waiting, and who has been waiting in this letter since 8:23. The groaning is real, and Paul never suggests otherwise. But the sentence is not may God crush. It is will. What is left is not the outcome but the interval.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. A benediction: the letter began with grace (1:7) and returns to it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers defeat Satan by their own strength. The God of peace crushes him. We stand in Christ’s victory.

How can I be innocent about evil without being naive? Know the good thoroughly, and do not go looking at evil to understand it. Those who are trained to spot forged banknotes learn the genuine note so well that a fake stands out at once. In the same way, the believer who knows Scripture, the gospel and the character of Christ deeply will sense what is false, without needing to immerse himself in it. That means being careful about what you watch, read and scroll through, not out of fear but because you do not need to be expert in sin. It also means being wise in the good: honest about how temptation and manipulation work, alert to flattery, and willing to ask a mature believer when something feels wrong.

Why has Satan not been crushed yet? He has been decisively defeated, and he is not yet destroyed. At the cross Christ disarmed the powers and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15); Satan is a beaten enemy who still prowls (1 Peter 5:8), but on a chain, unable to stop the gospel going to the nations (Revelation 20:1–3). Every time someone is converted, his house is plundered (Mark 3:27). God delays the final blow because he is patient, not wishing that any should perish, and the full number of his people is still being gathered (2 Peter 3:9). When the last of them is in, Christ will return, and the serpent will be thrown into the lake of fire for ever (Revelation 20:10).

In a sentence. Everyone has heard about your obedience, so Paul rejoices because of you; but he wants you to be wise about what is good, and innocent about what is evil. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus be with you.

On a Tuesday. When temptation comes this week, or accusation, or the fear that evil is winning, say this verse aloud: the God of peace will soon crush Satan under my feet. Then choose one way to grow wise in the good: a book of the Bible to read through, a mature Christian to learn from, a habit of goodness to practise. And choose one thing to be innocent of: an app, a channel or a kind of entertainment you do not need to know so well.

For worship. Satan is a defeated enemy. In the garden, on the day of the first sin, God promised the serpent’s ruin, and he has never once wavered. He sent the offspring of the woman, who let his heel be bruised on a cross and crushed the serpent’s head in the same act. And now the God of peace, who made peace by blood, will finish what he began, and will grind the enemy under the feet of the very people the enemy once held captive. The accuser of the brothers will be silenced, and the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ will be all in all. Praise the God of peace who will soon crush him under your feet.
verseByVerse.note: The promise echoes God’s word to the serpent in Eden.

parallels.desc: he shall bruise your head

verseByVerse.quote: Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen. I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen. I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.

Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you. Paul’s closest companion and spiritual son (Acts 16:1–3; Philippians 2:19–22). Timothy was with Paul through most of the Gentile mission, and Paul says there was no one like him, who would be genuinely concerned for their welfare.

So do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen. Fellow Jews. Lucius may be Lucius of Cyrene (Acts 13:1). Jason may be the man who hosted Paul in Thessalonica (Acts 17:5–9). Sosipater may be Sopater of Berea (Acts 20:4), who travelled with Paul to Jerusalem with the collection. Three Jewish co-workers in a largely Gentile mission: the very unity Paul has been describing, standing beside him as he writes.

I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord. Paul dictated his letters; Tertius was the scribe who wrote this one down. Here he adds his own greeting. Stop on this, because it is the only moment of its kind in the New Testament. For hours, more likely across several sittings, a man has been sitting with a pen, taking down the words of Romans as Paul spoke them. He has written the wrath of chapter 1 and the no condemnation of chapter 8. He has written out the potter and the clay. He has just taken down a list of more than twenty names. And at the end he is invited to add a line, or asks whether he may, and he writes his greeting. The pen looks up.

Three and Four. His name is worth noticing too. Tertius means Third. A verse later a brother called Quartus sends his greeting, and Quartus means Fourth. Numeral names like these were common among slaves and freedmen, sometimes given by owners who did not trouble to think of a name and simply counted. So the last stretch of the greatest letter ever written contains two men called Three and Four, one of whom physically wrote it. Neither, perhaps, was given a name anyone had troubled over. Both have been read aloud in every language on earth for two thousand years.

Paul’s own hand. Paul often signed the letter in his own hand at the end (Galatians 6:11; 2 Thessalonians 3:17). Using a scribe does not lessen the letter’s authority: the words are Paul’s, inspired by the Spirit (2 Peter 3:15–16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Tertius composed the letter. He wrote down what Paul said.

If humans wrote the Bible down, how is it God’s word? Because God was at work in the whole process. Scripture is breathed out by God (2 Timothy 3:16): men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21). God did not bypass their minds, personalities or circumstances. Paul’s logic, his warmth, his grief for Israel and his list of friends are all truly his. But God so superintended what they wrote that the result is exactly what he intended to say, without error. The scribe’s pen, the apostle’s voice and the Spirit’s breath all worked together. That is why we can read Romans as Paul’s letter to Rome and, at the same time, as God’s word to us (Westminster 1.2, 1.4).

In a sentence. Timothy, Paul’s co-worker, sends his greetings to you, as do Lucius, Jason and Sosipater, his fellow Jews. I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Think of the behind-the-scenes servants who have brought God’s word to you: translators, printers, the person who runs the sound desk, the church administrator, the Sunday school helper. Thank one of them this week. And if your own work for Christ is mostly holding the pen for someone else, do it with joy. Tertius never preached Romans, but he wrote it down, and the church has been reading his handwriting ever since.

For worship. The Holy Spirit used an apostle’s voice and a scribe’s pen to give the church its greatest letter, and he did not waste either. God chose a man named Third, perhaps a slave, perhaps a freedman, to set down in ink the gospel of justification by faith, and then let him sign his name in the margin of Scripture. That is the humility and the generosity of our God. He needs no one, and yet he delights to use everyone, and to honour the hands that serve him. The word of the Lord endures for ever, and some of it is in Tertius’s handwriting.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters; Tertius was the scribe who wrote this one down.

verseByVerse.quote: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.

Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Probably the Gaius whom Paul baptised in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14). He hosted Paul while he wrote Romans, and his house was big enough for the whole church in Corinth to meet. A man of sufficient means and sufficient generosity to open his home as the gathering place for the entire Corinthian congregation.

Erastus, the city treasurer. “City treasurer” (oikonomos tēs poleōs, steward of the city): a public official. An inscription found at Corinth names an Erastus who paved a public square at his own expense in return for his office as aedile, a city official. He may be the same man. The gospel reached people of high position as well as slaves.

And our brother Quartus, greet you. Quartus means fourth: perhaps a slave name. Paul places a city official and a man known only as our brother side by side. In Christ, both are equally brothers.

The whole argument in one room. Set the three men in this verse beside each other and the whole argument of the letter is standing in one room. Erastus holds municipal office, and an inscription that may be his records a street paved at his own expense. Quartus is called Fourth. Gaius is generous enough to be host to the whole church. They are sending a joint greeting. The city treasurer and the man named after a number are in the same sentence, on the same footing, and the only title Quartus needs is brother. In Corinth, outside that house, they may have had no relationship the law could have described. That is what Paul meant back at 2:11 when he said God shows no partiality, and at 10:12 when he said there is no distinction. He did not mean it as a sentiment. He meant that a room would eventually exist in which it was simply true, and he is writing from one.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should avoid public office. Erastus served his city as a believer.

How should a wealthy or powerful Christian relate to poorer believers? As Gaius and Erastus did: as a brother, and as a steward. Paul tells Timothy to charge the rich not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on uncertain riches, but on God, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–19). James tells the rich brother to boast in his humiliation, because he too will fade like a flower (James 1:9–11). In practice, that means opening your home, using your influence for the vulnerable, giving quietly and generously, and never expecting deference in church. In the congregation, your position counts for nothing; your service counts for much. And the poorer brother is to honour you without envy, as a fellow servant of the same Lord.

In a sentence. Gaius, whose hospitality Paul and the whole church here enjoy, sends you his greetings. Erastus, who is the city’s director of public works, and our brother Quartus send you their greetings.

On a Tuesday. Whatever your position, whether city official or ordinary worker, you can serve Christ in it and use it for his church. Ask this week what your position gives you that could serve others: a home large enough to host, a skill, a network, time. And in church on Sunday, notice whether you treat people differently by their status. If you do, remember Quartus, whose only title is brother.

For worship. In Christ the city treasurer and the man called Fourth are brothers, equally loved, equally forgiven, equally heirs. No other society on earth could have produced that sentence. It was made possible by the God who shows no partiality, and by the Son who, though he was rich, became poor for our sakes. He took the lowest place so that the high and the low could stand on level ground at the foot of his cross. Blessed be the Lord who gathers the powerful and the overlooked into one house, and calls them all his family.
verseByVerse.note: An inscription found at Corinth names an Erastus who paved a street at his own expense, perhaps the same man.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 24, with this benediction. The earliest and best manuscripts do not have it, so the ESV leaves it out of the text, and it is shown here from the margin. Nothing is lost: the same benediction already appears in verse 20. If your Bible skips from verse 23 to verse 25, that is why. It appears to be a copyist’s repetition of the benediction already given, a scribe reaching for a familiar ending. And the instinct behind the addition was sound, whoever had it. Grace is how this letter starts (1:7), and grace is how it should stop. A copyist who felt that the argument could not simply end had understood something about the book he was copying.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Grace (charis): the free favour of God in Christ, the theme of the whole letter. From first to last, Romans is a letter about grace: the grace of apostleship (1:5), the grace of justification (3:24), the grace in which we stand (5:2), the grace that abounds all the more where sin increased (5:20), the grace of election (11:5), the grace of spiritual gifts (12:6). With you all: strong and weak, Jew and Gentile, slave and free.

What it does not mean. It does not mean manuscript differences undermine Scripture. The differences are few and none affects any doctrine. God has preserved his word.

Can I trust that my Bible says what was originally written? Yes, with great confidence. The New Testament is by far the best-attested book of the ancient world: thousands of Greek manuscripts, some from within a few generations of the apostles, besides early translations and quotations by early Christian writers. Because there are so many copies, the occasional slip of a scribe can be seen and corrected by comparing them, as here. Modern Bibles are open about the few places where manuscripts differ, which is a sign of honesty, not weakness. And no doctrine of the faith rests on a disputed reading. God has kept his word pure in all ages by his singular care and providence (Westminster 1.8).

In a sentence. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen.

On a Tuesday. Next time you notice a footnote in your Bible about manuscripts, do not be unsettled by it. Let it remind you how carefully God’s word has been kept and checked. And take this benediction as a word spoken over you as you go out today: whatever comes, the grace of the Lord Jesus is with you.

For worship. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: there is no better word for a letter to end on, because there is no better word for what God has done. Grace found us ungodly and justified us. Grace reigns through righteousness to eternal life. Grace chose a remnant, kept it, and will bring in the fullness. And grace has guarded the very words that tell us of it, through centuries of copying by hand, so that we can still read them. The grace of the Lord Jesus is with you, today, because he has promised it and he does not change.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 24: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith—

The doxology. The letter ends with a long sentence of praise (vv. 25–27), which gathers up the great themes of Romans: the gospel, Jesus Christ, the Scriptures, the nations, the obedience of faith and the glory of God. It mirrors the opening of the letter (1:1–5).

Textual note. In a few manuscripts this doxology appears after 14:23 or after 15:33 instead of here, and in a few it appears twice or not at all (see the note on 14:23). The best and widest evidence puts it here, at the end of the letter, and its words fit Romans closely, echoing 1:1–5. Nothing in the text of Romans is in doubt because of this; the question is only where the closing praise stood.

Now to him who is able to strengthen you. “Strengthen” (stērizō) means establish, make firm, as in 1:11. God is able to keep them standing (14:4). And the opening verb closes a loop opened in the first chapter. Paul told them at 1:11 that he longed to come and give them some spiritual gift to strengthen them. He never managed it: hindered, then hindered again, and when he finally arrived it was in chains. So the letter ends by handing the task over. What the apostle wanted to do and could not, God can do without him.

According to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ. My gospel: the gospel entrusted to Paul (2:16), not a different one. The preaching of Jesus Christ: the proclamation about him. God strengthens his people through the gospel. The gospel is not merely information about Christ; it is the power by which God strengthens his people (1:16).

According to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages. A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God (11:25; Ephesians 3:4–6; Colossians 1:26–27). The mystery is the gospel of Christ, especially that Jews and Gentiles together would be saved through faith in him. Kept secret (sigaō, kept silent) for long ages. All that time, the promise to Abraham, the exodus, the law, the kings, the exile, the silence, God was holding something back that he fully intended to say. Nothing was being improvised. The nations were in the plan before there was a nation, and the ungodly were in it before there was anyone who was not.

But has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations. Revealed in the coming of Christ, and explained by the prophetic writings, the Old Testament (1:2; 3:21). The prophets spoke of it, but its full meaning was hidden until Christ came. And there is a deliberate paradox here: a mystery kept secret for long ages which has nonetheless been made known through the prophetic writings. Secret, and in writing the whole time. Which is exactly right, and anyone who has read chapters 9 to 11 has watched it demonstrated. Hosea and Isaiah and Moses and the Psalms were saying that the nations would come in. It was on the page in every synagogue. What was missing was not the information but the event that makes the information legible, and once Christ had come, Paul could go back through the same scrolls and show that they had been saying it all along. A mystery in Paul’s sense is not a puzzle nobody could solve. It is something that could not be seen until God did the thing it was about.

According to the command of the eternal God. The eternal God commanded that the gospel be preached to the nations (Matthew 28:19). The mission to the Gentiles is not Paul’s idea, nor the church’s strategy. It is the decree of the God who has no beginning and no end, carried out in time.

To bring about the obedience of faith. The same phrase as 1:5, framing the whole letter. The obedience that comes from faith, and the obedience that faith is. The gospel aims at a people who trust and obey. The first paragraph and the last paragraph of Romans say the same thing. Everything between is the argument for it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament was silent about the gospel. It means the gospel was there in promise, but could not be fully understood until Christ fulfilled it.

Does the obedience of faith make obedience part of what saves us? No. Paul means the obedience that faith is and the obedience faith produces: to believe the gospel is to obey God’s summons, and those who believe go on to obey. It is the same phrase as in 1:5, and the whole letter between those two verses has argued that we are justified by faith apart from works (3:28). Obedience is the fruit of faith, never its price.

How does God actually strengthen me? Through the gospel, as this verse says, and by the ordinary means he has appointed for it. He strengthens you when the gospel is preached and you hear it with faith; when you read and meditate on Scripture; when you pray; when you come to the Lord’s Supper and see Christ’s death set before you; and when fellow believers speak the truth to you in love. He works by his Spirit through these means, often quietly, so that you may not notice the strengthening until you find yourself still standing in a trial that once would have flattened you. So when you feel weak, do not look for something new. Go back to the old gospel, and to the means God uses to apply it.

In a sentence. Now to him who is able to establish you in accordance with Paul’s gospel, the message he proclaims about Jesus Christ, in keeping with the revelation of the mystery hidden for long ages past, but now revealed and made known through the prophetic writings by the command of the eternal God, so that all the Gentiles might come to the obedience that comes from faith,

On a Tuesday. When you feel unsteady, go back to the gospel. That is how God strengthens you. Take one passage of Romans that has held you up, perhaps 3:21–26, 5:1–11 or 8:28–39, and read it again this week, slowly, aloud. And read one Old Testament promise of the nations coming in, such as Isaiah 49:6 or Psalm 67, and thank God that you are part of its fulfilment.

For worship. Every page of the Old Testament was written by someone who did not know how the sentence ended, and was carried by Someone who did. The eternal God kept his secret through long ages, not out of reluctance, but because he was preparing the moment to reveal it: his Son, born of David, crucified for sinners, raised in power, preached to the nations. And he is able to strengthen you. Not the apostle, who could not reach Rome; not you, who cannot keep yourself standing; but him, who has never once let one of his own fall out of his hand. He commanded the gospel to go to all nations, and here we are, Gentiles who were never promised anything, made firm by the mystery now revealed.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.

To the only wise God. Only God is truly wise. His wisdom is seen in the plan of salvation, which no one could have imagined (11:33; 1 Corinthians 1:24–25). Not one wise being among many, but the only one whose wisdom is absolute, uncreated, inexhaustible and without rival. All of Romans has been a display of divine wisdom: the wisdom that designed salvation through the cross, so that God could be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (3:26); that included the Gentiles through Israel’s stumbling; that will bring mercy to Israel through the Gentiles’ fullness.

The sentence that breaks. It is worth admitting what the sentence does grammatically, because it is a small window into the man. Read verses 25–27 as one sentence and it does not quite resolve. It begins now to him who is able to strengthen you, accumulates clause after clause, according to my gospel, according to the revelation, kept secret, now disclosed, through the prophetic writings, according to the command, and then never returns to complete the thought in the expected way, arriving instead at glory to the only wise God through Jesus Christ. Commentators have worried at it for centuries. The plainest explanation is the human one. He set out to say something about God and could not get to the end of the subject, and the sentence simply gives way under the weight and turns into worship.

He has done this before. He has done it once before, at the end of chapter 11, when the argument about Israel ran out into oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God (11:33). Both times the same thing happens: the reasoning goes as far as reasoning goes, and then the only available next move is glory. That is not the failure of the theology. It is what the theology is for.

Be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Glory to God, through Jesus Christ: Christ is the one through whom God is glorified, and through whom our praise reaches God. The letter that began with the gospel of God concerning his Son (1:1–3) ends with glory to God through his Son. All glory returns to God through the Son, who is both the one through whom all things were made and the mediator of the new creation.

Amen. So be it. Truly. The only fitting response to Romans.

Where the letter ends. And so the letter stops. It began with a man calling himself a slave, set apart for a gospel promised beforehand through the prophets, sent to bring about the obedience of faith among all the nations (1:1–5). Sixteen chapters later, having been through wrath and justification and baptism and the wretched man and no condemnation and the potter and the olive tree and the living sacrifice and the weak brother and the greetings from Three and Four, it ends on the same three things: the gospel, the nations, and the obedience of faith. Nothing has been added to the first paragraph. It has been opened.

What it does not mean. It does not mean glory is given to God apart from Christ. All true worship goes through him.

What does it mean to give God glory through Jesus Christ? It means that all our praise reaches the Father by way of the Son. We cannot come to God on our own merit, and our worship, even at its best, is mixed with sin. But Christ is our great high priest, who lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25), and through him we continually offer up a sacrifice of praise (Hebrews 13:15). So when you pray or sing, you come in his name, trusting that he presents your praise to the Father, cleansed and accepted. It also means that God is most glorified in what he has done in Christ: the cross and resurrection are the brightest display of his glory there will ever be.

I have read Romans. What now? Do what Paul does at the end: worship. Then live out the letter. Rest your whole confidence on Christ’s righteousness, not your own (3:21–26). Fight sin as one who is dead to it and alive to God (6:11). Walk by the Spirit, assured that nothing can separate you from God’s love (8:38–39). Present your body as a living sacrifice (12:1). Welcome the brother who differs from you (15:7). Support the spread of the gospel to the nations (15:20–24). And come back to it. Romans is not a book to be finished but a book to be lived in, and the church has found for two thousand years that it never runs dry.

In a sentence. to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen.

On a Tuesday. Paul has argued them out of every ground of confidence they had and left them with a God who justifies the ungodly. There is only one thing to do with a God like that. So end today the way Paul ends: take five minutes, alone, and give God glory for one thing in Romans that has changed you. Tell him what it was, and say Amen.

For worship. To the only wise God. In the end there is no one else to give it to. Not the reader, who contributed nothing; not the apostle, who said so himself; not the church, which exists because of it; not the law, which could only measure the damage. One God, wise where nobody else could see, who found a way to be just and to justify the ungodly, who bound all over to disobedience that he might have mercy on all, and who will gather a people from every nation into one family through his Son. From him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forevermore, through Jesus Christ. The letter that began with a man calling himself a slave ends with the whole of creation going home to God, and the last word is not an argument. It is Amen.

16.text: <sup>1</sup>I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae,<sup>2</sup>that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well.<sup>3</sup>Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus,<sup>4</sup>who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.<sup>5</sup>Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.<sup>6</sup>Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you.<sup>7</sup>Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me.<sup>8</sup>Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.<sup>9</sup>Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.<sup>10</sup>Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus.<sup>11</sup>Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.<sup>12</sup>Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord.<sup>13</sup>Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord; also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.<sup>14</sup>Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them.<sup>15</sup>Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.<sup>16</sup>Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.<sup>17</sup>I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them.<sup>18</sup>For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive.<sup>19</sup>For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil.<sup>20</sup>The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.<sup>21</sup>Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen.<sup>22</sup>I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.<sup>23</sup>Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.<sup>25</sup>Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages<sup>26</sup>but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith—<sup>27</sup>to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.
